units.tr: To their lordships and his most gracious patrons, he offers, dedicates and consecrates this treatise on prolonging life in a good and healthful way, out of due observance, duty and submission, with a most humble hand,

units.la: Rodolphus Goclenius Med. D.

units.la: SANITATEM, Principes Illustrissimi, summum & maximum mum esse bonum & donum, vixq; haberefe vllum in hac vita præstantius, nemo, nisi cyclopica in barbarie natus, inficias ibit. Vndefequitur, eam medicinę partem longè cæteris esse præstantiorem, quæ docet rationem & modum sanitatis conferuandæ, & ex consequenti vitæ prorogandæ, absque enim illa hæc prorogari non potest. Sanitas illa potissimum consistit in opportuna & idonea qualitate, quantitate, vtendi ratione & occasione fumendorum, vt sunt esculenta ac potulenta, itemq; aer proximè mè nos ambiens. His tribus illegitimè intemperantiusq; adhibitis, malaq; qualitate vitiatis,magnę ac pernitiosę mortalib. struuntur insidiæ, unde sæpe perit homo funeris ante diem. Quapropter cum horis successiuis, legitimisq; officiis perfunctus meditari cœperim, seu potius efformandum susceperim universæ hygieinæ,hoc est,sanitatis prorogandæ corpus, proplasmaq; effingere uni-versum, ad quod angustius opus aliquādo dedolari possit,ægre tamen ac difficulter omnia pro animi sententia. perficere potui, ob varia quæ ex parte mea mihi obiecta sunt domi forisq; obstacula. Parté tantū, quantū per ingenii imbecillitaté licuit mihi esse industrio & otioso, in lucem emitto, malo enim in eo periculum facere, in quo errare foret leuius, & me in parte operis potius quàm in ipso toto censoriis hominū iudiciis exponere. Erunt, qui hunc meum conatum & la-borem improba contradicé-di cupiditate sunt improbaturi, quod post eximios viros, qui de hac materia scri-pserunt, ego inter hos obscurissimus idem argumentum tracto, inque medium proferre audeo. Non defuerunt, qui peculiares tractatus de hoc scripserunt erudite eruditè viri, nec forsan defuturi sunt, qui omnis doctrinae & laborum conficientissimi praestituri sunt id acrius & ingeniosius. In quos ego incidi, ii vel breuiter & strictè nimis, vel accuratè & methodicè minus materiam illam pertractarunt. Quapropter non gloriae cupiditate, quae praestantibus fere ingeniis omnibus est insita, adductus in tam trito à praeclaris viris argu-
units.tr: That health is the greatest and highest good and gift, and that there is hardly anything more excellent in this life, no one will deny unless he was born in Cyclopean barbarism, most illustrious princes. It follows that that part of medicine which teaches the reasoning and method of preserving health, and consequently of prolonging life, is far superior to the rest, since without it life cannot be prolonged. That health consists chiefly in the right and suitable quality and quantity of, the manner of using, and the occasions for taking, such things as food and drink, and likewise the air that immediately surrounds us. When these three are used unlawfully and intemperately, or are corrupted by bad quality, great and deadly snares are laid for mortals, whence man often perishes before his day. Therefore, when I had begun, in the hours left over after my lawful duties, to meditate on, or rather to undertake to shape, the whole of hygiene, that is, to set out the body of preserving and prolonging health and to fashion the entire model, from which a narrower work might someday be hewn, I have been able to complete everything according to my own judgment only with difficulty, because of the various obstacles raised against me at home and abroad. I publish only the part which, as far as the weakness of my talent allowed, I have worked on diligently and at leisure; for I prefer to make the trial where error would be less serious, and to expose myself to the judgment of critics in a part of the work rather than in the whole. There will be those who, out of a wicked desire to contradict, will disapprove of this effort and labour of mine, because after the distinguished men who have written on this subject, I, the most obscure of them, treat the same matter and dare to bring it before the public. There have not been lacking learned men who wrote special treatises on this, nor perhaps will there be lacking those who, most skilled in all learning and labour, will surpass it more keenly and ingeniously. Those whom I have come across have treated that matter either briefly and too narrowly, or accurately and methodically but less fully. Therefore, not led by the desire for glory, which is almost innate in nearly all men of outstanding talent, into a subject so worn by distinguished writers

units.la: EPISTOLA
units.tr: EPISTLE

units.la: argumento, ingenii quaero famam, qui ante me tanta arte & diligentia banc materi-am elaborarunt, elabora-tam illustrarunt, vt de eo-dem argumento agendi nullum sibi neque posteris locum reliquum fecisse vi-deantur. Verum, quemad-modum Ariftotelem à scri-bendo non deterruit ampli-tudo Platonis, neq; Cicero-nem M. Crassus, Antonius vel Hortensius Oratores à Romano foro prohibuerút. In magnis enim conatibus pulcrum est in mediis confi-stere: sic & mihi vitio non vertevertetur, in tam fertili medi-cinę agro, à diligentissimis illis, qui me præcesserunt, messoribus[?], relicta spicilegia, non mediocrem prouentus accessionem rei medicæ fa-ctura, postremus ego & infi-mus messor, siciliirem[?]. Publi-ca igitur vtilitas, cupiditas voluntati meæ satisfaciendi, & auctores viri graues, qui-bus hoc scriptum meum pla-cere & probari intellexi, me ad hunc fœtum excluden-dum compulerunt, cuius ca-put ac pectus, vobis, Serenis-simi Principes offero atque commendo, humiliter rogitans, vt clementi benignaq; manu præcipuas istas fœtus mei partes fouere, versare ac tractare, ad diuinæ maiestatis amplificationem & gloriam, Ecclesiæq; ac Reipublicæ vestræ salutem & emolumentum, deniq; totum vitæ vestræ curriculum salubriter, hoc est, temperanter, prorogandum, mentemq; sanam[?] in corpore sano[?] retinendam, non grauemini.
units.tr: I do not seek the fame of cleverness through a theme so worn by distinguished men, who have worked this subject with such skill and care and illuminated it so thoroughly that they seem to have left no room for anyone to treat the same subject again, either for themselves or for those who follow. But just as the magnitude of Plato did not deter Aristotle from writing, nor did M. Crassus, Antonius, or Hortensius, the orators, keep Cicero from the Roman forum, so in a great undertaking it is fine to take a middle place. In this fertile field of medicine, after those most diligent reapers who went before me, I hope I will not be blamed for gathering the leftover ears of grain, and for adding no small increase to the harvest of medicine. I am the last and lowest of the reapers, a gleaner. Therefore the public good, my desire to satisfy my own inclination, and the serious authors whose approval of this work of mine I have understood, have driven me to bring this offspring into the light. Its head and heart I offer and commend to you, most serene princes, humbly asking that you not be reluctant to cherish, turn over, and handle with your gentle and kindly hand these principal parts of my offspring, for the enlargement and glory of the divine majesty, for the salvation and advantage of your Church and commonwealth, and finally so that the whole course of your life may be wholesomely prolonged, that is, kept in moderation, and a sound mind kept in a sound body.

units.la: ROD. GOCLENII MEDIC. DOCTOR. RAPHAELIS EGLINI ICONII TIGURINI, SS. Theologiæ Doctoris, & Professoris Ordinarii in inclyta Academia Marpurgensi, Carmen.
units.tr: Poem of Rodolphus Goclenius, Doctor of Medicine, to Raphael Eglinus Iconius of Zurich, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Ordinary Professor in the renowned Academy of Marburg.

units.la: Laurea debetur duplici tibi nomine Phœbe, Quòd tua testudo est, quòd Medicina tua est.
units.tr: You deserve the laurel, Phoebus, for a double reason: because the lyre is yours, and because medicine is yours.

units.la: Herbarum inde tibi diuina potentia seruit; Inde genus Vatum surgit & ordo tibi.
units.tr: Hence divine power over herbs serves you, and hence the race and order of poets rises up for you.

units.la: Scilicet hinc ex te, Nymphaq; Coronide, nato Delubrum veluti constituere Deo.
units.tr: Surely from you and from the nymph Coronis a son was born, as if they had set up a shrine to a god.

units.la: Fallor an ambigua est Graiorum fabula? Nostris Debetur potius temporibusq; fides ?
units.tr: Am I mistaken, or is the Greek fable ambiguous? Does faith belong rather to our own times?

units.la: Ecce parens Vatum GOCLENIVS ille, RODOLPHVS, Ecce RODOLPHVS item filius ille Patris,
units.tr: Behold that Goclenius, the father of poets, Rodolphus; behold likewise Rodolphus, that son of the father.

units.la: Sunt & Apollo mihi, Nymphaq; Coronide nati, Queis delubra magis constituenda reor. Nulla Chelys tā docta fuit, nulla arsq; medendi, Quale opus est medicum docte RODOL-PHE tuum, Quale parentis opus, quo conciliauit amicè Dissimiles inter se, similesq; Sophos. Dicite Pierides lauro hic, an dignior ille[?] Et lauro hic dignus, dignus & ille fuit. Non bene conueniunt discrimina dissona uocū, Nec nisi concordi pectine grata lyra est: Sic nisi conueniant sapientum linguaq;, mensq;, Gratia quanta fuit, gratia tanta perit. Talis inest Patri sapientia, usq; docendi, Per quem iam coeunt, quae coitura neges: Qualis inest Gnato prudentia, usq; medendi, Per quem sanantur, quae moritura putes. Et quia non tantum laudatur acumine Pallas, Quantum laudata est utilitate Dea, Unde oleae inuentrix celebratur dia Minerua, Vsibus humanis commoda multa ferens:
units.tr: I also have Apollo, and the son born of the nymph Coronis, for whom I think shrines should rather be set up. No lyre was ever so skilled, no art of healing; what a work of a physician is yours, learned Rodolphus, what a work of a father, by which he has amicably united those unlike one another and yet like wise men. Tell me, Pierian Muses, is this one more worthy of the laurel, or that one? Each is worthy of the laurel, and each was worthy. Discordant tones do not agree well, and a lyre is pleasing only with a harmonious plectrum. Thus, unless the tongues and minds of the wise agree, however great the grace, so great grace perishes. Such wisdom dwells in the father, ever ready to teach, through whom those now come together who, you would say, will never come together. Such prudence dwells in the son, ever ready to heal, through whom those are saved who, you would think, are about to die. And because Pallas is not so much praised for her sharpness as the goddess is praised for her usefulness, whence the goddess Minerva, inventress of the olive, is celebrated, bringing many benefits for human use:

units.la: GOCLENIVS sic est Sophus hoc celeberrior, exse
units.tr: GOCLENIUS, so is he the sage more famous than this, ex-

units.la: Hoc quod opus nostris vsibus ille dedit, Nestoreos vitæ vsuræ qui extendat ad annos, Differat atq; tuum curua seneĉla pedem.
units.tr: This work which he gave for our use, he who may extend the years of life to Nestor's span and keep bent old age from setting its foot on you.

units.la: Qua non ars melior, qua non magis indiga vita est, Qua meritæ laudis non magis vlla feraæ:
units.tr: Than this no art is better, none is more needed by life, and none bears more of deserved praise.

units.la: Suauius banc tractas, iucundaq; pocla propinas, Et Medicina tuo grata fit eloquio.
units.tr: You treat it more sweetly and pour out pleasant draughts, and medicine becomes welcome through your eloquence.

units.la: Qualis quæ rutilo circundata fulgurat auro, Gemma nitens reficit lumina grata magis:
units.tr: As a gem set in glowing gold flashes, shining, it restores the eyes more pleasingly.

units.la: Sic tibi Romanæ facundia cognita linguæ, Nobilitat tua quoq; Musa peregrit opus.
units.tr: So the Roman tongue's well-known eloquence, and your Muse as well, ennobles the work of a stranger.

units.la: Salue ô Phœbe mihi: salue ô Epidauria proles; Tu Phœbus, Phœbi filius, esq; Nepos.
units.tr: Hail to me, O Phoebus; hail, O offspring of Epidaurus. You are Phoebus, the son of Phoebus, and his grandson.

units.la: ALIVD AD VIRUM CLARISS. Rod. GOCLENIUM Med. D. Compatrem carifs.
units.tr: Another poem to the most illustrious Rodolph Goclenius, Doctor of Medicine, my dear co-father.

units.la: VT nihil in vita vitali gratius auri,Nec generi humano dulcius esse potest:Sic nihil in vita maiori laude vehendum,Quam quod viuendi prorogat arte diem.
units.tr: As nothing in life is more pleasing than the gold of life, and nothing can be sweeter to the human race, so nothing deserves greater praise in life than what prolongs the days of living by art.

units.la: Cum tuus hoc praestet liber hic doctissime DoctorInsignis, nil hoc doctius orbis habet.Nec minor est virtus, quam quaerere, partaque tueri,Ut Salmonensis verba rotunda sonant:Dat natura animam: post ars conseruat eandem:Esse itidem hoc magnum quis negat artis opus?
units.tr: Since your book, most learned Doctor, offers this, the world has nothing more learned. Nor is it a lesser virtue to seek a thing and to keep what has been gained, as the well-turned words of the Salernitan school ring out: nature gives the soul, and then art preserves it. Who would deny that this too is a great work of art?

units.la: Si aliquis quaerat, liber hoc promittere quinam,Ausit, & in titulo quid tumor iste velit?Huic ego: quis stupor est? authoris perspice mentem,Cernesq; absurdi rebus inesse nihil.
units.tr: If anyone should ask what this book promises, and dares to make such a claim, and what that pomp in the title means, I answer him: what is there to be amazed at? Look into the author's mind, and you will see nothing absurd in his matter.

units.la: Finem qui statuit, medium quoq; destinat idem,Quo venit ad metam res mediante suam.Stat sua cuiq; dies, & inevitabile fatum,Ordinat vt vitae fons & origo, Deus.
units.tr: He who sets the end also appoints the means by which a thing reaches its goal, the means lying between. Each person has his day appointed, and an inevitable fate, which God orders as the fountain and origin of life.

units.la: Prima tamen rerum non tollit causa secundas,Sed iubet has currum quanq; tenere suum.Sic sunt certa quidem decreta stamina vitae,Ultra quae nullum vivere fata sinunt:
units.tr: Yet the first cause of things does not abolish the secondary causes, but bids these hold their own course. Thus indeed the threads of life are fixed decrees, beyond which the fates allow no one to live.

units.la: Ne tamen haec citra subsistat tempora vita,Vita hac deficiens arte iuvanda venit.
units.tr: Yet lest life stop short of these appointed times, a failing life comes to be helped by art.

units.la: Hoc titulus sibi vult: hoc est producere vitam.: Quam si, Mome, placet carpere: carpe nihil.
units.tr: This title means: this is to prolong life. If Momus wishes to carp at it, let him carp at nothing.

units.la: Ad te sed redeo, Phœbea qui decus ingens Artis, & Aonii gloria summa chori:
units.tr: But I return to you, whose great glory is the art of Phoebus, and the highest glory of the Aonian chorus:

units.la: Hic tuus, ecce, liber, vitæ qui regula, quiq, Ingenio summo scriptus & eloquio:
units.tr: Here, behold, is your book, which is a rule of life, written with the highest talent and eloquence.

units.la: Hic, inquam, vivat, summoq; habeatur honore, Tu quoq; Nelida secula vive senis.
units.tr: Here, I say, let it live and be held in the highest honour; and may you too live the years of Nestor, son of Neleus.

units.la: Vive diu, scriptusq; bonis bene perge mereri Nominis unde tui fama perennis erit.
units.tr: Live long, and, having written for good men, go on deserving well, from which your name will have an everlasting fame.

units.la: Ioh. Noviomag. Rector S.Bud.
units.tr: Ioh. Noviomag., Rector S. Bud.

units.la: DE VITA PRORO-GANDA TRACTA-TVS.
units.tr: ON PROLONGING LIFE, TREATED AT LENGTH.

units.la: Vitæ prorogandæ sanita-tisq; custodiendæ rationem Philosophi ac Medici præstantes sex rerum generibus sunt complexi, quorum justa debitaq; mensura atq; observatio diæta, conservatio sanitatis, modus tuendæ valetudinis, vel regimen sanitatis dicitur. Suntq; aer, cibus, potus, somnus, vigilia, {*}excretio, reten-tio, animiq; affectus, hæc legitimè & moderatè adhibita vitam prolongant, & incorruptam valetudinem conservant, unde & conservatrices appellantur causæ & salutares: immoderatè vero adhibita, insalubria evadunt & morborum causæ: indeq; res non naturales dicuntur, quod videlicet extrinsecus accedant. Ex nobis cum non nascantur, sinistreq; se habentia (ut cum aer est male affectus vel venenatus) corpus humanum alterant & ladunt, ut experientia id testatur quotidie.
units.tr: Philosophers and physicians of note have grouped the method of prolonging life and preserving health under six kinds of things. The just and due measure and observance of these is called diet, the preservation of health, the manner of guarding health, or the regimen of health. These are air, food, drink, sleep, waking, excretion, retention, and the affections of the mind. When these are applied lawfully and moderately, they prolong life and preserve sound health, and for this reason they are called conserving and healthful causes. But when they are applied immoderately, they become unhealthy and causes of disease; hence they are called non-natural things, because they come from outside. Since they are not born in us, and when they are disposed badly (as when the air is tainted or poisonous) they alter and harm the human body, as daily experience bears witness.

units.la: Proœmii autem loco sequentes quæstiones scitu discussuq; dignas, (de quibus etiam inter doctissimos non convenit) & ab instituto nostro minime alienas, premittere placuit.
units.tr: By way of preface, I have thought fit to set out the following questions, which are worth knowing and discussing (and on which even the most learned do not agree), and which are by no means foreign to my purpose.

units.la: DE VITA QUAESTIO I.
units.tr: THE FIRST QUESTION ON LIFE.

units.la: Circa operis hujus titulum:
units.tr: Concerning the title of this work:

units.la: An praefixi huic operi titulis inscri- ptionis fit aliqua necessitas, cum cuiq; vitae suae terminus praefini- tus fit, vt illa neq; prorogari, neq; ante tempus abrumpi possit?
units.tr: Is there any necessity for a title to be prefixed to this work, since the term of each person's life is fixed in advance, so that it can be neither prolonged nor cut short before its time?

units.la: ON abs re discutiendam in operis hujus vestibulo quaestionem hanc propono, quòd sciam, aliquibus eam otiosam & inutilem videri, fi scilicet praefini- ti sint fui cuiq; dies, vt nec temporius, nec fe- rius vitam praecidere alicui quid possit. Sed vehementer mirari subit, inuentiri quosdam Iamnode- polle & potuisse, qui hac de re dubitarent, ftieft & cum non tàm vtilis, quàm necessaria quaestio impru- fit, arduaq; : id quod fequentib: probatur ra- dentis te- tionib; quae, fi forsan primo intuitu alicui ap- paream non fatis firmae, vel accuratius expe- bruto ju- dantur, (quod prudentis est) vel inconcusse dicio relinquantur; (quod verecundi & modesti quidvis est.) Constat autem rem nullam corrumpi carpere. naturaliter, quantifper calor ejus congenitus Calor natdurat. Hic enim autor est, & conseruator tem tinus vi- peraturae, quâ incolumi permanente; nulla te cauf a refinterire pore st. Manet verò calor ille infi- conf er- tus tantisper, dum alimentum ei conueniens vitor. superest, habet enim fe instar flammae in El- lychlychnio, vel funiculo candelae accensae: alimentum vero ejus, seu pabulum est humidum illud primigenium, seu radicale à primordio generationis insitum & innatum, rationem habens lucernarum olei, vel sebi in candelis, in his enim flamma tam diu pascitur & viuit, quàm diu cera, sebum, vel oleum superest, quo absumto, ipsam quoque flammam (deficiente sc. nutrimento) interiri & extingui necesse est. Hoc igitur humidum in re aliqua, quo copiosius est & viscosius, eo difficilius dissipatur & absumitur, quo vero tenuius & aquosius est, eo facilius diffluit, reliquj cujusq; causa vitam seu durationem efficit breviorem. His ita positis, quis vitam arte produci ad illum terminum posse, quo rei cujusque calor insitus proprium humidum depopulat naturaliter, Dum enim damnus operam, vt calor ille praeter naturae modum non augeatur (vt in febribus fit) & humidum è contrario non minuatur vel dissipetur, rem certè ab interitu celeriori praeseruamus.
units.tr: I propose this question here at the threshold of the work, not irrelevantly, because I know that some think it idle and useless if the days of each person are indeed fixed, so that no one can shorten a life either sooner or later. But it astonishes me that some learned men have doubted the matter, and I find the question not so much useful as necessary and difficult. This is proved by the following arguments, which, if at first sight they seem to someone not firm enough, are either to be examined more carefully (which is the part of a prudent person) or left unshaken (which is the part of a modest and humble person). It is agreed that nothing is naturally corrupted so long as its innate heat endures. For this heat is the author and preserver of its life, and while it remains intact the thing cannot perish from any other cause. That heat persists as long as suitable nourishment remains. It is like the flame in a lamp wick or in the wick of a lit candle. Its nourishment, or fuel, is that primal or radical moisture, implanted and innate from the beginning of generation, which corresponds to the oil of lamps or the tallow of candles. In these the flame is fed and lives as long as the wax, tallow or oil lasts; when that is used up, the flame itself must die out and be extinguished for want of nourishment. So in any thing, the more abundant and viscous its moisture, the more slowly it is dissipated and consumed; the thinner and more watery it is, the more easily it runs off, and so it makes the life or duration of that thing shorter. Having laid this down, who could deny that life can be prolonged by art up to that limit at which the innate heat of each thing naturally consumes its own moisture? For while we take care that this heat is not increased beyond the measure of nature (as happens in fevers), and that the moisture is not diminished or dissipated, we certainly preserve the thing from a quicker destruction.

units.la: Videmus plantas, quae frigoris alioqui aut hiemis asperitate interirent, in cella, calido-ve aliquo loco positas, ad ver usq;, vel etiam intectas, multis annis conseruari. Fructus nonnullos arte, qui vix menses integri mansissent, per totum fere annum recentes seruari experientia satis testatur. Ob contrarias quoque causas à nonnullis arboribus & plantis tardiùs produci fructus & femina experimur. Ex quibus evidentissime proba- tur, calorem natiuum arte augeri conseruari minuiq; posse, ut eius operationes maturen- tur velimpediantur:pręcaueri item possit,ne pabulum ejus iusto celeriùs absumat: quod autem hoc praestat, ὑγίεια ἐστι[?], h. e. Sanitatis tuendæ ratio. Cum enim sanitas sit dispositio seu affectio naturalis corporis, à qua opera- tiones sane proueniunt, & plærag; animæ potentiæ organis utantur corporeis, ipseque homo propter animam fit homo, & organa quoq; ipsa aut nō agant, aut malè agant, nisi sint sana, facilè videre est, quantum sit situm in organorum omnium iusta temperie & sa- nitate, ipsiq; animæ interesse, ut corpus sit sa- num. Unde prudenter dixit Poeta:
units.tr: We see plants that would otherwise perish from the cold or the harshness of winter kept alive for many years when placed in a cellar or some warm place, until spring, or even when left uncovered. Experience amply testifies that some fruits, which would hardly have lasted whole months, are kept fresh by art for almost the whole year. We also find, from opposite causes, that some trees and plants bear fruit and seed more slowly. From this it is most evidently proved that natural heat can be increased, preserved and diminished by art, so that its operations are either hastened or hindered; and care can likewise be taken that its fuel is not used up too quickly. What does this is [ὑγίεια] hygieia, that is, the method of preserving health. For since health is the natural disposition or condition of the body, from which its operations rightly proceed, and since the powers of the soul make use of bodily organs, and man himself is man because of the soul, and the organs too either do not act, or act badly, unless they are sound, it is easy to see how much depends on the due balance and health of all the organs, and how much it concerns the soul itself that the body be sound. Hence the Poet wisely said:

units.la: Orandum esse, ut sit mens sana in corpore sano.
units.tr: It must be prayed for, that there be a sound mind in a sound body.

units.la: Itaq; etsi nobis omnibus moriendum se- mel, nec mors curâ aut medicinâ ullâ averti potest, differri eâ tamen sæpè posse non infi- ciandū est. Non enim, quia meta nobis possi- ta est & viuendi terminus, confiliūq; Deide vitæ termino ignoramus, officium nostrum deferere debemus, sed sedulo nobis faciendū est, quod ordinauit & mandauit, quicqd tan- dem Deo facere sit visum. An quia mortis ho- ram præfiniuit nobis Deus, necesse etiam nō habemus edere&bibere? An non deliraret, de alto se[?] loco præcipitem dare malle, quam per scalas descendere? An non tentaret Deũ, qui,cũ ex aquâ possset enatare, enatare nolit, quia Deus etiâ in aquis,quos vult,conserua-re potest? Iubet Deus ne solliciti sim*,qd edamus, quid bibamus, cࢅ & passerum & liliorũ agri curam gerat, prꝫterq; eius voluntatem ne capillus capitis nostri desluere possit.
units.tr: Therefore, although we must all die once, and neither death can be averted by care or any medicine, it cannot be denied that it can often be deferred. For because a limit has been set for us and a term to living, we are not therefore to abandon our duty, nor, since we are ignorant of the term of life, are we to neglect what God has ordained and commanded, whatever at last it may please God to do. Because God has determined the hour of death for us, do we therefore not need to eat and drink? Would not a man be mad who preferred to hurl himself headlong from a high place rather than descend by the stairs? Would not he tempt God who, though he could swim out of the water, refuses to swim, because God can preserve even in the waters whom he wills? God bids us not be anxious about what we shall eat or drink, since he cares for the sparrows and the lilies of the field, and without his will not a hair of our head can fall.

units.la: Idem interim Deus arare terram, metere, occare,triturare,vites colere, vuas colligere, fructus reponere pcipit & vt vno dicam verbo,Deus miraculosè vitam nostram nunc nõ sustentat,sed per media &instrumẽta ab ipso ordinata, vt ita successus à Deo expectandus sit,nostrum interim, quod est non negligen-dum.Dii enim facientes juuant,auxilioq; esse solent industriis & pro virili sua conantib.
units.tr: At the same time God also commands us to plough the land, reap, harrow, thresh, tend the vines, gather the grapes and store the fruits. In a word, God does not now sustain our life miraculously, but through the means and instruments he has ordained, so that success is to be looked for from God, while our own part, which is not to be neglected, is done. For "the gods help those who act," and are wont to aid those who strive with all their strength.

units.la: Qui igitur propterea juxta præscriptum Dei agere nolunt,fiduciaq; opis diuinæ industriâ remittunt, quòd sciunt, Deum ab æterno p-vidisse, quæ profutura sint nec ne, non sine culpa sua moriuntur, nec possunt non graviter ob neglecta media vulnerare conscientiâ, per quæ nihilominus suam nobis potentiam clementiamque liquidissimè Deus ostentat.
units.tr: Therefore those who refuse to act according to God's prescription, and relax their trust in divine help through idleness, because they know that God foresaw from eternity what would or would not profit them, do not die without fault. Nor can they fail to be gravely wounded in conscience on account of the neglected means, through which nonetheless God most plainly shows us his power and his mercy.

units.la: Quocirca non vtilis tantum est, verum etiâ necessaria proposita quæstio,nisi quis inscitè ac superciliosâ quadam statuitate affirmare ausit,prostigationem morborum,qui humi-dum congenitum dissipare ac depascere se-stinanter possunt, (vt sunt febres ardentes,) necessariam non esse.
units.tr: Wherefore the question proposed is not only useful but even necessary, unless someone should ignorantly and with a kind of supercilious assurance dare to affirm that the prevention of diseases which can swiftly dissipate and consume the innate moisture (such as burning fevers) is not necessary.

units.la: Non enim tollit artis exercitium Dei præscientia, quin & ipse Christus ægrotos medicis indigere affirmat, inque Dei populo fempet fuisse medicos, manifeste patet ex Gen. 50. Exod. 21. 2. Par. 16. & Eccl. 38. qui expresse ha- bet, ( quòd inprimis notandum) medicum à Deo creatum, propter eq; necessitatem hono- randum esse, tipendiumq; ei dari præcipit, additq; Deum ex artis medicæ miraculis & sanationibus laudari velle & prædicari, ipse nam inquit per medicamina sanat, doloribus- que hominis liberat. Qui igitur Dei ordinatio- ni sic paret, ac moritur nihilominus, bona conscientia coram Deo consistet, dum nulla sua culpa fe mortuum intelligat.
units.tr: For the exercise of the art is not abolished by God's foreknowledge. Indeed Christ himself affirms that the sick need physicians, and it is plain from Gen. 50. Exod. 21. 2 Par. 16. and Eccl. 38. that there have always been physicians among God's people. Ecclesiasticus expressly says (which is especially to be noted) that the physician was created by God, that for this need he is to be honoured, and that a fee is to be paid to him. It adds that God wishes to be praised and proclaimed for the wonders and healings of medical art: "for he himself heals through medicines and frees men from their pains." Therefore whoever submits to God's ordinance in this way, and yet dies, will stand before God with a good conscience, since he understands that he dies through no fault of his own.

units.la: QVÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: An subiectum morbi & sanitatis sit ipsius partis effentia, hoc est, an febris consistat in partium cordis conflitutione essentiali? N.
units.tr: Whether the subject of disease and of health is the very essence of the part, that is, whether fever consists in the essential constitution of the parts of the heart? No.

units.la: Ona Pfeudomedicorum parsin hac o- pinione consenuit, principium morbi materiale & formale in ipsius partis esse fixum substantia, cujus sententiæ falsitatem tem, tot quotidie monstrant errores in praxi. Morbus enim & sanitas non consistunt in essentiali partium constitutione, sed accidentali. Non enim, quicquid partem comcomponere, vel constituere dicitur, sanitatis & morbi subiectum est, essentialis enim forma vna cum materia non sanitatem, sed partium constitutionem essentiam: Sed est alia quaedam compositio, κατασκευὴ[?], quasi apparatus quidam, praeparatio, vel apta conformatio, quae accidens est, non substantia, quale in instrumentis contemplamur praeter materiam & formam, ut in gladio duritiem, aciem, nitorem, quib praeditus optime potest incidere: ejusmodi est in similari parte ipsa temperies, in organicis accidentalis forma, quae structura dicitur: accidentalis igitur partium constitutio, est apparatus quidam ad formae actiones exercendas, materiaq; & forma tanquam substantiae nunquam citra subjecti corruptionem abesse possunt, neque magis & minus recipere, temperies vero & structura multis modis immutantur, praeterid, quod separabilia sunt accidentia non minus quam sanitas & morbus: materiae item & formae nihil ut contrarium aduersatur, sed ipsa tantum privatio omnis transmutationis est autor, temperies vero & structura contrariorum expertia non sunt, quamobrem solius temperamenti integritas sanitatis nucupationem meretur, seruato enim temperamento seruantur actiones & sanitas.
units.tr: The Pseudo-physicians, who have been wedded to this opinion, hold that the material and formal principle of disease is fixed in the very substance of the part. The falsity of this view is shown every day by errors in practice. For disease and health do not consist in the essential constitution of the parts but in an accidental one. For not everything that is said to compose or constitute a part is the subject of health and disease: the essential form, together with matter, constitutes the essence of the part, not its health but its constitution. There is rather another kind of composition, a kind of katasceuē [κατασκευή], as it were an apparatus, a preparation, or a fitting arrangement, which is an accident and not a substance. We observe something of this sort in instruments, beyond their matter and form: in a sword there is hardness, edge and polish, by which it is excellently able to cut. Such in a similar part is its temperament itself; in organic parts it is an accidental form, which is called structure. The accidental constitution of the parts is therefore a kind of apparatus for carrying out the actions of the form. Matter and form, as substances, can never be absent without the corruption of the subject, nor do they admit more or less; temperament and structure, however, are changed in many ways. Besides, accidents are separable, no less than health and disease. Nothing is opposed to matter and form as a contrary; it is privation alone that is the author of every change. Temperament and structure, however, are not free of contraries; therefore the integrity of the temperament alone deserves the name of health, for when the temperament is preserved, the actions and the health are preserved.

units.la: QVÆSTIO III. An humores sint subiectum morbi & sanitatis? N.
units.tr: QUESTION III. Are the humours the subject of disease and of health? No.

units.la: NOn defuerunt, nec etiam nunc desunt, qui affirmatiuam defendendam susceperunt. Nonita pridem, cum negotiorum quorundam meorum causâ Budingâ irem Licham, incidi, certa tamen arreptaoccasione in Parochianû quendam, non quidem leuiter literis imbutum, sed saltem scelerata loquentia & impoftoria deblatera-tione de vrinaria inspectione infamem; Is ad-eo obstinate & pertinaciter affirmanti sen-tentiæ patrocinabatur, vt fcirrhum quis quâ-uis durissimum, citiùs concoxerit, quàm hàc ei opinionem ex animo eripuerit. Nullâ au-tem ratione aliâ negatiuam peruertere, suam vero prauam affirmatiuam tueri conabatur, quam quod sibi persuasum habebat, vnacû humoribus corruptis ac deprauatis, fiue per sudorem, fiue per vrinam, fiue per aluum exturbentur, etiam morbum expelli. Non absimile est, quod putidus quidam hyperbolicufq; Paradoxorum defensor fe vidisse fcribitvna cum vomitu rejectam febrim. Nam ei morbus in numero causarum est, causa vero morbi radix & seminarium[?] immutabi-le, quod suo loco excludi non possit. Sed hæc extra rem. Veritatis studiosi pro demonstrato habeant, quòd nulla sanitas vel ægritudo possit esse in parte aliquâ corporis, in quâ non exercentur operationes corporis, operationes enim sunt in compositis non cō-ponentibus, virtus enim vitalis in substantiâ cordis est, non humoribus & spiritibus, qui instrumentum sunt tantum, & vehiculum, vel principia & nutrimenta.
units.tr: There were not lacking, and even now there are not lacking, those who have undertaken to defend the affirmative. Not long ago, when I was going to Lich on some business of my own, I fell in, on a fitting occasion, with a certain parishioner, not indeed lightly versed in letters, but notorious for wicked talk and for quackish babbling about urine-inspection. He defended the affirmative opinion so obstinately and stubbornly that one could sooner digest the hardest scirrhus than tear this view from his mind. He had no other reason for overturning the negative, but he tried to uphold his own perverse affirmative on this ground, which he firmly believed: that when the humours are corrupted and depraved and are driven out, whether by sweat, by urine or by the bowels, the disease is expelled too. Not unlike this is what a foul and bombastic defender of paradoxes writes, that he saw a fever cast out together with vomiting. For disease is among the causes of that fever, while the root and seedbed of the cause is unchangeable and cannot be removed in its own place. But these things are beside the point. Let those who study the truth hold as demonstrated that no health or sickness can exist in any part of the body in which the operations of the body are not carried out. For operations belong to composite things, not to the things that compose them; the vital power resides in the substance of the heart, not in the humours and spirits, which are merely instruments and vehicle, or principles and nourishment.

units.la: Sic febris colerica dicitur, non quod in co-lera sit tanquam subiecto, sed quòd à colerâ eiusq; putredine dependeat, vt ita putredinis subiectum sit humor, febris verò ipsum cor, in quo humor flammam vel intermittentem vel continuâ primum concipit, nisi ea sit sym-tomatodes, h. e. aliunde cordi impetiatur.
units.tr: Thus we speak of a bilious fever, not because the bile is its subject, but because it depends on the bile and its putrefaction; so the subject of the putrefaction is the humour, while the fever itself is in the heart, where the humour first conceives a flame, either intermittent or continuous, unless it is symptomatic, that is, unless it is brought on the heart from elsewhere.

units.la: CAPVT I. DE AERE EIVSQVE CONDI-tionibus, essentia, qualitate, regionum, popu-lorum & locorum varietate, deq; vtendi mo-do, & peste aeris seu veneno aereo.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. ON THE AIR AND ITS CONDITIONS: ITS ESSENCE, QUALITY, AND THE VARIETY OF REGIONS, PEOPLES AND PLACES; ON THE MANNER OF USING IT; AND ON THE PESTILENCE OF THE AIR, OR AERIAL POISON.

units.la: INter sanitatis tuendæ decreta & capita primum sibi & principem locum vendi-cat aer, in omne corpus promtè penetrans. caloris nativi pabulum & refrigerium, quo sine nec sanitas conseruari integrè, nec mor-bus tutò profligari, imò ne quidem vitam a-gere homo potest.
units.tr: Among the rules and heads of preserving health, the air first claims the first and chief place, penetrating readily into every body. It is the food and refreshment of native heat, without which health cannot be kept whole, disease cannot be safely driven out, and a man cannot even live.

units.la: Vnde grauiss.& sapientiss.autores postèri-tati reliquerũt, pro vario cœlo multifariâ ho-minum naturam, mores, & morbos, numero-sam plantárũ, animaliũmq; prolem, simulq; sterilitatem & fertilitatem immutari : siqui-demaer ambiens, etiam nobis inuitis ad cor-poris tutelam hauriendus, corpus nostrũ vel conferuat, & tuetur, si temperatus : st & bone qualitatis, vel id labefactat & immutat, sifub-stantiâ vitiatus est, & immoderatæ qualitatis.
units.tr: Hence very serious and wise authors have left it to posterity that the nature, manners and diseases of men, the numerous plants and the offspring of animals, and likewise their barrenness and fertility, are altered according to the varying sky. For the surrounding air, which we must draw in for the protection of the body even against our will, either preserves and guards our body if it is temperate and of good quality, or weakens and changes it if it is vitiated in substance and of immoderate quality.

units.la: Itaq; danda est opera, vt summa animi cõ-tentione aeris effentia & qualitas accuratè obseruetur, vt sanitatem iucundius cõferua-re, & morbos tutius præcauere liceat. Et pri-mò quidem aeris effentia perpendenda est; pro vario cœlo, vrbium, locorũq; situ, pro-que diuerso solis accessu & recessu, ex quibus celerem sæpè mutationem subit.
units.tr: Therefore care must be taken, with the utmost effort of mind, that the essence and quality of the air be carefully observed, so that we may preserve health more pleasantly and guard against diseases more safely. And first the essence of the air must be weighed, according to the variety of the sky, the situation of cities and places, and the differing approach and withdrawal of the sun, from which it often undergoes rapid change.

units.la: Aer enim tenuis, purus, serenus, tempera-tus, tranquillus, tetroq; stagnorum, paludum, imbrium, cadauerum; habitu non confpur-catus, spiritus collustrat, ingeniumq; acuit, ac corpus in vigore conferuat.
units.tr: For thin, pure, serene, temperate and calm air, not tainted by the foul exhalations of swamps, marshes, rain, or carcasses, brightens the spirits, sharpens the wit, and keeps the body in vigour.

units.la: Hæc aeris constitutio ob cœli amœnitatem & puritatem hominũs facit venustiores, benigniores, maiores & efforminationes, quales Hipp.ait esse Asianos: Europæi ob cœli inco-stantiam magnitudine corporis varii existũt & differétes, audaces & robusti (quamuis hic nõ minor est vitus varii & discrepantis vis.)
units.tr: This constitution of the air makes people more graceful, kinder, and (as Hippocrates says of the Asians) more gentle and effeminate, because of the pleasantness and purity of the sky. Europeans, on account of the inconstancy of the sky, vary in bodily size and differ from one another, being bold and robust (although the force of vice and discord here is no less varied).

units.la: Aer Serenus est,qui nubibus & nebulis,seu su-
units.tr: Air is serene when it is free of clouds and mists, or of dark vapours.

units.la: mis careat: huic opponitur inserenus & nebulosus,Tranquillus, qui vel huic opponitur tumultuas,Tenuis defæcatum est purus & transparens:crassus contra opacus est & impurus.
units.tr: Its opposite is the unserene and misty air. Tranquil air is that which is not stirred by tumult, and its opposite is the turbulent. Thin air is purified and transparent; thick air, on the contrary, is opaque and impure.

units.la: Tenuis itaq;, purufq; aer sordida alicuius causæ externę illuuie nō infectus, omni ætati & temperamento saluberrimus est: impurus, crassusq; perniciosus. Hanc sententiam confirmat Gal. l.1. de sanit. tuend. c.11. Aerem, inquit, optimum in pulmones trahere omnib? salubre est: optimū aerem censeo, qui prorsus sit purus. Eiusmodi vero fuerit, q nec stagni, nec paludis halitus sit perturbatus, nec ex profundo specu pestilente aura spirante infectus, nec qui ex cloacis, quæ magnam aliquā vrbem aut numerosum exercitū purgent, vitium contraxit, nec, qui ob flumen vel stagnū vicinum, nebulosus est, nec, qui, editis vndiq; montibus, in cauo loco clausus nullum recipit perflatu. Suffocans enim putrisq; est, similis ei, qui in domibus quibusdā est inclusus, in quibus ob putredinem & perflatus defectū plurimus coaceruatur situs & corruptio. Huiusmodi ergo aer omni plane ætati est noxius, sicut è diuerso q purus est omninò, nulli nō ætati est vtilis. At vero, quæ ex calore, frigore, siccitate, humiditateue diuersitas aeris contingit, non perinde se ad omnes homines habet: sed corporibus, quæ sunt optimo temperamento,etiam optimè temperatus aer est, saluberrimus:in quibus verò exuperans qua-litas dominatur,iis vtilissimus aer est, qui ei qualitati maximè aduersatur, frigidus calidæ, calidus frigidæ,humidiori siccus,siccori quâ par est,tantò humidior, quantò siccitas ipsa modum excedit. Hactenus[?] Galenus.
units.tr: Thin and pure air, not infected by any filth from some external cause, is most healthful for every age and temperament; impure and thick air is harmful. Galen confirms this opinion in book 1 of On the Preservation of Health, chapter 11: "To draw the best air into the lungs is healthful for all; I hold that the best air is that which is entirely pure. Such air is not disturbed by the exhalation of a pond or marsh, nor infected by a pestilential breeze blowing from a deep cave, nor has it contracted fault from the sewers that cleanse some large city or numerous army, nor is it misty because of a nearby river or pool, nor is it enclosed in a hollow place with mountains rising on every side, receiving no breeze. For such air is suffocating and putrid, like that of certain closed houses, in which much filth and corruption accumulate through putrefaction and lack of ventilation. Such air is therefore harmful to every age, just as, conversely, the air that is wholly pure is useful to every age. But the differences of air arising from heat, cold, dryness or moisture do not affect all men alike. For bodies of the best temperament, air that is itself best tempered is most healthful; but in those in whom an excessive quality dominates, the most useful air is that which most opposes that quality: cold for the hot, warm for the cold, dry for the moist, and for the dry, moist to the degree proper, the more moist the more the dryness itself exceeds the measure." Thus far Galen.

units.la: Unde sanitati minus consulere videntur,q[?] circa stagna,paludes,nemora aut valles nullum flatum recipientes,aut flumé vicinū,aut loca austrū spectantia domicilia construunt. Sed longè peius faciunt Magistratus & proceres quidā,qui caulas,stabula & receptacula canū &equorū in arcib' extruunt vel loca cadaue-rū excoriandorū,sepulturamq; humanorum corporum in ipsis urbibus,vel prope cōstitu-unt etiam seuero edicto. Quid? quod apud quasdā gentes, cumprimis verò Danos,Sue-cos & his vicinos, nunc verò etiā Germaniæ proceres plerofq; mos inualuit,in cœnacula quosuis canes venaticos veftigiatores,pecua-rios,molossos,&villaticos recipere etiā feue-riffimo edicto,vt canè exire iubens citius pia-culum commisisse dicatur quam hominem.
units.tr: Hence they seem to take less care for their health who build their houses near pools, marshes, groves or valleys that receive no breeze, or beside a river, or in places facing south. But magistrates and certain nobles do far worse, who build pens, stables and kennels for dogs and horses in their citadels, or set up places for flaying carcasses and for burying human bodies within the cities themselves or close by, even under strict edict. And what of the fact that among certain peoples, above all the Danes, Swedes and their neighbours, and now also most of the nobles of Germany, the custom has prevailed of admitting into upper rooms any hunting dogs, trackers, herding dogs, mastiffs and house dogs, even under the strictest edict, so that a man who orders a dog out is said to have committed a greater offence than one who orders a man out?

units.la: Quid quæso sanitati magis obnoxium, quid fœdius & sordidius, quâ suauissimos ex cibis variis vaporesf[?] halitusq; exhalantes, tumq; cœnaculum complentes canū sterco-ribus & cletis obsolefieri & inquinari? Te-nuem enim & naturâ purum aerem eiusmodi exhalaexhalationibus facile vitiari, vitiatum a nobis inspirari, inspiratum ob arteriarum cū venis coadftomofin sanguini permisceri, permixtū spiritus, quorum præcipuum fomentum est, inficere & tenebricosos reddere, non dicam ipsum sanguinem incrassare, plus quam notū est. Quare totus debet esse Sanitatis custodiendæ studiosus in aeris effentia penitus exa-minanda, & in vario locorū ficu circūfpectius perlustrando, psertim vero qui humaniorib* literis operā dant, in arduisq; negotiis exhaurien-dis, officiis publicis administrandis sunt occupati, nec non valetudinarii in hoc vnicē inuigilabunt, vt aerem purum & temperatū habeant, vel industria, arteq;, si opus fuerit, talem præparent. Noster certē hicaer Budinga non adeo salubris est, quia rarò purus; cū, quia montib* altis vndiq; fere clausus & interceptus, nō est perflabilis, vnde putris euadit similifq; eiqui in domibus quibusdā, cauisq; habitationū locis inclusus ob perflatus & ventilationis defectū sæpe & facile corrūpitur: tum ob paludosam fossam lacunamq; mediam vrbem transeuntē, tetrumq; æstate halitum expirantem, vnde aerem vehementer infici & immutari testes sunt ipsi incolæ & quotidie fere inuadentes morbi. Huc accedunt validiores austrinorū ventorū afflatus, quib. Budinga nostra ex illa parte qua Fraco-furtum spectat & meridiē, maximē exposita & subiecta cernitur,nam certū est eiusmodi ventos multa sæpe inquinamenta & sparsa[?] morborum femina ex meridionalib? illis regionibus & locis huc depōhere[?], quæ postea in cauitatibus inclusa, atq; retenta rationem habét causæ efficientis & procreantis morbi, vt extrinsecus accidétia, & in corpore nostro non sponte generata. Ego, vt ab eiusmodi cō- tagione perstē irimmunis;itinerib?,crebro ex- ércitio, vel subdialibus montanisq; inambu- lationibus, Septentriones versus vel Orienté corpus soleo ventilare & perspirabile redde- ste, ex quib. postea me bené habere & valere testantur viri & amici optimi, eundé in finé id mecum ex suasu meo pertentantes. Hactenus de essentia aeris, Sequitur eius qualitas:
units.tr: What, I ask, is more harmful to health, what more foul and filthy, than that the most pleasant vapours and exhalations rising from various foods should be fouled and polluted by dogs' dung and filth, filling the upper room? For thin air, naturally pure, is easily vitiated by such exhalations; once vitiated and inhaled by us, it is mixed with the blood through the connection of the arteries with the veins; and the mixed spirits, of which blood is the chief fuel, it infects and renders gloomy, not to mention that it thickens the blood more than is generally known. Therefore everyone who is zealous for preserving health ought to examine thoroughly the essence of the air and to survey carefully the variety of places, especially those who devote themselves to humane letters, who are occupied in exhausting business and discharging public offices, and likewise invalids, who will watch vigilantly to this one end: that they have pure and temperate air, or prepare such air by diligence and art if need be. Our own air at Büdingen is certainly not very healthful, because it is rarely pure. Being shut in and cut off on nearly every side by high mountains, it is not open to breezes, so it becomes putrid like the air of certain houses enclosed in closed places, and, through lack of breeze and ventilation, is often and easily corrupted. Also, a marshy ditch and pool runs through the middle of the town, exhaling a foul vapour in summer, whence the air is strongly infected and altered, as the inhabitants themselves and nearly daily diseases bear witness. Add to this the stronger blasts of the southern winds, to which Büdingen is seen to be most exposed on the side facing Frankfurt and the south. For it is certain that such winds often bring many pollutions and scattered seeds of disease from those southern regions and places hither; these, afterwards shut in and retained in hollows, take on the character of an efficient and generating cause of disease, as things accidental and extrinsic, not spontaneously generated in our bodies. For my part, to remain free from such contagion, I am accustomed, through journeys, frequent exercise, or walks in the open air and the mountains, to air my body towards the north or east and make it open to perspiration. Afterwards my best men and friends testify that I am well and strong, and at my urging they try the same for the same end. So much on the essence of the air; there follows its quality.

units.la: Hæc non minus ad sanitatem tuendam, morborum; præcautionem conferr, quam ipsius essentia: Aer enim calidus confert frigido tempe- mento prædicitis, affectibusq; frigidis & diu- turnis: frigidus calidis, humidus siccis, siccus- que humidis opportune est accommodand?.
units.tr: This contributes no less to preserving health and preventing diseases than the essence itself. For warm air suits those of cold temperament and cold and long-standing affections; cold air suits the hot; moist air suits the dry, and dry air suits the moist, as is fitting.

units.la: Praeterea cōmoda & incomoda adnotare coducit,que vnaquæq; aeris qualitas secū af- ferre consueuit: Calidus aer corpora langui- diora reddit,breuiorisq; vitæ. Calorem n.in- satum & fluentem à centro ad circumferen- tiā educendo citius resoluit,cordiq; incomo- dat & morbis calidis, sed frigidis congruus est cerebrumq; recreat, & refocillat. Fri-
units.tr: It is also useful to note the advantages and disadvantages that each quality of air is accustomed to bring with it. Warm air makes bodies more languid and shortens life; for by drawing the unrefined and flowing heat outward from the centre to the circumference, it dissolves it quickly, is unfavourable to the heart, and suits hot diseases. But it suits cold diseases, and refreshes and revives the brain. Cold

units.la: Frigidus aer robusta, pertinacia & longa- tua facit alitq; corpora, testis Dania, Suecia, & caeteri Septentrionis populi, cerebro præter- ea incommodat, cordi vero refrigerium est.
units.tr: Cold air makes bodies robust, tenacious and long-lived, as Denmark, Sweden and the other peoples of the North bear witness. Besides, it harms the brain, but is a refreshment to the heart.

units.la: Humidus aer pinguia, mollia, glabra, moribusque humanioribus exornata profert corpora, ficcioribusque temperaturis, morbisque calidis & siccis plurimum opitulatur, pedum vero ac crurum vlceribus noxius.
units.tr: Moist air produces bodies that are fat, soft, smooth and adorned with gentler manners, and it greatly helps the drier temperaments and hot and dry diseases, but it is harmful to ulcers of the feet and legs.

units.la: Siccus humidis corporibus, affectibusque, pulmonum, vlceribus eximiè cōfert, sanitatiq; reseruadæ & tuendæ præ cæteris auxiliatur. Siccitates n. inquit Hipp. in aphor. imbribus sunt salubriores. Verum hoc tenendum, sicut aer siccus corpora ad morbos reddit minus pcli-uia, sed breuioris pfert vitæ, sic humidus corpora affectib. magis obnoxia reddit, sed vitæ longioris. Verum hic oriuntur dubia quaedam, quæ discutienda sunt. I. Cur Galenus aerem calidum & humidu vocet peffimu, cum tame in calore & humido cōsistat vita animaliu? II. Quodnam anni tempus sit salubrius, & an autumnus recte dicatur frigidus & siccus, vel calidum & humidum, ideoq; temperatum? R. ad
units.tr: Dry air is exceedingly beneficial to moist bodies and to affections of the lungs and ulcers, and above all others it helps to preserve and guard health. Dryness, says Hippocrates in the Aphorisms, is more healthful than rains. But this must be held: just as dry air makes bodies less prone to disease yet gives a shorter life, so moist air makes bodies more liable to affections but of longer life. Here, however, certain doubts arise which must be discussed. 1. Why does Galen call warm and moist air the worst, since the life of animals consists in heat and moisture? 2. Which season of the year is most healthful, and is autumn rightly called cold and dry, or warm and moist, and therefore temperate? Reply (R. ad) to the first: ...

units.la: I. Vitam in caloris innati humorem depascentis & humoris calorem fouentis legitima cō-stiture temperatione, ita accipiendum est, vt non excludatur frigidum & siccum, absq; frigido n. & sicco nulla esset caloris & humidi terminatio & unio, sed dissolutio, dissipatio humoris diffluxus. Hæc esse vera ostendunt Frigidi & animalia frigidioris & ficcioris temperamé-ti,quæ omniū longissimè viuunt,ut elephan-tes, cerui,corui,& in hominū tribubus melan-colici,qui omniū consensu sunt frigidi & sic-ci,& ratio hæc est,quod humor melancolic? Sed in causa est,ut humidum nō ita promtè & sa-lsa, colorq; dissipet,sed arctè uniátur & terminétur; Videbitur hoc multis parado-xon,sed si in experimento acquieuerint,re-ipsá cōperient,me nō plane falsum dixisse.Ac huius sententiæ veritate confirmant Septen-trionis populi,qui aerem spirant frigidum & siccum temparamento eorū familiarissimū, vnde diutissimè viuūt & innoxiè nisi frequés & crebrior salsamentorum vsus funeris ante-diem eos enecaret,pessimo in corporib.ipso-rum conducto inquilinoScorbuto.Cur autè Galenus aerem calidum & humidum vocet pessimum,facit ratione habitâad frigidum& siccum,id est,comparatè Verba eius [?]r. d:ré-per.c.4.hæc sunt. Ego vero,tantum abest,ut aut ut calidum & humidū pronūcién,aut sī quid temperatum est,calidum dicâatq; hu-midum, ut quod plane contrarium est affir-mem,omnium aeris ambientis temperamé-torum pessimum esse id,quod calidum & hu-midum est. Et paulò post , variorum affectu-um,quorum nullum aitesse, putredinis qui soboles non fit, enumerationem subiungit, quippe cum nec à sicco putrefieri quicquam fit aptum, nec à frigido: sic carnes & reliqua, quaecunq; alioqui ab hominibus solent, hæc sale, alia muria, alia aceto, vel alio quopiam, q; siccat, commodè præparantur: deprehendes & Borea vento natura frigido & sicco omnia quæ diutissimè impustria[?] durare, contra putrescere facilimè ven. o austrino, qui calidus & humidus est. Itaque nos in totum contra quam illi statuunt calidum & humidum esse ver, decernim[?], cum neq; tale sit, neq; si esset, utiq; salubre esset. Hac Galenus. Cū igitur promtissimè putrescant corpora calida & humida, teste eodem Gal. 1. de diff. febr. c.3. & quidem celerius in locis calidis & humidis, quam frigidis & siccis, ut demonstratum est, sequitur calidam humidamq; aeris ambientis constitutionem atque temperiem esse cæteris pejorem. Corpora autem calidiora humidioraque putredinis noxam (nisi difflentur & refrigerentur) citius contrahere, quam frigidiora & siccio̊ra, ostendunt febres humorales. Omnis h. humor alienus à natura corporis, in quo continetur, neque aptus ad eius nutritionem necessariò putrescit, febremq; accendit, putrescit autem celerrimè, cum locus, in quo fuerit collectus, est calidus: id quod ventriculus manifestat plus iusto calidior, nullus enim cibus immodicè calfactus, sine putredine in eo permanere potest, corrumpi n. cibum ob immoderatam caliditatem, & humidi defe&tum necesse est Verum de his commodius &c. explicatius cap. de cibis.
units.tr: I. The life that consists in a lawful balance between the innate heat, which feeds on moisture, and the moisture, which nourishes that heat, must be understood so that the cold and dry is not excluded. Without the cold and dry there would be no limit to the heat and moisture and no union between them, but dissolution and dissipation, the moisture flowing away. That these things are true is shown by cold creatures and animals of a colder and drier temperament, which live longest of all, such as elephants, stags and ravens, and among the tribes of men the melancholic, who by universal agreement are cold and dry. The reason is that melancholic humour is not so readily dissipated by heat, but is tightly bound and contained. This will seem a paradox to many, but if they rest on experience, they will find in fact that I have not spoken falsely. The truth of this opinion is also confirmed by the peoples of the North, who breathe cold and dry air, which is most familiar to their temperament, and so they live a very long time and harmlessly, unless the frequent and repeated use of salted foods carries them off before their day, scurvy taking up residence in their bodies as a most evil tenant. As for why Galen calls warm and moist air the worst, he does so with reference to cold and dry, that is, comparatively. His words, in the book De ... , chapter 4, are these: "I, indeed, so far from calling warm and moist the best, or calling anything temperate warm and moist, affirm the very opposite: that of all the temperaments of the surrounding air, the worst is that which is warm and moist." And a little later he adds a list of various affections, none of which, he says, is not an offspring of putrefaction, since nothing suited to putrefaction arises from the dry or from the cold. Thus meats and other things that men commonly keep are well preserved with salt, others with brine, others with vinegar or some other drying agent. You will also find that under the north wind, which is cold and dry by nature, all things last longest, whereas they putrefy most easily under the south wind, which is warm and moist. Therefore we, contrary to those who hold that the warm and moist is best, decide altogether that it is not so, since it is neither such a thing, nor, if it were, would it be healthy at all. Thus Galen. Since, then, warm and moist bodies putrefy most readily, as the same Galen witnesses in his book On Differences of Fevers, chapter 3, and indeed more quickly in warm and moist places than in cold and dry, as has been shown, it follows that a warm and moist constitution and temperature of the surrounding air is worse than the others. That bodies which are warmer and moister contract the harm of putrefaction more quickly (unless they are dissolved and cooled) than colder and drier ones is shown by humoral fevers. Every such humour, foreign to the nature of the body in which it is contained and not suited to its nourishment, necessarily putrefies and kindles fever, and it putrefies most quickly when the place in which it has collected is warm. The stomach shows this, being hotter than it should be, for no food that is excessively heated can remain in it without putrefaction, since food must be corrupted by immoderate heat and the lack of moisture. But concerning these matters, more conveniently and more fully, in the chapter on foods.

units.la: DE SECVNDO. Anautumnus, recte
units.tr: On the second question: whether autumn is rightly called cold and dry

units.la: Refponsio dicatur frigidus & siccus, hiems frigida & hu- ad alterā mida &c. acuté disputat Galenus /. de temper. quaestio- cap.3.6 4. perstringens cos, qui vere esse calidi nem. & humidi temperamenti ideoque tempera- tum, autumnum frigidum & siccum, ideoque intemperatum & morbiferum existimârunt, in qua etiam opinione bona physicorum pars permansit ; persuasum sibi habens, ver, quia calidum & humidum, esse saluberrimum. Ve- rum ex Galeni iudicio res se longe habet ali- ter. Non enim aduertunt antiquos Atta- lensis Athenaei sectatores temperatam crafin, statumque præteremisse, eiusque plane non meminisse.
units.tr: The answer. Autumn is rightly called cold and dry, and winter cold and moist, and so on. Galen sharply disputes, in his book On the Temperaments (chapters 3 and 4), those who thought spring, being warm and moist, is a temperate season, and therefore judged autumn, being cold and dry, to be intemperate and harmful. A good part of the natural philosophers remained in this opinion, persuaded that spring, because it is warm and moist, is the most healthful. But by Galen's judgement the matter stands quite otherwise. For they did not notice that the followers of Athenaeus of Attalia had passed over the temperate and balanced state, and did not remember it at all.

units.la: Sanitatis enim tuenda victum inuestigan- tes, calidiusque iusto corpus iubentes refrige- rare, vel frigidius calefacere, vel humidius sic- care, ficciusq; humectare, quid aliud intendat, quam temperatum quendam atq; mediocrem statum essicere ? Si igitur calidum & humi- dum excessus nomina sunt, non potest verum esse, quod verfit in omnibus mediocre. Siau- tem iccirco humidum est & calidum, quod s- state humidius est, hieme vero calidius, quid obstat, quo minus id frigidum etiam ficcumq; sit, propterea quod sstate frigidius & hieme calicalidus : hacque ratione erit omnia, calidum, humidum, frigidum & siccum : Sed quia 4. qualitates in vna eademque repræpollere non possunt, neque æstati neque hiemi vt compa- rare æquum est, sed potius ipsum per se æsti- mare. Neque enim hiems ipsa ea de causa fri- gida dicitur & humida, quod reliquis tempo- ribus humidior sit, frigidiorque, sed quod hu- miditas in ea superet siccitatem, & frigiditas calorem: ad eundem modum & æstas calida & sicca, quod in ea humor vincitur à sicco, & frigidum à calido. Sic & autumnus non recte frigidus dicitur & siccus, absolute, non enim frigidus est, si per se consideretur, vt hi- ems est, sed vbi cum æstate confertur, quâ fri- gidior est: & quia inæqualiter temperatus est, vtpote meridie multò calidior quam mane aut vesperi, nec in humido & sicco medium & æqualem statum obtiner, ita vt eodem die mo- dò frigus modò calor vrgeat, propter hanc in- quam, inæqualem temperiem morbiferū eum recte appellatum censendum est: vt ita 4. anni temporum quodlibet ex suapte natura non ex alterius comparatione calidum, humidum, fri- gidum vel siccum æstimandum sit & nomi- nandum. Quod autem Hippocrates ver vocat saluberrimum, ratio est, quod omnium excel- suum medium sit ver, id est, quia æqualitatem quandā tenet caloris, frigoris, humidi & sicci, obidq; morbis mortiferis minimè obnoxius.
units.tr: For those who seek a diet to preserve health, and who order the body that is warmer than is right to be cooled, or that which is colder to be warmed, or that which is too moist to be dried, or that which is too dry to be moistened, what else do they aim at than to bring about a certain temperate and moderate state? If, then, warm and moist are names of excess, it cannot be true that the mean lies in all things. But if something is moist and warm because it is moister in summer and warmer in winter, what prevents it from also being cold and dry, since it is colder in summer and warmer in winter? In this way everything would be warm, moist, cold and dry. But because four qualities cannot predominate in one and the same thing, it is not fair to compare it with summer or with winter, but rather to judge it by itself. For winter is not called cold and moist for this reason, that it is moister and colder than the other seasons, but because in it moisture exceeds dryness and cold exceeds heat. In the same way summer is called warm and dry because in it moisture is overcome by dryness and cold by heat. So too autumn is not rightly called cold and dry absolutely. For it is not cold when considered in itself, as winter is, but when it is compared with summer, by which it is colder. And because it is unevenly tempered, being much warmer at midday than in the morning or the evening, and because it does not hold a middle and even state between moist and dry, so that on the same day now cold and now heat presses upon us, it should be thought rightly called harmful for this reason, I say, its uneven temperament. And so each of the four seasons is to be judged and named warm, moist, cold or dry from its own nature, not from its comparison with another. As for Hippocrates calling spring the most healthful, the reason is that spring is the mean among all the extremes, that is, because it keeps a certain equality of heat, cold, moisture and dryness, and for this reason is least liable to deadly diseases.

units.la: Hallenus de quaestionibus propositis ex Galeni libris de fundamentis: Redeo ad ea, à quibus parum deflexi.
units.tr: Thus far on the questions raised from Galen's books on the foundations. I now return to the matters from which I have strayed a little.

units.la: Aer à tè- Verum enim verò, quia provatio accessu perte rece & recessu Solis, vaporum, pluuiarum & immensus dens quo- brium occurfione diuersam mutationem subi- modo tè- tamquè alterationem aer subit , facilè etiam perandus? corpora nostra eum variis afficere modis posse existimandum est. Itaque à temperie multum recedens impenfeq; calidior vel frigidior, eo- dem recessu, quo à temperie declinauit, corri- gendus est. Et quidem plus iusto frigidior igni- bus luculentis cum fuffumigiis aromaticis, vt lignoiuniperi, mastiche, thure, baccisiunipe- rinis, herbis etiam & floribus calfacientibus humi sparsis vel accensis & super caibones proiectis, vel, quod ego saluberrimum existi- mo, in crebroq; id viu habeo; licet aliis fit vel ignotum vel extra vsum) herbis leuiter deco- &tis, fumoque in conclaue immisso, vel nares recepto, vel reliquas partes externas, vt manus ac pedes eo imbuendo, vix enim credideris quàm hoc tempore frigidiore commodet: in- ter herbas praecipuam laudem obtinet lauen- dula, thymus, Satureia, rosmarinus, maiorana, hissopus, origanum, ferpillum, mentha, cala- mintha, betonica, saluia, & similes. Beatiores nis gentes nobis longe sunt Sueci & caeteri Septentrionis nobis bea populi, qui suis focis & caminis apponunt li- gna abiegna aliarum; refiniferarum, quarum illicabundantia maxima,(quercus enim rario-res ibi visuntur, ob idq; in magno pretio) quæ posteafuauiffimum, thuriq; similem odorem ex resina accensa fundunt,qui nares & cerebrū feriens miris id modis corroborat,inq; vigore confirmat. Solent autem & eiusdem cœli populi liquorem illum pinguem & flagrabilem ex arboribus prædictis affatim refudante colligere, collectum exiccare & thuris instar ad vsum reseruare. Ipse ego ex Suecia reduturiens imperitioribus quibusdam pharmacopęis im- ponens pro thure eum prædicaui, postea ad- monens, vt in simplicibus probè dignoscendis & discernendis sint cautiores.
units.tr: But because the air undergoes diverse changes and alterations through the approach and recession of the sun, through vapours, rains, and the immense violence of the winds, it is easy to think that it can affect our bodies in various ways. So when the air departs far from temperateness, becoming excessively hotter or colder, it must be corrected by the same withdrawal by which it departed from temperateness. And indeed, when it is too cold, one should use bright fires with aromatic fumigations, such as juniper wood, mastic, frankincense, juniper berries, and warming herbs and flowers scattered on the floor or set alight and thrown on the coals. Or, what I consider most healthful and use often (though to others it may be unknown or out of use), herbs lightly boiled, with the smoke let into the room, or received into the nostrils, or applied to the other outer parts, such as the hands and feet. For you would hardly believe how much this helps in cold weather. Among herbs, lavender, thyme, savory, rosemary, marjoram, hyssop, oregano, wild thyme, mint, calamint, betony, sage, and similar ones win the chief praise. Far happier than we are are the Swedes and the other peoples of the North, who put on their hearths and stoves logs of fir and other resinous woods, of which there is a very great abundance (oaks are rarer there and therefore highly prized). These, when burned, give off a most fragrant odour like frankincense from the kindled resin, which strikes the nostrils and brain and strengthens them in a wonderful way and confirms their vigour. The people of that same region also customarily collect that rich, inflammable liquid which flows freely from the aforementioned trees, dry it, and keep it for use in the manner of frankincense. I myself, returning from Sweden, passed it off as frankincense to some rather inexperienced pharmacists and recommended it; afterwards I advised them to be more careful in properly recognising and distinguishing simple remedies.

units.la: In Calidiori vero nobis offuso aere floribus frigidis, vt nymphęæ[?] rosarum, violarum anemones, hyacinthi, cichorii, balaustii, &c. herbis item frigidis, vt parietaria, chondrilla, lactuca, endiuia, acetosa, plantagine, trifolio a-ceroso[?], portulaca, & similibus vti conuenit.
units.tr: In a warmer air, however, it is fitting for us to use cooling flowers, such as water lilies, roses, violets, anemones, hyacinths, chicory, pomegranate blossoms, etc., and likewise cooling herbs, such as pellitory, gum-chondrilla, lettuce, endive, sorrel, plantain, trefoil, purslane, and similar ones.

units.la: Verum ventulum facere flabello optimum iudico. Ventilatio enim in aere calidiori quibusdam peculiaris est. Vbi tamen obseruan- dum vitiatum & corruptum aerem ventilandum non esse, nisi adapertis in conclaui fenestris, ex ea parte, qua ventus spirat Septentrio-nalis vel Orientalis, & si conclaue ab illa parte adapertile non est, corrigatur aer garyophyllis, baccis iuniperinis, mastiche, thureque, vel detineatur in ore paulatim, & sensim masticando radix angelicæ, Zedoariæ, galangæ, nux mofchata, garyophyllus, vel simile quid odo- riferum, de quibus paulò post exinstituto, vbi de veneno aeris, dicetur commodius.
units.tr: But I judge it best to create a little breeze with a fan, for ventilation is peculiarly useful in warmer air. Yet it must be observed that foul and corrupted air should not be ventilated unless the windows of the room are opened on the side from which the north or east wind blows; and if the room cannot be opened on that side, the air should be corrected with cloves, juniper berries, mastic, and frankincense, or else a root of angelica, zedoary, galangal, nutmeg, clove, or something similar and fragrant should be held gradually in the mouth and chewed slowly. Of these I shall speak a little later, where I discuss the poison of the air, more conveniently.

units.la: Accidit autem frequenter, vt per vrbium oppidorum, angustos, flexuosos, vicos cō- meanti putris è sterquilinii s vel cloacali vapor in nares & os obreptet, qui pofteain cerebrum delatus spirituum animalium consortium dif- gregat & conturbat. Quibus igitur necessa- rió per eiusmodi fœtentia loca est eundum, vel ftrophioli nodo ex garyophyllis & fimilib? a- romatis admoto naribus, vel spiritu fortiterre- tento, vel fi quid inopinato inspiratum fuerit, fortiter expirando, efflandoque à contagione possunt euadere immunes. Vnde videre est in- tempestiuas, exuperantefq; aeris immoderan- tias prorsus esse fugiendas.
units.tr: It frequently happens, however, that through the narrow, winding lanes of towns and villages a putrid vapour from a dunghill or sewer creeps into the nose and mouth, which afterwards, carried to the brain, scatters and disturbs the fellowship of the animal spirits. Therefore, for those who must necessarily pass through such stinking places, either a little bag of cloves and similar aromatics may be held to the nostrils, or the breath may be held firmly, or, if anything has been inhaled unexpectedly, one may breathe it out forcibly and so escape the contagion unharmed. Hence it is clear that unseasonable and excessive immoderations of the air are wholly to be avoided.

units.la: M. Aurelius Imper. diei pensum certis ho- ris partiebatur, maneq; non vigente adhuc ca- lore deambulabat, meridie verò in capitolio, quiescebat. Augustus Cæsar natura valetudi- narius domo non exibat, nisi prius aerem Sol colluftraffet.
units.tr: The Emperor Marcus Aurelius divided the day's work into fixed hours, and walked in the morning while the heat was not yet strong, but at midday he rested in the Capitol. The emperor Augustus Caesar, being sickly by nature, did not go out of doors unless the sun had first warmed the air.

units.la: Iccirco aer temperatus, vt matutinus, est o- mnium saluberrimus, Sole videlicet horofco- pum, duodecimum q; cœli locum occupante : meridianus calore exuperans, vt noctur nus- vapore exhalationeq; humefcens, insalubris & noxius. Vespertinus, Sole videlicet Cardinem occioccidentis peragrante, quanto cum desiderio pro cordis refrigerio à contentius æstate pere- grinantibus, vel subdiali ardore Solis nimioue salubris. exercitio labefactatis, hauriatur, nemini non est notum.
units.tr: Therefore the temperate air of morning is the most healthful of all, since the sun then occupies the horoscope and the twelfth place of the heavens. The air at midday, excessive with heat, and the air at night, moist with vapour and exhalation, are unhealthy and harmful. Everyone knows with what longing the evening air, when the sun is traversing the setting cardinal point, is drawn in for the refreshment of the heart by those who, wearied by the summer heat or by the excessive exertion of the sun's ardour out of doors, are travelling.

units.la: Cauendum tamen est, ne frigidior aer extrinsecus ad cutim, detecto scilicet capite pe-ctoreq; denudato, admittatur, densat enim cogitq; cutim, ac putredinosorum excremento-rum, humorumq; effluxum transpirare prohibet, vnde sæpe febres accendi videmus, aliaq; incommoda excitari. Qui tamen in continuo immodicoue sunt motu & exercitio, ne ob niam pororum cutaneorum relaxationem calor natiuus nimium expiret, his extrinsecus cutis spiracula perflari non est noxium, hoc enim modo cutanei meatus quodammodo densantur, calorque intus detinetur, qui alias perhalaret magno cum facultatum & actionum incommodo.
units.tr: Yet one must take care that the colder air from outside does not reach the skin, that is, with the head uncovered and the chest bared, for it thickens and compresses the skin and prevents the perspiration of putrid excrements and the outflow of humours, whence we often see fevers kindled and other ailments aroused. Yet for those who are in continual or immoderate motion and exercise, lest the natural heat be exhausted too much because of the relaxation of the pores of the skin, it is not harmful to let cool air blow on the skin from outside, for in this way the cutaneous passages are in some measure thickened and the heat is held within, which otherwise would escape to the great detriment of the faculties and actions.

units.la: Insolitæ etiam & subitæ mutationes tempestatum, & maximè austrinæ, graues sunt & periculosę corpusq; nostrum offendunt, testimonioq; Hipp. mentem percellunt: has iritur[?] sanitatis studiosus præcauebit, aut saltem se foras non debebit conferre, præsertim qui à rerum externarum, tempestatumq; immoderatarum occursatione prompte conflictantur.
units.tr: Therefore the person who cares for his health will guard against these sudden and unusual changes of weather, especially the southerly ones, which are grave and dangerous, injure the body, and, as Hippocrates testifies, strike terror into the mind. At the very least, he should not go out of doors, especially if he is easily overcome by encounters with external things and immoderate weather.

units.la: Hic vero & mundi regiones, regionum varietatem, ventorum vim, & quatuor anni tem-
units.tr: Here it is also worth carefully weighing the regions of the world, the variety of regions, the force of the winds, and the four seasons of the year, together with the mildness or harshness of the air,

units.la: pora cum aeris temperie, vel intemperie dili- genter perpendere expedit, vt quisque pro pe- culiari & vernacula natura aere competente & conueniente fruatur, noxiumq; euitet.
units.tr: so that each person may enjoy air that suits and agrees with his own particular and native constitution, and avoid what is harmful.

units.la: Primum mundi regiones seu cardines I V. vt Oriens calidus & siccus, Occidens frigidus & humidus, Septentrio frigidus & siccus, Meridies calidus & humidus : quibus cardinibus venti temperamento & natura correspondent, quod hi naturam fc.loci, per quem spirant, in- duant & affumant, auster videlic. calidus & humidus omnium infalubertrimus, pernitiofus n, semper, morborum namq; seminaria maligna ex meridionalibus illis locis & regionibus, vt Italia, Gallia, & bona parte Hispaniæ secum exportare, ac in Germaniam nostrā deponere sat testaturexperientia, quāuis & apud nos ra- dices & seminaria malignorum morborū im- mutabilia, quaq; interdum sua sede & loco ex- cludinō possint, sponte generari nō negārim.
units.tr: First, the regions or quarters of the world are four: the East is hot and dry, the West cold and moist, the North cold and dry, and the South hot and moist. The winds correspond to these quarters in temperament and nature, because they take on and assume the nature of the place (namely, the place through which they blow).
