The south wind, being hot and moist, is by far the most unhealthy of all and always pernicious, for experience sufficiently attests that it carries the malignant seedbeds of diseases from those southern places and regions, such as Italy, France, and a good part of Spain, and deposits them in our Germany. Yet I would not deny that among us too there are roots and seedbeds of malignant diseases that are unchangeable and that, at times, cannot be shut out from their own seat and place, and that they are generated spontaneously.

units.la: Zephyrus frigidus est & humidus. Boreas, iudicio Plinii, & testimonio populorum Septentrionis saluberrimus, vt & Eurus qui ab Oriente flat.
units.tr: The west wind is cold and moist. The north wind, in the judgement of Pliny and the testimony of the peoples of the North, is most healthful, and so is the east wind, which blows from the East.

units.la: Itaq; saluberrimi sunt dies sereni, meliores pluuiosi quam nebulosi, optimiq; hieme qui omnino vento carent, statim quibus Fauonius perflat. Occidentalem enim ventum, non plā- ne insalubrem esse & noxium testantur popu- li Occidentis : imò Euro sepe salubriorem eum inspirari æstiva docent experimenta.
units.tr: Therefore the healthiest days are clear ones; rainy days are better than foggy ones; and the best winter days are those entirely without wind, rather than those in which the west wind blows. For the peoples of the West testify that the west wind is not altogether unhealthy and harmful; indeed, experience in summer shows that it is often healthier to breathe than the east wind.

units.la: De anni temporibus, horumq; temperie, intemperieq; supra in quæstione, an autumnus rectè dicatur frigidus & siccus, abunde dictum est, quare lectorem eò remitto.
units.tr: Concerning the seasons of the year and their temperature or intemperature, enough has already been said above, in the question whether autumn is rightly called cold and dry; so I refer the reader there.

units.la: Mundi Regiones sequuntur, Asia, Africa, Europa, America.
units.tr: The regions of the world follow: Asia, Africa, Europe, America.

units.la: Europæi ob calidi innati & influentis ubertatem sunt audaces, robusti, longiorisq; vitæ, inter quos Germani, ut placuit Gale.2.de temp, & Seneca sunt iracundi, fortes, audaces, graves, armorumque cupidi.
units.tr: Europeans, because of the abundance of innate and inflowing heat, are bold, robust, and long-lived. Among them the Germans, as Gale.2.de temp, has pleased to say, and Seneca, are irascible, brave, bold, grave, and eager for arms.

units.la: Per Europæos intelligè Britannos, Germanos, Gallos, Hispanos, Italos. Sarmatas (h e. Polonos, Borussos, Effluos, <bl>Stefflender/</bl>Letuanos <bl>Littawer/Russos</bl>, <bl>Neuffen/</bl>Pomeranos <bl>Pommern/</bl>) Danos, Suecos, Dacos, <bl>Walachen/</bl> Transsyluanos, <bl>Siebenbürger</bl> / Pannones, <bl>Vngern/</bl> Tartaros, <bl>Tartern/</bl> Mœsos, <bl>Die in[?] Bulgarey/</bl>Pannonib.vicinos, Thraces, Macedones, Græcos, Dalmatas, Istros <bl>Hisferreich-cher/</bl>Italiæ attingentes ad mare Adriaticū, &c.
units.tr: By Europeans I understand the British, Germans, French, Spaniards, Italians; the Sarmatians (that is, the Poles, Prussians, Estonians, Lithuanians, Livonians, Russians, Pomeranians), the Danes, Swedes, Dacians, Walachians, Transylvanians, Siebenbürgers, Pannonians, Hungarians, Tartars, Mysians, the people of Bulgaria, neighbours of Pannonia, Thracians, Macedonians, Greeks, Dalmatians, the Istrians, and those who border on Italy at the Adriatic sea, etc.

units.la: Verum ut aerem & cœlum non habent hi unum & idem, sic etiam vita & moribus sunt diversissimis. Galli suffragiis Iustini, Cæsaris, Herodiani & Galeni sunt belliçosi & audaces, sed sitis impatientes. Pannonii teste Piur[?], sunt hebeti & tardo ingenio, sed ad bellum paratis-simi. Itali, teste Vitruvio, providi & sapientes sunt, compositi scilicet factiq; ex Mercurio &
units.tr: But just as these peoples do not have the same air and sky, so too their lives and customs are most diverse. By the testimony of Justin, Caesar, Herodian and Galen, the Gauls are warlike and bold, but impatient of thirst. According to Piur(?), the Pannonians are dull and slow of wit, but very ready for war. According to Vitruvius, the Italians are prudent and wise, being composed and made, of course, from Mercury and Venus, whence they seem to indulge in Venus more than the other peoples of Europe.

units.la: Venere, unde etiam Veneri plusquam caete-ra Europæ gentes indulgere videntur. Ligures montani Cic. resfe[?] sunt agrestes. Græci leues & mendaces, sed ob aeris siccitatem sapientio-res, quod siccitas, ut Plato prodidit, ingenium; humiditas vero stuporem gignat. Vides diuer-sas in diuersis terræ partibus, seu sub diuerso cœlo habitantium hominum proprietates. Hæ autem cum magnam partem ab influxu cœlesti dependeant, varientq; secundum di-uersitatem in lineis parallelis & angulis mun-di, qui sunt Oriens, Occidens, Meridies, Sep[?]-tentrio, lege iustitiæ admonitus, quæ regiones, prouinciæ, populi, quibus sideribus, stel-lisque subiiciantur & gubernentur in tractatu meoastrologico, quem adornandum jam sum aggressus, commodius & uberius paulo mea-éturum[?] polliceor.
units.tr: The mountain Ligurians are rustic, as Cicero reports. The Greeks are light and lying, but wiser because of the dryness of their air, since dryness, as Plato has taught, produces intelligence, whereas moisture produces stupidity. You can see the different characteristics of men who live in different parts of the earth, or under different skies. Since these depend largely on celestial influence, and vary according to the diversity of the parallel lines and angles of the world (which are East, West, South and North), I promise, admonished by the law of justice, that in my astrological treatise, which I have now begun to prepare, I will set out more conveniently and fully which regions, provinces and peoples are subject to and governed by which stars and constellations.

units.la: De Asianis, Africanis & Americanis incolis eorundemque variis naturis & motibus, mira sunt & fidem vix impetrare valentia, quæ Cosmographis literis mandata reperiuntur.
units.tr: Concerning the inhabitants of Asia, Africa and America, and their various natures and customs, there are marvels that can scarcely win belief, which are recorded in the writings of the cosmographers.

units.la: Ex Asianis ob aeris temperiem quidam, sunt clementiores & humaniores : quidam contra sylvestres, ferique, humanorum corpo-rum esu gaudentes.
units.tr: Among Asians, some, because of the temperateness of their air, are milder and more humane; others, on the contrary, are savage and wild, delighting in eating human flesh.

units.la: Africani minus vitam producunt, ob calo-ris innati & fluentis penuriam, unde & plæriq; sunt timidi, reperias tamen & inter eos vix ho-mines magisq; semiferos. Ameri-
units.tr: Africans live shorter lives, because of a shortage of innate and flowing heat, and so most of them are timid; yet among them you may find hardly any men, and rather more half-beasts.

units.la: Americanos inter crudelissimi sunt Antro-pophagi in sagittando certissimi, currendo ve-locifsimi, nudi incedentes, nulliq; obedientes, vniones aurumq; nihili facientes. Qui regio-nem Peru incolunt, feruntur humaniores & prudentiores, diuersarumque artium non ex-pertes, ac coloris crocei, cujusmodi sunt regio morbo seu ictero laborantes. Hos commercia & humanitatem excolere testantur, qui mer-catura amicè & perhumaniter, cum illis per-acta, velis remisq; inde redituriunt.
units.tr: Among the Americans the most cruel are the cannibals, very accurate in shooting and very swift in running, who walk about naked, obey no one, and think pearls and gold worthless. Those who inhabit the region of Peru are said to be more humane and prudent, not without skill in various arts, and of a saffron colour, such as those suffering from the jaundice or icterus. They are said to cultivate commerce and humanity: merchants who have dealt with them in a friendly and most courteous manner return from there with sails and oars.

units.la: Per Asianos intellige Ægyptios, Æthiopes sub Ægypto, Arabes, Syros, (qui in medio or-bis sunt constituti, cœlumq; habent tempera-tiffimum, adeo vt nec nimio calore torrean-tur, nec nimio frigore horreant:) Indianos, Chaldæos, Idumæos, Samaritanos, Interamnos, Galilæos, Persas, Scythas, Armenios, Parthos, Albanos, Colchos, (maximi veneficii autores) Cilices, Pamphylios, Lycios, Jones, Lydos, Phryges, (inter quos Trojani claruerunt) Ly-caones &c.
units.tr: By Asians understand the Egyptians, the Ethiopians under Egypt, the Arabs, and the Syrians (who are placed in the middle of the world and have a most temperate sky, so that they are neither scorched by excessive heat nor chilled by excessive cold); the Indians, Chaldeans, Idumeans, Samaritans, Interamnians, Galileans, Persians, Scythians, Armenians, Parthians, Albanians, Colchians (the greatest authors of witchcraft), Cilicians, Pamphylians, Lycians, Ionians, Lydians, Phrygians (among whom the Trojans were famous), Lycaonians, and so on.

units.la: Per Africanos, Mauros, Numidas, Libes, Cyrenæos, Carthaginenses, Æthiopes, Tingi-tanos, Cæsarienses, Ægyptios, Æthiopiæ con-terminos, &c.
units.tr: By Africans understand the Moors, Numidians, Libyans, Cyrenaeans, Carthaginians, Ethiopians, Tingitanians, Caesareans, Egyptians bordering on Ethiopia, and so on.

units.la: Regionum denique varietas, prout calida, humida, frigida vel sicca est, varias temperamentorum, humorumq; differentes producit naturas. Regio aspera & montosa homines alitin-gratos, stupidos & inhumanos, corpora ma-gna,aspera,crudelia,pertinacia,morbis calidis obnoxia:concaua pratis&latifundiis abundâs, corpora mollia,animos molles,morbos putri-dos & frigidos vtplurimum procreat. Vehe-menti & ancipiti temporum varietate flatu-umq;incursione crebro infestata corpora ma-gnitudine diuersa,robusta,animos audaces,in-dustriosq; sed instabiles,varios morbos,moref-que inducit, vt in Gallia videre est. In locis a-quosis degentes & humidis stupidi evadunt, carnosi, pingues, laborum impatientes,man-fuetiores,morbisq; pituitosis obnoxii, In lo-cis veró siccis contra sunt acutoingenio,proni ad iracundiam & febres ardentes. Regionem in ostiis sitam incolentes, vbi maximi fluuii mare vastum ingrediuntur, variis morbiscor-ripiuntur, quod aqua retenta in halitum con-vertatur,vnde postea aer conspurcatur & infi-citur. Morbosa est Regio,quæ magna antra, pa-ludes & loca halitibus tetris insectata recipit: Locus quoq; nulla ventorum vi exagitatus fa-cile corrumpitur,perflabilis vero & liber falu-berrimus est. Hactenus deaere,ejus effentia & proprie-tatibus &c. Sequitur de veneno & peste aeris.
units.tr: Finally, the variety of regions, according as a region is hot, moist, cold or dry, produces various natures of temperaments and humours. A rough and mountainous region generally produces men who are ungrateful, stupid and inhuman, with large, rough, cruel and stubborn bodies, liable to hot diseases. A hollow region abounding in meadows and great estates produces soft bodies, soft minds, and for the most part putrid and cold diseases. Places constantly troubled by violent and changeable weather, by variations of temperature and by gusts of wind produce bodies of diverse size, robust, minds bold and industrious but unstable, and various diseases and customs, as can be seen in Gaul. Those who live in watery and damp places become stupid, fleshy and fat, impatient of labour, more tame, and subject to phlegmatic diseases. In dry places, on the contrary, people are sharp-witted, prone to anger, and subject to burning fevers. Those who dwell in a region situated at the mouths of rivers, where great rivers enter the vast sea, are seized by various diseases, because the water held back is turned into vapour, whence the air is afterwards fouled and infected. A region is unhealthy which contains great caves, marshes and places infested with foul exhalations. A place not stirred by any force of wind is easily corrupted, but a place that is open to breezes and free is most healthy. Thus far concerning air, its essence and properties, etc. What follows concerns poison and pestilence in the air.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Sanitatis studio omnes teneri non posse, ut navigantes, peregrinantes & castra sequentes, ostendunt contagiosi gravissimiq; morbi, in quos saepe incidunt: Horum praecipuum seminarium est aer malignus, pestilentiq; qualitate infectus, per quem iter affectant, qui necessario cum spiritu attractus, inspiratuq; pulmones primo, & postea cor invadit, cum maxima inflammatione, & carbunculatione cito multos interimens, passimq; per expirationem & inspirationem in vulgus in volans, interdum multas peragrans regiones, frequentius unam, saepe unicum oppidum, vel etiam domum, quamuis frequenti pestiferorum halituum expiratione transpirationeq; tandem accidit, ut aer totius urbis vel oppidi evadat venenatus. Saepe etiam delitescit includiturq; in linteis, lana, indumentis pannis, locisq; obscuris, minimeque patentibus. Est in historiis ex arcula in templo quodam Graciae, saepe thesauri inveniendi a quibusdam perfracta, latens evolasse venenum, totaq; fere Graeciam infecisse. Scribit Bened. Alex. tempore patris sui, tegumentum, in quo venenum fuisse suspicio erat, in abditiore quodam loco fuisse repositum, & post 7, annum expromtum, probeq; ventilatum uni ex servis[?] pro tegmine impositum mortem accelerasse, pluresq; alios infecisse. Unde patefecit venenum extra etiam corpus humanum posse subsistere, contagioneq; ac mutua communi-tate tate contaminare ab ea parte primum, qua fit contactu, vt quotidiana id docent experimenta.
units.tr: Not everyone can keep to a regime of health, as is shown by those who sail, travel abroad, or follow armies, and by the contagious and grievous diseases into which they often fall. The chief seedbed of these is a malignant air infected with a pestilential quality. People who must travel through it breathe it in, and it first attacks the lungs and then the heart, causing a very great inflammation and carbuncles, and quickly kills many. Passing through the population by breathing out and breathing in, it sometimes spreads over many regions, more often over one, and often over a single town or even a single house. Through the frequent breathing out and exhaling of pestilential vapours, the air of a whole city or town at last becomes poisoned. Often, too, the poison lies hidden and is enclosed in linen, wool, clothing, rags, and in dark places that are little open to the air. There is a story of a small chest in a temple in Greece, which some men, seeking treasure, broke open; the hidden poison flew out and infected almost the whole of Greece. Benedictus Alexandrinus writes that in the time of his father a covering, in which poison was suspected, had been put away in a rather remote place, and after seven years was brought out, aired well, and laid as a cover on one of the servants, and that it hastened his death and infected several others. From this he showed that poison can persist even outside the human body, and can spread contagion by mutual contact, first in the part where the contact occurs, as daily experience teaches.

units.la: Quibuscunq; igitur necessario per ejusmodi infectum aerem vlti citroq; est peregrinandum, quia ejusmodi habitacula, quæ à maligni aeris contagio sint libera, habere non possunt, ij, ne in periculum quoddam deveniant, cau sa prius probe diligenter perpendentes, quæ aeri contagium corruptelam inferant, suffitibus, odoramentis maleficatoriis, contra externa ambientis aeris contagium se munire omni studio conabuntur.
units.tr: Therefore, since those who travel to and fro must of necessity pass through such infected air, and cannot have dwellings free from the contagion of malignant air, they should, to avoid falling into some danger, first weigh carefully what kinds of air-contagion bring corruption, and make every effort to protect themselves against the contagion of the surrounding air with fumigations and malodorous perfumes.

units.la: Loquor de peste aeris seu veneno aerio ad diffe rentiam veneni cuius contagium vel seminaria effunduntur ex aqua, terra, igne, & humanis etiam corporibus, humoribus, scilicet in iis ad summum putredinis gradum permutatis, cujusmodi fuit pestis quæ anno 1605. pervadere capit Fran cofurtum, & loca tandem vicina.
units.tr: I speak of the plague of the air, or aerial poison, as distinct from the poison whose contagion or seedbeds pour out from water, earth, fire, and even human bodies, that is, from humours changed in them to the highest degree of putrefaction. Such was the plague that began to invade Frankfurt in the year 1605, and finally the neighbouring places.

units.la: Hinc pestis, aeris, ignis, terra, aqua, & quæ ex humoribus in animantium corporibus corruptis & putrefactis effluit, potest pestis hominum appel lari.
units.tr: Hence the plague of air, fire, earth, and water, and that which flows from humours corrupted and putrefied in the bodies of living creatures, may be called the plague of men.

units.la: Non enim contagium vel seminaria pestis in sola aere ponenda sunt, nec ex humanis tantum corporibus ea effundi arbitrandum est, ut falso quidam opinantur ex arte myrepsica alimoniam magis & turpe lucrum, quam ægri salutem quæ rentes.
units.tr: For the contagion or seedbeds of plague are not to be placed in air alone, nor is it to be thought that they pour out only from human bodies, as some falsely suppose, following the mixer of ointments' art, who seek their own food and base gain rather than the health of the sick.

units.la: Sed hoc mirari subit etiam justissimo titulo Medicinam facilitantes hac pestilentia seminaria confundere, parum referre existimantes, num pestis sit hominis, aerus, aqua vel terra.
units.tr: But it is also surprising that some who rightly claim to make medicine easy confuse these seedbeds of plague, thinking it of little importance whether the plague comes from a man, from air, water, or earth.

units.la: Quidam falsò opinantur pestis contagium ex aere e semper primario effundi. Verum de his & similibus Pseudodoxis in tractatu meo de peste prolixè disserui.
units.tr: Some falsely suppose that the contagion of plague always pours out primarily from the air. But I have discussed these and similar false opinions at length in my treatise on the plague.

units.la: Unum hic meminisse oportet, pestis vocabulum equinocum[?] esse, aerium enim venenum, morbum ab eo illatum, nec non bubonem morbi comites, (a quibus rursus diuersa est febris pestilens) denotat.
units.tr: Here we must remember one thing: the word "pestis" is used in two senses, for it denotes both the aerial poison and the disease caused by it, as well as the bubo, the companion of the disease, from which in turn the pestilential fever differs.

units.la: Est enim pestis proprie seu Pestilentia nun-cupata ab aëre venenato & corrupto, venenosus scilicet vapor in aere conceptus animantium ge-neri perniciosissimus: is inspiratus spiritus cordis primum invadit alteratque, qui amissa temperie à natura imperio emancipati putrere incipiunt, aq; aliena caliditate occupati unà ascenduntur, & cum his ipsa cordis substantia, hinc per universum corpus venenum serpens in digniora viscera facit impetum, quae, quia tantam molestiam fer-re non possunt, in emissaria propria vel corporis habitum venenum protrudunt, unde bubo-nes, carbunculatio, herpes & erysipelata, & haec est origo febris propriae pestilentialis dictae: Sed est & alia ex similitudine pestilentialis dicta, quod scilicet est eiusdem ideae & characteristici, similiaque edit symptomata, perindeque habetur nonnũ-quã le: alij hoc fere distinguuntur, quod in vera pesti-
units.tr: For the plague, properly called pestilence, takes its name from poisoned and corrupted air: a poisonous vapour, conceived in the air, is most deadly to the race of living creatures. When this vapour is breathed in, it first attacks and alters the spirit of the heart. Having lost its temper, and emancipated from the rule of nature, it begins to putrefy, and, seized by the foreign heat, rises up together with the heart's own substance. From there the poison spreads through the whole body and attacks the nobler organs; since they cannot bear so great a burden, they thrust the poison out into the outlets of the body or its surface. From this come buboes, carbuncles, herpes and erysipelas, and this is the origin of the fever called properly pestilential. But there is also another fever called pestilential by resemblance, because it has the same nature and characteristics and produces similar symptoms, and is therefore sometimes so named. Some distinguish these chiefly by this: in true

units.la: Disseré-tia febris pestilen-tis vtræ & nothæ pestilenti necessario sit aliquis bubo, vel carbuncu- lus, (vel etiam papula) isq; latens vel manifestus, semper q; communem causam habeat aerem vene- natum : illa autem ex pravis corruptisq; alimen- tis, putridiq; humoribus in corpore excitari con- sueverit posse enim in nobis excitari, vel potius ge- nerari substantiam venenoproximam, excuiusq; vitæ proprio, experientia & rationibus manife- stum est.
units.tr: The difference of pestilential fever, true and spurious, is that the true pestilential fever necessarily has some bubo, or carbuncle (or even a papule), whether hidden or visible, and always has as its common cause poisoned air. The other, however, is usually produced in the body from bad and corrupt food and putrid humours; for it is clear from experience and reason that a substance akin to poison can be produced, or rather generated, within us, and that it also has its own life.

units.la: Nunc signa differentiarum pestis propo- nenda sunt, quæ à plerisque hodiè negligi sum- macum ægrotorum & attis jactura animad- uerto. Sympathias verò & antipathias myste- rium hic explorandum, quæ videlicet diuina quadam consortii lege conspirent, quæque in- terse dissideant.
units.tr: Now the signs of the differences of plague must be set out, which, I note, are today neglected by most people, to the great loss of the sick and of the art. The sympathies and antipathies are a mystery to be explored here: which of them agree with one another by a certain divine law of association, and which disagree.

units.la: Signa pestis terræ sunt apostemata cum pe- stilentia, difficilis omnis, color cutis lividus: in hac prosunt omnia medicamenta naturam terra participantia, ut caro talpæ, vulpis, lupi felis, &c.
units.tr: The signs of the plague of earth are abscesses with pestilence, every kind of difficulty, and a livid colour of the skin. Against this all medicines that share the nature of earth are helpful, such as the flesh of the mole, fox, wolf, and cat.

units.la: Pestis aeris signa sunt tibiarum hinc inde jactatio, tumores circa humeros, & infra brachia, astma siccum, cephalalgia ingens cum phrenitide: in hac prosunt passeres, merula, gallina, pavones, cornices, corvi.
units.tr: The signs of the plague of air are a jerking of the shins on both sides, swellings about the shoulders and under the arms, dry asthma, and a great headache with phrenitis. Against this sparrows, blackbirds, hens, peacocks, jackdaws, and ravens are helpful.

units.la: Pestis aquæ signa sunt sitis ingens; paucus so- mnus, tumor pedum & signa circa pudenda, potu- re nolunt, pedes, intumescunt, in hac prosunt pi- sces, ranæ, bufones, inprimis verò carnes ciconiæ & anatum, locis affectis applicata. Secretum. Pestis ignis signa sunt, somnus continuus & indefinens calor intensus, humores magnipost [?] aures, situm non habent: in hac venenum extrahendum est per alium & cepas, vel aliud specificum: atq; hic laudatur Xenechdon [?] Theophrasti. Has differentias diligenter expendere decet bonum & fidelem medicum, ex his enim cura instituenda est cum veris prognosticis, per quae medicus in sua arte, testimonio Hippocr. admirabilis censetur.
units.tr: The signs of the plague of water are great thirst, little sleep, swelling of the feet, and signs about the genitals; the patient is unwilling to drink, and the feet swell. Against this fish, frogs, and toads are helpful, and above all the flesh of storks and ducks, applied to the affected places. Secret. The signs of the plague of fire are continuous sleep, unceasing and intense heat, and great humours behind the ears that have no fixed place. Against this the poison must be drawn out by garlic and onions, or some other specific; and here the "Xenechdon" of Theophrastus is praised. A good and faithful physician ought to weigh these differences carefully, for the cure must be undertaken on the basis of them, together with true prognoses; by these the physician is judged admirable in his art, on the testimony of Hippocrates.

units.la: Aerem autem dupliciter immutari, vel in primis qualitatibus, vel in tota substantia, cum vi-delicet Extremam pravitatem malignitatemq; sortitus est, Physicorum documentum est.
units.tr: That air is changed in two ways, either in its primary qualities or in its whole substance, namely when it has received an extreme corruption and malignity, is a teaching of the natural philosophers.

units.la: In peste putrens & corruptus est non calore tantum, sed maligna et venenata etiam qualitate.
units.tr: In plague, the air is putrid and corrupted not only by heat but also by a malignant and poisonous quality.

units.la: Non igitur accidit pestis aeris, nisi aere se-[?]cundum substantiam corrupto.
units.tr: Therefore a plague of air does not occur unless the air has been corrupted in its substance.

units.la: Corrumpitur aer a corporibus coelestibus & terrestribus, ab illis, ut causa remota, ab his, ut propinqua.
units.tr: Air is corrupted by heavenly and earthly bodies: by the former as a remote cause, by the latter as a near cause.

units.la: Ab astris corrumpitur aer 1. Cum fiunt conjunctiones magnae, ut Saturni, Jouis & Martis, sicut anno elapso 1604. in Sagittario. II. Cum plures stellae tam fixae, quam errantes [?] Soli coniunguntur; cumulatur enim & intenditur calor illis locis & populus, ad quos conjunctio spectat. III. Virtus coelestis fortius agens in virtutes patientes terrestres aerem sensibiliter immutat & alterat, vel in naturam & statum ipsi homogeneum, ut cum naturali temporis caliditas mutatur in calidatem vehementem, vel heterogeneum € oppositum, ut siestas mutetur in frigiditatem € humiditatem, lædentem € contra communem naturæ cursum.
units.tr: Air is corrupted by the stars: (1) when great conjunctions occur, such as of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, as in Sagittarius in the past year 1604; (2) when several stars, both fixed and wandering, are conjoined with the Sun, for the heat in those places and among the people to whom the conjunction relates is then increased and intensified; (3) when heavenly power, acting more strongly on earthly passive powers, perceptibly changes and alters the air, either into a nature and state homogeneous with itself, as when the natural warmth of the season is changed into a vehement heat, or into a heterogeneous and opposite one, as when summer is changed into cold and damp, injuring the body and running contrary to the common course of nature.

units.la: Ejusmodi mutationes temporum inquit Hipp. 3.
units.tr: Hippocrates, in the third book of the Aphorisms, speaks of such changes of the seasons.

units.la: aphor. Si magna fuerint, subita & vehementer et pariunt morbos, € quando mortem. subita enim mutatione qualitatum alterarum, vehementer ter impertinentium forsan occurrentium, ut cali-ditatis in æstate, frigiditatis in hieme, mortem in-firmis aliquando accidere, & etiam nunc accidere posse patet, nam mortem, quæ infirmis æstate continget & hieme, potissimum à virtute cœlesti agentes, te naturalem aeris statum supra modum € subito immutante dependere animadversum est, in vere vero € autumno magis à causa inferiori € tempore restri.
units.tr: "If they are great, sudden and violent, they produce diseases and death." For a sudden change of qualities, which are contrary to one another and very violent, such as heat in summer or cold in winter, occurring perhaps unexpectedly, shows that death sometimes comes to the sick; and it is clear that this can still happen today. For the death that comes to the sick in summer and winter depends above all on the heavenly power acting, which changes the natural state of the air beyond measure and suddenly; whereas in spring and autumn it depends more on an inferior cause and on the season.

units.la: Inter causas inferiores, à quibus aer promtiùs corrumpi potest, sunt vapores, halitusque malignì terra quibusdam cauernis et aperturis expirantes, exhalantes, tum etiam sœda hominum € animalium strages, aquarum stagnantium € putri-darum corruptela, tetra, € contagiosa aliaruni rerum putrefactium, ut ex peco: sumus stabulis € cloacis, tum animalibus etiam quibus-dam venenosis.
units.tr: Among the lesser causes that can corrupt the air more readily are vapours and noxious exhalations that breathe out and escape from the earth through certain caverns and openings, also the foul slaughter of humans and animals, the pollution of stagnant and putrid waters, and the foul and contagious decay of other rotting things, such as from dung, stables and sewers, and also from certain poisonous animals.

units.la: Verum locus siue regio, regionis altitudo € bu-militas montium marium, vicinitas, ipsiusq; regio-nis terra hic perpendenda est. Non enim in ö-nt regione, € ubiq; semper, sed caeteris terra cavernis eiusmodi veneno[?]s halitus concludantur, qui eri-tis pentes aquam & aerem illius loci inficiunt, præcipue[?] vero per terra motum exclusi animalia interficiunt & inter ea primum oves pascentes, qui in locis p[?]sinis ubi vapores paulatim erumpunt, continuo quasi cum pastu exhalantem quandam putredinem hauriunt. Testatur Seneca, in terra motu tempore Neronis Imp. gregem sexcentarum ovium esse deletum, unaq; hominem aliaq; animantia contagio huic vicina.
units.tr: But the place or region, the height of the region, the lowness of the mountains and seas, the nearness of places, and the nature of the land itself must be weighed here. For such poisonous vapours are not confined to every region or everywhere at all times, but are shut up in certain caverns of the earth; when they break out, they infect the water and air of that place. Especially when they are shut in and released by an earthquake, they kill animals, and among these first the sheep that graze in low places where the vapours slowly come up, for they continually take in, as it were with their pasture, a certain putrid exhalation. Seneca testifies that in an earthquake in the time of the Emperor Nero a flock of six hundred sheep was destroyed, together with a man and other living creatures close by.

units.la: Idem vero halitus seu vapor intra terrae cavernas repulsus exitu videlicet ei interclusò, infernalis evadit & maxime pestiferus, ad auri pigmenti eminem aluminis & sulphuris specum venaq; detrusus ignescit, qui postea erumpunt subito & cito, quicquid comprehenderit, adurendo corrumpit atq; interficit, a qua etiam maligni a[?]e a quibusdam infernalem eum dictum reperio.
units.tr: The same vapour or breath, when it is driven back into the caverns of the earth, with its outlet blocked, becomes infernal and very deadly, and when it is forced into the veins and caves of gold-pigment, alum and sulphur, it catches fire. Afterwards it bursts out suddenly and quickly, and whatever it seizes it corrupts and destroys by burning. For this reason some call it malignant air, and I find that some have named it infernal.

units.la: A vivis animalibus quoq; aerem infici & corrumpi praeter experientiam nostri huius seculi exemplo sunt duo dracones, tempore Philippi Regis Macedoniae inter duos Armeniae montes, quam diu à multis salubriter tritam ita inficientes, ut transeuntes illico et subito è medio tollerentur. Accersitus à Rege Socrates, ut infectionis huius contagiique causam diceret, jussit aedificium aliquod erigi juxta montes, fecitq; speculum chalybeum planum, ut ad illud ex omni parte montium fieret reflexo & reverberatio. Ex qua radiatura catoptrica apparuerunt in speculo species draconum didu&lis apertisq; faucibus ex adverso se aspicientium, aeris intermedium oris ventrisq; ipsorum halitu maligno vitiantium, quibus postea jussu Regis interem-ptis factum est, ut is locus ex subita transeuntium inte necione nomen non amplius ceperit, memori-amq; prodiderit.
units.tr: That the air is also infected and corrupted by living animals, apart from our own experience, is shown by an example: in the time of Philip, King of Macedon, two dragons between two mountains of Armenia infected the place, so that those who passed through it were at once and suddenly carried off. King Philip summoned Socrates, so that he might tell the cause of this infection and contagion. Socrates ordered a building to be erected near the mountains and made a flat steel mirror, so that the reflection and echo of the mountains came to it from every side. From this catoptric radiation there appeared in the mirror the images of the dragons, with their mouths open and facing one another, polluting the air between their jaws and bellies with their malignant breath. Afterwards, at the King's command, they were killed, and so it came about that the place no longer took its name from the sudden death of those passing through, and handed down a memorial of it.

units.la: Ventos deniq; quosdam peft feros esse neme erit quiinficias iverit. Conflat ventos naturam & qualitates locorum, per que spirant, suscipere & inducere, aeremq;, five salubrem, five insalubrem & corruptum secum deferre, inq;, oppositam sibi plagam locumq; deponere, Exempl: grat. a, aere corrupto & infectoin plaga occidentis vel meri-diei, ventus contagium defert in plagam orientis vel septentrionis. Sed hic latitudines altitudinesq; locorum & cuiusvis perpendi(ffe oportebit. Contagium enim quod per ventos defertur prompti-subsidit in locis sublimioribus & editioribus, quod vero ex stagnantium aquarum, terra, alarumq; rerum putre(centium contagio tetroq; halitu e-manat atq; effunditur, loca vt plurimum in cavis vallibus sita infestare solet.
units.tr: Finally, no one who has looked into the matter will deny that some winds are very harmful. It is established that winds take on and carry the nature and qualities of the places over which they blow, and carry with them air that is either healthful or unhealthful and corrupt, and deposit it in the quarter opposite to them. For example: when the air is corrupted and infected in the western or southern quarter, the wind carries the contagion into the eastern or northern quarter. Here, however, the latitudes and altitudes of places and of any site must be carefully considered. For contagion carried by the winds quickly settles in higher and more elevated places, whereas that which emanates and spreads from the contagion of stagnant waters, earth and decaying things, and from foul breath, usually infests places lying in hollow valleys.

units.la: Iter igitur per publicas strages facientes, pa-ludes stagna, locaq; fetentia & veneno infi&la pratere-ntes, Pomambrus, odoriferis oleis, odoratis sacculis vel trocis maflicandis adversus eius-modi fetentes exhalationes fe debent munire.
units.tr: Therefore, those who travel through public places of slaughter, passing marshes, pools, stinking places and places infected with poison, should protect themselves against such noisome exhalations with pomanders, fragrant oils, scented little bags, or lozenges to be chewed.

units.la: POMAMBRUM.
units.tr: POMANDER.

units.la: Recip. laudani pinguis drachm. vnam fe-mis, styracis calamita crupulos duos, benzoi, storacis liquid. singulorum drachm. vnam ga-riophyriophylorum[?], cinnamomi; nucis moschatæ, macis, santali citrini, Zedoariæ, rosarum rubearum fing. drachm. semis, balsami garyophyllorum scr. semis, terebinthinæ quantum suffi. Cit ad incorporationem,
units.tr: Take: fat laudanum, one and a half drachms; storax, calamite, two scruples; benzoin, liquid storax, each one drachm; cloves; cinnamon; nutmeg; mace; yellow sandalwood; zedoary; red roses, each half a drachm; oil of cloves, half a scruple; turpentine as much as is sufficient. Mix into a paste.

units.la: Ditiores, quique cupiunt fragrantius & carius, addant moschi & ambræ, fing. grana ij. vel iij.
units.tr: Wealthier people, and those who want it more fragrant and costly, may add musk and ambergris, two or three grains each.

units.la: Aliud minus pretiosum pro pauperibus vel tenacibu.
units.tr: Another, less costly, for the poor or the frugal.

units.la: Recip. radic. enulæ, angelicæ, majoranæ, rorismarini, rosarum rub. ruthæ. Saluiæ, garyophyllorum, thymi vel satureiæ, singulorum partes æquales, camphoræ parum, fiat pulvis & incorporetur pro Pomambro.
units.tr: Take: roots of elecampane, angelica, marjoram, rosemary, red roses, rue, sage, cloves, thyme or savory, equal parts; a little camphor. Make a powder and mix it in for a pomander.

units.la: Sacculi fiunt ex rosis, violis, majorana, pulegio, basilicone, thymo, Satureja, radice iridis, calamo aromatico, garyophyllis, lauendula, serpillo, origano, rutha, stechade, coriandro, baccis juniperi, melissa, floribus hyssopi, lauendulæ, saluiæ, rorismarini, & similibus, serico insu-endis.
units.tr: Little bags are made from roses, violets, marjoram, pennyroyal, basil, thyme, savory, root of iris, aromatic calamus, cloves, lavender, wild thyme, oregano, rue, French lavender, coriander, juniper berries, balm, hyssop flowers, lavender, sage, rosemary, and similar things, sewn into silk.

units.la: Ego nullum ingredior iter absq; Zedoaria, garyophyllis, corticibus citri, arantiarum, radi-ce angelicæ, enulæ, valerianæ, vel galangæ, hæc enim & similia ore detenta & masticata venenatos habitus potenter discutiunt & avertunt. Certum enim est simplici veneno simplex medicamentum esse optimum, sed specificum, nam angelicæ in peste aqua improbatur. Possunt etiam prædicta simplisimplicia medicamenta contundi, & in electuaris formam cum melle, vel sirupo conuenienter, vt rosarum acetosi atq; citri, acetosae, scabiosae, cōtinnari. Acetū ex hisquoq, concinnata p[?]stantissima sunt. Sequentes in praeseruatione celebra[?]ssimum est, paratu a quouis facillimum vilique pretio.
units.tr: I never set out on a journey without zedoary, cloves, citron peel, orange peel, root of angelica, elecampane, valerian or galangal. For these and similar things, held in the mouth and chewed, powerfully dispel and turn away poisonous airs. For it is certain that against a simple poison a simple remedy is best, but a specific one is better; thus water of angelica is disapproved in plague. The aforesaid simple remedies can also be pounded and suitably made into an electuary with honey or syrup, such as rose, sorrel, citron, scabious, and the like. Vinegars made from these are also excellent. The following is very famous for prevention, easy for anyone to prepare, and of low cost.

units.la: Recip. baccarum iuniperi, corticibus nigris detractis, quantum lubet: folia rutae, iuglandis, desiij vel plures: Zedoariam, angelicam: quibus omnibus contusis in mortario cum melle electuarium, si [?]ē. Quia enim [?]suadet, et quoties sunt, super sub. Eodem etiam modo vsurpata theriaca cum tridati cum insignes praestant vsus, sed in curatione improbantur. Quia enim magna [?] tenuium ac calida partium, calorem febri-lem augent, quod notandum est: in primo tamen infultu ante febrim concedantur.
units.tr: Take: juniper berries with the black skins removed, as much as you like; rue leaves, walnut leaves, twenty or more; zedoary, angelica. Pound all of these together in a mortar with honey to make an electuary. In the same way, theriac used with trifera gives remarkable service, but in treatment it is disapproved, because, being of very thin and hot parts, it increases feverish heat; this should be noted. Yet at the first onset, before the fever, they may be allowed.

units.la: Consueui quoq; pradistorum simplicium vaginam quandam in crassiorem pulueream redigere, fericoq; infuere s[?] interiori pilei veltiara parti, vbi cerebellum contingit & verticem anne-ctere, non tam vitiati aeris emendandi, & a cerebro repellendi, quam ejusdem corroborandi gratia.
units.tr: I have also been accustomed to reduce some of these simple ingredients to a rather coarse powder, and to sew it into a silk sachet placed inside the hat or cap, on the inner part where it touches the brain and the crown of the head. I do this not so much to correct the foul air and drive it away from the brain as to strengthen the brain itself.

units.la: Olea quoq; & odorifera vnguenta naribus temporibusq; admota vel inuncta, sicut & cardiacam praestant vires, pulsus, manus, Spiritus ab omni contagio-ne feruant immunes.
units.tr: Oils and fragrant ointments applied to the nostrils and temples, or rubbed in, both give cordial strength and keep the pulse, the hands and the spirits free from every contagion.

units.la: Ex Oleis magis probantur, Oleum ex bac-cis juniperi, lauri, femine anisi, fœniculi, cymi-ni, ex hyssopo, thymo, spica, cinnamomo, ga-ryophyllis (hæc duo pretiosissima sunt) nuce mo-schata, mace, succino albo, terebinthinū, &c.
units.tr: Among the oils, these are more approved: oil of juniper berries, laurel, seed of anise, fennel, cumin, hyssop, thyme, spikenard, cinnamon, cloves (these two are most precious), nutmeg, mace, white amber, turpentine, etc.

units.la: Quia vero olea facile diffluunt, præstat in un-guento consistentiam ea redigere, vasculoq; in au-rato vel argenteo inclusa conservare.
units.tr: Since oils easily run off, it is better to bring them to a thicker consistency as an ointment, and keep it enclosed in a gilded or silver vessel.

units.la: Unguentum odoriferum pro delicatioribus.
units.tr: A perfumed ointment for the more delicate.

units.la: Recip. ambræ, moschi, zibetti, singul. granau-i, olei garyoph. vel cinnamomi, &c. guttas ij, cum oleo amygdalarum dulcium fiat unguen-tum.
units.tr: Take ambergris, musk and civet, one grain of each, and two drops of oil of cloves or cinnamon, etc.; make an ointment with sweet almond oil.

units.la: Aliud pretiosissimum.
units.tr: Another, most precious.

units.la: Recip. moschi, gr. vj. ol. garyoph. guttas iij. ambr. gr. ij. zibetti gr. viij. cum oleo e nuce mo-schata expresso ad drachm. unam, f. unguentum,
units.tr: Take six grains of musk, three drops of oil of cloves, two grains of ambergris and eight grains of civet; make one drachm with oil expressed from nutmeg, and form an ointment.

units.la: Aliud. Minus carum, & tamen efficax.
units.tr: Another. Less costly, yet effective.

units.la: Recip. ol. thymi, hyssopi, sing. guttas iij, ol. spicæ gutt. ij. ol. ex nuce moschata expressi drachm. semis vel scrup. duos, f. unguentum.
units.tr: Take three drops each of oil of thyme and oil of hyssop, two drops of oil of spike, and half a drachm or two scruples of oil expressed from nutmeg; make an ointment.

units.la: Qui vero eiusmodi habitacula obtinent, aqua vel plaudum, vel stagnorum rancori, vel etiam limi inquinamentis obuia sunt, & subiecta, ut dent operam, ut domus valuæ sint perflabiles & vento quidem septentrionis, vel orientis, vel aer recti fi-
units.tr: Those who occupy such dwellings, which lie exposed to water, to the stench of pools, or even to the filth of mud, should take care that their houses are well ventilated, open to the north or east wind, or that the air is corrected and purified

units.la: rectificetur & corrigatur accensoigne, sufficienti-giis ex ligno & baccis juniperi, thu e. mastiche.
units.tr: and purified by a lit fire, with sufficient fuel of wood and juniper berries, frankincense and mastic.

units.la: Igne enim contra aerem infectum nihil efficacius; vapores enim absorbet & dissipat. Unde Hippocrates, magnam illam luem Athenis & totum fere Graciæ igne publicis in plateis & computis accenso propulsauit: idem saepe Thaletem Milefium facisse reperiō. Ignes debent construi ex lignis juniperi, abietis, ypreffi vetularum, tamarifci, quernis, fagi-nis & similibus. Ligna refiniferarum arborum omnibus aliis præstant.
units.tr: Nothing is more effective against infected air than fire, for it absorbs and dissipates vapours. Hence Hippocrates drove off that great plague at Athens, and almost all of Greece, by lighting fires in the public squares and streets; I find that Thales of Miletus often did the same. Fires should be built from juniper, fir, cypress, tamarisk, oak, beech and similar woods. The wood of resinous trees surpasses all others.

units.la: Præstat etiam in ipso sanitatis statu præserim literis operam navantibus, singulis horis matutinus os & palatam diligenter aquà pura cum aceti modico vel pura rosacea abluere, vel aceto aquarofarum mixto, vel vino aquà rosarum temperato quod postremum oculis clarificandis optimum est. Frontis denique, temporum nariumque spersio aquâ rosar. vel lauendula, vel etiam aceto rosarum opitimum spiritum fomentum est: & tatum de aere nobis offuso, ac inuitis etiam ad corporis vigorem tutelamque, inspirando dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: It is also advisable, even in a state of health and especially for those labouring at their letters, to wash the mouth and palate diligently every hour, with pure water and a little vinegar, or with rose water, or with vinegar mixed with rose water, or with wine tempered with rose water, which last is best for clearing the eyes. Finally, sprinkling the forehead, temples and nostrils with rose water or lavender water, or even with rose vinegar, is an excellent fomentation of the spirits. Let it suffice to have said this of the air that surrounds us, which is breathed in even by those who are unwilling, for the vigour and protection of the body.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: De cibo, & potu, secundum locum inter Sanitatis prorogandæ præcepta & capita obtinentibus.
units.tr: On food and drink, which hold second place among the precepts and chapters for prolonging health.

units.la: Onstat quotidie aliquid de corporis nostri substantia decedere, viuereq; hominem minè distinon posse, nisi cibo & potu q̄ deflu-xit, reparetur, cibo quidem quicquid solidio-ris & hiccioris suntsubstantiæ, potu vero quic-quid humidioris ac spirituosæ exhaustum est, vt ita absque cibo & potu 7, vel ad longissimū 8. diesvitam protrahere nemo possit. Quod si à corporibus animantium nihil effluereret, sem-perque eadem substantiæ moles perduraret, cibis opus non esset.
units.tr: Every day some part of the substance of our body departs, and a person cannot live unless what has flowed away is restored by food and drink: by food, whatever is of more solid and thicker substance, and by drink, whatever is moister and more spirituous. So no one can prolong life without food and drink for more than seven, or at the very longest eight, days. If nothing flowed out of animate bodies and the same mass of substance always endured, there would be no need of food.

units.la: Est enim cibus squem nutrimentum, & ali-mentum appellant) substantia similis illi, quæ è corporibus defluxit, resarciens atque re-staurans, quod deperiit. Triplicis enim sub-stantiæ nostræ fluor perpetuus cibo & potu re-stauratur.
units.tr: Food (which the Latins call nutrimentum or alimentum) is a substance like that which has flowed out of the bodies, making good and restoring what has perished. For the perpetual loss of our threefold substance is restored by food and drink.

units.la: Iraque in legitimè & salubriter assumendis esculentis & potulentis, habita diligenti ra-tione qualitatis, quantitatis, vtendiqué modi, obseruentur proæmii loco sequentes præce-ptiones.
units.tr: Therefore, in taking food and drink lawfully and healthfully, with careful attention to quality, quantity and manner of use, the following precepts should be observed by way of introduction.

units.la: 1. Esculentorum & poculentorum quanti-tas non debet esse intempestiua, importuna, molesta & indecens, sed mediocris: Tantum enim cibi & potus, inquit Tullius in libr. de se-nest. adhibendum est, vt reficiantur vires non opprimantur. Reficiuntur autem, si edentes & bibetes modum teneant, qui est inter nimi-um & paucum: suffocantur vero & opprimun-tur, si in alterutram partem à mediocritate su-erit aberratum. Vnde Lycurgus Lacædemo-
units.tr: 1. The quantity of food and drink should not be untimely, inopportune, burdensome and unseemly, but moderate. For, as Tully says in his book On Old Age, only so much food and drink should be taken that the strength is restored and not overwhelmed. Strength is restored if those who eat and drink keep to the measure between too much and too little; but they are choked and overwhelmed if they stray from the mean to either side. Hence Lycurgus, when giving laws to the Spartans, ordered that each person be given only as much food as would suffice to keep the body in good health.

units.la: C s niis leges ferens tantum ciborum vnicuiq; di- ftribui iussit, quantum ad bonam corporis va- letudinem tuendam fatis effet.
units.tr: Lycurgus of Lacedaemon, when framing his laws, ordered that each man be given only as much food as would be enough for maintaining good bodily health.

units.la: Galenus in arte parua verè & sapienter dos[?] cet, certam cibi exhibendi mensuram ex natu- rali appetentia & coctione fumendam esse.
units.tr: Galen, in his little work on the art of medicine, rightly and wisely teaches that a fixed measure of food to be taken should be determined from natural appetite and digestion.

units.la: Huc accedit qnod[?] quantitas porrigendi cibi commodissime sumitur à calore magis vel mi- nus concoquente, qui pro varia corporum, humorum, ætatum, temporum, cœlíque natu- ra variat & mutatur. Vnde pro ætatum, tem- peramentorum, temporum & regionum vari- ætate, proq; vniufcuiufq; conditione & natura, cibi affumédi occasio fumédá est: Robustiores enim multum & frequentius comedent obica- loris innati & influentis copiam imbecillores vt senes pauco & frequenti ob calorem elan- guefcentem alimento indigent: Biliosi & ma- cillenti difficilius obesi & pituitosi facilius ine- diam perferunt, illic igitur paltus crebrior: hic rarior vtilior est. Æstate ob calorem influen- tem exiguum paucus cibus, sed potus dilutior offerendus est, hieme liberalius & meracius ob aeris frigida & humidam constitutionem veícendum & bibendum est. Pueri etiam fre- quentius ob copiam caloris innati & influen- tis, iuuenes ob calorisinfluentis acrimoniam dilutius, senes ob calorem imbecillum alantur frequentius. Itaque sanitati optime consulere volentes decentem ciborum mensuram, natu-[?] raeq; conuenientem sibi praescribant, eamque accurate, vel quoad fieri poterit, serulent, sic enim iucunde & salubriter totum vitae cursum abfq; morborum inuasione peracturi, corporis ac animi vires integras sunt conseruaturi.
units.tr: To this may be added that the amount of food to be given is best judged by the heat that digests more or less, which varies and changes according to the different natures of bodies, humours, ages, seasons and climate. Hence the occasion for taking food is to be determined by the variety of ages, constitutions, seasons and regions, and by each person's condition and nature. For the more robust, who have an abundant and strong innate and inflowing heat, will eat much and often; the weaker, such as the old, who have a feeble and waning heat, need little food, taken frequently. The bilious and lean find it harder to put on weight, while the phlegmatic and fat bear hunger more easily; so for the former a more frequent meal is useful, for the latter a rarer one. In summer, because the inflowing heat is slight, little food should be offered, but thinner drink; in winter, because of the cold and damp constitution of the air, one should eat and drink more freely and with undiluted wine. Children are fed more often because of the abundance of their innate and inflowing heat; young people, because of the sharpness of their inflowing heat, should be fed with more diluted food; the old, because their heat is feeble, should be fed more often. Therefore, those who wish to look well to their health should prescribe for themselves a fitting measure of food, suited to their nature, and keep to it carefully, or as closely as possible; for so they will bring the whole course of life to an end pleasantly and healthily, without the onset of disease, and will preserve the strength of body and mind whole.

units.la: Unde qui temperantiam & frugalitatem vitae constituerunt fundamentum, diutius vitam produxere, illustresq; euasere virtute & ingenio.
units.tr: Hence those who have made temperance and frugality of life the foundation have lived longer and become distinguished for virtue and talent.

units.la: Pythagoras Philosophus Samius, a multis escis sibi temperasse fertur, quoniam animo eas incommodare arbitrabatur. Ad vitem quoque non ingrediendum monuit, non ad ipsam scilicet vitem, sed vinolentiam fugiendam praeceptum dirigens. Vinum enim non attigisse aiunt, quin & parcissimi fuisse potus nullumq; obsonium degustasse, crebrius vero exiguo melle victitasse, omninoq; moderatissime vitam produxisse ab optimis autoribus proditum est.
units.tr: Pythagoras, the philosopher of Samos, is said to have abstained from many foods, since he judged that they were harmful to the mind. He also warned against touching wine, not, of course, the vine itself, but directing the precept at the avoiding of drunkenness. The best authors record that they say he did not touch wine, indeed that he drank very sparingly and tasted no delicacy, and that he lived mostly on a little honey, and altogether lived a most moderate life.

units.la: Socrates Philosophus Athenien-sis, parcissimi cibi extitisse & continentissimi victus omnium consensu fertur: famem sambulando obsonare dictitabat.
units.tr: Socrates, the Athenian philosopher, is said by universal agreement to have been the most sparing in food and the most abstemious in diet; he used to say that he seasoned his hunger by walking.

units.la: Plato Philosophus Athenien-sis, a praeceptoris frugalitate non discessit, quod testatur dictum Timothei, qui superiori die apud Platonem coenauerat, musicam tenuemque coenulam dixit, quique coenassent apud Platonem postero eos die bene agere. Mensas Italicas & Syracusanas nas vt opiparas & luxuriosas damnauit: quin morem illum, quo bis die faturum fieri lice- ret,detestatus est. Ficuum fuit amator,vnde φιλόσυκος[?] dictus fuit.
units.tr: Plato, the Athenian philosopher, did not depart from his teacher's frugality, as the saying of Timotheus shows: he had dined the previous day at Plato's, and called it a music-filled and slender little supper, and said that those who had dined at Plato's were doing well the next day. He condemned the Italian and Syracusan tables as lavish and luxurious; indeed he detested the custom by which one might be filled twice a day. He was a lover of figs, whence he was called "fig-lover".

units.la: Ariftotelem huius discipulum non sibi adé moderatum constat, Alexandrinæ procul- dubio illius victoriæ aut Perfici potius luxus contagione imbutum.
units.tr: It is not agreed that Aristotle, the pupil of this man, was so moderate; he was doubtless steeped in the corruption of Alexander's victory, or rather of Persian luxury.

units.la: Epaminondas Thebanorum dux clariffi- mus,sic in vita frugalis erat,vt è vicino ad cœ- nam vocatus, cum obsoniorum & bellariorū summum apparatum inuenisset,è veftigioab- ierit,dicens , Ego te sacrificare non lasciuire putabam,vnde in exercitu ventricofis obefisq; infensus erat,eosq; pellebat. In vestium veró moderatione laborumq; tolerantia clarum eŭ extitisse Plutarchus testis est.
units.tr: Epaminondas, the most famous leader of the Thebans, was so frugal in his life that, when invited to dinner by a neighbour and finding a very great array of delicacies and sweetmeats, he at once left, saying: "I thought you were sacrificing, not indulging yourself." Hence he was hostile to the paunchy and fat in the army, and drove them out. Plutarch bears witness that he was famous for moderation in dress and for endurance of labours.

units.la: Agefilaum illum Magnum Spartanorum Regem,à satietate vinolentiaq; penitus abfti- nuisse Historiæ tradunt. Huic Thefpii per su- um agrum iter cum exercitu facienti, farinam, aniferes, bellaria,libaq; & mellita opera aliafq; omnis generis escas,vina simul generofiffima miserunt. Verum is farina tantum recepta cæ- tera recusauit: tandem veró [precibus?] accipere coactus mancipiis distribuit,[afferens?] ingenuos & fortes ganeæ operibus non indigere.
units.tr: Histories relate that King Agesilaus the Great of the Spartans abstained entirely from satiety and drunkenness. When he was making his way with his army through the territory of the Thespians, they sent him flour, cakes, sweetmeats, honey-cakes and all kinds of other foods, together with the finest wines. He accepted only the flour and refused the rest; at last, when he was compelled to accept them, he distributed them to his servants, saying that free and brave men had no need of the works of the belly.

units.la: Chryfippus Philosophus Asianus Solenfis ad alendum homines nihil præter Cereris mu- nera & aquæ poculum opus esse cum Euripide afferebat.
units.tr: Chrysippus, the Stoic philosopher of Soli in Asia, used to say, with Euripides, that for feeding men nothing is needed beyond the gifts of Ceres and a cup of water.

units.la: Bion Borysthenes sapienter dixit non opor- tere voluptates ab epulis mensisq; proficisci, sed à sobrietate.
units.tr: Crates, that Theban philosopher, reproached Demetrius of Phalerum for sending him bread in a bag and a flask of wine, saying that he had no need of such things where there were springs. He threw all his money into the sea so that he might philosophize more freely.

units.la: Crates Philosophus ille Thebanus Deme- trium Phalereum reprehendit, quod panes in pera, & lagenam vini ad se misisset, dicens iis minimè se indigere vbi essent fontes: pecunias suas omnes abiecit in mare, vt philosophare- tur liberius.
units.tr: Cleomenes, leader of the Lacedaemonians, flourished in the glory of all the other virtues, and he kept a small daily dinner, befitting Spartan thrift. If he had received some elders or guests at a feast, he set a somewhat more generous table, not with the delights of spices or with a heaping of flavours in the seasoned dishes, but only so that the supply was a little more abundant and the wine somewhat sweeter. Gold was not greatly sought, nor was there any other pleasure, for he himself delighted and soothed the minds of his guests enough with his conversation.

units.la: Cleomenes Lacedæmoniorum dux, omni- um aliarum virtutum gloria floruit, cœnandi- que apparatum quotidianum exiguum habuit laconicæ parsimoniæ conuenientem. Quod si seniores quosdam hospitesue conuiuio excē- pisset, paulò lautius mensam struebat, non a- romatum iucunditate, aut saporum coarcer- uatione conditis dapibus, sed tantum vt copia largior paulò & vinum aliquanto esset suaui- us: Aurum non magnoperè expetebatur, nec alia oblectatio aderat vlla, ipse enim oratione animos conuiuarum satis delectabat atque de- mulcebat.
units.tr: Alexander the Macedonian too is said to have been most temperate in his belly and his food. He thought that for breakfast, night marches were the best seasoning, and for dinners, a slender breakfast; hence he removed the cooks from his army. In conducting affairs he was great above all, and sober and watchful, neither drunk nor raving like a Bacchant in the licence of power.

units.la: Alexander quoque ille Macedo ventris ci- biq; temperatissimus fertur, ad prandia enim, nocturna itinera, ad cœnas verò prandiorum tenuitatem optima esse condimenta putabat, vnde coquos ab exercitu suo remouit. In re- bus gerendis cum magnus inprimis fuit, tum verò sobrius & vigilans, non temulentus, nec imperii licentiâ bacchabundus.
units.tr: That Macedonian Alexander too is said to have been most temperate in belly and food: he thought that for breakfasts a night march was the best seasoning, and for dinners a meagre fare of breakfasts; hence he removed the cooks from his army. In conducting affairs he was great above all, and also sober and watchful, not drunk with wine, nor raving like Bacchus through the licence of power.

units.la: Adeò autem exquisitorum cibotum coti-temtot extitit, vtab fe èlohginquo transmissa obsonia elegantissima inter amicos partitetur, nihilque ex iis sibi reliquum faceret. Graues tamen autores tradunt, tum Philippum pa-trem, tum Alexandrem filium vinolentos ex-titisse, multaque per temulentiam crudelitet perpetrasse. Alexandrum ad vina pronum fuisse, & apud Mediam vini fortis bibisse con-gios duos, paulo; post extinctum Plutarchus autor est.
units.tr: Yet he was so fastidious about the choice of food that he would share the most elegant dainties sent from afar among his friends, and would keep nothing of them for himself. Nevertheless, grave authors relate that both his father Philip and his son Alexander were given to wine and committed many cruelties through drunkenness. Plutarch is the authority that Alexander was prone to wine, and that near Media he drank two congii of strong wine, and a little afterwards died.

units.la: Demosthenes Atheniensis Orator aquam
units.tr: Demosthenes the Athenian orator

units.la: bibit, noctes vigilauit, totus curis follicitudi-nibusq; intentus, vnde orationes eius lucerna olere prouerbio iactatur, vitamque egit longè contrariam vitæ Demadis oratoris æqualis fuit. Hic enim scortabatur, ebrietatiac vinolentiæ totus deditus, fingulisq; diebus in concionibus & conciliis distentus discumbebat, plenoque ventre accubabat.
units.tr: He drank water and kept watch through the nights, wholly intent on cares and anxieties; hence the proverb that his orations smell of the lamp. He lived in a way quite opposite to that of Demades the orator, his contemporary. For Demades was a whoremonger, wholly given over to drunkenness and wine-bibbing, and each day, busy in public assemblies and councils, he reclined at table and lay down with a full belly.

units.la: Cato Censorius in amplissima fortuna te-nuissime vixit, ex rapis sua sibi manu iucundis-simum parans obsonium, eoq; vt saluberrimo vescebatur.
units.tr: Cato the Censor lived most frugally in a very splendid fortune, preparing for himself with his own hand the most pleasant relish from turnips, and he ate this as the most wholesome food.

units.la: In Hispaniam nauigans, vnde cum tri-umphorediit, nonaliud bibit vinum quam regimes: mensam amicorum parentem & procreatricem dixit. A puero, laboribus, moderatá viuendi ratione, & ex rei militaris consuetudine bonam valetudinem & constan-tissimum. tissimum nactus est corporis habitum. In exercitu sitiens fere semper bibit aquam. Quod si gravriori tentaretur, aceti hausftu crebriori sitim leuabat & calorem, si vero infirmior sibi videretur pro pristinis viribus recuperandis leuiusculi vini aliquid degustabat, eodemq; pane & vino vsus est, quo sui, Imperator & Consul.
units.tr: When he sailed to Spain, from where he later returned in triumph, he drank nothing but what was prescribed as a remedy. He called the tables of friends the parents and mothers of wine. From boyhood, through labours, a moderate way of living, and the habits of military life, he gained a good and very steady condition of body. In the army, when thirsty, he drank water almost always. If he was troubled by a heavier fever, he eased thirst and heat by drinking vinegar more often; if he felt weaker, to recover his former strength he tasted a little lightish wine. He used the same bread and wine that his soldiers did, as an Imperator and Consul.

units.la: Curius Dentatus Romanorum Imperator frugalitate & felicitate victoriarum clarissimus rapis vixisse[?] fertur. Quare Samnitum legatis aurum ei plurimum offerentibus, respondet, auro illi non opus esse qui talia cænaret, ostendens rapam quam foco torrebat in cibo[?].
units.tr: Curius Dentatus, the Roman Imperator, most famous for his frugality and the success of his victories, is said to have lived on turnips. So when the envoys of the Samnites offered him a great quantity of gold, he replied that he had no need of gold who dined on such things, showing the turnip he was roasting on the hearth as his food.

units.la: Pompeius Virad omnia summa natus, multis felicissimè confectis bellis & victoriis clarus, insignis in victus ratione fuit, de quare hoc tantum commemorasse sufficit quod cum morbo decumbeti, & cibos fastidieti medicus turdum illi apponi iussisset, hunc que venalem non invenirent famuli, quoniam id temporis non ferebat, a quodam indicatum est apud Lucullum posse reperiri, qui eos toto anno in a-viariis educaret: verum Pompeius respondisse fertur, nos igitur sine Luculli luxu viuere non possumus? aliumque cibum facile parabilem sumpsit.
units.tr: Pompey the Great, born to the highest rank, famous for many very successful wars and victories, was remarkable in his manner of living; of this it is enough to mention only that when he lay sick and loathed food, his physician ordered a thrush to be set before him. When his servants could not find one for sale, since it was not the season, someone reported that one could be found at Lucullus's house, where he kept them in aviaries all year round. But Pompey is said to have replied: "So we cannot live without Lucullus's luxury?" and he took another food that was easily got.

units.la: Ciceronem cibi potusq; fuisse temperati-simum nemo opinor ambiger, qui scripta eius evoluerit.
units.tr: I suppose no one who has read through his writings doubts that Cicero was most temperate in food and drink.

units.la: Augustus Cæsar cibo minimo atque vulga-ri usus est, pisces enim minusculos, panem se-cundarium[?] & caseum bubulum manu pres-sam, ficusq; virides maxime expetiisse aiunt. Vini naturâ erat parcissimus, pro potione su-mebat perfusum aqua frigida panem, aut cucu-meris frustum aut lactucæ thyrsum, aut recens acidumue pomum succi vinosioris. Vescebatur quocunque tempore & loco, quod stoma-chus desiderabat. Querentem de inopia & ca-ritate vini populum Romanum seuerissima obiurgauit oratione, utpote satis prouisum à genero suo Agrippa, productis pluribus aquis, ne homines sitirent.
units.tr: They say Augustus Caesar used the very simplest and commonest food: he especially liked small fish, second-grade bread, cow's cheese pressed by hand, and green figs. He was very sparing of wine; for his drink he took bread soaked in cold water, or a piece of cucumber, or a sprig of lettuce, or a fresh or sour apple of a thinner juice. He ate at whatever time and place his stomach desired. When the Roman people complained of the scarcity and dearness of wine, he rebuked them in a very severe speech, saying that it had been amply provided for by his son-in-law Agrippa, who had brought forth many waters so that men should not thirst.

units.la: Agrippa Augusti gener in victu rusticitati potius, quam delitiis fuit propior.
units.tr: Agrippa, Augustus's son-in-law, in his diet inclined more to rustic plainness than to luxury.

units.la: Tiberius Augusti successor integra fuit va-letudine, eaque vsus est toto imperii sui secundi tempore, sine consilio & medicorum adiumento octauum & septuagesimum annum attigit. Annonam macelli quotannis tempe-randam censuit, dato ædilibus negotio, popi-pas ganeasque eousque inhibendi, ut ne operā quidem piftoria venalis sinerent. Et ut parsi-moniā publicam exemplo quoq; corroboraret atque iuuaret, folennibus ipsè coenis pridiana sepeacsemesfa obsonia apposuit, dimidiatūq; aprum, affirmans hæc omnia eadem habere quæ totum, quamuis à viniauiditate pro Tibe-rio Biberium eum dictum reperio.
units.tr: Tiberius, Augustus's successor, had sound health, and he kept it throughout the second period of his reign; without advice or the help of physicians he reached his seventy-eighth year. He decided that the price of meat in the market should be regulated each year, by giving the aediles the task of restraining the pomp and gluttony so far that they did not even allow the cooks' work to be sold. And so that he might strengthen and support public thrift by example, he himself set before his guests at great dinners the leftovers of the previous day and of the day before, and half a boar, asserting that all these things had the same value as the whole. Yet I find that, because of his greed for wine, Tiberius was called "Biberius" (the wine-bibber).

units.la: Marcus ille Crassus Romanorum ditissimus, P. Crassi iurisperiti filius, Licinii Crassi Pontificis nepos, in omni victu frugalis fuit atque modestus. Parua in domo tenui censu vna cum fratribus parce admodum educatus est, viuisq; adhuc parentibus vxores ducentes vnà & domo & mensa simul omnes visos reperio.
units.tr: That famous Marcus Crassus, the richest of the Romans, son of Publius Crassus the jurist and grandson of Licinius Crassus the Pontifex, was frugal and modest in all his food. He was brought up very sparingly in a small house, on a modest income, together with his brothers; and I find that while his parents were still alive, all of them, when they took wives, were seen to live together under one roof and at one table.

units.la: Ad coenas atq; conuiuia homines plerumq; ex media plebe vocare consuesse Crassum historiae prodiderunt. Neminem Romanorum debere esse, dixit, quibusdam de eius liberalitate, con-querentibus, qui parum se possidere arbitretur, cum tantum habeat soli, quod ad victum praebendum abunde sufficiat, dederat enim iis singulis 14. agri iugera.
units.tr: Historians record that Crassus often invited to dinners and banquets men mostly from the common people. When some complained of his generosity, saying that he thought too little of what they possessed, although he had enough land to supply their food in abundance, he replied that no Roman ought to be rich. For he had given each of them fourteen iugera of land.

units.la: Tanta fuit Prisci illius seculi Imperatorum & illustrium virorum temperantia & frugalitas.
units.tr: Such was the temperance and frugality of the Imperators and illustrious men of that ancient age.

units.la: Contra verò, qui intemperantiæ voluptatisq; illecebris & lenociniis diffluxerunt, mi-rè vixerunt, mortemq; præcipitem matura-runt, vel veneno sublati, alioue mortis violentæ genere, vt suffocatione, prolapsu ex equis, scalis[?], transfossione in concursibus nocturnis, (vinum enim in prælia tradit inermem) igne, aquâ, decollatione, strangulatione, & vt pluri-mum morbosâ corporis dispositione, quæ luxum continuum comitatur, vel denique ventrem in amplitudinem pinguissimum & distentissimum adepti.
units.tr: On the other hand, those who dissolved themselves in intemperance and in the allurements and enticements of pleasure lived shamefully, and hastened a headlong death: some were carried off by poison, or by some other violent kind of death, such as suffocation, a fall from horses, from ladders, being pierced through in night skirmishes (for wine delivers a man unarmed into battle), by fire, by water, by beheading, by strangling; and most often they came to a diseased condition of the body, which accompanies continual luxury; or finally they grew into a huge, very fat and bloated belly.

units.la: Dᴱ VITA
units.tr: On Life

units.la: Euergetes 7. Ægyptiorum Rex, ab Alexandrinis dictus Καχιίγέτης ob luxuriam & delicatam victus rationem ventrem ad-ductus ptus est pinguissimum & diftentiffimum: quin & filius huius Alexander, qui matrem regni sociam interfecit. Hi fuere adeo ventricofi, vt vix pedem efferre possent, raroque in conspectum prodirent.
units.tr: Euergetes the Seventh, king of the Egyptians, whom the Alexandrians called Kakergetes [Κακεργέτης] because of his luxury and delicate way of living, grew to have a belly that was enormously large and swollen. So too did his son Alexander, who killed his mother, his partner in the kingdom. They became so pot-bellied that they could scarcely lift a foot, and they rarely showed themselves in public.

units.la: Dionysius Heracleorum Tyrannus ad immodicam corporis molem adoleuit ob intem-peratiffimas voluptates & quotidianam vora-citatem.
units.tr: Dionysius, tyrant of Heraclea, grew to an immense bulk of body from his most intemperate pleasures and daily gluttony.

units.la: Fuit item Pitho Bizantius, Rhetor obefiffimo aqualiculo, pariterque vxor eius, gulæ & vitio & ventris intemperantiæ.
units.tr: There was also Pitho of Byzantium, a rhetorician with a huge paunch, and likewise his wife, both afflicted by gluttony and by intemperance of the belly.

units.la: C. Caligula portentiffimorum ciborum atque epularum fuit autor, omniumque ganeo-forum gulosorumque ingenia fuperaffe dicitur. Pretiosas Margaritas aceto liquefactas absorpsit, panesque ex auto atque etiam obfo-niaappofuit.
units.tr: Gaius Caligula was the author of monstrous dishes and banquets, and he is said to have surpassed the spirit of all the gluttons and gourmands. He swallowed pearls dissolved in vinegar, and he served up bread made of gold and even of game-birds.

units.la: Claudius Cæsar vinum cibosque quocunque tempore appetebat auidissime, conuiuia celebrabat assidua & ampla, nec triclinio ab-fceffit nisi madens & distentus. Erat boletorum cupidissimus. Quare per hanc ei occasionem venenum datum ab Agrippina coniuge: quo facto illa retris venenum alterum sibique ante omnes Neronem dedit.
units.tr: Claudius Caesar craved wine and food with the greatest eagerness at any hour, held frequent and lavish banquets, and never left the dining couch except drunk and stuffed. He was very fond of mushrooms. For this reason poison was given to him on that occasion by his wife Agrippina; after doing so she gave another poison to her own son, and before all others she gave it to herself, to Nero.

units.la: Neroad principatum eue&us vulgaria ci-baria baria recusauit, sordidum enim ei oblatum panem fame etiam stimulante aspernatus est, in tantum dissimilis clarissimis illis Regibus & Ducibus, qui cruentas aquas & cœnolas; panesq; atros & cibarios assumpserunt.
units.tr: Nero, once raised to power, refused the common food: when bread was set before him, he rejected even the coarse bread, though hunger was pressing him. He was thus wholly unlike those famous kings and leaders who drank bloody and muddy water and ate black, coarse bread.

units.la: Vitellius trifariam semper, quandoque etiam quadrifariam epulas dispertiebat, in ientaculà, prandia, cœnas & commessationes, qui- bus vt sufficeret, vomitibus vtebatur assidue, quod etiam Claudium factitasse reperio pinnâ & in os indita. Famosissimam illam verò supra alias Vitellio à fratre datam cœnam quis non miretur, in qua duo millia electissimorum pi- scium, & 7. auium apposita traduntur? Pati- nam Vitellii, cui faciendæ fornax in campis exædificata est non minoris quam ducentis se-stertiis, hoc est, quinque millibus aureorum cō- stitisse proditur, in qua scarorũ iecinora, Phœ- nicopterorum linguæ & murenarum lactes commiscebantur; erat autem Phœnicopterus auis ratissima, & primum M. Apitii mensis cognita: Murenarum lactes etsi in ipso Italico mari frequentes reperirentur, nihilominus ab externis littoribus asportatæ gratiores vide- bantur: à Carpathio enim sq;, fretoq; Hispa- niæ petitæ sunt: Vnde manifestum euadit sor- didissimæ & profusissimæ Vitellium fuisse vi- tæ, cum nouies millies sestertium paucis eum mensibus interuertisse, Tacitus autor sit.
units.tr: Vitellius always divided his feasts into three parts, and sometimes into four: breakfasts, lunches, dinners and drinking-parties. To get through them he constantly used vomiting, which I find that Claudius also practised, with a feather put into his mouth. Who would not marvel at that most famous dinner which his brother gave Vitellius above all others, at which two thousand choice fishes and seven birds are said to have been served? Vitellius's platter, for which a furnace was built in the Campus Martius at a cost of no less than two hundred sesterces (that is, five thousand gold pieces), is said to have held a mixture of the livers of scarus fish, the tongues of flamingos and the milt of moray eels. The flamingo was a very rare bird, and was first known at the time of Marcus Apicius. Although moray milt is common in the Italian sea itself, it was thought more delicious when brought from distant shores; for it was fetched from the Carpathian sea and from the Strait of Spain. From this it is clear that Vitellius's life was most squalid and most extravagant, since Tacitus records that he squandered nine thousand times a thousand sesterces (nouies millies sestertium) in a few months.

units.la: Lucullus, qui primus luxum Romam inBudeo, uexit & auxit, ingentes opes, quas deuictis vnde ftu- duobus potentissimis & maximis RegibusTi- penda i- grane & Mithridate, sibi comparauerat, con- ftius fecu- terere Romam regressus omnino studebat, lilüxuria quod tamen efficere non potuit, seu hortorum concipi spectes amoenissimorum impensam intolera- potest, bilem, seu piscinarum, praetoriorum, aedium & coenationum amoenissimarum structuram, seu deniq; lautissimorum conuiuiorum quoti- dianum apparatum. Vndein prouerbium abi- erunt delitiae Luculli. Vnicuiq; loco coenarum taxata & ordinata erat summa: quod testatur apparata coena illa impendio quinquaginta millium, hoc est, mille & ducentorum quin- quaginta aureorum, tanta celeritate & lautitia, vt Cicero & Pompeius, quibus illa dabatur, obstupescerent.
units.tr: Lucullus, who first brought luxury to Rome and increased it, had gained great wealth by defeating the two most powerful and greatest kings, Tigranes and Mithridates. When he returned to Rome, he was eager above all to spend it, which he could not wholly manage. Whether it was the cost of the most pleasant gardens, which is hard to bear, or of the fishponds, the pavilions, the houses and the most delightful dining-rooms, or finally the daily preparation of the most lavish banquets, the proverb arose: "the pleasures of Lucullus." For each dinner a total cost was fixed and set down. This is shown by that dinner he gave, prepared at a cost of fifty thousand, that is, one thousand two hundred and fifty gold pieces, with such speed and elegance that Cicero and Pompey, to whom it was given, were astonished.

units.la: Apitius Marcus nepotinis helluationibus hunc longè superauit, Hinc coenae Apitianae prouerbii loco circumferuntur. Sexcenties enim sestertium, id est, quindecies centena au- reorum milliain explebili illa ingluuie heilua- tus est: cumq; potuisset adhuc ducentis quin- quaginta millibus vitam lauto victu producere, tamen venenum miser hausit, ne patrimonio tanto fuperefflet, quod iam fe defecturum vide- batur. Plinius aptissimum omnium nepotum gurgitem appellauit. Suidas in luxum & in- usitatos sumtus multas eum argenti myriadas in ventrem absumpsisse autor est. Degebat autem crebrius in Campaniæ vrbe Minturna-rum, vt caricas, quæ illic amplissimæ gignuntur, luxuriosè manderet. Quin tanta erat hominis huius gulæ insania, vt in Lybiam nauigarent ventrem ficubus explendi graria: merces verò sociis comportantibus, cum ad reditum iam omnia spectarent, Apitius sparteis aliquot corbibus ficus bene compactas, in naue comportari iussit, vt & domi, si venter desideraret, earum possit esse copia. Verum exorta subito turbulentissima tempestate, nulla salutis spe affulgente, morte, vt saxum Tantalo, impendente, Apitius, ne vacuo ventre interiret, ficubus probè & ad saturitatem vsq; eum farsit, reliquas in mare proiectis, quibus postea sedatâ tempestate, ægerrimè carere ipsum oportuit.
