Signum ingenii ad omnem luxum mirandi.
units.tr: Marcus Apicius far surpassed him in his extravagant gluttony. From him the "Apician dinners" are passed around as a proverb. For he consumed six hundred million sesterces, that is, fifteen hundred thousand gold pieces, in that insatiable gorging. And although he could still have lived on two hundred and fifty thousand in a sumptuous way, he unhappily drank poison, so that he would not be left with a fortune which he saw was about to run out. Pliny called him the most fitting whirlpool of all the spendthrifts. Suidas reports that he spent many myriads of silver on luxury and unusual expenses, all on his belly. He used to live often in the Campanian town of Minturnae, where he greedily ate the figs which grow there in great abundance. Indeed the madness of this man's gluttony was such that men sailed to Libya to fill his belly with figs. When his merchants brought them, and all were looking forward to the return voyage, Apicius ordered several rush baskets of well-packed figs to be stowed on the ship, so that at home he would have a supply of them if his belly wanted them. But a sudden and most violent storm arose, no hope of safety shone forth, and death hung over them like the stone over Tantalus. Apicius, so as not to die with an empty belly, stuffed himself well with figs up to his fill, and threw the rest into the sea; afterwards, when the storm had calmed, he was forced to go without them, and with great difficulty. This is a sign of a mind to be wondered at for every kind of luxury.

units.la: M. Antonius exquisitissimis quotitidiè e-pulis se saginabat; & per luxum inusitatum debacchabatur, exhausisseq; fertur & impendisse ducenta millia talentum, hoc est, centies & vi-cies millies mille aureos.
units.tr: Mark Antony fattened himself on the most exquisite foods every day, and he raged in unheard-of luxury. He is said to have used up and spent two hundred thousand talents, that is, one hundred and twenty-thousand times a thousand gold pieces.

units.la: Cleopatra Ægypti Regina lautitiam eius omnem apparatusque splendorem fastu meretricio detrectabat, dictitans vna se cœna centies sestertium absumturam. Condicta cœna Regina magnificam alias epularem struem, sed quotidianam posuit. Irridente autem & com-putationem Antonio expostulante, confirmabatin ea fe cœna taxationem confumturam. Quare mensam fecundam inferri iubens, di- stitans totum alium apparatum corollarium vel procemium siltem esse, detractumq; auri-busvnionem aceto mersit, & liquefactum ab-sorpsit.
units.tr: Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, scorned all his elegance and the splendour of his display with a harlot's pride, declaring that she would spend a hundred million sesterces on a single dinner. A dinner was arranged. The queen set out a magnificent banquet, but an ordinary one. When Antony laughed and demanded an account, she insisted that the cost of that dinner would come to the sum she had named. Then, ordering a second course to be brought in, she declared that all the other display was only a kind of preface or prelude. She took out one of her earrings, dropped it into vinegar, and when the pearl had dissolved, swallowed it.

units.la: Singulare & ferè vnicum naturæ opus, ait Plinius, aurib. gerebat Cleopatra, quis que-so nō obstupescat, vno ferculo secundæ mensæ centies sestertium, h.e. ducenta & quinquaginta millia aureorum absumta? Experta hæc cer-tè est, quid in gloria palati saperent margaritæ. Quis dubitet in aulis huiusmodi perditissimo-rum principum multos fuisse, qui se non vi-&tui[?] solum, sed cæteris etiam eorum moribus accommodarent? Quin & nostra memoria in aulis Magnatum inueniuntur non infimum obtinentes locum, gulæ ganeæque deditiffi-mi,nullusque iam feré habetur pluris, quam qui peritissimè censum Domini mergit. Vide-mus nostra ætate priscum illum morem perdi-nacissimè perdurare.
units.tr: "A unique work of nature," says Pliny, "Cleopatra wore in her ears." Who, I ask, would not be astonished that a hundred million sesterces, that is, two hundred and fifty thousand gold pieces, were spent on a single dish of the second course? She certainly proved what pearls are worth in the glory of the palate. Who would doubt that in the courts of such utterly depraved princes there were many who adapted themselves not only to their food but also to their other habits? Indeed, even in our own memory, at the courts of the magnates there are found men holding no low position, most given over to gluttony and gorging. Hardly anyone is now considered more valuable than the one who most skilfully wastes his master's estate. We see in our age that this ancient custom lasts most stubbornly.

units.la: Vina enim hac nostra ætate tam profusè prodiguntur, vt videantur ad perdenda ea ge-niti,ita vt nullam operosiorem lautioremque vitam nostro seculo inueniamus, quam in proè luendis vinis. Apud nos enim sine lege, sine modo bibitur.
units.tr: For wine is squandered so lavishly in our age that it seems born only for destruction, so that we find no more elaborate or more lavish way of life in our century than in pouring out wines. Among us people drink without law and without measure.

units.la: Germanorum bibacitas ante cunctas alias gètes nobilitatur, atq; inter miracula celebra-tur, tur,cum singuli quaternos quartarios vno prā-dio hauriruntur,& hodiè vasa cernutur potoria, quæ plus quam vnam mensuram ciuilem capiant, quibus hospites externos liberalissimè inuitant & proluunt. In conuiuiis enim nostris omnes certamus pro luxus patina & principa-tu. Nam quò quisque exquisitissimorum obso-niorum varia genera, epularumq; varios appa-ratus & lautos dat profusius, eò magis com-mendatur. Dolendum sanè nos eo venisse,vt cibis maximè pereamus. Innumerosissimum illud morborum agmen & satellitium nouum, quod indies gulæ culpâ emergit, quâ plurimū plurimi funeris ante diem intereunt, ad tem-perantiam & vitæ modestiam deberet nos in-citare. Tantum verò abest,vt hoc fiat,vt etiam luxus Luculli, Cœnæ Apitianę,& quadripar-tita Vitellii Epularum, in ientacula, Prandia, Cœnas , & commessationes dimensio maio-rem longè hodie quam olim laudem in Ma-gnatum aulis mereatur,vtq; asoti illi crudi po-stridie rursus ingurgitent, vt cum Cic. de fini-bus loquar,de mensa & conuiuiis auferuntur, pinnaq; in os inditi vomitum proritat, quod à multis hodie factitari more Epicuri de grege porcorum animaduertitur magno sæpe & cor-poris & animi damno. Verum de vomitu mor-bofo & non morboso suo loco.
units.tr: The heavy drinking of the Germans is famous above all other peoples, and is celebrated among wonders: they empty four quartarii at a time in one draught. Today, too, drinking vessels are on show which hold more than one civic measure, and with these they invite and regale foreign guests most generously. For at our banquets we all compete for the first place in extravagance. The more lavishly someone gives the rich variety of the choicest dishes and the sumptuous preparations of feasts, the more he is praised. It is truly to be lamented that we have come to this, that we perish above all by food. That innumerable host of diseases and that new retinue, which daily rises up through the fault of gluttony, and by which very many die well before their time, ought to urge us toward temperance and a modest life. Yet so far is this from happening, that the luxury of Lucullus, the Apician dinners, and Vitellius's fourfold feasts divided into breakfasts, lunches, dinners and drinking-parties, deserve far greater praise today at the courts of the magnates than they did in former times. And those wretched spendthrifts, the next day, gorge themselves again, and, to use Cicero's words from De finibus, they are carried away from the table and the feasts, and a feather put into the mouth provokes vomiting. This is noticed to be practised by many today in the manner of Epicurus's herd of swine, often with great loss to both body and mind. But more on morbid and non-morbid vomiting in its proper place.

units.la: Non tamen hic prætereundum est, voraci-tatis & bibacitatis quoddam vitium à natura quiddam[?] quibusdam innasci,aliis etiam ab ipsa consue-tudine proficisci,cum sepe videamus alios a-liis esse edaciores à tenero,eosq; vitæ processu moderantiores fieri. Sed de externa & intem-perátissima voracitate & ingluvie hic sermo est; Cuiusmodi fuit Milonis Crotoniatæ ath-letæ robustissimi,qui in certamine Olyinpico taurum vivum circumtulisse stadio unius cur-riculi prædicat,ipsumq; postea ictu nudæ dex-træ iugulatum ipso die solum vorasse. Quin & uno cóniótu[?] carnium xx. pondo, totidemq; panum absumere,vini vero choas tres exhau-sse consueuit,teste Arben.lib.10. Verum in prodigioso robore prodigiosa certè minus vi-debitur gula,
units.tr: Yet it must not be passed over here that a disposition to greed and drinking is inborn in some people from nature itself, while in others it arises from habit. We often see some people eat more greedily than others from childhood, and as life goes on these become more moderate. But the present discussion concerns outward and most intemperate greed and gluttony. Such was that of Milo of Croton, the most robust athlete, who is said to have carried a live bull around the stadium of a single course at the Olympic contest, and afterwards to have slaughtered it with one blow of his bare right hand and eaten it entire on the same day. He also used to consume twenty pounds of meat and as much bread at one sitting, and to drain three choes of wine, as Arrian reports in book 10. But in a prodigious strength, gluttony hardly seems prodigious.

units.la: Omnes autem athletas assueuisse plurimo cibo ad corporis vires ampliandas Hippocra-tes etiam & interpres eius Galenus in apho-rifmis non tacuerint. Habitum enim corpo-ris ipsorum periculosum esse confirmant,quo-rum etiam sententiam Hieronymus contra Io-vianum usurpavit. Athletas,inquit Galenus, in exhortatione Medicinæ, nec posse vivere diu nec sanos esse, animasq; eorum in nimio sanguine & adipibus quasi luto involutas ni-hil tenue, nihil cœleste, semperque de carni-bus & ructu, ventris ingluvie cogitare. Suillam itaq; Galenus suadet ut valenter alentem.
units.tr: Hippocrates and his interpreter Galen, in the Aphorisms, did not fail to note that all athletes accustomed themselves to a great quantity of food in order to increase their bodily strength. They affirm that the physical condition of athletes is dangerous, and Jerome, against Jovinian, took up the same opinion. Galen, in his Exhortation to Medicine, says that athletes can neither live long nor be healthy, that their souls are wrapped up in excess blood and fat as if in mud, that they think of nothing fine or heavenly, but always of meat, belching and the gluttony of the belly. Galen therefore advises that those who want to be strong should eat pork.

units.la: Theagenes Thasius athleta[?] taurum solus e-debat.
units.tr: Theagenes of Thasos, an athlete, alone ate a bull.

units.la: Astidamas athleta Milefius, qui terin O-lympia euasit victor, deuorabat, quantum no-vem hominibus aliis satis esset: & plerumque omnia quae apud Ariobarzanem Persarum Regem in conuiuio parata offenderet, solus abiumebat.
units.tr: Astydamas of Miletus, an athlete who won the victory at Olympia, devoured as much as would be enough for nine other men, and whatever he found prepared at the banquet of Ariobarzanes, king of the Persians, he alone would eat up.

units.la: Herodorus Megarensis tibicen & saltator, [?]trium plus minus cubitorum altitudine & pro-ceritate, alias tamen bonis lateribus constans, panis sex choenices, carnis libras 2o. edebat, vi-niq; duas choas, h.e. 12. Sextarios seu congios 2. hauriebat vno conuiuio. Dignahercle gula harpiis rapacibus,
units.tr: Herodorus of Megara, a flute-player and dancer, about three cubits tall and of that height and stature, otherwise sturdy in build, used to eat six choenixes of bread and twenty pounds of meat, and at one banquet drank two choes of wine, that is, twelve sextarii or two congii. Truly a gluttony worthy of the rapacious Harpies!

units.la: Gulosus ille Phago, cujus meminit Flavius Vopiscus, Aureliano Imperatori fuit in deli-tiis, quod vno prandio integrum aprum deuo-raret, veruecem unum, praeterea porcellum & panes 100. exiccaretq; vini orcam, quibus o-mnibus in ventrem exceptis, perconctatus est coquum, quanam hora fit redeundum ad coe-nam. Sed an capacitati ventriculi ejusq; am-plitudini id fit acceptum ferendum, an vero ventriculi infirmitati vel firmitati, quod Bu-daeus voluit, quaeritur? Capacitatem certe & amplitudinem ventriculi cibi & potus majo-rem copiam expetere, firmioremque visceris constitutionem arguere, contra vero angustiā & paruitatem, imbecillitatem, esculentorum-que ac potulentorum parsimoniam praeter jam dicta etiam consuetudo ipsa suadet, plurimum enim eam valere exemplo sunt Parthi, qui quanto plus biberint, tanto plus sitiunt.
units.tr: That gluttonous Phago, whom Flavius Vopiscus mentions, was a favourite of the Emperor Aurelian, because at one meal he devoured a whole wild boar, a ram, a suckling pig and a hundred loaves, and drained a jar of wine. When all this had gone into his belly, he asked the cook at what hour he should return for supper. But is this to be ascribed to the capacity and size of his stomach, or to its weakness or strength, as Budaeus held? Certainly the capacity and size of the stomach seek a greater quantity of food and drink and indicate a stronger constitution of the viscera; on the other hand, a narrow and small stomach, weakness, and a sparing use of food and drink, besides what has been said, custom itself also recommends. For the Parthians are an example of how much custom avails, since the more they drink, the thirstier they become.

units.la: Græci poculis certarunt, præsertim diebus festis agentes inferias, quiq; cæteris præbibebat, promachus dicebatur quasi prepugnans, quatuorq; choas ebibebat. Alexander aliquando conuocatis & amicis & ducibus solenne constituit conuiuium, in quo vinariæ potationis certamen indixit, victori proponens coronam: bibacissimus omnium Promachus quatuor ingurgitans congios palmam retulit, vniusq; talenti coronam accepit, h.e. aureorum sexcentorum. Romani Tricongium Torqua-rum appellarunt à tribus vno impetu congiis exhaustis, & Bicongium à duob.congiis Ciceronis filium.
units.tr: The Greeks competed in drinking cups, especially on festival days when they held funeral feasts. The man who drank before the others was called Promachus, as if "fighting in front." He drank four choes. Once Alexander, having summoned his friends and commanders, arranged a customary banquet, in which he proclaimed a contest of wine-drinking, offering a crown to the winner. Promachus, the most bibulous of all, gulping down four congii, carried off the palm and received a crown worth one talent, that is, six hundred gold pieces. The Romans called Torquatus "Tricongius" from the three congii that he drained in one go, and Cicero's son "Bicongius" from two congii.

units.la: Xenarchus Rhodius Metretes dictus est ab immodica potione.
units.tr: Xenarchus of Rhodes was called "Metretes" from his immoderate drinking.

units.la: Maximinus Patęr amphoram Capitolinam siceabat sæpe in die, teste Capitolino, amphora vero 8. capiebat congios.
units.tr: Maximinus the Elder often drained the Capitoline amphora in a day, according to Capitolinus; the amphora held eight congii.

units.la: Tiberius ignotissimum quendam nobilissi-mi [?] santeposuit, ob epotam in conuiuio, propinante se, vini amphoram: quin & eodem nomine atq; prodigiosa bibendi ostentatione L. Pisonem vrbis curatorem delegit, quòd biduo duabusq; noctibus per potationem continuasset apud ipsum iam Principem.
units.tr: Tiberius placed ahead of a certain quite unknown man of most noble birth, because he had drained a jar of wine at a banquet when he was toasted by Tiberius himself. Indeed, for the same reason, and for this prodigious display of drinking, he appointed Lucius Piso curator of the city, because Piso had kept up his drinking for two days and two nights in the presence of the Emperor himself.

units.la: De quodam vini potatore reperitur Syracusius tandiu potare solitum, donec ab eo cooperta ovain terra fœtum ederent, teste Aristotele & Plin.
units.tr: Of a certain wine-drinker it is recorded that he was a Syracusan who used to drink so long that the eggs, which he had covered over with earth, hatched their young. This is reported by Aristotle and Pliny.

units.la: Bonosus imperator, ut scribit Flavius Vo-piscus, bibit, quantum alius nemo: & si quando legati barbarorum gentium vndecunq; venif-fent, ipsis propinauit, vt eos vino obrueret, sic-que ab ebriis consilia eliciebat.
units.tr: Bonosus the emperor, as Flavius Vopiscus writes, drank more than anyone else. And whenever envoys of barbarian nations arrived from wherever, he plied them with drink to overwhelm them with wine, and so drew out their plans from them while they were drunk.

units.la: Protheas Macedo apud Alexandrum bibacissimus fuit, & valenti corporis robore, tandé tamen vino periit.
units.tr: Protheas the Macedonian was the most bibulous man at Alexander's court, and although he had a strong body, he nevertheless perished from wine in the end.

units.la: Illyrii cubantes cœnabant & bibebant, teste Periandro &c.
units.tr: The Illyrians dined and drank reclining, according to Periander, etc.

units.la: Scythas, Iberos, Thraces, Gallos, Persas & Lydios vinolentiæ deditos fuisse Plato prodidit.
units.tr: Plato has recorded that the Scythians, Iberians, Thracians, Gauls, Persians and Lydians were given over to drunkenness.

units.la: Ariæi conuiuia celebrabant quotidie, & inebriabantur, quare Galli, qui bellum aduersus eos gerebant, id animaduertentes, dolum co-menti sunt. Singuli enim Gallorum duces prandium exquisitissime in tabernaculis suis apparauerunt, cibariisq; adiecerunt herbam quandam medicamentosam quæ aluum deiiciendi & violenter purgandi vim obtineret: vnde quotquot ex iis edissent, ad vnum extin-cti sunt omnes.
units.tr: The Ariaei held banquets every day and got drunk. Therefore the Gauls, who were waging war against them, noticed this and devised a trick. Each of the Gallic leaders prepared a most elaborate lunch in his tent and added to the food a certain medicinal herb that had the power of loosening the bowels and purging violently. Consequently, all who ate of it were killed to a man.

units.la: Præterea & flumina eadem herba infecerant, quæ postea hausta aluum immodice purgarunt. Constat certe multos & inuictos exercitus militum vinolentiâ fuisse prostratos. Germanis nostris olim in bello Gal-lico simile quid accidisse plusquam notu est.
units.tr: Moreover, they had also poisoned the rivers with the same herb, which those who drank it purged excessively. It is certain that many invincible armies have been overthrown by drunkenness. Something similar happened to our Germans in the Gallic war, and this is more than well known.

units.la: Carthaginenses non sinebant in castra vi- num deferri. Contra vero Neftor vel graui in- stante pugna à vini potu non abstinuit, quam etiam gloriam nostri seculi duces & milites quaerunt pertinaciffime, vt adeo in confesso fit, neminiq; dubium, maximam priscæ illius luxuriæ ad nos fluxisse partem, inueniriq; qui eam avidissimè sectentur, non tam in virorum quam foeminarum tribubus. Foeminarum ge- nus vini auidum fuisse & etiamnunc esse, for- fan quispiam dubitet. Dubitare autem desinet Romanorum annales qui euoluerit. Romulo regnum obtinente Egnatius Me- tentinus vxorem, quod vinum e dolio bibisset, interfecit, cujus etiam caedis à Romulo fuit absolutus.
units.tr: The Carthaginians did not allow wine to be brought into their camp. On the other hand, Nestor did not abstain from drinking wine even when a heavy battle was at hand. The commanders and soldiers of our age pursue this same glory most stubbornly, so that it is generally agreed and no one doubts that a great part of that ancient luxury has flowed down to us. And some are found who pursue it most eagerly, not so much among the men as among the women. Whether women have been, and still are, greedy for wine, someone might doubt. But anyone who looks through the annals of the Romans will doubt no longer. In the reign of Romulus, Egnatius Metentinus killed his wife because she had drunk wine from the cask; and he was acquitted of that murder by Romulus himself.

units.la: Est quoq; inter exempla, mulierem à Cneo Domitio dote multatam, quod viro inscio, plus vini hausisse visa effet, quam valetudo ex- posceret.
units.tr: There is also among the examples a woman whom Gnaeus Domitius fined her dowry, because, without her husband's knowledge, she was seen to have drunk more wine than her health required.

units.la: Polybius apud Athenaeum scribit non licu- isse Romanorum foeminis vinum bibere. A- pud Maffilienfes lex quoq; fuit, qua mulieres aquam potare jubebantur hancq; eandem le- gem Mileti sua aetate floruisse Theophraftus autor est.
units.tr: Polybius, in Athenaeus, writes that it was not permitted for Roman women to drink wine. Among the people of Massilia there was also a law by which women were ordered to drink water; and Theophrastus is the authority that this same law flourished at Miletus in his own time.

units.la: Cato censuit osculum foeminis dari debere à propinquis, vt fcil. scirent an vinum olerent. Nostræ certe hodie cautiores sunt & callidio- res quæ à vini haustu aromata commanducant aut anisum, coriandrum, vel fœniculum sac-charo intectum, quo diuerticulo imponunt maritis suis atq; adulteris. Vidi in inferiori Germania potissimum vero Coloniæ tam profusè vina à fœminis prodigi, ut vino plenissimæ velut attonitæ in plateas conciderint, ac publicum propudium exiterint, quo tamen opprobrio cæterarum se absterreri minimè patiuntur, sed potius mori morem gerere pertinaciter pergunt, parìque sæpe ebrietatis vitio conspiciuntur viri & fœminæ, ut merito antiqui proverbii veritas hic locum tenere videatur, Cascus Cascam ducit, Cœcus Cœcam, Ebrius Ebriam. Sed mirum, in tanta Colonia tot esse leges bene viuendi, & inter eas nullam quæ sacram illam vinolentiam puniat, hac enim impunitate efficitur luxus ille quotidie capitalis.
units.tr: Cato judged that women should be kissed by their relatives, namely so that they might know whether they smelled of wine. Our women today are certainly more cautious and cunning: after drinking wine they chew aromatics, or anise, coriander or fennel coated with sugar, and by this trick they deceive their husbands and lovers. I have seen in Lower Germany, and especially at Cologne, women so lavish with wine that, completely full and as if stunned, they have collapsed in the streets and become a public disgrace. Yet they are not at all deterred from this shame by the disgrace of other women, but stubbornly persist in following the custom of dying. Men and women are often seen with the same vice of drunkenness, so that the truth of the old proverb seems to hold its place here: "The dotard leads the dotard, the blind man the blind woman, the drunk the drunk woman." But it is strange that in so great a city there are so many laws for living well, and among them none that punishes that sacred drunkenness; for by this impunity that luxury, which is deadly, is daily increased.

units.la: Apud Persas quidem pignus & fœdus hospitii habebatur, mulieres vxores filiasq; coniuiis adhibere, si quando hospites laute & splendidè excipere vellet, qui etiam mos apud nos durat, verum illis propinare ut vino intemescant, sicut Periander scriptum reliquit, Illyrios in vsu habuisse, & ipsæ postea è coniuiis viros exturbent, ut nostra ætate sæpius contingit, hoc, inquam, an egregium sit & pulcrum, facile quilibet prudens secum reputaverit.
units.tr: Among the Persians indeed a pledge and bond of hospitality was held to be this: that when a host wished to receive his guests lavishly and splendidly, he would bring his wives and daughters to the banquets, a custom that still survives among us. But to ply the guests with drink until they were soaked with wine, as Periander left it written that the Illyrians practised, and afterwards for the women themselves to throw the men out of the banquets, as happens more often in our age: whether this is excellent and fine, anyone who is prudent can easily consider for himself.

units.la: Illyricæ potantes aluum sibi fasciis zonisq; cingunt: primum quidem leuiter & modicè, postea vero cum liberalius bibunt, atĉius validiusq;: quem morem Scythis etiam fuisse in bello, vt diutius & constantius famem tolerarent; graues autores tradiderunt. Nostræ, ne mentem animumq; vinum nimium obtundat atq; etiam adimat, ciborum luxuriæ vnâ vacant, plurisvinolentiam, quàm opes facientes.
units.tr: Illyrians who drink bind their bellies with bands and belts: first lightly and moderately, but afterwards, when they drink more freely, more tightly and more firmly. Serious authors have recorded that the Scythians also had this custom in war, so that they might endure hunger longer and more steadily. Some of our people, so that wine may not dull and even take away the mind and spirit, at the same time abstain from luxury in food, setting more store by drunkenness than by riches.

units.la: Non possum silentio hic præterire memorabilem bibacitatem, quâ apud nos tres mulieres ciuicæ fe nobilitarunt, vno prandio quindecim mensuras vini ciuiles in ventrem absumentes, constante adhuc mente & animo, vt ita in totum dixisse liceat, fœminarum genus vini auidissimum esse.
units.tr: I cannot pass over in silence the remarkable drinking capacity by which three citizen women among us made themselves famous: at a single dinner they consumed fifteen civic measures of wine, and their minds and spirits remained steady throughout. So one may say, in general, that the female sex is the most avid for wine.

units.la: Sed cesso ne insanis illis Bacchis fiam Archilochicus.
units.tr: But I will stop, lest I become an Archilochus against those mad Bacchantes.

units.la: Hactenus de quantitate cibi.
units.tr: So much for the quantity of food.

units.la: Sequitur præceptio II. de tempore cibum fumendi: differ corpus reficiendi: Non vescendum prius quàm appetitus & fames adsit.
units.tr: Follows precept II, on the time for taking food: do not put off refreshing the body. Do not eat until appetite and hunger are present.

units.la: Non intelligo hic famem morbosam, quæ cibum expetit corpore non indigente. Præsente igitur fame cibus non est protrahendus, juxta illud vulgatum: Non toleranda fames nam ventrem humoribus implet;
units.tr: I do not mean here morbid hunger, which craves food when the body has no need of it. So when true hunger is present, food should not be delayed, according to the common saying: Hunger is not to be endured, for it fills the stomach with humours.

units.la: Ventriculus enim vacuus à venis proximis & membris alimentum expetentibus stimulatur & impellitur, vtque eorum desiderio morem gerat, lacessit Oesophagum vnde, alimen-to non subsequente, viciosus eum humoribus impleri necesse est, è vicinis partibus eos ad se allicientem.
units.tr: For the empty stomach, cut off from the nearby veins and limbs that seek nourishment, is stimulated and driven. To satisfy their desire, it provokes the gullet. If food does not follow, the gullet must necessarily fill with harmful humours, drawing them to itself from the neighbouring parts.

units.la: Certissimus igitur & fidus cibi noui ingerendi index est fames seu appetitus edendi. Vnde non approbo, quod quidam certam, opportunam & consuetam in sumendo cibo horam sibi eligunt, persuasum habentes naturā felicius sic coctioni indulgere. Sæpe enim contingit, vt hora illa ordinaria & consueta ventriculum exinanitum cibisq; vacuum, purumq; non reperiat, nullumq; edendi adsit desiderium, vt ita certum edendi tempus præscri-bere non facile ausim, sed potius suadeam, vt qui suae spontis est, edat bibatque quoties & quandocunq; cibum ventriculus efflagitat, id est naturae instinctu.
units.tr: The surest and most trustworthy sign that new food should be taken in is therefore hunger, or the appetite to eat. For this reason I do not approve of those who choose for themselves a fixed, convenient and customary hour for eating, persuaded that nature favours digestion more happily in this way. For it often happens that this ordinary and usual hour finds the stomach not emptied, clean and free of food, and no desire to eat is present. So I would not readily dare to prescribe a fixed time for eating. I would rather advise that a person of sound mind eat and drink as often as, and whenever, the stomach demands food, that is, by the impulse of nature.

units.la: Quapropter reprehensione non immeri-tò digni sunt, qui, sine vllo appetitu, ventricu-lo non postulante, priori alimento nondum plene concocto, nouum cibum ingerunt, studiosè pro-curato iaculo, prandio mox subsequente, non neglectis etiam coenis & commessationibus, quæ sæpe in aulis magnatum, vbi præci-puam hodie merentur laudem, in multam no-ctem protrahuntur nō sine corporis dispendio.
units.tr: Therefore they deserve reproof, and not undeservedly, who, without any appetite, while the stomach is not asking for it, put new food on top of earlier food not yet fully digested. They eagerly procure a bout of eating, with dinner following soon after, and do not neglect suppers and drinking parties, which are often prolonged far into the night in the courts of great men, where they today win especial praise, and not without harm to the body.

units.la: Fieri enim non potest, vt in tanta ingluuie vi-res corporis possint constare integræ. Sunt multi qui, voluptatis tantum gratiâ, vt sibi hoc nomine alios deuincant, fame etiam non fti-mulante, jentant[?] & commessantur, qui postea molestam totius corporis grauedinem sentiunt & lassitudinem. Ego illis edonibus aureum il-lud Gorgiæ Rhetoris Siculi responsum tan-quam saluberrimum sanitatis custodiendæ re-medium imitandum & custodiendum suase-rim: is enim interrogatus, quanam ratione tantum temporis, hoc est, centum & nouem annos salubriter optimeq; vixisset, respondit, nihil voluptatis gratiâ faciendo. Hippocrates conseruationem sanitatis esse dixit, vesci citra satietatem. Galenus nunquam fatur de mensa surrexit, quâ etiam ratione vitam inextremam vsq; produxit senectam. Nunquam igitur sa-turum de mensa surgere, est frugaliter & tem-peranter viuere.
units.tr: For the body's strength cannot remain intact amid such gluttony. There are many who, merely for the sake of pleasure, so as to bind others to themselves by this means, feast and carouse even when hunger does not stimulate them, and afterwards feel a troublesome heaviness and weariness of the whole body. I would advise imitating and keeping as the most wholesome remedy for preserving health that golden answer of Gorgias, the Sicilian rhetorician. When asked by what method he had lived so long, healthily and well, that is, a hundred and nine years, he replied: by doing nothing for the sake of pleasure. Hippocrates said that the preservation of health consists in eating without satiety. Galen never rose from the table full, and by this method too he prolonged his life into extreme old age. Therefore, to rise from the table never sated is to live frugally and temperately.

units.la: Concoctu facilia, liquida, & quæ facilè pu-trefcunt primum sunt ingerenda, citius enim ventriculo elabuntur, nam si extremis epulis sumeretur, praposteroque ordine concoctu difficilia præcederent, concoctionis opus im-pediretur, prohiberetur; ne concoctu facilia è ventriculo exirent: adde quòd liquida, & quæ facilè corrumpuntur, primis mensis fuit[?] offerenda, vt citius è ventriculi officina depel-lantur, autequam putrescant. Unde ciborum varievarietas, mensæq; dubiæ (in quibus dubitatur potissimum, quid sit sumendum) illaudantur, diuersæ enim naturæ cibi eâdem mensâ assum-ti contumaciter à naturæ robore edomantur, magnoq; negotio à ventriculo concoquun-tur, faciliusq; putredinis labem induunt. Unde Homerus unum & simplex alimentum, ut carnem bubulam assam Principibus & duci-bus appositam esse prodidit. Hoc nomine Chrysippus Euripidis sæpe sententiam in ore habebat, qui ad hominum alimentum nihil præter Cereris munera & aquæ poculum o-pus esse contendebat.
units.tr: Foods that are easy to digest, liquid, and those that spoil easily should be eaten first, for they pass more quickly out of the stomach. If they were taken at the end of the feast, and foods hard to digest came first in a reversed order, the work of digestion would be impeded and hindered, and the easily digested foods could not leave the stomach. Add that liquids and foods that corrupt easily should be offered at the first courses, so that they may be driven more quickly from the workshop of the stomach before they putrefy. Hence a variety of foods and doubtful courses, in which it is chiefly unclear what should be taken, are disparaged. Foods of different natures eaten at the same table are stubbornly subdued by the strength of nature, are digested by the stomach with great labour, and more easily take on the taint of putrefaction. Hence Homer reported that a single, simple food, such as roast beef, was set before princes and leaders. For this reason Chrysippus often had on his lips a saying of Euripides, who maintained that for human nourishment nothing is needed beyond the gifts of Ceres and a cup of water.

units.la: Quid tibi deesse potest, modicus si panis & unda, Prandia, vel cœnam si tibi præbet olus.
units.tr: What can be lacking to you, if you have modest bread and water, or if vegetables provide your lunch or supper?

units.la: Quanquam consuetudinis hic ratio haben-da est, tanquam alterius naturæ. Etenim cibi præter consuetudinem plurimum, aut repen-tè ingesti ventriculum aggrauant, & non parū offendunt. Ventriculus enim consuetis gau-dere solet, cibumque familiarem majori cum voluptate amplectitur. Ubi tamen memineris consuetudinem sanitatis tempore esse immu-tandam, si sit praua, cibisq; omnibò[?] mali succi quispiam vesci consueuerit, ut fungis, oleribus quibusdam, & leguminibus. Non tamen dere-pente & subitò immutanda est. Mala enim victus ratio, inquit Hippocrates, modo sit fa-miliaris & assueta, tutior est, quam si repente in aliam, & quidem meliorem fiat transmuta-tio: tio: quin tantam consuetudinis esse vim idem nos monet. 7. & 2. aphorifm. vt, quae longo tempore consueta sunt, licet sint deteriora, minus laedant insuetis: quem locum enarrans Gale-nus consuetudinem videtur aequalle naturae, cibos & potus consuetos dicens naturam facere readuentitiam. Hac consuetudinis efficacia, ingenitaq, solidorum & fimiliarium membrorum temperatura & proprietate, non solius natiui caloris virtute, venena & pharmaca digerat, geriinq; alimentum conuerti exemplo funtas nates, & palumbi hyoscyami pastillis inescati, praeterea coturnices & sturni ex hellebori & cicutae paitu obesi, ac pisces nuce vomica capti, struthio ferrum digerens, pastores pleriq; in Graecia integros hellebori manipulos citra noxam, & Turcae opium deuorantes. Hac len-te primum & moderate acquisita assuetudine puella Indica puellari Venere decora, praefen-tiffimo Napelli veneno enutrita est, à Rege In-dorum Alexandro Magno, dolo, muneri data, cujus scintillantes & serpentum more nictan-tes oculos cum Ariftoteles ipsius praeceptor vidisset, Caue tibi ab hac, inquit, O Alexander, hac nempetibi exitium paratur. Nec judicio Ariftotelis defuit euentus, nam fere omnes proci virginis concubitu intoxicati interie-runt. Sic venena quotidie fere hauft a, praesum-tis tamen remediis, Mitridati à consuetudine fuerunt innoxia adeo, vt captus à Pompejo M. in vinculis veneno se interimere non potuerit. Cicutæ autem succum esse venenum soporiferum, & puluerem quoq; lethalem, Atheniensium indicant supplicia, qui morte condemnatos sorbitione cicutæ interemerunt, quam & Socrates condemnatus in carcere hausit. Ex quibus patere arbitror, quid consuetudo cum ingenita totius substantiæ membrorum similarium proprietate citra etiam natiui, & à corde influentis caloris auxilium valeat. Illa autem proprietas cum sit diuersa in diuersis corporibus & animalibus, accidit, vt hic cafeum, alius vinum natura abhorreat, cotumices & capræ Elleboro, numna-sturni cicuta vescantur. De quare docte ceci-nit Lucretius l.4. & 5.
units.tr: Yet here the rule of custom must be observed, as though it were a second nature. For foods taken in great quantity, or suddenly and contrary to custom, weigh down the stomach and offend it not a little. The stomach is wont to rejoice in what is customary, and embraces familiar food with greater pleasure. Yet you should remember that custom must be changed even in health if it is bad, as when someone has been accustomed to eat foods of wholly bad juice, such as mushrooms, certain herbs and pulses. Yet it must not be changed suddenly or abruptly. For a bad regimen, says Hippocrates, provided it is familiar and habitual, is safer than a sudden change to another, and indeed a better, regimen. The same author warns us of the great power of custom, in Aphorisms 7 and 2: things that have been customary for a long time, although they are worse, harm less those who are unaccustomed to them. Expounding this passage, Galen seems to equate custom with nature, saying that customary foods and drinks make nature a second nature. This efficacy of custom, together with the innate temperament and property of the solid and similar parts of the body, digests poisons and drugs, and converts them into nourishment, not by the power of natural heat alone. Examples: pigeons baited with pastilles of henbane; quails and starlings fattened on a diet of hellebore and hemlock; fish caught with nux vomica; the ostrich digesting iron; most shepherds in Greece eating whole bundles of hellebore without harm; and the Turks devouring opium. By this gentle and moderate acquisition of habit, a girl of India, graced with girlish charm, was nourished on the most potent poison of aconite, and was given as a gift to Alexander the Great, king of the Indians, by treachery. When Aristotle, his teacher, saw her sparkling eyes, which blinked like those of serpents, he said: "Beware of her, O Alexander, for death is being prepared for you through her." Aristotle's judgment was not without its outcome, for nearly all her suitors died poisoned by her embrace. So too poisons taken daily, though remedies were taken beforehand, were so harmless to Mithridates through habit that when he was captured by Pompey the Great and held in chains, he could not kill himself with poison. That hemlock juice is a soporific poison, and its powder lethal, is shown by the executions of the Athenians, who killed condemned men by making them drink hemlock, the draught which Socrates too swallowed in prison when condemned. From these examples I think it is clear what custom can accomplish, together with the innate property of the whole substance of the similar parts of the body, even without the aid of natural heat flowing from the heart. Since this property differs in different bodies and animals, it happens that one animal shuns cheese, another wine by nature; quails and goats feed on hellebore, and starlings on hemlock. On this Lucretius sang learnedly:

units.la: Est vtiq; serpens, hominis quæ tacta saliuis Disperit, ac sese mandendo conficit ipsa, Præterea nobis veratrum est acre venenum, At capris adipes & co'u' nicibus auget. Quippe videre licet pinguescere sæpe cicutâ Barbigeras pecudes, hominis quæ est acre venenum.
units.tr: There is indeed a serpent, which perishes when touched by a man's spittle, and by biting itself destroys itself. Moreover, hellebore is a sharp poison for us, yet it increases the fat of goats and of ... For one may see bearded flocks grow fat on hemlock, which is a sharp poison to man.

units.la: Plura vide apud Plin. l. 10. c. 23. Aristl. l. 1 de hist. plant. Gal. lib. 3. de simplic. med. l. 2. de alim. Theoph. l. 9. de hist. plant c. 18. Arist. in l. de regimine principum. Averrh. in procem. 3. phys.
units.tr: See more in Pliny, book 10, chapter 23; Aristotle, book 1 of the History of Plants; Galen, book 3 of On Simple Medicines, and book 2 of On Foods; Theophrastus, book 9 of the History of Plants, chapter 18; Aristotle in the book on the government of princes; Averroes in the proem to the third book of the Physics.

units.la: De Eudemo illo Chio tradit Theophrastus, quod neque vomitu, neq; alui dejectione E purgari potuerit. Multi aluum habent fequa-cem, pharmacoq; facilè cedentem. Nouiin regio Haffnienfi myropolio quendam, qui, quotiefcunq; volebat, solo pillularum formā- darum olfactu aluum irritabat, vt ita congeni-tæ totius membrorum substantiæ proprietati, quæ in indiuiduis variat, hæ diuersitates indiuiduificæ sint acceptæ fetendæ, ftruthionum[?]-que ventriculum ferrum & numismata, quæ vix igne domari possunt, feruentifq; aquæ calidior ventriculo liquefacere aptus non est, concoquere ob eandem rationem fit cre-dendum.
units.tr: Theophrastus relates of that Chian, Eudemus, that he could be purged neither by vomiting nor by a discharge from the bowels. Many people have a bowel that is sluggish and yields readily to medicine. In an apothecary's shop in Copenhagen I once knew a certain man who, whenever he wished, could stimulate his bowels merely by smelling a particular form of pills. Thus the diversity of individuals, which varies in the innate property of the whole substance of the members, must be accepted as an individualising difference. And it must be believed for the same reason that the ostrich's stomach digests iron and coins, which can scarcely be tamed by fire, and that a stomach hotter than boiling water is not apt to liquefy them.

units.la: Occasio noui cibi ingerendi aliquando humorum cruditate interturbatur.
units.tr: An opportunity to take new food is sometimes disturbed by a raw, crude state of the humours.

units.la: Itaq; qui laborant ex cruditatibus,& calorem ventriculi habent imbecilliorem, minuf-que vigentem, videant, ne affumtione noni ci-bi ventriculi vigorem vel opprimant, planeue prosternant.
units.tr: Therefore those who suffer from crudities, and whose stomach heat is weaker and less vigorous, should take care that taking new food does not overwhelm or utterly prostrate the stomach's strength.

units.la: Verum cum cruditas literarum studiosos plerumq; infestare soleat, iifq; inimica fit, plu-rimumq; morborum radix, teste Cicer. de fato, operæ pretium me hic factum putaui, fi hu-manioribus literis operam dantibus, quorum in gratiam hic potissimum de tuenda sanitate tractatus est conscriptus, de cruditate ejusque causis & signis breuiter & perspicuè aliquid adiicerem.
units.tr: But since crudity is wont to plague students of the humane letters most often, is hostile to them, and is the chief root of diseases, as Cicero, On Fate, bears witness, I thought it worth the effort here to add something briefly and clearly on crudity and its causes, for the benefit of those who devote themselves to the humane letters, for whose sake this treatise on preserving health has been written chiefly.

units.la: Cibus in ventriculo vel plane non alteratur,
units.tr: Food either is not altered at all in the stomach,

units.la: & dicitur ἁπλῶς, id est, simpliciter cruditas, vel alteratur, non tamen sicut oportet, & dicitur cruditas κατὰ τί, id est, secundum quid, vel alteratio depravata. Haec alteratio depravata vel fit tarde, cum videlicet cibi convenientem mutationem nondum susceperunt, & dicitur βραδυπεψία[?], id est, tarda coctio; vel fit corrupte, cum videlicet cibi corrumpuntur, & dici potest chylificatio corrupta: mutatio enim cibi in chylum, id est, eam substantiam quae in sanguinem potest converti, a medicis dicitur chylificatio, sicut chyli in sanguinem conversio sanguificatio.
units.tr: and this is called simply (haplōs) [ἁπλῶς] crudity, that is, crudity in the plain sense; or it is altered, but not as it ought to be, and this is called crudity in some respect (kata ti) [κατὰ τί], that is, in a certain respect, or a depraved alteration. This depraved alteration either happens slowly, when the food has not yet undergone its proper change, and it is called slow digestion (bradypepsia) [βραδυπεψία], that is, slow concoction; or it happens corruptly, when the food is spoiled, and it may be called corrupt chylification. For the change of food into chyle, that is, into the substance which can be converted into blood, is called chylification by physicians, just as the conversion of chyle into blood is called sanguification.

units.la: Causarum magna differentia est. Contra- huntur potissimum ex ciborum copiosa varietate, commessationibus & comportationibus assiduis, unde ventriculus frigidior evadit, vel calidior, nativusque calor imminuitur, vel opprimitur.
units.tr: The causes differ greatly. They are contracted chiefly from a copious variety of foods, from drinking parties and from constant overloading, whence the stomach becomes either colder or hotter than it should be, and the innate heat is diminished or suppressed.

units.la: Signa in genere sunt flatus, ructus, morsus & ventriculi pondus, gravitas, & circa diaphragma compressio.
units.tr: The signs in general are flatulence, belching, gnawing, and a heaviness and weight of the stomach, and a pressure around the diaphragm.

units.la: In specie vero, signa cruditaris sunt excrementa mutata. Si cibi ingesti nullam suscipiunt alterationem, ut cum integri ova iterum deiiciuntur, signum coctionis ablitae est: Sicut imminutae coctionis signum est, cum cibi longo tempore concoquuntur: corruptae denique signum cognoscitur e ructibus tum acidis tum nidorulentis,illi frigiditatis, hi calidi-tatis noxam denunciant.
units.tr: More particularly, the signs of crudity are altered excretions. If the food taken in undergoes no alteration at all, as when whole eggs are passed again, this is a sign of abolished concoction. Diminished concoction is signalled when the food takes a long time to digest. Finally, corrupt concoction is recognised from belching, both sour and fetid; the former announces the harm of coldness, the latter the harm of heat.

units.la: Cruditates vel admittunt coctionem, vel nonadmittunt. Sinon admittunt, (vt in ascite aqua, quæ omnem coctionem respuit) euacu-andæ sunt. Si crudi humores coctionem ad-mittunt, vel quiescunt vel mouentur. Si qui-efcunt[?], conducit primum digerere, postea purgare. Si mouentur, mouentur ad loca con-uenientia vel non conuenientia. Si ad conue-nientia, promouendi sunt & expurgandi. Si ad non conuenientia, h. e. ad partem aliquam principem vel principi cognatam, ilico, negle-cta concoctione, exturbandi sunt, pillulis ex hiera simplici, alephangineis, maftichinis vel similibus.
units.tr: Crudities either admit of concoction or do not. If they do not admit it (as in ascites, where the water rejects all concoction), they must be evacuated. If the crude humours do admit concoction, they either remain still or are moved. If they remain still, it is advisable first to digest and afterwards to purge. If they are moved, they are moved either to suitable places or unsuitable ones. If to suitable places, they must be advanced and purged out. If to unsuitable ones, that is, to some principal part or one akin to a principal part, they must at once be driven out, neglecting concoction, with pills of simple hiera, of aloe with ginger, of mastic, or similar remedies.

units.la: Præfentiffimum remedium est vomitus, qui fi spontaneus non est, irritabitur haustu olei, aquæ & aceti tepidè mixtorum, vel digito oleo intincto ac in fauces immisso: quo facto ventriculus statim roborandus est nuce mo-fchata conditâ, corticibus citri vel arantiarum conditis, Zinzibere vel galanga conditâ, vinò absinthite, vel similibus.
units.tr: The most ready remedy is vomiting. If it does not come on of its own accord, it should be provoked by a draught of oil, water and vinegar mixed lukewarm, or by a finger dipped in oil and put down the throat. Once this is done, the stomach should at once be strengthened with preserved nutmeg, preserved citron or orange peel, preserved ginger or galangal, wine of wormwood, or similar things.

units.la: Qui vero caloris congeniti & nativi im-becillitatem & defectum per fe sentiunt, omni studio conabuntur, substantiam caloris adau-gere, prorato & firmo habentes, omnia quæ calorem innatum adaugere experientia testatur, etiam ventriculi concoctionem promouere. moueré, vt sunt aromata deglutita, fomentationes, cataplasmata, frictiones, inunctiones, exercitia, balnea & id genus temperata fomenta, vt catellus, aut puer, puellaeue senili flaccido-que stomacho accumbens. Sic Dauid septuagenarius cum senili torpore frigeret, nec pellibus coopertus incalesceret, in spectati decoris puellae amplexibus caste condormiuit, vt ejus calore stomachi robur foueretur. Est in experimentis, quosdam jam fere tabe & atrophia consumptos solo lacte ex vegetae & florentis mulieris uberibus sucto esse restitutos, vt ita constet, calorem naturalem & à corde infusum non modo esse spirituum vehiculum, sed praecipuum concoctionis organum, facultatumque animae instrumentum, teste Arist. 2. de anima.
units.tr: Those who feel by themselves the weakness and deficiency of their innate and natural heat should strive with all zeal to increase the substance of their heat, holding as settled and certain that all those things which experience shows increase innate heat also promote the concoction of the stomach: such as swallowed aromatics, fomentations, poultices, rubbings, anointings, exercise, baths, and that kind of gentle warming applications, such as a puppy, or a boy or girl lying beside a chilled and flaccid old stomach. So David, when in his old age he grew cold with senile torpor and could not grow warm even when covered with skins, slept chastely in the embrace of a girl of notable beauty, so that the strength of his stomach might be fostered by her warmth. There is experience that some who were already nearly consumed by wasting and atrophy have been restored by sucking milk alone from the breasts of a vigorous and flourishing woman. Thus it is established that natural heat, infused from the heart, is not only the vehicle of the spirits but also the chief organ of concoction and the instrument of the faculties of the soul, as Aristotle bears witness in the second book of On the Soul.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt generales praeceptiones de cibo & potu:
units.tr: So far these have been general precepts concerning food and drink.

units.la: Sequitur de variis cibi & potus generibus, quae in usum hominum admittuntur, cum primis vero quae nostras mensas subeunt.
units.tr: There follows an account of the various kinds of food and drink which are admitted into human use, and chiefly of those which come to our tables.

units.la: HIC vero me non inanem plane operam sumpsisse arbitrabor, si sequentes prius quaestiones in medicorum & philosophorum Scholis etiamnunc controversas, difficultate, utilitate & jucunditate non carentes discutiendas propositurum, quam varia cibaria degustanda exhibuerim.
units.tr: Here I shall think I have not undertaken the task altogether in vain if, before setting out various foods to be tasted, I propose to discuss the following questions, which are still disputed in the schools of physicians and philosophers, and which are not without difficulty, usefulness and pleasantness.

units.la: Hippocr. 1. Aphor.
units.tr: Hippocrates, Aphorisms book 1.

units.la: 1. An cœna prandio debeat esse liberalior, hoc est, an largius fit cœnandum, quam prandendum?
units.tr: 1. Should supper be more generous than dinner, that is, should one eat more at supper than at dinner?

units.la: 2. Utrum magus lædat valetudinem, vorando an potando modum excedere?
units.tr: 2. Does excess harm health more when it is in eating or in drinking?

units.la: 3. An omnino fit abstinendum à potu interme-dio inter cœnam & prandium tempore?
units.tr: 3. Should one abstain altogether from drinking in the interval between supper and dinner?

units.la: 4. An hieme propterea plus esitandum[?] quàm æstate, quòd ventres sint calidiores?
units.tr: 4. Should one eat more in winter than in summer, because the stomachs are warmer?

units.la: 5. An alimentum sit tantum dicendum quod nutrit?
units.tr: 5. Should only that be called nourishment which nourishes?

units.la: 6. An nutritio sit assimilatio:
units.tr: 6. Is nutrition assimilation?

units.la: 7. An mo:bi[?] communes etiam oriantur à bo:rum[?] malo:um[?] copia & culpa?
units.tr: 7. Do common diseases also arise from an abundance and fault of bad humours?

units.la: 8. An ciborum natura & potestas ad varia gen'ium ac populorum ingenia morefq; aliquid conferat? Ubi & de singulari alimentorum vi.
units.tr: 8. Does the nature and power of foods contribute something to the various talents and customs of peoples and nations? Here also concerning the particular power of foods.

units.la: 9. Morbi quod quibusdam gentibus peculia-riter accidant, an victus[?] ratio in causa fit? & cur quidam repente hominibus nascantur in certis[?] membris?
units.tr: 9. Is the reason for diet a cause in the fact that certain diseases befall certain peoples peculiarly? And why do some suddenly arise in certain limbs of human beings?

units.la: In his quæstionibus ventilandis apud me valebit prisc̈um illud: In sententia permaneto[?], ni alia fit melior. Itaque si quid rectius & verius videro vel audiuero, lubenter id amplectar. Neque enim inconstantis est, repudiatis falsis vera amplecti & defendere. Veritatem vel infirmare vel obscurare, aqui[?] viris sapientibus & doctis temere: dissentire evidentissimum stultitiae & inscitiae argumentu est. Omnia sibi tribuere,reliquis nihil vel parum,superciliosę fatuitatis est. Turpes & ridiculas potius causas & rationes quærere, quam de ignorantia confiteri improbum nec ingenuum est, cum sapientissimi & doctissimi quique multa se ignorare, & multa sibi etiam atque etiam discenda esse,sint confessi,referente Cic.3 Tuscul. Ingenuè suam imbecillitatem indicabat Fallo-pius, cum se ignorare causam, cur argentum viuum gallicam luem sanet,scriberet: Hippocrates solertissimus Medicinæ instaurator, cum popularium & incurabilium morborum causas & curationes explicare nequiret, ipsum Deum quasi ad hominum errores explicandos accire non dubitauit, seu diuina potestate illos cieri modestè confessus est,quem secutus fidelissimus eius interpres Galenus, cum seminis viam admirabilem intueretur, nec causas animaduerteret, diuinum quid in eo latitare scripsit. Aristoteles ignorantiæ se palam accusare non erubuit. Socrate inter Græcos iudicio Apollinis nemo erat sapiens, & tamen assiduè discens plurima fiebat senex, vt de se ipso refert.
units.tr: In examining these questions, that old maxim will hold good with me: one should remain in one's opinion unless another is better. So if I see or hear anything more correct and truer, I shall gladly embrace it. For it is not the mark of an inconstant person to embrace and defend the true after rejecting the false. To weaken or obscure the truth, and rashly to dissent from wise and learned men, is the most evident proof of folly and ignorance. To attribute everything to oneself and nothing, or little, to others is the mark of a supercilious foolishness. It is rather base and ridiculous to seek shameful and absurd causes and reasons than to confess one's ignorance, which is not a mark of an honest and well-bred person, since the wisest and most learned men have confessed that they know many things not, and that they must learn many things again and again, as Cicero reports in the third book of the Tusculan Disputations. Fallopius openly indicated his weakness when he wrote that he did not know the cause why quicksilver cures the French pox. Hippocrates, the most skilful restorer of medicine, when he could not explain the causes and cures of epidemic and incurable diseases, did not hesitate to summon God himself, as it were, to explain human errors; modestly confessing that these things were stirred up by divine power. His most faithful interpreter Galen followed him, and when he looked upon the admirable passage of the seed and did not notice its causes, he wrote that something divine lay hidden in it. Aristotle did not blush to accuse his own ignorance openly. Among the Greeks, by the judgment of Apollo, no one was wiser than Socrates, and yet, as he himself reports, he became an old man while learning constantly many things.

units.la: Verè igitur eruditi & sapienter literati intra hominem consistunt & naturam.
units.tr: Truly, then, those who are learned and wisely lettered keep within the limits of man and nature.

units.la: Verum cum præsidium in nobis sit diuinæ imaginis, hoc est, artificiosus & rationalis igniculus, non plane etiam is nullus putandus est, licet graduum sit diuersitas, adeò vt nimiaduer-
units.tr: But since there is in us a defence of the divine image, that is, the skilful and rational little spark, it should not be thought that it is altogether absent in anyone, even though there is a diversity of degrees, so much so that those who notice more carefully

units.la: {y} sciolos & arrogantes. tant aliquid in acutis & superioribus inferio- res,quod admirari quidem,imitari verò vix va- leant. Quod quidem ego in magni ingenii vi- ris lubens agnosco, naturæq; præstantiam in illis magnifacio , me ad illorum exemplum, quantum per naturæ genium mihi licebit, to- tum conformans. Sapere vltra hominem ex fe nulli concessum esse.
units.tr: {y} the shallow and arrogant. Some of the keener and more eminent men grasp things that the lesser ones can admire but scarcely imitate. This I gladly acknowledge in men of great genius, and I greatly value the excellence of nature in them, shaping myself wholly after their example, as far as the genius of nature shall allow me. To be wise beyond man is granted to no one of himself.

units.la: QVÆSTIO I. An largius fit coenandum quam prandendum? Difting.
units.tr: QUESTION I. Should more be eaten at supper than at lunch? A distinction.

units.la: [?]Etsi & constans opinio est parcius pran- dendum esse quam coenandum,pluraq; s valentiora alimenta in cœna, quam in- prandio esse offerenda,quòd quies, somnus & nox calorem natiuum ad centrum reuocant,unde ad- auctus[?] ad coctionem excitatur,ventriculum & vi- scera corroborat, sicq; coctio m ægis complentur, quæ in vigilia, in quâ calor ad cutis & partes corpo- ris externas eximiâq;[?] reuocatur & influit, unde ex immodicis vigiliis cruditates coacernantur. In somno autem interiora omnia calent magis, vir- tutes spiritusq;, naturales plus vigent quam in per- vigilio, in quo magis dissipantur.
units.tr: Although the common opinion holds that one should eat less at lunch than at supper, and that more and stronger food should be served at supper than at lunch, for rest, sleep and night draw the natural heat back to the centre, and from there it is roused to aid digestion, strengthening the stomach and viscera, so that digestion is completed. In waking, by contrast, the heat is drawn out to the skin and external parts of the body and flows there, so that crudities accumulate from excessive waking. In sleep, however, all the inner parts are warmer, and the vital and natural spirits are more vigorous than when one stays awake, when they are more dissipated.

units.la: Nullus quoq; cibus melius digeri argumento est mentis ingenii, acumen mane longe expedi- tius, quo uno noctuarnam ferculorum cœna concoc- tionem diurnâ longè vegetiorem efficit magis, exassam[?] demonstratur. Huc accedit noßurnus & humidus Luna splendor. Lunæ enim astrum ad cibariorum concoctiones multum conferre nemo negauerit, nisi Lunam è cælo suo deturbans. Est enim putrefactiui[?], id est concoctio ante quaedam putrefactio est. Vilissima certè noßurna sunt digestibiliores, nam & ligna ad Lunæ splendorem cæsa citius putrefiunt.
units.tr: That no food is digested better is shown by the argument from the keenness of the mind, which is far quicker in the morning; this alone shows that a supper of night-time dishes makes digestion much more vigorous than a daytime meal. Add to this the moist light of the moon. No one would deny that the moon contributes much to the digestion of food, unless he tore the moon from its heaven, for it has a putrefactive power, and digestion is a kind of putrefaction. Indeed, the cheapest foods are more digestible at night, for wood cut by moonlight also rots more quickly.

units.la: Hæc sententia vetustissima & salubérrima Heroum vitæ ratione corroboratur. Magis enim opiparè & maiori ferculorum apparatu instruxisse cœnas quàm prandia veteres, testatur apud Homerum Eumæus subulcus, Ulyssi adventi duos mactans porcos, carneq; suilla in veru tosta cænam ei, addito vino optimo, instruens. Gracifru-gi fere semper ientare & prandere solitifunt. Athletæ quoq; & palæstritæ, quamuis variis palæstræ exercitiis valentiori alimento corporis robur sibi comparare omnibus modis studerent, interdum tamen à ferculis variis sibi cauebant, & in prandio solùm panem cophinum <bl>(Krafftbrodt)</bl> edebant: at in cœna liberali genio indulgebant, præcipuè vescentes carne suilla, quia copiosè nutriret.
units.tr: This opinion is supported by the most ancient and most wholesome way of life of the heroes. That the ancients prepared suppers more lavishly, with a greater array of dishes, than lunches is attested in Homer by Eumaeus the swineherd, who, when Ulysses arrived, slaughtered two pigs and, roasting the pork on a spit, served him supper with the finest wine added. The frugal Greeks were almost always in the habit of breakfasting and lunching. Athletes and wrestlers, though they strove by every means to build strength with more nourishing food to suit their varied exercises, nevertheless sometimes kept away from rich dishes and at lunch ate only bread and basket-bread (Krafftbrodt); but at supper they indulged their generous appetite, especially by eating pork, because it nourished abundantly.

units.la: Antoninus Pius Cæsar iam senex, mane antequam salutatores venirent, solo pane sicco robur virium conseruauit, Capitolino teste. Pythagoricos non aliud quàm panem cum melle attico prandere solitos, referri Aristoxenus. Quid? quod Galenus ipse 7. method. copiosè docet, semper studi-
units.tr: Antoninus Pius Caesar, already old, kept up his strength on dry bread alone in the morning, before the greeters came, as Capitolinus testifies. Aristoxenus reports that the Pythagoreans were accustomed to eat nothing but bread with Attic honey at lunch. What of the fact that Galen himself, in the seventh book of his Method, teaches at length that one should always strive

units.la: studendum ut valentius alimentum vesperi exe-bibeamus, quoniam non solum quies & somnus, verum etiam longius tempus naturalem huius concoctionem excipit. Et Corn. Celsus lib. 1.c.3. inquit: plus edere hieme communit, sed minus meracius bibere, prandenti vero utilius esse exi-guum quid, & ipsum siccum sine carne, sine potione fumere: quae certe Celsi sententia plurimum in se habet momenti. Inter intendum enim vel prandendum potando & vorando modum excedens, cum primis vero bibendo, dic amabo te mihi, an non toto illo die sommolentia corripiatur, ac facile obdormiscas (nisi colloquio sominum impediatur,) & ad quaestus negotia obeunda reddat ineptus nemo opinor inficiatur: Et licet somno meridiano vel dimo medelam malo quam experiri, tamen ita capiat vaporibus repletum cum tanta gravedine, ut cyclopas tibi in id migraffe iuret quae alternatim illud feriant ictibus, quae certe corporis lassitudo capitis gravedo nec contingit largius cum antibus (nisi communitatio ex potatione ad mediam vel ultra nocte primo trahantur, & horae publicum iterum sit fargendum colliore sicut non peracta, vaporibus, non difficiles) quae eniam somnum, noctumque, calor, unitio, compulsu vel reliquias meri in venis turgentibus humore, crudos exalibus concoquuntur digerunt: quod per quam norunt potatores.
units.tr: to take the more nourishing food in the evening, since not only rest and sleep but also a longer time receives its natural digestion. And Cornelius Celsus, book 1, chapter 3, says: "In winter it is generally better to eat more but to drink less undiluted wine; for one who lunches, it is more useful to take a little, and that dry, without meat and without drink." Certainly Celsus's view carries great weight. For if you drink and gorge beyond measure at midday or at lunch, especially drinking, tell me, pray, whether you are not seized with drowsiness the whole day and easily doze off (unless conversation prevents it), and whether no one, I think, would deny that you become unfit for business. And although I would rather try a midday or afternoon sleep as a remedy, one is so weighed down by the vapours that he swears Cyclopes had migrated into his head, each hammering it in turn with blows. Such weariness of body and heaviness of head do not come on so much after drinking that is carried on into midnight or beyond, when the public hour must be waited out, not by hangovers. For sleep, night, the heat, and the rest of the wine in the swollen veins digest the crude humours, as drinkers know very well.

units.la: Hi enim ob nocturnam hefternamq; crapulam, corporis capitifq, lassitudinem gravedinemq, per-sentis comsentificentes totum fere diem flerunt somnoq; indulgent, sicq; malo medentur: & recte quidem: præstat enim ad coctionis vsq; complementum dormire, quam crudo ventriculo surgere, h.e. cibo nondum coctò ventriculo egresso. Pro quantitate enim & qualitate alimentorum & celeriùs robore citius aut serius concoquitur. Percipitur autem cibum è ventriculo elapsum esse, (quod fit 6. vel 7. plerumq; horis) si nullis flatus, nulli rustus, nulla gravitas, morsus, tumor inflatione circa ventriculi regionem vatigant: horum signorum vero maior pars si sentiatur, signum est non tantum cibum è ventriculo non egressum, sed ad dimidium etiam vix coctum esse. Tale quibus contingit, id est, qui vel nimium se replerunt, vel parum concoxerunt, vomitus utilis est, inquit Corn.ille[?] Celsus.
units.tr: Hence drinkers, feeling after the night's and the previous day's drunkenness the weariness of body and head and the heaviness, spend almost the whole day in sleep and so cure the evil; and rightly, for it is better to sleep until digestion is complete than to rise with a crude stomach, that is, with food not yet digested that has left the stomach. Digestion is quicker or slower according to the quantity and quality of the food. It is perceived that food has left the stomach (which usually happens after six or seven hours) if no flatulence, belching, heaviness, gnawing, or swelling by inflation troubles the region of the stomach. But if most of these signs are felt, it is a sign that the food has not only failed to leave the stomach but is barely half digested. For those to whom this happens, that is, who have either overfilled themselves or digested poorly, vomiting is useful, says Cornelius Celsus.

units.la: Recentiores quidam, inter quos est clarissimus Philosophus & Medicus Ioh. Pincier, veterum illam prandendi, cœnandiq; rationem videntur impugnare non infirmis rationibus. Primò concedunt, vigilantes extrinsecus plus calere, dormientes verò frigere, eò quòd vigilantes plerumq; corpus exerceant, dormientes non item: calor q; revocetur quidem ad suum principium videlicet cor venasq;, non verò ventriculum, qui caloris principium & subiectum non est; ideoq; meliorem etiam coctionem non fieri in ventriculo noctu affirmant: Exercitio autem calorum nativum non tantum refocillari in nobis & excitari, verum etiam quaquaversum[?] distribui omnibus non est notum, & per motum auctio calore melius absolui collationem probant qui labore corporis victum sibi quaerunt; fabri lignarii, ferrarii, agricolae, qui prandio cœna non contenti ientaculum etiam merendam sibi dari potuerunt. (Sed et Troiani belli tempore poribus Graeci 4. comedendi tempora obseruabant, ut sunt acratissima seu ientaculum, ariflos prandii, befperifma merenda, & dipnos (cœna), quae adeo illis frugi instituebatur, ut in acratismate solo pane macerato vescerentur, sub vesperam instituebatur merenda, post vero occasum solis cœna.) Praeterea cum etiam illis, qui vigilantes ad corporis agitationem & exercitium absinent, idem quod dormientibus euenire solet, sequitur non ideo in somno frigere exteriora, quia homo dormiat, sed quod corpus non exerceatur. Adde quod tunc praecipue est somno indulgendum, cum ventriculus calore maxime indiget: atque nunquam eo magis indiget, quam mox a cibo, cum videlicet adhuc crudus est, ut ita faturi somno se dare quam primum debeant. At vero eos, qui id faciunt, male cibos coquere & liquefacere, documenta sunt, nausea, rustus, inflatio dolorq; ventriculi: & qui pro sono tanquam ventriculi coquentis admiratore tanto operere decertant, duarum horarum spatium inter cœnam somnum interuenire oportere, & debere praecipiunt, quo mandato nihil aliud te statuunt, faciunt, quam (somnum) chylificationis impedi-mentum porius esse quam adiumentum, aliquin confestim à somno dormire iuberent.
units.tr: More recent writers, among whom is the most distinguished philosopher and physician Johann Pincier, seem to attack that old practice of lunching and dining, and not with weak arguments. First, they concede that those who are awake are warmer on the outside and sleepers colder, because the waking mostly exercise the body and sleepers do not. Heat is indeed drawn back to its source, namely the heart and veins, not the stomach, which is neither the source nor the seat of heat; therefore they affirm that digestion is not better in the stomach at night. That the natural heat is not only revived and roused in us by exercise but also spread everywhere is not known to everyone; and those who earn their living by bodily labour, carpenters, smiths, farmers, who are not content with supper and could be given breakfast and an afternoon snack, prove that digestion is completed better by motion, which increases heat. (But even in the time of the Trojan War the Greeks observed four times for eating: the early morning meal, breakfast, lunch, the afternoon snack, and supper. Breakfast was so frugal that they ate only bread soaked in wine; the afternoon snack was taken towards evening, and supper after sunset.) Moreover, since those who are awake but abstain from bodily activity and exercise usually suffer the same as sleepers, it follows that the outer parts are not cold in sleep because a man sleeps, but because the body is not exercised. Add that one should indulge in sleep especially when the stomach most needs warmth; and it never needs it more than soon after eating, while the food is still raw, so that those who have eaten should give themselves to sleep as soon as they can. But that those who do this digest badly and dissolve food poorly is shown by the evidence of nausea, belching, swelling and pain in the stomach. And those who contend so eagerly for sleep, as admirers of the stomach's digestion, instruct that two hours should pass between supper and sleep. By this rule they make sleep more of a hindrance than a help to chylification; otherwise they would order sleep straight after the meal.

units.la: Deinde, quo tempore maior fit resolutio, eo maiori opus est refectione.
units.tr: Further, the greater the dissolution at a given time, the greater the restoration needed.

units.la: A tempore prandii, ob vigilias precedentes & subsequentes, resolutio fit euidentior & maior, quam tempore cœnæ. Ergo in prandio maiori opus est refectione, ante enim prandium & diu à prandio exercitiis se solent homines oblectare.
units.tr: At lunchtime, because of the waking before and after it, the dissolution is more evident and greater than at supper. Therefore a greater restoration is needed at lunch; for people usually take their pleasure in exercise before lunch and for a long time after it.

units.la: Ad extremum experientiâ, se muniunt, quæ testantur vigiliam concoctionem maturare, vigilantes enim plus cibi 8. horarum spatio conficere, & 15. vel 16. horis dormientes: adducitur quoque autoritas Plinii, qui pernigilio cibos præcipuè vinci ait. Et Hippocr. 6. Epid. vigiliam homines reddere edaces afferentis, quod motu, quo viuntur vigilantes excitetur calor & augeatur. In hac controuersia quid statuendum? Ante omnia hic quemlibet nosse corporis sui naturam oportet: mihi perinde est, sive largius cœnem sive parcius, modo bene cœnem, hoc est, citra virium corporis iacturam: prout plura pauciorumue [?] alimenta in prandio vel cœna, sive domi sim mea, sive aliena, offerantur, ita & esto, nunc in prandio largius, nunc in cœna, pro appetitu desiderio.
units.tr: Finally, they rely on experience, which testifies that waking hastens digestion: those awake digest more food in eight hours than sleepers do in fifteen or sixteen. The authority of Pliny is also cited, who says that food is overcome especially by wakefulness. And Hippocrates, in Epidemics 6, says that wakefulness makes men voracious, because the motion in which the waking are engaged stirs and increases the heat. What is to be decided in this controversy? Above all, each man must know the nature of his own body. For me it makes no difference whether I eat more at supper or less, provided I eat well, that is, without loss of bodily strength. As more or fewer, or stronger, foods are set before me at lunch or at supper, whether I am at home or elsewhere, so let it be: now more at lunch, now at supper, according to appetite and desire.

units.la: Ego vitius rationem eam esse optimam existimarem, quâ nec plura, nec pauciora, nec valentiora alimenta in prandio apponerentur, quàm cœna, ut ubiq; æquabilitas mereretur laudem, quæ sicut in omni vita pulchra [?] est, ita esset hic maxime. Quorsum enim quasi [?] prodest, exquisito se saginare prandio, in cœna vero ieiunare,
units.tr: I would judge the best rule to be one that sets before a person neither more, nor fewer, nor stronger foods at dinner than at supper, so that evenness everywhere deserves praise. As it is beautiful in all of life, so it is especially so here. For what good is it to stuff oneself with choice food at dinner and then fast at supper, or to sup sparingly and then at the next day's dinner devour black bread with yesterday's broth?

units.la: velexquifi è cœnare, & postero prandio atrum, ex hesterno iure deuo·are panem? Verum uberius cœnandum esse sanis & amorbo conualescentibus veteres medici,palestrita gymnaste acpancratia- ste summopere approbârunt, (nisi à puero alia edendi consuetudo obstiterit) frugalius vero prandendum. Valetudinarii ue ò,quiq, ventriculo suni infirmo, cerebrumq, habent frigidius humi- diusq, liberalius prandere quam cœnare expedit: ex la ga enim illis cœna vapores sursum elevati cerebrum imbrium instar humectant, qui postea suffusiones aliaq, capitis symptomata proriant.
units.tr: The ancient physicians, and the trainers, gymnasts and pancratiasts, have strongly approved of eating more fully at supper for the healthy and for those recovering from illness, unless a different habit of eating from boyhood stands in the way, and of eating more frugally at dinner. Invalids, however, whose stomach is weak by nature and whose brain is cold and moist, find it more advantageous to dine more generously than to sup. For after a large supper, vapours rising upward moisten the brain like rain, and these afterwards bring on suffusions and other symptoms of the head.

units.la: Valetudinariorum enim longe alia est ratio quam sanorum. Quibusdam enim venter est imbecillis & frigidus adeo, ut copiam cibũ nõn digerere non possit,id quod postero die ventriculi cibariorum odorem eructans, & hypochondria flatu turgentia indicant: quibusdam ob venarum sin visceribus obstructionem alimentum per corpus non distribuitur, excrementaq, cibi humida & cruda per alvum deiciuntur, unde atrophia & absumptio totius: illis diu ob humorum crudita- tem dormire, ac corpus straguli repore fouere & exercere, plus meri bibere, parciusq, eo die cœnare suadet Hipp.l. de salubri diaet.in sin. Hos panem bene in furno tostum ac vino intinctum comedere, vinumq, bene temperatum bibere, ac semel tantum comedere, vel vino tantum cibariorum genere vesci, & aчbo quiescere iubet id. m. Quibus vero semel, bis aut serebrum in die, parum vel plus cibi esseofferendum,id valetudinis natura, anni tempus, ætas,edendi assuetudo,viresq; perito Medico facilè indicabunt. Antiochus Medicus Ascalonita ea ratione victus in senio suo usus est, ut sensibus illæsis membrisq; omnibus integris ad extremum vsq; vitæ duranerit. Plus quam octogenarius tr[?] in die comedebat, nec tamen desidem domi vitam agens, sed quotidie in forum ad civium concilium, & ad visendos ægros, ad trium stadiorum iter pedes conficiens: & si qua longius erat progrediendum, in sella deferebatur, aut vehiculo vehebatur postea, deinde prius aluo[?], in aliquo fori loco, remotis arbitris circa horam diei tertiam vel quartam, panem cum melle Attico esitabat[?]. Deinde aliquid legens ipse, aut cum aliis de rebus gravioribus communicans, vsq; ad horam diei sextam in foro perseverabat: deinde in balneo publico frictione & exercitiis senili suæ ætati opportunis curatus domi mediocriter prandebat, primum his assumptis quæ alvum laxarent, posthæc piscibus, maximè saxatilibus vel in alto mari degentibus, vescebatur, at in cœna piscibus abstinuit, aliquid boni succi, quod non facile putresceret, ut alicam ex mulso, auemq; iure simplici coctam edebat, merumq; bibebat.
units.tr: The case of invalids is indeed quite different from that of the healthy. For some have a stomach so feeble and cold that it cannot digest a large amount of food, as the belching of food-odours the next day and the swelling of the hypochondria with wind show. For others, owing to an obstruction of the veins in the viscera, food is not distributed through the body, and the humid and raw excrements of the food are passed through the bowels, whence comes atrophy and wasting of the whole body. Hippocrates, in his book On the Healthful Diet, at the end, advises the former to sleep much on account of the rawness of their humours, to warm and exercise the body by lying still, to drink more unmixed wine, and to sup more sparingly that day. He bids the latter to eat bread well toasted in the oven and soaked in wine, to drink well-tempered wine, and to eat only once, or to eat only one kind of food with wine, and to rest in bed. Those who must eat once, twice or three times a day should be given a little or a larger amount of food; a skilled physician will readily judge this from the nature of the health, the time of year, age, habit of eating and strength. Antiochus the physician of Ascalon, by such a regimen of diet, kept in old age his senses unimpaired and all his limbs whole, and lasted to the end of life. Though more than eighty, he ate three times a day. Yet he did not live an idle life at home, but every day went on foot to the forum, to the assembly of citizens and to visit the sick, covering a walk of three stadia. If he had to go farther, he was carried in a chair or conveyed in a carriage. Afterwards, first sitting somewhere in the forum, with observers removed, about the third or fourth hour of the day, he ate bread with Attic honey. Then, reading something himself or discussing weightier matters with others, he remained in the forum until the sixth hour of the day. Then, cared for in the public bath by rubbing and by exercises suited to his old age, he dined moderately at home. At dinner he first took those things which loosen the bowels, and afterwards ate fish, especially rock-fish or those living in the deep sea.
