But at supper he abstained from fish, and ate something of good juice that would not easily putrefy, such as gruel made of mulsum and a bird boiled in plain broth, and he drank unmixed wine.

units.la: Telephus Grammaticus Antiocho ætate provectior natus 100. annos, diebus quibus non lavabatur, tertiam circa diei horam cum exigua fricatione oleo inunctus, mox mel optimum crudum aliceaqua coctapermixtum edebat, quo solo proientaculo fuit contentus: prandebat hora 7. aut paulo citius primum oleribus, deinde piscibus aut auibus comestis: vesperi pane tantum vino diluto madidum edebat, vinum, senilis ataiis neclar bibebat. Hæc de horæ fenū victu Gal. l. 5. falubr. &c.
units.tr: Telephus the grammarian, born older than Antiochus, lived to 100 years. On days when he did not bathe, about the third hour of the day, after a light rubbing with oil, he ate excellent raw honey mixed with boiled water, and was content with this alone as breakfast. He dined at the seventh hour, or a little earlier, first on vegetables, then on fish or birds. In the evening he ate only bread soaked in diluted wine, and drank wine, which is nectar to old age. Galen, in the fifth book of On Healthful Diet, etc., reports these things about the diet of the aged.

units.la: De calore in somno & nocte per antiperastasin ad suum fontem & principium confugiente videl.
units.tr: On heat in sleep and at night, retreating by antiperistasis to its source and origin, namely

units.la: cor venasq;, non ventriculum, expeditiorem q; pro- pterea fieri in venis concoctionem nocte & in somno quamvis die, assentior interim tamen calor ad centrum suum repulsi portionem etiam ven- tricmlo per venas & arterias impertiri negari non potest, & per consequens calorem ventriculi robur siorem euadere. Vide quæst. 4.
units.tr: I assent that concoction in the heart and veins, not in the stomach, is therefore made quicker in the veins at night and in sleep than by day. Meanwhile, however, it cannot be denied that the heat driven back to its centre imparts a portion also to the stomach through the veins and arteries, and consequently the heat of the stomach becomes stronger. See question 4.

units.la: Nocte autem cibos & alimenta melius & vegetius digeri, eò quòd meius ingenio, vis mane sit vetior & acutior, non est de omnibus universa- liter verum. Mihi quoties à cœna edulis abstinere omnino, id fere semper contingit. Mulis meis amici sima Lucubratio est: non aurora. Non à me dif- sentiunt, quibus lucubratoria sunt lectiscula.
units.tr: That food is digested better and more vigorously at night, because the mind is sharper and more alert in the morning, is not universally true. For me, whenever I abstain entirely from supper, this almost always happens. Late-night study is most agreeable to my friends, not the dawn. Those for whom reading-couches are made do not disagree with me.

units.la: QUÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: Vtrum magis sit noxium, potando an vorando excedere modum?
units.tr: Whether it is more harmful to exceed the measure in drinking or in eating?

units.la: Vi potus intemperantiam nocentio- rem existimant quàm cibi, sequenti- busq; astruunt rationibus: I. quòd po- tus Ventriculum omnes confestim penetret, subeatq; crudus & plane incoctus, unde sanguini infertur noxa. II. quod neruos tentet & cerebrum mentemque perturbet. Verum potum citius meatus corporis penetrare quam cibum facile datur, interim tamen non sequitur, plane incoctum & crudum eum permeare, dum enim e ventriculo per venas transfit, alterari eum aliqua ex parte, (licet non perfecte) negari non potest: idque ostendunt color, odor, qui in celeri etiam & frequenti eius emissione bi-bacibus visitatissima, deprehenduntur longè diuersi, quam in materia ipsa potulenta, cum primum ingurgitatur. Adde quod plus laffitu-dinis, gravedinis, incommodiq; persentiscunt[?], qui nimia se ciborum copia vel semel inferse-runt, quàm qui dies etiam continuos vinum cerevisiamque plenis buccis absque vlla etiam molestia in se ingurgitant, propterea quod liquida citius descendunt, penetrant, & in vesica collecta excernuntur, solida verò & cibaria tardius & secedunt, & digeruntur, & nutriunt, ut ita longè securius sit grauari potu quàm cibis.
units.tr: Some think that intemperance in drink is more harmful than intemperance in food, and they support this with the following reasons: (1) drink passes straight through the stomach and reaches the blood raw and quite undigested, whence harm comes to the blood; (2) it attacks the nerves and disturbs the brain and mind. It is true that drink passes through the body's channels more quickly than food, but it does not follow that it passes through raw and wholly undigested. While it passes from the stomach through the veins, it cannot be denied that it is altered in some part, though not perfectly. Colour and smell show this: in the quick and frequent discharge of drink in the most frequented drinking places, they are found to be very different from the liquid as soon as it is swallowed. Add that those who have once crammed themselves with an excessive quantity of food feel more weariness, heaviness and discomfort than those who for days on end swallow wine and beer in full mouthfuls without any trouble at all. This is because liquids go down more quickly, penetrate, and collect in the bladder to be excreted, whereas solids and food pass more slowly, are digested, and nourish. So it is much safer to be burdened by drink than by food.

units.la: Potum autem quod quidam nutrire negant, mirari subit. Siquidem ipsius Hippocratis iudicio & autoritate facilè conuincuntur.
units.tr: It is strange, however, that some deny that drink nourishes. It is easily refuted by the judgment and authority of Hippocrates himself.

units.la: Facilius enim est impleri cibo quam potu, inquit aph. ii. sect. 2. Galenus hoc explicans, humida, etsi non nutriunt ut solidiora, superare tamen ait nutriendi celeritate. Quod iterum confirmat Hipp. l. de alimẽt. quicunque veloci appositione indigent , his humidum ad reficiendas vires optimum medicamen , qui-cunq; vero adhuc velociori opus habet, rectif-fimè reficiuntur per olfactum. Quibus autem tardior appositio est necessaria, solido alimen-to vtantur: vnde potum esse alimentum , faci-liufque digeri quam esculenta & cibaria mani-feftû est, etiam exinde, quod qui hesterna co-na largius biberunt, parcius autem efitarunt, longè melius postero die fe habere testantur, quam fi vna cum copioso potu copiosum etiã cibum deglutiissent: quamuis id non semper probari potest, cum in larga potatione ventri-culo (sed perinterualla & vices) aliquid fit ob-iiciendum in quod agat, & quod meri viribus resistat, quaealias confertim irreperent in ce-rebrum idq; conturbarent. Verum de dolore capitis à temulentia & crebrietate excitato, apud multos non parum gratiæ me initurum per-suasum habeo, fi in præfentia aliquid dixero.
units.tr: "It is easier to be filled with food than with drink," says Aphorisms 2, section 2. Galen, explaining this, says that moist things, although they do not nourish as solid things do, surpass them in speed of nourishing. Hippocrates confirms this again in his book On Diet: those who need quick application should be given moist liquid, the best remedy for restoring strength; but whoever needs an even quicker restoration is best restored through smell. Those who need slower application should use solid food. Whence it is evident that drink is food and is digested more easily than edibles and solid food. This is also shown by the fact that those who drank more freely at yesterday's dinner but ate more sparingly report that they feel much better the next day than if they had swallowed a copious amount of food along with copious drink. Yet this cannot always be proved, since in heavy drinking something must be thrown at the stomach, at intervals and in turns, which acts against and resists the force of the neat wine; otherwise the wine would rush straight into the brain and disturb it. But I am persuaded that I will win no little gratitude from many if I say something now about the headache caused by drunkenness and frequent drinking.

units.la: Sunt multi , & inter hos viri temperantiæ & frugalitati deditissimi quidem. sed tamen inci-dente & postulante occasione largius fe quoq; ex pridia- mero perfundentes, qui postea capite vini va-poribus cruditatibusque repleto languent va-rieq; afficiuntur, afferentes, omnibus fe Crae-fi diuitiis carere potius malle, quam eiusmodi semper dolores ex crapula perpeti.
units.tr: There are many, and among them men most devoted to temperance and frugality, who nonetheless, when an occasion arises and invites them, drench themselves more freely the day before. Afterwards, with their heads filled with wine vapours and indigestion, they languish and are afflicted in various ways, declaring that they would rather go without all the riches of Croesus than always endure such pains from surfeit.

units.la: Symtomata adsunt varia, dolor capitis, fuffufiones, obscuritas visus, oculorum caligo, nausea, fastidium, cor palpitans, venæ inflatæ & turgentes, ructus, flatus, & similia. Quidam Zinzibere condito, brodi- gallinæ, pilosum, vel vini saccharati, aromatisque vt cinnamomo, cubebis, garyophylis, cardamomis, galanga, piperibus & similibus, symtemata, vel mitigari vel propulsari sibi plane habent persuasum. Quidam generosa vina, vt maluatica, Hispanica, alii lulapia [?]liantib. expetunt buccis. Sed fallaci experimento & iudicio cæco.
units.tr: Various symptoms are present: headache, suffusions, dimness of vision, darkness before the eyes, nausea, loathing of food, a palpitating heart, swollen and distended veins, belching, flatulence and the like. Some are firmly persuaded that these symptoms can either be eased or driven off by preserved ginger, chicken broth, a hair of the dog, or sugared wine, and by spices such as cinnamon, cubebs, cloves, cardamom, galingale, pepper and the like. Some crave generous wines, such as Malmsey and Spanish wine; others, juleps. But this is a deceptive experiment and a blind judgment.

units.la: Primo enim sciendum, num malum hæreat in ventriculo nec ne? Si malum hæret in ventriculo cruditasque turget, male faciunt, qui brodiis aromatisque conditis, vel vinis generosis quærunt leuamen, hæc enim cruditates in ventriculo magis faciunt effumare, vnde dolor recrudescit.
units.tr: For first one must know whether the evil sticks in the stomach or not. If the evil sticks in the stomach and the crudity swells it, those do badly who seek relief in broths, spiced drinks or generous wines. For these make the crudities exhale more in the stomach, whence the pain breaks out again.

units.la: Si malum cruditas q; non est in ventriculo sed venis, quæ ex meri reliquiis turgent, frustra brodia, aromata, maluatica, lulapia, & similia assumuntur in ventriculum, non tantum eniam prius malum non aufertur, sed nouu subinde oboritur, noua scilicet vaporum generatione & conturbatione. Itaq; malo hærente in ventriculo indeq; vaporibus in caput & cerebrum repentib9, vomitu expurgandum quic-quid in ventriculo vel permansit, vel in eū resorbuit, postea vero ventriculus aromatis conditis, & vino generoso venit corroborādus pa-ne videlicet tosto vel aromatis consperso, vel vinoimbuto, prout quifq; voluerit vel affue-uerit. Vacuato enim ventre & tamé dolore nó remittente, vini noxam potum vini eiusdem (non quidem specie) eluere nó fine ratione af-seuero: quia pimirū, quæ mala calidæ tenuifq; suæ substantiæ copiá inuexit, eadem sua quali-tate & vicalefaciendi exiccandiq; vicissim tol-lit, eo inquam modo vapores crassos nebulo-fosq; dispergit, quo dolores oculorum inde ortos scripsit Hip.fe.6.l.2. Epidem. meracá po-tione discuti. Contrarium verò fi euenerit, id est, fi vini noxam vini potio non tollit, malum & rectudefcit & augetur,
units.tr: If the evil is a crudity that lies not in the stomach but in the veins, swollen with the leftovers of the neat wine, it is vain to take broths, spices, Malmsey, juleps and the like into the stomach. For not only is the former evil not removed, but a new one arises straightaway, namely through a fresh generation and disturbance of vapours. So when the evil sticks in the stomach and vapours rush up into the head and brain, whatever has remained in the stomach or been reabsorbed into it must be purged by vomiting. Afterwards the stomach is to be strengthened with spiced foods and generous wine: namely toasted bread, either sprinkled with spices or soaked in wine, as each one wishes or is accustomed. For when the belly is emptied and yet the pain does not relent, I maintain, not without reason, that the harm of wine is washed away by drinking the same wine (though not of the same kind). For the same quality that the hot and thin substance of wine has brought in, it removes in turn by its power of warming and drying. In that way, I say, it disperses the thick, cloudy vapours, just as Hippocrates wrote that eye pains arising from them are dispelled by neat drinking (Epidemics 6, book 2). But if the contrary happens, that is, if drinking wine does not remove the harm of wine, the evil both grows worse and increases.

units.la: Vomere autem vél non valentibus, vel mo-leftè & difficulter vomentibus ieiunium & in-ediam optimum esse remediū experientia te-ftis est, somnum prææerea, quietem optimam, ventriculi fomentü & linimentum, quibus e-goaddo leuem frictionem capitis & ventris, Sæpe frustra tentantur omnia vaporibus fcili-cet crassis & crudis in venas, cerebri profun-dum, &neruorum substantiam relapsis, cumq; spiritibus mixtis, vnde torpidi, obscuri, ingna-uiqueredditi lassitudinem illam membrorum tantisper fouent, dum per motum vapor ille fuerit dispersus atque resolutus. Itaq; mo-tionem & obambulationem diuturniorem & paulò celeriorem ante cibum plurimum plurimis hic prodesse & profuisse in experi-mentis est, à cibo autem lentiorem & bre-uiorem. uiorem[?] commendari reperio, idq; duabus aut tribus horis post. Postero igitur die hesternā crapula disturbati diligenter animadvertent, num excrementa in illis & humores crudi sint revocati & propulsi ad centrum, an vero ventriculum eiusque orificium afficiant? illic exercitium & motus ante cibum, vel somnus ad tertiam etiam diei partem, teste Hipp. absque interruptione extractus laudatur: hic vomit*, inedia, fomenta, linimenta vel frictiones circa ventriculi regionem magis commendantur. Unde male sanitati consulunt, qui ventriculo ex immodica fortioris meri potione aestuanti & sitienti refrigerium quaerunt potu frigido aquae vel cerevisiae, quam ad aliquot saepe mensuras a Germanis ingurgitari ieiuno stomacho passim videas.
units.tr: For those who cannot vomit, or who vomit with difficulty and discomfort, experience bears witness that fasting and abstinence from food is the best remedy. Besides these, sleep is the best rest, and fomentations and liniments of the stomach help, to which I add gentle rubbing of the head and belly. Often everything is tried in vain, because the crude, thick vapours have slipped back into the veins, the depths of the brain and the substance of the nerves, and mixed with the spirits. Hence they cherish that weariness of the limbs for a while, making the body dull, dim and sluggish, until that vapour is dispersed and dissolved by movement. Therefore I find, in experience, that a longer walk and a somewhat quicker pace before food have done, and still do, very much good for many people; after food, a slower and shorter walk is recommended, two or three hours after eating. So on the following day, those disturbed by yesterday's surfeit should carefully observe whether the excrements and crude humours in them have been recalled and driven to the centre, or whether they affect the stomach and its orifice. In the first case, exercise and movement before food, or sleep for even a third part of the day, drawn out without interruption (as Hippocrates testifies), is praised. In the second case, vomiting, fasting, fomentations, liniments or rubbing around the region of the stomach are more commended. Hence those do ill for their health who, when the stomach is seething and thirsty after an immoderate draught of stronger wine, seek refreshment by drinking cold water or beer. You may see the Germans gulp these down on an empty stomach everywhere, often several measures at a time.

units.la: Sed dum calorem eo remedio deferbere putant, feruentiorem eum paulò post & auctiorem deprehendunt, quo enim plus bibunt, eo plus sitire incipiunt, non secus ac in lapidibus excalfactis videmus, qui, si aqua frigidissima asperguntur, multò sentiuntur calidiores, nutriente videlicet in ipsis humida substantia aridam caliditatem, ut ita hoc medicandi ventriculo excalfacto modo nihil fit nocenti*.
units.tr: But while they think that the heat is cooled by this remedy, they find it a little later hotter and increased. For the more they drink, the more they begin to thirst, just as we see with heated stones: if they are sprinkled with the coldest water, they feel much hotter, because the dry heat is nourished by the moist substance in them. So this way of treating an overheated stomach achieves nothing but harm.

units.la: Qui de noctu sitiunt, decenti & conuenienti utantur potu, & postea redormiant, id enim bonum esse ipse Hipp. asseruit. Qui tamen adhuc graviori siti tentantur atque premuntur post redormitionem,iis potum non interdico, cum omninò ab eo abstinere insalubre prorf[?] est, ob adustionem humidi, intemperieique siccæ,quâ nihil periculosus,metum. Vehementius igitur sitientes ventriculum æstuantem potione diluent & irrigabunt, potione in-quam, in quâ panis tosti frusta puluere nucis mofchatæ vel cinnamomi asperso macerata sint, ficenim ventriculus minus offendetur. Apud Septentrionis gentes vidi in frequenti vsu esse crapulosis,potum ex vino vel cereuisia Rostochiana cum sufficiente saccharo, cinna-momo, nuce mofchata, cubebis, & similibus concinnate, adiecta panis bis coeti sufficiente quantitate,s[?]ftum enim ventriculi mirifice ex-tinguit,ipsamq; ventriculum roborat, cum panis ipse,tum etiam aromata.
units.tr: Those who are thirsty at night should take a suitable and fitting drink, and then go back to sleep, for Hippocrates himself asserted this to be good. Yet those who are still tormented and oppressed by a more severe thirst after going back to sleep, I do not forbid drink, since to abstain from it altogether is plainly unhealthy, because of the drying up of moisture and dry intemperance, than which nothing is more dangerous, I fear. Those who are more vehemently thirsty should therefore dilute and water the seething stomach with a drink, I mean one in which pieces of toasted bread have been soaked, sprinkled with powdered nutmeg or cinnamon; for so the stomach will be less offended. Among the Northern peoples I have seen the drunken commonly use a drink made of wine or Rostock beer, prepared with sufficient sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, cubebs and the like, with a sufficient quantity of twice-baked bread added. For it marvellously quenches the thirst of the stomach and strengthens the stomach itself, both the bread and the spices doing so.

units.la: Mirum in modum me sæpius eo refectum sensi,meos primo mores adillum morem con-formans. Saccharo destitutus fumo eius loco mel despumatum, & panis nostri cibarii inue-terati medullam,quæ in micas friatur conteri-turq;ac postea aromatis in puluerem redactis commiscetur. Ad extremum optimè sibi con-sulent profpicientq; potatores, frequenter in-ter potandum sale vtentes. Salenim torpen-tem ventriculi excitat appetentiam,teste Plin. lib.31.c.9. & Plutarch. l.de causis natur. quæst. 9. & salsugo illa naturam stimulat ad celeriorem excretionem,ne vasa & vtres nimium diften-dantur dantur: salsuginem enim illam fero permisce-ri testantur, qui crebrius salsis cibis utentes sal-siorem mingunt urinam, & contra. Quamuis haec non à me dicuntur, vel in apertum prose-runtur, ut tansam alicui ministrem aut fenestrā aperiam ad potandum, sed ut aut moderatè bibere omnes assuescant, aut si occasione incidente liberalius & meracius sit bibendum, id fiat citra noxam & incommodum corporis. De Ebrietate autem naturali quadam proprietate repugnantibus, inter quæ amygdalas amaras, brassicam, cardamomum, persicorum nucleos, succum foliorum persicæ arboris expressum, absinthii pontici dilutum, & nostrum etiam vulgare absinthium præcipuam obtinuisse laudem reperio, suo dicetur loco & ordine.
units.tr: I have often found myself wonderfully refreshed by this, having first conformed my own habits to that custom. Lacking sugar, I use instead skimmed honey and the crumb of our stale bread, rubbed and crushed into crumbs and then mixed with spices reduced to powder. Finally, drinkers who look to their own good often use salt during drinking. For salt rouses a sluggish stomach to appetite, as Pliny attests (book 31, chapter 9) and Plutarch (Natural Questions, question 9). That saltiness also stimulates nature to quicker excretion, so that the vessels and bladder are not overstretched: those who eat salty food more often are said to pass saltier urine, and the reverse also holds. I do not say these things to offer anyone a tansy or to open a tap for drinking. I say them so that either everyone becomes accustomed to drinking in moderation, or, if an occasion arises when drinking must be more generous and neat, it is done without harm or discomfort to the body. Concerning drunkenness, I find that among the remedies with a natural property, bitter almonds, cabbage, cardamom, peach kernels, juice pressed from peach leaves, diluted Pontic wormwood, and our common wormwood have won the chief praise. These will be discussed in their proper place and order.

units.la: QVÆSTIO III. An à potu omninò sit abstinendum intermedio prandii & cœnæ tempore?
units.tr: QUESTION III. Should one abstain from drink altogether in the interval between lunch and supper?

units.la: HIC vero modeste discedo ab iis, qui quasi prætorio edicto inter prandium & cœnam omnem potum interdicunt, putantes clausum ventriculum potu frigido crudoq; aperiri, coctionemq; interturbari. Ri-gidam nimis hanc in victu præceptionem vix ab uno inter millenos video observari, imo verius dixerim à nullo mortalium.
units.tr: Here I modestly part ways with those who, as if by a praetorian edict, forbid all drink between lunch and supper, supposing that a closed stomach is opened by cold and raw drink and that digestion is thrown into disorder. I scarcely see this overly rigid precept in diet observed by one in a thousand; or rather, to speak more truly, by no mortal at all.

units.la: Quis enim potu omninò abstinere juberet falsuram vel suillæ carnis, vel halecesex muria,
units.tr: For who would order someone to abstain from drink altogether at lunch when he eats salted pork or herring preserved in brine,

units.la: aliofque pifcesaut carnes infumatas, vel etiam aromatis confperfos & conditos cibos devo- rantem in prandio? hac enim vehementiorem excitabunt fitim. Conftat falfum faporem lin- guam quidem non admodum calefacere, fed aeriter ficcando corrodere, fincerumq; falfo- rum efum nimium humores & fanguinem la- befactare, ob ficcitatem quas in falfo fapore major eft quam caliditas. Id quod chymico- rum falfus fapor vi chymica elicitus demon- strat, nullum enim fere corpus eft quo & calx & proprius fal non extrahi poffit arte vul, cania, at vero ejufmodi acerrimi caloris effeac in plerifq; caufticum, id eft, viadurendi predi- tum, guftus vnicuiq; indicabit. Quapropter ci- bum in ipfo etiam coctionis opere humecta- re, ne exuratur, aflétur & corrumpatur, opti- mum & faluberrimum judico, non fecus ac coqui inter elixandum folidioribus obfoniis, quae tardius coctionis terminum affequantur, affundere aquam confueuerunt, priori ante perfectam coquitam abfumta, minus interef- fe experientia edocti, elixationem paululum interturbare quam concedere, vt cibus in le- bete comburatur. Verum quemadmodum aquam fape & multum affundere elixationem non interpellat tantum, verum ipfam coctio- nem impedit, suffocato fcilicet ob nimiam hu- mectationem calore, vel potius actione feu o- peratione ejus laesa ac retusa: fic & cibus in ventri.
units.tr: or other fish or smoked meats, or even food seasoned and spiced with aromatics? These will excite a stronger thirst. It is established that salt does not greatly heat the tongue, but by drying it fiercely it corrodes it; and that excessive eating of salted foods weakens the humours and blood, because of the dryness that is greater than the heat in a salty taste. The salty taste of chemical substances, drawn out by chemical force, demonstrates this. For there is almost no body from which both lime and its proper salt cannot be extracted by art; but a taste will show to everyone that this most bitter kind of heat, which in most cases is caustic, that is, endowed with the power of burning. Therefore I judge it best and most salutary to moisten food even during the work of cooking, so that it is not scorched, burnt and spoiled. Cooks, too, are accustomed to pour water over solid dishes that take longer to reach the end of cooking, while the first water is used up before boiling is complete. Experience teaches that it matters less to disturb the boiling a little than to let the food burn in the pot. Yet just as pouring on water often and in quantity does not merely interrupt boiling but actually hinders the cooking itself, namely by smothering the heat through excessive moistening, or rather by injuring and blunting its action or operation, so too food in the stomach...

units.la: {y} Salchymi corum tm penfecal- dus imo caufticus. ventriculo immoderatius humectandus non est ob causas easdem.
units.tr: {Marginal note} Salt of the chemists, though warm, indeed caustic, is not to be moistened too immoderately in the stomach, for the same reasons.

units.la: Quos praeterea grauis inter prandium & coenam sitis non vrget, iis (nisi sint temperamenti cholerici, hoc est, calidioris & siccioris, ii enim vt plurimum sunt siticulosi) vt a potu abstineant plane, suasor sum. Si quando tamen voluptatis vel officii gratia bibendum est, decenter id fiat & conuenienter, &c.
units.tr: As for those whom a heavy thirst does not press between lunch and supper, I advise them to abstain from drink altogether (unless they are of a choleric temperament, that is, hotter and drier, for such people are usually very thirsty). If, however, drinking must be done for pleasure or from duty, let it be done decently and suitably, etc.

units.la: QVÆSTIO IV. An hieme plus edere conueniat quam æstate, propterea quòd ventres sint tempore hiberno calidiores, æstate verò frigidiores?
units.tr: QUESTION IV. Is it fitting to eat more in winter than in summer, because the stomachs are warmer in winter and cooler in summer?

units.la: COpiosiora alimenta offerenda esse hieme quàm æstate, tempore hiberno cibum melius faciliusQque digeri, plus etiam homines appetere, vetus a veterrimis repetita autoribus, & per multa secula sapientum judicio & ratione confirmata sententia est. Causa, ob quam hæc ita se habeant, assignatur ab Hippocrate lib.1.aphor. 15. Cum ait ventres natura calidissimos esse hieme & vere, obq; id copiosius cibandos. Calidissimi sunt non absolute & simpliciter, sed calido naturali influente, quod tempore hiberno propter circumstan[?]tiam extrinsecus frigiditatem continetur, cohibetur, & ad interioriinteriora refugit, ob quod coctiones, sanguificatio-nes & nutritiones magis procedunt, tempore vere estiuo idem calidum a sibi affini videlicet exterio-ri ad extimas corporis partes evocatur, dissolu-tur atq; dissipatur, unde natura opera magis langue-scunt astate quàm hieme. Cum enim calor innatus sit omnium naturalium operationum causa, sequi-tur, ubi is plurimus est & superabundat, cibi ap-petentiam intendi, coctiones, melius procedere & felicius absolui.
units.tr: That richer food should be offered in winter than in summer, that in winter food is better and more easily digested, and that people also have a greater appetite, is an opinion handed down from the oldest authors and confirmed through many centuries by the judgment and reason of the wise. The cause for which these things are so is given by Hippocrates, Aphorisms book 1, aphorism 15: since he says that by nature the stomachs are hottest in winter and spring, and for this reason they should be fed more copiously. They are hottest not absolutely and simply, but by the natural heat flowing in; in winter this heat is held back and confined, and retreats to the interior parts, because of the external cold surrounding the body. For this reason, concoctions, sanguification and nutrition proceed more vigorously. In spring and summer the same heat is drawn by its kinship with the outer air to the outermost parts of the body, is loosened and dissipated, and so the operations of nature grow more sluggish in summer than in winter. For since innate heat is the cause of all natural operations, it follows that where it is most abundant and superabundant, the appetite for food is intensified, and concoctions proceed better and are completed more happily.

units.la: Et vero plurimum eum est, hiberne tempore validiorem, indicio sunt naturae operafortiora; ac tiones enim augentur, plus generatur sanguinis, corpus efficitur crassius, super fluitates, in so-nis longioribus expurgantur, & omnia melius in corpore animalis admiscentur tempore hi-berno quàm estate, quâ calor circumfusus non tan-tum inuisilia, sed etiam ea, quae secundum natu-ram in corpore continentur, una d' slusi per ec-culam diffusionem quidam calor innatus operatur. Hinc enim beneficio non tantum alimen-tum conficitur, singuliq; partibus proprium ag-glutina ur, verum etiam omnes superfluates bu-jus excernunt, ut atq; extenuat ur, quaedam ex-quisi e per cutem, quae vero in vapores converti-ut per expirationem, sufficientem vero habentem crassi udinem per urinas, in quibus etiam plus fe-dimentiest quàm per efatem, propterea quod ca-Ratio felicius pr ficitur, corpora se undum carnem plus argentum plus etiam boni sanguinis cumulat-[?] tur hieme mediocritate seruante, quae omnia vi-gorem & robur caloris innati denunciant. ¶Adde quod occulta perspiratio seu diffusio, quo magis effi[?]t sensum, eo fortius arguit calidum innatum; vnde sudores fratres natu am[?]sunt, quia sensibilis humor insensibiliter per cutim non excernitur, si in animali corpore rite omnia administratur, alimentumq; probe a natura conficitur: (Sudores enim in balneis, vehementioribus exercitiis, vel aestuo calore excitati a causis violentis habent originem) probe autem omnia administrari in animali corpore, alimentumq; a natura bene conficiti tempore hiberno praeter sensum, rationem, experientiam, ostendunt: supe[?] fluitates quae insensibiliter & per occultu spiracula magis disflantur & expurgantur hieme quam aestate, vt ita in totum dixisse liceat, vere & stè ab Hipp. d[?]uum esse ventres hieme & vere esse calidissimos, quare per ea tempora alimenta copiosiora exhibenda: etenim tunc calor innatus plurimum est, intusq; viget, vnde & pluribus opus est al mentis.
units.tr: And indeed, where it is most abundant, the heat is stronger in winter; the evidence is that the operations of nature are stronger. For the functions are increased, more blood is generated, the body becomes denser, superfluities are purged in longer sleeps, and everything in the animal body is mixed together better in winter than in summer. In summer the surrounding heat, which diffuses by a kind of expansion, operates not only on the things that are external, but also on those that are contained in the body according to nature. For by this benefit not only is food digested and each part given its proper nourishment, but all superfluities of the body are also excreted: some are dissolved and thinned out through the skin, others are turned into vapours and breathed out, and those of sufficient thickness leave through the urine, in which there is also more sediment than in sweat. This is because digestion is more happily accomplished, and the bodies accumulate more flesh, more silver, and more good blood in winter, while keeping a moderate mean. All these things announce the vigour and strength of innate heat. Add that the hidden perspiration, or diffusion, the more it escapes the senses, the more strongly it shows innate heat. Hence sweats are rightly said to be of a sensible kind, because the sensible humour is not excreted insensibly through the skin when everything in the animal body is properly managed and the food is well digested by nature. (Sweats excited in baths, by very vigorous exercises, or by summer heat, have their origin in violent causes.) That all things in the animal body are properly managed, and food is well digested by nature, in winter time, apart from sense, reason and experience, is shown by this: the superfluities which are dispersed and purged more by hidden and insensible openings in winter than in summer. So that one may say, in short, that Hippocrates was right that the stomachs are warmest in winter and spring; therefore more copious food should be given in those seasons. For then the innate heat is greatest and flourishes within, and so more nourishment is needed.

units.la: ¶Accedunt nox & somnus longissimus, in quo interna omnia magis calent, vi tutes & Spiritus naturales plus vigent, qui in vigiliis corporis sensuumq; laboribus magis dissipantur.
units.tr: Add to this the night and the longest sleep, in which all internal things grow warmer, and the powers and natural spirits are more vigorous, whereas in the wakefulness and labours of the body and senses they are more dissipated.

units.la: Quid? quòd hieme quo[?] daum parcius paucas comedentes, r[?] frigeri atq; uendi, liberalius vero ac copiosius vescentes in nullos tamen ex re[?]leti-one morbos incidere ipsa experientia ostendit manifeste.
units.tr: What of the fact that in winter, people who eat sparingly, eating few things, become cold and weak, yet those who eat more freely and copiously fall into no diseases from overeating? Experience itself shows this plainly.

units.la: Rationem addit Galenus in comment. quòd ni-mirum corpora differentur promtius per sensui oc-culta foramina & spiracula, unde alimento egent quoniam evacuantur: quod si enim nihil à corporibus nostris effluueret, sed semper aqua subftan-tia nostra moles seruaretur, nulla foret alimenti necessitas. Hac veterum sententia tot seculis tan-tò, consensu ab antiquitate approbata, haßlenus, stans inconcussa à recentioribus quibusdam argu-té improbatur.
units.tr: Galen, in his commentary, adds the reason: namely, that bodies are more quickly diminished through the hidden pores and openings of the senses, and therefore they need food because they are emptied. For if nothing flowed out of our bodies, but our substance always remained the same mass of water, there would be no need of food. This opinion of the ancients, approved by antiquity and by the consent of so many centuries, has hitherto stood unshaken; but it is cleverly rejected by certain more recent writers.

units.la: Ac primo adducunt autoritatem Hippoc.& Galen. qui volunt corpora calidissima esse æstate, quoniam id anni tempus calidissimum est, frigi-diffimum hieme, quoniam hiberno tempore frigi-dus nullum. Hippocr.l.3.de diæt. Tempore exi-stente frigido ac compacto, consimilia patiuntur etiam animalia ipsa: (scilicet extrinsecus, sicut æstate extrinsecus calent) & de salubri dieta, sic his, vbi astas fuerit, uti oportet, ut frigidum sit corpus & molle, tempus enim calidum est & sic-cum, redditq; corpora astuosa & squalida. Vbi, inquit Hippocrates, fuerit astas, curare oportet ut corpus sit frigidum, quid ita? quia tempus cali-dum est: jubet igitur ac vult Hippocrates, ut tempore astiuo, cum astu flagrat totum corpus, ap-plicemus adhibeamusq; frigida, ut nimirum cu-tis spiracula porig, paululum paulatimq; conden-sentur atq; constringantur, ne ob caloris interni nimium diffluxum (ab externo enim evocatur, dissipatur, disperditurq;) totum corpus, cumpri-mis uemis vero interiora marcescant viresq; labascant, quod certè æstate crebrerrimè accidere vidimus peregrinantibus, dum potu destituuntur: Una enim cum calore exhalante etiam humidum diffluere, obidq; siccitura magisq; frigida, reddi corpora, quis est qui infic'as ibit? Adducitur quoq; Galenus[?], quem idem asserere ajunt in comm.in 1. Hipp.de natura humana, cum circumfuso scil. aeris statu vna animalium corpora affici, siccari in sicco humectari in humido, &c. Unde concludunt nihil aliud voluisse Hipp.& Gal. quàm no- stra corpora hieme frigere, æstate vero calere, propterea quod hieme pituitam augeri, æstate bilem. Hippocrates & experientia testantur, hieme enim homines pituitosissima expuere atq; emungere, unde sequi ajunt corpus æstate calidius esse, hieme frigidius. Verum Galenus comment. in l.Hipp. de natur.human. copiosioris pituitæ per hiemem hanc affert causam, quod homines id temporis multis pituitosis vescantur cibis, ut oleribus, rapis, leguminibus, fructibus, carnibus agninis & porcinis, & idgenus aliis quæ facilè in pituitam vertuntur: quod item bibant vinum novum, ex quo non minus promte generetur pituita.
units.tr: And first they adduce the authority of Hippocrates and Galen, who hold that bodies are hottest in summer, because that is the hottest season of the year, and coldest in winter, because in winter the cold is greatest. Hippocrates, On Diet book 3: "When the time is cold and compact, the animals themselves suffer similar things (namely from without, as in summer they are warmed from without)." And on healthful diet: "So in the season when summer comes, one must use such diet that the body becomes cool and soft, for the time is hot and dry, and it makes bodies fiery and squalid. Where summer comes, says Hippocrates, care must be taken that the body is cool. Why so? Because the season is hot." He therefore bids and wishes that in summer, when the whole body glows with heat, we apply and use cold things, so that the pores of the skin gradually close and tighten, lest, from the excessive outflow of internal heat (for it is drawn out by the external heat, dissipated and scattered), the whole body, and especially the inner parts in spring, wither and lose strength. This we certainly see very often happening to travellers in summer when they lack drink. For when the heat is exhaled, the moisture flows away with it, and the bodies are made drier and colder by the dryness. Who would deny it? Galen is also cited, whom they say asserts in his commentary on the first book of Hippocrates' On the Nature of Man that animal bodies are affected by the state of the surrounding air: dried in dryness, moistened in moisture, and so on. Hence they conclude that Hippocrates and Galen meant nothing else than that our bodies grow cold in winter and warm in summer, because in winter phlegm increases and in summer bile. Hippocrates and experience bear witness: in winter people spit out and blow their noses most phlegm, whence they say it follows that the body is hotter in summer and colder in winter. But Galen, in his commentary on the same book of Hippocrates, gives this cause for the more copious phlegm of winter: at that season people eat many phlegm-producing foods, such as vegetables, turnips, pulses, fruits, lamb and pork, and other such things that are easily turned into phlegm; likewise they drink new wine, from which phlegm is no less readily generated.

units.la: Sed illi regerunt etiam per æstatem tali-bus cibis non vesci & pituitosioribus, omnis scilicet gene-ris fructibus, iisq; crudis, ut fragis, cerasis, prunis, pomis, pyris, & in acetariis lactucâ, endiviâ, ace-tosa, portulacâ, &c.
units.tr: But they reply that in summer too people do not eat such phlegm-producing foods, namely all kinds of fruit, and those raw, such as strawberries, cherries, plums, apples, pears, and among salads lettuce, endive, sorrel, purslane, and so on.

units.la: Hic verò quæritur cur horum ciborum pituitosorum tosorum immoderatus vsus sit noxius magis esse ate [?] quàm bieme [?], ac vtplurimum diarrhœas procreet ac dysenterias? Anid sit ob caloris natiui penuri- am ac imbecillitatem, quæ maior est astate, quàm vt exuperantiam illam ciborum moderari possit ac domare, unde pituita crassa ac viscida in intestinis colligitur, eruditates cumulantur, quapro- ꝓ vam qualitatem adepta à calore nec supcrari, nec mitigari possunt? Nemo opinor existet, qui con- tradistur sit. Illa enim omnia astiuo calere promtiùs putrescunt, interstina horum, venas vel licant atq; exulcerant, complexionem ventriculi intestinorum, immutant, quam complexionis mutationem prædictæ symptomata s. b sequuntur: contra vero hieme melius omnia in animalis cor- pore administrari supra demonstratum est. Præ- terea verè & rectè ab Hipp. dictum esse la- lubr. diæt. oportere & ad ætatem, & ad annitem- pus & ad corporum habitus dietas constituere sta ut caloribus & humidibus nos oppnamus, sic enim homines maximè sore saños, ipse Galenus scribit in commentar. Et licet eundem pro se adducat, scribentem in eodem commentario, corpus, quod immoderatius excalfactum est, aut calefit, refri- gerandum esse, refrigeratum calefaciendum: Et Celsus l. de re medica c. 3. dicentem naturale esse potione astuantem ventriculum refrigerari, sri- gentem calefieri: Item calidum hominem srige- rare se deberet inde tamen non elicitur, propter ea astate æstate nos magis vesci cibis frigidis & humidis, quod ventriculus sit calidior secundum essentiam primo & per se sed potius ut ventriculus flaccidus, humido scil. in eo per resolutionem & evaporatio-nem tenuium partium absumto, refrigerando & humectando corroboretur, villi resoluti ac relaxati astringantur: his enim laxatis appetitus per-ditur, qui iisdem astrictis restituitur. Cum enim calorem immodicum & redundantem consecuti-ve & necessario comitetur siccitas, quâ in corpore humano nihil periculosius, (ut vidimus in corpo-ribus tabidis & emaciatis, quae sunt sicca absumto videlicet humido radicali) ad hanc præ-canen-dam ventriculum frigido humidis roboramus, cu-jus alias vires prorsus conciderent atq; resoluerentur. Deinde calor æstate sentitur magis in exteri-oribus evocatus scilicet à centro suo ad circum-ferentiam ac per universum corpus dispersus. Atq; hoc est quod Hipp.l.3. de diæt. inquit, cibis mol-lioribus & paucioribus utendum esse ob debilem ventriculi calorem, & maza magis quàm pane, potionibusq; albis, mollibus & aquosis, sc.ad humec-tandum. Consentiunt cum his quæ habentur l. de salubr. diæt. Æstate maza molli alioportet & potione aquosa multa, obsonisq; omnibus elixis; & his ita utendum est, ut corpus si frigidum & mol-le. Huc accedit authoritas Celsi, qui inquit, æstate potione & cibo corpus sæpius egere quia videlicet calor externus multum depascitur: calor em ex-ternum nominat & circumfusum non internum, qui
units.tr: Here, however, the question is asked why the immoderate use of these phlegmatic foods should be more harmful in summer than in winter, and should most often produce diarrhoeas and dysenteries. Is it because of the lack and weakness of the natural heat, which in summer is too feeble to moderate and tame that excess of food, so that thick and viscid phlegm collects in the intestines and crudities accumulate, which, having taken on a corrupting quality from the heat, can be neither overcome nor softened? I think no one will arise to contradict this. For all those things putrefy more readily in summer's heat; they corrode and ulcerate the intestines and veins, and they alter the complexion of the stomach and intestines, and the aforesaid symptoms follow this change of complexion. On the contrary, in winter everything is better managed in the animal body, as has been shown above. Moreover, Hippocrates rightly and truly said in On Healthful Diet that diets must be arranged according to age, season and bodily constitution, so that we oppose heat and moisture; for thus, Galen himself writes in his commentary, people are kept most healthy. And although Galen cites the same author in his favour, writing in the same commentary that a body which has become excessively heated, or is becoming so, must be cooled, and what has been cooled must be warmed; and although Celsus, in book 1 of On Medicine chapter 3, says it is natural to cool a stomach that is seething with drink and to warm one that is chilled; and although a hot man ought to cool himself, yet it does not follow from this that in summer we should eat cold and moist foods more, on the ground that the stomach is hotter in its essence, primarily and in itself. Rather, the stomach, being flaccid because its moisture is consumed by resolution and evaporation of the fine parts, is strengthened by cooling and moistening, so that its loosened and relaxed villi are braced. For when these are relaxed, appetite is lost, and when they are braced again it is restored. Since excessive and superabundant heat is necessarily accompanied by dryness, than which nothing is more dangerous in the human body (as we see in wasted and emaciated bodies, which are dry because the radical moisture has been consumed), we strengthen the stomach with cold and moist things to forestall this, lest its other powers utterly collapse and dissolve. Then, too, in summer the heat is felt more on the outside, being drawn out from its centre to the circumference and dispersed through the whole body. This is what Hippocrates means in book 3 of On Diet when he says that softer and fewer foods should be used because of the stomach's weak heat, barley-cake rather than bread, and white, soft and watery drinks, namely to moisten. These agree with what is found in On Healthful Diet: in summer one should eat soft barley-cake and much watery drink, and all boiled foods; and these should be used so that the body remains cool and soft. Add to this the authority of Celsus, who says that in summer the body more often needs drink and food, because the external heat is greatly consumed: he means the external heat that surrounds the body, not the internal, which is weaker.

units.la: {G} qui debilior est. Ad morbos pergunt sensum & ex- perientiam aettestari aientes, aestate utplurimum grassantes morbos calidio: es & ardentiores esse,q;
units.tr: {G} which is weaker. They go on to appeal to the senses and experience, saying that the diseases which mostly rage in summer are hotter and more fiery.

units.la: negari non potest. Verum hoc queritur, num hoc fiat propterea quod ventriculus cateraq; viscera calore abundent? an vero quia calor internus è cetro suo et sede dimot? p uniuersum corpus quae- si volitans tenuiores sanguinis partes & schores in- flammat et accendit, bilem puto, secundum Hippocratis iudicium ad eiusmodi pra reliquis humo-rib. exarsionem et incendium estate et sua natu-ra qua calida et sica est, aptissimam : calescente enim sanguine exhalat maxime per hunc aquosus humor febrili incendio infestissimus, relinquitur au'em[?] pinguis et lenis, qui biliosus est et febris a- flua potissimum nutrimentum, copiosus enim. et accommodatius nutrimentum febri bilis ipsa suppeditat inquit Hipp. 4. de morb,
units.tr: This cannot be denied. But the question is whether this happens because the stomach and the other viscera abound with heat, or rather because the internal heat, removed from its centre and seat, flies through the whole body like a wandering fire and inflames and kindles the finer parts of the blood and the humours. I think bile, according to Hippocrates' judgement, is most apt for such burning and conflagration in summer, above the other humours, by its nature, which is hot and dry. For when the blood grows warm, the watery humour, most hostile to feverish fire, is exhaled most; what remains, however, is the fat and smooth humour, which is bilious and most of all supplies nourishment to the fever. For, says Hippocrates in book 4 of On Diseases, bile itself supplies the more copious and more suitable nourishment for fever.

units.la: Quid? an propterea calidiores morbi generari dicentur, quod corpus fit calidius, aliis dijudican-dum relinquo? Hippocrates enim 1. de veter. med. calidum vult, qua calidum non esse morbi cau-sam, nam inquit, ego hoc maximum signum esse puto, quod non propter calidum hominis febrici-tent simpliciter, neq; hoc sit simpliciter affectionis causa, sed est amarum et calidum idem, et cali-dum ac acidum et salsum, sic et frigidum cum a- his[?] facultatibus coniunctum.
units.tr: What then? Shall diseases be said to be generated hotter because the body becomes hotter? I leave that to others to judge. For Hippocrates in On Ancient Medicine wishes heat not to be the cause of disease. He says: "I think this is the greatest sign, that people do not become feverish simply because of heat, nor is heat simply the cause of the affection; but bitter is the same as hot, and hot is the same as sharp and salty, and so too cold when joined with these qualities."

units.la: Bilis autem calida est et amara, maxime vi-gentes aestate, ac propter pinguedinem tenuitatem, adfead febrilem exarsionem promptissima est calore sc. excitato atq; per omne corpus sursum & deorsum volitante, putredinemq; in humore primum pinguiori tenuioriq; ad inflammationem longe aptiori accedente non secus ut in aedificio incenso palea primo flammam concipere, postea trabes, auлo vero incendio non solum paleas, & ligna, sed & lapides rumpi videmus; calidiores igitur & ardentiores morbi contingunt aestate ratione bilis flammae facile ac prompte concipientis, sua etiam natura nec simpliciter calida, sed calida ac amara. Antiperistasi denique nihil vel parum ponderis & virium hic concedunt. I. quod qui gelu enectantur, in illorum se corpora ambiens frigus penitissime insinuet caloremq; natiuum extinguat. Sed hoc ipsum frigoris intensissimo ascribendum est: frigiditas enim ἀντιμέτρῳ [?] & reducens altissime & violenter penetrans calorem quasi in suo centro quiescentem extinguit, quod neutiquam fieret si calor per universum corpus distributus, quod certissimum argumentum est caloris ad intima penetralia animadversa hoste efugientis.
units.tr: Bile, however, is hot and bitter, most vigorous in summer, and because of its fatness and thinness it is most ready for feverish burning, once the heat is excited and flies up and down through the whole body, and putrefaction arises first in the fatter and thinner humour, far more apt for inflammation. Just as in a burning building the straw first catches fire and afterwards the beams, and in a great conflagration we see not only straws and wood but even stones split, so hotter and fiercer diseases befall us in summer by reason of bile, which catches fire easily and promptly, and whose nature is not simply hot but hot and bitter. Finally, they concede little or no weight or force here to Antiperistasis. First, those who are dying of cold: the surrounding frost penetrates most deeply into their bodies and extinguishes the natural heat. But this must be ascribed to the most intense cold itself: for cold, by counter-measure, reducing and penetrating very deeply and violently, extinguishes the heat that rests as if in its own centre. This would by no means happen if the heat were distributed through the whole body, which is the most certain proof that heat, when it notices the enemy at its innermost recesses, flees.

units.la: Cum enim calor & frigus sint contraria, unde se mutuo prohibent, fugant & fugiunt, necesse est debiliorem a fortiori fugari & vinci. Prate[?] ea calorem ri[?] fugere quidem ac repelli ob antiperistasin, sin ad interiora concedunt, verum ad suum primum videlicet cor, non vero ventriculum. Sed quis caloris ad principium suum repulsi partem etiam per venas arteriasq; ventriculo communicari neganegabit? ad infinitum enim ventriculi calorem, quia plus accesserit caloris influentis eo evadit fortior, & felicius cibus conficitur. Instant, multos biber- ni frigoris [?] interemisse [?] valde frigentes seminorum vorum instar rigere, cibumq; ac potum aversari quam diu non recalfacti fuerint, ergo cali- lori innato tanta vires non sunt, ut frigori ambien- ti resistat, seu eo intendatur. Hic responderi potest, hoc fieri ratione nervorum, musculorum & extre- morum, in quo frigus penetravit, seq; insinuavit, unde extrema rigida & congelata deprehendun- tur, motu sensuq; expertia: quod si vere intensi- us frigus est, diutiusq; durans, ulterius etiam pe- netrando calorisofficinam ita coarctat atq; occlu- dit, ut calor extinguatur atq; suffocetur. Reliqua negantis partis argumenta æquo ac erudito lectori pensitanda relinquo, liberum cuiq; faciens, hoc ne an illud approbet statuatne: veritas ipsa se non quasita prodet.
units.tr: Since heat and cold are contrary, and so mutually hinder, drive out and flee one another, the weaker must necessarily be driven out and conquered by the stronger. Besides, heat may indeed flee and be repelled because of antiperistasis, but if it retreats inward, it does so to its first principle, namely the heart, and not to the stomach. But who would deny that part of the heat driven back to its source is also communicated to the stomach through the veins and arteries? For the stomach's heat, since more of the inflowing heat has come to it, becomes stronger, and food is digested more readily. They object that many who died of the intense winter cold became stiff like tree trunks, and shrank from food and drink until they were warmed again; therefore the innate heat does not have such strength that it can resist the surrounding cold or be strengthened against it. Here it can be answered that this happens by reason of the nerves, muscles and extremities into which the cold has penetrated and insinuated itself, whence the extremities are found rigid and frozen, without motion or sensation. But if the cold is truly more intense and lasts longer, penetrating further, it so constricts and shuts the workshop of heat that the heat is extinguished and suffocated. I leave the remaining arguments of the opposing side to be weighed by the fair and learned reader, leaving it free to each to approve this or that and to decide which is true: truth itself will reveal itself without being sought.

units.la: I. Si, inquiunt, bieme constricta cute calor in- corpore cohibetur & intensior fit, astate autem ca- loris extra evocato frigus succedit, sequitur astate generari pituitam, bieme vero bilem, astate vitiu- tendum esse calido, bieme frigido, astate calidas naturas bene se habituras, bieme frigidas quasi Hip. & Galeni placitis sunt aduersa. Ego vero sumin- ea sententia & pituitam & bilem tam astate, quam bieme generari, illam tamen copiosius bieme, hanc astate: pituitam astate generari ostendunt alii profluvia ex crudorum ciborum immodico essu, quæ postea pituita æstivo calore putrescens acris e-vadit & corrosiva: bilem vero etiam hieme genera-ri manifesto offendunt biliosi vomitus. Idem Iudicium sit de bile atra, quam non mi[?]nus æstate, ve-re, hiemeq; quam autumno generari certum est.
units.tr: I. They say that if in winter the skin is constricted and the heat is held within the body and becomes more intense, while in summer the heat is drawn outward and cold follows, then it follows that phlegm is generated in summer and bile in winter; that in summer the hot constitution is harmed and in winter the cold; that in summer hot natures will do well and in winter cold ones; and that these things are contrary to the opinions of Hippocrates and Galen. I, however, am of the opinion that both phlegm and bile are generated as much in summer as in winter, though phlegm more abundantly in winter and bile in summer. That phlegm is generated in summer, others show by the flows that follow immoderate eating of raw foods, which phlegm afterwards, putrefying in the summer heat, becomes sharp and corrosive. That bile is generated also in winter is clearly shown by bilious vomiting. The same judgment should be made about black bile, which is certainly generated no less in summer, spring and winter than in autumn.

units.la: II. Quod hieme quàm æstate sumus edacio-res, escamq; minori negotio digeramus, aiunt non esse certum signum abundantis in ventriculo caloris, qui enim laborant canina appetentia, voracissimi sunt, quorum tamen ventriculi omnium medicorum judicio sunt frigida intemperie affecti.
units.tr: II. They say that we are more voracious in winter than in summer, and digest food with less effort, but this is not a certain sign of abundant heat in the stomach. For those who suffer from canine appetite are most voracious, and yet, by the judgment of all physicians, their stomachs are affected by a cold intemperature.

units.la: Hic ignoratur Elenchus.
units.tr: Here the refutation is ignored.

units.la: Quod enim pro confesso ac demonstrato assumitur adhuc probandum restat. An enim frigidus ventriculus plus appetat quam calidus, rationum & argumentorum viribus ponderandum est. Pueri certè plus cibi appetunt, augmentumq; capiunt non quod longius profunditusq; dormiant, ut quidam putant, sed quod plurimo calido innato abundent. Appetitus igitur nec omnis, nec semper a frigido est, sed moderatè seu temperatè calido. Phlegmatici & pituitosi parum & tardè appetunt, ob calorem remissum & torpidum; contra qui natiui caloris qualitatem acriorem experiuntur inedias nocentissimè ferunt, identidemq; itèrato pastu uti coguntur, ut sunt biliosi, quæ certè expressè contradicunt posterioris sententiæ patro-nis, contrariumq; satis demonstrant.
units.tr: For what is assumed as admitted and demonstrated still remains to be proved. Whether a cold stomach desires more than a warm one must be weighed by the force of reasons and arguments. Surely children desire more food and gain growth, not because they sleep longer and more deeply, as some think, but because they abound in much innate heat. Appetite, therefore, is neither universal nor always from cold, but comes from heat moderately or temperately present. Phlegmatic and phlegmatic-natured people desire little and slowly, because their heat is slack and sluggish; on the other hand, those who experience the sharper quality of innate heat bear fasting most harmfully, and are obliged to eat again and again, as bilious people do. These things certainly contradict the advocates of the latter opinion expressly, and sufficiently demonstrate the contrary.

units.la: III. Quod æstate ciborum sumus minus appe-tentes aut assumptos difficulter concoquimus, non frigoris aiunt fieri culpâ, sed immoderati caloris, id m enim nobis astuantibus evenire quod febri-citantibus, qui cum maxime ardeant, cibos tamen auersantur, aut si comedant, grauantur magis quam refocillantur. Hoc vero ipsum est, quod vo-lui, appetentiam silicet oriri a calore moderato seu temperato: quo etiam sensu potest concedi a frigido posse excitari appetentiam, non simpliciter & absolute seu quâ frigido, sed quatenus cum ca-lore contemperatum, adq; naturâ conuenientem tem-peramentum redactum est.
units.tr: III. That in summer we are less inclined to eat, or digest with difficulty what we have eaten, they say is not the fault of cold but of excessive heat; for this happens to us in the summer heat just as it does to the feverish, who, though they burn most fiercely, nevertheless shrink from food, or if they eat, are weighed down rather than refreshed. But this is exactly what I wished to show: that appetite arises from moderate or temperate heat. In this sense it may also be granted that appetite can be aroused by cold, not simply and absolutely, as cold, but insofar as the temperament has been brought into a state tempered with heat and suited to nature.

units.la: IV. Quod deniq; hieme potu frigido minus delectemur, magis autem eduliis calidis, argu-mento esse contendunt, ventriculum hieme frigi-dum esse, non calidum.
units.tr: IV. Finally, they contend that we take less pleasure in cold drink in winter, and more in warm foods, as proof that the stomach is cold in winter, not warm.

units.la: Item quod appetamus vi-na calidiora & generosa ad ventriculum calfaci-endum. Vera hæc esse concedo de iis qui liberiori aeri crebro se exponunt, horum enim ventriculos eduliis calidioribus generosisq; vinis foueri expe-dit, ut a violenti penetrantisq; frigoris ambientis iniuria interiora sint tutiora, fortiusq; circumfusa frigiditati resistant.
units.tr: Likewise, that we desire warmer and more generous wines to warm the stomach. I grant that these things are true of those who often expose themselves to the open air: for it is advantageous that the stomachs of such people be cherished with warmer foods and generous wines, so that the interior parts may be safer from the harm of the violent and piercing cold of the surrounding air, and may resist more strongly the chill that surrounds them.

units.la: Deinde quibus ventriculus est infirmus, generosis vinis eduliisq; calidis quo-cunq;, loco & tempore uti innoxium erit, ut scilicet calor innatus sibi affini & simili adauctus atq; adjutus in vigore & operationibus con-seruetur.
units.tr: Furthermore, for those whose stomach is weak, it will be harmless to use generous wines and warm foods at any place and time, so that the innate heat, increased and aided by what is akin and similar to itself, may be preserved in its vigour and operations.

units.la: AD QVAEST. V.
units.tr: TO QUESTION V.

units.la: An alimentum sit tantum dicendum quod nutrit?
units.tr: Whether food should be defined only as that which nourishes?

units.la: Alimentum familiare, simile, proprium, facultateq; idem cum eo esse quod nutritur, aq; naturæ majestate vnicuique animantium proprium atque peculiare tributum esse, nulli est dubium. Verum cum triplex sit apud Galenum & Medicos alimentum, sciendum quodnam vere & proprie dicatur nutrire.
units.tr: That food is familiar, similar, proper to the one nourished, and has the same faculty as that which it nourishes, and that by the majesty of nature a peculiar and particular allotment belongs to each living creature, no one doubts. But since, according to Galen and the physicians, food is threefold, we must know which is truly and properly said to nourish.

units.la: Primum enim alimentum iis dicitur quod vere & jam actu nutrit: Secundo quod velut nutrimentum est, nondum tamen nutriuit. Tertio quod futurum est, seu aliquando alitu-rum est.
units.tr: For first, that is called food which truly and already actually nourishes. Second, that which is as it were nourishment but has not yet nourished. Third, that which will be food, or will at some time nourish.

units.la: Alimentum igitur quod proximè & proprie nutrit, exquisitè assimilatum esse oportet: quod autem veluti nutriens est, nondum vero nutriuit, cujusmodi est quod agglutinatur & apponitur, æquiuocè nutrimentum est. In venis autem ac in ventriculo magis existens, si probè pleneq, conficiatur, alimentū futurum nuncupatur: atq; hoc est, quod Galenus aphor. 29. l. 5. ait, alimentum non nisi coctum nutrit; qua ratione & modo cibi omnes nutrimenta possunt appellari, non quòd animal iis proximè jam alatur, neque quod tales sint, qualia vere nutrimenta esse oportet, sed quòd probè conse-
units.tr: Therefore the food that nourishes most closely and properly must be thoroughly assimilated. But what is as it were nourishing and has not yet nourished, such as what is stuck on and applied from outside, is nourishment only in an equivocal sense. Food that is more within the veins and the stomach, if it is well and fully digested, is called food that will nourish. This is what Galen means in aphorism 29 of book 5 when he says that food nourishes only once it is cooked. On this principle and manner all foods can be called nourishments, not because the animal is already being nourished by them, nor because they are of the kind that are truly to be nourishments, but because, when well digested and prepared, they will nourish.

units.la: confecti & subacti nutrituri sint: vbiadno-tandum paucos admodum medicos præter v-num Galenum ejusque fectatores has alimen-torum distinctiones nouisse & explanasse.
units.tr: Here it should be noted that, apart from Galen and his followers, very few physicians have known or explained these distinctions of food.

units.la: Ex his facilè patebit alimenti simpliciter sic dicti, alimenti medicamentofi, & medica-menti differentia. Ex propria enim cujusque substantia & forma ea innotescit. Alimen-tum corpori nutriendo ita simile est, vt id nu-triat, augeatque: exuperante vero aliqua qua-litate id immutante, licet substantia quodam-modo sit simile, alimentum medicamentosum est, vt lactuca, vina generosa, mala cotonea, &c. Nulla autem qualitate corpus manifeste afficiente præditum, substantiaque corpori-lendo plane dissimile, neque inter alimenta, neque medicamenta censeri debet. Quod denique in substantia nobis prorsus dispari qualitates ab alimenti natura omnino remo-tas obtinet, corpusque nostrum manifeste immutare aptum est, vsquequaque medica-mentum est, vt hyoscyamus, pirethrum, alu-men, sena, aloe, rhabarbarum, &c. Manife-sta qualitate homines jugulantes, venena sunt & deleteria, vt euforbium, arsenicum, scammonium, antimonium mal-lè præparatum, &c.
units.tr: From these points it will readily be clear what the difference is between food so called in the plain sense, medicinal food, and medicine. For each thing is known from its own substance and form. Food is so similar to the body to be nourished that it nourishes and increases it. But when some quality predominates and alters the body, the food is medicinal, though in substance it is somewhat similar; such are lettuce, generous wines, quinces, and so on. Again, that which has no quality that clearly affects the body, and in substance is wholly unlike the body to be nourished, should be counted neither among foods nor among medicines. Finally, that which in substance is entirely foreign to us, has qualities wholly remote from the nature of food, and is fit to alter our body clearly, is altogether a medicine, such as henbane, pellitory, alum, senna, aloe, rhubarb, and so on. Substances that kill men by a manifest quality are poisons and deadly, such as spurge, arsenic, scammony, and antimony better prepared, and so on.

units.la: Ꝺ
AD QVÆST. VI. An nutritio fit assimilatio?
units.tr: TO QUESTION VI. Whether nutrition is assimilation?

units.la: VEram nutritionem nihil aliud esse, quam eius quod nutrit, assimilationem ad id quod nutritur, seu repositionem, instaurationem vel repletionem eius quod effluxit, in Medicorum scholis tritum est. Verum an nutritio fit assimilatio vel unio, ad unguem nosse poterit nemo, nisi nutritionis modum, eius instrumenta ac gradus pronoverit: hoc enim ignorare, homine, qui eruditus perhiberi vult, nihil turpius: Nempe qua ratione ex pane domorato generetur sanguis, depositio sc. al-bore, sensim ruberem accipiente: sanguine enim facilon i a magno negotio generabitur caro, cum in id, quod natura illius, quod mutatur vicinius est, facilior semper est mutatio. At vero ut sanguis fiat os, multo labore et mutatione opus est, longoque temporis intervallo. Unde nemini mirum videri debet, ea quae nutriuntur singula proprium e sanguine succum primum trahere, toque instrumentis in alendo providam naturam esse usum, ad mutandos, alterandos, perficiendos, deducendosque cibos idoneos. Ac quidem os primus meatus est, quo cibi in ventriculum ingrediuntur, fitque prima quasi praeparatio cibi in ore masticando, dentibusque conterendo, qui postea per oesophagum seu gulam in ventriculum (vulgo stomachum) delabitur ac deducitur.
units.tr: It is commonplace in the schools of the physicians that true nutrition is nothing other than the assimilation of that which nourishes to that which is nourished, or the replacing, restoring, or refilling of what has flowed away. But whether nutrition is assimilation or union, no one can know precisely unless he has examined the manner of nutrition, its instruments and its stages. For to be ignorant of this is most shameful for a man who wishes to be thought learned. Consider how from bread, for instance, blood is generated: the deposit, namely the whitish part, gradually takes on a reddish colour. For flesh is generated from blood without great difficulty, since change is always easier into that which lies nearer to the nature of what is changed. But for blood to become bone, much labour and change are needed, and a long interval of time. Hence no one should think it strange that the parts that are nourished each first draw their own proper juice from the blood, and that nature, provident in nourishing, uses instruments suited to changing, altering, perfecting and conducting the food. The mouth is the first passage by which food enters the stomach, and there is a first preparation of the food in the mouth, by chewing and grinding with the teeth. Afterwards it slips down and is conveyed through the gullet, or oesophagus, into the stomach (commonly called the stomach proper).

units.la: Hic primum subit in cibis laborem, ac insita
units.tr: Here the food first undergoes labour, and the innate

units.la: Prima quadam facultate cibum in substantiam quanda concoctio conuertit, quae dicitur chylus, qui conuenientem adeptus qualitatem in epate postea in sanguinem convertitur, atque hac prima concoctio est, quae fit una vice in ventriculo, s. aut 6. 7. etiam in quibusdam horarum spatio. Huius concoctionis excrementa sunt alui seces.
units.tr: By a certain first faculty, concoction converts the food into a certain substance, which is called chyle. This, having obtained a suitable quality, is afterwards converted into blood in the liver. This is the first concoction, which takes place in one go in the stomach, in some cases in six or seven hours. The excrements of this concoction are the dregs of the bowels.

units.la: Secunda ventriculus igitur chylo satiatus in intestina concoctio[?] expers a cum deponit, ubi vene meseraice sensim fit in epate hunc exugunt, et ad epar amandant, in cuius officio tertia concoctio, quae sanguificationem in singulis corporis membris fit, conficit[?] quae confecta et perfecta tertia subsequitur. Vt autem ventriculus primum ea, quae in esca sunt impura et inutilia dilu-genter repurgat, ita quoq; secoris munus est, utile ab inutili secernere.
units.tr: Then the stomach, having been satisfied with chyle, deposits it into the intestines, where the mesaraic veins gradually draw it out and convey it to the liver. In the liver's office the third concoction takes place, which completes the blood-making in the individual members of the body; this completed concoction follows the third. And just as the stomach first carefully cleanses out what in the food is impure and useless, so too it is the office of the liver to separate the useful from the useless.

units.la: Dum enim succus ille a ventriculo in epar diffusus in sanguinis probe massam alteratur et contertitur, gignuntur duo excrementa, quorum alterum tenue, et quasi innatans spuma, alterum crassum, lutulentumq; est, vtrumq; in fabricatum â natura receptaculum fecregatur, lene illud, spumosum[?] mosum et fatuum vasculo recipitur. Epati adhaerenti, vesicula vocant, coenosum et facculentum in lienem recipitur, aquosus vero ferofus liquor, qui sanguini semper admistus est, eiq; pro vehiculo existit: ob angustiam enim venarum exilitatem, sanguis facile permeare non potest, nisi fluidum quid et aquosum effet, permistum) maneret, suo functionis natura... animalis non amplius[?] utilis, noxius (scilicet & molestu[?] vasorum generi, per renes à sanguine secernitur, perq; exi-tes meatus vreteres dictos in vesicam demissi, & laxatum ibi musculum effunditur excernitur ꝗ, sicq; sanguis ab omni alieno & inutili liquore re-purgatus totum corpus sursum permeat atq; de-orsum.
units.tr: For while that juice, poured from the stomach into the liver, is altered and blended into the mass of the blood, two excrements are generated. One is thin and like a floating foam; the other is thick and muddy. Both are separated into receptacles fashioned by nature. The light, foamy and frothy part is received into a little vessel attached to the liver, which they call the gall-bladder. The thick and dregs-like part is received into the spleen. The watery, serous liquor, which is always mixed with the blood and serves it as a vehicle, is not useful, but harmful to the animal, because the veins are narrow and thin and the blood cannot easily pass through them unless it is fluid and watery and mixed with this. It is separated from the blood by the kidneys, and through narrow passages called ureters it is sent down into the bladder, and there the relaxed muscle expels it. So the blood, purged of every foreign and useless liquor, passes throughout the whole body, upwards and downwards.

units.la: Atq; tantum de nutritione & nutritionis mo-do, vbi & gradus annotasse oportebit, nam ipsam naturam gradatim in ea procedere spectatur, suc-cus enim ille, qui omnes animalis partes nutritur ꝗ est, in eas primum diffunditur, seu apponitur, seu dispergitur, mox agglutinatur, deinde assimilatur & vnitur.
units.tr: Thus much concerning nutrition and its manner, where it will also be fitting to note the stages. For nature is observed to proceed in this gradually. That juice, which is the nourishment of all the parts of the animal, is first diffused into them, or applied, or dispersed; then it is stuck on, and then assimilated and united.

units.la: Sunt itaque ad nutritionem gradus necessarii appositio, agglutinatio, assimilatio & vnio. Vl-timus igitur nutritionis gradus est vnio eius, quod nutrit cum parte nutrienda. Si enim, quod nutri-re carnem debet, in locum eius, quæ abiit, succede-re, atque idipsum fieri, quod illa fuerat, oportet, necessario sequitur, illud ipsum carni quæ nutri-tur, primò assimilari, deinde vniri, hoc est, carnem specie & natura fieri eandem cum ea, quæ nutritur, & quod talis caro fieri non potest, nutrimentum eius esse non potest. In vera igi-tur nutritione idem restituitur in locum euacua-ti, & quod in vacuati locum per nutritionem suc-cedit, proprium est & familiare, vnde alimen-tum dicitur facultate idem cum eo esse quod nutrinutritur, idq; veritas pronunciati illius Physicæ confirmat, vnumquodq; scil. eo nutriri, ex quo de principio constiterit, cuius sepe apud Galen. & A-ristot. fit mentio.
units.tr: There are therefore necessary stages in nutrition: application, agglutination, assimilation and union. The last stage of nutrition, then, is the union of that which nourishes with the part to be nourished. For if what is to nourish the flesh must succeed into the place of that which has departed, and must become the very thing that the other was, it necessarily follows that it is first assimilated to the flesh that is nourished and then united with it; that is, the flesh becomes the same in kind and nature as that which is nourished. And since such flesh cannot be made, it cannot be its nourishment. In true nutrition, therefore, the same thing is restored into the place of what was emptied, and what succeeds into the place of the emptied part through nutrition is proper and familiar. Hence food is said to have the same faculty as that which it nourishes. The truth of that physical proposition confirms this, namely that each thing is nourished by that from which it has its origin, a point often mentioned in Galen and Aristotle.

units.la: Nec obstat, quod diuersitas reb. vescamur, quod multis esculentis vtantur, quib. diuersa animalia gaudent, nam de vltimo alimento, videl. sanguine accipienda est prædicta enunciatio. Sanguis enim, licet ex variis cibis conficiatur, natura tamen in eius costione partes tantum cognatas & homogeneas colligit, nostris vero corporibus inimica separat & secernit, & sic nobis reddit familiarem. Idem de aliis animalibus iudicandum est. Est enim suus & canes pane nobiscum vescerentur, nontamen eundem specie sanguinem, eundem nostro generarent, quia non eodem modo coquuntur, nec eadem partes segregant, quas noster calor separat: quod manifestum primo euadit ex specie excrementorum, qua qualitatibus & substantia sunt dissimilia: deinde quod nostris delestantur, sua abominantur:
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that we eat various things, and that many foods are used which different animals enjoy. For the aforesaid statement must be understood of the final food, namely blood. For blood, although it is made from various foods, nevertheless in its concoction nature gathers only parts that are kindred and homogeneous, and separates and secretes what is hostile to our bodies, and so makes it familiar to us. The same must be judged of other animals. For though dogs eat bread with us, they would not generate from it the same blood in kind, the same as ours, because it is not cooked in the same way, nor do they separate the same parts that our heat separates. This is first made plain from the kind of excrements, which are unlike in quality and substance; and then because they delight in our things, while they loathe their own.

units.la: Cur exe-adem materia & alimé-to in di-uersis a-nimalib° non ge-neretur idem fan-guis?
units.tr: Why does the same blood not arise in different animals from the same matter and food?

units.la: nunquam vero id facerent, si non in nostris relin-querentur partes ipsis gratae: quare alias partes no-si natura, alias ipsorum inter coquendum fer-mauit ac reiecit, alterq; omnes coxit & mutauit, vtitatidem sanguis non sit, qui ex eadem materia genitus est. Causa hæc est, quod idem agens res di-uersis agentibus eodem modo non alte-ratur & immutatur. Nunquam igitur calor ignis expane facit sanguisanguinem & chylum, quod ventriculi calor facit. Nunquā epar expane chylum, sicut nec ex chylo venter unquam producet sanguinem. Idem chylus aliter ab eodem epate sano & agro permutatur, sanum chylum in sanguinem bonum, agrum, ut in hydrope, in aquam convertit.
units.tr: They would never do so, if the parts pleasing to them were not left among ours. For nature sets aside some parts and, during digestion, they reject others; so they cook and change everything else, and the blood is not the same, even though it was generated from the same matter. The cause is this: the same agent does not get altered and changed in the same way by different agents. So fire's heat never makes blood and chyle out of bread, as the heat of the stomach does. Nor does the liver ever make chyle out of bread, just as the stomach never produces blood from chyle. The same chyle is changed differently by the same liver, when it is healthy and when it is diseased: a healthy liver turns the chyle into good blood, but a diseased one, as in dropsy, turns it into water.

units.la: Et tantum de hac quaestione.
units.tr: And so much for this question.

units.la: AD QUÆST. VII. An morbi communes etiam oriantur ex[?] malorum ciborum copia & culpa?
units.tr: AD QUÆST. VII. Whether common diseases also arise from a surplus and fault of bad foods?

units.la: MOrbus communis dicitur, non tantum qui causam habet communem, actuque uno tempore plurimos corripit, sed etiam qui ad plures alios sese per contagium potest extendere & promouere. Causa communis est nō solus aer, verum etiam aqua putris, cibus aut potus vitiosus. Hic igitur quaeritur, num morbi cōmunes, puta pestis, origine trahant à malorum ciborum culpa? Sunt qui pestis seminaria in solo aere ponūt. Alii ex hominum tantum corporibus pestis contagia effundi arbitrantur. Alii hoc ipsum negant. Quidā ex aeris coeliq; iniuria, ut magnis & insolitis tempestatibus, magnis planetarum coniunctionibus. Verum neque in solo aere pestis seminarium contineri, neque ex aeris semper iniuria coeliq; inclementia dependere, neq; ex hominum corporibus tantum erumpere oftendunt[?] putridi illi halitus ex lacubus, spelúncis[?], brutorum cadaueribus putrefactis exhalantes corporaq; noftra inficientes.
