Qui verò ex hu-manis corporibus, diæteq; culpa, vt ptauis ali-mentis humoribusq; putridis, communes mor-bos oriti poffe inficiantur, contendentes mor-bum communem effe, cuius femper commu-nis fit caufa, videlicet aer venenatus, conta-giofus, nonconfiderant poffe in nobis ge-nerari fubftantiam quandam eiufdem cum ve-neno ideæ[?] & characterifmi, æquè pernitiofam contagiofamq; vt ipfa peftilens eft. In annonæ æftuantis caritate quot funt qui alimentis prauis, vt bulbis, brafficis, raphanis, cæpis, oleribus agreftibus, radicib?, arborumq; foliis & germinib?, vefcétes grauiffimis poftea mor-bis correpti funt? eiufmodi cibis magnos fæpè exercitus deletos effe conftat. Validos exerci-tus fœdarum aquarū potū concidiffe, quin etiā frugū viciatarū vfu, hiftorie tradunt. Fit namq; interdū vt diutiffimè feruata frumenta ac cere-alia femina putrefcant, & malè condita repofi-taq; humoré contrahant atq; fitū. Hipp. refert; eos qui leguminib? in Ænofame prémente in cibatu vfi fuiffent, crurib. debilitatos, genuúq; dolore tentatos: quafdam n.tetras iniqui fucci legumina oleraq; producere in cófeffo eft. Sed quid multis? Ex variis cibis diuerfarū qualitatū, viriūq; contrariarū difficiles & contumaces ægritudines generari nemo inficiabit, qui alios acres,alios falsos, alios summè frigidos, cali-dos,humidos,siccos,austeros,astringentes, a-maros,alios deniq; venenosis qualitatibus esse praeditos, vt cicutā,ferulā,tytimallū, hyoscya-mū, quib. saepe homines in famis inclementia vescuntur,praenouerit. Sic Gal.ex semiputrido tritico morbū ortū communé asseruit. Ex vitiosę cereuisiae potu,quę ex semiputrido hordeo parata fuerat,vidi vno in loco tépore eodé,multos decubuisse eodé morbo,aliis sic nuspiā affectis. Aliquot ab hinc annis celebratae sunt nuptiae in quodā pago,in quib.cū carnes ob ae-stum putrescere coepissent, quidā ex illis,q; eas auidius comedissent,decubuerunt,plures verò ex contagione in eundem morbū lapsi perie-runt.Proinde cauendū vnicuiq; imprimis est, ne improbi succi cibos vsurpet,vnde tot valetudini vitaeq; ipsi incommoda impendent.
units.tr: A common disease is called one that not only has a common cause and attacks many at the same time, but also one that can spread and pass on to many others by contagion. The common cause is not only the air, but also putrid water and tainted food or drink. So the question here is whether common diseases, such as plague, derive their origin from the fault of bad foods. Some place the seeds of plague in the air alone. Others think the contagion of plague is poured forth only from human bodies. Others deny even this. Some ascribe it to an injury of the air and the sky, such as great and unusual storms or great conjunctions of the planets. But that plague is not contained in the air alone, nor does it always depend on an injury of the air or on the harshness of the sky, nor does it burst forth only from human bodies, is shown by those putrid exhalations from pools, caves and rotting carcasses of beasts, which poison our bodies. Those who insist that common diseases can arise from human bodies and from the fault of diet, from bad foods and putrid humours, maintain that a common disease is one whose cause is always common, namely a poisonous and contagious air; they do not consider that in us there can be generated some substance of the same nature as the poison, with the same form and character, as deadly and contagious as the pestilence itself. In a time of dear grain, how many are there who, eating bad foods such as bulbs, cabbages, radishes, onions, wild herbs, roots, and leaves and buds of trees, were afterwards seized by most grievous diseases? It is established that large armies have often been destroyed by such foods. Histories relate that strong armies have collapsed from drinking foul water, and even from using spoiled grain. For it sometimes happens that grains and seeds stored for a very long time rot, and when badly preserved and stored they contract moisture and mustiness. Hippocrates reports that those who in the time of Aenofame ate pulses were weakened in their legs and troubled by pain in the knees; for it is agreed that certain pulses and vegetables produce foul humours from a bad juice. But why say more? No one will deny that various foods of diverse qualities and contrary powers generate difficult and stubborn sicknesses. Anyone who considers that some foods are sharp, others salty, others very cold, hot, moist, dry, astringent, bitter, and others endowed with poisonous qualities, such as hemlock, giant fennel, spurge, and henbane, on which people often feed in the harshness of famine, will see this. Thus Galen asserted that a common disease arose from half-rotten wheat. I saw, in one place and at the same time, many people fall ill with the same disease from drinking beer made from half-rotten barley, while others were not affected in this way anywhere. Some years ago a wedding was celebrated in a certain village, where, since the meat had begun to rot in the heat, some of those who had eaten it more greedily fell ill, and more who fell into the same disease by contagion died. Therefore everyone must above all take care not to consume foods of bad juice, from which so many discomforts to health and life threaten.

units.la: AD QUÆST. VIII.
units.tr: AD QUÆST. VIII.

units.la: An ciborum natura & potestas ad varia gentium ingenia moresque aliquid conferat?
units.tr: Whether the nature and power of foods contribute anything to the varied dispositions and customs of peoples?

units.la: ADmiranda plane gentium populorumq; deprehenduntur ingenia, variiq; animo-rum mores. Hos autem temperatu-ram corporis sequi, temperaturam vero con-stare succorum spirituumq; confusione, atque com-moderaPersea non est vulgaris pomi Persici arbor, vt quidam putant. moderatione testes praeter Platonem sunt Philoso- phi & Medici. Pro ciborum autem diuersitate & mutatione temperamenta variari [?] q, immutari non inficiasiturus est, qui alimentorum vim me- morabilem ac singularem ab omnibus Philosophis celebribus, Medicis proditam considerauit. Per-se [?] pro moniana sua & inhospita regione plantam ac fertilem occupare cupiuerunt : Vetus [?] Cyrus, quod sciret, vt plantis femina, sic hominum vitas regionibus similes fieri.
units.tr: Truly wonderful dispositions of nations and peoples are discovered, and varied customs of minds. Now that these follow the temperament of the body, and that the temperament consists in the mixing and moderation of the humours and spirits, is witnessed by philosophers and physicians, besides Plato. That the temperaments vary and are changed with the diversity and change of foods, no one will deny who considers the remarkable and singular power of foods, recorded by all the famous philosophers and physicians. [Persea is not the common Persian peach tree, as some think.] Cyrus, knowing that, just as plants become like their seeds, so the lives of men become like their regions, wished to occupy a fertile plant in his own mountainous and inhospitable region.

units.la: Planta enim quae transferuntur saepe toto genere immutari conspiciuntur. Causam praecipuam nutrimento affcribunt naturae prudentes, quam & caeli virtus hic non est proscribenda, plurimum enim referre testibus quotidiana experientia est. Ex ferocibus & syluestribus quia negabit vrbanas fieri & mites plantas? Coeli solique mutatione naturam immutare tam est verum quam quod verissimum. Exigui namque interualli mutatio ac- què translatio hoc est, suorum trium plurimum passuum transitus maximas efficit differentias. Arbores translatas mutari, fatis testatur Persea, quae in Perside natapestilens est, seferuntur deportata ur- ro & translata in Aegyptum mutata natura in cibos recipitur, succosq, noxios deponit. Sape arbor leta acnitens in aliquam trapofita locum deteriorit terra succo & alimento deperuisse visa est. Arbores fotelus, Plato, Theophrastus, ceteriq, Philosophi, quid de sito orbis literis mandarunt, si animan- tia ab alimentis immutari testantur superiorum verò aquarum mirabili vi id contingere prodiderunt. Traduntur & inveniuntur fontes, amnes, lacusq; quorum hausta memorabiles & insignes fiunt alterationes: sunt quaedam aquae quae nigredinem, quaedam quae candorem potu pecoribus afferunt.
units.tr: For plants that are transplanted are often seen to be changed in their whole kind. Wise men ascribe the chief cause to nourishment, though the power of the sky is not to be excluded here, for everyday experience bears witness that it makes a great difference. Why would anyone deny that wild and savage plants become cultivated and gentle? To change nature by a change of sky and soil is as true as what is most true. For even a slight change of place, a transfer of only three or so miles, makes the greatest differences. That transplanted trees are changed is well attested by the Persea, which, being native to Persia, is deadly there; but when it is carried and transplanted into Egypt, its nature is changed, it takes in food and loses its harmful juices. Often a tree that seemed healthy and flourishing in some transplanted place has been seen to deteriorate, having lost its strength from the soil and its nourishment. What Theophrastus, Plato and other philosophers committed to writing about the situation of the world, if they testify that animals are changed by their food, and have declared that this happens through the wonderful power of the waters above? It is also reported and found that springs, rivers and lakes, by drinking from which, become remarkable and notable alterations: some waters bring blackness to cattle that drink them, others whiteness.

units.la: Apud Æthiopes Macrobios quib. dimidio vita protensior est quam nostra, est lacus, quo perfusa corpora velut oleo nitescunt, adeoq; nitidus est, ut ne caducas quidem vehat frondes, sed illico folia lapsa ad fundum demittat laticis tenuitate.
units.tr: Among the Ethiopian Macrobii, whose lives are about half again longer than ours, there is a lake in which bodies bathed in it shine as if with oil; and it is so clear that it does not even carry falling leaves, but at once lets the fallen leaves sink to the bottom because of the thinness of its water.

units.la: In oppido Garamantum [?]Debri fons est alternis vicibus die frigens, noctu fervens: ac per eadem venarum commercia interdum igne vapore æstuat, interdum glaciali horrore algescit. Quis non miretur fontem frigere calore, calere frigore? occasu enim mundum a calore temperante ita incipit incalescere, ut intactu abstineas, contigisse noxium sit. Rursus cum ortu solis incanduerit radiisq; ferventa sint omnia, sic glaciales euomit scaturigines, ut hauriri etiam a sitientibus nequeat. Stupenda sane & incredibile memoratu, quod tam brevi temporis curriculo natura tam dissonam sui faciat mutationem. Scamandrus ille Homericus exiguo amnis Xanthus appellatus, existimatur, quod flamas redderet oves. Euenire autem id a succo, quem ex terris, per quas transeunt, fluunt, concipiunt, manifestum est. Nam & arborum plantarum radicis succos ex terra visceribus sugere trahere, inq; alimentum convertere ostendunt alii aliq alii saporem differentiaq; fructum[?]. Quod si enim sic nō nutrirentur, unus effet omnium in omnibus sapor frugum, fructuum, aliorumq; feminum. Arabia, India, Syria, caeterarumq; regionum poma & fruges tanta gustus odorumq;, varietate non distinguere-tur, nisi terra dissimilia succorum genera continerent. Hinc tot vinorum genera prodigiosa. Vinum in Arcadia foecunditatem feminis apporrare, vis autem rabiei in Arcadia quoddam genus esse, quae abigatur part[?], Trochenii potu non generare, aliud quod somnum conciliet, alterum quod perniciem faciat, etiam usam esse, quae abortus faciat, & haud dubie terrarum maleficos pestilentesq;, succos, aquas & fruges fructuumq;, omnes noxios infalubresq;, reddere, ut a quibus alantur, & nutrimentum capiant, apud gravissimos auctores Aristotelem, Theophrastum, Athenaeum, Plinium, & alios scriptum repe-ritur. Differentiam aquarum quotidie sentimus, de quib. alibi seorsim[?], Deo dante, & copiose differemus.
units.tr: In the town of the Garamantes, Debri, there is a spring which by turns is cold by day and hot by night; and through these exchanges of its veins it sometimes boils with fire and steam, and sometimes grows cold with icy chill. Who would not marvel that a spring is cold from heat and hot from cold? For at sunset, when the world's temperate heat begins to lessen, it grows so hot that you must abstain from touching it, as touching it would be harmful. Again, when the sun rises and it has grown hot and all things are glowing with rays, it pours forth icy springs, so that not even thirsty people can draw from them. It is truly astonishing and incredible to relate that nature makes so unlike a change in so brief a course of time. That famous river of Homer, called Scamander, was thought to be a small stream named Xanthus, because it made the sheep yellow. It is clear that this happens from the juice which the waters take up and carry from the earth through which they flow. For others show that the roots of trees and plants suck up juices from the bowels of the earth, drawing them and turning them into nourishment, and some give one flavour and others another to their fruit. For if they were not nourished in this way, there would be one taste of all fruits, produce and other seeds in everything. The fruits and crops of Arabia, India, Syria and other regions would not be distinguished by such a variety of tastes and smells, unless the soil contained kinds of juice differing from one another. Hence come so many prodigious kinds of wine. It is written by the most weighty authors, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Athenaeus, Pliny and others, that wine in Arcadia brings fertility to seeds, while there is a certain kind in Arcadia which drives away the part; that a Trochenian drink does not generate, another which induces sleep, another which causes destruction, and that they also use one which causes abortion; and that the poisonous and pestilential juices, waters and crops of the lands, and all fruits, make harmful and unwholesome whatever they nourish and from which they take nourishment. We daily perceive the difference of waters, of which, God willing, we shall speak elsewhere separately and at length.

units.la: Sed ad animalia pergamus, quae quibusdam in locis carent felle, praesertim in parte quadam agri Chalcidici. In Euboea pecora eo carent, quod non aliunde quam a pabulo accidere indubitatum putatur. In Ponto quoq; eo carent, quae vescuntur absinthio, cum tamen illo eximie pinguescant.
units.tr: But let us pass on to animals, which in some places lack gall bladders, especially in a certain part of the Chalcidic region. In Euboea the cattle lack it, which is thought beyond doubt to come from nothing but their fodder. In Pontus too they lack it, those that feed on wormwood, although they nonetheless fatten up remarkably well.

units.la: Gallis gallinaceis in officinis Ferrariis educatis, lienem non reperiri certissimi auctores tradunt.
units.tr: Certain authorities report that domestic cocks raised in the Ferrara workshops are found without a spleen.

units.la: Pecora, quae in alveis aut canalib. ex Tamarisco fabricatis bibunt, sine splene inveniuntur, cum primis suis. Unde praeceptum est lienosis & melan-colis cibum potumq; dare in vasis ex ea factis.
units.tr: Cattle that drink from troughs or channels made of tamarisk are found without a spleen, along with their first offspring. Hence the rule that people with spleen trouble and melancholy should be given food and drink in vessels made of it.

units.la: In Naxo fere omnib. quadrupedib. adeo gran-de fel esse Aristot. scripsit, vt qui sacra fecerint ad-uena, stupescant, rem scil. prodigii loco arbitrantes: quam sane amplitudinem, vel a potu, vel a pabu-lo contingere verisimile est.
units.tr: Aristotle wrote that on Naxos almost all four-footed animals have so large a gall bladder that strangers who make sacrifices there are astonished, regarding the thing as a portent. It is indeed probable that this great size comes either from their drink or from their fodder.

units.la: In suibus & anseribus dulcibus cibariis enutri-tis iecur incredibile pene incrementum assumere omnib. non est nō notum: unde veteres culinaria in o-peribus ganea mirifice id commendarunt.
units.tr: It is not unknown to anyone that in pigs and geese fed on sweet food the liver takes on an almost incredible growth; for this reason the ancient cooks in their works praised it wonderfully.

units.la: Mille vescentes populos longam ætatem age-re & sanam[?], Athenæus testis est. Septentrionis quidam populi id optime norunt, mulsam bibendam iis præcipientes, qui animi sunt præparati & pusilli, quasi eius miti leniq; succo vis anima robo-retur atq; augeatur. Celebre est Pollionis Romuli exemplum, quem centesimum excedentem annum, cum Augustus Cæsar hospes interrogaret, qua-nam ratione maxime vigorem illum animi cor-poriq; custodivisset, ille respondit, intus mulso, foris oleo.
units.tr: Athenaeus is a witness that a thousand peoples live a long and healthy life. Certain northern peoples know this very well, prescribing mead to those who are timid and of weak spirit, as though the strength of the soul were strengthened and increased by the mild and gentle juice of it. The example of Pollio Romulus is famous: when Augustus Caesar, as his guest, asked by what method he had so long preserved that vigour of mind and body, he being past a hundred years of age, Pollio replied: "Mead within, oil without."

units.la: In Hispaniola insula greges pecorum ex nostris terris in ea deportatos, papulo quidē illius soli pin-guescere, verum carnes eorum in cibis insuaves esse & sentiri testantur, qui de sitz orbis nuper inventi li-teris mandarunt: Quin ossa eorum aut medullæ ex-pertia inveniri, aut si continent, aquosiore omni-no spectari, sues quoque tales in insula egregie obesari a-greftib. pomis, carnesq; gustui incudiores nancisci, cicures item sues in sylvas feros effici, & sylvestres quibusdam in locis suis nostris minores, cauda pedibusq, dissimiles carnes prabere maxime falsta-res pracipuiq, saporis experimento compertu bambent. Id quod cibariorum praftantia & natura tribui vere potest.
units.tr: Those who have recently written letters from the New World, from the regions of that new-found orb, testify that herds of cattle brought over to the island of Hispaniola from our lands grow fat on the pasture of that soil, but that their flesh is unpleasant to eat and tastes of it. They also report that their bones and marrow are found empty, or, if they contain marrow, that it appears altogether more watery. Pigs of this kind, they say, are excellently fattened on the island by wild fruits, and they obtain flesh less pleasing to the taste; likewise domestic pigs become wild in the woods, and wild ones in some places become smaller than ours, unlike in tail and feet; and they are found to yield meat that is most savoury and of a special flavour. This can truly be attributed to the excellence and nature of the food.

units.la: In hominibus memorabilis horum natura non minus conspicua est, cum proipforum diuersitate & mutatione temperamenta immutentur. Quis enim ignorat, temperatas escas, boniq, succì cibos, temperatos humores spiritusq, puriores gignere, indeq, mentem puriorem, defecatiorem & prudentiorem euadere, rationemq, constantiorem & solidiorem effici. Animum adipe & sanguine suffocatum nihil cœleste sublimeq, meditari posse, Galen asserit.
units.tr: In human beings the notable nature of these things is no less evident, since the temperaments are changed by the difference and alteration of the foods themselves. For who does not know that temperate foods and wholesome juices produce temperate humours and purer spirits, and that from these the mind becomes purer, clearer and wiser, and reason is made steadier and more solid? Galen asserts that a soul choked with fat and blood cannot contemplate anything heavenly or lofty.

units.la: Vinum prastantissimum nutrimentum vtentium moribus sese applicare non negabit, quistar-diores eo incendi & excitari mobiliores reddi, contra vero mobiliores dissolui pigrofq, reddi, obser-uarit, vt ita nunc retardos, nunc superbos, nunc infanibundos efficiat. Zeno dicere solitus est, se à vino perinde affici atq, lupini ab aqua, qui in ea macerati omnem amaritudinem deponunt, dul-cesq, reddantur.
units.tr: No one will deny that wine, the most excellent nourishment, adapts itself to the habits of those who use it: he who has observed that those who are sober are warmed by it and roused, and that the more lively are dissolved and made sluggish by it, so that it makes some slow, others proud, others raging. Zeno used to say that he was affected by wine in the same way as lupins by water: when they are soaked in it they lose all their bitterness and become sweet.

units.la: Cœlum, solumq, maximum momentum ad facili-ores difficiliores q, cibos generandos obtinere, naturæ rerum prudentes vnanimi afferunt consensu.
units.tr: Those who know the nature of things agree unanimously that the sky and the soil have the greatest influence in producing foods that are easier or harder to digest.

units.la: Nec dubium est pro cœli aeriq, clementia ac benignitate solum quoq, succos benignos adipisci atq, salubres, quibus deinde enutrite plantæ alimenta exhibet[?] salubriora. Vnde cœli, quo necessario[?] cun[?]Ela aluntur, aerisq; sub Luna concavo temperatura statuq; imprimis animadvertenda. Tempora enim anni si sunt constantia, & tempestiue tempestiua in iis omnia reddunt, fructus quoque terrae meliores proueniunt atq; utiliores. Quod si praepo-sterae sint tempora & intempestiua, terra etiam fundet dabitq; alimenta infalubriora, ut si frigora sint intempestiua, imbres & calores intepestiui & immoderati. Ab his enim corporis temperationem deprauari, animiq; mores mirum non est. Obser-uatur hoc in tractibus & regionibus, in quib. coelu adeo est iniquum & invidum, ut temporum anni temperatum ordinem non seruet, unde incolarum ingenia animiq; mores necessario etiam intemperantiam non mediocrem sortiuntur. Hippocrates morum temperaturas locis aeriq; acceptas retulit. Vult enim mores temperatos & probos fieri in locis & terris temperatis, contra in intemperatis. Ideoq; Europaeos feros, indomitos, iracundos & in-sociabiles aferit: Asianos[?] mitiores, ignauos, imbel-les animisq; abiectiores: quod etiam a Lucano di-[?]lum eleganter reperio,
units.tr: And there is no doubt that, through the mildness and kindness of the sky and air, the soil also acquires kindly and wholesome juices, by which the plants nourished in turn provide more wholesome food. Hence the temperature of the heavens, by which the things that necessarily nourish us are sustained, and of the air beneath the concave of the moon, must above all be considered. For if the seasons of the year are steady, and each season yields everything at its proper time, the fruits of the earth also come forth better and more useful. But if the seasons are out of order and unseasonable, the earth too will produce and give less wholesome food; for example, if the colds are unseasonable and the rains and heats unseasonable and immoderate. For it is no wonder that the temperament of the body is thereby corrupted, and the morals of the mind. This is observed in regions and climates where the sky is so unkind and hostile that it does not keep the temperate order of the seasons; hence the dispositions and morals of the inhabitants necessarily acquire no small intemperance as well. Hippocrates ascribed the temperaments of morals to places and to the air. For he wishes morals to become temperate and upright in places and lands that are temperate, but the opposite in intemperate ones. Therefore he calls Europeans wild, untamed, quick to anger and unsociable; Asians milder, lazy, unwarlike and of more abject spirit. I find that Lucan also expressed this elegantly:

units.la: Emollit gentes clementia coeli.
units.tr: The mildness of the sky softens nations.

units.la: Temporibus autem anni omnia haec imputantur. Faba, teste Theophrasto, quodam in loco ab af-flatu quodam incoctilis est: fruges item & reliqua femina cerealia a succo telluris[?], in quam seruntur, incoctilia proueniunt. Haec igitur in cibatu probi alimentum minime dabunt, corpus namq; atq; animum deprauabunt. Galli fe- Gallis leuitatem innasci, & audaciam omnib* cundum fere Romanis historiis proditum est, cuius causam Iul. C. & nullam aliam crediderim, quam coeli inconstan- alios le- ... Intemperatam enim Galliam esse, affidius, ues & cau- flatibus agitari confiat, quin & crebrioribus im- daces, fi- bribus obnoxiam. Proinde licet vinorum omnium, tisq; im- fere cibariorum ad vitam sustinendam necessario- patientes, rum feracissima sit, non tamen adeo salutaria a-limenta [?] quod patet in tritici probatione apud Theophrastum & Plinium.
units.tr: All these things, moreover, are attributed to the seasons of the year. Beans, according to Theophrastus, grow in certain places as a result of a certain blast of wind; grain and the other cereal seeds likewise come forth from the juice of the earth in which they are sown, as if cooked. These, therefore, will by no means give a good man nourishment in his food, for they will corrupt both body and mind. It is said, almost according to Roman histories, that lightness and boldness are inborn in the Gauls; I would believe the cause of this, as Julius Caesar's, to be nothing other than the inconstancy of the sky. For it is established that Gaul is intemperate, stirred by constant winds, and, moreover, subject to more frequent rains. Therefore, although it is most fertile in all wines and in nearly all the foods necessary for sustaining life, it does not have foods so wholesome, as is clear from the testing of wheat in Theophrastus and Pliny.

units.la: Aphros & maxime Carthaginenses perfidos o- minimum confessi dictos inuenimus, Memorabile illud Cic. est in Orat. pro l. Agraria, dum ait, ingenerari hominibus mores non tam a stirpe generis & feminis, quam ex his rebus, quae ex ipsa natura loci, & a vita consuetudine suppeditantur, quibus alium [?] visitimus. (Chartaginenses mendaces sunt ac fraudulenti non genere sed natura loci, quod propter portus suos multis & variis mercatorum adventantium sermonibus ad studium fallendi studio quaestus ducebantur.
units.tr: We find that Africans, and especially the Carthaginians, are called faithless, and this is confessed by almost all. That famous saying of Cicero is in the speech for the Agrarian law, where he says that morals are produced in men not so much by the stock of their race and their seed as by those things which come from the very nature of the place and from the habits of life that they are supplied with, by which we are led to other things. (The Carthaginians are liars and deceivers, not by their race but by the nature of their place: because of their harbours, from the varied talk of many arriving merchants, they were led by the desire of gain to the practice of deceiving.)

units.la: Ligures montani duri atque agrestes sunt, quod docet ager ipse nihil ferendo, nisi multa cultura labore quaesitum.
units.tr: The Ligurians of the mountains are hard and rustic, as the land itself shows, bearing nothing unless it is won by much cultivation and labour.

units.la: Campani semper superbi, ob agrorum bonitatem, fructuum magnitudinem, urbis salubritatem.
units.tr: The Campanians are always proud, on account of the fertility of their fields, the size of their fruits, and the healthfulness of their city.

units.la: Hispanos ac Lusitanos iactabundos & aestuosos videmus, quae partim a solo caelo, partim a vita accidere dubium non est.
units.tr: We see the Spanish and the Portuguese to be boastful and fiery, and there is no doubt that this comes partly from the soil and sky, partly from their way of life.

units.la: Aristot. in animantibus a sanguinis consistentia & & substantia petere videtur prudentiam, fortitudinem, timiditatem. Tenuem enim & purum atq; mundum sapientiores efficere credidit. In quibus e- nim humor subtilior atq; purior, ius sensus quoque subtiliores puriores atq; insunt: timidiores qua aquo- sim nimis & dilutum obtinent: animosos, irascun- dos, furibundos, quibus crassius biliosus & feruens. Sanguis enim quia ultimum corporis alimentum habetur, alimentū ante materia est, facit vt per- multa animalib. eueniant, tum per mores, tum per sensum, si calidi aut frigidi existat, tenuis & crassus, turbulenti, splendidus aut nitidus. Hæc Arist. Plato huic suffragatur, improbos succos corporis anima noxios esse volens, indeq; varios & multiplices, graviores & leviores agritudines exoriri, quæ eam pro loco adquē resederint, afficiunt. Vnde ad principem eius facultatem denuenientes oblitiones, atq; hebetudines, convulsiones, stupores, tremores, phrenitides, melancoliam, vertiginem, apoplexias, lethargos: sin ad cor, iracundias, audacias, timiditates, febresq; inferent.
units.tr: Aristotle, in his book on animals, seems to seek prudence, courage and timidity from the consistency and substance of the blood. For he believed that thin, pure and clean blood makes people wiser. For in those in whom the humour is finer and purer, the senses too are finer and purer, and are present in them; those who have a rather watery and diluted humour are more timid; the spirited, the angry and the furious are those with a thicker, bilious and fervent humour. For since blood is regarded as the final nourishment of the body, it is the material that precedes the others, and it makes many things happen to animals, both in their morals and in their senses, whether it is hot or cold, thin or thick, turbid, bright or clear. So Aristotle. Plato supports this, holding that corrupt humours are harmful to the soul, and that from them arise various and manifold diseases, both graver and lighter, which affect the soul according to the place where they settle. Hence, when they reach its chief faculty, they bring forgetfulness and dullness, convulsions, stupors, tremors, frenzies, melancholy, vertigo, apoplexies, lethargies; but when they reach the heart, they bring anger, rashness, timidity and fevers.

units.la: Idem animam corporea humiditatis potestate in oblivionem labi eorum, quæ ante, quàm corporis effet coercita vinculis, coperta habebat, videturq; sentire, nimiam hanc humiditatē esse causam dementiæ & stultitiæ, siccitatem vero ad prudentiam adipiscendam plurimum conferre. Quorum igi-tur corpora sunt humidiora, vt in terris frigidis & humidis, minus sunt prudentes calidiq;, sed simplices: at calidarum & siccarum terrarum populi versuti & prudentes indicantur. Hinc gra-ci lenes & mendaces quidem, sed ob aeris siccitate sapientiores. Itali prouidi ingeniosi & Venerei sunt, teste Vitruuio, Gasconès iracundos & furi-bundos dicunt non aliam ob causam, quam quod bilioso imprimis victu vtantur, allio, scilicet, cepis, raphanis, vinisq; vehementissimis.
units.tr: The same Plato thinks that the soul, through the power of bodily moisture, slips into forgetfulness of those things which it held in mind before it was confined by the bonds of the body; and he seems to hold that this excessive moisture is the cause of madness and foolishness, while dryness contributes greatly to the attainment of prudence. Therefore those whose bodies are moister, as in cold and wet lands, are less prudent and hot-tempered, but simple; whereas the peoples of hot and dry lands are reckoned crafty and prudent. Hence the Greeks are gentle and, indeed, deceitful, but wiser because of the dryness of the air. The Italians are provident, ingenious and fond of love, according to Vitruvius. The Gascons are called angry and furious for no other reason than that they use a diet especially rich in bile: garlic, onions, radishes, and very strong wines.

units.la: Verum ingeniorum morumque varietatem, non naturae loci tantum, vitae consuetudini, aeris tem-peries intemperiei, verum etiam generis stirpi femini non raro acceptam ferendam esse, fate-bitur, qui animum ad similitudinem causas retu-lerit. Deprehendet certè mirum naturae artificium ingenium.
units.tr: Yet the variety of talents and manners must be attributed not only to the nature of places, to the habits of life, and to the temperate or intemperate character of the air, but also, not rarely, to the stock of the race in the female line. Anyone who has looked into the causes by analogy will admit this. He will surely discover in it the marvellous craftsmanship of nature.

units.la: Sepe in familiis transitus fit per sobolem, Vi-deniss plerumq; parvulos modo cicatrices, modo qualescunq; origines fuenotas ferre.
units.tr: It often happens in families that a trait passes down through the offspring, who usually seem to bear small scars or other marks of origin, of whatever kind they are.

units.la: Bizantius nobilis pugil, qui matrem habuit ex Æthiope per adulterinum conceptam, quæ nihil patrem comparandum reddidisset, in Æthiopem aerum degeneravit.
units.tr: Byzantius, a noble boxer, whose mother had conceived him with an Ethiopian through adultery, a union which left the father in no way comparable, degenerated into the appearance of an Ethiopian.

units.la: Regem Antiochum Arteon quidam ex plebe Syriaca, sic facie amulâ mentitus est, ut possimo-dum Laodicea uxor regia obiecta papulari isto tam-dius, diffimulasse defunctum maritum, quoad ex arbitrariu sius regni successor ordinaretur.
units.tr: A certain man from the Syrian common people so falsely imitated King Antiochus Arteon in appearance that Laodice, the royal wife, put this impostor before the people and for so long pretended her husband was still alive, until a successor to the kingdom was appointed by her decision.

units.la: Inter Cn. Pomp. & Vibium bis mili loco natum, tantus error extitit de patribus lineamentis, ut Ro-mani Vibium Pompeii nomine Pompeium Vibii vocabulo cognominarent.
units.tr: Between Gnaeus Pompey and Vibius, who were born in the same place, such a great resemblance of features arose that the Romans called Vibius by the name Pompey and Pompey by the name Vibius.

units.la: Oratorem L. Plancum Rubrium Histriofic expressit, ut & ipse Plancus a populo nominaretur.
units.tr: He made the orator L. Plancus look like the actor Rubrius, so that Plancus himself was called Rubrius by the people.

units.la: Armentarius Mirmillo & Cassius Severus oratorita se reddiderunt mutuo ut si quando pariter viderentur, dignosci non possent, nisi discrepantiam indicaret habitus.
units.tr: Armentarius the Mirmillo and Cassius Severus so resembled each other that when they were seen together they could not be told apart, unless the difference in their dress showed it.

units.la: M. Messala Censorius & Menogenes ex facie vulgi, hoc fuerunt uterq;, quod singuli, nec alium Messalam quam Menogenem, nec Menogenem alium quam Messalam putarunt.
units.tr: M. Messala the Censor and Menogenes were so alike in the common view that each took the other for himself: Messala thought there was no Messala but Menogenes, and Menogenes thought there was no Menogenes but Messala.

units.la: Quid? quod n[?]stro etiam seculo nostrisq; inter-ris indiscreti vulgus corporisq; miracula exstet. At licet plerique sentiant, nullum posse excedere 7.pedū longitudine, quod intra hunc modum fuerit Hercules, deprehensum tamen est Romanis temporibus sub D. Augusto Pusionem & Secundillam denos pedes & amplius habuisse proceritatis, quorum reliquiæ adhuc in conditorio Sallustianorum ante annos aliquot visæ sunt: Sicut postmodū sub D. Claudio principe nomine Gabbaras ex Arabia advectus novem pedum fuit & totidem unciarum quamuis annis ferme mille ante Augustū huiusmodi forma non apparuit, sicut nec post Claudium visa est.
units.tr: What of our own time, when among our contemporaries there still exist monstrous wonders of body and of the crowd? Although most people think that no one can exceed seven feet in height, which was the measure of Hercules, it has nevertheless been established that in Roman times, under the deified Augustus, Pusio and Secundilla had a stature of ten feet and more, whose remains were seen some years ago in the burial place of the Sallustians. Likewise later, under the emperor Claudius, Gabbaras, brought from Arabia, was nine feet and as many inches tall; yet almost a thousand years before Augustus no such form appeared, and none was seen after Claudius.

units.la: Scripta quoq; ex antiquitate memorias revocant in fidem veri, quod bello Cretico, cum elata flumina impetu plus quam vi amnica inuecta terras rupissent, post fluctuum discessum inter plurima alia humanum cadauer repertum sit cubitum trium atq; triginta, cuius spectandi cupidine L. Flaccum Legatum, atq; Metellum ipsum, quod
units.tr: Written records from antiquity also confirm the truth of such things by recalling that in the Cretan war, when rivers swollen beyond the force of any river had burst over and broken the lands, a human corpse of thirty-three cubits was found among very many other things after the waters withdrew. Out of eagerness to see it, the legate L. Flaccus and Metellus himself, who had rejected the report on hearsay,

units.la: auditu refutarant, cum oculis aspicerent, miraculo quasi captos, eadem memoria receptum est. Non omiserim Euthymenis filium Salamiam, qui in triennio creuit in sublimitatem tria cubita, sed incessu tardo, sensu hebeti, robusta voce, pubertate festinâ, verum morbus statim plurimus vexatus immoderatis aegritudinum suppliciis praecipitem incrementi celeritatem compensavit.
units.tr: looked at it with their own eyes, and were struck as if by a marvel; the same record has preserved this. I should not omit Salamis, son of Euthymenes, who in three years grew to a height of three cubits, but with a slow gait, a dull sense, a robust voice, and hasty puberty; yet he was at once beset by much sickness, and the severe torments of his illnesses made up for the headlong speed of his growth.

units.la: Possem hic multa adducere, quae fastidio parcens praetereo. Vide Solinum cap. 5.
units.tr: I could bring forward much more here, but out of distaste I pass it over. See Solinus, chapter 5.

units.la: AD QVAEST IX.
units.tr: TO QUESTION IX.

units.la: Morbi quòd quibusdam gentib. peculiariter accidant, an victus ratio incausa sit? & cur repente quidā hominib. exoriantur in certis membris? consuetudinem deniq; plurimum valere.
units.tr: Whether diseases arise peculiarly among certain peoples, whether the manner of diet is not the cause, and why some men suddenly break out with illness in certain limbs; and finally, how greatly custom prevails.

units.la: Morborum plurimorum causam vel abundantiam, vel cibariorum diversitatem esse, potissimam vero rerum naturalium abusum, illegitimā intempestiuamq; earum administratione, (vt cū bona dieta negligitur, aerq; male affectus non corrigitur, cū euacuatio, retentio, somnus, vigilia, & affectus animi finistrē & immoderate se habent) inter omnes Medicinę peritos conuenit. Quosdam etiam morbos terris quibusdam & populis peculiares esse, quos aeris coeliq; inclementior status improborumq; alimentorum vsus excitare consueuit, notius est quàm vt explicari fusius debedebeat. Quosdam verò repetè certis membris innasci, hominib. optima etiam constitutione praeditis à natura, mirabile aliquib. videbitur, praesertim iis qui ignorant cibaria, per quae vi-vunt. Elephantiasin Ægypti peculiare malum esse, Alexandrinosq; magis infestare, vt quorū victus ex farina elixata est & lentib. quae illic in magna copia proueniunt, testatur ille, qui Elephantiasin morbū esse scripsit nascentē propter flumina Nili in media Ægypto. Vescuntur item cochleis & salsamētis largissimè, asininis quoq; nonnulli carnib. quę crassos succos atraq; bilem pariunt, qui poftmodū humores ob cœli feruidam constitutionem ad cutim euocati eā foeda ficcaq; scabie deformant, evaditq; morb. plane detestandus, elephantorum cuti similis, per multa durans secula, & quasi haereditario jure pertinaciter etiā in posteris haerens. Britones, Nortmanni & Narbonensis provinciae populi huic malo sunt opportuniores. Apud Pleumofios, vulgo Flandros, frequentissimū est. Caulae adscribuntur esui piscium creberrimo & liberaliori, tū potib. ex corruptis frugib. cócin-natis, operi ite lactario, quo imodice eos vti conflat: quamuis Gal. nusquam hunc morbum apud Scythas, quos [illegible, ~12 letters] nūcuparūt, vagari censet: quin & in Germania haereditaria eam esse, rarissime sentitur, vt plurimum verò per contagium inducitur. Italiae ante Pompeii M[?]agni aetate ignota fuisse Elephantiasin Plin. constanter aflerit , vt ita nullum hodie fit du- bium Alexandrinorum mores, delitiafque oes Asianas Italiam inuasisse. ' Carbuncalum Narbonensi prouinciæ pe- culiarem, & Parthis obindifcretos cibos, gra- uem oris halitum esse testatur idem. In Alpibus aliifq; regionibus aquarum vi- tio atq; culpa homines gutturofos effici testis experientia est. Strumosi magis Lufitani. Hippocr. Eunuchos podagra non laborare scripsit in Aphor. quod tamen Galen. diligen- tissimus ejus interpres suo suo aliter contigit, seuidit , ob malam scilicet viuendi rationem, Podagram Italiæ incognitam aliquando fuisse traditum est, colicumq; dolorem Tiberii prin- cipatu irrepsisse, nec quenquam priorem ipso Imperatore id malum sensisse : Nunc per oēs gentes disseminatum pertinacissime durat. Lues Venerea, quæ ab Hispanis ortum ha- buit, Hispanis primum & Gallis peculiaris su- it, nunc ex Venereo concubitu vniusq; impu- ritate & inquinamento sensim in vniuersum orbem est disseminata. Scorbutus, pessimus corporis humani in- quilinus, non ita pridem Septentrionis gentes & loca maritima arctica inhabitantes cœpit af- sigere, germ. Schurbock/Schurmund, alio- cis in quibus externis signis primo malitiam suam & contagium prodidisse compertum est: Septen- Vere-
units.tr: It is agreed among all skilled in medicine that the cause of most diseases is either excess or variety of foods, but above all the misuse of the natural things, through their illegitimate and untimely handling (as when good diet is neglected, the air is not corrected when it is ill-disposed, when evacuation and retention, sleep and waking, and the affections of the mind are disordered or immoderate). That certain diseases are peculiar to certain lands and peoples, which the harsher state of the sky and air and the use of bad foods are wont to stir up, is too well known to need explaining at length. That certain diseases repeatedly arise in certain limbs, even in men endowed by nature with the best constitution, will seem marvellous to some, especially to those who do not know the foods by which they live. Elephantiasis is a peculiar evil of Egypt, and it chiefly attacks the Alexandrians, as he testifies who wrote that elephantiasis is a disease arising from the rivers of the Nile in the heart of Egypt, since their diet consists of boiled meal and lentils, which grow there in great abundance. Some also eat snails and salted foods very freely, and some eat asses' flesh, which produce thick humours and black bile; these humours later, because of the hot climate, are drawn out to the skin and disfigure it with a foul, dry scab, and the thoroughly detestable disease results, like the hide of elephants, lasting through many ages and clinging stubbornly, as if by hereditary right, even to descendants. The Britons, the Normans, and the people of the province of Narbonne are more liable to this evil. Among the Pleumosii, commonly called Flemings, it is very frequent. It is ascribed to the very frequent and more generous eating of fish, to drinks made of corrupted grain and fermented, and to that milk-diet, by which it is clear they use it immoderately. Although Galen thinks this disease nowhere wanders among the Scythians, whom [illegible] they called..., and though it is very rarely felt in Germany as hereditary, it is for the most part introduced by contagion. Pliny firmly asserts that elephantiasis was unknown in Italy before the time of Pompey the Great, so there is now no doubt that the customs and luxuries of the Alexandrians and of all Asia have invaded Italy. The same writer testifies that the carbuncle is peculiar to the province of Narbonne, and that the Parthians have a heavy breath from indiscriminate foods. Experience bears witness that in the Alps and other regions people become goitrous through the fault and defect of the waters. The Lusitanians are more often afflicted with goitre. Hippocrates wrote in the Aphorisms that eunuchs do not suffer from gout; yet Galen, his most diligent interpreter, observed that this happened otherwise to him, namely because of a bad manner of living. It is recorded that gout was once unknown in Italy, and that colic crept in under the principate of Tiberius, and that no one before the emperor himself had felt that disease. Now it has spread through all peoples and lasts most stubbornly. Venereal disease, which had its origin among the Spaniards, was at first peculiar to the Spaniards and the French, and now, through venereal intercourse and the impurity and pollution of everyone, it has gradually spread through the whole world.

units.la: Veteres de eo nihil certi prodiderunt, nisi quòd gingiuarum affectum stomacacen dixerunt, cum videlicet illis corrosis & putrefactis dentes cum foedo odore, vel sponte excidunt, vel digitis apprehensi absque ulla molestia & dentifrangibulo eruuntur. Origo huius mali non aliunde est quàm ex rancidorum, salidorum, induratorum infumatorumque alimentorum continuo esu usuq;, cereuisiaeq; praepinguioris & dulcioris potu, unde sensim & paulatim, assiduaq; vitae affluetudine primum sanguinis oficinam lienemq; adoritur inficitq;, tandem irrepit absque ullo etiam doloris sensu in omnes partes, gingiuas tamen primum & dentes inuadens, liuidis etiam quandoq; & fuscis maculis crura circa tibias inprimis deformans cum genuum dolore, quod malum scelotyrbe dicitur certissimum & confirmati scorbuti signum, non enim quaeuis gingiuarum putrilago foetorq; scorbuti index est, ut temere & imperite chirurgi opinantur, cum saepe gingiuae ex acri-um calidorumq; humorum superno affluxu inflammentur, & putrescant, scorbuticæ vero gingiuarum putrilaginis origo ab epate semper ac liene dependet, meatuumq; inter haec viscera obstructione.
units.tr: The ancients delivered nothing certain about this, except that they called the affection of the gums stomacace, namely when the teeth, with the gums corroded and rotten and a foul smell, either fall out of their own accord or are taken hold of by the fingers and drawn out without any pain and without a tooth-puller. The origin of this evil is nothing other than the constant eating and use of rancid, salted, hardened and smoked foods, and the drinking of very fatty and sweet beer; from these causes it gradually and little by little, through a continual abundance of life, first attacks and infects the workshop of the blood and the spleen, and at last creeps into all parts without any sense of pain, attacking the gums first and the teeth, and also marking the legs, especially around the shins, with livid and dusky spots, with pain in the knees. This evil is called scelotyrbe, and it is a most certain sign of confirmed scurvy. For not every putrefaction and stench of the gums is an indicator of scurvy, as rash and unskilled surgeons suppose; the gums are often inflamed and rot from an upward flow of sharp and hot humours, but the origin of scorbutic putrefaction of the gums always depends on the liver and spleen, and on obstruction of the passages between these viscera.

units.la: Quamobrem minime mirum videri debet, si noui quotidie & priori aeuo incogniti acci-dunt morbi, ex terrisq; in alias terras transfe-runtur ac deportantur, & peculiariter quibus-dam
units.tr: It should therefore seem not at all surprising if new diseases, unknown in earlier ages, arise every day, and are carried and transported from lands into other lands, and befall certain peoples in particular; and that certain people may suddenly be born with such afflictions and break out in certain limbs. For when a new way of living is adopted and introduced into our lands from foreign ones, who will deny it, or who will not think that from the badness of foods...

units.la: dam gentibus contingunt: etiam quosdam hoc minib. repente nasci & exoriri in certis mem- bris posse. Cum enim ratio viuendi noua vfur- petur,& ex alienis terris in nostras introduca- tur, quis inficias ibit, vel non censebit à cibo- rum improbitate gulæq; intemperie certis et- iam membris morbos importari posse? Ab In- discibum petentes contagium simul sperare oportet. Nam quis salubritatem in peregrinis illis & incognitis spondeat? Quot sunt, quoru renes grauiter tentantur calculo? Colica quot torquentur? quot vehementissimis capitis do- loribus? quot stomachi dolore debilitateque? oculorum hebetudine atq; caligine quot? quot digitorū manuumq; sæuissimis tormentis ex- cruciantur? Immodicum horum omnium v- sum improborum ciborum auctorem esse ar- gumento est, quod ipsa anima ciborum vitiis inficitur, id quod Parthis precipue accidere ob cibos indiferetcs, dictum est.
units.tr: ...dam peoples, and that some diseases happen to certain peoples; and that men may even suddenly be born with, and arise in, certain limbs. For when a new way of living is adopted and carried over from foreign lands into ours, who will deny, or fail to think, that diseases in certain limbs may be brought in by the badness of foods and by intemperance in eating? Those who take up Indian foods must also expect to catch their infections. For who can vouch for the wholesomeness of those strange and unfamiliar foods? How many have their kidneys grievously troubled by stone? How many are racked by colic? How many suffer the most violent headaches? How many are wracked by stomach pain and weakness, by dullness and dimness of the eyes, by the most savage torments of fingers and hands? That excessive use of all these bad foods is the cause is shown by the fact that the very soul is infected by the faults of foods, which, as was said, happens especially to the Parthians because of their indiscriminate eating.

units.la: Sed id nunc terris etiam nostris familiare est: & verisimile est ejusmodi animas peftilen- tes fieri haud aliter atq; innocua quædam ani- malia, quæ venenis pasta noxia fiunt & ipsa, vt apri in Pamphilia. Ergo vitæ multum interest, diligenter considerare quibus alamur cibis. Siquidem qualis natura fuccîq; cibi extiterint, talem quoq; sanguinem, h.e. ipsos corporis hu- mores praftabunt, crassos, lentos, vifcidos, te- nues, calidos, frigidos, mordaces, acres, qui in partes aliquas imbecillas delapsi illicq; confi-stentes dolores excitant & morbos, quifq; pro naturæ suæ & loci etiam cui impactus & infar-ctus est, conditione, vt minum non fit quam-obtem, qui fine delectu cibos ingerunt nul-lamq; rationem alimentorum habentinfignes corpore mutationes sentiant, variofquæ mor-bos. Corpus scatens atra bile hanc referet, morbisque atrabiliariis obnoxium est: pituitâ refertum carnem pituitofiorem referet, & fe-rosam.
units.tr: But this is now common in our own lands too, and it is likely that such people become pestilential in soul, just as harmless animals, fed on poisons, become noxious themselves, like the boars in Pamphylia. Therefore it matters greatly to life to consider carefully what foods we are nourished by. For whatever the nature and juices of a food are, such will be the blood, that is, the very humours of the body it produces: thick, sluggish, viscous, thin, hot, cold, biting, sharp, which, sinking into some weak parts and lodging there, provoke pains and diseases, each according to the nature of its own kind and the condition of the place where it is lodged and blocked. So it is no wonder that those who swallow foods without discrimination, with no regard for what nourishes them, notice remarkable changes in their bodies and various diseases. A body full of black bile will reproduce that, and is liable to melancholy diseases; a body stuffed with phlegm will produce flesh that is more phlegmatic and also fierce.

units.la: Verum consuetudinem, vt in aliis multis, ita in cibis plurimùm valere non est dubium. Id quod peregrinantes,& continuas commef-sationes voluptatis & honoris gratiâ agentes, dum à domestica affluetudine recedere cogun-tur crebrò experiuntur.
units.tr: But that custom counts for a great deal in food, as in many other things, is beyond doubt. Travellers experience this often, and those who keep up constant feastings for pleasure and for the sake of status, when they are forced to leave their domestic abundance behind.

units.la: Nec in hominum solùm genere, sed & in pecorib.quoq; id spectatur. Insueta enim pa-bula, tota plerumq; armenta totosq; greges p-diderunt. Peregrina namq; licet suauia sentiã-tur & facilia, vescentibus tamen insignem af-fe-runt mutationem & perturbationem. Alexan-dri exercitum in India ciborum nouitate pene deletum historia proditum est: quin & in ea-dem India apud Arianam gentem repertus est frutex pestilens, lauri folio, odore equos invi-tante atq; alliciente, qui penè omni equitatu Alexandrum orbauit, & quidem primo in-troitu. Incolis autem iste propter affluetu-dinem dinem minus noxius, adeò à tenèris assuescere multum est.
units.tr: This is seen not only in the human race but also in cattle. For unfamiliar pastures have often destroyed whole herds and whole flocks. Foreign fodder, though it seems pleasant and easy, brings a striking change and disturbance to those who eat it. History tells that the army of Alexander in India was nearly destroyed by the novelty of the food; and indeed in the same India, among the Arian people, there is found a pestilent shrub with the leaf of a laurel, whose smell invites and attracts horses, and which all but robbed Alexander of his whole cavalry, and that at the very first encounter. For the inhabitants, because of their long familiarity with it, are less harmed by it; so much does it matter to be accustomed to such things from childhood.

units.la: Qui nostra memoria de situ orbis Indici nuper patefacti scripserunt, variis ægritudini-bus incommodisque affectos primo intuitu prodiderunt eos, qui illuc commeárant, tum ob cœli mutationem, tum vero & inprimis ob pomorum radicumq;, quibus salubriter vescebantur incolæ, atq; etiam ipsorum animalium esum.
units.tr: Those who have written in our own time about the situation of the recently opened Indian world reported that those who travelled there were at first sight affected by various sicknesses and discomforts, both because of the change of climate and especially because of the fruits and roots on which the inhabitants fed healthily, and also because of the eating of their animals.

units.la: Quid? quod mirabilius possit videri quod Mithridates maximus sua ætate Regum quo-tidiè bibere venenum excogitauit, ut scilicet consuetudine redderetur innoxium, clandesti-nasque epularum insidias euitaret, quo etiam pacto tutum corpus aduersus veneni pericula effecit. Sic enim de eo Martialis l. 5.
units.tr: What could seem more remarkable than that Mithridates, the greatest king of his age, devised daily drinking of poison, so that by habit he would be rendered harmless, and might avoid secret plots at banquets; and in this way he made his body safe against the dangers of poison. For Martial speaks thus of him in book 5:

units.la: Profecit potò Mithridates sæpe veneno / Toxica ne possent sibi nocere sibi.
units.tr: Mithridates indeed often profited from poison, so that poisons could not harm him.

units.la: Consuetudine prætereà venena inalimo-niam conuerti Indica testatur puella, ab Indo-rum Rege Alexandro Regi dono missa, illius contagioso concubitu ut inficeretur, & anus illa attica, quæ à momento cicutæ, quod natu-ra euincere & concoquere posset, assuetum integros cicutæ manipulos innoxiè devorare, cū cicutæ succus eiusq; puluis sit lethalis[?], aliàs & soporiferum venenum, id quod Atheniensium supplicia indicant, qui morte condemnatos sorbitione cicutæ interemerunt, quàm & So-cratem. cratem impietatis condemnatum in carcere hausisse ferunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Indian girl testifies that by habit poisons are turned into nourishment: she was sent as a gift to the king of the Indians, Alexander, so that she might be infected by his deadly embrace; and that old Athenian woman, who, accustomed to swallow hemlock from the very beginning, could eat whole bundles of hemlock without harm, since she could overcome and digest what nature allows. Yet the juice of hemlock and its powder is lethal, and otherwise a soporific poison. The executions of the Athenians show this, who killed those condemned to death by having them drink hemlock; and they say Socrates, condemned for impiety, drank it in prison.

units.la: Eadem pene ratio Pharmacorum & medi-camentorum quorundam est, quorum vires in assuetis debiliores deprehenduntur, in nonnullis etiam plane inertes. Quicquid enim à natura, calore, aut cogenita vel ex consuetudi-ne acquisita corporis proprietate alteratum in corporis alimoniam conficitur & digeritur, id alito venenum esse non potest, adeo plurimum pollet consuetudo & natura acquisitita, vt scil. qui venenorum esui sensim assueuere, congeniti caloris substantia existente forti, ea tandem digerant, iisque alantur, sicque in nutrimentum versa medicamentorum nomen plane amittant, id quod non in Attica illa anu tantum, quae ab initio cicutae momentum hauriens, ad liberalissimum haustum progressa sine vllo valetudinis incommodo diu superstes mansit, manifestum est, sed etiam id factitasse alios in historiis reperitur, & quidem, qui Elleborum, opiumq; in magna quantitate deuorarunt innoxiè, teste Theophrasto, quod hodie adhuc ipsos Turcas factitare audio. Refert Theophrastus, quosdam totos Ellebori manipulos esitasse, nihilq; affectos esse, Chiumq; Eudemum viginti duos aliquando haustus Ellebori uno etiam die sumpsisse. Anus attica triginta cicutae succi potiones tolerauit, vt ita manifestum sit, omnem cibum similem debere esse ... nutrito, nec omnem cibum omnibus conue- nire, ob proprietatem quandam temperaméti quæ omnibus cibariis ineft, huicque naturæ confentiens eft, illi vero auerfatur atq; contra- ria eft. Sic fuibus ferpentes aprifque propabu- lo funt: generi gallinaceo bufones, araneæ & colubri: coturnicibus & furnis helleborus & cicuta: anatibus hyofcyamus, bufones, ferpé- tes, ranæ, &c. Sibi igitur conueniens & familiaris aréalimentum áflumens calorifq; beneficioin fuam naturam conuertens natiui caloris fub- ftantiam augeri fentiet: quod enim fecundum naturam eft, fuaue eft & gratum, & carum cui- que fuaueque eft, quod per & fecundum natu- ram habetur. Sic biliofis mel eft infeftum, pi- tuitofis fuaue & familiare: acria, falfa, amara pituitofis magis quam biliofis conueniunt, vt non tàm vefcendorum, quàm vefcentium ra- tio hic habenda fit, &c.
units.tr: There is almost the same reasoning for certain drugs and medicines, whose powers are found weaker in those accustomed to them, and in some cases quite inert. For whatever is altered by nature, by heat, or by a bodily property either innate or acquired by habit, and is then prepared and digested into the body's nourishment, cannot be poison to the one who takes it; so much does habit and acquired nature prevail, that those who have gradually grown accustomed to eating poisons, when the substance of their innate heat is strong, at last digest them and are nourished by them, and so, turned into nutriment, they entirely lose the name of medicines. This is clear not only from that Attic old woman, who, starting with the power of hemlock, advanced to very large draughts and remained long alive without any harm to her health; but it is also found in histories that others have done the same, namely those who swallowed hellebore and opium in large quantities without harm, as Theophrastus relates, and as I hear the Turks themselves still do today. Theophrastus reports that some ate whole bundles of hellebore and suffered nothing, and that Eudemus of Chios once took twenty-two doses of hellebore in a single day. The Attic old woman endured thirty drinks of hemlock juice. So it is clear that every food ought to be similar to and nourishing for the one who eats it, and that not every food suits everyone, because of a certain property of temperament which is in all foods: it agrees with one nature and is opposed and contrary to another. Thus serpents and wild boars are food for pigs; toads, spiders and snakes for the fowl kind; hellebore and hemlock for quails and thrushes; henbane, toads, serpents and frogs for ducks, and so on. Therefore one who takes in food suited and familiar to him, and turns it by the benefit of heat into his own nature, will feel the substance of his natural heat increased; for what is according to nature is sweet and pleasing, and dear to each, and sweet to each, which is held to be so through and according to nature. Thus honey is hostile to the bilious, while it is sweet and familiar to the phlegmatic; sharp, salt and bitter things suit the phlegmatic more than the bilious, so that here the question is not so much of the foods as of the people who eat them, and so on.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: De Primo, & vario mirabiliq; diuerfifi- marum gentium victu.
units.tr: On the primitive and varied, and wonderful, diets of the different peoples.

units.la: Ibariorum facultates nofe ad unguem, vite hominum, fupra quam cuiquam cre- dibile eft, utile erit. Sunt enim non morbo- rum tantum, fed & fecundæ valetudinis commu- nia prafidia: nec valetudo noftra ftabiliri firma- rig, potest, fi fundamenta corporis, b.e. fucci, quib. &c nu& nutritio ipsa & vita subsistit, vitiosa sint. Itaq; in alimentorum variis generib. viribus & natura studiose enucleandis atq; explicandis animus occupatus est, quantum per naturam licebit ei esse sagaci & industrio. Sed prius de primo mortalium & postea vario genitu quae nostro victu & in cibis delectu differendum est, ut sc. palam fiat, victus hominum gradus quosdam habuisse, quibus a summa rusticitate & feritate ad humaniorem elegantiorem eq; & tandem ad celsa luxuriae fastigia devenentum fit.
units.tr: It will be useful to know thoroughly the resources of human life, beyond what anyone would believe. They are the common safeguards not only against disease but also of good health. Our health cannot be established or made firm unless the foundations of the body, that is, the juices on which nutrition and life itself depend, are sound. So the mind has been occupied with the various kinds of foods, and with studiously unfolding and explaining their powers and natures, as far as nature allows a mind to be shrewd and diligent. But first we must discuss the diet of the earliest mortals and then the varied diets that arose later, which have a bearing on our own way of living and on the choice of foods. This will make clear that the diet of humankind passed through certain stages, rising from the greatest rusticity and savagery to a more civilised and refined way of life, and at last to the lofty heights of luxury.

units.la: Constat autem inter omnes tum Philosophos tum historiarum scriptores, primum hominum genus in sylvis & nemoribus, ut feras degisse, ac glandiferis baccijerisq; arboribus victitasse, h. e. sylvas arboresq; prima mortalibus alimenta suppeditasse in glandibus, pomis ac baccis.
units.tr: It is agreed among all philosophers and historians that the first human race lived in forests and groves like wild beasts, and fed on acorn-bearing and berry-bearing trees. That is, the woods and trees supplied the first mortals with food in acorns, fruits and berries.

units.la: Deinde ex hac vita in aliam descenderunt pastoritiam. Etenim ex animalibus ob eandem vitalitatem sylvestria deprehenderunt atq; manusfecerunt, inter quae oves primum assumtas verisimile est, tum propter placiditatem, aptissima enim sunt ad vitam hominis, ad cibos, caseum ac butyrum, tum propter corporis tutelam & vestitum, ad quem vellera adhibuerunt.
units.tr: Then from this life they descended to another, the pastoral. For, on account of the same need for sustenance, they caught wild animals and tamed them, and among these it is likely that sheep were taken up first. They were chosen for their gentleness, since they are very well suited to human life, providing food, cheese and butter, and also for the protection and clothing of the body, for which people used their fleeces.

units.la: Tertio a vita pastorali ad agriculturam animum adhibuerunt, qua maxime accepta vitae fuisse satis testantur populorum erga eam amor ingens & diligentia admirabilis, cum illis seculis nihil antiquius habuerint, quam agros studiose excolere, illumq; amplissime laudatum existimabant, quae virum bonum colonum appellari audirent, tunc, pascua & fruges folaregum & gentium vetlngalia erant, annonae, vilitas erat incredib lis: haudq, dubie aurea illa secula vere extiterunt, in quibus tam innocenti vitu homines uterētur,is vid. qua benigna tellure prouenirent vescentes, eoq, quod honestis excultum effet manibus.
units.tr: Thirdly, from the pastoral life they turned their minds to agriculture. That this was most welcomed in life is sufficiently attested by the great love and remarkable diligence that peoples showed towards it. In those ages they held nothing more important than cultivating the fields diligently, and they thought a man was praised most highly when he was called a good farmer. Then pastures and crops were the common wealth of kings and nations; provisions were abundant and prices incredibly low. Indeed, those golden ages truly existed, in which men lived on such innocent food as the kindly earth produced for those who ate it, because it had been tilled by honest hands.

units.la: In hoc caelesti munere quantum vita posteapro- fecerit, & quantum foleruia ingeniaq, hominum curam eam per gulam irritamenta auxerint, satis superq, testatur aureum illud vita genus jublatu, luxuria gradu repente innecto & jubfecuto: atq, hic postremum gradus nostri [?]seculi est: hac vita, quam beatiorem solent dicere, quinouis mo- rib. & luxui fauent. Hinc tot panificii genera, tot pulmenta, tot cofeta, tot obsonia parantur, atq, conflantur in usus vitae hominum, tot denique videas lautitias atq, deliciasque fine quib. vita vix possit consistere, & creditur, a ganeoforum portentosis ingeniis excogitatas. Verum non unum olim fuisse gentium victum, sed varium mirabilemq, imo innumeros & totidem pene quot gentes hominum[?] numeros, lingua, testatur inter alios, quires populorum historia prodiderunt, quiq, de situ orbis monumenta reliquerunt, Iul. Caef. in Clarissimis illis suis commentariis de rebus bellicis. Non solum enim Gallorum alium fuisse victum, alium Britannorum, alium vero Germanorum prodidit, verum etiam inter ipsos Germanos varium eum extitisse mirabilem, atq, etiam inter ipsos Gallos.
units.tr: How far later life progressed beyond this heavenly gift, and how much the rising pleasures and talents of men, through gluttony, increased the cares of that life, is amply shown by the fact that the golden way of life was abolished. Luxury followed suddenly and stepped in close behind it, and this is the last stage of our age. This is the life that people call happier, and it favours every kind of vice and extravagance. Hence so many kinds of bread, so many dishes, so many confections, so many delicacies are prepared and compounded for the uses of human life. In short, you may see so many luxuries and pleasures, without which life could scarcely continue, and they are believed to have been devised by the monstrous talents of gluttons. But that there was once not one diet for all peoples, but a varied and wonderful one, indeed countless ones, almost as many as there are nations and tongues, is attested among others by Julius Caesar in his most famous commentaries on his wars. Those who have handed down the histories of peoples, and who left records of the world's geography, have also testified to this. Caesar not only reported that the diet of the Gauls was one thing, that of the Britons another, and that of the Germans yet another, but also that among the Germans themselves there was a remarkable variety, and likewise among the Gauls.

units.la: Apud Petragonos & Lemouicos castanea & rapa à vino & melle tertium honorem adpi-scebantur: rapa etiam Allobrogibus & Subaudis in cibis mirifice grata, sicut & castanea montanis Lugdunensibus fuere.
units.tr: Among the Petragorians and the Lemovices, chestnuts, turnips, wine and honey held the third place of honour. Turnips were also wonderfully pleasing in the food of the Allobroges and the Subaudi, as chestnuts were among the mountain-dwellers of Lyon.

units.la: Montium Cemannorum populi Aruernis & Velleis proximi vice panificii vtebantur, & etiamnunc vtuntur castaneis, quippe festis tantum diebus, vel non infima sortis ac fortuna homines panificium illic ex frugibus vsurpant.
units.tr: The peoples of the Cevennes mountains, next to the Arverni and the Vellavi, used chestnuts in place of bread, and still use them today, but only on feast days. Or men of no low rank and fortune there take bread made from grain.

units.la: Gasconum gens Aquitaniæ nobilissima inter præcipua pulmentaria alia habet & cepas, quorū olfactum & gustatum in delitiis gula vertit & suauia condimenta: hi nunc quoq; pra cæteris Gallis ventri indulgere magis creduntur: vulgatum enim & maxime nobilitatum apud eos jactatur prouerbium, satius esse ventrem belle farcire epulis, quam corpus veste molli & pretiosa ornare, adjuntq; Burgundioni ventrem esse sericeum.
units.tr: The Gascons, a most noble people of Aquitaine, have other choice side dishes, and onions, whose smell and taste the palate turns into delights, and pleasant seasonings. These people are even now believed to indulge the belly more than other Gauls. For the widespread and most celebrated saying among them runs that it is better to stuff the belly well with feasts than to adorn the body with soft and costly clothing. They add that a Burgundian has a silken belly.

units.la: Aruerni caseo frequentius vtitare consue-uerunt.
units.tr: The Arverni were accustomed to use cheese rather often.

units.la: Nortmanni malis pyrisq; crudis ac coctis vē-scebantur liberaliter, suosq; ex illis concinnabant potus, carnibus praterea omnigenis vtebantur.
units.tr: The Normans ate apples and pears, raw and cooked, generously, and made drinks from them. Besides, they used meats of every kind.

units.la: Narbonensis Gallia pisces habet frequentes, tum sale conditos, ante cuncta autem oleuas condi-tas capparesq; manducat, ficus item vuasq; recentes, mala citria, arantia, limones inter lautiores cibos habet & gula irritamenta: vina apud eos generosissima: oues pascuntur thymo, quo pabulo mire pinguescunt. Armonicarum regionum populi inter se vi-vendi ratione differunt.
units.tr: Narbonese Gaul has many fish, both salted and fresh; above all, it eats pickled olives and capers, and likewise fresh figs and grapes. Among its more luxurious foods and provocations of the palate it has lemons, citrons, oranges and limes. Its wines are very fine, and its sheep are fed on thyme, by which fodder they grow remarkably fat. The peoples of the Armorican regions differ among themselves in their way of living.

units.la: Brittones enim & Brittonifantes vi&lu ma-gis utuntur fero & barbaro : at Gallobrittones maximam civilitatis urbanitatis, Francica partem frequentant, apud quos panificia lauta ex frugib. parantur, vinaq, non ignobilia abfarbentur.
units.tr: For the Britons and the Britons-in-Gaul live on rather wild and barbarous food. But the Gallo-Britons, who frequent the greatest part of civility and urbanity, that is, the Frankish part, prepare fine breads from grain, and drink wines that are not contemptible.

units.la: De moribus Germanorum prodidit Cornelius Tacitus, quod cibi illis olim fuerint simplices, agrestia poma, recens[?] fera aut lac concretum si-ne apparatu, sine blandimentis ad famem sedan-dam, sed adversus sitim non eandem fuisse tempe-rantiam, quoniam diem noctemq; in potu continuarent, qui mos apud illos nostra etiam memoria pertinacissimè perdurat, ut videantur ad perden-da vina genitiq[?], nomine nunc apud Romanos, Hispanos & Gallos male audiant, quamuis cer-tum est Germaniam a Romanis minimè fuisse cognitam: & hodie, licet longè mitiori ur-baniores[?], victu degant vivandi[?], nihilominus ta-men ferina & prisca illius vita vestigia quaedam retinuerunt, maximè quo propiùs accedunt ad Septentrionem.
units.tr: Cornelius Tacitus reported about the customs of the Germans that their food was once plain: wild apples, fresh game, or curdled milk, without preparation or delicacies, serving only to satisfy hunger. But their restraint against thirst was not the same, since they kept up their drinking day and night. This custom among them has lasted very stubbornly even in our own memory, so that they seem to have been born to squander wine, and among the Romans, Spaniards and Gauls they now have a bad name for it. Yet it is certain that Germany was little known to the Romans. And today, although the more civilised Germans live on much milder food, they have nonetheless kept certain traces of their wild and ancient way of life, especially the more closely they approach the North.

units.la: Britanni qui nunc Angli, pecorum magnum numerum, leporem vero, gallinam, anse-remq; gustare fas non putabant, animi tantum vo-luptatuq[?] gratiâ educabant. Hodie à pristinis illis moribus longè recesserunt, humaniores facti, in-que omni exercitiorum[?] genere (corporis puta & animi) spectabiles, Cœlum temperatius illis esse quam Gallis, frigoriq; asperitatemq; ab iis abesse experientia abunde testatur.
units.tr: The Britons, who are now the English, did not think it right to taste a great number of sheep, nor hare, hen or goose; they bred them only for the sake of pleasure and delight. Today they have departed far from those old customs and have become more civilised, and they are notable in every kind of exercise, both of body and of mind. The sky is milder for them than for the Gauls, and experience amply testifies that the harshness of the cold is far from them.

units.la: Scoti, quibus Diuus Hieronymus feritatem & barbariem asscribit, in quorum etiam numero habentur Septentrionis quidam populi, ut Dani, Sueci, Effui, quos omnes feros adhuc & agrestes inveneris ni alie gentes eos cicurarint atq; expolierint. Nunc vrbanitate & humanitate nemini fere cedunt. Miseram olim autem vitam conditionem Scotis fuisse historia testantur, frumentis enim adventitiis ut plurimum utebantur, bulbulamq; in cibis largissime assumebant.
units.tr: The Scots, to whom Saint Jerome ascribes ferocity and barbarism, and among whom certain peoples of the North are also counted, such as the Danes, Swedes and Esthonians, all of whom you would find still wild and rustic, unless other nations had tamed and refined them. Now they yield to almost no one in urbanity and humanity. Histories testify that the Scots' condition was once wretched, for they mostly used foreign grain and consumed a great deal of bulbs in their food.

units.la: Italia pro trastuum[?] differentia imperiiq; incremento victum pariter mutauit. Romani enim qui initia imperio dederunt, tum etiam quiid provexerunt, cibos expetebant tantum qui vitam sustinerent, famemq; depellerent. Capitale erat bouem mactasse gulæ causâ: piscibus statim à Roma condita praesertim marinus vsos esse constat antiquorum scriptorum monumentis: carnes omnino parcius esitasse quam ceteros populos verum videri potest, nam & nostra memoria parcissime iis vescuntur. Vini obseruationes memorabiles apud Romanos fuerunt, auctoritatem enim post centesimum urbis annum coepisse aiunt, Romulumq; ipsum latte non vino libasse, & Numam sanxisse, ne rogum vino respergerent, nec licuisse foeminis primum id bibere, postea concessum valetudinis tantum causa: eorum autem qui secuti sunt cura fertilior felicior, industria in vitibus fuit excolendis: vini quidem in vniuersum sunt auidi, sed modum potionibus adhibent, sicut & Hispani.
units.tr: Italy, too, changed its diet in step with the differences in its ways of life and the growth of its empire. For the Romans, who gave the beginnings of the empire and then advanced it, sought only foods that sustained life and drove off hunger. It was a capital offence to slaughter an ox for the sake of gluttony. It is established by the monuments of ancient writers that, especially from the founding of Rome, they used sea fish most of all. It can be seen to be true that they ate meat more sparingly than other peoples, for even in our own time they eat it very sparingly. The Romans had remarkable rules about wine. They say that its use only began after the hundredth year of the city, that Romulus himself offered milk, not wine, in libation, and that Numa decreed that the funeral pyre should not be sprinkled with wine. Women were not permitted to drink it at first, and later it was allowed only for the sake of health. But among those who followed, care and industry were more productive and more successful in cultivating vines. Indeed, they are generally fond of wine, but they keep their drinking within limits, as do the Spaniards.

units.la: Vitius autem Romanorum rationem variaffe pro Reipub. recta depravatae gubernatione, & ftea Imperatorum virtute temperantiaq, atq; etiam libidine ac luxuria, dubium nullum est: inde enim tot emerserunt leges fumtuaria & censoriae, quibus non exotica solum cibaria sed & domefti- ca quaedam prohibebantur, atq; etiam ex suae per- necoenis detrahebantur. Pisces simul cum carnibus vna in patella seu lance, mensis veteres Romani apponebant, pariterq; herbas quasdam ut asparagum: panificia varii generis conficiebant: lepusculi & perdices raro illorum mensis subibant ob inopiam scilicet, catera autem aliorum genera frequentius. Vitulina nulla illic caro pretiosior. Vernecina non admodum grata.
units.tr: The Romans' diet changed as the good government of the republic decayed, and with the virtue and temperance of the emperors, and also with their lust and luxury; there is no doubt of this. From this came so many sumptuary and censorial laws, forbidding not only foreign foods but certain domestic ones, and even removing some from their dinners. The old Romans served fish together with meat on one dish or platter, and likewise certain herbs such as asparagus. They made breads of many kinds. Hares and partridges seldom came to their tables, certainly from poverty, but other kinds more often. No veal was more prized there. Lamb was not very pleasing.

units.la: Hispani sordes in vivendo peculiares habebant, quoniam fi suis alebantur loculis, domi esuriebant, & famelici biabant, at quando alie-na quadra illis frui licebat, nulla gens aeque vorax cernebatur, quem etiam morem nostra aetate in quibusdam Hispaniae locis perdurare animaduersum est. Viuunt praterea carnibus immodicis, pifcibusq;, tum amnicis, tum marinis: pomorum vbertas apud eos varia atq; multiplex, maxime citriorum omne genus, punicorum, ficuum, vuarum, quas siccatas in alias terras mit-tunt: tunt : vina illis vehementissima: secundis mensis quernas glandes adhibent dulcedine praestantes.
units.tr: The Spaniards had a peculiar meanness in living. If they were fed from their own purses, they went hungry at home and lived starved. But when they were allowed to enjoy another's expense, no people was seen to be so voracious, and this custom has been observed to persist in our own age in some parts of Spain. They also live on immoderate amounts of meat and fish, both river and sea.
