Their abundance of fruit is varied and manifold, above all every kind of citron, pomegranates, figs and grapes, which they send dried to other lands; wines very strong; for dessert they serve acorns of oak, excellent in sweetness.

units.la: Lusitaniae montanas gentes querna glande vesci Strabo autor est.
units.tr: Strabo is the authority that the mountain peoples of Lusitania feed on acorns of oak.

units.la: Græcis diuersa victus & studiorum fuit ratio: aliter n. Lacedemonii vivebat, aliter Athenienses. Lycurgus leges Lacedemoniis condens tantū cibi unicuiq; elargiri iussit, quantum ad bona corporis valetudine esset satis: certum itaq; numerum frumenti singulis, in singulos annos emetiri mādauit, & liquores pro ratione, atq; id uberius viris, fœmi-nis parcius. Instituit praeterea publica conuiuia, in quibus nulla, praeter vulgares, esca apponebantur, probrosū existimās & inutile animis corporibusq; coquorum condimentis, & saporū coacernationib. saginari. Solebant praeterea Lacedemonii epulas suas condire laboribus in venatu, sudore, cursu, fame, siti: unde Dionysio Siculo neganti, se iure illo nigro (erat enim inter obsonia hoc illis celebratissi-mum) quod caput coenae fuerat, delectatum, respo-disse[?] fertur, qui illud coxerat, minime mirum, co-dimenta n. defuerunt. Sybaritae gloria virtutisq; loco delitiis mollitieiq; diti vitam despiciebant.
units.tr: The Greeks had different systems of diet and of pursuits. The Lacedaemonians lived differently from the Athenians. Lycurgus, when he drafted laws for the Lacedaemonians, ordered that each person be given only as much food as was enough for good bodily health. So he commanded that a set measure of grain be allotted to each person for each year, and liquids in proportion, more generously to men and more sparingly to women. He also instituted public messes, at which no food was served apart from common fare, since he thought it shameful and harmful to souls and bodies to be fattened on the seasonings of cooks and the mixing of flavours. The Lacedaemonians also used to season their feasts with the labours of hunting, sweat, running, hunger and thirst. Hence it is reported that when Dionysius of Sicily said he did not enjoy that black broth (for among their dishes it was most celebrated), which was the chief part of the meal, they replied that it was no wonder the man who had cooked it found it so, for seasonings were lacking. The Sybarites, in place of virtue, despised life for delights, and were rich in softness and luxury.

units.la: Spartani vero & vivendum liberaliter & moriendum censebant, utrumq; cum virtute, teste Plutarcho. Verum Atheniensium longe alia fuit vivendi ratio, quippe luxui omnino deditos fuisse graeci fere omnes testati sunt, ipsiq; Poeta Comici Atticas inprimis coenas riserunt. Socrates cibos detestabatur, quinō esuriente inuitarei[?] adedendū, similiter & potum, qui non sitientes ad bibendum. Est in exemplis parasitum quendam interrogatum, cum coena Attice Chalcidicus lautiores effent[?], an vero hac Atheniensibus praestarent, respondisse, Chalcedonicum praemium pretiosius esse & sua-uius, quàm Atticorum totum apparatum, appellant praemium coenarum, ostrearum multitudinem & varietatem.
units.tr: The Spartans, indeed, judged that one should live generously and die generously, both with virtue, as Plutarch testifies. But the Athenians' way of living was quite different. Almost all the Greeks have testified that they were wholly given over to luxury, and the comic poets above all mocked Attic dinners. Socrates detested foods that one should eat when not hungry, and likewise drink for those not thirsty. There is an example of a certain parasite who, when a Chalcidian at an Attic dinner (the Chalcidians lived more lavishly) was asked whether they surpassed the Athenians in this, replied that the Chalcedonian prize was more precious and pleasant than the whole Attic array. They call the prize of dinners the multitude and variety of oysters.

units.la: Persas praeter naufragium[?] ad panem nihil adbibuisse. Xenophon testis est. Sed de eorundem luxu ganeaq[?], apud omnes fere scriptores passim communi plura tradita leguntur.
units.tr: The Persians, apart from [a word I cannot read], added nothing to their bread. Xenophon is the witness. But about the luxury and gluttony of the same people, much is commonly recorded, passed on almost everywhere by nearly all writers.

units.la: De aliarum gentium vitiis[?], quae a grauissimis autoribus literis sunt assignata, scio permulta esse, quae vix fidem merentur, multiq; ea videantur incredibilia, praesertim iis qui a patrio solo non multum discesserunt.
units.tr: Concerning the vices of other peoples, which have been recorded in writing by very serious authors, I know there are many that scarcely deserve belief, and that many seem incredible, especially to those who have not gone far from their native soil.

units.la: Sed quia ex illis mundi partibus, quarum gentium ritus mirabilemq; victum[?] enarraturus, homines, fruges, legumina, aues, animaliaq;, nobis incognita, creberrime ad nos terra marique comportantur, fidem facile iis adhibendam esse censeo. Ferunt ante annos aliquot apud nostrates habitas esse, cochleis, vescitur, vanis, testudinibus. At in vniuer-sa ferè Gallia & Italia inter praecipuas mensa-rum delicias reponuntur. Thraces quosdam canis-busvitiaffe Picus Francifcus autor est. Hircani vescebantur venatibus, quorum varietate abundabant, teste Marcellino. Geris quoque ... vsu omnino ignoratum, quin & frugum vitellum illis [illegible, ~8 letters] ovillum pecus cōmodat, ex quo Nomadū Getarūq; plurimi Columella teste, galactopotæ dicuntur.
units.tr: But because men, grain, pulses, birds and animals unknown to us are very often brought to us by land and sea from those parts of the world whose peoples' customs and wondrous diet I am about to describe, I think they should be readily believed. They say that some years ago snails were eaten among our own people, and frogs and tortoises as well. Yet in almost all of Gaul and Italy these are counted among the chief delicacies of the table. Picus Franciscus is the authority that some Thracians used to eat dogs. The Hyrcanians fed on game, of which they had abundant variety, as Marcellinus testifies. Among the Geri too the use [...] was altogether unknown; nay, they keep flocks of sheep, from which, as Columella testifies, most of the Nomads and Getae are called milk-drinkers.

units.la: Orientis populi plurimi, q imperio Magni Cham parent, potus suos ex oryza & genere aromatū coquinant[?], carnesq; crudas primū, deinde aromatis respersas, oleisq; odoratis imbutas vorāt: serpentib. etiamnunc, q illic nascuntur copiosissimæ & grandissimæ in cibis vtuntur, inq; delitiis habēt carnes humanas, hominis scil. morbo non extincti, sed in bello ab iis trucidati.
units.tr: Many peoples of the East who obey the empire of the Great Khan make their drinks from rice and a kind of spice. They eat meats raw at first, then sprinkled with spices and soaked in fragrant oils. They still use serpents, which are born there in very great numbers and of great size, as food. They also count human flesh a delicacy, of men who did not die of disease but were slaughtered by them in war.

units.la: Matthias Michon de Sarmatia Asiana scribens, Tartarorū quoq; meminit, omniq; frumēto carere asseuerat, omni quoq; leguminū genere, excepto milio, quod magna cura ab iis feri[?] idem tradit: equorum prætereà greges educant, quorum carnes manducant, sanguine verò equinum milio commiscent, coquuntq; simul ac vorant, quin etiam ipsum solum potāt, idq; & barbaris olim placuisse testatur Virg. carm. Bucolico:
units.tr: Matthias Michon, writing about Asiatic Sarmatia, also mentions the Tartars. He asserts that they lack all wheat and every kind of pulse except millet, which, as the same writer records, they cultivate with great care. Moreover they raise herds of horses, whose flesh they eat; they mix horse blood with millet, and cook and devour them together. Indeed they drink the blood alone, and Virgil testifies that this once pleased even the barbarians, in the Bucolics:

units.la: Et lac concretum cum sanguine potat equino.
units.tr: "And they drink milk curdled with horse blood."

units.la: Acido lacte oblectantur, id nam q; stomacho tum salutare esse persuadent, tum alvo deiiciendæ idoneum experimentis comprobarunt: si quando verò epulari splendidius illis animus est, lac equinum sublimatum bibunt, quod mirabile dictu, promtissimè atq; ocyssimè in cerebrum penetrans inebriat.
units.tr: They delight in sour milk, which they persuade themselves is healthful for the stomach and which they have proved by experience to be suitable for purging the bowels. If at any time they want to feast more splendidly, they drink sublimated mare's milk, which, wonderful to say, penetrates the brain very quickly and easily and intoxicates.

units.la: A Tartaris Turcas Oriundos censet idem, qua-re ab eorum victu[?] non procul recedere.
units.tr: The same writer thinks the Turks are descended from the Tartars, wherefore they do not depart far from their diet.

units.la: Qui de Rhodi expugnatione historiā scripserūt, omnino gentē illam immundam atq; obscœnā tradunt. In Sarmatia Europæa Podolia fertilitate nobilitata est: potus illic ex melle concinnantur, quod ibidē abundantissimē gignitur, atq; etiam in Ruscia. Moscoviæ idem Matthias faciens mentionem potûm incolis esse scribit, ex aqua & melle confectum: aromatis utuntur crebrius, nam & eacū[?] melle arte chymica sublimant, existimantes (&c verè) hanc potionē viscerib. calorē excitari, adeo insignem & salutarē, ut possit inclementissimis frigoribus fortiter repugnare: auenam ipsam sublimant, ex quā sublimatione elicitur liquor, quem aquā ardentem vocant, aquæ ac apud Germanos, Italos, Gallos, ex vinis vehementioribus. Mosco-vitis parent Scythæ humanis corporib. vescentes, sine vllo degentes panificio, vino aliûq; potibus: viscera offag, humana vorare, ipsumq; sanguine glaediatorij bibere, & quidem ex homine ipso, ex ipsa vena sectâ calentem adhuc & spirante adhuc sorbere efficacissimum putant. Paulus Jovius testatur Moscoviam Melopepones ferre, quod mirari subit, quippe gelidissimis Borea flatib. tenerrima quaq; exuruntur. Certissima illic messis in melle atq; cera est, namq; illic apes in arborum cannis mella conficiunt, & probatissima, & copiosissima: domi opi-parè & lautè epulantur, gallina siquidem & anates singulæ profingulis argenteolis numinis venenit: venatio & aucupia mensas magnatum opulen-tant, vina nesciunt præter exotica, utq; utuntur in sacrificiis & conuiuiis luxurioforibus ostenta-tionis gratiâ. Lapponum gens supra quam credi-bile est fera & agrestis, neq; enim fruges, neq; vina,
units.tr: Those who have written the history of the capture of Rhodes report that that people is wholly unclean and obscene. In European Sarmatia, Podolia is made famous for its fertility: drinks are concocted there from honey, which is produced there in great abundance, and also in Russia. Matthias, speaking of Muscovy, writes that the inhabitants have a drink made of water and honey. They use spices rather often, for they also refine oats with honey by chemical art, thinking (and truly) that this drink stirs heat in the bowels, so remarkable and wholesome that it can strongly resist the harshest cold. They also distil oats, and from this distillation they draw a liquor which they call burning water, like the aqua vitae of Germans, Italians and French, made from stronger wines. The Scythians who obey the Muscovites live on human bodies, without any bread, wine or other drinks. They devour human entrails and flesh, and drink gladiators' blood. Indeed they think it most efficacious to sip it from the man himself, from an opened vein, still warm and still breathing. Paulus Jovius testifies that Muscovy bears melons, which is surprising, since the most tender kinds are scorched by the cold blasts of the north wind. The harvest there is most certain in honey and wax, for there bees make honey in the hollows of trees, and it is both excellent and plentiful. They feast richly and lavishly at home, since a hen and ducks are each sold for a small silver coin. Hunting and fowling enrich the tables of the great. They know no wines except foreign ones, and use them in sacrifices and in luxurious feasts for show. The race of the Lapps is wild and rustic beyond what is credible, for they know neither grain, nor wines,

units.la: neq; poma nouit, sagittandi sola arte victum quaritar, & ferarum occisarum tergoribus vestitur. In Oriente pori o traditur quosdam esse populos, qui sine vllis arboribus, sineq; frutice degant. Plurima quoq; gentes frugum, arborum, quin & pecorum innocuntur[?] expertes. Fuerunt & apud Graecos, qui scrupulose hominum viscera sunt persecuti, eorumq; sapores. Aethiopum gens, cuius regio a Meroe ad fluuium Hydaspin porrigitur, scorpionibus vescebatur & aspidibus. Quintinus Heduus scribit, se vidisse in infula Melita, qui scorpionem ederet innoxie. Supra Borysthenem Scythiae fluuium maximum esse gente Saucomatum, quae tertio semper die capiat cibum: ad extremos vero Indos gente astomorum fuisse sine ore, corpore toto hirsutam, vestitam frondium lanugine, halitibus tantum viuentem & odore quem narib. trahebant, memoria proditu est: quae si vera sunt, quis miretur Democritum melius odore vixisse? Qui Athon monte incolebant, viperinis carnibus alebatur, itaq; nec capiti nec vestibus eorum noxia corpori animalia innascebantur. Gens Medunnorū animalium, quae Cynophalos appellabant, lacte[?] vi-vebat * Arimphaei gens baccis[?] alebatur. * Celenophagi testudinib. vescebantur, quarum testis casas suas integebant, id genus hominum noua alit India. Candei serpentibus vesci assueti, & ob id ophiophagi dicti. Libes ouillam non gustabant, erat enim apud eos id inexpiabile, si quis edisset. * Cyno-cephali Iudaei atq; Aegyptii non vescebantur suilla. Tro-
units.tr: nor fruit. They seek food by archery alone, and clothe themselves in the hides of the wild beasts they have killed. In the East it is handed down that some peoples live without any trees or shrubs. Many peoples too lack crops, trees, and even livestock. Among the Greeks too there were some who scrupulously pursued human entrails and their flavours. The Ethiopians, whose country stretches from Meroe to the river Hydaspes, fed on scorpions and asps. Quintinus of Autun writes that he saw a man on the island of Malta who ate a scorpion without harm. Beyond the Borysthenes, the greatest river of Scythia, is the people of the Sauromatae, who take food only every third day. At the farthest Indians is a race of Astomi without a mouth, whole body hairy, clothed in a down of leaves, living only by breath and by the odour they drew through their nostrils; this is recorded in memory. If these things are true, who would wonder that Democritus lived better on smell? Those who inhabited Mount Athos were fed on viper flesh, so that no harmful creatures were born on their heads or in their clothes. The tribe of the Medunni, called Cynophali, lived on milk. The Arimphaei were fed on berries. The Celenophagi ate tortoises, whose shells they used to cover their huts; India too nourishes this kind of men. The Candei, accustomed to eat serpents, were therefore called Ophiophagi. The Libyans did not taste sheep's flesh, for among them it was an inexpiable thing if anyone ate it. The Cynocephali, Jews and Egyptians did not eat pork.

units.la: Athos mons inter Ma-ced.& Thraciae tantae altitudinis, vt vmbra ad infula vsq; Lem non por-rigere dicatur. * Cyno-cephali
units.tr: Mount Athos, between Macedonia and Thrace, is said to be so high that its shadow reaches as far as the island of Lemnos. Cynocephali.

units.la: gloditae ferae sunt
units.tr: The Glodytae are savage beasts.

units.la: in æthiopia gloditæ specus subibant, alebantque serpentibus pia cani- Riphæis bacca erant alimenta. Nonnullis India na habé- populis casorum parentiū uisceribus epularī fas erat: tes capi- Carmani fine fuge ac uelle, fine pecore, fine fedi- ta, cæterā bus degebant, pisci uelcebantur, eorumq;, cute sæpe hominis velabant Pharufi pecoribus alebantur tautum. In similes, Æthiopia cū hominū multiformes miraq; effigies violentæ reperiuntur, ut uitium rationi incredibile: illic enim ad saltū, gentes esse ore concreto naribus carentes, unoq; morsu &c tantū foraminefpirantes, & potū auena calamus latratu trahere, stradiderūt prisci. Acridophagi vermib. fera. alitur, iudeq; necatur, cibus illorū p omne tempus * Carma est locuftarū uitulus, q; uenis tempore Zephyrus in nia regio maxima copia ad eos ex deferto defert. Has sale, Indiscó- qui apud eos plurimus est fernant. Vita sunt bre- termina, uiuiffima, annoficinimus enim 40. non excedit annos. populi Quibusdam ignorum fuisse ignis usum narrat toto cot- ante Ptolomæum Latyram Ægypti regem, atq; pore præ illic fuisse Nomades, qui Elephantis uiueuerunt. ter capi- Agriophagi Pantherarum carnes leonumq;, ede- ta hirsuti bant. Pamphagi omnia vorabant. Alii Orientes sunt. populi pisces uiuunt tum piccatis tum recentib, quorum capturæ uberrima fit Martio, Aprili, Maio, contritos eos ¶ in massam redactos in panificia cognunt, piccatas, in annua cibaria repo- nunt. Fortunatarum insularum incolæ beatiores sunt, quibus sua fonte tellus abundantissimè sup- peditat alimenta. De uictu & cibo nouæ Indiæ, fiue noui orbis non ita pridem à Christianis pa- fatti conflat variam eum esse fertilitate foli alibi, alibi vero infœcunditate nobilem: alit autem omnes, aliaq; pecora, aprosq; affatim, melle, saccharo, vitibusq; abundat, quae illic plus fundunt uvarum quam foliorum.
units.tr: In Ethiopia the Glodytae lived in caves and fed on snakes. The Riphaei lived on berries. Some peoples thought it lawful to feast on the flesh of their own parents, and some lived without cattle, without flocks and without fire, feeding only on fish, and clothed themselves in the skins of seals. In Ethiopia, which is the most fertile in monstrous and marvellous shapes of men, there are reported to be, as is hard to believe, peoples with their mouths sealed shut and no nostrils, breathing through one small hole and drawing their drink through a reed, as the ancients wrote. The Acridophagi feed on locusts, which are salted and dried and, for them, the whole year's food, and which the west wind carries to them from the desert in great numbers. Their lives are short and rarely exceed forty years. Some write that fire was unknown to the people of India until the time of Ptolemy Latyrus, king of Egypt. There were also nomads there who lived on elephants' milk. The Agriophagi ate the flesh of panthers and lions. The Pamphagi devoured everything. Other peoples live on fish, both salted and fresh, which are caught most abundantly in March, April and May; they grind them into a paste, make them into cakes, and store them as provisions for the year. The inhabitants of the Fortunate Islands are happier, since their land supplies them with food in abundance from its own soil. Concerning the food and diet of New India, or the New World, which Christians recently discovered, it is established that its fertility varies: in some places it is famous for the richness of its soil, in others for its barrenness. It feeds all men and other livestock, and wild boars in plenty; it abounds in honey, sugar and vines, which there yield more grapes than leaves.

units.la: Qui terras incolunt, prima Americi Vspucii[?] navigatione visas, omnino frumenta ignorant, cibariaq; iis sunt poma atq; herba, ac quoq; pisces, radicem quandam in farinam redigunt, quâ vice panis utuntur, hanc alii Juccam, alii Chambi appellant: carnes nullas attingunt praeter humanas. Qui primi è nostro orbe in eas terras habitatū sunt deducti, duraverunt quidem aliquot annis solis herbis, pomis, radicibusq; viventes, verum postea ad alia cibaria descenderunt, invenerũntq; cibos, quos primum exitiales experti sunt, innoxios reddere. Etenim jucca radix, primum degustata illis mortifera fuit, verum procedente tempore, cum id venenum in radicis solo succo delitescere comperissent, aqua coctâ acigne totam madere coeperunt absq; noxa.
units.tr: The people who inhabit the lands first seen on the voyage of Americus Vespucius know nothing at all of grain. Their food is fruit and herbs, and also fish. They grind a certain root into flour, which they use in place of bread; some call it yuca, others chambi. They touch no meat except human flesh. The first people brought from our world to those lands lived for some years on herbs, fruit and roots alone, but afterwards they turned to other foods, and found ways to make harmless the things that had first proved deadly to them. For the yuca root, when first tasted, was fatal to them; but as time went on, when they discovered that the poison lay only in the juice of the root, they began to soak it in water, boil it or dry it by the fire, and eat it without harm.

units.la: Nauigatione Josephi Indi compertum habetur, regionem Indicam, quae Carangonora dicitur, sita inter astium tropicum & æquatorem, nucib. Indicis abundare, incolasq; herbarū 24. radicib. vesci, ex oryza vero panes coficere: sunt etiamnum Pal-meta, quorum ex fructibus panes conflant, vinum elicunt: acetum temperant, oleum exprimunt, atque etiam saccharum, quod ideo minus mirabile videtur, quod Sirabenem auctorem gravem, eandem penè in libris suis de orbis situ tradidisse reperitur. Ex palma enim fieri panem, mel, acetum & oleum oleum scripto mandauit. Calechutani laste[?] cybu-tyro vescuntur, panesq; factitant fine frumer[?] toin foco tantū cocłos &c cinere. Oryza apud eos abun-dantia summa, eaq; cymbalis, faltationib. omniq; laetitiæ genere ferunt, damonia sua pręcātes vt sit oryzæ vberrimus prouentus, hæc n. varias epulas conficiunt, ex palmis potant liquoré, carnibus pi-scibusq; promiscuè vescuntur, à bubalatamè absti-nent, boues namq; sacrosanctos putant. Quicolunt Infulā, quæ S. Iohannis porta dicta est, canes alit saginantq; in vsum cibarii, verum nullus illis la-tratus est, rostrumq; habent vulpinū. Infima plebs piscatu nutritur, muriumq; venatu. Mameluchi, qui Sultano parebant Ægyptio, equorū, camelo-rū, bubalorū, carnib. vtilis ārunt. Arietes in illis locis grandes & memorabiles vsuntur magnitudi-ne asinos æquantes, quorū aliqui cauda gestant li-brarū 40. adeò obesi vt pꝓgredi[?] vix valeant: capras præterea grandes illic reperiri traditur, quæ vno partu quatuor hœdos enitantur. Apud quasdā O-rientiū gentes sunt gallinæ, quæ pro pennis pilos ge-rant nigricantes, quib. vescuntur, pariterq; ipsarū carnes q; sunt saporis suauissimi. Liquores ex sau-ciatis arboribus emanantes in potum assumunt: quin & sub earum corticibus farinā reperiri præ-dicāt, q; præbeat incolis pulmēta suauiāq; cibaria. Pygmei, (quorum tota cohors cubito non est al-tior vno, vt ait Iuuenalis) pro frugib. aduerso gru-es dimicabant: nā & tantillos homunculos mitio-ribus alimentis vti natura docuit: fabulosam aute[?] & fictitiam pygmæorum gentem non esse Aristote- les in illis suis præclaris de animalib. historiis scri- psit. Atq; hæc de vario mirabiliq; gentium victu a- spergere placuit, ut scil. compertum quis habeat, si forsan rudis in istiusmodi rerum auditionib. repe- riatur, quantum exoticus ille victus a nostro diffe- rat: ubi hoc adnotasse oportebit, si ab exoticis istis abscesserimus, adq; domestica exempla venerimus, permulta futura, quæ visa primum admiratione allatura sint, ut fide carere quis ea existimet, etiā ab homine probo audita & grauì.
units.tr: From the voyage of Josephus the Indian it is known that the region of India called Carangonora, which lies between the Tropic of Capricorn and the equator, abounds in Indian nuts, and that its inhabitants eat the roots of twenty-four herbs and make bread from rice. There are also palm trees, whose fruit they use to make bread, wine, vinegar and oil, and even sugar. This seems less wonderful because the grave author Sirabenus is found to have written almost the same in his books on the geography of the world. He committed to writing that bread, honey, vinegar and oil are made from the palm oil. The Calechutani eat milk, cheese and butter, and make bread without grain, baking it only on the hearth in the ashes. Rice is extremely abundant among them, and they celebrate with cymbals, dances and every kind of merriment, praying to their demons for a plentiful rice harvest. They prepare various feasts, drink a liquor made from palms, and eat meat and fish indiscriminately, but they abstain from buffalo beef, for they consider oxen sacred. The inhabitants of the island called St John's Gate fatten dogs for food. These dogs do not bark, and have foxlike snouts. The lowest class of people live on fishing and on hunting mice. The Mamelukes, who obeyed the Egyptian Sultan, were fed on the flesh of horses, camels and buffaloes. In those regions there are rams as large as donkeys, some with tails weighing forty pounds, so fat that they can scarcely walk. Large goats are also said to be found there, which bring forth four kids at a birth. Among some eastern peoples there are hens whose feathers are replaced by dark hairs; they are eaten, and their flesh is very sweet. They drink the liquids that flow from trees that have been wounded, and it is said that flour can be found beneath their bark, which supplies the inhabitants with porridge and sweet food. The pygmies, whose whole tribe is no taller than a cubit, as Juvenal says, fought with cranes over grain; for nature has taught even such tiny men to live on gentler food. Yet Aristotle, in his famous books on animals, wrote that the race of pygmies is not a fable or a fiction. I have thought fit to set out these things about the varied and wonderful diets of peoples, so that anyone who is untrained in hearing such matters may learn how far that foreign diet differs from ours. When we have left these foreign examples and come to domestic ones, I shall note many things which, though at first sight they will cause wonder, may make someone think them unworthy of belief, even when heard from an honest and serious man.

units.la: Multi, cum quis ab Italis colubras tuto edi re- fert, minimè credent: cum item in Alpium iugis & Septentrionis quibusdam locis, ut Noruegia, Suecia, Liuonia, &c. cādidos lepores, ursos & vul- pes conspici, atq; ab illorum locorum incolis edi au- dierint. Ut enim externa illa & exotica nobis mi- raculo sunt ita visissim nostra illis. Et ut homines equo insidentes antiquitas Centauros dixit, ita & Indi illi nostros equites, ranauigia[?], remigan- di q; artem sunt demirati.
units.tr: Many people, when someone tells them that Italians eat snakes safely, will not believe it at all. Likewise, when they hear that in some places on the Alpine ridges and in the north, as in Norway, Sweden, Livonia and elsewhere, white hares, bears and foxes are seen and eaten by the inhabitants of those places, they will not credit it. For as those foreign and exotic things are a marvel to us, so are our things to them. And just as the ancients called men who ride horses Centaurs, so those Indians marvelled at our horsemen and at the art of rowing and sailing.

units.la: CAPVT V. De alimentorum diuisione, generibus, & differentiis generatim, decq; mirâ terrarum quarundam fertilitate.
units.tr: CAPVT V. On the division of foods, their kinds and differences in general, and on the remarkable fertility of certain lands.

units.la: PRimus mortalium victus, & exotica gentium quarundam cibandi ratio exhibita est, quæ si cui ganeoso forsan saluiam moue-
units.tr: The primitive diet of mortals, and the manner of feeding of certain foreign peoples, has been set out here, which, if perhaps it stirs the appetite of some glutton,

units.la: mouerit,videatis quomodo vlteriore atq; lautiore quodam ferculo palatum explere possit: auribus percipiendam,oculifq; lectitandam eam proposui,non etiam degustandam.
units.tr: has stirred it, you may see how he could satisfy his palate with a more lavish and refined dish. I have proposed that this be perceived by the ears and read over with the eyes, not tasted.

units.la: Nos melioribus(vtinam non peioribus)viviuédi institutis deliniti placidiorefq; redditi, quod ex cibis ferum omninò est, relinquamus illis,alimentorumq; vim ac naturam memorâdam,diligenter perpendamus.vt suauia,familiaria & amica distinguamus ab iis,quæ naturę ac vitæ hominum noxia sunt & inimica.
units.tr: We, soothed by better (would that they were not worse) institutions of living and made more calm, should leave to those people what is altogether savage in food. Let us carefully weigh the force and nature of foods so that we may distinguish the pleasant, familiar and friendly from those that are harmful and hostile to human nature and life.

units.la: Omne autem animans sibi conueniente nutritur alimento. Alimentum est quo alimur, vel fine quo corpus ali non potest. Conueniens vnicuiq; alimentum est, q̃ aflimilari corpori alendo potest: ciborum enim ratio est,assimilari & vniri substantiæ corporis cibandi.
units.tr: Every living creature is nourished by food suited to it. Food is that by which we are nourished, or without which the body cannot be fed. Food suitable to each is that which can be assimilated to nourish the body, for the function of food is to be assimilated and united with the substance of the body it feeds.

units.la: Alimentum affimilandû vel efculentû est vel potulentum. Esculentum est q̃ esui est aptum.
units.tr: Food to be assimilated is either edible or drinkable. Edible food is that which is fit for eating.

units.la: Esculenta fiue cibi quæ in hominum vsus admittuntur,veniunt vel à vegetabilibus,vt frugibus,leguminibus,fructibus: vel ab animalibus horumq; partibus, vel ab iis, quæ ab animalib. pueniunt, vt sunt oua,lac,mel,sanguis.
units.tr: Edibles, or foods admitted to human use, come either from plants, such as grains, pulses and fruits; or from animals and their parts; or from things that come from animals, such as eggs, milk, honey and blood.

units.la: De omnib.autem & singulis in specie esculentis,quæ vel à vegetabilib', vel ab animalib' depromi possunt in vsus humanos,tractare instituti,& consilii mei non est, sed deiis solummodo,quę nostra ætate crebrius veniunt in cibos & mensas. Ac qui de cibis hominû tractarunt, runt,ab arborum pomis & baccis, quæ primò vitam mortalium aluerunt, ut vitæ ordinem sequerentur, exordiri maluerunt. Verum nos, quoniam salubriora subsecuta[?] sunt secula, mitioraq; cibaria ex frugibus inuenta sunt, fugū[?] naturas prius persequemur atq; inde cibaria[?], præsertim cum ex iis firmissimum & probatissimum cibi ac potus vinculum videl. panis cōficiatur, & præcipua hominum cibaria. Mira profecto frugum natura & eximia gratia, quod sine iis vix vlla esca placere potuit. Vnde nō immerito agricultura ab antiquis Romanis adeò commendata est, vt quæ non solum sanis, sed etiam ægrotantibus alimenta suggerat. Romanorum aratores triumphales exiterunt & laureati, qui femina non leuiori cura tractabat quam bella, qui eâdem diligentia agros disponebant atque castra: vnde tunc in Italia annonæ vilitas erat incredibilis, nulla enim prouinciarum Italiam alebat. Athenienses licet pascuo magis indulsisse[?] vidi sunt quàm agricolationi, maximo tamen in honore agricolas habuerunt frugûq; inuentores. Quid? quod optimi quiq; pariterq; dignissimi rei rusticæ operâ dabant, nam nec imperatores pudebat manibus triumphalibus tum agros colere, tum femina tractare ipsosq; ligones: & cùm virum bonum laudabant, eum bonum agricolam bonumq; colonum appellitabat. Hodie ita abiecta est, vt tellus aranda committatur in seruitute quasi redactis, prouentusq; abiis & vectigal accipiatur. Felicissimum rerum statum tunc fusse,cum aranti Cincinato viator afferret dictaturam,& Serranum ferentem oblati invenirent honores, extra dubium est.Sed ad propositum.
units.tr: I have not undertaken, nor is it my intention, to treat of all and each of the edibles, whether drawn from plants or animals, for human use, but only of those that in our age are more frequently found in foods and on tables. Those who have written about human food preferred to begin with the fruits and berries of trees, which first nourished mortals, so that they might follow the order of life. But we, since more wholesome ages have followed and gentler foods have been discovered from grains, will first pursue the nature of grains and from there the foods, especially since from them is made bread, the firmest and most approved bond of food and drink, and the chief food of men. Truly marvellous is the nature of grain and its outstanding grace, since almost no food could please without it. For this reason agriculture was not undeservedly commended so highly by the ancient Romans, since it supplies nourishment not only to the healthy but also to the sick. The Roman ploughmen became triumphant and laureled, who handled the farm with no less care than war, who arranged fields with the same diligence as camps. Hence in Italy at that time the cheapness of the grain supply was incredible, for no province fed Italy. The Athenians, although they seem to have indulged more in pasturing than in farming, nevertheless held farmers and the inventors of grain in the highest honour. What more? The best men and those most worthy of the task devoted themselves to rural work, for generals were not ashamed then to till fields with triumphal hands, to handle the plough and the hoes themselves; and when they praised a good man, they called him a good farmer and good cultivator. Today it has been so cast down that the earth is committed to ploughing by those reduced to slavery, while the produce and tax are taken from them. That the state of affairs was most happy when Cincinnatus, while ploughing, was brought the news of his dictatorship, and when they found Serranus threshing when honours were offered him, is beyond doubt. But to our purpose.

units.la: Omnes frugum species & differentiæ autore Theophrasto, Columella,& alis[?],sub frumentis & leguminibus tanquam summis generibus comprehenduntur. Varias autem cerealium seminum differentias invenire, testantur, qui per Italiam,Galliam,Indiam,Aegyptum,Hispaniam,Angliam,Germaniam, Daniam,peregrinationes suscepe-runt. Causas coelo soloque tribuerunt naturae Solertes, ad frugum enim fructuumque nobilitatem auti-[?]gnobilitatem,facilitatem aut difficultatem in cibis foecunditatem aut sterilitatem, coelum aut solum plurimum valere animadverterunt. Differentias itaq; frugum scire & cognoscere inprimis oportet vitae salubritati consulturum & peregrinationes suscepturum. In quibus-dam enim locis quaedam praecoces cernuntur, quaedam serae: quaedam multum ferentes,quaedam parum,quedam pauciores intra dies con-summantur, ut Euboicae, quae intra 40. dies perficiuntur, quaedam ponderosae sunt & firmae,quaedam leves, quaedam parum obtinent furfuris, quaedam multum, quaedam Spicam effundunt,quaedam cristam,&c. Sunt etiam quaedam loca quae semper coctilia & cibo facilia ferant,
units.tr: All the kinds and differences of grain, according to Theophrastus, Columella and others, are comprehended under cereals and pulses as the highest genera. Those who have undertaken journeys through Italy, Gaul, India, Egypt, Spain, England, Germany and Denmark attest that there are various differences among the cereal seeds. The skilled students of nature have attributed the causes to climate and soil; for they have observed that the climate or the soil counts for most in the quality of grains and fruits, in their ease or difficulty of digestion, and in their fertility or sterility. Therefore it is especially necessary to know and recognise the differences of grains, for one who would look after the health of life and undertake journeys. For in certain places some are seen to be early, some late; some yield much, some little; some are used up within a few days, as the Euboic grains, which ripen within forty days; some are heavy and hard, some light; some have little bran, some much; some pour out the ear, some the crest, and so on. There are also places that always produce grains that are easy to cook and digest,

In Lemno non nisi coćtilia proueniunt , quoniam ager calidus, stercorosus,tenuis,soliq; expositus est. Ægy-ptus cœli soliq; gratiâ coćtilia affert, caliditas enim coćtilitati atq; digestioni perutilis est at-que pnecessaria.Quę igitur agro ferueri & leni proueniunt,coćt lia erunt: quæ algido,spisso, lento,atq; etiam madido & palustri erumpunt solo,incoćtilia sentiuntur omnia,ob vberi? nimirum alimentum val diusq;.nam & frequen-tioribus imbrib. incoćt lia seri constat, & de-teriora,putredinîque magis obnoxia. Pluuia certè à satione protinus secuta incoćt litaté af-fert,Solis siccitas,licet min⁹ reddat suauia. co-ćtilia tamen efficit.Certissimū autę in proban- disfrumentis & leguminib. experimentū est, quod vnicuique debet esse ad manum , siqui- dem ad vitę salubritatem optimum funda- mentum:estque huiusmodi.Semina aquâ per- funfundantur aut madescunt, & quæ ocyus ex his s̃il. bonã intu nefcunt, molliorâq; euadūt, aridiratemq; corpori ac dacritiem statim eximunt, præstantiora iudi-
units.tr: while others always produce grains that are hard to cook and difficult for food. Indeed, in the same crop one may sometimes find some easily cooked and others hard to cook, separated only by a furrow. This might seem a marvel to someone, unless in matters of diet this too were considered. Here "easily cooked" is said of what can be softened readily and quickly altered by cooking; "hard to cook," by contrast, is what is not changed at all or only with difficulty. The former is soft and loose, able to receive the warmth and moisture by which it is softened; the other resists and opposes by its density. All these things come about from the influence of the climate and sun. In Lemnos only easily cooked grains are produced, since the field is warm, dung-rich, thin and exposed to the sun. Egypt, by the favour of its climate and sun, yields easily cooked grains, for warmth is very useful and necessary for cooking and digestion. Grains that grow in a warm and light soil will therefore be easily cooked; those that break forth in a cold, dense, sticky and even wet and marshy soil are all found to be hard to cook, because of their abundant and lasting nourishment. For it is agreed that grains sown in very frequent rains are hard to cook and inferior, and more liable to rot. Rain falling immediately after sowing brings hardness, while the drying of the sun, though it makes them less pleasant, still makes them easy to cook. Moreover, the most certain test of grains and pulses, which everyone ought to have at hand, since it is the best foundation of a healthy life, is this: seeds are soaked or steeped in water, and those that soften more quickly and become more tender, and at once shed their dryness and hardness, will be judged the better;

units.la: cabunt urque verò pristinam ariditatem duri- tiemq; diu retinent, necin coquendo tumef- cunt, necinsignitermollefcunt, cibis abdican- da fant, constant enim terrestri & crassa effen- tia, ac difficulter à ventriculo & venis confi- ciuntur ac digeruntur, quamobrem crudus succus in vescentium corporibus procrea- tur, qui variorum morborum causa existit; quæ verò ocyus videmus intumescere & mol- lescere, cibis idonea & facilia iudicantur, nam à ventriculo facile digeruntur, & cosiciuntur.
units.tr: but those that retain their former dryness and hardness for a long time, and do not swell in cooking nor soften noticeably, are to be rejected from food. For they consist of an earthy and gross substance, and are with difficulty processed and digested by the stomach and veins; therefore crude juice is produced in the bodies of those who eat them, and this is the cause of various diseases. But those which we see swell and soften more quickly are judged suitable and easy for food, for they are readily digested and processed by the stomach.

units.la: Vitæ falsa Hæc diligenter obseruare oporteb it eum, cui brevitas s- vitæ salubritas, quâ inter omnia dona & bona nimbus nihil præstant us, cure est: quis verò inter mor- maxime tales est, qui eam non expetat? Hanc ne- debet ess. gligere, quid aliud est quàm morbis ipsis præ- cura. bere initia? Cæterum defrugum satione, agricolatione, frugum ipsarum permultis dif- ferentiis, earum messe, & repositione, plura qui desiderat, consulat rei rusticæ scriptores, naturæ; prudentes & inter alios. Varronem,
units.tr: One who is concerned with a long and healthy life, which surpasses all gifts and goods, ought to observe these things diligently. For who among mortals does not seek this most of all? To neglect it is nothing other than to give the beginnings of disease to disease itself. As for the sowing of grain, its cultivation, the many differences of the grains, their harvest and storage, let whoever wants more consult the writers on rural matters, the wise students of nature, and among others Varro, Columella, Theophrastus, Pliny, and so on.

units.la: Q. s̃ter- Columellam, Theophrastum, Plinium, &c. rein Eu- Vnum hic præterire minime decet, quæ vide- rove se- licet terræ in Europa fœcunditate magis sint scundistate s̃ bilitatem? Europam terrarum pulcerrimam celebres esse, saluberrimam iuxta ac fructuosissi- mam, s̃sient mam, adq; colendum magis idoneam, quam ceteras. cæteras orbis partes, qui de situ orbis literis mandarunt, propemodum astruunt omnes.
units.tr: One thing it is by no means fitting to pass over here: why is the earth of Europe more fertile than the others? That Europe is the most beautiful of lands, most healthy and most fruitful, and more suitable for cultivation than the other parts of the world, almost all who have committed the situation of the world to writing affirm.

units.la: In hac Germania nostra sita est, hodie plu- rimis suis partibus agrorum cultu insignis, frugum abundantia commendabilis, genero-sisq; virtbus consita, diues clarorum virorum, animosisque populis frequens, ferarum, aliorumque animalium, qui in cibos hominum pro nutrimento admittuntur, fœcundissima, quibusdam tamen in locis magnis syluis multisq; fluminibus inuia cernitur: olim non admodum ferax frugum fuit, quia teste Cæsare, agrorum cultum neglexerunt, nolentes studium gerendi belli agricultura commutare, vitaq; omnibus erat in venationibus. Vnde maior pars illorum victus in caseo, lacte, carne, consistebat, neque quisquam apud eos agri modum certum aut fines proprios habebat. Hodie quoque pleræque Germaniæ gentes vinum ignorant, vt quæ sub cœlo frigidiore & asperiore sitæ sunt, externa tamen conquirunt terrâ mariqúe, qualia sunt Gallicum, Hispanicum, Rhenanum. Sed certum est totam Germaniam à Priscis non fuisse cognitam. Hodie certè in victus vrbanitate, morumq; comitate nullis aliis populis Germani cedunt.
units.tr: Our Germany lies in this region. Today, in most of its parts, it is distinguished by the cultivation of its fields, commended for its abundance of crops, planted with noble virtues, rich in famous men and populous with spirited peoples; it is very fertile in wild animals and other creatures that are admitted as nourishment for human food. Yet in some places it appears unfit, with great forests and many rivers. Formerly it was not very fruitful in grain, because, as Caesar testifies, they neglected the cultivation of the fields, unwilling to exchange the zeal for waging war for agriculture, and their life consisted entirely in hunting. Hence the greater part of their food consisted of cheese, milk and meat, and no one among them had a fixed measure or proper boundaries of land. Even today most German peoples are ignorant of wine, since they live under a colder and harsher sky, yet they seek foreign wines from land and sea, such as the Gallic, Spanish and Rhenish. But it is certain that all of Germany was unknown to the ancients. Today, certainly, the Germans yield to no other peoples in the refinement of their food and the courtesy of their manners.

units.la: Galliam florentissimam regionem esse, solisque vbertate felicissimâ, amœnam, salubrem, frumenti pabuliq; feracem, quin & vitibus maxima ex parte consitam, omnium feré scripta prædicant. Unum non leue incommo-dum habet, quod assiduis agitatur flatibus, humoribusq; & pluuiis plurimum obnoxia cernitur, algoribusque premitur vehementibus. Quidam tam opulentam hodie Galliam esse existimant, quàm Priscis temporibus Hispania fuisse aut Persis perhibetur. Undecimi Galliarum Regis Ludouici elegans dictum hic usurpare libet, pratum enim graminosum & late patens Galliam nominabat, quod toties fit retibile[?], quoties usum[?] fuerit fœnisecio opus esse, quo dicto omnium aliorum regum opes suis minime æquandas intellexit.
units.tr: It is commonly said in nearly all writers that Gaul is a most flourishing region, with a very happy fertility of soil, pleasant, healthy, rich in grain and pasture, and indeed for the most part planted with vines. It has one not slight drawback: it is seen to be much exposed to constant winds, moisture and rains, and is pressed by fierce cold. Some think Gaul is today as wealthy as Spain or Persia are said to have been in ancient times. It is worth adopting here the elegant saying of Louis, eleventh king of the Gauls: he called Gaul a grassy meadow spreading far and wide, which must be mown whenever there is need of haymaking; by this saying he indicated that the wealth of all other kings could not be compared with his own.

units.la: Italiæ veterum, tum Latinorum, tum Græcorum scriptis admirabilis fertilitas celebratur, inq; frugibus, vitibus, arboribus, aliisq; ad vitam necessariis cibis beatissima semper habita est. Ipsam tamen Romam Venetiasq; sine a-liarum vicinarumq; terrarum frumentis stare non posse constat.
units.tr: The admirable fertility of Italy is celebrated in the writings of the ancients, both Latin and Greek, and it has always been regarded as the most blessed in grain, vines, trees and other foods necessary for life. Yet it is agreed that Rome itself and Venice cannot stand without the grain of other and neighbouring lands.

units.la: Hispaniam quoq; fertilitate mirè commendabilem graues autores tradiderunt, maximè verò ob metallorum copiam, quibus universa scatet: frugibus enim non ubique abundare, & præsertim ubi metallorum est ferax, Strabo pro-didit: rarum enim est inuenire regione utroq; munere claram. Solinus nihil in ea ociosum, nihilq; sterile inueniri affirmat, siue soli ubertatem, siue vinearum prouentus, siue arbora-rios rios respicias. Sed hæc felicitas cœli aerisque temperationi non parum accepta ferenda est, quippe flores, rosæ scilicet, violæ & asparagus etiam, tribus tantum mensib.in anno illis defi-ciunt. In quibusdam etiam locis agros fertiles esse adeò traditur vt, cum semel sata frumenta sint, subinde recidiuis feminibus segetem novantibus septem minimum, interdum plures etiam ferant messes.
units.tr: Serious authors have also handed down that Spain is remarkably commendable for its fertility, but chiefly for its abundance of metals, with which the whole land teems. For Strabo has recorded that a country is not everywhere abundant in crops, and especially where it is rich in metals; for it is rare to find a region famous for both gifts. Solinus affirms that nothing in it is idle or barren, whether you look at the richness of the soil, the yield of the vineyards, or the trees. But this happiness must be credited not a little to the temperature of its sky and air, since roses, violets and even asparagus fail there for only three months of the year. It is also related that in some places the fields are so fertile that, once the grain has been sown, they bring forth at least seven harvests, and sometimes more, since the fallen seeds renew the crop.

units.la: Hæc Romanis ante Dictatorem Cæsarem parū fuit cognita, vt ex historiis patet: plæriq; enim fictā eam, nusquamq; extare omninoq; fabulosam contenderunt, teste Plut. Temperatius in ea & salubrius cœlum est quam in Gal-lia: imbribus tamen ac nebulis crebriorib. ma-didum. Frugum pecorumq; fœcundum est ibi solum, Fruges citò proveniunt, sed tardè mitescunt, omnibusque iis quæ tàm pecora, quàm homines benignius alant, præclarè abundat. Hibernia iniquum habet ad maturanda semina cœlum, verùm herbis lætis & dulcib. adeo luxuriat, vt se exigua diei parte pecora imple-ant, & nisi pabulo prohibeantur, difficiliant diu-ti[?] sc.pasta. Vina in Anglia nulla, à Gallis enim Germanisque ea petunt, & quidem fortiora, quia imbecilla vecturam non ferunt.
units.tr: This was little known to the Romans before the Dictator Caesar, as the histories make plain; for most of them maintained that it was fictitious, nowhere existed, and was entirely fabulous, as Plutarch testifies. The sky there is more temperate and healthier than in Gaul, though it is more often troubled by showers and mists. The soil is fruitful in crops and livestock. Crops come up quickly but ripen slowly, and it abounds splendidly in all those things which feed both beasts and men more generously. Ireland has an unkindly sky for ripening seed, but it is so lush with cheerful and sweet herbs that the cattle fill themselves in a small part of the day, and unless they are kept from the pasture they would burst. There is no wine in England; they seek it from the Gauls and Germans, and indeed the stronger kinds, because weak wine does not bear carriage.

units.la: Sicilia, cui Anglia maximè similis nonnul-lis videtur figura sc.triquetra, fertilitate nullis pene terris comparanda venit. Tulit Cererem frugum inuentricem : Unde fit vt quicquid gignat, optimum esse judicetur. Hujus felicitas ex orat. Cic. in Ver. manifesta euadit. Theophraftus autor est in quadam ejus parte cele-rem quandam fieri confirmationem feminum ferorum, esse namque sementem eorum sex menses, pascua quoq; habere mirifica, frumentiq; omnino perfertilem praedicant: horreum Romanorum jure nominatae est, ut quae in singulos annos ingentem frumenti copiam penderet, ut quidam non sibi sed Romanis agros arare atq; ferere eam dixerit. Leontinorum in ea ager ante cuncta foecunditate nobilitatus reperitur centesimum granum dens.
units.tr: Sicily, to which England seems most similar in some respects, namely in its triangular shape, is to be compared in fertility with almost no lands. It bore Ceres, the inventress of grain; hence whatever it produces is judged to be the best. Its happiness is made plain from Cicero's Verrines. Theophrastus is the authority that in one part of it wild seeds are made to sprout quickly, since their sowing takes only six months. They also say its pastures are wonderful, and that it is altogether very fertile in grain: it was rightly called the granary of the Romans, since it paid in each year an immense quantity of grain, so that some said it ploughed and sowed its fields not for itself but for the Romans. In it the field of the Leontini is found to be most renowned above all for fruitfulness, yielding a hundredfold.

units.la: Sed & cæteras Europæi orbis terras fertiles esse opinifq; segetibus non deficere testantur qui in illas iter adornarunt, & ad tempus in iis moram fecerunt, vel visendarum illarum gratia, vel etiam certorum negotiorum expedi- undorum causa. De Suecia & Dania hoc vere possum affirmare, licet sub asperiore & algidi- ore sint coelo sita illa loca, nihil tamen, quic- quid ad hominum vitam humaniter & benig- ne sustentandam pertinet, naturam iis dene- gaffe, Brabantiam, Flandriam, Hollandiam, Frisiam totam, &c. Multis nominibus earum rerum ubertate & foecunditate, quae salubritati hominum conducunt, nobilitatas reperi-mus. Sed ob tumultus bellicos frumentorum aliarumq; rerum pretium plus justo adauctum, annonaeq; caritas major.
units.tr: But the other lands of the European world also are testified to be fertile and not lacking in plentiful crops, by those who have set out on journeys into them and stayed there for some time, either for the sake of seeing them or for the sake of conducting certain business. Concerning Sweden and Denmark I can truly affirm this: although those places lie under a harsher and colder sky, nature has nonetheless denied them nothing that pertains to sustaining human life humanely and kindly. We find Brabant, Flanders, Holland, all of Friesland, and so on, famed under many names for the abundance and fruitfulness of those things which serve the health of men. But on account of warlike tumults the price of grain and other goods has risen beyond what is just, and the dearness of provisions is greater.

units.la: Sed quid memorem Africae, Asiaeque loca quaedam fœcunditate adeo nobilitata ab autoribus gravissimis, ut fidem pene excedat omnem.
units.tr: But why should I mention certain places of Africa and Asia, made so famous for fruitfulness by the most weighty authors that it almost exceeds all belief?

units.la: Inprimis vero Babylonica felicitas commendatur. Etenim, Theophrasto prodente, bis illic in anno semper & quasi ordinate tondent triticum, tertio vero pecus admittunt, sic enim caulem mittit, cum alioquin foliis tantum lasciviat. Quid? quod negligentius colentibus quinquagesimo cum fœnore messes reddunt, diligentius vero cum centesimo quinquagesimo. Refert Curtius inter Tygrim & Euphratem jacentia tam vberi & pingui esse solo, vt à pastu repelli pecora dicantur, ne suffocentur. Causam memorandæ huius fertilitatis tradit, humorem ex vtroque manantem amne per certas aquarum venas.
units.tr: Above all, the happiness of Babylon is commended. For, as Theophrastus reports, they always cut wheat there twice a year, as if by a fixed order, and in the third they let the flock in, for the stalk then sends forth a shoot, whereas otherwise it would run riot only in leaves. What more? Those who farm more carelessly get harvests with a return of fiftyfold, while those who farm more diligently get a hundred and fiftyfold. Curtius relates that the land lying between the Tigris and the Euphrates is so rich and fat that the flocks are said to be driven back from pasture lest they choke. He gives as the cause of this memorable fertility the moisture flowing from both rivers through certain veins of water.

units.la: Theophr. Asiae quodam in loco adeo grande frumentum produci ait, vt grana singula magnitudine sua olivæ nucleis æquiparentur, illicq; omnia rore coalescere. Mirabile dictu & auditu, q; Procurator in Byzantia Africae campo Divo Augusto ex eo loco misit ex vno gra-no quadringenta paucis minus germina. Misit & Neroni similiter trecentas quadraginta stipulas ex grano vno. Cotinet in circuitu eximiæ ferti-
units.tr: Theophrastus says that in a certain place in Asia grain grows so large that each single grain equals an olive stone in size, and that everything there thrives on dew. It is wonderful to say and hear that a procurator in Byzantium, in the plain of Africa, sent to the deified Augustus from a single grain of that place a little under four hundred shoots. He likewise sent to Nero three hundred and forty stalks from one grain. The tract of that remarkable fertility is said to contain in its circuit two hundred and fifty thousand paces, yielding to the farmers a return of a hundredfold. Yet it lacks oil and wine, though it shows itself sufficiently glorious in its harvests.

units.la: fertilitatis illius tractus ducentos quinquaginta millenos passus, cum centesima fruge agricolis fœnus reddens. Oleo tamen ac vino caret fatis gloriæ in messibus exhibens.
units.tr: The outer shore of Mauretania is said to be so fertile and rich in soil that it bears very generously all kinds of grain and shows a vine bearing twice a year, and two harvests, according to Strabo.

units.la: Mauritanie oram exteriorem adeò fertilem esse traditur, foloq; diuitem, vt frugum genera & benignissimè proferat, & vitem biferam ostendat, duasq; messes, teste Strabone. Mirabilissimum est, quod in Chalcia Rhodiorum infula fieriproditum est Theoph. & Plin. autoribus, locum videlicet repertum præcocem fertilemq; adeò, vt hordeum in eo fatum, cum cæteris sereretur in locis, meterent coloni, itemq; ferere, atque cum reliquis vnà frugibus turfus metere possent. Sed beatiores longè sunt Infulæ fortunatæ, in mari Cafpio, quæ liberne cultu fertiles, omni frugum genere fructibus abundant sua sponte genitis, fubindeq; aliis fuperaliis innascentibus.
units.tr: Most remarkable is what is reported of Chalcia, an island of the Rhodians, on the authority of Theophrastus and Pliny: a place was found so early and fertile that barley sown there, while other places were sown at the same time, was reaped by the farmers, and they sowed again and could reap together with the other crops. But the Fortunate Islands in the Caspian Sea are far happier: they are fertile without cultivation, abound in every kind of grain produced of their own accord, and sometimes one crop springs up among another.

units.la: In Hispaniola infula ejusdem orbis (sc. Nouæ Indiæ) ter anno maturescere demetiq; segetes testantur qui de ficu nouæ Indiæ scripfe- runt: expertes enim sunt algoris hiemalis ob lineæ æquinoctialis viciniam: illic præterea ocyfsimè erumpere hortensia femina, fructufq; mitescere ac maturari tradunt: Cucumeres enim pepones & id genus, vigefimo à jacto femine die maturescunt, aut ad summum 28.
units.tr: Concerning the island of Hispaniola in the same world (that is, the New Indies), those who have written about the fig of the New Indies testify that the crops ripen and are harvested three times a year; for they are free from winter cold because of their nearness to the equinoctial line. Moreover, they report that garden seeds there sprout very swiftly, and that fruits ripen and mature quickly: cucumbers, melons and that kind mature on the twentieth day from the sowing of the seed, or at most the twenty-eighth.

units.la: Theophraft in Melo Infula intra 30. aut 40. dies meti fruges testatus est.
units.tr: Theophrastus records that on the island of Melos the crops are reaped within thirty or forty days.

units.la: Arabes beati felicesq; appellati sunt, quod frugibus, palmitibus, odorum suauitate multiplici, fluuiorumq; perspicua multitudine abundent, teste Marcell. Temperies praeterea apud eos coeli terraeq; admirabilis, adeo vt ad extremam eis felicitatem nihil videatur deesse[?]: quin & pretiosissimae ex mari apud eos margaritae petuntur, habent enim mare felicissimum. Thus illic duplici colligitur vindemia, primò circa canis exortum, hinc verno tempore.
units.tr: The Arabians were called blessed and happy because they abound in grain, vines, the manifold sweetness of spices, and the clear abundance of rivers, as Marcellinus witnesses. Moreover, the temperature of their sky and land is admirable, so that nothing seems lacking to their utmost happiness. Indeed, precious pearls are fetched from the sea among them, for they have a most fortunate sea. There the frankincense is gathered in a double vintage: first about the rising of the Dog Star, and then in springtime.

units.la: Judæam terram fertilitate insignem, nulliq; alteri inferiorem esse inter Historicos orbis scriptores pene omnes conuenit. Solum apud eos feracissimum est, maximeq; balsamo nobilitatum. Insula, in qua Meroe ciuitas cernitur, triticum ferre atq; hordeum, quæ in tantâ adolescent proceritate, vt facile homo equo aut Camelo insidens occultetur eorum segetibus, & à nemine conspici potest, Heliodorus testis est. In Olynthia agros quotannis restibu-los esse Varro scripsit. Vix in nostris fœcundif-fimis etiam atq; maxime opimis latifundiis a-gros restibulos inuenire est, ac in summa etiam terrarum vbertate rarissimè ac fere nunquam semen cum decima fruge reddi, quod partim hominum negligentia, præcipue verò telluris ac temporum culpâ accidere manifestum est. Hactenus de mirabili terrarum quarundam fer-tilitate, redeamus nunc ad ipsa frumentacea, quibus potissimum aluntur homines, & ex
units.tr: Almost all the writers of history of the world agree that the land of Judea is distinguished by its fertility and inferior to no other. Its soil is most fruitful and is especially celebrated for balsam. The island in which the city of Meroe is seen bears wheat and barley, which grow to such height that a man sitting on a horse or a camel can easily be hidden by their crops, and cannot be seen by anyone; Heliodorus is the witness. Varro wrote that in Olynthus the fields are fallow every year. Scarcely can one find, even in our most fruitful and especially rich estates, fields left fallow; and in the greatest fertility of lands it is very rare, and almost never, that seed is returned with a tenfold yield; and it is clear that this happens partly through the negligence of men, but chiefly through the fault of the soil and of the seasons. So far concerning the wonderful fertility of certain lands; let us now return to the grains themselves, on which men mainly feed, and from which

units.la: quibus præcipua hominum cibaria cõstant atque conflantur. Ubi tamen adnotandum dē frumentorum speciebus inquisitionem ambi- guam valde esse, quod, referente Plinio, non eadem vbiq; sint ss umenti genera, & si eadem, neque tamen vbique isdem nominibus appellantur: pleruntur : proindeque superfluum puto, sruc mentorum nomina præcipere, quæ aut loco subinde, aut ætate mutantur, sacileque esse, eaque eligere ac explorata habere, quæ nostris in regionibus vel sata proueniunt vel aliunde advehuntur.
units.tr: These are the staple foods from which people's chief diet is made up and prepared. Yet it should be noted that enquiry into the kinds of grain is very uncertain, because, as Pliny reports, the kinds of grain are not the same everywhere, and even where they are the same, they are often not called by the same names everywhere. Therefore I think it superfluous to lay down the names of the grains, which change from place to place or with the age, and it is easy enough to choose and keep in mind those that grow sown in our regions or are brought in from elsewhere.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De alimentis quæ veniunt à vegetabilibus & plantis.
units.tr: On foods that come from vegetables and plants.

units.la: NExor si bḗ caput memmimisse velim leḡo- rem amplioris ulterioriq, intelligentiæ gratiā, varias alimentorum dinifiones apud autores occurrere, pro variis atq; diuersis eorum facultatibus & viribus. Primo enim quedam proprie dicuntur alimenta, alendi tantum corporis potestatem habentia, non etiam alterandi: quedam non tantum alunt solum, sed alendo etiam alterant & immutant & nutrimenta, si alimenta appellantur, immutant, inquam calefaciendo, vel refrigerando, vel humectando, velexiccando. Deinde quedam sunt ευχυλα boni succi, quedam ꝓ ἁυλα ꝓ succi, que quoq; difficulter concoquuntur & perficiuntur sicut prior a facile digeruntur & nu- triuntur.
units.tr: Now, if I wish to recall, for the sake of wider and deeper understanding, the division that is commonly found in the authors, there are various divisions of foods according to their different faculties and powers. First, some foods are properly so called, having only the power to nourish the body and not also to alter it. Others not only nourish but also alter and change by nourishing. Nourishments, if they are called foods, change things by warming, cooling, moistening, or drying. Next, some foods are of good juice (eucyla), others of poor juice (aucyla?), and the latter are digested with difficulty and are not fully made into nourishment, while the former are easily digested and nourish.

units.la: I. Alimentorum variæ distinctiones.
units.tr: I. Various distinctions of foods.

units.la: II. Alimentorum succi boni et mali. triunt. Tertiò quædã sunt infirma parū sed prom-tènu rientia[?], quædam firmissima ex quibus plu-rimum alimenti coacernantur[?], vt succolenta craf-fa & grauia: quædam inter hæc ambigunt nulla in emperie donata, optimum frugiue succum effi-cientia, in quorum numero sunt panis benè iuba-ftus & fermentatum gallinarum, caponum, phasi-anorum perdicum, columbarum, turturum, tur-dorum, merularum, omnisq; generis avicularum carnes, aliaq; laudabiles lucci, vt vitulina, verve-cina, pisces saxatiles, vinum generosum, mel, lac, & ova sorbilia. Quædam vero insitâ quadam-sympathia & familiaritate alunt, vt elleborus co-turnices, ferrum Struthiocamelum. Deniq; à condimentis differunt alimenta. illa enim ad ob-sonia condienda fiunt, graecis ὀψώματα, ἐδύσμα-ματα[?] dicuntur, alimenta vero proprie sunt, sine quib. corpus alimento posset. Nunc de singulis seorsim & speciatim pertractare instituti operis ratio re-quirit. Et primo quidem ex plantis in cibū venit aut semen, aut radix, aut folia, aut fructus, aut flos, quib. addi possunt tubera & fungi quos terra spon-te ut superuacua protrudit. Inter feminā primas obtinent frumenta & legumina. Frumenta (sic dicta à fruendo, id est, vescendo, frumen enim summa pars gulae est) spicas habent cū arista, aut spica mutica: Legumina (sic dicta à legedo, unde etiā legumeta dicuntur, non n. secantur, sed vellendo legūtur) siliquis seu thecis includūtur. vnde dicuntur Inter cerealia præcipuè numerantur triticum, &c.[?]
units.tr: II. Good and bad juices of foods. Some are weak, scarcely nourishing, and quickly passing through; others are very firm, from which a great deal of nourishment is gathered, such as foods that are juicy, thick and heavy. Some lie between these, being of no extreme quality, and yielding the best and most wholesome juice. Among these are well-baked bread and fermented (leavened) bread, the flesh of hens, capons, pheasants, partridges, pigeons, turtle-doves, thrushes, blackbirds, and all kinds of small birds, and other praiseworthy meats such as veal, mutton, rock fish, good wine, honey, milk, and soft-boiled eggs. Some foods nourish by a certain innate sympathy and affinity, such as hellebore for quails, and iron for the ostrich-camel. Finally, foods differ from seasonings: the latter are prepared to season dishes and are called in Greek opsomata, edysmata [ὀψώματα, ἐδύσματα], whereas foods properly are those without which the body could not be sustained. Now, the plan of the present work requires that I treat each one separately and in particular. And first, from plants there comes to food either the seed, the root, the leaves, the fruit, or the flower, to which can be added the tubers and mushrooms which the earth puts forth spontaneously as superfluous growths. Among seeds, grains and pulses hold the first place. Grains (so called from enjoying, that is, from eating, for the grain is the chief part of the gullet) have ears with awns, or ears without awns. Pulses (so called from picking, whence also they are called legumes, for they are not cut but plucked) are enclosed in pods or husks. Among the cereals, wheat, and so on, are especially reckoned.

units.la: Siligo, hordeum, Zea, far, oryza, avena, milium, ocymum, panicum, sesamum.
units.tr: Rye, barley, maize, spelt, rice, oats, millet, basil, panic grass, sesame.

units.la: Triticum alendis hominibus accommodatissi-mum est, interq; fruges primam semper obtinuit autoritatem: Plurima eius notantur genera, Africum, Thracium, Assyrium, Ægyptium, Italicum, Gallicum, Germanicum, &c Non aliunde quàm à terris sortita nomina, colore tamen, specie, magnitudine & proprietate differentia.
units.tr: Wheat is most suited to feeding humans and has always held the first place of authority among the grains. Very many kinds are noted: African, Thracian, Assyrian, Egyptian, Italian, Gallic, German, etc. They have received their names not from anything but the lands, yet they differ in colour, appearance, size and quality.

units.la: Optimum probumq; triticum est ponderosum, densum, tota substantia adeo compacta, ut dentib. vix teri diuidiq; queat: quod item plus farinæ reddit, quod aquâ maceratum vel etiam præcoctum ocyus intumescit, ( hoc enim modo agricolationis naturaq; rerum peritî cerealia femina probare solent, probitatisq; vel improbitatis indubitatum id habent experimentum.) Dentib. verò facilè cedens facileq;, frangibile, fractumq;, sirarum & laxum cernitur, magna mole & quantitate exiguum præbet alimentum. Non enim superficies tantum externa consideranda est, sed frangi debet & diuidi. Ut enim venire solet, ut quod extra flauum ac densum sit, pinsitum postea fractumq; rarum, leve, intus, album appáreat. Plurimum enim vitæ interest, tritico uti electo, vescio, quod non sit mucidum, situm corruptionemve redolens, aq; gurgulionibus arrosum, quod bene pinsitum ac molitum, quod lolio, melampyro, aliisq; feminum quisquiliis careat, id liquidum permitto-sum vescentibus graues autores cum experientia tra[?]radunt: panificia enim ingrata, tum odore & colore, tum gustatu reddit. Non igitur parum vitæ interest pistorum diligentia aut negligen-tia: negligentius enim ventilate & expurgate fruges, lolio aliisq; id genus vitiis mixta plerumq; in cibos assumte ingentes morborum causas præ-bent. Quoties panificum & frumentariorum auaritia fraude, accidere videmus, ut in pani-ficia veniat triticum mucidum atq; gurgulio-nibus arrosum? frumenta scilicet impurgata relinquunt, ne mensuræ aliquid detrahatur, quas imposturas quidam hodie ad unguem tenent, & per experimenta docuunt. Lolii pessimi esse succi, caput ferire, & vertigines ciere multis exemplis probare superuacaneum iudico: hinc prouerbiū, Lolio vitiare vsurpatur in eos, qui cacutiunt, & de rebus peruerse iudicant. Aeram quoq; in-ter frugum vitia numerat Plinius, & cum est in pane, celerrimè ait, vertigines facere. In Asia, Græciaq; balneatores, cum volunt turbam pelle-re, carbonibus id semen initiant. Melampyrum in siculo tritico peculiariter innasci traditur, nō tamen æque noxium ac lolium. In nostris segeti-bus prosilit herba, quæ nigella dicitur, cuius semē pinsitum, & in panificia redastum, non admodū ingratum gustu est, est enim tota planta sine odore, excepto semine, quod odoratum solum est, ideoq; panibus potest compinsi, sicut sæniculum & carui. Porro vitiari & corrumpi semina fre-quentioribus imbribus, imprimis vero triticum-
units.tr: The best and soundest wheat is heavy and dense, its whole substance so compact that it can hardly be crushed or split by the teeth. Such wheat also yields more flour, and when soaked in water or even parboiled it swells more quickly. (This is how those skilled in husbandry and the nature of things usually test cereal seed, and they regard it as an unfailing proof of good or bad quality.) Wheat that yields easily to the teeth, is brittle, and when broken looks porous and loose gives little nourishment despite its great bulk and quantity. For one must consider not only the outer surface but also break and divide the grain. As often happens, what is yellow and firm on the outside, once ground and broken, appears thin, light and white within. Much of our health depends on using selected wheat: flour that is not mouldy, does not smell musty or rotten, is not gnawed by weevils, is well ground and milled, and is free of darnel, melampyrum and other weed seeds. Serious authors who have tested this by experience teach that such flour is wholesome to eat, since impure flour makes bread unpleasant in smell, colour and taste. It matters a great deal to our health, then, whether bakers are diligent or careless. Grain that is carelessly winnowed and cleaned, mixed with darnel and similar faults, and then eaten, commonly causes serious illnesses. How often do we see bakers and corn-dealers, out of greed and fraud, put mouldy wheat gnawed by weevils into their bread? They leave the grain unclean so that nothing is taken from the measure. Some today master these tricks perfectly and teach them by practice. I judge it superfluous to prove with many examples that the juice of darnel is very harmful, striking the head and causing dizziness; hence the proverb "to spoil with darnel" is used of those who are dim-witted and judge matters wrongly. Pliny also counts tares among the faults of grain, and says that when it is in bread it very quickly causes dizziness. In Asia and Greece, bath-attendants, when they want to drive off a crowd, fumigate it with charcoal. Melampyrum is said to grow especially among Sicilian wheat, though it is not as harmful as darnel. In our fields there springs up a herb called nigella, whose seed, when ground and put into bread, is not very unpleasant in taste; the whole plant is without smell except the seed, which alone is fragrant, and so it can be ground into bread, as fennel and caraway can. Moreover, that seeds are spoiled and corrupted by frequent rains, especially wheat

units.la: & bordeum, ftercoratione quoq;, quando, tum cantharidibus, quæ tritico, & suum adhuc in spicis est, innascuntur, experientiâ compertum est. Exstercoratione virus redolere, cantharides spargi, na erodere, exindeq; contagione fruges infici, plan- nè verisimile est. In frequentioribus plurimis imbribus plus prosilire lolium quam in ficcita- tibus tepstantur præter experientiam nauseam rerum agricolationisq; prudentes. Quid? quod ipsa femina cariosa, arrosa, & im beccilla fruges vitiant? Quapropter summa diligentia adhibenda est, ut fruges a tempestiua messe rite condan- tur. Recentes enim & ventilatæ & pulcriores sunt, ponderosiores, & diu vero in horreo asseruata exusta deprehenduntur, & leuiores, minusq; fa- rineæ reddunt. Plurimum etiam refert ante ex- actam & completam maturitatem fruges, cum- primis veteres triticum & hordeum non demete- re: ante enim tempus decipiamur, mole suatoris consta- re deprehenduntur, multoq; melioris ac laxio- res: Superuacua humiditatis industria, unde ar- gumentum: Sic enim recondire hominem studio con- calefacientem corruptionem contrahunt, & putre- scunt: unde deteriores euadunt tum ad seminem tempus adulterium cibariorum Interempsi- seue igitur demittere fruges incorruptas seruari non possunt, & etiam in intensissima aestate perditussimo frumentariorum dolo & fraude. Caterum pure frumentaria, quæ in annos reponuntur, repurgari subet. Columella: quanto enim sunt expoliti Columella minus à gurgulionibus arrodúntur : sin verò protinus ad vsum assumantur, satis erit in vm-brarefigerari[?] inq; granarium reponere.
units.tr: and barley, and also by manuring, and when there are cantharides, which breed on wheat while it is still standing in the ears, is established by experience. That manure gives off a stench, that cantharides are scattered and gnaw the grain, and that the crop is infected by this contagion, is not at all improbable. That darnel springs up more in frequently rainy seasons than in dry ones is attested by experience and by the sensible men who know farming. And what of the fact that the seed itself, when decayed, gnawed or weakened, spoils the crop? So great diligence must be applied to storing the grain properly after a timely harvest. Fresh grain that has been winnowed is finer and heavier, but grain kept for a long time in the granary is found to be dried out, lighter, and yields less flour. It also matters a great deal not to gather the grain, especially old wheat and barley, before it has fully and completely ripened: for if we are deceived by the timing, it is found to be shrunken in bulk, though it is then much better and fuller. Superfluous dampness, from which an argument arises: when grain is stored with too much moisture it heats, contracts corruption and rots, and so becomes worse, with the adulteration of food following at the same time. Therefore grain that is not dried cannot be kept uncorrupted, even in the most intense summer, and it is ruined by the greatest deceit and fraud of corn-dealers. But pure grain that is stored for years must be cleaned again. Columella: the better the grain is cleaned, the less it is gnawed by weevils. But if it is to be used at once, it is enough to dry it in the shade and put it in the granary.

units.la: Nec statim à messe in vsum cibarium sunt assumenda, vt maior fere pars nostris temporibus & locis facere cor: fuerit[?], sed loco sicco condenda sunt ac reponenda, modicèq; siccanda, absumtâ sc. aliena in ii humiditate post adeptâ quadâ excoctione. Cauendum quoq; diligenter, ne præ-ter modum arescant, decedente sc. ab iis & exhalante natiua humiditate: immodicè enim sicca-ta in cibis damnantur, quamuis absolute improba dici non possunt. Certum est, quæ in annos multos reposita durauerunt, vires validiores habere: vetusta autem & diutissime serua-ta sequenti experimento discernes, quippe dissipata ac fracta pulusculum quendam tenuissimum effluentant atque emittunt, taliaq; in usu cibario ingratissima sunt, sicut & erosa à noxiis animalculis valetudini obesse non dubitandum: ad diuturnitatem vero & durationem in multos annos plurimum facit frugum matura deci-sio & collectio in siccitatibus, repositioq; in loco sicco, quo aer humorq; nō pertingit, nisi cum advu-sum promuntur, unde auster damnatur & meridies, aura[?] humidiores nonnunq; propinquis è locis aut amnibus expirates: laudatur aura aquilonaris frigida & sicca, hæc enim perennitatem affert conditis frugibus. Vnde mirari non subitin Germania nostra fruges tam diu durare non posse ob imbrium s. abundantiam, quà robustissi- ma etiam grana corrumpi videmus. Fruges e-nim reposita, si diu incorrupta manere debent, quotannis ventilanda sunt & repurganda, mo-nente Columella. Qui denique de re rustica po-steris praeceptis reliquerunt, in universum subent omnes messem fieri, antequam extoto grana in-durescant, equaliter si flauescentibus, sic enimnecimmodicè sicca, nec etiam nimis madidadeprehenduntur. Haetenus de variis frugum cerealium, feminum corruptionis causis inter-nis & externis, remotis & propinquis: redeamus nunc ad triticum.
units.tr: Nor should grain be taken for food straight from the harvest, as most people in our times and places do, but it should be kept and stored in a dry place, and dried moderately, so that the alien moisture is removed and, after a certain kind of cooking, the grain is ready. One must also take care not to dry it beyond measure, when its native moisture departs and evaporates from it: for grain that is dried too much is condemned as food, although it cannot be called absolutely bad. It is certain that grain which has lasted many years in store has stronger powers; you will tell old and long-kept grain by this test: when crushed or broken it gives off and emits a very fine dust, and such grain is most unpleasant as food; likewise grain gnawed by harmful little creatures should not be doubted to harm health. For durability and lasting many years, what matters most is harvesting the grain when it is fully ripe and in dry weather, and storing it in a dry place, where air and moisture do not reach it, unless it is brought out facing the wind. For that reason the south wind and midday are condemned, and the damper breezes that sometimes blow from nearby places or rivers; the cold, dry north wind is praised, for it brings lasting preservation to stored grain. Hence it is no wonder that in our Germany grain cannot last so long, because of the abundance of rains, by which we see even the sturdiest kernels corrupted. For stored grain, if it is to remain uncorrupted for long, must be winnowed and cleaned every year, as Columella advises. Finally, those who have left precepts on country life to posterity all agree that the harvest should be made before the grain has hardened all over, and equally when it has turned yellow, for thus it is found neither excessively dry nor too damp. So far on the various internal and external, remote and near causes of corruption in cereal grain and seeds. Let us now return to wheat.

units.la: Natura tritici est mediocriter siccare & ca-lefacere, hominig prabere alimentum inter o-mnia frumenta familiare & salutare. Vsus eius pracipuè & maximè in pane sentitur: quippe a-liter esum, siue crudum, siue elixum, succum crassum generat & lentum.
