Est enim crudi tri-ticinflari aluum indubitatum est, ex volupta-te verò & dulcidine plus efitatum durumpit. Elixato rusticos [?] Galenus testis est, concottu tamen esse difficile & crassi succū af-ferat, ideog cibus abdicandum: quae sista sunt videant quifrumentatam, ut vocant, hoc est Ptisanam ex tritico confectam liberalius essumunt, olim enim hanc sorbitionem, & etiam num quibusdam admodum placuisse: & place-re, sinsimamq, plebem in sesunis quadragenariis quandoque se ea solari atque reficere confuēsse obserobseruatum est. Olim celebrata ex tritico Ptisana est ad eadem commoda adque hordacea, scilicet ad asperae arteriae exulcerationem, nisi Ptisanæ quod triticea valentioris alimenti, et ad ciendas urinas efficacior perhibetur, & hordacea vero glutinosior, obq;id pulmonis trachaeae, vlcerationi ceae vi-utilior[?]. Cum itaq; non ex tritico tantum, sed hordeo, oryza & similibus Ptisanæ fieri consueuit, & in libris omnium Medicorum Ptisanæ sorbitione nihil sit magis protritum atque decantatum, præsertim in febrium acutorum morborum cura, non ἀλόγως me hic fecisse existimaverim, si de Ptisanæ huiusmodi confectionibus generatim aliquid adiecero.
units.tr: The nature of wheat is to dry and warm moderately, and among all grains it is a familiar and wholesome food for humans. Its use is felt chiefly and most of all in bread, for otherwise, whether eaten raw or boiled, it produces a thick and sticky juice. That raw wheat causes flatulence in the bowels is beyond doubt; eaten with relish and sweetness, however, it is brought up more easily. Galen bears witness that boiled wheat is hard to digest and yields a thick juice, and so it should be avoided as food. Let those who eat frumentata, as they call it, that is, ptisan made from wheat, more freely consider these points. For this broth was once, and still is, pleasing to some, and it has been observed that the common people in their forty-day fasts have often comforted and refreshed themselves with it. Ptisan made from wheat was once celebrated for the same benefits as barley ptisan, namely for healing an ulcerated windpipe; yet wheat ptisan is considered the more nourishing and more effective at promoting urine, while barley ptisan is more glutinous and therefore more useful for ulceration of the lungs and windpipe. Since ptisan is commonly made not only from wheat but also from barley, rice and similar grains, and since nothing is more worn and repeated in the books of all physicians than the broth of ptisan, especially in treating acute fevers, I do not think I have acted irrationally [ἀλόγως] in adding something here about such preparations in general.

units.la: Sciendum vero Ptisanam proprie, sicut ex antiquis & recentioribus scriptoribus liquet, dici de hordeo vel decorticato solum atq; degluba-to, vel etiam de hordeo decocto, vt ita Ptisana proprie nihil aliud sit, quam pulmentarium, sorbitio vel cremor ex hordeo in mortario contusa & decorticato. Cremor vero lac seu succus ex grano macerato elicitur. Vnde in comitio dipnosophistarum griphus iactabatur, succum hordei decorticati depsitum bibe. Athen. l.10. dipnosoph.
units.tr: It should be noted that ptisan, properly speaking, as is clear from ancient and recent writers, is said of barley either merely husked and hulled, or also of boiled barley. Thus ptisan properly is nothing other than a pottage, broth or gruel made from barley pounded in a mortar and husked. Cremor (gruel) is drawn out as a liquid or juice from the macerated grain. Hence at the assembly of the Deipnosophists a riddle was tossed about: "Drink the juice of husked barley, let it settle." Athenaeus, Deipnosophists, book 10.

units.la: Impropriè vero & generaliter Ptisanæ appellatione veniunt omnia frumentacea, deglubata ac pistillis decorticata, [illegible, ~9 letters] hoc est, tundere vel decorticare, hinc Ptisanam quibus ex dicatur?
units.tr: Improperly and in a general sense, under the name ptisan are included all grain foods that are hulled and husked with pestles [illegible], that is, pounded or husked. Hence, from what things is ptisan said to be made?

units.la: ex zea, tritico, hordeo & oryza apud Galenum, Plin. & Hippocrat. concinnatam legimus. Tei- stis, describatur deomnibus his non crudis folium & deglubatis, sed etiam aqua cotlis, Plin. lib. 18. c. 17. Galen. 8. meth. & 7. c. 6.
units.tr: We read that it is prepared from maize, wheat, barley and rice in Galen, Pliny and Hippocrates. As evidence, let it be described from all of these, not only raw and hulled, but also boiled in water: Pliny, book 18, ch. 17; Galen, Method, book 8, and book 7, ch. 6.

units.la: Genuina autem & antiqua Ptisanæ conste- ctio. Elionis ratio hæc erat: hordeum maturum, me- dulla plenum, non strigosum, sed crudum adhuc aquâ irrigatum manibus fricabatur fortiter, donec exterior cortex bene abstergeretur: hoc ita aliquoties manibus subactum, sole siccatum in pilam coniiciebatur, velut si in mola tritum pinsebatur, contusum suo cum polline ad neces- sarios usus in vase sictili condebatur, ex quo pti- sanæ sorbitiones, pultem & cremorem concoque- bant.
units.tr: The genuine and ancient preparation of ptisan was this, according to Elion's method: ripe barley, full of marrow, not shrivelled but still raw, was moistened with water and rubbed vigorously by hand until the outer husk was well scoured off. This was worked by hand several times, dried in the sun, and thrown into a mortar; as if ground in a mill, it was pounded, and the husked grain with its fine meal was stored in an earthen vessel for necessary uses. From this they boiled ptisan broths, porridge and gruel.

units.la: Pollen tenuissimum est & purissimum, in farina pulueris instar molis adhærescens, & proprie est in tritico, sicut flos in silii- gine.
units.tr: The pollen is very fine and very pure, clinging to the flour like dust from a mill. Properly it is found in wheat, just as the flour is in siligo.

units.la: Porro simplex hordei decoctio per colum tra- ctæ ptisanæ colatæ, sucus hordei & bordeata dicitur. Item aqua hordei, pars enim succulenta retinetur, terrestrior vero abiicitur: In qua ve- rò grana hordei colo vel cribro ab eorum succo segregata non sunt, ptisanæ non colatæ dicitur, sorbitio.
units.tr: Moreover, the simple decoction of barley drawn through a strainer is called strained ptisan, barley juice, or bordeata. Likewise barley water, for the juicy part is kept and the more earthy part is thrown away. That in which the grains of barley, not separated from their juice by a strainer or sieve, remain, is called unstrained ptisan, or broth.

units.la: Varius autem modus ptisanam condire sole- bant, saleto, melle, sapa, cyminio, amygdalis, pi- nea, & similibus, pro suo magis vel minus nutri- entes. trientem, refrigerantem, abstergentem, præcordia humectantem, asperitatem pectoris demulcentem, ventrem lubricantem, sitisq; extinguentem, reddere eam studebant. Optima conditura est cum lacte feminis peponum vel amygdalarum dulcium & saccharo, pro plus vel minus nutriendi ac refrigerandi scopo. Si enim magis eam nutrire optamus, multa portio hordei adiicienda erit, multumq; bullire permittendum: Si maior cura refrigerandi est, pauciore erit hordei portio, atq; non tam diu bullire concedendum. Fuerunt quoq; alia operosiores & lautiores ptisanæ decoctiones, ut cum melle, aceto, oleo, porro, anethiq;que, quas Apitius (qui arte culinaria paterna abligurierat bona) & Galen passim mo-strant, sicut & Ægineta lib. 1. & Oribasius in Euporistis, qui tamen minus aquæ accipit, unam nempe hordei præparati heminam, hoc est, dimidium sextarii in X. tantu aquæ heminis coquit, donec medulla hordei fuerit eliquata, tum mel, acetum & salis mucil[?], & postquam in ebullitione hordeum detumuit, porrum & anethum quoq; addere solitus est.
units.tr: They commonly seasoned ptisan in various ways, with salt, honey, must (sapa), cumin, almonds, pine nuts and the like, according to whether they wished it to be more or less nourishing. They aimed to make it nourishing, cooling, cleansing, moistening the praecordia, soothing the roughness of the chest, loosening the bowels and quenching thirst. The best seasoning is with the milk of pumpkin seeds or sweet almonds and sugar, according to whether the aim is more or less nourishment and cooling. If we wish it to be more nourishing, a large portion of barley must be added and allowed to boil for a long time; if cooling is the greater concern, the portion of barley will be smaller and it should not be boiled so long. There were also other more elaborate and refined ptisan decoctions, with honey, vinegar, oil, leek and dill, which Apicius (who squandered his father's fortune on culinary art) and Galen show in many places, as do Aegineta, book 1, and Oribasius in the Euporista. Oribasius, however, takes less water: he boils one hemina of prepared barley, that is half a sextarius, in ten heminae of water until the marrow of the barley is dissolved; then he adds honey, vinegar and salt, and after the barley has swollen in boiling, he is accustomed to add leek and dill too.

units.la: Ægineta vero accipit aquæ partes XV. paululumq; olei, & postea ebullitionem acetum addebat, post vero exactam coctionem param salis friabilis inspergebat: atq; hoc modo ptisana etiam extrusso & oryza ad varios usus coctinnari praepariq; potest. Ad extremum vulgaris nostra ex hordeo aqua, quâ frequenter utimur in febrium cura, conficiendi modus non est apud omnes unum.
units.tr: Aegineta takes fifteen parts of water and a little oil, and afterwards adds vinegar during the boiling; when the cooking is complete he sprinkles in a little crumbled salt. In this way ptisan can also be cooked and prepared for various uses from spelt and rice. Finally, our common barley water, which we often use in treating fevers, is not made in the same way by everyone.

units.la: § idem: quidam simpliciter aquâ macerant, quidam eam, vt ex hordeo [?] ʒ ythum praeparant.
units.tr: Likewise: some simply macerate it in water, while others prepare it as [?] of barley.

units.la: Galeno fisse eam ignorant inde constare qui- busdam videtur [?], quod quidem explicaturus Hippocratem 4.acutorum libro, iubentem, vt febricitantes ad sedandam sitim aquae bordeacee potum bibant, dicit, bordei poculum esse [?] ... ἀδιψον, hoc est, sitis extinctivum, sed non docet quâ ratione hordeum praeparetur. Oribasius V. Juliani Imp. medicus id videtur docere, quan- do inquit, non oportet febrientibus hordeum in- pila tundere, sed grana compressa dilatare et coquere in aquâ, hordeum, in aquâ tepidâ bis abluere, deinde illius hordei heminam, hoc est, di- midium sextarii (<bl>cinhalb Nòffeln</bl>) in x. aquæ heminis ad hordei usque crepaturam coquere, tandem colare: in fine decoctionis quidam ad- dunt cinnamomum, nucem mosch-atam, Zinzi- ber, vel galangam, vel etiam post decoctionem modicum croci integri, priusquam morbus requirit, habita ratione simul naturae patientis, aetatis & temporis.
units.tr: That it was made by Galen is not known to some, and seems to be doubted for this reason. Indeed, in explaining Hippocrates, book 4 of the Aphorisms (Acutorum), where he bids febrile patients drink barley water to quench their thirst, he says the barley drink is thirst-quenching [ἀδιψον], that is, thirst-extinguishing, but does not teach by what method the barley is prepared. Oribasius, physician to the Emperor Julian, seems to teach this when he says that barley should not be pounded in a mortar for febrile patients; rather the compressed grains should be softened and boiled in water. The barley should be washed twice in warm water, then one hemina of that barley, that is half a sextarius (<bl>cinhalb Nòffeln</bl>), should be boiled in ten heminae of water until the barley cracks; finally it is strained. At the end of the boiling some add cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger or galangal, or, after boiling, a little whole saffron, before the illness requires it, having regard at the same time to the patient's nature, age and the season.

units.la: De pultibus, placentis, panes, extritico, & hordeo, de cereuisia, huiusce coctione commodius dicetur suo loco post frugum (c. tractationem).
units.tr: On poultices, flat cakes, bread made of wheat and barley, and beer, their preparation will be discussed more conveniently in its place, after the treatment of grains (chapter).

units.la: Hucusque igitur de Ptisana, sequuntur nunc aliquae tritici speciales, quas hic negligere, quam gloria illud sua faudare [?].
units.tr: So much, then, on ptisan. Now follow some special kinds of wheat, which it would be wrong to neglect here rather than to praise them for their own sake.

units.la: Annotatum vero supra est naturam eius et species modicè [?]. modice calfacere & exiccare, propterea praestantissimum & delicatissimum ex eo panem concinnari. Expertum praeterea est farinam eius in aqua vel lacte cum butyro bene decoctam, vel etiam cum oleo amygdalarum dulcium (quodin experimentis habeo, licet non apud omnes in usu fuit) contra tussim, arteriam exasperatam, cruentas & sanguinolentas excreationes pectorisque catera vitia efficacem esse.
units.tr: It was noted above that its nature and kinds are moderately warming and drying, and therefore a most excellent and delicate bread is made from it. It has also been tested that its flour, well boiled in water or milk with butter, or also with oil of sweet almonds (which I have tried in my own experiments, though it was not in use among everyone), is effective against cough, a roughened windpipe, bloody and blood-streaked expectorations, and other ailments of the chest.

units.la: Sextum Pompeium in tritico coelo adge-nua usque sedendo podagra liberatum historia tradunt.
units.tr: Histories relate that Sextus Pompeius, freed from gout by sitting in wheat up to his knees.

units.la: Farinam triticeam cum aqua & melle decoctam, quamvis phlogosin & inflammationem discutere, emplastri vice illitam atque apposi-tam, qui dubitat, experiatur.
units.tr: Whoever doubts that wheat flour boiled with water and honey, though it disperses phlegmon and inflammation, works as a plaster when applied and laid on, let him try it.

units.la: Furfures tritici aqua cum melle decocti, percolatiq;, colli palatiq; inflammationes sanant, gargarizatu & collutione: colluatur autem os tepide: si vis, adde flores malvae hortensis, qui Germanis dicuntur, Ehrnrofen/Herbst-rofen, hi enim maxime in oris colliq; inflammationibus commendantur: si adsit oris exulceratio, collioni adde alumen.
units.tr: Bran of wheat boiled with water and honey, then strained, cures inflammations of the throat and palate when used as a gargle and rinse. Let the mouth be rinsed warm. If you wish, add the flowers of garden mallow, which the Germans call Ehrnrofen/Herbst-rofen, for these are especially recommended for inflammations of the mouth and throat. If there is ulceration of the mouth, add alum to the rinse.

units.la: In aceto vero & vino tritici furfures decocti utilissime adhibentur membris nervisque luxatis, fanant serpigines, pruriginem, & mammarum inflammationes: efficacius operantur si addideris rutham & agrimoniam: si vero luxationibus illorum decoctum tantum adhibens dum est, infine decoctionis adde crocum, vel quod melius est post remotionem ab igne. Fermentum ex. ritico extenuandi, ex- trahendi, maturandi, concoquendi aperiendi, vi pollere ostendunt furunculi caterag, tuber- cula cutanea maturanda, concoquenda atq; a- perienda, ut materia putris intus conclusa egre- diatur: adiiciendum vero modicum falis est, emplastri, vice applicandum. Triticum quoq; prolem est amylum, farina fine tritico fine mola confecta: dictum enim quod sine mola conficiatur: optimum ex trime-ftri fit tritico, huius [?] inventionem deberi in[?]fule Chio prodidit Plinius; idq; [?] datissimum: Dioscorides laudat Creticum & Ægyptium. Probatur lenitate, & ut candidum accrecens sit, nec tactu asperum. Emplasticum vere est, bene est tenacius adhærescendo obstruit & infarcitum implet, siccat & absorbet, quare sanguinis vi ectiones potest cohibet, cum faccha-rō & modico croci prodest tussientibus & asth-matieis, faucibus item exaspera tis, cum oleo ve-ro amygdalarum dulc. decoctum admixto sa-charo Candi pectoris apostema fanat, imbu-endum autem, antequam coquatur in aqua per noctem est contra oculorum denig fluxus pu-tulas cavas, ulcera illum efficax est. Confici-endi modum antiqui fatis fatiscat, tradiderunt. &Ægineta ex purgato tritico fieri sub Canicule feruoribus tradit. Vulgaris modus talis est. Triticum in aquam frigidam recentem iniicitur, spiusq; in die agitatur, indies recentem affundendo: quinto die effunditur aqua sensim, cum sc. triticum fuerit emollitum, vasculoq; puro excipitur, contusumq; triticum per pannum colatur, aqua autem effusa nonnihil ei admisceatur ob facilliorem penetrationem, colatum in sole siccatur, aquam vero innatantem omnem effundas vel effluere sines, & ita confectum est.
units.tr: Bran boiled in vinegar and wine is very useful when applied to dislocated limbs and sinews. It heals creeping ulcers (serpigines), itching, and inflammations of the breasts. It works more effectively if you add rue and agrimony. If, however, the decoction alone is used for dislocations, add saffron at the end of boiling, or, what is better, after the pot has been taken off the fire. Bran also has the power to thin, draw out, ripen, concoct and open, as furuncles and other cutaneous tubercles show. These are to be ripened, concocted and opened so that the putrid matter shut up inside may come out. A little salt should be added, and it is applied in the manner of a plaster. Wheat also yields starch (amylum), made from flour prepared without wheat-bran and without a mill; it is called "without a mill" for that reason. The best comes from the wheat of Chios: Pliny reports that its invention is owed to the island of Chios, and it is the most excellent kind. Dioscorides praises the Cretan and Egyptian kinds. Good starch is tested by its smoothness, by its whiteness when it is crushed, and by not feeling rough to the touch. It is truly emplastic: because it adheres very tenaciously, it blocks up and fills stuffed places, dries and absorbs, and so it can restrain bleeding. With sugar and a little saffron it helps coughers and asthmatics, and also rough throats. With oil of sweet almonds, decocted and mixed with sugar candy, it heals an abscess of the chest. It should be soaked overnight in water before it is boiled, and it is effective against hollow pustules and ulcers, and against discharges from the eyes. The ancients handed down methods of preparing it, though the accounts are rather scanty. Aegineta says it is made from cleaned wheat during the heat of the dog days. The common method is this. The wheat is put into fresh cold water and stirred every day for five days, adding fresh water each day. On the fifth day the water is poured off gradually, once the wheat has softened. The wheat is then taken out into a clean vessel, crushed, and strained through a cloth. Some of the water that was poured off is mixed in, to make it penetrate more easily. The strained mixture is dried in the sun, and any water floating on top is poured off or allowed to drain away, and so it is finished.

units.la: Ex triticis deniq; aliud præcocius, aliud se-rius prouenit, aliud plures, aliud pauciores emit-tit culmos. Legitur vno ex tritici grano 30. aut 40 quandoq; exiisse spicatos culmos, quod tamè terræ bonitati, fertilitati & diligenti culturæ ac-ceptum ferendum est: atq; huc respexisse Sal-uatorem nostrum extra dubium est, cum dicit in parabola ad populum, sementem quæ in bo-nam terram ceciderit, aliam quidem centu-plum, aliam sexagecuplum, aliam deniq; trige-cuplum tulisse fructum. Eandem habet ratio-nem, quod quædam loca adeo præcocia & ferti-lia deprehenduntur, vt circa Thracium Si-num & in Chalcia Rhodiorum insula &c. vt quadragesimo à satione die triticum maturē-scat, testante Plinio & Theophr. lib. 9. hist. Plant. quoddam 9. mens. in agris moratur, vt in quibus-dam locis hibernū: quoddam 7. à satione mense hor-reis mandatur, vnde septimestre dici meretur: quoddam 3. à satione mense erumpit, vt staniū a-melforn [?]/ex quo optimū fit amylū, et trimestre Dioscoridi appellatur. Sed eiusmodi benignitas fertilitasq; nostro solo denegata est, apud nos enim quinto demum mense maturatur, adeo fruges alio atq; alio solo inter se distant, alio atq; alio gaudent cœlo, suumq; cuiq; frumento tempus, quo ad maturitatem perducitur, pro ter-varum diuersitate in singulis regionibus depu-tatum cernimus. Tantum de tritico.
units.tr: Among wheats, one kind ripens earlier and another later; one sends up many stalks and another fewer. It is read that from a single grain of wheat there have sometimes come forth 30 or even 40 spiked stalks. This, however, must be credited to the goodness of the soil, its fertility and careful cultivation. That our Saviour had this in mind is beyond doubt, when in the parable he tells the people that the seed which fell on good ground bore fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold. For the same reason, some places are found so early and fertile, such as the region about the Thracian Sea and the island of Rhodes in Chalcia, that wheat ripens forty days after sowing. Pliny and Theophrastus (Plinio & Theophr. lib. 9. hist. Plant.) bear witness to this. Some wheat stays in the fields for nine months, as it does in some places where it is sown in winter. Some is stored in granaries seven months after sowing, whence it deserves to be called "seven-month" wheat. Some sprouts three months after sowing, such as the wheat called "amelforn," from which the best starch is made, and which Dioscorides calls "three-month" wheat. But such a generous and fertile character has been denied to our soil, for with us wheat is not ripe until the fifth month. So different are the crops from one soil to another, and they rejoice in different skies. We see that each kind of grain has its own season for reaching maturity, assigned in each region according to the variety of the lands. So much for wheat.

units.la: A tritico proximam sibi dignitatem vendicant Siligo & Hordeum.
units.tr: Next in rank to wheat are rye (siligo) and barley.

units.la: De Siligine non parua controuersia inter doctos rei frumentariæ scriptores exorta est, quo patto videl. veteribus fuerit hoc frumenti genus appellatum? quid? quod & nostra ætate doctissimi quoq; medici in frugibus antiquorum discernendis non parum ambigere video, cum de vulgatissimo & notissimo bordeo dubitare illos animadvertam. Plinius vir alioquin acerrimi ingenii plurima hic confuse tradidit. Galenus de frumentis & feminibus, quæ in usu cibario erant, diligenter admodum sed tamen non usquequaq; aperte disseruit: ut sunt. Veteribus Siligo non tantum altera triticispecies erat, in quam triticum tertio anno degenerabat, sed quoq; depuratissima à furfuribus farina, <bl>flat schön Weitzenmehl</bl>/ quam Plinius obid tritici dicitas appellat. l.18.c.8. & 10. ac 11. Et Cornelius Celsus l.2.c.17. ex triticoinquit firmissima sitgo. Et idem Plinius, ex Siligine aut firmissimus panis, qui pistus dicebatur Siligni-tisicut Semidalitis, hoc est, Simila, qui conficiebatur. ebatur extritico non exquisite à furfuribus de- purato,& fyncomistus à Dioscoride appellaba- tur à farinæ cum furfuribus commixtione, ni- hil enim furfuris cribro ab eo excussum est, vt ita exquisitepura tritici farina, & excea panis siligo, similago, & semidalis dicta fit veteribus. Fuisse autem siliginem frugem Italiæ notissimam, magnamq; in panificijs gratiam obtinuisse offendit Iuuenalis carmine Satyrico Romanorum diuitum morem reprehendens, qui alium sibi ac delicatiorem quam communis panem apponi iubebant:
units.tr: Concerning rye, no small controversy has arisen among learned writers on grain: by what means was this kind of grain called by the ancients? Indeed, I see that even in our own age the most learned physicians are not a little uncertain in distinguishing the grains of the ancients, since I notice that they doubt even the most common and well-known barley. Pliny, a man of otherwise the keenest intellect, has handed down a great deal here in a confused way. Galen, in his work on grains and seeds that were used for food, discussed them very carefully, though not always clearly. For example: among the ancients, rye was not merely a second kind of wheat, into which wheat degenerated in the third year. It was also a very pure flour, freed from bran, which Pliny calls "flour of wheat" (flor tritici). See Pliny, book 18, chapters 8, 10 and 11. Cornelius Celsus, book 2, chapter 17, says that the strongest bread is made from wheat... and the same Pliny says that from rye comes the strongest bread, which was called "pistus," and the rye-meal called "semidalis," which is "simila," the finest flour. Pure flour from wheat not carefully freed from bran was called "syncomistus" by Dioscorides, from the mixing of flour with bran, for nothing of the bran had been sifted out of it by the sieve. Thus the finest wheat flour was called, by the ancients, "siligo," "similago," and "semidalis" bread. That rye was the most famous grain of Italy, and had gained great favour in baking, is shown by Juvenal, who in his satire censures the custom of the rich Romans, who ordered that a finer bread than common bread be set before them.

units.la: Ecce alius quanto porrexit murmure panem Vix fractum solidæ jam muccida frusta farinæ, Quæ geminum agerent non admittentia morsum: Sed tener & niueus molliq; siligine factus Seruatur Domino.
units.tr: Look how another, with what a grumble he pushed forward the bread, scarcely broken, already hard-crusted pieces of solid meal, which could not admit a double bite. But the soft and snow-white bread, made of smooth rye, is kept for the master.

units.la: Panis hic siliginei meminit vt lautissimi ac primarij, venusteq, & eleganter Romanos luxum in pane querentes exagitat.
units.tr: This bread is mentioned as the most elegant and principal kind, and with wit and refinement he lashes the Romans who look for luxury in bread.

units.la: Alij in hoc consentiunt siliginem veterum esse quod Germani Korn oder Rocken appellant. Et ex omnibus sestimonijs [?] veterum congestis liquido constare arbitror, siliginem, triticum, sicut & Speltam congeneres esse sruges, nam & Columella l. 2. c. 6. siliginem secundum triticigenum facit, & Theophrastus Siligi-nem tritico similem esse dixit, vocans eam bo-ζειόπυρον [?]: Dioscorides quoque, Speltae generi eam annumerat. l. 2. c. 2. ut ita in totum dixisse licet, at Siliginem nostram, quam German. Rocken appellant, cuius grana in molis tunduntur, quod crassius est, pro pecorum nutrimento a farina separatur, furfures nominant, a vete-rum siligine longe esse diuersam, cum siligo illis non tantum fit granum delicatissimi tritici, ve-rum etiam interdum medulla siliginei grani: Summa enim panis laus siliginis bonitate C prestantiâ apud illos constabat, ac panis ex ea conficiebatur delicatissimus & dulcissimus, cum ex nostra siligine insuauior, crassior ac atrior e-nadat pro locorum tamen terrarum, ac coeli temperatura varia. Bucuq, de siligine.
units.tr: Others agree that the rye of the ancients is what the Germans call "Korn" or "Rocken." I think it is clear from all the testimonies of the ancients gathered together that rye, wheat and spelt are kindred grains. Columella, book 2, chapter 6, makes rye second to wheat-kind, and Theophrastus said that rye is like wheat, calling it "zeiopyron" [ζειόπυρον]. Dioscorides also counts it among the spelt kind (book 2, chapter 2). So it may be said in general terms. But our rye, which the Germans call "Rocken," whose grains are ground in mills, and whose coarser part is separated from the flour for feeding animals, which they call bran, is quite different from the rye of the ancients. For the rye of those times was not only the grain of the finest wheat, but sometimes also the marrow of the rye grain. For the highest praise of bread among them rested on the goodness and excellence of the rye, and the bread made from it was most delicate and sweetest, whereas our rye produces a bread that is less pleasant, coarser and darker, though this varies with the temperature of the regions and the sky. So much for rye.

units.la: Submonitio ad locum de Siligine.
units.tr: Note on the passage concerning spelt-wheat (siligo).

units.la: Sunt qui existimant, quod Germani rocken nominant id esse siliginem veterum & [?] fecale, nec non triticum secundum Columellam, olyram vero appellatam Theophrasto & Dioscoridi. Sunt praeterea qui siliginem Romanorum idem esse cum olyra Graecorum esse putant, nam Theodorus Gaza fidelissimus Aristotelis interpres pro olyra siliginem vertit. Plinius [?] de siligine & olyra tractat, unde cadit illorum sententia, qui olyram siliginem esse Plinium prodidisse credidisse [?]. Alii Germanorum siliginem antiquorum typhon esse tendunt: alii esse diuersa, quod tri-tici [?] ticum, siligo & hordeum te[?] Plin. in area ex- teruntur, Zea vero cuius species est olyra mola exteritur & cum suis follicutis feritur. At olyrá Africanam siliginem esse Plinius sequentur, af- firmat verbis l.18.c.10 Ex ea dulcissimus fit pa- nis, inquit Plinius, est ipsa quam far, & ponde- rosior, raroq, modius granorum eius non sexde- cim libras farina adimplet, exteritur in Gracia difficulter, propterea iumentis dari Hom. tradi- dit: hoc enim est inquit quam vocant olyram. Olyra v. Ægypto peculiaris est, sicut & Gal- li, qui eam arincam nominant, Italiq, Theoph. Ide plantis, olyram inter ea, quæ tritico hordeoq, sunt similia, retulit, maturcq, feri prodidit, quam & multiplici folio includi, molliorq, atq; infir- miorem typha, avena, Zea, colore item candido. Non desunt qui nostrā siliginem typhā potu esse q olyrā sep[?]icantur: Est nam q typha Galeno te- ste 2 de alim. cereale frumenti, cuius granum gluma sine invoolucro velut tritico & hordeum vestitur, pinsitq, totum in panes densatur, color illi tritice flavior, corpus strigosum, tritico exil.* unde & parum triticum quibusdam appellatur. Ha- ebenus de siligine, cuius disceptatio, sicut & cete- rorum frumentorum ideo ambigua est, quod, sicut aliquoties meminì, non eadem ubique, sunt fruméti genera, & fideadem, neq, tamen iisdem nominib. appellantur. Sufficit illa frumentorū genera ex- plorata habere, quæ in nostris regionib. fata pro- mentur, quorumq, vis ac vires sunt perspectæ atq; probatæ. Hordeum ad varios medicinæ vsus vsur- patum ab antiquitus inuenitur, & nobilissimum ab iis frumentum appellatum est. Hodie raro lautiorum atq; magnatum mensas subit, nisi cortice suo castratum, mundatum bordeum ap- pellatum, rundendo enim deglubitur, oder geschelte Gersten / elixum enim primo cibo iuxta solet, stomacho non ingratum præfer- tim si aceti modicum fuerit permixtum: quod si vero diu satiue elixum non fuerit, inflat, & ventriculo noxium est, minus enim abstergit. Plurimum eo in papatu vescuntur in ieiunio illo quadragenario. Caeterum cum bordeum cuiq; notissimum sit, hic illud delineare opera pretium est, quod si, aut in alijs, mini sse & hic oportet, omnia fœmina, præcipue vero frumenta pro locorum natura varia, cœlo, statu in quo fata sunt & ænatæ, boni tatem adipisci vel malignitatem. Maturius feriētur quam triticum, & primo ex omnibus fru- mentis erumpit à primo satu, die vt plurimum septimo, magis, festinat quam triticum. In Ægypto sertio quarto sue dieprovenit, sexto verò à satu mense metitur, in Hellade septimo, in Peloponneso ostauo, Æthiopes non aliam quam mili & bordei frugem nouerunt. Melius autem deteriùs, fit cultura & foli natura. Terram requirit optimam & bene stercoratam, quæ sit destituitur, facile in lolium transit & degene- rat præsertim pluuio sa tempestate. Causam hujus
units.tr: Some hold that what the Germans call rocken is the rye of the ancients, and also the wheat that Columella describes, while Theophrastus and Dioscorides call it olyra. Others think the Roman siligo is the same as the Greek olyra, since Theodorus Gaza, the most faithful translator of Aristotle, renders olyra as siligo. Pliny treats of siligo and olyra, and from this comes the opinion of those who believe Pliny reported olyra to be siligo. Others argue that the German rye is the typhon of the ancients. Others hold that they are different things. Pliny, in book 18, chapter 10, says that the African siligo is the one that follows, in words: "From it comes the sweetest bread," says Pliny, "it is the same as far, and heavier; and a bushel of its grain rarely fills sixteen pounds with flour. It is threshed with difficulty in Greece, and so Homer reports it was given to beasts of burden; for this, he says, is what they call olyra." Olyra is peculiar to Egypt, as also to the Gauls, who call it arinca, and to Italy. Theophrastus counted olyra among plants similar to wheat and barley, and reported that it ripens late, and that it is enclosed in a many-layered husk, softer and weaker than spelt, oats and zea, and likewise white in colour. There are those who think our rye is the typha or the olyra. For typha, according to Galen in book 2 of On Food, is a cereal of wheat whose grain is covered by a husk without an outer skin, as wheat and barley are, and when ground it is made into dense loaves. Its colour is yellower than wheat, its body meagre, and for this reason some call it "poor wheat." So much on siligo. Its discussion is uncertain, as are those of the other grains, because, as I have mentioned several times, the kinds of grain are not the same everywhere, and though they are the same, they are not called by the same names. It is enough to know those kinds of grain that are produced in our regions, whose force and powers have been examined and tested. Barley, used from ancient times for various medical purposes, was called by them the most noble of grains. Today it rarely comes to the tables of the wealthier and the great unless it has been stripped of its husk and cleaned, and is called pearl barley; for it is peeled by rubbing. oder geschelte Gersten It is usually boiled first, and is not unpleasant to the stomach, especially if a little vinegar is mixed in. But if it has not been boiled long enough, it causes bloating and is harmful to the stomach, for it cleanses less. They eat a great deal of it in the papacy, during that forty-day fast. Since barley is very well known to everyone, it is worth describing here that all grains, and especially cereals, vary according to the nature of the place, the climate, and the condition in which they were sown and grew, in their goodness or badness. It ripens earlier than wheat, and for the most part, of all grains, it sprouts soonest after sowing, usually on the seventh day. In Egypt it appears on the fourth or third day, and it is harvested in the sixth month after sowing; in Greece on the seventh, in the Peloponnese on the eighth. The Ethiopians know no other crop than millet and barley. It turns out better or worse according to cultivation and the nature of the soil. It requires the best land, well manured; if it is neglected, it easily turns into darnel and degenerates, especially in rainy weather.

units.la: buius rei assignat Galenus aliquam l. de alim. cum ait, a patre suo agricolationis perit ssimo, longo vsu obseruatum fuisse, semina tritici cum sufficiora fuerint s imperfectiora, distingus intra humum delituerint, non facile fructus bonum edere posse, sed potius conuertisse in loliuum herbam sc. segetibus inimicam. Theophrastus ait hordeum primum in triticum, in hordeum vero triticum mutari, atq; ita deinceps ex vitro generi lolium. Sed id fortasse in agro Atheniensi, vbi maximum optimum sir- missimum hordeum repe: itur, euen re scet. No- ster sermo de germanico hordeo est. Porro laudatissimum hordeum id est, quod fractum s pinsitum candorem representat, quod densum, planum ac ponderosum est laxum enim gracile s lene imp obatur. Sed certissimum vitio s hordei indicium est, quando e fractio s diuiso excidit pulmisculus quidam quo significatur in- terna corruptio caries, situ ac putredo.
units.tr: Galen, in the book on food, gives a reason for this, when he says that it was observed by his father, a most skilled farmer, over long experience, that when seeds of wheat were less full or imperfect, and lay hidden in the ground, they could not easily produce a good crop, but rather turned into darnel, a weed hostile to the crops. Theophrastus says that barley first changes into wheat, and wheat in turn into barley, and so on successively into the worst kind, darnel. But this perhaps happens in the Athenian countryside, where the largest, best and heaviest barley is found. Our discussion concerns German barley. Moreover, the most praiseworthy barley is that which, when broken and ground, shows a white colour; that which is dense, flat and heavy is good, for a loose, slight and light one is rejected. But the most certain sign of a defect in barley is when, on breaking and splitting it, a certain dust falls out, which indicates internal corruption, decay and rot.

units.la: Verum quastio hic occurrebat, quæ difsi- An fru- hienda est, an hordeum sicut s alia semina, pro- menta tinus a messe s tritura sint melior, an vero nouella certotempore post? Quosdam non patiexicari annicu- triticum s hordeum Theophrastus meminit, lis præ- propterea quod ad reddendam farinam meliora tent, an minus arefacta putantur, unde in acernostam vero hæc triticum quam hordeum redgere solent: in hac illis? etiam sententia agricolationis peritè quidam esse seperiuntur. Alij semina non protinus a tritura s
units.tr: Here a question arises, which is debated: whether grain should be kept, like other seeds, and be better for being used immediately after harvest and threshing, or rather some time after. Theophrastus mentions that some do not allow wheat and barley to be used at once, because they are thought to make better flour when they have dried out a little. In this view, men skilled in agriculture are also said to be divided: some prefer the new crop to the old, and others the older grain. Yet in the case of wheat, some think it is better than barley for making bread.

units.la: meliora esse quam certo tempore post, nec no- uella anniculis prastare inde consistunt, quod necesse sit, ut veluti excoctionem quandam atq; potessatem capiant, exacto sc. quod fuerit in iis alienum: humor enim supernatans concoquendus erit in loco sicco et minime humenti, primum in vsum cibarium veniant, mediocriter siccata, salutaria sunt et cibis idoneo: a Columella affirmat frumenta decisa tempestive inde emensa tum postea capere, quae si pura deinde in annos reconduntur, reppurgari debent, quanto enim sunt expoliticra, tanto minus a gurgulionibus exeduntur si in protinus vsui destinantur, sati est in umbra refrigerari, et ita granario infer- ri: intempestive vero demessa incorrupta dies tius seruari non posse videmus, sic enim condita concalescunt et putrefiunt. Prior sententia vera esse potest de certo tritici et bordei genere: est namq; tritici sicut et bordei genus trimestre, sic appellatum quod trium mensium spatio possit perfici, ideo in cibo hominis facilius est gratius, quod videl minus terra infit propter temporis breuitatem, germ. Sommergersten Hoc obi- ter notandum frumentaris negotiatoribus et annonam flagellantibus relinquo, frumenta im- modice si cata, quaeq; reposita in multos annos duraverunt, vires innalidiores et imbecillores habere, cuius rei, ut antea memini est indicium evolans dunifis ac fractis granis palmis culmus. Sed eiusmodi Da danarios, sic enim Ulpianos eos appelappellat, qui omnia praemunt ut carium ea postea distrahant, capite de vinis, veriorib[?]us coloribus depingam.
units.tr: Others maintain that seeds are not better immediately after threshing than at a certain time afterwards, and that grain a year old is preferable to new grain, because it must, as it were, take on a certain ripening and strength once what is foreign to it has been driven out; for the moisture that rises to the surface must be digested in a dry place, and not at all damp. Grain that is only moderately dried is wholesome and fit for food, if it is used first for eating. Columella affirms that grain cut at the proper time, and then measured, keeps well; but if it is stored for years, it must be cleaned, for the more polished it is, the less it is eaten by weevils. If it is destined for immediate use, it is enough to cool it in the shade and so put it in the granary. But we see that grain harvested at the wrong time cannot be kept long without spoiling, for stored in that state it heats and rots. The former opinion may be true of a certain kind of wheat and barley: there is a kind of wheat, as also of barley, called trimestral, because it can be brought to maturity in the space of three months. Therefore it is easier to digest and more pleasant as human food, because it stays less time in the earth, owing to the shortness of its season; in German, Sommergersten (summer barley). I note this in passing and leave it to grain merchants and to those who drive up the price of corn: grain that is excessively dried, and that has been kept for many years, has weaker and feebler strength; the sign of this, as I mentioned before, is that the stalk flies out in dust when the grains are pressed and broken. But such men, whom Ulpian calls danarii, who hoard everything so that they can later sell it at a high price, I will describe under the heading on wines, with truer colours.

units.la: Apud Campanos κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν ἀνοβιλι[?]-tate scilicet & frugis praestantia semen appella-tum est: quin ex ea praestant simum atq; salu-berrimam alicam confici prodidit Dioscor. l. 2. c. 8o. & Plinius l. 18. c. 8. In Campania p. ove-niebat laudatissima, ac in multis quoq; Italia loci. Typhe perquam similem esse scribit Theophrastus; maturęq; seri dicitur solo pingui & leto: granum multiplici tunica includitur, facilimum, omnibusq; animantibus gratissimum. Qui sar non habent, loco eius utuntur Zea.
units.tr: Among the Campanians, the seed was called by the Greek word [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν] simply by excellence, that is, of the seed of outstanding quality; indeed, Dioscorides in book 2, chapter 80, and Pliny in book 18, chapter 8, report that from it is made a most excellent and wholesome groats. In Campania, and also in many places in Italy, it grew most praiseworthy. Theophrastus writes that it is very like spelt; it is said to be sown late, in rich and fat soil. The grain is enclosed in a many-layered husk; it is very easily prepared and most pleasing to all living creatures. Those who do not have sar use zea instead of it. Some, however, think it is sar.

units.la: Quidam tamen sar eam esse putant. Duorum autem est generum, una simplex, altera in binis putaminibus bina grana iuncta gerens, unde dicoccos appellatur. Scribit Dioscorides (Chon-dron ex ea, qua dicoccos dicitur, & Crimnon, hoc est, farinam crassiorem seu crassulentam confici, ex qua faciebant pultes abunde alentes, sed quae agre conficiuntur. Galenus rerum na-tura prudentissimus 1. de alimento, nihil certi videtur de Zea statuere, aut enim se numquam vidisse nec ab ullo alio audiuisse semen esse aliquod frumentaceum, quod vulgo appella-tur Zea, inq; totum vult, nullam aliam esse exquirendam praeter olyras & typhas.
units.tr: Some, however, think that this is far. There are two kinds: one is simple, the other bears two grains joined together in two husks, which is why it is called dicoccos. Dioscorides writes that from the kind called dicoccos, and from crimnon, that is, a thicker or coarser meal, a porridge is made that nourishes abundantly but is hard to digest. Galen, most learned in the nature of things, in book 1 of On Food, seems to establish nothing certain about Zea. For he says either that he has never seen, nor heard from anyone else, any cereal grain commonly called Zea, and he wants it said outright that no other grain is to be sought besides olyra and typha.

units.la: Idem quedam esse femina testatur, quæ partim in hordei aut typha, partim in typhæ oly ræ aut tritici medio sunt loco, quædam vero esse quæ ad olyræ, alia ad hordei aut typhæ, alia ad tritici, alia ad panici, alia quæ ad milii naturam proxime accedant quæ nomina habent, alia simplicia, ut in Italia, alia composita, ut in Cappadocia ψυμνόκεφρον[?], hoc est, hordeum nudum ac corticis expers. In Bithynia autem minoris Asiæ regione Zeopyron, hoc est, ex Zea quod tritico nomen conflatum est, ut ita adeo differant, ut ei non nisi ad ea, quæ sunt ex tritico, quo nomen maius est, de eis feminibus exquisite differre.
units.tr: The same author testifies that there are certain kinds of grain which lie partly between barley or typha and the typha olyra or wheat; some are close to the nature of olyra, others to that of barley or typha, others to wheat, others to millet, and others to the nature of millet, and these have names. Others are simple, as in Italy; others are compound, as in Cappadocia, where there is a grain called psymnokephron, that is, naked barley without husk. In Bithynia, a region of Asia Minor, there is zeopyron, that is, a name compounded from Zea and wheat (triticum). So the kinds differ so much that he treats these grains exactly only in relation to those made from wheat, whose name is the greater.

units.la: Quidam Galeniinte pretes Chondrum far verterunt, ut Linacer vir utraque literatura clarissimus. Quid hoc die fit pa-um coffare vi- deo. Ruellius scribit in Gallia farris duo genera: , rase ut vn- ma rutilo colore, arufitus agricola lis rutilum frumentum appellatum, ge. man. Kerni alte um candidum, quod clam finum purum tatur, germ. Spelt oder Dinckel, Columella farris 4, descriptgenera, Venuculum rutilum, venuculum album germ. Teutsch Reiß/ryage manica, clusinum gen. Spelt/ zimen, deniq, trimestre alias halcaft um, germanis Ammelkorn / quod pondere bonitatem, pracipuum est: unde non cadit illorum sententia, quæ Chondron, hoc est alicam & far adoreum Co- lamella, lumelle, Spelte seu Zea faciunt speciem. Exi-mium autem fuisse farri a prisci's Romanis bo-norem tributum ex eo constat, quod ipsam glo-riam a farris honore adoream vocarunt: Tanta autem erat farris copia, ut nulla provinciarum Italiam pasceret, modiusq; farris ad singulos asses redactus erat. Numa instituit far ipsum torrere, tunc enim salubrius censebatur, unde fornacalia farris torrendi feriae instituisse fer-tur : arista caret, interq; hiberna frumenta an-numeratur : omnium frumentorum durissi-mum, contraq; hiemes firmissimum est. Roma-nis far triticumq; vulgatissima fuisse frumenta comperio, quamuis & aliis terris communia. Varro Campanum praestantissimum appellavit. Ex omnibus autem veterum testimoniis colligere est & concludere licet, far adoreum, alicam & chondrum idem significare, & nunc quidem pro frumento peculiari, nunc pro mola, hoc est, farre ofto ex Zea confecta accipi. Far autem factitium an fuerit apud antiquos disceptatur, Archigenes apud Athen. l. 9. c. 45 manifeste monstrat, Romanos far ex frumento madefacto, siccato, & in crassoribus partes diffratto, parasse: alii & quid in recentioribus, inter quos est Hiero. Mercurialis l. 2. variar. lect. contra afferunt, nullum, far aliud praeter natiuum adoreum vocatum, unquam nominasse: In his & similibus parum iunat diutius immorari, quare relinquo illu litem: nolo enim hic esse ambitiose diligens.
units.tr: Some of Galen's translators rendered chondrum as far, as Linacer, a man most distinguished in both literatures, did. What is done today I see is little to be wondered at. Ruellius writes that in Gaul there are two kinds of spelt: one with a reddish colour, called in German Kerni or Dinkel, and the other white, which is called clean and pure. Columella describes four kinds of far: the reddish venuculum, the white venuculum, the one called in German Reiß or Zimen (or Spelt), the clusinum, and finally the trimestre, otherwise called halcaft, which is called Ammelkorn in German and is especially prized for its weight and goodness. So the opinion of those who make chondron, that is alica, far, adoreum, Columella's lumelle, spelt or Zea, the same kind, does not hold. Moreover, that the ancient Romans gave far especially high honour is clear from the fact that they called glory itself adoreum from the honour of far. The supply of far was so great that no province fed Italy, and a measure of far had been reduced to a single as. Numa instituted that far be parched, for then it was considered more wholesome; hence it is said that the Fornacalia, a festival of parching far, was instituted. It lacks the awn and is counted among the winter grains; it is the hardest of all grains, and on the other hand the firmest against winters. I find that far and wheat were the most common grains among the Romans, although they were also common in other lands. Varro called the Campanian far the finest. From all the testimonies of the ancients it can be gathered and concluded that far adoreum, alica and chondrum mean the same thing, and that they are taken now for a particular grain, now for meal, that is, spelt-flour made from Zea. Whether far was ever made artificially among the ancients is debated. Archigenes, cited in Athenaeus book 9 chapter 45, clearly shows that the Romans prepared far from wheat that had been soaked, dried and crushed into coarser pieces. Others, among them Hieronymus Mercurialis in book 2 of the Variae lectiones, argue on the contrary that no one ever named any far other than the natural grain called adoreum. I think it is not much use to linger longer over these and similar matters, so I leave this dispute aside; for I do not wish to be ostentatiously meticulous here.

units.la: Submonitio.
units.tr: Preliminary note.

units.la: Plinius tragum cerealem et typham cerealem inter frumentacea genera reponit, & quidem ab Oriente adducti prod dit, atq; ex ipsa typha in suo orbe oryzam fieri retulit: dicitur tragus cerealis ad differentiam tragi herba. Ex tritici femine fieri tragum in Campania tantum & Aegypto Plinius affirmat: Galenus vero roex nobilissima olyra decorticata: tragum ex Chondro fieri scriptores graeci tradiderunt. Columella c.6.lib.2. far candidum tragum cerealem nominat, alii oryzam germanicam, Dioscorides tragum frumentaceum l.2.c.85. & 86. Eiusdem cum chondro natura est, nisi quod difficilius in ventriculo conficiatur. De typha Dioscorides omnino tacuit, quod mirari subit, cum Theophrastus lib. de plantis multa de typha prodiderit. Quin & Plinius nihil praeterea de ea notatu dignum reliquit. Hoc adducere unum opera est pretium, quod Theophrastus scribit, nullum frumenti genus comperiri, quod totum in aliud transfire aptum sit, atq; typha & Zea. Galenus large in Asia provenire tefatur, regionibus praecipue quae supra Pergamum sunt. Panes ex tritico in panificia cogi, quoniam triticum in oppida deportetur, ad hanc pa- nis typhinos olyrinis longe praestantiores praedicat. Illi calen[?]tes nimirum sint calentes: si enim diutius asservantur, ferventur, sepsis evadunt deteriores, ventri- culumculumq; instar concreti luti grauant. Hac Ga-lenus.
units.tr: Pliny lists tragus cerealis and typha cerealis among the grain kinds. He says they were brought from the East, and that rice is made from typha itself in its own region. Tragus cerealis is so called to distinguish it from the herb tragus. Pliny affirms that tragus is made from wheat seed only in Campania and Egypt. Galen, however, says it is made from the most noble husked olyra, and the Greek writers have handed down that tragus is made from chondros. Columella (2.6) calls white far tragus cereal, others call it German rice, and Dioscorides (2.85 and 86) calls it grain-tragus. It has the same nature as chondros, except that it is digested with more difficulty in the stomach. Dioscorides said nothing at all about typha, which is surprising, since Theophrastus in his book on plants said much about typha. Indeed Pliny also left nothing else about it worth noting. It is worth adding one thing Theophrastus writes: no kind of grain is found that can be wholly changed into another, as typha and zea can. Galen says it grows abundantly in Asia, especially in the regions above Pergamum. Bread is made from wheat in the bakeries, since wheat is carried into the towns, but for this purpose he declares typha bread far superior to olyra bread. Loaves of course are hot when they are hot; but if they are kept longer they ferment, turn sour, and weigh down the stomach like clotted mud. So Galen.

units.la: De alica velim in hac submonitione le- Elorem[?] in transcursu quasi meminisse eam nunc frugis genus esse, nunc ex fruge factam fari-nam, indeq; pulticulam vel sorbitionem. Pro fruge accipitur à Plin. l.18.c.7. vbi de frumen-tis per tempora satis inquit, aliqui verna, myli-um, panicum, lentem, cicer, alicam appel-lant.
units.tr: Concerning alica, I would like to note briefly in this preliminary remark that it is sometimes a kind of grain, sometimes flour made from grain, and from that a pulse or gruel. Pliny (18.7), speaking of grains by the seasons, says that some call the spring grains, millet, panic, lentil, chickpea and alica by this name, so he takes it as a grain.

units.la: Et Celsus l.2.c.17. inter frumenta expresse numerat alicam. Cap. item 19. inquit: Boni succi sunt triticum, Siligo, Zea, Alica, Amy-lum: vt ita quartum farris genus Columella.
units.tr: Celsus (2.17) expressly counts alica among the grains. In chapter 19 he also says: "Wheat, siligo, zea, alica and starch are of good juice." Columella thus counts it as a fourth kind of spelt.

units.la: sc. halicastrum si: alica. Ab eodem quoque Plinio alica pro pulte accipitur, sicut & ab aliis, in sanitatis quidem statu locum habens, sed diuersis locis diuersimode præparata, vt patet ex Plin. l.18. c.11. vbi varia eius genera conficiendique modos ponit, & ex Zea fieri tradit, &c.
units.tr: Pliny also takes alica as a pulse, as do others. In health it has its place, but it is prepared in different ways in different places, as is clear from Pliny (18.11), where he sets out its various kinds and methods of preparation, and says it is made from zea, and so on.

units.la: De Secali hoc sub huius submonitionis sinem adiiciendum existimo, quod latinis quibusdam vt Plinio fuerit notum, à gracorum vero nullo proditum. Rei scriptores rusticæ Romani, Cato, Varro, Columella & Palladius nullam fecerunt de ea mentionem, vel quia vsum eius ingratissimum putarunt, saque Subalpinis familiarem, aut quia non dignam arbitrati sunt quae posteris vulgaretur, Plinius farraginem vocat: gratissimus eius vsus in panificiis est rusticus, sicut es infima media plebi, potentiorum enim es procerum mensis abdicatur, nisi quod quandoq; miscetur tritico, ut panis inde confectus firmitudinem quandam recipiat, cum aliis panis, ex sola fecalis farina ater fit es ponderosus: quidam Secale vulga- rem nostram siliginem esse existimant de quo cap. de Siliginc dicendum est.
units.tr: I think it should be added at the end of this preliminary note about rye (secale) that it was known to some Latin writers such as Pliny, but was reported by no Greek. The Roman writers on farming, Cato, Varro, Columella and Palladius, made no mention of it, either because they thought its use very unpleasant (it being familiar to the Subalpines), or because they judged it not worth passing on to posterity. Pliny calls it farrago. Its most agreeable use is in rustic bread-making, among the lowest and middle sort of people; for it is banished from the tables of the powerful and great, except that it is sometimes mixed with wheat so that the bread made from it gains some firmness. Otherwise bread made from coarse flour alone becomes dark and heavy. Some think secale is our common siligo, about which we must speak in the chapter on siligo.

units.la: Oryzam peregrinam Galenus inter legu- mina numerat; Plinius es Celsus inter frumen- ti genera. Indica terra populis vulgatissimus es gratissimus cibus est, apud quos magna cum su- perfitione feritur. Hodie in quibusdam Italiae locis feritur. Orientis Indiaq; populi potissimum
units.tr: Foreign rice Galen counts among the pulses; Pliny and Celsus count it among the kinds of grain. In the Indian land it is the most common and most welcome food of the peoples there, among whom it is sown with great abundance. Today it is sown in some places in Italy. The peoples of the East and of India in particular

units.la: Calechutani oryzam in panes coguntur, potus ex ea concinnant [accharo variisq; aromatis con- ditos, quibus facilius occiuntur, capita granare aiunt, quam vini potentioris bauftu. Oryzae aut apud eos [umma abundantia, eamq; cymbalis ac saltationibus, omniq; laetitiae genere ferunt, sua daemonia precantes, ut fit oryza uberrimus pro- ventus, hac enim varias epulas conficiunt. In re- gione quoq; Indica quae Carangonora dicitur, panes ex oryza confici nauigatione Iofephi Indi compertu est. Duo facit: eius generis gra- norubente quod rarius est, alterum candido aq, nonnullis bordeum galaticum appellatur, hoc e- legantiorum mensis subit, variisq; praeparatur modis, estq; boni succi edulium, crassiorem tamen tiritatem generat non, vt decet preparatum: de pulmbus & sorbitionibus eius agetur infra cap. de pultibus. In Germania nondum nasci est ad- prehensa, quam enim nos vulgo vocamus ory-zam, aliud s umenti genus est, tota s. b̄stantia oryza illa peregrina minus, nostra tamen ex Sy-ria, Asia, Egypto, vbi copiosissime prouenist translatain multis quoq; Europa locis hodie se-ritur, vnde ad nos exportatur.
units.tr: The Calechutani make rice into loaves and prepare drinks from it, seasoned with sugar and various aromatics; by these, they say, heads are more easily overturned than by drinking stronger wine. Rice is found among them in the greatest abundance, and they celebrate it with cymbals, dances and every kind of joy, invoking their demons so that the rice harvest may be most plentiful, for from it they prepare various feasts. In the Indian region also called Carangonora, bread is made from rice, as was learned from the voyage of Joseph the Indian. He mentions two kinds of this grain: one reddish, which is rarer, and the other white, which some call Galatian barley. This white kind comes to the tables of the more refined and is prepared in various ways; it is a food of good juice, though it does not produce thicker juice as it ought when prepared. Its purées and gruels will be treated below in the chapter on pultes. In Germany it has not been found to grow. What we commonly call rice is a different kind of grain, wholly unlike that foreign rice in substance. Ours is brought from Syria, Asia and Egypt, where it grows most abundantly, and today it is also sown in many places in Europe, whence it is exported to us.

units.la: Milium frumentum est non contemnen-dum, mul is enim gentibus in cibis fuit gratis-simum, & hodie quoq; esse inter omnes constat. Festus à milliaria summa derivatum latinis pu-tat. Varro à Graeco id deducit, melinemq; ab its nuncupari voluit, licet alii melinem panicum intellexerunt. Basin anno feritur, vere & initio Iunii quidam sub Vergiliarum exortum Maio semense ferifelicius suadent. Addersus sniu-riam auicularum indesensum existit, sicut & a-mena ocymum q. Omnia enim frumenta armā-tur, vel aristis acutis & asperis, vt triticum, bor-deum, siligo, vel gluma & folliculis includuntur, vt spelta, huiusq; genera: milium vero, aneua, & ocymum femina sua in tenuissimis continent membranis, vnde etiam facilius auicularum in-iurijs obnoxia redduntur. Omnium autem frugum fertilissimum est milium, ex vno enim gra-no ternos sexiarios gigni affirmat Plin.l.18.c. 17. feriq; debere locis vliginosis & humidis. Idem loco citato multos ad milii remedia no[?]la rabetam aruo circumferre solere, priusquam farria-tur, defodiq. in medio inclusam vase fictili vbe-ret, ut ... [?] cum nocent, et sic ... [?] velut ... [?] ... vermes nocere. Hoc vero remedium an superstitione careat, non ... [?]
units.tr: Millet is a grain not to be despised, since it was most pleasing as food to many peoples, and is still today known among everyone. Festus thinks it derives its Latin name from the total of the thousands (miliaria). Varro derives it from the Greek and wished it to be called melinē, though others understood melinē as panic. It is sown every year; some advise sowing in spring, in May or early June, under the rising of the Pleiades, as more favourable. It is exposed to the injuries of small birds, as is also canary grass and basil. For all the other grains are armed either with sharp, rough awns, as wheat, barley and siligo are, or are enclosed in husks and pods, as spelt and its kinds are. Millet, panic and basil, however, keep their seeds in very thin membranes, and so are more easily harmed by birds. Yet millet is the most fertile of all grains: Pliny (18.17) affirms that from one grain come three hundred six-rowed ears, and that it should be sown in damp, marshy places. In the same passage he says that many people, against the remedies for millet, were accustomed to carry the root around the field before it is threshed, and to bury it inside a clay vessel, so that [unclear]; and that [unclear] worms do harm. Whether this remedy is free of superstition, I [unclear].

units.la: Est autem alia consimile, quod Indicum appellatur, latur in Italiam sub Neronis principatu con-sectum, colore nigrum, granco, amplum, sed hoc nihil ad nos, cum peregrinum sit.
units.tr: There is also another similar grain, called Indian, which was brought to Italy under the reign of Nero. It is black in colour, with a large grain. But this has nothing to do with us, since it is foreign.

units.la: Proxenit quoque in quibusdam asperioribus Germaniae locis frumentum, cuius semen tritum exiguum milio adeo simile est, ut difficile ... [?] buiusmodi, seu agre-fte. Vnde & milium exiguum seu agrestè dicitur, aliis paniculum, & typha iuba illa paniculata, seu quia spicas fert inter typhas aquaticas, pra-densis acceratas granis, verum quia typha ap-pellat aliis frugibus nimirum tritico & oryza at-tribuitur, milium agreste dicis paretes.
units.tr: In some rougher parts of Germany grain also grows, whose seed, when threshed, is very like millet in size, so that it is hard [unclear] of this kind, or wild. Hence small or wild millet is also so called; others call it panicle, and typha the panicled plume, either because it bears ears among the water-typhas, crowded with grains, or because typha is attributed to other grains, namely wheat and rice; wild millet, however, I call panicle.

units.la: Quod verò ex Italia nouum frumenti genus in Germaniam adductum est, femen habens len-ticulas nofras forma & magnitudine referen-tia, paululum tamen acuminatum, quia Ger-manico nomine deflituitur, milium Italicum appellari potest, & Panicum, cuius Plinius 4. facit genera lib.18.cap.7. & 8. candidum, ni-grum, russum, & purpureum, nobis non-nisi russum cognitum est. Eodem modo
units.tr: As for the new kind of grain brought into Germany from Italy, having seed that resembles our lentils in shape and size, though slightly pointed, it may be called Italian millet, since it is named in German after... and panic, of which Pliny (18.7 and 8) makes four kinds: white, black, red and purple. Only the red is known to us. In the same way

units.la: eodem modo ... [?] quo milium in panes subigitur, minus tamen nutrit.
units.tr: In the same way [unclear] it is made into loaves as millet is, though it nourishes less.

units.la: Inter peregrina quoq; frumenta recensetur Turcicum, a mercatoribus primum in nostras terras exportatum, nostrumq; solum coepit eiusdem liciter assuefieri: requirit autem solum pingue & bene stercoratum. 4. autem huius frumenti spicae inveniuntur genera: quaedam enim granaruffa, quaedam purpurea, quaedam lutea, quaedam candida grana proferunt: phaseoli agrestis, magnitudine mobilis; culmi in hoc frumento virides adhuc & faeculenti dulcedine saccharum superant. In Asia vltra Bactriam fluuium adeo grande fieri tradun (Theophrast. lib. 9. c. 4.) vt nucleos olivae sua aequiparet magnitudine: non inepte etiam hoc frumentum typha magna appellari potest.
units.tr: Among the foreign grains is also counted Turkish corn, first brought into our lands by merchants, and our soil has begun to grow accustomed to it. It requires rich soil that is well manured. Four kinds of ear of this grain are found: some bear reddish grains, some purple, some yellow, some white. The beans of the wild kind are of mobile size; in this grain the green stalks, still juicy and sweet, surpass sugar cane. Theophrastus (9.4) says that in Asia beyond the river Bactria it grows so large that it equals the stones of an olive in size. It is not inappropriate to call this grain the great typha.

units.la: Sesamum à veteribus inter fruges fuit numeratum, hodie paucis cognitum. Aegyptii olei ex eo praestantissimum tum ad cibos, tum ad alia confecerunt, oleo communi longe praestantius: hodie devenit in contemptum, vbi primum Italia oleas plantare coepit. Apud veteres fuit in magno pretio, quia pani compingitur incundum et dulcem saporem conciliat, quamplurimum vero saccharum coepit vsurpari, non solum magnitudine aestimatum est, sed ne plantatum quidem postea. Caeterum, quae affatim inter lini segetes vbique locorum, maxime vero in Alsatia & tractu Rheni prouenit planta, sesamum.
units.tr: Sesame was counted among the grains by the ancients, but today it is known to few. The Egyptians made from it an oil far superior to common oil, both for food and for other uses. Today it has fallen into contempt, from the time when Italy first began to plant olive trees. Among the ancients it was held in great esteem, because it is pressed into bread and gives a pleasant, sweet flavour. Sugar cane began to be used much more, and sesame was valued not only for its size but was not even planted afterwards. Meanwhile, the plant sesame grows abundantly among flax crops everywhere, but especially in Alsace and along the Rhine.

units.la: {y} Sesamum nostrum. sefami genus est, quod ipsa ratio & descriptio indicat, excepto quod Ægyptiacum efficacius est & candidius. Hoc nostrum sesamum ab omnibus anulla tanquam inutile reiicitur, cum tamen ipsum emollire & calfacere, planiam [?] vero ò viridum vino decoctum inflammationem dolorésq, oculorum certò sedare experimentum sit. Quin & pani commixtum jucundum & dulce et aporem conciliat: per se vero ù usu patum stomacho non admodum confert, est enim oleosum & pingue, unde pingue alimentum praestat, crassum [?].
units.tr: Our sesame. It is a kind of sesame, as its nature and description show, except that the Egyptian is more effective and whiter. Our sesame is rejected by everyone as useless, although it is known from experience to soften and warm, and when the green plant is boiled in wine it certainly calms inflammation and pain of the eyes. Moreover, mixed into bread it gives a pleasant and sweet flavour; but taken alone it is not very good for the stomach, since it is oily and fat, and so it provides a rich, thick food.

units.la: Placentae [?] succum. Cum melle crudo placentas ex eo confi-ciebant, quas [?] vocabant. Apud Athe-nem lib.14. huiusmodi placentas finguntur ex melle & sesamo torrefactis addito oleo: meminit praeterea & aliarum, quas ab uni-ue sa Sicilia [illegible, ~6 letters] appellatas asserit, quae ex sesamo & melle mulieribus pubis formam fingebantur, has enim feminae Dearum altaribus cir-cumferebant.
units.tr: Cakes and juice. With raw honey they made cakes from it, which they called ... Athenaeus, book 14, describes such cakes made of honey and roasted sesame with oil added. He also mentions other cakes, which he says were named after a place in Sicily [illegible], and which were shaped from sesame and honey into the form of the female pubis, for women carried these around the altars of the goddesses.

units.la: Ad hanc haud penitendum f[?]umenti genus est. In [?] infulis quibusdam sola auena homines vi-vere memoriae productum est, utpote effonte [?] proeuenientes. Mos [?] fcrip ut Matthias Michon, aenam sublimant, ex qua sublima-tione elicitur liquor, quem aquam ardentem vi-tae vocant, ut apud Germanos, Italos, Gallos, ex vinis vehementioribus, bancq; summo eos habere pretio testantur, quibus legatione functi ut ii [?] redierunt domum. Quidam ex eis lenitor [?]
units.tr: To this grain there is no need for regret. In some islands, where oats alone are produced, people are said to live, as they grow spontaneously. Matthias Michov reports the custom of distilling in a copper vessel, from which distillation a liquid is drawn off, which they call burning water, as the Germans, Italians and French do from strong wines; and they testify that they hold it in the highest esteem, those who on returning home have discharged an embassy.

units.la: [Footnote lines at the foot not clearly legible; see notes.] leniter tusa pinsitaq; edulium agrotis parant, eoq; quadragenario tempore quoq; diuites ac pauperes pariter viuntur. Ægrotis edulia aenea-ceanon facile obtinerim[?], nisi sint sorbitiones rite praeparata, & ad certum vsum destinata ex medici praescripto atq; consilio. Eiusmodi enim sorbitiones (cum croco & melle) sufficientibus utiliter propinantur. Cogitur quoq; in panis in aspe-ris quibusdam & montosis regionibus, aliàs pro pabulo equorum praecipuè hodiè seritur. Certum est pultes[?] auenaceas probè confectas optimè convenire sanis, licet enim alvum sistant, nutriunt tamen mediocriter propter calorem quem habet sua natura avena, ut enim cibus calidae temperaturae est, ut vero medicamentum frigidae & sicca.
units.tr: Some of them, gently pounded and ground, prepare soft food for the sick, and in Lent rich and poor alike live on it. Oatmeal foods are not easily obtained for the sick, unless there are properly prepared gruels, intended for a fixed use and given according to the physician's prescription and advice. For such gruels, with saffron and honey, are usefully given to the sick. It is also sown as bread in some rough and mountainous regions, but today it is chiefly sown as fodder for horses. It is certain that well-made oat porridge suits the healthy very well; for although it constipates the bowels, it nourishes moderately, because of the warmth which the nature of oats has: as food it is of warm temperature, but as medicine cold and dry.

units.la: Quod vero Plinius Germanos nonnihil notat barbariei nescio cuius, ob pultem auenaceam, quae frequenter & plurimum viuntur, non morandum, cum ii, qui auenacea pultes victitare assueuerunt, non solum prosperiori valetudine, validi sint, bene curati, formaque egregia conspiciantur, sed etiam diutius viuant, quam Plinius vixerit, quam ii qui vel in Italia vel Gallia ij sunt in tritici delitiis vinoq; generosissimi, pulmo affatim vtuntur. Puranii[?] forsan vir aliàs accerrimo indicio, eiusmodi pultes ex mera aqua & pura farina confici. Si foret reditum atque probè confectas degustaret, sponsionem facerem, & salubriores palato stomachoq; eas gratas esse sit affuera-turus. Idem plane indicium sit de pultibus ex
units.tr: As for Pliny's remark that the Germans are somewhat marked by a certain barbarism because of oat porridge, which they eat frequently and in large quantities, this need not detain us. Those who are accustomed to live on oat porridge are not only healthier and sturdier, well cared for and of notable appearance, but also live longer than Pliny lived; whereas those who in Italy or France indulge in wheat and the most noble wine, use it in plenty. Perhaps Puranius, a man otherwise of the keenest judgement, thinks that such porridges are made of plain water and pure flour. If he had tasted them when they are returned and properly made, I would wager, and he would testify that they are pleasing to the palate and more wholesome for the stomach. The same judgement clearly applies to porridges made from ozymum.

units.la: ocymo, quibus in quibusdam nostris terris nihil vulgatius. Quidam farinam torrere solent, s in Pultis a- pulsem postea cogere: videoid mulis in locis ea- uenacea vulgatum, vt etiam tá aueide s alacriter vscen- ncom- tes ad efficandum meuna pellexerint. Verum moda, si melancholicum succum exinde generari, obstru- non pro- Hippocrates, viscerum manife ste descrebendi atq, ob- bè fit pa- seruans in uis, qui largius s sapius eá sunt usi, rata. Cateant igitur sibi ab eiusmodi pulsibus, quibus Censura. humor melancholicus non expurgatur in sple- nem, vt propriam receptaculum, qui laborant calculo ventriculo, frigido. Cum laste, sale, s bui yro cenio so probant s quidam delicatio- res addunt saccharum: qui bui yro destinantur, loco eius usurpent: lardum, quod in stili vel sar- tagine torrendum est: quibus non inuisum est mel, possunt id permiscere, hæc enim singula essi- cunt, vt s secundus s salubrius edantur: hoc etiam modo parandæ sunt pultes ex ocymo, cato- ri, frumenti, quain vsum cibarium admi- Quidin- tentur. Inprimis vero hic opera danda, ne primis consistentia harum pulliculorum sit nimis cras- circa pul sa, descensa s compatta, sed mediocris, hæc enim tes obser ratione s mantus ventriculum s valenter alunt, uandum. nimis crasse, solidaq, meatus obstruunt, difficul- Præcepit, terq, concoquuntur: Sic vero consigerit, ut s fame- non cō- licus quispiam ex aliorum eduliorum defectus temnen- crassiorem quam parcitur, deuorant, s largiore dum. vini haustu eam imbuat. ita enim condensatio dissoluetur, prohibitum prohibeat, si nelentore tunc ad- bere-
units.tr: ...ozymum, which in some of our lands is nothing more common. Some are accustomed to roast the flour, and afterwards to thicken it into porridge; indeed, in places where oats are common, they have so enticed people to eat it that they even eagerly... Yet if it generates a melancholic humour from this, and obstructs the viscera, as Hippocrates clearly describes, especially in those who use it more freely and often, let them beware of such porridges, by which the melancholic humour is not purged into the spleen, its proper receptacle, for those who suffer from stone or a cold stomach. They approve of it with milk, salt and butter; and some more delicate people add sugar; those who are destined for butter may use lard in its place, which must be roasted in a pan or frying pan; to those who do not dislike honey they may mix it in, for these things each make it more pleasant and wholesome to eat. In this way porridges of ozymum, oats and wheat are also to be prepared for food. Above all, care must be taken here that the consistency of these little porridges is not too thin, nor too thick and compact, but moderate; for these nourish the stomach strongly and well, while if too thick and solid they block the passages and are digested with difficulty. And so it happens that anyone who lacks other foods devours a porridge thicker than is appropriate, and let him soak it with a generous draught of wine; for thus the thickness will dissolve, and it will descend more easily and inflate and distend the stomach less, if he ... (the remainder of this sentence is illegible).

units.la: Hippocrates hærefcat: facilius etiam descendet, minusq; inflabit atq; distendet ventrem.
units.tr: Hippocrates ... It will descend more easily, and will inflate and distend the stomach less.

units.la: De ozymo miror quod controuersia fit, cum denomine potiùs quàm reipsa contentio sit. Qui dicunt id: isse basilicum nostrum hallucinantur, siquidem basilicum in magno habetur à nobis pretio, nec pecoribus saginandis vt ozymum adhiberi, sed latificans corda appellatur à Galeno.
units.tr: I am surprised that there is a dispute about ozymum, since the contention is more about the name than about the thing itself. Those who say that ozymum is our basilicum are mistaken; for we hold basilicum in high esteem, and it is not used to fatten cattle like ozymum, but Galen calls it the gladdener of the heart.

units.la: Ozymum igitur est illud, quod vulgo appellatur Heydenkorn / multis gentibus, cumprimis Septentrionalibus, frigidiora item ac aspera loca inhabitantibus notissimum. Pultes ex eo conficiunt cum lacte & butyro, & adarcendam etiam famem pantis. Pultes probè paratae, consistentiam mediocrem nactae, non ingratæ sunt palato, ventre enim firmant & corroborant, valentiores. Aliqui. Nam magni nominis Reges & Principes, quibus auenaceæ & ex ozymo pultes in cibis suorum & sui gratissimæ, cumprimis vero vena & siliquis, uel ultro citroque, peregrinantibus. Pisanam quoque, extritis granorum putaminibus è granis, & ex ieiuno cum aliis coquunt ad esum. Quapropter qui hoc frumenti genus cibis abducendis existimant, inscienter id palam facere offendero.
units.tr: Ozymum, then, is that which is commonly called Heydenkorn, very well known to many peoples, especially the Northerners and those who inhabit colder and rough regions. They make porridges from it with milk and butter, and also use it to ward off hunger in bread. Porridges well prepared and of moderate consistency are not unpleasant to the palate; for they firm and strengthen the stomach, making people more vigorous. Indeed, kings and princes of great name, to whom oat and ozymum porridges are most pleasing in their own and their people's diets, especially when travelling to and fro, cook them with other things for eating, as well as the Pisanum, its grains' husks crushed, from the grains, and from the fasting... Wherefore those who think this kind of grain should be removed from food will, I fear, be doing so openly and foolishly.

units.la: Videmus homines pallidè ex ozymo frequentius viitantes, validos esse, bene curatos, ac laudabiles corporis habitu, præcipuè in Lugdunensi montanorum tractu, Foresti & Arverno, Suecia, & Da-niaq, & in nostri etiam Comitatus Ferbugici parte, quæ septentriones, vulgò Bogelberg.
units.tr: We see men who eat ozymum rather often, looking pale, yet they are healthy, well cared for, and praiseworthy in bodily build, especially in the mountain region of Lyon, in Forez and Auvergne, in Sweden and Denmark, and also in part of our county of Ferbugicum, which is in the north, commonly called Bogelberg.

units.la: Berg / vb: hoc frumentum vulgatissimum est.
units.tr: Berg: this grain is very common.

units.la: Ego soleo adiicere modicum boni croci, cum dei bita quantitate piperis trita, (quamuis crocus in omni pulis genere laudatur) butyro salito super natante, sic enim paratae ne tantillum quidem noxe inferre valent: piperè enim calor ventri- culi excitatur, prohibeturq; ne venter influtur a'q; diffendatur crocus ob itricinem prohibet, ventriculoq; ex humiditate debili succurrit, me- aluq; urinarioi ferunt apertos: butyrum falsis est quasi vinculum totius maff. , vehiculemq; virtutis crocea, piperis ipfumq; esculenti affinitate landi addit prarerea crocus, ad prohibendam oculorum caliginem, quam ocymum per fefiptis commeftum inferre creditur. Oziofis tamen sedentariam vitam agentibus non adeo esse viti- le semper dixerim. Consuetudinis nihil ominus
units.tr: I am accustomed to add a little good saffron, ground with a fitting quantity of pepper (although saffron is praised in every kind of porridge), with butter floating on top; for thus prepared they can cause not the slightest harm. For pepper excites the warmth of the stomach, and prevents the stomach from being flooded and distended; saffron, because of its dryness, prevents it, and helps the stomach against weakness from moisture, and they say it opens the urinary and menstrual passages. Butter is as it were the bond of the whole mass, and the vehicle of the saffron's virtue; besides, the pepper adds its own affinity to the food. Saffron is also added to prevent the dimness of the eyes which ozymum eaten by itself is believed to cause. Yet I would always say it is not very suitable for those who lead a sedentary life. Nevertheless, custom...

units.la: Cur ru- hic magna vi.
