In Dania, S recia vidi magni ftici lon- nomine foeminis inter multa alia cibaria pulte glorem exocymo nihil vulgarius, eq, prefferrima vale- vitam cu tudine ac nitidiffima forma confpicuntur. A q, firma va- hoc ipsum in causa est, quod rufici agricole letudine longiorem atarem cum firmiori valeat adine at- atcingat, tingant, quia nimirum innocentia ac simplici quam cibo sunt contenti & aqua potu, quam qui quo- didiffime, delicatiffimeq, viuunt, quotidie q, ma- tidie o- gna & lanta epularum fruite mensas fias opu- piparè ac lentant : quin potius conflat & foleipfo clarius fplendi- est , eluxuriofis ille coquentes & culinas olueres dè epu- morbos quam vlla alia ex causa proinanare, & lantur. licet manifestum hoc fit omnibus , nemo tamen est, qui deliciis his carere velit.
units.tr: Why do rustic folk here live longer and enjoy firmer health? In Denmark and Greece I have seen, among many other dishes, that the women serve a porridge of basil, nothing more common, and yet they are the most robust and sprightly in appearance. The reason is this: farmers and rustics, who eat simple food and drink water, and who are content with plain fare, are healthier and stronger. Those who live daintily and luxuriously, who every day prepare and enjoy lavish feasts and sumptuous tables, are pale and sickly. It is even clearer than this that the cooks and kitchens are the cause of most diseases. Although this is plain to everyone, nobody is willing to give up these delights.

units.la: O fortunatos nimium, (inquit Maro) sua si bona norint, Agricolas, quibus ipsa procul discordibus armis Fundit humo facilem victum iustissima tellus.
units.tr: O too fortunate farmers, if only they knew their blessings, to whom the most just earth pours out easy sustenance, far from the clash of arms. ## Submonitio

units.la: Hodiè, Deum immortalem, quam omnia in peius eunt, deteriora[?] quotidie euadunt? Infa- ne gulæ irritamentis & nepotinis helluationibus interire videmus homines, regna, urbes. Inipsos urbium agros luxuriam penetrasse spectamus, quippe & India ipsa in cibos adducatur, cum nullam escam lautam probiq; paratam arbi- trantur multi, quae Zinziberè, cinnamomo, ma- ce, piperibus, croco, caterisq; id genus non condia-tur. An non vesani luxus argumentum est, cibos ita aromatis condire, ut etiam in paropsidum margnibus luxurient, & quod inprimis deplo-randum est, apud infimam etiam & exhaustam plebem, qui non minus in conuiuiis suis pro luxu patina certant ac principatu, quam magnates & diuitiores. Constat quibusdam in Germania nostra locis celebrari conuiuia, quae puerperialia seu baptismalia vocantur, & lu- strica à die quo infantes lustrantur & nomen ac- cipiunt, adeo luxuriosa ac sumptuosa, ut sicut in- fans[?] aqua fuit extrinsecus aspersus, ita viri pari- ter atque mulieres vino immodico intrinsecus ita se abluunt, ita baptizantur, ut neque mens brari fo- neque sensus officium suum munus, obire ans Vita im p- plus possint. Hic quo quisq; exquisitissimorum banda, & obseniorum varia genera, epularum, variis multis apparatus dat profusus, eo magis commenda- nomini- tur, vt itanihil aliud ista conuiuia dicere licet buscafti- at, quam ad perdenda vina operefum inuen- ganda tum ac fumtuofum gule irritamentum: hanc iunt. vitae intemperantiam etiam hic apud nos quoti- die adhuc debacchari videmus magna cum rei Plebsin- familiaris detrimento: sunt enim multi qui fima per conuiuia eiusmodi celebratuer tanto id faciunt côtinua- cum luxu & fumtu, tantis cum expensis, vt co- ta ista cô gantur possea atrum ex beferno ure demorare viuia ex- panem, vix anno uno atque alteromeritoria hauritur: manu recolligentes, quantum una cœna pran- opesque dione profundebatur. Sic itaque miseri illi necessa- quod unciatim comparant, uno cor ut ut ab- riz abfu- ligurient. darnach geben fie zum Brunnen muntur. fauffen Waffer, vnd freffen Salat. Con- fuerudo igitur lustrum illum diem laxi riofis conuiuiis celebrandi vel abroganda est, vel pu- blica animadue fione legum, fanctionib. mul- Ratiões, landa & coercenda, vitiis vero moderatus at- cur luxu- que sobrius iudem castodiendus atq; confirman- riofa cô- dum: quo nomine magistratus amice tantum co- uiuia sint pellandus venit, non admonendus: prim ò ensim abrogá- maxima in Deum fit iniuria, cuius veneranda da, vel le sacramentum, quo infans in sanctorum album gibus co est affiriptus, fodiffime pollutur ac contamina- ercenda? tur, dum vidi. nos ecdem flatim die, quo ci- fanus fantis & nostro nomine, sanctè spopondimus, e-brittatis gulaq, sordibus nos inquinamus, si-s instar lutulenta ad pristinum proinus latium coenumq; se volutantis. 2. Insanus istis ac sumtuo-sis conuiuiis opes ad infantis & puerperæ sus-ten-tationem necessarie absumuntur in impurissi-mum ventrem, sicq; misellus ille infantulus ina-pietatq; familia relinquitur. quid? quod sepe propter infantum baptismalium huiusmodi epularum apparatum baptismus differtur, magna cum in Deum, tum in infantem iniuria. Tertio notis-simum est, luxuriosas istas ac sumptuosas com-messationes contentionum, rixarum, conuiuio-rumq; esse femina ex quibus funesta sæpe odia, inimicitiæ, cædesq; oriuntur, adq; tuendam & confirmandam amicitiam nihil, sed disturbandam potius, pacemque ac concordiam dirimendam valere plurimum. Quod ele-ganter celebri Epicharmi dicto, cuius me-minit Atheneus libr. 1. notatur, ex sacri-ficio conuiuium, ex conuiuio potio, expotione lascivia, ex hac insania, ex insania iudicium, a[?] iudicio condemnatio, hinc compedes, sideratio-nes, multa.
units.tr: Good God, how everything goes from bad to worse, and what further decline we see each day! We see men, kingdoms and cities perishing from the incitements of insane gluttony and the feasting of their grandchildren. We see luxury creeping even into the fields of the towns themselves, for even India is brought in for food, since many think no dish is fine and properly prepared unless it is seasoned with ginger, cinnamon, mace, pepper, saffron and the like. Is it not a sign of mad luxury to season food with spices in such a way that they run riot even in the dishes, and what is most to be lamented, that even among the lowest and most impoverished common people, who compete no less in their feasts for the glory of the pot than the great men and the richer folk do? It is well known that in some places in our Germany there are banquets called lying-in or christening feasts, and the festivities of the day on which the infants are purified and receive their name are so extravagant and costly that, just as the child is sprinkled with water from the outside, so men and women alike wash themselves inwardly with immoderate wine, and are so baptized that their minds and senses can no longer perform their office. The more exquisite and varied the dishes and the more lavish the preparations a host provides, the more he is praised, so that these feasts can be called nothing else than an occasion for wasting wine and a costly incitement to gluttony. We see this intemperance of life still raging daily among us here, to the great loss of families. For there are many who hold such feasts with such continual luxury and expense, at such cost, that the common people, gathering up with their hands what was once squandered on a single dinner, can scarcely earn a living by a year's or two years' labour. So those wretched people, in their necessity, go hungry bit by bit, and afterwards go to the well, drink water and eat salad. Therefore the custom of celebrating that day of purification with luxurious feasts must either be abolished or else restrained and checked by public punishment under laws and sanctions; and the magistrate should be urged, not merely asked as a friend, to restrain those who are prone to vice, and the sober should be kept and confirmed in their soberness. Why do we not first abolish these luxurious feasts, or at least check them? First, the greatest injury is done to God, whose venerable sacrament, by which the infant is enrolled in the register of the saints, is most foully defiled and polluted, since on the very day on which we solemnly promised in the name of the child and for ourselves, we defile ourselves with filth and gluttony, returning straightway like a sow wallowing in mud to its former filth. Second, through these insane and costly feasts the resources needed to sustain the infant and the mother are consumed in the most unclean belly, and so that poor little infant is left in poverty and neglect. And what is more, because of the preparation of such christening feasts, baptism is often postponed, a great injury both to God and to the infant. Third, it is very well known that these luxurious and costly carousings are the source of quarrels, brawls and banquet-rooms, from which deadly hatreds, enmities and killings often arise, and that they contribute very little to preserving and strengthening friendship, but rather disturb it and break up peace and harmony. This is elegantly expressed in the well-known saying of Epicharmus, which Athenaeus mentions in book 1: from sacrifice comes the feast, from the feast drinking, from drinking wantonness, from wantonness madness, from madness judgment, from judgment condemnation, and hence fetters, imprisonment and many other evils.

units.la: Ne itaque infantum vulgus ita belluetur, & familiam pecuniamq; prandiorum gurgitibus proluat, certis legibus, ac edislis[?] luxus coercendus est,
units.tr: Therefore, so that the common people are not gorged in this way, and so that feasts do not wash away family and money in the whirlpools of banquets, luxury must be restrained by fixed laws and edicts.

units.la: quibus decernendum q., quantum cuiq; in fine galas coenas e7 conuiuia insumere consueuiat. Hinc illustres ille Rom snorum fumtuaria ac ci- barie leges fun prumulgate. Lege enim Pha- niacaucbaiur,ne quis carum obsonare. Lex Fannia lade Romanus, item Plebeis es Satur- nalibus in singulos dies centenos eris infumi co- cessit, decem q, alii diebus in singulis mensibus tricenos,cateris vero omnibus dies. Lex Li- cinia nuptiis ducenos indu fit, ceterig, diebus tricenos,tum et carnis aride et fulfamentorum certa pondera in singulos dies conflitut. Orchia (quae omnia,quae de coenis late sunt, fuit prima) consueuerunt tantum numeri um prefcribebat, luxui nihil derogabat. Lege Didia, prandia coenas, maiori fumtu paranres tenebat. Lex Aemilia non sumtus coenarum, sed ciborum ge- nu et modum prefiniebat. Postremo veni Iulia ad populum, queprofeffus diebus ducentos permisit, Calendis, Idibus et nonis recentios, nu- tus accreponit, b. e. postridie nuptiarum (esse- tios mille qui quinq, et 20. aut eis cor. aftimantur. Nisi tre nuptiae nostra statelonge fuit lu- ruofio es et fumtuofiores, quiipe vel quotidiana consuetua hanc taxationem excedunt, fefer ii- nim ducenti in singulas coenas quinq, affimant tur coronati aurei. Oportet adum sane eff ut Chriftianirerumpubl, mode aores ad Ethnico- rum illorum exemplum et imitationem infan- ilam et immanem consuetudinem luxuriam fe- veris. verù legum sanctionibus, atq; inprimis sobria vi- tamq;[?] vitæ legis exemplo refrenarent atq; co- coercerent. Id si fieret, melius cum R. publ. Christiana multum in locis agereatur[?], pretia omnium rerum non quotidie adaugerentur, nulla esset annonæ flagellatio, aroma optimarum[?] crumena minus tangeret. Verum enimuero ne quis exi- met, me omnem epularum apparatum abiicere, velle, vt Christiani ab omni profusa consuetudine[?] conuiuiali omnia consuetudine[?] tanquam monopolagi sint alieni, et ex mul-is hoc vnicum dico, tantum abesse, vt ta- le quid sentiam, vt etiam in veteri & nouo testa- mento pios & religiosos homines conuiuia & alios apparatus, & inuitatos aliorum conuiuia admi- se, quin & Deum ipsum conuiuia læta populo suo præscripsisse atq; mandasse, non ignorem, facile q; si opus esset, id probari possit. Ipse Christus ex- emplorum rationumq; loco nobis de- bet esse, quem Euangelica historia tradit, & con- uiuio alios excepisse, & ad aliorum conuiuia ac- cedere, atq; adeo cum improba fama hominibus, publicanis & meretricibus sæpe numero conui- uiari minimè dubitasse, nō libidine quadam immoderatâ, cibi potuq; auiditate, sed, vt Hieron. c.9. Marth. differt, vt occasionem ha- beret docendi, vq; illorum invitationes cum spi- ritualibus epulis compensaret, illoq; hac occasione ab improba vita ad bonam frugem perduce- ret. His adde Salomonis in Ecclesiaste testi- monium, nihil, dicentis, homini ferè optabilius esse. eff.,quam lætari,conuiuari, & soluta quadam animi libertate eff:nec non Siracidis c.31.&32. docentis conuiuia iucunda eff: &c. Sit igitur Christus cum Pharisæis, publicanis atq; meretri-bus. Cibus conuiuari solitus est, nobis quoq; an hoc li-bertatem Christianis in sacris literis interdici, quam etiam ipse Paulus reliquit liberam, 1. Cor. 10. sed nimium conuictum prohiberi, cum videlicet quis amicè magno studio & voluptate-te consuetudinem eorum sectatur, cum dictis vel facilis illorum superstitionibus impietatis, prae-best affectum, cum religionem veram criminan-di submini strat occasionem, & Christi exemplo contrarium, in impietate & superstitionibus ipsis confirmat, cum præcipuus conuiuiorum finis sit, omnia facere ad Dei gloriam. Inordinata igi-tur, immoderata, luxuriosa, monstrosa, portenta-tofa, & sumptuosa conuiuia damnantur, quæ non ex honestis & caritatis erga Deum & proximum studio, sed ex ambitione, & inexplebili quadam voluptatum cupiditate infitium-tur.
units.tr: By these laws it should also be decreed how much each person may spend on feasts and banquets at the end of the day. Hence the famous sumptuary and food laws of the Romans were published. By the law of Fannia, no one was allowed to spend more than a fixed sum on dinner; the Plebeians were allowed a hundred asses a day during the Saturnalia, and ten or thirty on other days in each month, and on all other days. The Licinian law allowed two hundred for weddings, and thirty on other days, and it also fixed certain weights of dried meat and seasonings for each day. The Orchian law (which was the first of all the laws about dinners, and is widely discussed) only prescribed the number of guests and did not restrain luxury at all. By the Didian law, those who prepared lunches and dinners at greater expense were held to account. The Aemilian law regulated not the cost of dinners but the kind and quantity of foods. Finally came the Julian law, which, proposed to the people, allowed two hundred sesterces on the Calends, Ides and Nones, and a thousand on wedding days, that is, on the day after the wedding, which are reckoned at about twenty-five gold crowns. Yet our present weddings are far more lavish and sumptuous than these, since daily custom exceeds this assessment, for two hundred gold crowns are reckoned for a single dinner. Surely it is fitting that the commonwealth of Christians should follow the example and imitation of those heathens, and restrain and check the unlawful and monstrous custom of luxury by the sanctions of laws, and above all by the example of sober and temperate life. If this were done, the commonwealth of Christians would be better managed in many places, the prices of all goods would not rise every day, there would be no whipping of the market, and the purse would be less touched by the expense of the finest spices. But, lest anyone suppose that I wish to reject every kind of banquet preparation, so that Christians should be strangers to all profuse feasting, as though they were monks, I say this one thing among many: far from thinking any such thing, I know that in both the Old and New Testaments pious and religious men held feasts and other gatherings, and were invited to the feasts of others; indeed God himself prescribed and commanded joyful feasts for his people. This could easily be proved if there were need. Christ himself, whom the Gospel history presents as our pattern and rule, both took part in feasts and went to the feasts of others, and he did not hesitate to dine often with men of ill repute, tax-collectors and harlots, not out of some immoderate desire or greed for food and drink, but, as Jerome says on Matthew 9, so that he might have the opportunity to teach, to balance their invitations with spiritual feasts, and by this occasion to lead them from a wicked life to good conduct. To this add the testimony of Solomon in Ecclesiastes, who says that nothing is better for man than to rejoice and feast, and to enjoy a certain free ease of mind, and also Sirach 31 and 32, which teaches that pleasant feasts are good, and so on. Let Christ therefore sit with Pharisees, tax-collectors and harlots, and let him eat and drink at feasts. Do we also deny Christians this liberty, which Paul himself left free, in Scripture? See 1 Cor. 10. But excessive dining is to be forbidden, namely when someone pursues the company of those people with great eagerness and pleasure, when by their words or easy approval he favours their superstitions and impieties, when he gives occasion for slandering the true religion, and when by his example he confirms in impiety and superstitions what is contrary to Christ's example, since the chief end of feasts is to do all things for the glory of God. Therefore disorderly, immoderate, luxurious, monstrous, prodigious and sumptuous banquets are condemned, those which are not undertaken from honest zeal for love of God and neighbour, but are set up out of ambition and some insatiable lust for pleasures.

units.la: Contra vero frugalia, munda, parca, moderata, iucunda, sana, quæ honestis & liberalibus iocis sunt condita, quales vere elegantes ac eruditi homines solent afferre & musicarum sacrarium) maximè probantur, sunt enim laxus existi-mant doli[?] ignara.
units.tr: On the other hand, frugal, clean, sparing, moderate, pleasant and wholesome meals, seasoned with honest and liberal jests of the kind that truly refined and learned men are accustomed to bring, and with the music of the Muses, are most highly approved. For such people think that those meals are free of any vulgar or dishonest pleasure.

units.la: In horum censu fuit cœna Saturnia, quæ à Cœna Sa poetis aureo seculo tributur prouerbialiq; sropo turnia, dicitur pro beata. (cœna Ioci Medici Tarentini, cuius vitæ parsimonia in proverbium abiit. Me- Cœna minit ꝯLiani alieni cu usdam Icci Taren- Icci. tini latloris, quem toto certaminis tempore temperatissime vix s. suenerisq; omnisuisse ex- pertem scribi. Inter frugales quoque & mo- deratam cœnas reserentur philosophica frugali- sime Athenia Diogenis, Antipatris, & Pa- Philoso- netiastis instrustle, vt moderaiè & erudite de phorum, rerum natura dissererent. Conuiuium quoq; sermo- sicum pro mediocri temperatoq; passim nes cõui- apud authores acceptt testantur Atheneus libr. uiales de 10. dicens, conuiuio exceptus mediocri & musi- bent esse co: & Plutarch in præc. salubrib. Timotheum eruditi& ꝯAtheniensium ducem cœnasse dicit in Aca- temperâ- demia apud Platonem musicam & frugalem tes,non cœnam : atque hinc Lucianum, conuiui- Baccho unn sapientum virorum μυσῶν appellasse atq; Ve- puto. nere su- Cœnam quoque Platonicam prouerbialiter tiles & & paraemiacè pro mediocri & frugali vsur- obscoeni. patam inueniso , propterea quod si Philoso- Conui- phus eiusmodi cœnæ suisse delestatus scribi- uium tur. Vnde Timotheus Cononis filius sum- musicū. tuofis cœnis indulgens, à Platone exceptus Cœna tenui , musico ac moderato vitu, di- Platoni- xit, eos qui apud Platonem cœnarent, ca.
units.tr: Among these is the Saturnian feast, which the poets assign to the golden age, and which is proverbially called "blessed." (The dinner of Icius the Tarentine jester, whose frugality passed into a proverb, is also counted here. Lucian writes that Icius, a certain jester of Tarentum, was almost entirely free of the vices of wine, sex and gluttony during the whole of the contest.) Among the frugal and moderate dinners are also reckoned the dinners of the Athenian philosophers Diogenes, Antipater and Panaetius, who gathered together so that they might discuss the nature of things moderately and learnedly. Ancient authors also testify that a sociable meal, with a moderate and temperate table, is everywhere accepted as a feast of the philosophers, the banquet of wise men, which Athenaeus in book 10 describes as a meal with moderate food and music. Plutarch, in the Precepts on Health, says that Timotheus, the leader of the Athenians, dined in the Academy with Plato on music and a frugal meal. Hence Lucian called such dinners the "feasts of the wise," and I think Plato's dinner is found proverbially and paraemiacally used for a moderate and frugal meal, because the philosopher is written to have been delighted by a dinner of this kind. Hence Timotheus, the son of Conon, who was given to lavish dinners, after being entertained by Plato with a slender, musical and moderate fare, said that those who dined with Plato felt well the next day.

units.la: N 4 stridi postridie bene se habere. Horatius lib. 2. Satyr. s. cœnas quoque rusticas vocat tenues minimeq[?]. sumtuosas, dicit q[?], post eas se nocles ducere quietas & tranquillas. De his conuiuiis vere & conuenti-enter dicitur, quod sint mutua hominum cari-tatis, amicitiæ, benevolentiaq[?], vincula s[?] fyn-bola. Vnde verbe[?] à conuiuendo dicuntur, vi-tæ, coniunctione s[?] quasi conuiuiu[?], quoditmc maxime simul vivatur, teste Ciceron. l. de se-nect. Nonius Marcell. epularem amicorum accubationem vocat. Ariftotelesin Ethicis conuiua[?] tones hominum amicitiæ tuendæ ac sta-bilendis perquam accommodatas esse scribit. Cicero Patum monet, viscum viris boni[?], iuscun-dis, [?]uiq, amantibus vivat, sermone enim fami-liari, qui in conuiuiis est dulcissimus, vita nihil honestis-aptius esse, nihil, ad beatè vivendum accom-modatius: ac plurima alia praclara doctissimorum testimonia adhuc conuiuiorum finem demon-strandum extant: vnum tantum producam, quod est Plutarchi lib. 4. Symposi. problem. 1. vbi conuiuii finem esse dicit amicitiæ vel generat-tionem, vel confirmationem iunctam cum volun-tate, vnde conuiuium definit viuendi ratio-nem per vini vsum in amicitiam definen-tem.
units.tr: Horace, in book 2 of the Satires (satire 6), also calls the rustic dinners slender and by no means costly, and says that after them he passes quiet and tranquil nights. Of these feasts it is rightly and fittingly said that they are bonds of mutual human charity, friendship and goodwill, and symbols of life together. Hence they are called convivia from living together (convivere), as if it were a convivium, because people live together most of all in them, as Cicero says in his book On Old Age. Nonius Marcellus calls the reclining of friends at a feast an "epular" gathering. Aristotle in the Ethics writes that the dinners of men are especially well suited to preserving and strengthening friendship. Cicero advises that the man who lives with good, pleasant and friendly people should know that nothing is more honourable, and nothing more suited to living well, than familiar conversation, which is sweetest at dinners. Many other excellent testimonies of the most learned men still exist to show the purpose of feasts. I will produce only one, from Plutarch, Table Talk book 4, problem 1, where he says that the purpose of a feast is either the begetting or the confirmation of friendship joined with goodwill; hence he defines a feast as a way of life, by the use of wine, leading to friendship.

units.la: Hinc sestiuae admodum Romanus ille solus a- ligando cœnans eo die se non cœnasse dixit, sed edisse tantum, innuens cœnam semper commucommunione & amicitia veluti condimento indigere. Neq, vero ad amicitiam tuendam, stabiliendam, tantum conuiuia valent, sed & ad simultates inimicitias auferendas: graues enim diuturnas, priuatorum hominum simul-tates, odiaq;, conuiuia extinčta legimus ac et-iâ nunc hodie sæpe hominum capitalibus à se inui-cem odiis dissidentes conuiuiorum occasione sibi inuicem reconciliari. Sic M. Crassus (Cicero-nī reconciliatus conuiuio est. Scipio & Hasdru-bal conuiuio sibi inuicem reconciliati: ut vere dixisse liceat, mensâ posita contentionem tolli, hoc est, mensæ communione sæpe tolli rixas, inimicitiasq;, gratiamq;, reconciliari, cùm reiex-emplum proferatur de Isbo setho filio Saulis, in cuius adibus cum exarsisset altercatio, ferunt eum adornato conuiuio dicitur eam diremisse. Babet enim nescio quid philtri in se vinum ad amorem reconciliandum. Atq; hæc de con-uiuiis frugalibus & moderatis, quæ si nimis sunt sordida & parca, recte appellantur Cynica & Timonia: Cynicorum enim Philosophorum vi-tus erat vilissimus, tenuissimus & sordidus, si-quidem videl. & legumina. Timonia à Timo-ne, cui humanum genus exosum erat, dicta dida sunt, si enim vitam sequebatur feram, in cibis-que vilissimis & à reliquis hominibus prope-modum damnatis acquiescebat. Hæc referun-tur cœnæ terrestres, quæ nil nisi terra producuntum continent, quas Horatius cœnas sine sanguine N 5 -VOCAB
units.tr: Hence that Roman who, when he had dined alone on a summer day, said that he had not dined but only eaten, implying that a dinner always needs fellowship and friendship as its seasoning. Feasts are of value not only for preserving and strengthening friendship, but also for removing enmities and quarrels. We read that serious and long-standing hatreds and feuds between private men have been ended by feasts, and even today men who are at mortal odds with one another are often reconciled at a dinner. So Marcus Crassus was reconciled with Cicero at a feast; Scipio and Hasdrubal were reconciled with each other at a feast. So one may truly say that when the table is laid, strife is removed; that is, by sharing a table, quarrels, enmities are often removed and favour is restored. Also cited is the example of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, in whose house, when a quarrel had flared up, they say that he settled it by preparing a feast. Wine has I know not what love-charm in itself for reconciling people. So much for frugal and moderate feasts. If they are too squalid and meagre, they are rightly called Cynic and Timonian. For the food of the Cynic philosophers was very cheap, very slender and squalid, namely lentils and pulses. Timonian feasts are named after Timon, who hated the human race; for if he followed a wild life, he was content with the cheapest food, which other men almost rejected.

units.la: hominū eiusdem cibi po-tus ac ser monis commu-nio, mu-tuiamo-tis ami-citiæque gratiâ in-stituta, Conui-uiis ini-micissi-mi sæpe reconci-liati.
units.tr: These are the meals of earthly fare, which contain only what the earth produces, which Horace calls dinners without blood. They are established for the sharing of the same food and drink and the same conversation, and for the favour of mutual exchange and friendship. Bitter enemies are often reconciled at feasts.

units.la: Conui-uia sordida quæ? vocat: Et pafferinum conuiuium, proexigue bolo es minuto, quantum vel passer absumat. Sordidum deni, nimis, tenue conuiuium est. Vere lu- absq; fumo, in quonibus cocti obscuri, apponi- xuriosi q tur. Quemadmodum gitur, qui nimia conui- sint? niorum crebritate atq; frequentia, eorumque profuso, splendido ac fumuoso apparatu gau- dent, in excefu peccant, itaque contra in defectu Quinam sint vere ford de delinquunt, l. quia a communi ali con- sordidi? fuerud ne abhorrent, ut neq; alios ad fe, epula- rumq; suarum communionem vnquam inui- tet, neq; invitati ad aliorum conuiuia accedant, id quod fere cuiusdam immanitatis esse videtur, quippe cum ipsa natura atq; humanitas, Tria ge- hanc vitæ cænarumq; consuetudinem postulet. neta lor- ll. Cum quis inuitatus liberiter quidem es pro- didorum pte aliorum conuiuio fe sistit, at ille inuitat ne- hominū. minem, id quod auaritia ingratitudinisq; cum- Sordida iusdam flagitiosissime vitium est, quo quis la- omnis borans ἀλόγος ἰοφάγοι rectè dicitur, cui ni- mono- mirum dulce est aliena vi uere quadra. Horum phagia passim reperiuntur plurimi, quos neq; pudet, est, sicut neq; piget, neq; pœnitet inconuiuentiæ suæ & illibe- monophagia sordidissime, et fi quando bonefti- ralis ribus liberalioribusque conuiuiis adhibentur, ἀλόγος alienamque quadram arrodere ac lingere illi ἐφαγία, licet, tantum cibrum inglutie fe infarciunt uno Parasiti- prandio cænatus, quanta vix decem alii accusa- rifeunt natura et genio existimantes, fi intanta cum & epularum strues apparatuque eorum defrauda- sed una rent.
units.tr: Which banquets are sordid? Pliny calls it a sparrow's feast, with a tiny morsel, just as much as a sparrow can eat. A banquet is sordid when it is too meagre and thin. Truly luxurious feasts are served without smoke, with the food cooked and kept out of sight. As, then, those who rejoice in too frequent and crowded dinners, and in their lavish, splendid and smoky display, sin by excess, so on the other side those who sin by defect are the ones who shrink from sharing a common meal, so that they neither invite others to their feasts nor accept invitations to the banquets of others. This seems almost a kind of savagery, since nature and humanity themselves demand this custom of life and of dining together. There are three kinds of sordid people: (1) the greedy man who accepts an invitation gladly but never invites anyone in return, a vice most shamefully base, and rightly called a parasite's lack of reason [ἀλόγος], for he finds it sweet to live on other people's food. Many of these are found everywhere, men who are neither ashamed nor sorry for their unsociability and their illiberal ways, and who, when they are admitted to more generous and liberal banquets, gnaw and lick at another's dish and stuff themselves with so much food at one lunch that ten others could scarcely eat as much, thinking themselves wise by nature and genius, yet defrauding their hosts of the great spread and display of their feasts. (2) the man who entertains guests too meagrely and sordidly, and sends away half-starved and thirsty those whom he has invited, setting out a narrow and scanty table, which might be called petty-minded [μικροπρεπῶς]; and (3) the man who cannot take part in such meagre gatherings at all, because he is hindered by sickness, burdened with many affairs, or lacking means.

units.la: Hieronymus, Epistola ad Nepotianum. rent. III. Cum quis ad conuiuium à fein-mitatos nimis tenuiter fordideq; tractat, eosq; fe-mifamelicos atque sitientes dimittit, qui μικροπρεπῶς[?] potest appellari, hoc est, par-nam & angustam mensam ponens: vbitamen excipiendi, qui aduersa valetudine impediti, vel negotiorum multitudine districti, vel deniq;, ex inopia & egestate conuiuali huiusmodi ossi-cio fungi minime possunt: quamuis & hic a-maritis sordibus polluti inuentiantur, qui con- uiuia quidem asymbola, quae solus conuiuatoris sumtibus constant ac apparantur, [?]ante ore ac promptissima mente accedunt, ad symbolica ve-ro & collatitia, ad qua singʼuli conuiuia certas quasdam portiones, vel esculentorum, vel pocu-lentorum, vel etiam pecuniae certam summam, amoris, amicitiae, mutuae declarande ac conci-landa gratia, conferre solent, inuitati, quouis[?] vel leui etiam pratextu se excusant, interesse, se conuiuio nunc non posse, iam iam accepisse se li-teras, ad quas protinus nullaque interposita mo-ra sit respondendum, tentari se, nescio, qua capi-tis grauedine, vertigine, oculorumque caligine, sentire se insignem corporis alterationem, vel oc-cupari se necessariorum negotiorum mole: his similibus pratextis multi bodie, trygobii, trysi-bii, ac quoniam luto lutulentiores, legitima su bo-mantra conuiuia refugere norunt, ne scilicet de suo in conuiam[?] aliquid conferant, cyclopica qua-
units.tr: Jerome, Letter to Nepotianus. When someone entertains guests too meanly and sordidly, and sends them away half-starved and thirsty, he may be called petty-minded [μικροπρεπῶς], that is, one who sets out a small and cramped table. Yet those who are defiled by similar meanness are also found in the other kind of company: people who come eagerly and with ready minds to banquets that cost the host alone, but who, when invited to shared dinners, to which each guest is accustomed to contribute a fixed portion of food or drink, or even a set sum of money, to declare and win friendship and mutual goodwill, excuse themselves on any slight pretext. They say they cannot come to the dinner now; they have just received a letter which must be answered at once without delay; they say they feel some dizziness, a heaviness of the head, or a dimness of sight, or a marked change in the body; or that they are occupied with a weight of necessary business. With such pretexts, many today, who are lazy, dull, and muddier than mud itself, know how to avoid lawful feasts, lest they should contribute anything of their own to the common meal. Driven by a kind of Cyclopean misanthropy or avarice, they prefer to shun others, to live anxiously, to feed on the leaves of trees, and to dine meanly, rather than be joined with others in mutual goodwill and friendship, or contribute certain portions to those shared banquets.

units.la: quadam misanthropia,vel anaritia dutti, sece. vititare, anxieq, viuere, ficiq, arboris foliis vesci, fordideq, coenare malunt, quam mutua beneuolentia amicitiaq, cum aliis coniungi, quam certas quasdam portiones ad fympofiatilla collatitia conferre.
units.tr: Driven by a certain misanthropy or avarice, they prefer to withdraw, to shun company, to live anxiously, to eat fig leaves and tree foliage, and to dine squalidly, rather than to join with others in mutual goodwill and friendship, or to contribute certain fixed shares to those communal dinners.

units.la: Huiusmodi collatitiarum coenarum illustria exempla fuerunt dilectiones illae Christianorum primitiuae Ecclesiae, quae quidem inter diuites & pauperes, amicos, vicinos & propinquos agitarent promiscue etiamnunc consuevere-runt ex collectis fiue symbolis, quae a singulis conferrentur. Paschales similiter epulae, quae apud Christianos nonnullos summa cum laetitia quotannis celebrantur ex collectis, con- tant fiue symbolis, dona enim atq; munera, ut ova, placentas, panes, saccharatos, & mellitos, carnes, & vina ad festivitatis illius celebrationem colliguntur atq; conferuntur. Legislatores quotidianam etiam, syffitia dicta, & phiditia, ut quoda-facilius ciues in officio parsimoniae frugalitatis, studio imprimis vero mutuo amore beneuolentiae & bene-tia atq; concordia continerent, instituerunt. Hanc quoq; victum quotidianam communionem probat Plato, s.de legibus, vbi singulis in locis adq; fru-cus oportere esse syffitia, in quibus simul omnibus galitate contuuandum sit, aperit: qu in [illegible, ~8 letters] affuefa- ctis polititio.7. Syfftia approbat, conducibilia esse in- quiens communi omn. um conferuit bene confti-tutis. tutis ciuitatibus Syssitia, multitudinemq; oportere in syssitia siue sodalitates esse distributam. probatq; ibidem antiquam esse syssitiorum τάξιν[?], omniumq; antiquissima esse Italica, à quibus reliquorum populorum syssitia fuerunt deducta, vt Cretensium, Spartanorum, Lacedæmoniorum, quorum meminit Cicero 6. Tuscul. Chartaginensium, Atheniensium, quibus non inepte Germanorum syssitia, collegia, siue sodalitates comparari posse existimo, in democraticis praesertim Reipublicis publicas commessationes ac quotidianas in frequenti usu esse neminem non est notum, in quem etiam usum ampla & splendida coenacula extructa cernuntur, quae vulgo à potatione gentilitia lingua appellantur Trinckstuben/Gesellstuben / sodalium domus, in qua eiusdem muneris atq; officii artifices homines, eadem vitae genere vtentes conueniunt atq; coeunt, tum ad mutuam benevolentiam atq; amicitiam tuendam, tum etiam ad honestam legitimamq; foedera atq; conuenta sancienda atq; confirmanda. Vbi vero commessationum & compotationum existit intemperantia, quam in pluribus hodie ciuitatibus & oppidis debacchari, imo maximam fere orbis partem perbacchari videmus, cumq; factionis cuiusdam metus suspicio, subest, syssitia magistratus autoritate iunt abolenda, euertenda, & dissoluenda, vt illicita, noua illegitima, & intemperantia, in quibus sc. menses sumtuosis accumbentes bentes voracium instar pecudum Epicuri què de grege porcorum vino ciboq, adeo se obruunt at- que infarciunt, vt omnem mentis rationisque vsum amittant, irapiis nefariisque contra De- VM & Proximum patris foederibus, se obstrin- gant atque deuinciant, unde maxima mala at- que calamitates necessario enascuntur. Verum sat commessatum est, sat prolixe coenatum; adeo pulluciibiles coenas conuiuiaque varia va- rio ferculorum apparatu exhibuit unicum illud ocymum, ex eoq, puls: saliuam si forsan alicui mouerim, cà se saturet, vlteriore enim & lau- tiore ferculo palatum explere non valeo. Et ba- lenus de frumentis eorumque variis differen- tiis, sequuntur nunc panificia, pultes, placenta & libamina, quae ex iis conficiuntur.
units.tr: Such contributory dinners had their famous examples in the love-feasts of the Christians of the primitive Church, which, from the collections or contributions each person made, were held without distinction between rich and poor, friends, neighbours and relatives; and they are still held in the same way. Likewise the Paschal feasts, which some Christians celebrate every year with great joy, are made from collections or contributions, for gifts and presents such as eggs, cakes, breads, sugared and honeyed things, meats and wines are gathered and contributed for the celebration of that festival. The legislators also instituted daily common meals, called syssitia and phiditia, so that citizens might more easily be kept to the duty of thrift and frugality, and above all to zeal for mutual love, goodwill and concord. Plato too approves this daily common eating in his Laws, where he declares that there ought to be syssitia in every place and district, in which all are to be kept together in fellowship. He approves the syssitia, saying they are useful in well-ordered states, and that the multitude ought to be distributed into syssitia or fellowships. He also holds that the syssitia are of ancient custom, and that the Italian ones are the oldest of all, from which the syssitia of the other peoples were derived, such as those of the Cretans, Spartans and Lacedaemonians, which Cicero mentions in the sixth book of the Tusculan Disputations, and of the Carthaginians and Athenians. To these I think the syssitia, guilds or fellowships of the Germans may not inappropriately be compared. That in democratic commonwealths especially public and daily feasts are in frequent use, everyone knows; and for this purpose ample and splendid dining halls are built, which in the common German tongue are called Trinkstuben or Gesellstuben, the houses of companions, where men of the same trade and office, living in the same way of life, meet and gather, both to keep up mutual goodwill and friendship and also to ratify and confirm honest and lawful covenants and agreements. But where intemperance in feasting and drinking arises, which we see raging in many cities and towns today, indeed running wild over almost the greater part of the world, and where there is some suspicion of faction, the syssitia should be abolished, overthrown and dissolved by the authority of the magistrate, as unlawful, new, illegitimate and intemperate. In these, men reclining at sumptuous tables, like voracious beasts or swine from Epicurus' herd, so overwhelm and stuff themselves with wine and food that they lose all use of mind and reason, and bind themselves by wicked and impious covenants against God and neighbour, whence the greatest evils and calamities necessarily arise. But enough of feasting, and enough of dinners described at length. That single dish of basil, and the pottage made from it, has so served up its humble meals and banquets, with such a varied array of courses, that if I have perhaps stirred anyone's appetite, let him satisfy himself with this; for I cannot delight the palate with a further and richer course. And so much concerning grains and their various kinds; now follow the bread-foods, porridges, cakes and offerings made from them.

units.la: CAP. VII. Depane, placentis, pultibus, va-riifq; eduliis.
units.tr: Chapter VII. Of bread, cakes, porridges and various other foods.

units.la: X frugibus hactenus com-memoratis fiunt panificia. Inter omnia enim alimenta primas tenet panis, esculen-torum potulentorumque fir-missimum & probatissimum vinculum. Vnde & sacræ literæ sub nomine pa-nis omne genus alimenti comprehendunt: qua de re etiam Euripides impulsus ad ali-mentum hominum nihil præterCereris mu-nera & aquæ poculum opus esse pronuncia-uit. Et quæ quæ[?]scopulmentariis aliisq; ciba-riis vtilitas esse potest atq; voluptas, si citra panem edantur. Animam iis grauiter infici, qui panem in cibis abstinent, vulgi opinioquę-dam est: quin iis quoq;, qui parcius eum mi-scent cæteris eduliis, fœtere ora manifestum est. Vidi & noui ipse multos, quibus hoc peculiare fuit, multis carnibus, pauco autem pane vesci, vnde illis in pœnam contigit fœtidissimus oris halitus. Complures nihilominus inuenias, quib. à juuenta carnes, aliis quibus oua, aliisquibus pisces, multos quib. cafei fuerint fastidio, quib. vero panes, pauci. Certissimum est maximam hominum partem, vel solo pane, vel ex vino, vel ex jure aliquo contentam viuere, nulloque alimento magis contineri vitam, quam optimo pane. Est in exemplis senes quosdam panem ex melle edisse, eoque cibo vitam diutius prorraxisse. Permulti, cum per occupationes non licet vberiores ingerere cibos, panem ex vino mandunt cum saccharo: Saluberrimum & suauissimum inuentum, hoc est, literarum studiosis & vitam sedentariam agentibus commodissimum. De modo autem sumendi, panis certi all-quid singulis constitui non facile potest, quippe alii minori contenti viuunt, alii maiorem expetunt, intense enim laborantes vt fossores, messores, helcijarii, bajuli, athletæ-que copiosiorem edunt, iisq; inutilis est candidus & qui celeriter conficitur, vtiles vero iis sunt ejusmodi panes, qui neq; bellissime cocti, neq; plurimum fermentati sunt, crassi enim lentiq; succi alimentis indigent, quæ haud facile exhalent & corrumpantur. Candidi autem panes probe parati ac cocti eximie conueniunt liberaliorem vitam sequentibus: quâ de causa Sacerdotibus & Monachis lautissima panificia constituta sunt, aliquin otio marcidi, frequentissime ægrotarent. Electi igitur probiq; panes sunt eligendi, pondufq; pro pulmentariorum aliorumq; cibariorum natura & copia augeri miniue potest, vbi etiam laborum hominum-que varietas consideranda venit. Vetusta-tem in panificiis medicina damnat: calentes itemrecentioresque : veteres supra modum ficciores redduntur, proinde ægrius conficiuntur, qui calent. Siticulosi sunt, flatufq; pariunt, & obstructiones insignes: recentes jucunde & salubriter efitantur: hesterni ab illis sunt fecundi, id est quijam consederunt, ab his biduani triduanique qui vltra durâtunt, inutiliter eduntur. Quapropter pterillarum gentium morem improbo,quæ inaliquot menses coquunt panes & in esum recondunt, nullam aliam ob causam, quam quod parcius vorantur ob duritiem & sicci-tatem. Locus quoque in quo feruantur pa-nificia non parum addit detrahitve bonitati vel malignitati, calentes enim in locum gra-ueolentem repositi, facile vitofam vim alli-ciunt, vi caloris trahentis, locis autem hu-mentioribus facile mucefcunt, situmque contrahunt, redolentque : apud quasdam gentes in subterraneis cellis vinariis innoxie feruantur, aliii in tabulatis & locis foco pro-ximis, panes suos recondunt, sed hanc cu-ram matribus vel patribus familias relinqui-nus suscipiendam.
units.tr: Bread is made from the grains mentioned so far. Among all foods bread holds first place, the firmest and most approved bond of foods and drinks. Hence Sacred Letters also comprise every kind of food under the name of bread. For this reason Euripides, pressed about human food, declared that nothing was needed except the gifts of Ceres and a cup of water. What use or pleasure can side dishes and other relishes have if they are eaten without bread? It is a popular opinion that those who abstain from bread with their meals are badly tainted in the breath, and it is plain that the mouths of those who mix bread sparingly with other foods stink. I have seen and known many people for whom this was a peculiar trait: they eat much meat but little bread, and as a punishment they have the most foul breath. Nevertheless you will find many people who from youth avoid meats, others eggs, others fish, many who dislike cheese, but few who dislike bread. It is certain that the greatest part of mankind lives on bread alone, or on wine, or on some broth, and that life is sustained by no food more than by the best bread. There are examples of old men who ate bread made with honey and by this food prolonged their lives. Many people, when their occupations do not allow them to take in more substantial food, chew bread with wine and sugar: a most wholesome and pleasant invention, especially convenient for students of letters and those who lead a sedentary life. As to how much bread should be taken, a fixed amount cannot easily be set for each person, for some live content with less, others desire more. Those who labour hard, such as diggers, reapers, carters, porters and athletes, eat more abundantly, and for them white bread, which is quickly made, is unsuitable. Breads that are neither very finely baked nor much leavened are useful to them, for thick and sluggish humours need foods that do not readily evaporate and decay. Well-prepared and well-baked white breads, however, suit those who lead a more refined life. For this reason fine breads have been provided for priests and monks, who otherwise, weakened by idleness, would very often fall ill. Good and wholesome breads, therefore, are to be chosen, and their weight cannot be increased in proportion to the nature and quantity of the side dishes and other foods; the variety of men's labours must also be considered. Medicine condemns old bread in the making of loaves, and likewise bread that is still warm or too fresh. Old bread becomes excessively dry and so is digested with difficulty, and warm bread is digested with difficulty too. Such loaves make people thirsty, produce wind and cause marked obstructions. Fresh bread is eaten pleasantly and healthily; yesterday's bread is fruitful, that is, bread that has already settled; bread two or three days old, which lasts longer, is eaten to no good purpose. Therefore I disapprove of the custom of those peoples who bake bread for several months and store it up to eat, for no other reason than that it is eaten more sparingly because of its hardness and dryness. The place where bread is kept also adds or takes away not a little from its goodness or badness. Warm bread placed in a foul-smelling place easily draws in a noxious quality by the drawing power of the heat; in damper places it readily grows mouldy, contracts a musty taste and smells. Among some peoples bread is kept harmlessly in underground wine cellars; others store their loaves on shelves and in places near the hearth. But we leave this care to be undertaken by mothers and heads of households.

units.la: De panibus furnaceis & clibani-tis,
units.tr: On oven breads and clibanus breads.

units.la: CVm panis furnaceus inter ea quæ nutri-unt primum tenet locum, nonq, parum ad valetudinis vitæq, conseruationem eius coctura refert, opera pretium erit, de eo panca bicinter-ferere.
units.tr: Since oven bread holds first place among the foods that nourish, and its baking contributes not a little to the preservation of health and life, it will be worth the trouble to discuss it briefly.

units.la: Panes autem ipsitas seu furnaceos à clibanitis differre Plinius l.8. & Athen. l.3. clavein- dicant. Furnacei enim in magnis furnis co-quuntur, clibanite in tefliis aut furnis portati-bus, illi innocentiores sunt magisq, nutriunt bi-O. sicficciffimi sunt, ob testa[?] nimiam humiditatem, exugentis calorem, quam etiam sententiam ex- presse expressit Hipp. 2. de diæt. Ipnite igitur magis nutriunt, quam verubus aut craticulis cocti, quod minus ab igne, quam illi adurun- tur.
units.tr: Pliny in book 8 and Athenaeus in book 3 indicate that furnace breads differ from clibanus breads. Furnace breads are baked in large ovens, clibanus breads in tiles or portable ovens. The former are more harmless and more nourishing; the latter are the driest, because of the excessive moisture of the tile, which draws out the heat. Hippocrates expressly states this opinion in book 2 of On Diet. Therefore bread baked in an oven nourishes more than bread cooked on spits or gridirons, because it is less scorched by the fire.

units.la: Ad clibanitas panis biscoctus refertur nauticus, quo praecipue utuntur vncti atq; ad scalmum redacti in triremibus: Item milites nauta in longioribus nauigationibus: in septem- trionalibus regionibus à nonnullis etiam sub te- stis coquitur, non ingratus ut quidam putant, ob nimiam siccitatem, sed famelici cis meliores inopia pressis acceptissimus, cuius rei ipse possum esse testis: coctus autem in partes scinditur ac recoquitur, ut perduret, non mucescat, sittimq; minus contrahat.
units.tr: To clibanus bread belongs the ship's biscuit, twice baked, which is especially used by the oarsmen who are chained to their benches in triremes, and by soldiers and sailors on long voyages. In northern regions some bake it under tiles. It is not unpleasant, as some think, because of its great dryness, but it is most welcome to the hungry and to those pressed by want, of which I myself can be a witness. When it is baked it is cut into pieces and baked again, so that it lasts, does not go mouldy, and draws in less moisture.

units.la: Quitorretur sub craticula, et sub finem coena apponi solet, diciitur Efcharitis, Anteinen- tionem clibanorum et furnorum veteres torre- bant panes suos feruenti loco, vel fictilibus pati- nis,cinere et carbone, qui adhuc mos barbaris quibusdam gentibus peculiaris est, subcinerit ui panibus maxime vescentibus.
units.tr: Bread that is roasted under a gridiron, and is commonly served at the end of a meal, is called eschariten [ἐσχαρίτης]. Before ovens and clibani were in use, the ancients roasted their loaves in a hot place or in earthenware pans, in ashes and charcoal. This custom is still peculiar to certain barbarian peoples, who eat bread mostly baked under the ashes.

units.la: Quin et nostra atate fepius nunc fornaces, seu furni, nunc ligna omnibus locis et tem- poribus, maxime veroin bellis ac mari, item ritè neribus haberi nequeunt, ut ita subcinerit ui panibus ad focum vel cacabum aut prunis co- ctis esurientes vesci cogantur. In laminis quoq; ferreis aut aneis &c. ci-ffime[?] panes coquuntur, Vnde lixa in militia ta-les laminas vt & farinam, in sacculis coriaceis, nefcilicet peruolet, secum gerunt, vt fugati vel exutinere defatigati, cibum in eiusmodi lami-nis cito possint parare. Sed & furnos subter-raneos ad colles (fcil. & montes, vbi glebofum fo-lum est, quidam fodiunt, quod hodie Turcas factitare audio: alii vero fornaces cupreas pen-siles secum vehunt currum in flar suspensi-lum.
units.tr: Even in our own age, ovens or furnaces cannot always be had in every place and at every time, especially in wars and at sea, nor likewise in the countryside; so hungry people are forced to eat bread buried under ashes at the hearth or pot, or in hot embers. Cakes are also baked very quickly on iron or bronze plates. Hence soldiers in the field carry such plates, and flour in leather sacks, so that when they are fleeing, or worn out by fatigue, they can quickly prepare food on such plates. Some also dig underground ovens into the hills (that is, the mountains where the ground is clayey), which I hear the Turks do today. Others carry copper hanging ovens with them on a wagon, suspended in a frame.

units.la: Damnantur autem omnes qui feruenti loco, cineribus atq; carbone torrentur, intus au-tem crudi existunt. Subcineritius vero coctura ratione omnium improbatur maxime, barbaris & a cultu humanitatis remotis conuenientes: minus ab igne vsti, æqueq, intus & extra coctu in-nocentiores deprehenduntur, vt sunt panes fornis coctu. Non hic praetereundum est, ab vrbe condita annis super quingentis ostogin-ta Pistores Romae non fuisse mulierum, id tunc opus fuisse, ipsos, Quirites panes finxisse. Vxor Catonis, autore Plutarcho, pinsendi munus à sua dignitate alienum non putauit: Denique vero Persia atq; Asia omnis generis delitiæ Romanorum confluxerunt, unde adhuc pistores illi dulciarii, qui placentas & catera dulcia panificia format, carnes incrustant, vt in amplis vrbibus, magnatum familiis videre est.
units.tr: All those are condemned who are roasted in a hot place with ashes and charcoal and remain raw inside. Baking under ashes is rejected by every reasoning and suits only barbarians and those remote from civilised culture. Breads baked in ovens are found to be less scorched by the fire, more harmless, and cooked equally inside and out. It should not be passed over here that more than five hundred and eighty years after the founding of the city there were no bakers at Rome; the women then did this work, and the citizens themselves baked their own bread. Cato's wife, according to Plutarch, did not think grinding corn beneath her dignity. Finally, when Persia and all Asia poured every kind of luxury into Rome, those confectioner bakers remained who shape cakes and other sweet breads and coat meats, as can be seen in the households of great men in large cities.

units.la: De coctura panis.
units.tr: On the baking of bread.

units.la: Coctura quoque ratio diligenter ei, qui vitae salubritati studet, tenenda est, Pistorum enim intolerabili auaritia atq; negligentia fit, ut identidem panes justam coctionem non adipiscantur, quia minus coctos ponderosiores existere certum est ob humo-ris copiam intus manentis: saepe torrentur potius quam coquuntur; quo errore haud dubie valetudo tentatur, immodico enim ignis calore non alienus tantum humor ab-sumitur, sed etiam lentus ille, genuinus & dulcis succus, qui velut anima farinae est exhalat atque deuritur. Quamobrem vr-bium praefecti inprimis debent cauere ne in hac rei cibariae parte adeo grauiter & frequenter peccetur, sed potius, qui ex jurisdictione hoc habent inquirere poenis multandisque in eos debent animaduertere, quos tantas vitae insidias moliri comperierint.
units.tr: Care in baking must also be taken by anyone who studies the wholesomeness of life. Through the bakers' intolerable greed and carelessness, loaves repeatedly fail to bake properly. It is certain that loaves less thoroughly baked are heavier, because of the moisture that remains inside them. They are often scorched rather than baked. This error undoubtedly endangers health, for with excessive heat not only is the foreign moisture driven off, but also that soft, natural and sweet juice, which is like the life of the flour, is breathed out and burnt away. Therefore the city prefects above all must take care that such grave and frequent faults are not committed in this part of our food. Rather, those who hold the power of inquiry by their jurisdiction should inquire, punish with fines, and deal sharply with those whom they discover to be plotting such great dangers to life.

units.la: De farina & aqua qua subigi-tur.
units.tr: On the flour and the water with which it is kneaded.

units.la: Farina quoque natura viresque non sunt negligenda: ut enim panis sit optimus, optimeque nutriat, facilisque conficia-tur, requiritur I. frumenti bonitas. II. [illegible, ~8 letters] eius molitura ac pistura. III. ut farina fit tenuis, non vermiculosa, ut fit candida & ab omni furfure pura, sic enim facilius in ventriculo alteratur, probius concoquitur, facilius in corpus distribuitur, promtiusque alit. IV. mistio fermenti plurima, falis modica. V. Subactio exacta. VI.Proba coctura.
units.tr: The nature and strength of the flour must also not be neglected. For bread to be excellent, to nourish best and to be easily digested, the following are required: (1) the goodness of the grain; (2) [illegible] its milling and grinding; (3) that the flour be fine, not wormy, white and free from all bran, for so it is more easily altered in the stomach, more properly digested, more readily distributed through the body, and nourishes more promptly; (4) a large quantity of leaven and a moderate amount of salt; (5) exact kneading; (6) proper baking.

units.la: Quod igitur in farina durum relinquitur atque furfureum, ut in aqua id extrinsecus dissolui non potest, eadem ratione neque intus ventre quidem madefactum dissoluetur, sed totum ut fuit ingestum, indi-gestum atque indigestum permanet, unde etiam panes furfuracei & crassi maiorem stercoris copiam conficiunt quam necesse est propter subsidentiam furfurumque vim abster-soriam.
units.tr: Whatever in the flour is hard and bran-like remains, and since it cannot be dissolved from outside in water, by the same reasoning it will not be dissolved inside the belly even when softened there. It remains undigested, just as it was swallowed. For this reason coarse bran breads also produce a greater quantity of excrement than is necessary, on account of the sediment and the scouring power of the bran.

units.la: Aquæ porro maximam habendam esse rationem, non dubitandum est, vitiosa enim aquæ insalubres panes reddit, ut plurimum continent hieme: largiori etiam aquâ farina perfundi debet, ut sua spongiosa inanitate panis multum admittat aërem.
units.tr: Furthermore, there is no doubt that great regard must be paid to the water. Bad water makes bread unwholesome, as it mostly does in winter. The flour should also be sprinkled with a larger amount of water, so that the bread, by its spongy emptiness, admits much air.

units.la: Panificum grex peruersus neque aquæ, neque salis, neque fermenti etiam habet rationem. Salitos enim panes salubriores esse iudicant omnes, cum in cibo eruditi palati homines iudicant omnes. Salem exsiccat omnem humorem, qui a calore solet putrescere, quod manifeste indicant sale imbutæ conditæque carnes, quas in vsum cibarium salitas diu videmus per-durare, qua ratione etiam in panificiis humor a sale consumetur, qui fi insideret pondus aduceret. Praterea sal modicus inomni cibo excitat auiditatem, coctionem q, iuuat..
units.tr: The perverse flock of bakers pays regard neither to water, nor to salt, nor even to leaven. All men judge salted loaves to be more wholesome, since men of trained palate judge so in their eating. Salt dries up all moisture, which from heat is apt to putrefy, as salted and pickled meats clearly show; we see these, when salted for eating, last a long time. By the same reasoning, in bakery goods the salt will consume the moisture which, if it stayed, would bring weight. Moreover, moderate salt in every food stimulates appetite and also aids digestion.

units.la: Panis denig, fermentatus esse debet, qui ζυμωτός[?] dicitur: fermentum enim panificiis fa-lubritatem affert & gratiam. Infermentatum dicitur ζυμωτός[?], qualis fuit Iudaicus panis. Cornelius tamen Celsus panem fine fermento idoneum dicit, fermentatum vero a-lienum, facilius quàm intus corrumpi, cui Galenus caterig, posteriores medici contradicunt, panes plurimum fermentatos facilime concoqui, eos vero qui fine fermento finguntur nemini omnino utiles esse constanter asseuerantes; quin & utiliores fieri fi caseus admisceatur, conftatq; hoc panificii genus tum apud maiores, tum no-ftra etate agricolis & rulticis in summo honore fuisse inque vsu frequentissimo etiamnunc esse: a quibus tamen panibus literarum studiosos omnes quique otio dediti vitam tranfiguunt, ubeo abstinere, namq, fossores, mefores q, ipsos baiu-losq, esu illorum ladi constat..
units.tr: Finally, bread ought to be leavened, which is called [ζυμωτός] leavened. For leaven brings wholesomeness and pleasantness to bakery goods. Unleavened bread is called [ἄζυμος], such as the Jewish bread was. Cornelius Celsus, however, says that bread without leaven is suitable, while leavened bread is less so, as it more easily corrupts inside. Galen agrees with him in other respects, but later physicians contradict this, firmly asserting that very leavened breads are most easily digested, while those made without leaven are altogether useless to no one. Indeed they become more useful if cheese is mixed in. It is established that this kind of bread was held in the highest esteem by our ancestors and is still in very frequent use among farmers and country folk. Yet all those who spend their lives devoted to literary studies, or to leisure, I bid abstain from these breads, for it is well established that diggers, millers and even the idle and the bathers are harmed by eating them.

units.la: Esse autem fermentatos panes non inutiles inde constat, quod fermentum fit tenuum partium, modiceque calidum, & ut verius dicitur, ex contrariis facultatibus temperatum, quipquippe propter aciditatem frigida cuiusdam naturæ particeps est, & caliditatis etiam ex putredine oborta, quin & aliquid à sale accipit & farinæ naturæ.
units.tr: That leavened breads are not useless is clear from the fact that leaven consists of fine parts and is moderately warm; and, to speak more truly, it is tempered from contrary qualities. For on account of its acidity it partakes of a certain cold nature, and also of a heat arising from putrefaction; moreover it takes something from the salt and from the nature of the flour.

units.la: Pro ritu autem gentium fermentum variis fit modis, quos, nimis laboriosum esset [?], hic recensere: teneamus nos nostram faciendi fermenti rationem nobis obviam: hoc unum observandum, subactum fermentum plus minus quindecim dies servari posse, ultra vero vitiari.
units.tr: According to the custom of nations, leaven is made in various ways, which would be too laborious to list here. Let us keep to our own method of making leaven, which lies closest to hand. This one thing must be observed: kneaded leaven can be kept for about fifteen days, but beyond that it spoils.

units.la: Modus quoq; statuendus: modicum enim fermentum totam massam corrumpit, plurimumq; deperdit gratia.
units.tr: The amount also must be set: for a small amount of leaven corrupts the whole mass, and loses much of its goodness.

units.la: Per se deniq; fermentum cumprimis ex farina tritici extrahendi maturandiq; virtute pollere experimentis constat, callos enim pedum clavosq; extenuat, caterasq; tubercula & furunculos ex sale concoquit aperitq;.
units.tr: Finally, it is established by experience that leaven, especially that drawn from wheat flour, has great power for drawing out and ripening: for it thins calluses of the feet and corns, and by means of salt it digests and opens other tubercles and boils.

units.la: De variis panis generibus & differen-tiis.
units.tr: On the various kinds of bread and their differences.

units.la: PAnis varia genera ac differentias omnes literis mandare ut superuacuum, ita dif-ficilimum est, discrimina tamen ad rem no-stram pertinentia, ascribam.
units.tr: To commit all the kinds and differences of bread to writing would be as superfluous as it is difficult; nevertheless I will set down those distinctions which pertain to our subject.

units.la: Conuenit autem inter omnes delica- tiffimum praeftantiffimumq; panem fieri ex tritico, quitamen protritici natura non exi- guas differentias : alii enim pu- riffimi, alii farfuribus paucis, alii multis, quidam polline furfuribusque simul consu- fis finguntur, pro gentium ritu, homi- numque peculiari uiuendi ratione*; alius, enim hoc , alius illo panis genere delecta- tur. Ut enim olim apud antiquos, tum Graecos, tum Romanos multiplex fuit pa- nis varietas , sic nostra quoque aetate hic & alibi permulta sunt discrimina , quippe primarii , vt regii , procerumque ac ma- gnatum , secundarii , tertiarii & quartarii cernuntur , quanquam magnos imperato- res & magnates secundario etiam pane ob- lectatos fuisse constat , & hodie in plurium Dominorum mensis atri panes confpiciun- tur.
units.tr: All agree that the most delicate and excellent bread is made from wheat; yet even within the nature of wheat there are no small differences. Some breads are made of the purest flour, some with few bran-flakes, some with many, and some are shaped from fine flour and bran sifted together, according to the custom of peoples and the particular way of life of men. For one man delights in this kind of bread, another in that. Just as among the ancients, both Greeks and Romans, there was a manifold variety of bread, so in our own age, here and elsewhere, there are very many distinctions. For there are seen primary bread, such as the bread of kings and of nobles and magnates, secondary, tertiary and quaternary bread. Although it is established that great emperors and magnates were pleased even with secondary bread, and today black loaves are seen on the tables of many lords.

units.la: Siligineus summae fuit auctoritatis in mensis Romanorum , quorum mos hodie quoq; in amplis familiis pertinaciter durat. Porro doctrinae gratia talis panis dichoto- mia, institui potest, ut quidam dicuntur ex- tremi, quidam intermed.j. Extremi triticei seu purissimi, & furfuracei : inter hos Interje-[?] &ti[?] sunt hordeacei, siliginei nostri, auenacei, farracei, fpeltacei & ex ocymo. Triticei omnium sunt purissimi. Furfuracei omnium sordidissimi, leuissimeque alunt,ocyffimè per aluum deiiciuntur, quos nisi famma vrgente inopia edi non vide-mus.
units.tr: Siliginous bread was of the highest reputation on the tables of the Romans, and their custom still stubbornly persists today in great households. Further, for the sake of teaching, such bread may be divided by dichotomy, so that some kinds are called extreme and some intermediate. The extreme kinds are wheaten or purest, and bran bread. Among these [illegible] are barley bread, our siliginous or rye bread, oat bread, farro bread, spelt bread, and bread from ocymum. Wheaten bread is of all the purest. Bran bread is of all the coarsest; it nourishes very lightly and is most quickly passed through the bowels. We see it eaten only when pressing want forces hunger.

units.la: Hordaceos & reliquos,qui antiquis fue-runt vsitatissimi, cibis quidam abdicandos iubent, quadrupedumq; refectibus tantum idoneos,sed nullo iudicio.
units.tr: Some order barley bread and the rest, which were most in use among the ancients, to be abandoned as food, fit only for the feeding of four-footed beasts; but this is said without judgment.

units.la: Hordaceus namq; tritico feré nihil cedit, ita vt etiam Hipp. teste, proximum ab eo oc-cupet locum. Siquidem ipsi saluatori nostro panes hordacei miraculi materiam prœbue-runt,nonigitur ex humana vita panes horda-ceifunt proscribendi. Constat eos qui pani-bus hordaceis vescuntur,morbo pedum non tentari. Experimenti via facilis,quibus res est cum podagra. Experimentum cuiq; fit libe-rum &obuium. Multos certe reperias in no-stris etiam regionibus & locis illis asperis montofiq; ac fyluis illis, quas Germani dent Westerwaldt vnd Odenwaldt vocant, vt & in nostra etiam ditionis & Comitatus I- fenburgici parte,quæ auimontium appellari potest, Bogelsberg/auenàfola, ocymoque plurimum victitantes,melius nutriri fariati-que,quam qui tritico abundant, (præsertim sbi farina auenacea pollinario cribro exacte fuerit cribrata,farfuribusque purgata ) imò non tantum prosperiori vti eos valetudine, sed diutius etiam viuere iis constat,qui vel in
units.tr: For barley bread yields almost nothing to wheat, so that, as Hippocrates bears witness, it occupies the next place after it. Indeed, barley loaves provided the material for a miracle to our Saviour himself; therefore barley bread is not to be banished from human life. It is established that those who eat barley bread are not troubled by disease of the feet. The way of testing is easy for those who have to do with gout, and anyone may make the experiment freely and openly. Certainly you will find many in our own regions, and in those rough, mountainous and wooded places which the Germans call Westerwald and Odenwald, and also in our own district and in the part of the county of Isenburg which may be called the mountain country, Bogelsberg. Living mostly on oats, barley and spelt, they are better nourished and fattened than those who abound in wheat (especially if oat flour has been carefully sifted through a bolting sieve and cleansed of bran). Indeed, it is established that they not only enjoy a more prosperous state of health, but also live longer, than those who have plenty of wheat and wine in Alsace or Italy and who every day devise new dishes after the manner of Apicius.

units.la: Alfatia, vel Italia tritici & vini habent copi-am, quiqúe Apitii more quotidie noua fer-cula excogitant. Quare prudenter gladia-tores & athletæ veteres ab hordei tanquam optimi cibi ad nutriendum accommodatiffi-mi vsu,se deterreri non sunt passi, licet à ple-risque contumeliosè hordeacii appellaren-tur.
units.tr: Therefore the ancient gladiators and athletes wisely did not allow themselves to be deterred from the use of barley, as the best food most suited to nourishment, although by many it was insultingly called barley-food.

units.la: Ac vt multa paucis expediam, omnia fru-menta mutuò in hominibus alendis sibi suc-cedere posse vsus docuit: quemadmodum enim qui vinum non habet, cereuisiam, qui hac destituitur,aquam bibat, ita cui per vitæ suæ rationem, triticum, speltam, hordeum-umque vlurpare concessum non est,is vulga-rem siliginem, auenam, ocymumue vsurpet, non minus enim his quam tritico natura contenta est, præsertim si iis quis assue-uerit, non enim assuetis grauitatem ven-triculo inferunt, difficulterque conco-quuntur, malleatoribus verò, phalan-gariis, agricolisque conuenientissima sunt.
units.tr: To set out many things in few words: experience has taught that all grains can stand in for one another in feeding people. For just as one who has no wine drinks beer, and one who lacks beer drinks water, so the one to whom, by the manner of his life, it is not permitted to use wheat, spelt or barley, let him use common rye, oats or ocymum. For nature is content with these no less than with wheat, especially if one has become accustomed to them. For to those not accustomed they bring heaviness to the stomach and are digested with difficulty; but for hammermen, soldiers and farmers they are most suitable.

units.la: Ex siligine nostra seu secali,sale fermento bono, aquaque simplici præstantissimum fit tetraphatmacum famis, vbiuis vsitatissi-mum ac longo vsu probatissimum, <bl>Rocken brodt</bl>. Rité autè & proportionaliter inter se quatuor illa sunt contemperanda & perco-quenquenda. Salubrior panis efficitur, si bene fermentatus est, & probe salitus.
units.tr: From our rye, or secale, flour, with salt, good leaven and plain water, is made the most excellent famine bread of four ingredients, everywhere the most common and proven by long use: <bl>Rocken brodt</bl>. These four must be mixed together and baked properly and in due proportion. Bread is more wholesome if it is well fermented and properly salted.

units.la: Romani & delicati Graeci hunc panem sordidum appellarunt, sed iniquè. Vtinam eiusmodi sordibus horrea & penuaria tempore caritatis annonae plena essent.
units.tr: The Romans and the fastidious Greeks called this bread coarse, but unjustly. Would that granaries and pantries were full of such coarseness in times of dearth.

units.la: Verum, ne vnquam alicui aliquid durissimae etiam & miserandae famis, nec non summae frumentaceorum feminum penuriae tempore deesse videatur, subsidia quaedam aut saltem subleuamina, naturaliaque & artificiosa simul cibi vicaria seu locum tenentia, annotabo, pauperculis & egenis fameque perituris pernecessaria.
units.tr: But lest anyone should ever seem to lack some remedy in a time of most severe and pitiable famine, and of extreme scarcity of grain, I will note certain aids, or at least alleviations, both natural and artificial, substitutes or stopgaps for food, most necessary for the poor, the needy and those about to perish of hunger.

units.la: Ac primò quidem paupertas in frumentorum penuria artificiosè didicit concinnare panes ex pisis, fabis, ciceribus, lupinis, vi- ciis, lentibus, milio, oryza, orobis, glandibus, &c. horum enim farina frumentaceae vel parte media, vel etiam largius admiscetur: fa- melicorum autem stomachum sufficienter replent, famem retardant, paucitate satiant, firmiusque praebent nutrimentum, praeferdim glandini, castaneati, cicerini, quique ex oryza fiunt & milio, hi enim nec inusitati sunt, nec insalubres. Pulcriores autem &gra- tiores erunt eiusmodi panes, si feminibus ex- corticatis prius parentur, Quibus vero leguminum flatulentia su-specta est, ii carui, fœniculi, anisi vel cymini feminæ adiecto eam emendare possunt, mor-bidisq; corporibus sunt accommodatiores, quia hac ratione medicati euadunt.
units.tr: First, poverty, in a shortage of grain, has learned to make breads skilfully from peas, beans, chickpeas, lupins, vetches, lentils, millet, rice, orobus, acorns and so on. Their flour is mixed in with grain flour, either in part or even more generously. These fill the stomachs of the hungry sufficiently, delay hunger, satisfy with a small quantity and provide firmer nourishment. This is especially true of acorn, chestnut, chickpea, and those made from rice and millet, for these are neither unusual nor unwholesome. The breads will be pleasanter and more agreeable if the seeds are first husked. For those who suspect legumes of causing flatulence, the addition of caraway, fennel, anise or cumin seed can correct this, and they are more suitable for sick bodies, since they become medicinal in this way.

units.la: Dira quoque, tabida & rab da fames pa-nes ex siliquis cereuisiariis <bl>Drabern/nefũ</bl> hominum transferre coegit: quin & ex fur-ibus, qui tamen extra annonæ caritatem in Magnorum aulis in pastum canum & alti-lium pinsuntur. Minimè enim hi panes tam propter extremam paganorum famem le-thalem (quam Deus auertat) quam ob vtili-tatem ac comparandi facilitatem fuerunt praetereundi. Carius enim vita nihil est, quomodocunque illa tandem conferuetur. Lupulus siliquis adiectus earum fœculenti-am fa ilè corriget, purredinem enim arcet, sanguineunq; mundificat.
units.tr: A dire, wasting and ravenous hunger has also forced men to turn to breads made from brewers' husks, <bl>Drabern/nefũ</bl>, and even from bran, which outside times of dearth is ground in the courts of the great for feeding dogs and cattle. These breads should by no means be passed over, both because of the deadly extreme hunger of the common folk (which God avert) and because of their usefulness and ease of procurement. For life is nothing dearer, however it may be preserved. Hops added to the husks will easily correct their muddiness, for they prevent putrefaction and cleanse the blood.

units.la: Fit quoq; panis laudabilis ex pomis con-cisis siue excorticatis, siue non, vel elixis in forma pultis. vel furno tostis, sicvt farina pri-us probè fermentata & salita subigatur, & ma-ne media pomorum præparatorum pars ad-misceatur.
units.tr: A praiseworthy bread is also made from apples, cut up whether peeled or not, boiled into a pulp or toasted in an oven. The flour, first well fermented and salted, is kneaded, and a middle portion of the prepared apples is added in the morning.

units.la: Rectius tamen coquuntur in pulmenti formam, coloque traiiciuntur, & postea fa-rinæ subiiciuntur. Tot autem sunt huius panis differentiæ, quot & pomorum. Ex dulcibus sunt meliores & εὐχυμοι. Eodem modo ex pyris tam sylvestribus quàm domesticis, prout libet, panes confici possunt.
units.tr: However, the apples are more properly cooked into the form of a pottage, strained through a cloth, and afterwards added to the flour. There are as many kinds of this bread as there are kinds of apples. Sweet apples make the better breads, and they are of good flavour. In the same way breads can be made from pears, wild or cultivated, as one pleases.

units.la: Fiunt quoq; panes ex cerasis, prunis, a-catiis nostris cotoneis;amygdalis, castaneis, nucibus iuglandibus & avellanis, baccis iuniperinis & lauri.
units.tr: Breads are also made from cherries, plums, our apricots and quinces; from almonds, chestnuts, walnuts and hazelnuts; and from juniper and laurel berries.

units.la: Cerasati sic conficiuntur. Exiccata ce-rasa per totum annum in hunc & alium usum reponuntur, postea recocta præbentur, vel electuarium farinæ commiscetur, vel per se in pane triticeo & pane placentarum pistaro devorantur.
units.tr: Cherry breads are made as follows. Dried cherries are stored for the whole year for this and other uses. Afterwards they are offered re-cooked, or mixed as a confection with the flour, or eaten by themselves in wheat bread and in a bread of pastry cakes.

units.la: Nuclei verò, sicut & consimiliū fructuum cum cortice pistrino moli, & in pollinem redigi possunt albicantem, farinæ subigendæ addendum pro pane augendo, & largius exiguâ massa cibando: talesq; panes inutiles planè & noxii esse non possunt, eins-modi enim nuclei cum suis ossibus[?] & corticibus contra calculum colicamq; commendantur.
units.tr: Kernels, however, like those of similar fruits, can be ground with their shells in a mill and reduced to a whitish powder, to be added to flour when kneading, to enlarge the bread and to feed generously on a small mass. Such breads cannot be wholly useless or harmful, for such kernels, with their bones [?] and shells, are recommended against gravel and colic.

units.la: Eodem modo coquuntur myrtilli, mora, fraga, similesq; fructus in formam ele-ctuarii adq; usum reseruantur.
units.tr: In the same way bilberries, mulberries, strawberries and similar fruits are cooked into the form of an electuary and kept for use.

units.la: Amygdalæ cum corticibus suis si mo-luntur, farinam replentem exhibebunt & nutrientem.
units.tr: If almonds are ground with their skins, they will yield a filling and nourishing flour.

units.la: Sunt & panes faginei, rosacei, rosis cum farinæ particula contemperatis, funtq; utilissimi & salubérrimi, efficati enim omnes alui cruen-
units.tr: There are also beech breads and rose breads, with the roses mixed with a little flour. They are very useful and wholesome, for all of them check bloody stools and immoderate flux of the bowels.

units.la: cruentas deiectiones menfiumqueimmodi-cum fluxum fiftunt. Ficulnei, paffulati, qui fiunt ex ficubus caricisque prxpinguibus & paffulis, fi videlicet cum farina fubigantur, funtque non inutiles: fed ne hi panes aluum citius foluant, folido & ftiptico medicamen- to fiunt diftemperandi, vt pifis glandibus, vel falrem aquá chalybeata.
units.tr: Fig breads, made from fat dried figs and raisins, are not useless if they are kneaded with flour. But so that these breads do not loosen the bowels too quickly, they should be tempered with a solid, astringent medicine, such as peas or acorns, or with chalybeate water.

units.la: Ex floribus quoque fambuci coctis, in eles- &uarii formam fit panis in dyfenteria cele- bratiffimus. Recipiantur baccæ fambuci contufæ, in mortario & farina é mola iam iam calens adhuc allata, hæc inter fe mifce- antur, coquantur vel pinfantur: fruftum dé hoc pane vino optimo iniicitur, &pro teftin- guenda fiti cbibitur faluberrimo experi- mento.
units.tr: Bread made from boiled elder flowers, formed into an electuary, is also a very famous remedy for dysentery. Let crushed elderberries be taken and mixed in a mortar with flour just brought from the mill and still warm; these are mixed together and then cooked or pounded. A piece of this bread is steeped in the best wine and swallowed to quench thirst, a most wholesome remedy.
