units.la: Ex omnis generis prunis coctis vel toftis, vbi fcilicet vberior eorum prouentus eft, fa- rinæ fubactis, panis bene nutriens hume- ctansque parari poteft. Poffunt commodiffi- mè torreri & reponi, vt totoanno panis in promtu, neceffitate vrgente & poftulante, effe queat.
units.tr: From plums of every kind, cooked or toasted, wherever their yield is plentiful, a bread that nourishes well and keeps moist can be prepared, when they are mixed with kneaded flour. They can very conveniently be dried and stored, so that bread may be at hand throughout the year when necessity urges and demands it.

units.la: Ex fungis prætera rufticiexiccatis, &in pollinem tritis panes cibosq; parare confue- uerunt: verum cautiffimè funt colligendi, quia quidam venenofi funt: eiufmodi tamen periculum præcauendum, vtque omnianni tempore edules fungi haberi possint, albi populi cortex humotenus sectus, aquaque calida, quae fermentum excepit, perfulus, quatriduo spatio fungos esui proferet aptif-limos.
units.tr: Besides, country people have been accustomed to prepare breads and food from dried mushrooms ground to powder. But they must be gathered with the greatest care, since some are poisonous. To guard against this danger, and so that edible mushrooms can be had at all times of the year, bark of white poplar, cut at ground level and steeped in warm water that has received leaven, will for four days yield very suitable mushrooms for eating.

units.la: Sed nevnquam cuiquam aliquid deeflevi- deatur, in famis & penuriae tempore fcien-dum,etiam ex radicibus,vt rapis,napis,petro- felino,iride,caepis,& ex ipsis stagneis arundi-netis panem parari facile salubrem posse: I- tem,ex herbis,vt cichoriis,acetosis,rosis, be-tis,blitis,braffi cis,buglofis,lactucis, & fimi- libus polychreftis simplicibus. Ex arborum quoque foliis,vt prunorum,pyrorum,fago-rum,quercuumque torridis,inque pollinem redactis, cotritis scilicet vel pistrino molitis, quin & arborum quarundam corticibus, vt betulae,(quod vidi ipse in Suecia anno 98.cu annonae caritas grauissima flagellaret totum regnum)molere farinam inque panis vsum spissare ineuitabilis fames famelicos coegit.
units.tr: But lest anyone lack something, it should be known that in times of famine and dearth bread can easily be made wholesome also from roots such as turnips, rapeseed, parsley, iris and onions, and from the reeds of marsh beds; likewise from herbs such as chicory, sorrel, roses, beets, orache, cabbage, bugloss and lettuce, and similar simple medicinal herbs. Also from the leaves of trees, such as plum, pear, beech and oak, dried and reduced to powder, that is, crushed or ground in a mill; and even from the bark of certain trees, such as birch. (I saw this myself in Sweden in the year 98, when the grievous dearth of grain scourged the whole kingdom.) Unavoidable hunger has compelled the starving to grind these into flour and thicken it for bread.

units.la: Foliaquoq; coxerunt atq; deuorarunt.
units.tr: They also boiled and devoured leaves.

units.la: Ex foeno quoque & cordo in extrema ne-ceffitate pistrino molito,& cum farina lauda-bili vsitata commixto,panem paratum inue-nio. Nec id absurdum est, aut penitus in-auditum,cum Hierosolymis id factum elfe, Iofephus testetur. Sed malum hoc paterne auferat,auertatq; Deus.
units.tr: I find bread also made in extreme necessity from hay and straw, ground in a mill and mixed with the usual praiseworthy flour. Nor is this absurd or wholly unheard of, since Josephus testifies that it was done at Jerusalem. But may God in fatherly fashion remove this evil and avert it.

units.la: Snntquoque panes vinosi,acetati,facchâ- rati,melliti. Spissantur & panes expifcibus sole siccatis, tostis etiam vel assis inque pul- uerem attritis & cum farina subactis, vtin- Norvvegia,Islandia,Finlappia. Quibus etiam populis caseati panes in frequenti sunt vsu.
units.tr: There are also wine breads, vinegar breads, sugared breads and honeyed breads. Breads are also thickened with fish dried in the sun, toasted or roasted, ground into powder and kneaded with flour, as in Norway, Iceland and Finland. Among these peoples cheese breads are also in frequent use.

units.la: Panis lacteus optimus est,& valdè nutri- ens:fit ex lacte ἀζύμος vel fermentatus, tamen bidis vtilissimus. Notandum hic, lacteos hosce panes multò magis satiare, fi laridum frixum addatur, vocanturq; in Wetterauia Specksuchen. Holandi & Heluetii etiam extra famem cafeum recentem seu pressi co- piam lactis cum pane interunt,& vix purio- re pane etiam diebus dominicis vtuntur ii, qui ex rusticis ditioribus sunt, quorum census æstimatur 5000 flor. Non ergo abfurdû, sitempore caritatis hi panes trahantur in vsum.
units.tr: Milk bread is excellent and very nourishing; it is made from milk, either unleavened or fermented, and is very useful for the sick. It should be noted that these milk breads satisfy much more if fried bacon is added; in the Wetterau they are called Specksuchen. The Dutch and the Swiss, even outside times of famine, eat fresh cheese or a plentiful amount of pressed milk with their bread, and those of the richer peasants, whose property is valued at 5000 florins, scarcely use finer bread even on Sundays. Therefore it is not absurd that in times of dearth these breads should be brought into use.

units.la: Neque verò prætereundi sunt panes,qui ex ouis fiunt saluberrimi ac præstantissimi, magis enim cæteris panibus satietatem indu- cunt, laudabilissimumque corpori præbent nutrimentum,cumprimis quando sacce cere- uisz melioris fermentatus aut subactus fue- rit, quod optimè norunt matresfamilias o- mnes in Wetterauia,quæ ob pinsendi (heb- doatim enim in magna id faciunt copia, ma- ximè verò diebus dominicis & sacris) artificium conterminis sibi populis omnibus pre- ripuerunt palmam.
units.tr: Nor should breads made from eggs be passed over; they are most wholesome and excellent. For they induce satiety more than other breads and give the body most praiseworthy nourishment, especially when they have been fermented or kneaded with good beer. All the housewives in the Wetterau know this well, and by their skill in kneading (for they do it weekly in great quantity, especially on Sundays and holy days) they have won the palm from all the neighbouring peoples.

units.la: Inter non naturales denique panes Cinerei sunt, qui ex cineribus radicum, item arborum & gleba- condensantur, quibus usi sunt in nauigatio- ne Indica, ut à famelica sese morte vindica- rent. Cineres autem cum aqua subegerunt & comederunt. Sic fieri potest pa- nis ex puriori terræ gleba, ut bolo armeno, terra sigillata, quorum in defectu & paucita- te commode usurpari potest bolus Hungen- fis, Niddanus, vel Laubacensis. Hi enim Hungen- ia summa penuria farinæ commiscentur: li- fis, Lau- cet enim plus repleant quam nutriant, ine- bacensis tamen penuria & fames victum et- materia iam horrendum sapidum reddit. Sic anno panis pre-98. in Suecia pauperes obintolerabilem fa- bere pof- mem glebam furnorum deuorasse, cortices- sunt. que betularum in panificium redegisse meis vidioculis, quam tamen plus quàm lupinam famem Deus paterne & clementer postea mitigauit.
units.tr: Finally, among unnatural breads are the ashen ones, which are made from the ashes of roots, likewise of trees, and from clods of earth. Those sailing to the Indies used these to save themselves from dying of hunger: they kneaded the ashes with water and ate them. So bread can be made from a purer clod of earth, such as Armenian bole or sealed earth, and where these are lacking or scarce, the Hungen, Nidda or Laubach bole can conveniently be used. For these are mixed with flour in times of great scarcity at Hungen; they fill more than they nourish, yet dire hunger makes even this unpleasant matter palatable. Thus in the year 98 in Sweden I saw with my own eyes poor people devour clods of earth from the ovens and turn birch bark into bread, though God later mercifully and kindly relieved this, which was worse than lupin hunger.

units.la: De peculiaribus quibusdam panis usi- busfaluberrimis q; inuentis ad sani- tatem conferuandam.
units.tr: On certain especially wholesome kinds of bread, also discovered for preserving health.

units.la: Quibusdam[?] torretur in tenuissimas lami- nas dissectus[?] nouitio medicinæ inuento, postremoq, loco sumitur prafertim ab obefioribus, putant enim corpora obefiora esu huius frequentiori gracilefcere, abfumiq, pituitam ventriculo infartlam[?].
units.tr: Some toast bread sliced into very thin sheets. This is a novel invention of medicine, and it is taken last, especially by the overweight, for they think fleshier bodies grow slimmer by eating it often, and that it clears phlegm lodged in the stomach.

units.la: Panem alii tostum vino intingunt, deinde pulmentis excinnamomo, nuce mofchata, macę, laudatissimo, facchar o confergunt, coq, tum in fecunda tum in aduersa valetudine plerique v-tuntur ad cibi auiditatem excitandam, tandem atque titillandam, ipsumque ventriculum corroborandum. Compertum quoque stum panem gravitatem odorum in cubiculis e-mendare, sicut seorsum fœtorem, quo nihil est cer-tius, vtrum item ingratum odorem et saporem in-sacculis addutum.
units.tr: Others dip toasted bread in wine, then sprinkle it with cinnamon, nutmeg, mace and the most praised sugar. People use this both in good and in poor health, to rouse and tickle the appetite and to strengthen the stomach itself. It is also known that toasted bread corrects the heaviness of odours in bedrooms, and likewise a stench, which is quite certain. Whether it also removes unpleasant smell and taste when added to bags is less clear.

units.la: Elotum panem mirifice celebrat laudibus me-dicina, leuiter enim alit, obstructiones q, vsceri-bus non creat, quicquid enim in eo antea lentoris a[?]q, crassi[?] continebatur, omnino exactis-simi est, leuissimus scilicet ac aerius factus. Subte-ris autem in molem in aquam conicitur, fupersluitaque, post lotionem appendatur, mirabiliter singularem lenitatem.
units.tr: Medicine greatly praises washed bread. It nourishes lightly and does not create obstructions in the viscera, for whatever sliminess and thickness it contained before is entirely removed, and it becomes very light and airy. The bread is ground fine and put into water, and after washing the surplus is weighed, giving a remarkable and special softness.

units.la: Fit praterea edulium ex pane sanis aegrotis, summo expetitum, Panatellam vocant seu patinam, nam friatum : friatur enim manibus panis, deinde aliquot horis sinunt aqua madescere calida vel frigida, quae ter quaterue mutatur, exinde ollis inditur, leniori igne coquitur ex aqua butyro adiecto, aliquè pinguiusculo liquore: lautius fit autem, si carbonibus decoquatur ex iure gallinacei pulli aut gallinæ, saepè & diutius cochleari versando, adiecto paulùm cinnamomi, zinzibe-ris modico, laudatiffimoq; saccharo, confert esum eruditatis stomachi ex immodica crapula co-traëtis, iisq; qui à cibo largiori abstinere cupi-unt.
units.tr: There is also a dish made from bread, much desired by the healthy and the sick alike, called panatella or patina. Bread is rubbed in the hands, then left for some hours to soak in warm or cold water, which is changed three or four times. Then it is put into pots and cooked over a gentle fire in water with butter added, and some fattish liquid. It is richer if boiled over embers in the broth of a cockerel or hen, stirred often and long with a spoon, with a little cinnamon, a moderate amount of ginger and the most praised sugar added. It helps a stomach weakened by immoderate gluttony, and those who wish to abstain from heavier food.

units.la: Huc pertinet panis distillatus optimum nu-tritiuum & refectiuum, inter extra[?]ta nutritiua merito principem obtinens locum, tabidis morbo exhaustis conuenientissimum.
units.tr: Here belongs distilled bread, the best nourishing and restorative food, rightly holding first place among nourishing foods, and most suitable for those wasted and exhausted by disease.

units.la: De panificiis quæ dicuntur placentæ.
units.tr: On bakers' products called placentae (cakes).

units.la: AD panis categoriam proximè accedunt placentæ, Græcè πέμματα[?] & πλακοῦντης[?], & bellaria, quorum omnium rationem, numerum & differentias, nominaque conscribere infiniti esset operis.
units.tr: Next to bread in kind come the cakes, in Greek [πέμματα] and [πλακοῦντες], and the sweetmeats; to set down the method, number, varieties and names of all of them would be the work of an endless task.

units.la: Pro locorum enim & gentium varietate, temporum varia diuersitate & ratione variare ea certum est.
units.tr: For it is certain that they vary according to the diversity of places and peoples, and according to times and customs.

units.la: Ex farina autem tritici , ouis , lacte, flore eius , melle , saccharo , cafeo ac butyro praecipuè confici & subigi con-stat.
units.tr: It is generally agreed that they are made and kneaded chiefly from wheat flour, eggs, milk, its fine flour, honey, sugar, cheese and butter.

units.la: Quae ex lacte,cafeo,ouis,butyro, melle, aut saccharo subactis conflantur, totum feré annum in vsu esse possunt. Quaedam zsta-te fiunt ex fructibus arboreis,cerasis,prunis, malis, pyris,atque id genus aliis : ex fragis item ineunte zstate, vere verò ex grosulis, uisque passis, quae stomacho non ingratae sunt.
units.tr: Those made from milk, cheese, eggs, butter, honey or sugar, kneaded together, can be in use for almost the whole year. Some are made in summer from tree fruits: cherries, plums, apples, pears and the like; in early summer from strawberries; in spring from gooseberries and raisins, which are not unpleasant to the stomach.

units.la: Hissopus,thymus,saluia,cinnamomum, rosmarinus, maiorana, piper, huiusmodi alia mediocriter admixta acriores eas faciunt & salubriores.
units.tr: Hyssop, thyme, sage, cinnamon, rosemary, marjoram, pepper and other such things, mixed in moderately, make them sharper and more wholesome.

units.la: Erunt itaque placentae vernae, hiemales, autumnales & aestiuae.
units.tr: There will therefore be spring, winter, autumn and summer placentae.

units.la: Vernae ex farina butyro,ouisque,absynthio,chelidonia,violis, mentha, hedera terrestri, porro, allio, cepisque[?] admixtis concin-nantur, salubberrimaeque existunt ac proba-tissimae.
units.tr: Spring placentae are made by mixing flour with butter, eggs, wormwood, celandine, violets, mint, ground ivy, leek, garlic and onions. They are very wholesome and most approved.

units.la: Aestate admisceantur, rosae, flores borraginis,buglossae,rosmarini, hissopus, melis-sa,nasturtium hortense &c. Autumno autem apium , cyminum , foeniculum , rutha, fumaria, centaurium, lingua cerui-na,&c. Hieme nafturtium aquaticum, piper, thymus, satureia, saluia, galanga, radix arizinziber, & similia: hæc enim moderatè & mediocriter admixta, palato eas gratiores reddunt minusque noxias.
units.tr: In summer they may be mixed with roses, borage flowers, bugloss, rosemary, hyssop, balm, garden cress and so on. In autumn, celery, cumin, fennel, rue, fumitory, centaury, hart's tongue, and so on. In winter, watercress, pepper, thyme, savory, sage, galangal, ginger root and similar things. For these, mixed in moderately, make them more pleasing to the palate and less harmful.

units.la: Quæ ex amygdalis, pistaciis, nucibusque pineis conficiuntur, atrophia laborantibus pthificisque saluberrimæ sunt, possuntque & melle condiri, quas placentas Græci, credo, [illegible, ~9 letters] appellant, apud antiquos enim mel placentis & tragematis fingendis obtinebat primas, hodie sacchari polline nihil feré est, quod non conficiatur vel saltem conspergatur.
units.tr: Those made from almonds, pistachios and pine nuts are most wholesome for those suffering from atrophy and consumption. They can also be seasoned with honey, which the Greeks, I believe, call by a name I cannot read. Among the ancients honey held the first place in shaping placentae and tragemata. Today there is almost nothing that is not made, or at least sprinkled, with sugar dust.

units.la: Fiunt quoque pugillares pastilli ex nucleis pineis, & saccharo: ex piftadis item & amygdalis saccharoque conficiuntur placentulæ, quas vulgus panes martios appellat. Quid? quod similago & saccharum in omnes figuras duci possunt atque trahi.
units.tr: Small pastilles the size of a hand are also made from pine nuts and sugar. Little cakes, which the common people call Mars' bread, are made from pistachios, almonds and sugar. And why not? Fine flour and sugar can be drawn and shaped into all sorts of forms.

units.la: Pythagorici non aliud quam panem cum melle Attico prandere soliti sunt, fuitq; placentæ genus, quod ex butyro, femidale & melle conficiebatur, gratum palato obsonium, ac salubre.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans ate nothing but bread with Attic honey for their dinner. There was also a kind of placenta made from butter, semidale and honey, a dish pleasing to the palate and wholesome.

units.la: In placentarum quoque albo est panis ille absque fermento dulciarius seu infermenta- tus,quem Hebrei septem diebus in azymo- rum festo edebant: coquebatur autem ex fa- rina tritici, cafeo & mellein clibano sub te- staceo operculo, censeturque inter Græco- rum pemmata. Unde Galenus libr.1.de ali- ment. ait ,quæcunque azymorum pemmata in clibano coxerint,exemta statim in mel ca- lidum cóiiciunt,vt penitus melleimbuátur, & hæc, inquit, de placentorum genere sunt. Et lib. de alimēnt.boni & mali succi,ait,omne ex tritico pistorium sine fermento opus pemma di&um, præcipuèaddito cafeo len- tos crassosque humores generat, succosque crudos.
units.tr: Among placentae too is that sweet or unleavened bread, which the Hebrews ate during the seven days of the feast of unleavened bread. It was baked from wheat flour, cheese and honey in an oven under a tile lid, and it is counted among the Greek pemmata. Hence Galen, in book 1 of On Foods, says: whatever pemmata of unleavened dough they have baked in the oven, they immediately take out and put into warm honey, so that they are thoroughly soaked with it; and these, he says, are of the kind of placentae. And in the book On the Juice of Good and Bad Nourishment he says that every pastry made by the baker from wheat without leaven, especially with cheese added, generates thick, viscous humours and crude juices.

units.la: Quare salubérrimus panis est is,qui plu- rimum salis & fermenti participat,cuius ma- za primum manibus bene subacta ac depsta tandem probe in clibano decocta suerit. At panis infermētatus, quamuis corpus impin- guat, si bene digestus fuerit ,quo & athletæ ob id siginabantur, vifcidos tamen humo- res generat, aluumque & viscera obstruit, cum fermentum contra suo feruore ma- zam panis friabilem reddit iusumpta e- ius viscositate, illiusque dum turget flatus tus discutit, faciliu(que digeritur. Omnes ta- men panes azymi venerem languentem & frigescentem excitant. Sunt & alia pemmatum apud veteres ge- nera, quæ liba appellarunt, ac ex cafeo, fa- rina siliginea aut tritica, ouisque fiebant, quidam addunt crocum lactisque pinguedi- nem.
units.tr: Hence the most wholesome bread is that which has much salt and leaven, whose dough is first well kneaded and pressed by hand and finally thoroughly baked in the oven. Leavened bread, although it fattens the body if well digested (for which reason athletes were once marked with it), nevertheless generates viscid humours and obstructs the bowels and viscera. Leaven, by its own heat, makes the dough friable, and once its viscosity has been taken away, it dispels the wind as it swells and is digested more easily. However, all unleavened breads excite languid and cold desire. The ancients also had other kinds of pemmata, which they called liba, made from cheese, rye or wheat flour and eggs; some add saffron and the fat of milk.

units.la: Huius generis est itrion dictum, cu- jus sæpe mentionem facit Galenus & a- lii, componiturque ex sesamo & mel- le, hodie loco sesami sumunt amygda- las.
units.tr: Of this kind is the thing called itrion, which Galen and others often mention. It is made from sesame and honey; today almonds are taken instead of sesame.

units.la: Est Tracta, mixtura quædam ex fermento & farina compacta, manibus sæpius in for- mam longam planamque tracta, vnde et- iam nomen emanauit. Itali Tiratas à tra- hendo nominant, si subigitur vuæ passæ fuc- co melior fit & suauior.
units.tr: There is the tracta, a mixture of leaven and flour pressed together, often drawn out by the hands into a long, flat shape, whence it also got its name. The Italians call them tiratae from the verb "to draw" (trahere). If it is kneaded with the juice of raisins it becomes better and sweeter.

units.la: Infitiaetiam huc referre licet, siue insicia, quæ fiebant ex variis carnibus tritis pi- pereque commixtis, vel etiam ex pi- scibus diuersis, teste Alexandro Tralli- ano.
units.tr: One may also refer here the infitia, or insicia, which were made from various minced meats mixed with pepper, or also from different fishes, according to Alexander of Tralles.

units.la: Simile huic edulium tetrapharmacum est Adriano Imperat. carum, quod ex phasiano, sumine, perna, & crustulo compositum fuit- se, narrat Spartanus.
units.tr: Similar to this is the tetrapharmacon dish, which Spartian reports was a favourite of the Emperor Hadrian, composed of pheasant, sow's womb, ham and a crust.

units.la: Qui primò Itria, Tractam, & id genus liba in mensis ponunt, illaudandi sunt: nam cer- tum est eiusmodi panificiorum genera nullo tanda. fermento imbutainfalubria esse, quin & co-quendi apparandique modo. Videmus ple-runque, quod foris est retorridum, intus esse incoctum, ideoque vix conficiuntur, ftoma-cho enim negotium facessunt, crudumque succum ac flatus generant.
units.tr: Those who first put itria, tractae and that kind of pastry on the table are to be blamed. For it is certain that these kinds of bakery, steeped in leaven, are in no way unwholesome, nor is the manner of cooking and preparing them. We commonly see that what is dried out on the outside is undercooked within, and therefore they are barely digested; for they cause trouble for the stomach and produce crude juice and wind.

units.la: Fiunt quoque panificia celebratiffima ex medulla tritici aqua vinoque albo diligen-ter macerata agitataque, deinde ouorum lu-teis pluribus adiectis, sale modico ac faccha-ro: ferramenta autem habent peculiaria, qui hos panes expetunt, non tam alte, neque tam patenter exsculpta, sed tantum ad fauo-rum rudimenta, quæ oleo aut butyro illinun-tur, Germani vocant <bl>Kuchenfen / Eifenku-chen.</bl>
units.tr: Also very celebrated bakery is made from wheat marrow, carefully steeped and stirred in water and white wine, then with several egg yolks added, a little salt and sugar. Those who desire these breads have special moulds, not cut very deep or very openly, but only to the rudiments of honeycombs, which are smeared with oil or butter. The Germans call them Kuchenfen or Eisenkuchen.

units.la: Apud quosdam ex similagine, alios ex polline tritici conflantur opera piftoria, bu-tyro, ouis, lacte, melle aut saccharo fubigen-tes, quidam crocum adiiciunt, gustuque lunt suauissima.
units.tr: Among some, bakery is made from fine flour, among others from wheat pollen, kneaded with butter, eggs, milk, honey or sugar. Some add saffron, and they are most pleasant to taste.

units.la: Alii similam triticeam adiecto melle aut saccharo subigunt, quibus postea cinnamo-mum, piper, aliaque id genus confunduntur. Quidam anisum, fœniculum & cymi-num inspergunt, grati optimique lapo-ris, quibus etiam communis noster pa-nis siligineus salubriter perspergi potest. Plura panificiorum placentarumq; genera exhibent in inclytis vrbibus aulifq; magna-tum pistores dulciarii, cupedinarii, libarii, fcriblitarii, mira subtilitate & elegantia va- ria panificia concinnantes: hinc ferinam o- pera piftoria incrustatam cernimus, hincin-crustatos gallos, capones, pisces, variasque formas, quarum quaedam triangulae, quaedam oblongae sunt, quaedam fphericae, quaedam pudenda muliebria repraesentant, quaedam virilia, adeo degenerárunt mores Chri- ftianorum, vt obscæna & pudenda in cibis hodie delectent, sunt enim quos cunnos saccharatos[?] vocant. Sed longum foretin hif-ce singulis enumerandis tempori inseruire, praesertim cum ad gulae irritamenta pertine-ant luxuriamque, in quaita Christiani pro-fecerunt, vt eorum culinae monstrificarum potius epularum, quam necessariorum stru-cturam[?] doceant.
units.tr: Others knead wheat semolina with honey or sugar added, and afterwards cinnamon, pepper and such things are mixed in. Some sprinkle anise, fennel and cumin, of pleasant and excellent flavour, and our common rye bread can also be wholesomely sprinkled with them. In famous cities and at the courts of great men, confectioners, pastry cooks, makers of sweetmeats and makers of writing-tablet cakes present many kinds of bakery and placentae, preparing various breads with wonderful skill and elegance. Hence we see game encrusted in pastry; hence we see encrusted cocks, capons and fish, and various shapes, some triangular, some oblong, some spherical; some represent female genitals, some male. So far have the morals of Christians degenerated that obscene and shameful things now delight them in food; there are those who call sugared cunts a delicacy. But it would take too long to list these one by one, especially since they serve the incitements of gluttony and the luxury to which Christians have advanced so far that their kitchens teach the construction of monstrous feasts rather than of necessary food.

units.la: Hactenus de placentis. DePultibus,
units.tr: Thus far on cakes. On porridges.

units.la: Vltè[?] non pane longo tempore vixisse Romanos certum & manifestum est, vnde pulti-phagi fuerunt appellati. Ex farina autem, aqua vel lacte, melle, caseo, ovo, vt plurimum cinnantur[?]. Ex diversis vero fiunt feminibus tri-tico, hordeo, siligine, milio, oryza, avena, ozyme. Certum est omnes pultes bene probeq, co- Elas ac praeparatas valenter nutrire, ac firmare Triticeæ corpus: praestant tamen triticeæ, quia enim saepius reliquis iis utuntur, melioris esse habitus deprehenduntur: pizeltant tur, facilius enim coquuntur et conficiuntur, ing, crudos humores non convertuntur. Ex occy- mo avena, milio, oryza confecta pultes putantur cruditates signere, exiccare atque affringere, quod de improba non exacta collatione concepta fero: crassiorem enim consistentiam naeta valide laborantibus. ut sunt baioli, agricolae, mefores, fossores, apprime conuenient, liberaliorem vero vi&tum fa&tantes ac sedentariam vitam agentes, butyro, lattiq, pinguedine, croco vel saccharo eas reddent lautiores, molliores, ac delicatiores, qua etiam ratione salubriores evadent. Apud quosdam in frequentissimo vsu est pultieula ge-nus, quod concinnatur ex pane friabili (siue tri-ticeum fit, siue siliginem, cui tamen ille preferuntur) latte et butyro: lautius evadit, si vino faccha- rogo, adiecto cinnamomi modico, praeparetur: fa- luberrimum hoc edulium est stomachoq, uti- liffimum, quod ipse sapius comperi, licet nulli- rum et opus sit et inuentum.
units.tr: That the Romans lived for a long time on bread not at all is certain and well attested, whence they were called pultiphagi, porridge-eaters. Porridges are usually made from flour with water or milk, and honey, cheese, or egg are added to them. They are made from various grains: wheat, barley, rye, millet, rice, oats, and spelt. It is certain that all porridges, when well cooked and properly prepared, nourish vigorously and strengthen the body. Wheat porridges, however, are considered the best, since they are used more often than the others and are found to be of better quality. They are also easier to cook and digest, and they do not turn into crude humours. Porridges made of spelt, oats, millet, or rice are thought to dispel and dry up indigestions and to bind the bowels; this I take from an improper, unexamined comparison. Their thicker consistency makes them especially suitable for those who labour hard, such as carters, farmers, reapers, and diggers. But for those who live more liberal diets and sedentary lives, they can be made richer, softer, and more delicate with butter, milk fat, saffron, or sugar, and in this way they become more wholesome. Among some people there is a very common kind of porridge, made from crumbly bread (whether of wheat or of rye, though wheat is preferred), milk, and butter. It turns out more luxurious if it is prepared with wine, sugar, and a small amount of cinnamon added. This is a very wholesome dish and most useful for the stomach, as I have often found myself, although it is neither necessary nor an invention of ours.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Leguminibus.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. On Pulses.

units.la: Actenus fuerunt femina Cerealia, & quae ex his conficiuntur, alimenta, fe- quuntur.
units.tr: So far we have dealt with cereals and the foods made from them. Next come pulses and legumes.

units.la: quantur legumina & legumenta, àlegendo dicta, quod videl.non secentur, sed vellen- dolegantur. Horum tractatio jure à fru- mentis proxima est, quia fecundas in vsu ci- bario tenere videntur, & aliquando vicem panis excoctaimplent,inque multiplices ci- bariorum vsus à plebeis conuertuntur. Quin etiam magnatum mensas frequenter exornant, praesertim in papatu tempore je- juniorum. Complura autem leguminum sunt genera, de singulis hic scribere nihil attinet, multo minus de eorundem satione, & vni- uersa cultura, quorundam duntaxat nobis scilicet magis vsitatorum ac familiarium, na- turam & mirabiles vires persequemur, vt intelligatur, quae noxia sint, quae innoxia.
units.tr: Legumes (legumina) and pulse crops (legumenta) are named from legere, to gather, because they are not cut but picked. Their treatment rightly follows that of grains, since they seem to hold second place in diet. When cooked they sometimes take the place of bread, and the common people turn them to many culinary uses. Indeed they often grace the tables of the great, especially in the Papist time of fasts. There are many kinds of pulses. It is pointless to write here about each one, still less about their sowing and general cultivation. We shall trace the nature and remarkable powers of only a few, namely the more commonly used and familiar ones, so that it may be understood which are harmful and which harmless.

units.la: Vbi in transcursu notandum, legumi- na incoctilia, coctilibus deteriora semper esse, propterea quod aegre conficiuntur, ac difficulter mutantur. Salubriora evadunt o- mnia, fi inter coquendum sinapis momentu adijciatur, tuncenim resoluta penitus tabe- fcunt,&ocyffime fatiscunt,alias cacochymia ac flatus parere, continuatus eorum vsus do- cet. Verum coctura hic diligentissima habe- da ratio nimium enim coquendo & ad lucu- lenta flamam, exorbet atq; exhalat, quicquid nutrimentalis humidi in eis continetur, juftu vero coctionis termin non adepta, retinent quicquicquid flatulentum est & crudum, quod inprimis prosperâ valetudine frui cupientes, sedentariamque vitam agentes obserua-bunt.
units.tr: Here it should be noted in passing that pulses eaten uncooked are always worse than cooked ones, because they are digested with difficulty and changed with difficulty. All of them become more wholesome if a little mustard is added during cooking, for then they dissolve thoroughly and break down very quickly. Otherwise, continued use teaches that they produce bad humours and wind. But the cooking must be done with great care. If they are boiled too long and over a fierce flame, they lose and exhale whatever nourishing moisture they contain. If they are not brought to the proper end of cooking, they retain whatever is windy and raw. Those who wish above all to enjoy good health, and who lead a sedentary life, will observe this.

units.la: Ex leguminibus quædam sunt culina-ria, quorum maxime vsus in culina est & ci-bo, quædam medicamentosa, quorum vsus est potissimum in medicina; & ex his quæ-dam medium obtinere locum videntur, ob idq; mixta appellari possunt.
units.tr: Some pulses are culinary, and their main use is in the kitchen as food. Some are medicinal, and their use is chiefly in medicine. Some of these seem to hold a middle place, and for that reason they may be called mixed.

units.la: Culinaria legumina sunt faba phaseo-li, pisa, lentes.
units.tr: The culinary pulses are beans, kidney beans, peas and lentils.

units.la: Medicinalia, semen lini, cannabis, cy-mini, sesami, fœnugræci, papaueris, orobus, lupinus, cicer: hæc licet olim fuerint inter alimenta numerata, hodie tamen in medi-camentorum magis habentur censu.
units.tr: The medicinal ones are linseed, hemp, cumin, sesame, fenugreek, poppy, orobus, lupine and chickpea. Although these were once counted among foods, today they are rather counted among medicines.

units.la: De Fabis.
units.tr: On Beans.

units.la: Naturam leguminum fagaciter disquire-re vitæ plurimum interest. De Fabis sciendum, maximam semper eorum fuisse auctoritatem inter legumina, quippe ex iis tenta-tus panis apud quosdam populos. Dicta faba q. phaga, ἀπὸ τῆς Φαγεῖν [?] a comedendo, quod primum hoc legumine homines sint usi. Diversa autem de fabis inueniuntur eruditorum opiniones. Pythagoras omnino ab illorum esu abstinuisse, eamque vetasse multorum monumentis tradi-
units.tr: It matters greatly for life to inquire carefully into the nature of pulses. Concerning beans, it should be known that their authority has always been greatest among pulses, since among some peoples bread was made from them. The bean is so named from eating [φαγεῖν], because men first used this pulse for food. Scholars' opinions about beans differ widely. Pythagoras is said to have abstained entirely from eating them and to have forbidden it, as many records hand down. He thought that the mind is disturbed by them, the senses dulled, and sleep troubled by tumultuous dreams. He also believed that women who ate them became barren.

units.la: traditum, tum quod mentem eo perturbari, sensus obtundi, somnoq; sopitus, tumultuosa somnia excitari existimarent, tum quod comesta mu-lieres infœcundas redderent. apud Gell. l. 4. c. 11. banc opinionem refellit, affirmans nullo legumine sapius usum Pythagorā quam fabis, quod is cibus & alium [?] subducere, duceret & levigaret. Galen. quoq; meminit, fabas, fi bellè nutriunt, & flatulenta sint, fœcunditatem potius, quam sterilitatem inducere debere. In tanta opinionum diuersitate attenden-dum, quid vero sit similius. Theophrastus l. 5. de causis plantarum c. 21. scribit, fabarum putamina radicibus aut germinibus plantarum novellarum appositā earum vim penitus tollere, quae etiam sententia à Clemente Alexandrino & Apollonio in mirabilibus historiis citata in-tuentur. Qui addunt, domesticas gallinas iisdem putaminibus ingiter vescentes sterilescere. Qua si ita se habent, facile à fabarum esu frequentio-re aliquem deterrere debent. etiam modo ac ratione paratam, atq; conditam, fabam noxiam proclamant, eo quod vim generandi statuit coctura non amittat, quod equidem miror, cum nihil sit tam noxium, quod coquen-di arte ac vi igne non efficiatur innoxium, quin & venenati serpentes ac vipera arte coquendi artificio, condiendi innoxie in cibos vsurpari posse, praeter experimentum testantur leprosi, qui pro potu bibunt vinum, in quo vipera viva fit ex-
units.tr: Gellius (book 4, chapter 11) refutes this opinion, affirming that Pythagoras used no pulse more often than beans, since this food draws off and smooths. Galen too mentions that beans, if they nourish well and are windy, ought to promote fruitfulness rather than sterility. Given such great diversity of opinion, one must consider which view is more probable. Theophrastus (book 5, On the Causes of Plants, chapter 21) writes that bean husks placed at the roots or shoots of young plants wholly destroy their power. Clement of Alexandria and Apollonius, in his Marvellous Histories, cite this view too. They add that domestic hens which constantly eat those husks become sterile. If these things are so, they ought easily to deter someone from frequent eating of beans. Yet some proclaim the bean harmful even when it is prepared and seasoned in this way, because they think cooking does not remove its power to generate wind. I marvel at this. Nothing is so harmful that it cannot be made harmless by the art of cooking and the power of fire. Indeed, venomous serpents and vipers can safely be used as food by the skill of cooking and seasoning, as lepers testify beyond experience. They drink wine in which a live viper has been

units.la: extinƈta, iubenturq, earum carnem ab[?]cifs[?]otas. pi[?]se & cauda ad putrilaginem coctam cum iure conuenienti edere, in[?]culumq, sorbere. Quid? quod gentibus quibusdam peculiare est vesci, serpentibus, quod Nomadas Scythas, facere a- pud Scriptores seperio, est enim illorum regio serpentum fertilissima. Gentem Æthio- pum, cuius regio ad Meroe ad fluvium Hyda- spis porrigitur, scorpionibus & aspidibus vesci, literis proditum est. Sed forsan illis minus vene- nati sunt, vel etiam venenti omnino expertes, ut in quibusdam locis scorpiones. Certum est in- nostris regionibus virus mortiferum terrestres omnes continere, sed mitiores vero esse colubros, aquaticos, qui anguillas cognati sunt. Verum, quis forsan vel voluptatis gratia vesani luxu palatig, gloria proleftatus iis deleftaretur, ante contagiose ac maligne scabiei metu vefcissedem. cogeretur, ut sequentem collionis modum obser- nabit quem à quibusdam, sponsione ac stipula- tione certa pecunia se provocantibus, orta videl. interspsos quastione an collustrá venenum expel- latur, ipse adhibitum vidi.
units.tr: extinguished. They are ordered to eat the flesh of the viper, boiled down to a pulp with a suitable broth, and to sip the broth. What then? It is peculiar to some peoples to eat serpents. Writers report that the Scythian Nomads do so, for their region is most fertile in serpents. It is recorded in writing that the Ethiopian people, whose land stretches to Meroe by the river Hydaspes, eat scorpions and asps. But perhaps these creatures are less poisonous for them, or even wholly free of venom, as scorpions are in certain places. It is certain that in our regions all land creatures carry deadly poison, but water snakes, which are kin to eels, are milder. Perhaps someone, for the sake of pleasure, mad with luxury of the palate and delighting in notoriety, would eat such things. Or, from fear of contagious and malignant scabies, he might be compelled to do so. He would then observe the following method of purging, which I myself saw applied by certain men. They challenged one another by wager and a binding agreement for a sum of money, the question arising among themselves whether the poison is expelled by this purging.

units.la: Coquatur serpens, vel vipera aquâ fontâ- na, abiiciatur ius ex coctione reliquum, verissi- mum enim est, maximam venenti partem in il- lud deponi: affundatur aqua pura recens scenu- do fiat decoction, iterum, vt prius, si abiicien- dum, coquatur tertio vino & aqua, vel si mani- vino tantum, aromatisq, convenientibus, ut cinna-
units.tr: Let a serpent or viper be boiled in spring water. Throw away the broth left from the boiling, for it is most true that the greatest part of the poison is deposited in it. Pour on fresh pure water and make a decoction again as before. If it must be thrown away, let it be boiled a third time in wine and water, or, if you prefer, in wine alone, with suitable aromatics, such as cinnamon,

units.la: cinnamomo, corticibus arantiarum vel citri, ga-ryophyllis, piperibus & similibus ius condiatur esui referuandum. Ferinum multis videbitur vescì serpentibus, cochleis, ranis, testudinibus, a-sinum vero carduis : at in vniuersa fere Italia & Gallia inter praecipuas mensarum delicias reponuntur. In longis obsidionibus vrbium, canes ac feles, mures ac glires, gratum palato obscenium extitisse testantur biftoria. Qui à patrio solo nuquam discesserunt, non finefaftidio ac admiratione etiam, hac legent, tanquam veritatis fidem excedentia.
units.tr: cinnamon, orange or citron peel, cloves, pepper and the like. Let the broth be seasoned and kept for eating. Many will think that only wild peoples eat serpents, snails, frogs, tortoises, and asses eat thistles. Yet in nearly all of Italy and France these are placed among the chief delicacies of the table. Histories testify that during long sieges of cities, dogs and cats, mice and dormice became a pleasing and savoury food. Those who have never left their native soil read these things with no small disgust and wonder, as exceeding the bounds of credibility.

units.la: Ego lectorem relego ad autores, qui de his dubiis rogati certi aliquid affirmabunt, inter quos Athenæum & Plinium studiosiores ac copiosiores reperiet. Sed adrem. Si igitur noxia & venenata coctura & conditura reddunt tur innoxia, efuiq, apta, quid quefo prohibebit, quominus & fabis per coctionem vis generandi flatus, ventremq, distendendi adimatur ? rides tamen & recentes magis commendantur inre escaria, aviditime enim a gula proceri- bus quibusdam in regionibus, praesertim Gallia & Italia, expetuntur. Siccata relinquuntur operariis.
units.tr: I refer the reader to the authors who, when asked about these doubtful matters, affirm something certain. Among them he will find Athenaeus and Pliny more studious and fuller. But to the point. If harmful and poisonous things are made harmless by cooking and seasoning, and fit for eating, what, I ask, will prevent beans from losing their power to generate wind and distend the belly by cooking? You laugh, yet fresh beans are more highly recommended as food, for they are eagerly sought after by gluttons among certain nobles, especially in France and Italy. Dried beans are left to labourers.

units.la: Parantur autem ex iis infcula: quandoq, in sartagine, ex lardo, butyro, aut oleo, adiectà Satureia, apio, thymo, anethi vel cyminifemine friguntur, prius tamen decorticata. Virides post carnes loco bellariorum olim esitas fuisse, Athenaeus & Mercurialis l.4.varia-rum lect.docent: assumebantur quoq; parentan-do. In quibusdam Galliae & Italiae locis molâ parum prius frangantur, deinde delibrantur ac percoquuntur, inq; album quoddam crassamentum formantur ac rediguntur, quod per urbis compita, dieb. quadragesimae venale pro-stat, idq; postea in patinis ex butyro aut oleo len-to igne paratur ad esum, nonq; ingratum est e-dulium.plebi, quas familiariter eo utitur. Ut fit, studiosi literarum ab immodico fabarum esu abstinebunt, praesertim vero pueri, quia gra-vem inde ingeniorum patiuntur iacturam, in otio quoq; degentes, ac ventriculi imbecillitate laborantes ab illarum esu se contineant, inflant. Enim agreq[?], conficiuntur, cuius vei argumentum est, quod frequentius colico dolore; ructi-[?]bus crepitibus, conflictentur, qui Pythagorae praceptis non obtemperant.
units.tr: Sweet dishes are made from them. Sometimes they are fried in a pan with lard, butter or oil, with savory, celery, thyme, dill or cumin seed added, though first shelled. Athenaeus and Mercurialis (Various Readings, book 4) teach that green beans were once eaten after the meat in place of dessert. They were also taken at funeral feasts. In certain places in France and Italy they are first lightly crushed in a mill, then soaked and thoroughly cooked, and formed and reduced to a white paste. This is sold through the city crossroads during Lent and afterwards prepared in pans with butter or oil over a slow fire for eating. It is not an unpleasant food for the common people, who use it as an everyday dish. Accordingly, students of letters should abstain from immoderate eating of beans, especially boys, since they suffer a serious loss of wit from it. Those who live in idleness, and those suffering from a weak stomach, should also keep away from them, since they cause swelling. For they are digested with difficulty. This is shown by the fact that those who do not obey Pythagoras's precepts are more often troubled by colic, belching and wind.

units.la: Hinc trita illa & celebrata de faba pro-verbia, à fabis abstineto: fabas ne comedas: faba alba, hac enim antiquitus in fortibus usa est, cui enim contigisset et permittebatur in convi-vio & ocio agere aliis laborantibus: faba nummus-mus, fabis enim olim ferebantur suffragia, ac denotantur proverbio corrupta suffragia. Sic fabarum arrosor dicebatur, qui in creandis magistratibus vendebat sua suffragia accepta pecunia, quod certe & hodie fieri atq; usuvenire vividemus in proceribus & orbis monarchis creandis: fabulibus denique victitare diceba-tur de homine nimis sordido, qui qui-busvis cibis vilissimis etiam fabarum furfuri-bus & repurgamentis pra nimia parsimonia ve-scitur. Hactenus de fabis, quarum maxi-mam fuisse inter legumina olim autoritatem, expraditus facile est coniicere: unum hic no-tandum venit quod, quae de vulgaribus nostris fabis hic sunt assignata, eadem quoq; dephafeo-lis seu fabis Italicis, quarum species quoq; est Smilax hortensis, sint intelligenda: faba vero AEgyptia nostras longe amplitudine superat, humidioris, est temperatura, radixq; eius lau-te ab incolis cruda atq; decocta adhibetur.
units.tr: Hence the familiar and well-worn proverbs about beans: "Abstain from beans," and "Do not eat beans." Also "white bean," for in antiquity beans were used in drawing lots, and whoever drew the white bean was permitted to take his ease at feasts while others laboured. "Bean money" refers to the fact that votes were once cast with beans, and so corrupt votes are called that by proverb. Thus one who took payment for his vote when magistrates were chosen was called a "bean-nibbler," which is surely still done, and may be seen today in the choosing of nobles and monarchs of the world. Finally, a man who is too mean is said to live on bean-husks, since out of excessive thrift he eats even the bran and refuse of beans. So much about beans, and from this their once very great authority among pulses is easily inferred. One point must be noted here: what has been said of our common beans applies also to the phaseoli or Italian beans, of which the garden smilax is a kind. The Egyptian bean, however, far surpasses ours in size; its nature is moister, and its root is used by the locals both raw and boiled in lye.

units.la: De phafeolis in specie notetur, quod fecun-dum Galenum, Aëtium & Paulum, medium inter alimenta boni maligi, succi obtineant lo-cum, & inter ea quae exiguum corpori praebent, bona & nutrimentum, & quae plurimum, inter ea, quae mala te- flatus gignunt, & quae non gignunt, & inter ea, nent lo- quae facile & difficulter concoquuntur. Colu- mella vero Phafeolum inter legumina maxime grata & in vsu cibario posuit, quod nostri coquu-tur, quibus nunc familiares esse coperunt, miris modis phafeolum coquentes in iure galli-naceo: In cibis crebrius vsurpati melancoliam augent, atrum reddentes sanguinem, unde Ga-leni exacte siccatos atq; repositos tutioris esse vsu-tradidit, & ut pisa vsurpari posse.
units.tr: Concerning phaseoli in particular, it should be noted that according to Galen, Aëtius and Paulus they hold a middle place among foods, both in the quality of their juice, good or bad; among those that give the body little nourishment and those that give much; among those that cause wind and those that do not; and among those that are digested easily and those that are digested with difficulty. Columella, however, counted the phaseolus among the most agreeable pulses and among foods in common use. Our cooks, to whom it has now become familiar, prepare it in wonderful ways, cooking it in chicken broth. Eaten too often, they increase melancholy and make the blood dark, and so Galen taught that they are safer to use when carefully dried and stored, and that they may be used in the same way as peas.

units.la: Innocentiores quoq; in cibis reddunt ut, si cum sinapi aut cari femine edantur, adiecto piperis momento. Semen deniq; generare, venerem remq; stimulare, praesertim si ex lacte bubalo ca[?]- quantur experimentum est. Quidam, ut legu- minum omnium noxas vitent, cepas simul decoquunt, & quidem prudentissime, licet alii aliter sentiant, concalfaciunt enim, pariterq; attenuant, discutiunt simul ac dissipant, quod adeò flatulentum, idq; a coquis & culinis vellem diligenter observari, escarum enim notare noxas cauti & prudentis est.
units.tr: Less harmful too, when eaten with food, provided they are eaten if with mustard or caraway seed, with a pinch of pepper added. Lastly, they generate semen and stimulate lust, especially if they are cooked in buffalo milk; this is established by experience. Some, to avoid all the harm of pulses, cook onions along with them, and very prudently, although others think differently; for onions warm and at the same time thin, disperse and dissipate the wind-producing quality. I would wish this carefully observed by cooks and kitchen-staff, for it is the mark of a cautious and prudent person to note the harms of foods.

units.la: Hactenus de Phaseolis.
units.tr: So far concerning phaseoli.

units.la: De Pisis.
units.tr: On Peas.

units.la: Inter omnia leguminum genera nostrâ memoriâ vix vllum pisis praestantius reperitur atque vsitatius: lautissimas enim mensas ea subire, magnatesque gratissime mandere videmus: quin & nobile foeminarum genus auidissime iis praesertim suilla[?] in- coctis vescitûr ac delectatur, ex lautissima etiam ac magnifica variarum epularum strue[?] ambabus quasi manibus ea praeripiens.
units.tr: Among all kinds of pulses, in our own memory scarcely any is found more excellent or more commonly used than peas. For we see them grace the most lavish tables, and magnates eat them with the greatest pleasure. Indeed the noble sex eagerly eats them, especially when stewed with pork, and takes delight in them, snatching them up with both hands even from the most lavish and magnificent array of various dishes.

units.la: Apud veteres quoq; in gratia fuisse dubium non est, quippe de iis ab antiquis & medicis & rei rusticae scriptoribus traditum est. Hodie fabis longe praeferuntur. Saturandi enim alendi, nutriendiq; vi praepollent. lent , nec perinde ac fabæ flatus gignunt, quod præter experientiam ipse Galenus pi-stribuit[?], licet Hippocrates lib.2.de rat. vict. in morbis acut. fabam minus inflare asserat, quod tamen contrà experientiam dictum videtur. Ratio Hippocratis videtur esse hæc, quod nimirum fabæ facilius descen- dant & celerius, ob substantiam earum gra- uem & densam, unde concludit, ob celerem illum descensum minus inflare. Galenus contra censet pisa minus inflare, seriusque peraluum excerni, ventremque permeare quam fabas, ob leuem & fungosam illorum substantiam,quà fit ut pigre descendant, me- liusque nutriant quam ipsæ fabæ. Hæc Ga- leni sententia confirmatur sequente Syllo- gismo.
units.tr: That peas were also in favour with the ancients there is no doubt, for they were recorded by ancient physicians and writers on agriculture. Today they are preferred far above beans, for they have great power to satisfy, feed and nourish. Nor do they cause wind to the same degree as beans, as Galen himself points out, beyond what experience shows. Hippocrates, in book 2 of On Regimen in Acute Diseases, asserts that beans inflate less, which, however, seems to be said against experience. Hippocrates' reasoning appears to be this: beans descend more easily and quickly on account of their heavy and dense substance, and he concludes that because of this rapid descent they inflate less. Galen, on the contrary, judges that peas inflate less, and that they pass through the bowels more slowly and are evacuated later than beans, on account of their light and spongy substance; so they descend sluggishly and nourish better than beans themselves. This opinion of Galen is confirmed by the following syllogism.

units.la: Quod celeriter per ventrem & intestinum dilabitur,id minus nutrit,requiritur enim diuturnior cibi commoratio in intestinis,ne facilis transitus causam præbeat voracitati, venisq; mesaraicis necessarius succus inter- cipiatur[?]: fabæ celerius per ventrem descen- dunt ob gravitatem & densitatem, Ergo mi- nus nutriunt, & qa vix aut raro & fere nunq vigita[?] sunt expeditæ & lubricæ, & ab infar- stib[?]: libere, ut cib. cū impetu possit dilabi & ꝑmeare, cōsequēs est, fabas, cū transitu phi- bētur, plusq; iusto detinētur crassorū humo- rū colluvié, ꝑcreare flatuumq; copiā maiorem, quam vel unquam ulla pisa, quæ ob substantiam raram & leuem, viis etiam im-peditis & obstructis, penetrando possunt permeare. An vero quod celeriter defcen-dit, inque intestinis non diu commoratur, possit in transitu flatus excitare ac procreare, quæsitum est utile ac discussu dignum, cum potius contrarium quis verum dixerit, vide-licet ex diuturniore cibi in ventre mora fla-tus excitari.
units.tr: What passes quickly through the belly and intestine nourishes less, for a longer stay of food in the intestines is required, lest easy passage give occasion for voracity, and the nutritive juice be intercepted for the mesaraic veins. Beans descend more quickly through the belly on account of their heaviness and density; therefore they nourish less. And since they are seldom or almost never smooth and slippery, and cannot pass freely from the intestines so that the food slides and passes through with force, it follows that when beans are impeded in their passage they are held back longer than is right by a gathering of thick humours, and they create a greater quantity of wind than any pea, which, because of its thin and light substance, can penetrate and pass through even impeded and obstructed passages. Whether what descends quickly and does not stay long in the intestines can excite and produce wind in its passage is a useful question and worth discussing, since one might rather say the opposite is true, namely that wind is excited by a longer stay of food in the belly.

units.la: Hanc quæstionem enodandi occasio-nem dabit tractatus de potu & inprimis ce-reuisia. Vide cap. de potulentis. Porro o-mnia juscula & brodia ex pisis commen-dantur : multipliciter vero & varijs modis à coquis præparantur.
units.tr: The occasion for unravelling this question will be given by the treatise on drink, and especially on beer; see the chapter on drinks. Moreover, all broths and soups made from peas are commended, and cooks prepare them in many ways and by various methods.

units.la: Spina suis sale condita pisis decocta suauis est : grata etiam palato est Lucanica cum lardo, gratissimum si pani in scu[?]ta te-nuiter dissecto, butyroque torrefacto, jus-culum pisorum affundatur, ut-que salubrius e-uadat[?] lautiusque, crocus sufficiente quanti-tate cum cymini vel cari femine & simili-bus, adiiciendus est, habereque insignem cor-roborandi ac nutriendi vim, ex grato odore, sapore, & colore, odorem conciliat crocus sicut & colorem, saporem panis butyro to-stus & cyminum, quod etiam flatuum discu-tiendorum gratiâ adjectum est. Viridia cum siliginis costa maximam in mensis & aulis magnatum obtinent[?] autoritatem: defidera- tiffima funt,fi cum pullaftris coquantur, aut plateffis. Id veroin infantia fieri oporter, nam vbi jam adoleuerint,duriora euadunt& ingratiora. Gratiffimi deniq; faporis ac odo- ris funt, falubritatiq; maxime conducunt,fi cum radice petrofelini,mace,rofmarino,thy- mo,aut faluia coquantur : thecis auté fuis & valuulis fint fpoliata fic enim multipliciter præparari & condiri poffunt. Ridendi igitur potius funt quam refutandi, qui pifa conco- &tu difficilia effe fcribunt,craffumq; fuccum parere , eumq; flatulentum contendunt,de adultis & durioribus , rutilis ac rubentibus, eximiæq; amplitudinis , inq; plenum perco- &tisid verum effe fcitur ratione & experi- entiâ, in plenum enim percocta &ad perfe- &tum maturitatis terminum perducta,admi- niculis item vel palis non fulta deteriora ea euadere minufque durare conftat , eo quod hac ratione foli terræq; humorem attrahant imbibantq;. A gurgulionibus (à quibus ma¢[?] xime infeftantur) arrofa cibis abdicanda funt,licet fationi fic cotrofa idonea effe agri- colationis periti affirmant , quod mirum eft.
units.tr: Bacon seasoned with salt and boiled with peas is pleasant, and Lucanica sausage with lard is agreeable to the palate. Most pleasing of all is pea broth poured over bread cut thinly into slices and toasted in butter, which goes down more wholesomely and more elegantly; saffron, in sufficient quantity, should be added, along with cumin or caraway seed and the like, and this gives the dish a remarkable power to strengthen and nourish, through its pleasant smell, taste and colour. Saffron supplies the smell and the colour, the buttered toast and the cumin supply the taste, and cumin is added also for the sake of dispersing wind. Green peas cooked with the pod of rye hold the greatest authority at the tables and courts of magnates. They are most desirable if cooked with young fowl or with plaice. This must be done in the early stage, for when they have grown older they become harder and less pleasant. Finally, they are most pleasing in taste and smell, and most conducive to health, if cooked with root of parsley, mace, rosemary, thyme or sage; but they must be stripped of their pods and shells, for in this way they can be prepared and seasoned in many ways. Those therefore who write that peas are difficult to digest, and produce thick and windy juice, are rather to be laughed at than refuted. This is true of mature and harder peas, reddish and ruddy, of very large size, and of those thoroughly cooked. It is known from reason and experience that peas which have been fully cooked and brought to the full term of ripeness become worse and last less well if they are not supported by props or stakes, because in this way they draw in and soak up the moisture of the soil. Peas that are gnawed by weevils (by which they are especially infested) must be rejected as food, although skilled farmers affirm that such peas are fit for sowing, which is strange.

units.la: Quodigitur Auicenna lib. 2. capite de eo quod comeditur ac bibitur,nulla legumi- na , quatenus cibi rationem fubeunt, fanis conducere fcribit,& Galenus lib.4. de victu morb.acut.legumina vniuersa,ceu suam sin- gula malignitatem habentia,à consortio bo- norum ciborum sejungit, nonabsolute & ὡς sed, κατὰ accipiendum est, de adul- tioribus enim & durioribus, crudeque in- gestis ac comestis eos locutos esse mani- festum est, cum omnibus fructibus & legu- minibus, quæ cruda viridiaque comedun- tur, hoc commune fit, vt alimentum præ- stent humidius,superfluitatibusq; abundans, vnde cruditates &flatus generari necesse est. Manifesto exemplo sunt faba ipsa & pisa cruda & viridia commesta, persica quoque, pruna, pepones, cucumeres, de quibus sin- gulis vide suo loco.
units.tr: Avicenna, in book 2, in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk, writes that no pulses, insofar as they serve as food, are good for healthy people; and Galen, in book 4 of On the Diet in Acute Diseases, separates all pulses, as each having its own malignity, from the company of good foods. But this must be understood not absolutely [ὡς] but in a particular sense [κατά]: it is clear that they spoke of the more mature and harder pulses, eaten raw and crude. For it is common to all fruits and pulses that are eaten raw and green that they provide a more watery nourishment, abundant in superfluities, whence crudities and wind must necessarily be generated. Clear examples are beans and peas eaten raw and green, and also peaches, plums, melons and cucumbers, each of which is to be considered in its own place.

units.la: De Lentibus.
units.tr: On Lentils.

units.la: Entes philosophi olim in cibo maxime placuisse,& apud Græcos magno in pretio fuisse, passim ex antiquis literarum mo- nimentis confiat. Apud Atheneum Zenonem lentes coxisse inuenitur, vnde stoicorum dogma erat, (teste Athenæo l. 4.) Sapientem omnia agere, & lentem diligenter condire, persuasum enim sibi habebant vescentibus iis æquanimitatem fieri, quam opinionem, nec probo, nec im- probo, naturæ enim huius leguminis sagacitas in- suisse veritatem autoritati præferet.
units.tr: That philosophers of old were especially fond of this food, and that it was highly prized among the Greeks, is clear from many ancient literary records. In Athenaeus we find that Zeno the Stoic cooked lentils. Hence it was a dogma of the Stoics (as Athenaeus reports, book 4) that the wise man does everything and seasons his lentils carefully, for they were persuaded that equanimity came to those who ate them. I neither approve nor reject this opinion, since the sagacity of this pulse's nature will, if anything, prefer its own truth to authority.

units.la: Est autem lens leguminum omnium fere minimum, sed fertilissimum, teste Theophrasto
units.tr: Lentils are almost the smallest of all pulses, but the most productive, according to Theophrastus.

units.la: lib.9.cap.3. Cotlupertinax est, ac inuenias, quae non mollescant nisi aqua coelesti cottae, cuius rei rationem reddit Theophraftus libr.9.c.9. affir-mans fabam & lentem maxime cotlu difficiles, idq; fieri coeli conditione, quae in his duobus leguminibus maiorem mutationem pariat. Hanenus Theophraftus. Unde etiam rarius apud nos in mensas magnatum veniunt, frequentiori enim earum esu atram bilem, & ex hac peruicaciores morbos, ut Cancrum, Lepram, Scorbutum, generari existimatur, crassa enim & arida alimenta humori atrabiliario Quænā[?] procreando sunt aptissima: oculorum quoq; acie alimenta natura siccis hebetare, humentioribus vero vi-atram bi-lem tueri compertum habetur, unde utilissima lem gi-gnant? putantur ut, qui cachexia confli&antur, inutiles. Ves vero ariditate & qualore laborantib. Aquâ Lentium cotta, in fulmina, illud sale aut ga o conditum contra-bauftumq, aluum haud dubie soluet, gratiores riz vires concoctuq, faciliores euadent fi pulegium, thy-diligen-mum vel satureiam adieceris. Bifcotta & terobfer percutta fi comedantur aluum sistunt, ventri-uandae.
units.tr: Book 9, chapter 3. They are very stubborn to cook, and you will find that they do not soften unless boiled in rainwater. Theophrastus gives the reason in book 9, chapter 9, affirming that beans and lentils are the hardest of all to cook, and that this comes from the condition of the sky, which causes the greatest change in these two pulses. So far Theophrastus. Hence they also come less often to the tables of the great among us, for by frequent eating of them black bile is thought to be generated, and from this more stubborn diseases such as cancer, leprosy and scurvy. For thick and dry foods are most apt for producing the melancholy humour. It is also known that dry foods dull the sharpness of the eyes, while moister foods preserve it. Hence they are thought most useful for those who labour with dryness and heat, but useless for those who struggle with cachexia. Lentils boiled in water, seasoned with salt or garum, certainly loosen the bowels, counteract the heat, and become more pleasant to the taste and easier to digest if you add pennyroyal, thyme or savory. Twice-boiled and lightly pounded, if eaten, they stop the bowels and strengthen the stomach admirably when drenched in vinegar.

units.la: culumq, egregie corroborant aceto perfuso.Opti-mae[?] sint qua facililime coquuntur, maxime[?] aq[?] sorbent: cum carnibus suillis sale conditus cotta stomacho gratiores sunt, licet crassos humores augeant: peculiare enim malum salis carnibus est[?] quamvis melancolicum gignere, prafertim in autumno, hieme enim eduntur tutius. Optima[?] nasci circa oppidum Pelusium, vnde les Pelufiaca. dicta videtur, Inq. Ægypto maximeq;, Ale-xandria peculiarem eius fuisse vsum certissimi. Autores tradunt, vnde non mirandum si elephas morbus in Ægypto fuerit vulgatissimus. Heraclidi Tarentino edulium ex beta lentibus dicebatur [illegible, ~8 letters], quem ci- [?]. Bumtum[?] bene, tum male valentibus exhibebat, constatq; expugnantibus naturis, beta enim mi-nus, lens autem magis subducitur, unde e[?]mentum, quod ex bis in corpus distribuitur, tri-q;, naturam referre necesse est. Panis denig; ex lentibus rarissime aut nunquam confectus invenitur.
units.tr: The best are those that are most easily cooked and soak up the most liquid. Lentils boiled with salted pork are more pleasing to the stomach, although they increase thick humours; for salt has a particular harm when combined with meats, even though it generates melancholy, especially in autumn. They are eaten more safely in winter. The best lentils grow around the town of Pelusium, whence they seem to be called Pelusiac, and especially in Egypt, where their use was most certainly peculiar, and at Alexandria. Authors relate this, so it is no wonder that elephantiasis was most common in Egypt. A dish of beet and lentils was called [illegible] by Heraclides of Tarentum, which he gave to both the healthy and the sick. It is agreed that beet is less absorbed by the body and lentils are more so, so the nourishment that is distributed through the body from these must necessarily reflect their nature. Finally, bread made from lentils is very rarely or never found.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt culinaria legumina, se-quuntur medicinalia: (De vicia enim, eruo, [?] similibus hic multum dissere, opera pre-tium non est, cum inter pecudum pabula magis enumerentur, quam alimenta hominum, ac non nisi annona e[?]ftuante[?] fame urgente me-
units.tr: So much for the culinary pulses; the medicinal ones follow. (For to discuss vetches, bitter vetch and similar plants at length here is not worth the trouble, since they are counted among animal fodder rather than human food, and are admitted into human diet only when grain is scarce and famine presses.) We leave these to the druggists of physicians, since they certainly have no fixed place at the tables of the more refined.

units.la: liorum q; penuria in hominum cibatum admit-tantur) quae Medicorum [?] pharma-copolis committimus, in humaniorum enim [?] nitidioris vita hominum mensis nullum ha-benus, [?]tenus obtinuisse locum certum est, quare abdi-canda sunt.
units.tr: For in the tables of people of more polished life they have no place; how far they have held a fixed place is certain, and so they are to be rejected.

units.la: Lupinos protogeni pi-ctori comedendos re-linquimus. Cicer sen pi(s)um rubeum raro epipa-rasmen[?]subit, in medicina autem [?] lupi-num, [?] cicer praeclaros habere vsu comper-tum est. Semine (cannabino antiquitatem olim vice bel-lariorum & tragematum vsam constat, quas tamen delitias nostrum seculum penitus ignorat, nisi in annonæ difficultatibus, vt in retrodi-ctis prænmonitum est, vti eo cogamur. Idem iudicium esto de semine lini, sfœnugræci, &c.
units.tr: We leave lupins to be eaten by the painter Protogenes. Chickpea or red pea rarely makes its way into the diet as a relish, but in medicine both lupin and chickpea have been found to have excellent uses. Hemp seed was once used, as is known, in place of bread-cakes and sweetmeats, delicacies which our age entirely ignores, unless in times of scarcity of grain, when we are forced to use it, as was noted above. The same judgment is to be made concerning linseed, fenugreek, and so on.

units.la: CAP. IX. De alimentis, quæ sumuntur ex radicibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. Foods that are taken from roots.

units.la: Hucusq; de leguminibus, sequuntur radices.
units.tr: So far on pulses; the roots follow.

units.la: Maximè iucundas ac vitæ mortalium salutares cibos ex hortis peti; nemini non est notum : ideoque vbique terrarum hortorum cultus nostra ætate celeberrimus habetur, quin &apud antiquos auctore Plinio, in magno honore fuerunt hortí, damnabat enim antiqua frugalitas pulmentaria, quæ egerent alio pulmentario. Hodiè Magnates & Principes quidam herbis cognoscendis non modò impensè dant operâ, verum etiam nullis sumtibus parcunt, nullisq; impensis, quò horti variarum arborum plantarumque famâ percelebres extruantur.
units.tr: That the most pleasant foods, and those most healthful for human life, come from gardens is known to everyone. For this reason the cultivation of gardens is now most celebrated everywhere in the world. Nor was it otherwise among the ancients: according to Pliny, gardens were held in great honour, since the old frugality condemned side dishes that needed another side dish to go with them. Today certain magnates and princes not only devote great labour to the study of herbs, but also spare no expense and no outlay in laying out gardens made famous by their variety of trees and plants.

units.la: Ex radicibus præcipuam laudem obtinét, rapa, napus, pastinaca, petroselinum, Q_s rapharaphanus maior & minor, caepa, allium, porrum.
units.tr: Among roots, the chief praise goes to the turnip, the rape, the parsnip, parsley, the radish (greater and lesser), the onion, garlic and the leek.

units.la: De rapis.
units.tr: On turnips.

units.la: Inter Romanos Plinius rapis tantam tribuit autoritatem, vt à frumento protinus, aut certè faba de iis dixisse (inquit) conuenit. Et certè gentium multarum opes sunt, inque cibis commendantur plurimis modis, omnibus animalibus non in nouissimis: quapropter pluribus commoditates raporum hic commemorare operæ pretium esse non puto, vt quæ vulgò notissimæ sint. Crescunt autem quibusdam in locis amplitudine mi-rabili, Plinius lib.13.cap.18. se vidisse testatur 40. libras excedentia, id quod credibile est, cum & apud nos ingentis amplitudinis inveniantur. Quædam in latitudinem finguntur, & amplitudinem rotunditatemque maxima glomerantur, idque rariore fatu, densiore enim masculescunt, hoc est, in oblongam ex-crescunt figuram. Cum lacte cocta palato gratissima sunt, ac bene nutriunt satiantque. Cum verveccina percocta nutriunt, multisque gentibus desideratissimus cibus sunt, magnatum etiam mensas exornans. Venerem languentem stimulant, visumque clarificant: caut[?] brodium & iusculum eorum modice croca-
units.tr: Among the Romans, Pliny gave turnips such authority that he said people agreed they came straight after grain, or at least after beans. Certainly many peoples are rich in them, and they are recommended in many ways in foods, and not least to all animals. For this reason I do not think it worth the effort to recount here the many advantages of turnips, since they are very widely known. They grow in some places to a remarkable size; Pliny, in book 13, chapter 18, says he saw some weighing more than forty pounds, which is believable, since in our own country turnips of huge size are also found. Some are shaped broad and round and are gathered into very large bulbs; these are less common, since the denser ones become firmer and grow into an elongated shape. Cooked with milk they are very pleasant to the palate and nourish and satisfy well. Boiled with mutton they nourish, and they are a most desired food for many peoples, adorning even the tables of the great. They stimulate faded desire and clear the sight. I have learned by experience that a broth and soup of them, moderately saffroned, is remarkably good for a cough. It is established that they generate wind and in turn expel it.

units.la: crocatum tussi eximie conferre experimen- to didici, Flatus generare eofdemque vi- ciffim expellere constat.
units.tr: I have learned by experience that a broth or soup made of these, lightly saffroned, is remarkably good for a cough. They are known both to generate wind and in turn to expel it.

units.la: Cruda noxia sunt cumprimis edacibus pueris, ideoque ab iis abítinendum. Per- cocta manducantur vtilius. Quidam cine- recalido torrent vel carbonibus, tosta per- mixto butyro & modico sale, salubriter efitantur.
units.tr: Raw ones are harmful, especially to greedy boys, so they should be avoided. Cooked ones are eaten with more benefit. Some roast them in hot ashes or on coals, then eat them tossed with butter and a little salt, which is wholesome.

units.la: His victitaffe Curium Imper. Roma- numhiftoriæteftantur, & inuentum à Le- gatis Samnitum aurum offerentibus rapum torrentem in foco. Apud Septentrionis gentes vidi ex iis cum lacte percoctis & butyro, concinnari pulticulam suaui ffimi & saluberrimi saporis, procerum mensis commendatissimam, quà sæpè palatum e- gregie expleui. Pruinis & frigore rapa ali, dulcioraque & grandiora fieri constat : ne autem tabescant & putrescant, scrobes & foueas fodiunt, quibus hieme appropin- quante conduntur & feruanturincorrupta: ad restim enim quædam gentes rem rediisse clamant, vbi rapa gelu fuerint exusta, aut alia iniuria aliqua cœli foliue per- ierint.
units.tr: Roman histories testify that Curius, the Roman emperor, lived on this diet, and that when the envoys of the Samnites came to offer him gold, they found him roasting a turnip on the hearth. Among the peoples of the North I have seen them cooked with milk and butter into a porridge of most pleasant and healthful flavour, highly recommended at the tables of the nobility, and I have often filled my palate with it to great satisfaction. Turnips are nourished by frost and cold, and it is said they become sweeter and larger. So that they do not rot and decay, people dig pits and trenches, and when winter draws near they are stored there and kept uncorrupted. Some peoples insist that matters come down to a pinch when frost has scorched the turnips or some other harm from the sky or the leaves has destroyed them.

units.la: Ad raporum quoque catalogum refertur napus & rapunculus seu rapum fylueftre.
units.tr: The napus and the rapunculus, or wild turnip, also belong to the catalogue of turnips.

units.la: Napus radices habet prælongas, tres fere palmos in terram descendentes crassitudine staphylino luteo pares, in cibo propter infi-gnem dulcedinem gratissimæ, suaues ac falu-bres, præsertim cum carnibus præcipuè fuil-lis & veruecina coctæ, has enim mita suaui-tate condiunt: fi quis vero flatuum prouen-tum ex crudo illarum succo pertimescat, is ex sinapi coctas edat, hoc enim modo flatus dissipabuntur. Sabulo in subterraneis cellis incorruptæ feruantur, durant enim sic con-ditæ in multos menses. Has eduntex butyro in Papatu, diebus quibus carne vesci vetitum est, præsertim ieiunio illo quadragenario.
units.tr: The napus has very long roots, going about three palms down into the earth, as thick as a yellow grape. As food it is most pleasant, on account of its remarkable sweetness, and it is sweet and wholesome, especially when cooked with meat, chiefly with fowl and mutton, for these it seasons with its mild sweetness. If anyone fears the generation of wind from its raw juice, let him eat it cooked with mustard, for in this way the winds will be dispersed. Buried in sand in underground cellars it is kept uncorrupted, for so preserved it lasts for many months. They eat these fried in butter in the Papacy on the days when it is forbidden to eat meat, especially in that forty-day fast.

units.la: Rapunculus rapum exiguum seu mini-mum napi genus, estur vere in acetariis. Sed tenendum vsum huius ante primum ver esse noxium, frigore scilicet terræ meatibus ad-huc occlusis, foliisq; nondum apparenter e-rumpentibus: vere quoque tepido & humi-do, certum eftefum huius minus salutarem esse. Videant igitur, qui liberalius eo vtuntur. Cocta radix cum planta gustui in acetariis magis arridet, minusque est noxia, quamque in terræ visceribus malignitatem contraxit, eam coctionis vi amittit.
units.tr: The rapunculus, a small turnip or the smallest kind of napus, is eaten in spring in salads. But it must be borne in mind that using it before the first spring is harmful, namely because the ground is still cold, its pores still closed, and the leaves not yet sprouting. Also, in a warm and damp spring, the known effect is that it is less wholesome. Let those who use it freely take note. The cooked root, with the plant, pleases the taste better in salads and is less harmful, since by the force of cooking it loses the malignancy it contracted in the bowels of the earth.

units.la: Rapunculi
units.tr: Rapunculi ## On the Parsnip.

units.la: De Pastinaca.

Pastinacæ quoq; sunt in hortis & cibi bonos est, feritur enim studiosissimè. Candida & lutea in summa apud gentes quasdam sunt autoritatis cum carnib. decoctæ salubriores sunt ac suaviores, habent enim aromaticum quid, stomacho, haud inutiles sunt, urinam quoque promovent, veneremq; stimulant. In miram autem crescunt amplitudinem, præsertim si folia rescentur, durantq; in veris tempora in sua terra, unde insignes usus præbent circa id tempus diui-tibus & pauperibus solennitatis quadragesi-mali.
units.tr: Parsnips are also grown in gardens, and they are good food, for they are cultivated with the greatest care. The white and yellow kinds are held in highest esteem among certain peoples; boiled with meat they are more wholesome and pleasanter, for they have something aromatic, and they are not useless to the stomach. They also promote urine and stimulate lust. They grow to a remarkable size, especially if the leaves are cut off, and they last into spring in their own ground, whence about that time they provide notable food for rich and poor alike during the solemnity of Lent.

units.la: Huc pertinent Carota, Satiua, Pastinacæ spe-cies, culinis notissimæ, Germani vocant, rothe vnd gelbe Rüben / magni apud nos usus & gratiæ in cibu, urinæ Veneriq, stimulandæ accom-modatæ. Rubram coquunt aquam, tesselatim, incifam in acetariis cum pipere, aniso vel fœni-culo mandunt. Albain cibos frequentius assu-mitur, verum colla in iure aliquo, cruda enim e-stata inflat, ac concoctu difficilis est, unde proba-renon possum, quod quidam hæc incommoda et-iam concoctæ attribuant. Non protinus enim damnandum, aut cibis abdicandum est, à quo quis vel abhorret naturâ, vel errore quodam externo.
units.tr: To this group belong the carrot, the cultivated species of parsnip, very well known in kitchens, which the Germans call red and yellow turnips. Among us they are of great use and favour as food, and suited to stimulating urine and lust. The red kind they cook in water, cut into slices, and eat in salads with pepper, anise or fennel. The white kind is taken more often as food, but it should be cooked in some broth, for raw it causes inflation and is hard to digest. Hence I cannot agree that some attribute these inconveniences even to the cooked root. One must not straightway condemn a food or renounce it because someone is averse to it by nature or from some external error.

units.la: De petroselino, seu apio hortensi.
units.tr: On parsley, or garden celery.

units.la: Vix reperias in Germania nostra culi-nam, in qua herba & radix huius, suum inter praecipua olera locum non occupet. Quid? quod apud Romanos & Græcos in maxima autoritate fuisse propter renum calculos & vrinæ difficultatem, ad quæ maximè radix & semen expetuntur, graues autores literis mandarunt. Apitius nepotum gurges, vt eum appellat Plinius, & Platina magno in honore petroselinum sem-per habuerunt. Carnes elixas & assas mirè commendat praecipuè veruecinas, quin etiam pisces atque ouain sartagine tosta: ægris pariter atque bene valentibus datur: vina reddit gratiora & suauiora, sicut & aquas in coctum. Stomacho & suaue & gratum esse testatur Galenus. Lactucis quoque in aceta-riis miscetur, vt earum frigus contemperet. Peculiaris quoq; gratia crudo est, fœtidum e-nim illum halitum è frustis esculentis vinum redolentibus, oreque vino nimium fœtente exhalantem retundit atque hebetat. Graues autores, inter quos est Plinius, literis mandarunt frequentiorem eius vsum Comitiales & epilepticos facere, visusque claritati obesse, quod si verum est, mirari subit cur in cibis tam frequens eius fit vsus. Verum de nostro petroselino seu apio hortensi id minimè accipiendum esse puto, sed de syluęstri & aquatico, licet Manardus lib. 18.
