Epist. 1. dubitet, quodnam genus sit, quod in Comitiali morbo damnatur. Alexander damnat Smyrnium, Plinius vero indiscriminatim alimenti ratione, apium omne, quod non probatur, siquidem nemini non constat, nostri petroselini radices & folia in cibis vtilissima esse peculiarem quę obtinere gratiam, id quod Galenus expressè testatur, cum scribit, stomacho & suaue & gratum esse: Veteres namque id ex aceto & sale & garo mandebant, qui tamen mos an quibusdam adhuc gentibus sit peculiaris, an vero exaruerit, affirmare verè non ausim. Hactenus Petroselinum.
units.tr: You will hardly find a kitchen in our Germany in which the herb and root of this plant do not hold a place among the chief vegetables. Indeed, serious authors have written that it was held in the greatest esteem among the Romans and Greeks because of kidney stones and difficulty in passing urine, for which the root and seed are chiefly sought. Apicius, the glutton of the nephews, as Pliny calls him, and Platina always held parsley in great honour. It is especially commended with boiled and roast meats, above all mutton, and also with fish and with eggs fried in a pan. It is given alike to the sick and to the healthy. It makes wines more pleasant and agreeable, as it does waters used for cooking. Galen testifies that it is both soothing and agreeable to the stomach. It is also mixed with lettuces in salads, to temper their coldness. It is especially pleasing when raw, for it dulls and overcomes the foul breath that rises from food scented with wine and from a mouth that smells too strongly of wine. Serious authors, among them Pliny, have written that frequent use of it brings on epilepsy and the falling sickness and harms the clarity of sight. If this is true, one wonders why it is used so often in food. But I think this should not be taken of our common parsley, or garden celery, but of the wild and water kinds, although Manardus, book 18, letter 1, doubts what kind it is that is condemned in the falling sickness. Alexander condemns smyrnium, and Pliny, in regard to food, condemns indiscriminately every kind of celery that is not approved. For it is known to everyone that the roots and leaves of our parsley are most useful in foods and enjoy a special favour, as Galen clearly testifies when he writes that it is both soothing and agreeable to the stomach. For the ancients chewed it with vinegar, salt and fish sauce. I would not dare to affirm truly whether this custom is peculiar to some peoples even now, or whether it has died out. So much for parsley.

units.la: De raphano vtroq.
units.tr: On both kinds of radish.

units.la: Omnibus fere orbis gentibus admodum placere in cibatu raphanum minorem, (German. Rettich) seu radiculam, nemo est, opinor, qui ignoret. Plebs infima & lautiores mensæ mirè eo delectantur. Quidam eo solo ex sale cum pane sese sustentant. Eligendus autem est qui modicè dulcescit, mitiorque est,nec adeò vehemente acrimonia linguam vel-licat,quam costione amitti expertum est:In pro- band? autem raphano spectandum maxime est, si frangenti s: contumax, fragilis namq; facile commendatur. Prelongus napis similis,dulcior & mitior est. Verum quastionem,an radiculam ante vel post alios cibos mandere conuenientius sit & utilius, opera pretium est hic discutere, tum quia graues autores hic dissentiunt,tum quod in omnibus fere liberalioribus conuiuiis à dictis eam proponi animadverti. Galenus eum vult alios cibos praecedere, atq; ex garo,cui modicum aceti permixtum sit, edendum praecipit,alui scilicet eiiciende gratia, facilius enim sic aliquam subire exireq; dicit, ac citius & minori cum incommodo do extima ventriculi parte, in qua costio praes-pue cosficitur,adintestina transire,hacq; ratione ori ventriculi minus nocumentiu inferre: debet n.q alius facile subeunt,q corruptibilia sunt, & humida omnia in principio sese dari, teste Gal.
units.tr: Almost all the peoples of the world, I suppose, are very fond of the smaller radish (German Rettich), or radicula, in their diet; nobody is ignorant of this. The lowest common people and the more refined tables delight in it greatly. Some sustain themselves on it alone, with salt and bread. One should choose the kind that is slightly sweet and milder, and that does not pluck at the tongue with too violent a sharpness, which is known to be lost by cooking. In testing a radish, one must above all look to whether it is firm when broken, for a stubborn radish is brittle and easily spoils. The very long kind, like a turnip, is sweeter and milder. But the question whether it is more fitting and more useful to eat the little radish before or after other foods is worth discussing here, both because serious authors disagree on it and because I have noticed that it is offered at almost all the more generous banquets, at the beginning. Galen wishes it to precede other foods, and he directs that it be eaten with salt to which a little vinegar has been added, namely to help the bowels move; for thus, he says, it passes through more easily and quickly, and with less discomfort passes from the outer part of the stomach, where the chyle is chiefly made, into the intestines, and in this way does less harm to the stomach's mouth. For things that are easily corrupted and all moist things, he says, are given first, as Galen testifies in the first and third books of On the Regimen in Acute Diseases, especially where the aim is to soften the bowels, lest they be given after the food and corrupt it. But things that strengthen the belly and stomach, such as sour apples, or pears moderately roasted in hot ashes, are to be offered immediately after the food. So far Galen. Others disagree; they assert the contrary, namely that the radish, because it is opposed to the stomach, should be given after food. For in this way, they say, it helps digestion, whereas if taken before, it hinders and delays the chyle, and draws in raw humours, which afterwards injure and irritate the mouth of the stomach. Paulus Aegineta, Aetius, and several others confirm Galen's opinion; Dioscorides has the Trallians as his defenders. But Galen marvels at those physicians who swallow raw radish after dinner to help digestion.

units.la: 1. & 3.l.de ratione vict.in morb.acut. praeser-tim ubi intentio est mollire aluum ne sic cibo den-tur,eum corrumpant. Quae autem ventrem sto-machum, corroborant,ut poma acerba,aut py-ra cineribus calidis mediocriter astata, statim cibo sunt offerenda. Hac Galenus. Discordant contrarium asserit videlicet radiculam,quia sto-macho aduersetur, à cibo dandam esse, hoc enim modo digestionem eam adiuuare,contrario vero costionem impedire & suspendere, crudosq, bu-<bl>mores</bl> mores attrahere, qui postea orificium ventriculi laedant atq; lacessant. Galeni sententiam confirmant Paulus Ægineta, Ætius, & nonnulli alii, Dioscorides patrocinantem habet Tralliani. Sed Galenus medicos illos miratur, qui radiculam crudam à cœna ad coctionem iuuandam ingerunt.
units.tr: Simon Seth, in his chapter on the radish, briefly settles this controversy. For he holds that if the stomach is easily loosened and not disposed to swelling or the generation of wind, the radish is more conveniently given before food; but if the contrary is the case, after food. From these points it is gathered that a moist stomach is windy, because winds are generated from moist matter, not dry; for heat, as the efficient cause, acts on food and humours, but feebly, that is, in relation to the matter itself, which it partly thins and dissolves but does not perfectly digest. Therefore those who are hard in the bowels and have a windy stomach should eat radish with salt and a little vinegar after food, but before food if the opposite is the case. Yet because raw food of whatever kind, however taken, excites belches and wind, disturbs the brain and eyes, and is harder to digest, it is best eaten with oil, for thus it cannot provoke belching from the stomach. The kind that has a thin skin and a moderate sharpness, tempered so that it is hardly felt, is preferred to the others; yet it should not be entirely free of sharpness. There is a kind that has a very thick skin, beneath which lies a great deal of bitterness (which is nevertheless removed by salting), and this must be rejected from food. Therefore rustic and dull palates seek that kind of bitterness and sharp flavour in the radish.

units.la: Simon Sethi cap. de radicula hanc controuersiam breuiter dirimit, vult enim, si ventriculus faciлe fluat, nec ad inflationem seu flatuum genera-tionem sit dispositus, radiculam ante cibum dari commodius, sin contrarium fuerit à cibo. Ex quibus colligitur ventriculum humidum esse flatulentum, quia flatus generantur ex materia humida non sicca, calor enim tanquam causa efficiens in cibos quidem & humores agit, sed dimi-nuté, respectu scilicet ipsius materiæ, quam qui-de aliqua exparte attenuat atq; dissoluit, nō ta-men perfectè conficit. Vndequi duriore sunt al-uo, & ventriculum habent flatulentum, radicu-la cum sale & modico aceto vesci debent à cibo, ante vero si contrarium fuerit. Verum quia quo-modocunque modo sumta cruda eructationes & flatus excitat, cerebrum oculosq; turbat, ac con-coctu difficilius est ex oleo comedenda est, sic enim de ventriculo eructationis ciere non potest. Quæ corticem habet tenuem, modicamq; acrimoniam, eamq; ita temperatam, vt vix sentiatur, cateris præfertur: nō tamen debet esse omnes acrimonia expers: quoddam genus est quod corticem habet crassissimum, cuius subest amaritudo plurima (quæ tamen salsugine eximitur,) ac cibis abdicandū. Quare rustica & stupida palata sunt, qua eius-modi amaritudinem acremq; illum saporem in raphano quaerunt.
units.tr: Simon Sethi, in his chapter on the radish, settles this controversy briefly. He holds that if the stomach empties easily and is not prone to swelling or the generation of wind, it is more convenient to give the radish before the meal, but if the opposite is true, after it. From this it follows that the stomach is moist and windy, because winds are generated from moist rather than dry matter. Heat, as the efficient cause, acts on food and humours, but feebly, relative to the matter itself: it partly thins and dissolves it, yet does not fully digest it. Therefore those whose bowels are harder and whose stomachs are windy ought to eat radish with salt and a little vinegar after the meal, but before it if the opposite is true. Yet because a raw radish, however it is taken, provokes belching and wind, troubles the brain and the eyes, and is hard to digest, it should be eaten with oil, for in this way it cannot cause belching from the stomach. The kind that has a thin skin and a mild sharpness, tempered so that it is scarcely noticed, is preferred to the others; yet it should not be altogether free of sharpness. There is a kind with a very thick skin, beneath which lies a great deal of bitterness (which, however, is removed by saltiness), and this must be banished from food. Therefore rustic and dull palates are those that seek this kind of bitterness and sharp flavour in the radish.

units.la: Raphanus maior, seu thlaspi maius ger-man. Merrettich / feruentior in omnibus & efficacior est, ad salsamentarios usus cum sale & aceto tusa radix conditur, embammatis enim seu condimentis ex aceto, quae ad condienda sunt obsonia, ut pisces, carnes, adiungitur, & maxime idonea est ad excitandam appetentiam, pellendam urinam & calculum, sed immodicus eius usus capiti noxius est, quare aliis conveni-entibus contemperanda est. De raphano mino-ri, germ. Rettich / hoc minime praetereundum est, quod ieiuno stomacho manducatus cum sale & pane veneno potenter resistit, experimenti via facilis & certa.
units.tr: The greater radish, or greater thlaspi, in German Merrettich is more fiery and more effective in every respect. For the uses of salting, the root is pounded with salt and vinegar and seasoned; it is added to vinegar-based embammata or condiments, which are used to season relishes such as fish and meats, and it is most suitable for arousing appetite and driving out urine and stone. But its excessive use is harmful to the head, so it must be tempered with other suitable things. Concerning the lesser radish, in German Rettich , this must not be passed over: when eaten on an empty stomach with salt and bread, it powerfully resists poison, an easy and certain method by experiment.

units.la: De Caepis.
units.tr: On Onions.

units.la: APud Ægyptios piaculum ducunt vesci caepis aut allio, propterea quod haec illorum sint numina, quae de re extant in :5 Juvenalis Satyr. elegantes versus
units.tr: Among the Egyptians it was counted a sin to eat onions or garlic, because these were their deities. Juvenal, Satire 15, says about this in elegant verses:

units.la: Oppida tota canem venerantur, nulla Diana Porrum & Cœpe nefas violare acfrangere morsu, O sanctas gentes, quib. hac nascuntur in hortis Numina.
units.tr: Whole towns worship a dog; no town reveres Diana. It is wrong to violate the leek and the onion, or to break them with the teeth. O holy nations, in whose gardens such deities grow!

units.la: Causam hujus superstitionis ex fequen-tibus verbis Ruelliiin historia cepæ, facile quis intellexerit. Id mirandum, inquit, occurrit, quodapud Plutarchum 4. in Hefiod. commentario legitur, Cepa enim reuirescit & congerminat luna decedente, contra autem marcescit eâdem adolescente : eam causam dicunt Sacerdotes Ægyptii, cur Pe-lufiotæ Cœpam non edant, eo quod solum olerum omnium contra fyderis incrementa & decrementa vices minuendi & augendi habeat contrarias, cum omnia quæ crefcen-te Luna gliscunt, eâdem senescente tabe-fcunt, quod in ostreis & cancris aperte cognoscitur, quos fyderis juuenta complet & vberiores facit, senium deplet macrosque reddit.Hæc ille.
units.tr: From the following words of Ruellius in his History of the Onion, one can easily understand the cause of this superstition. "This is remarkable," he says, "which is read in Plutarch, in the fourth book of his commentary on Hesiod: the onion revives and sprouts again as the moon wanes, but on the contrary withers as the moon waxes. The Egyptian priests give this as the reason why the Pelusiotes do not eat onions: it alone of all vegetables has effects opposed to the increase and decrease of the stars, diminishing and augmenting in the reverse way. For all things that swell as the moon grows waste away as it wanes, which is clearly seen in oysters and crabs: the youth of the star fills them and makes them fuller, while its old age empties them and makes them thin." Thus far Ruellius.

units.la: Nos vero Germani acribus istis Ægyptiorum Diis carere non possumus, in nostris enim culinis cepis nihil fere frequentius, aliumque cultum Ægyptiacis Diis præstare non possumus, quam vt iis mane & jejuno stomacho cum sale & pane deuoratis à peste & veneno nos præferuemus.
units.tr: We Germans, however, cannot do without those sharp onions of the Egyptian gods. In our kitchens nothing is more common than onions, and we cannot pay the Egyptian gods any other worship than by eating them in the morning on an empty stomach with salt and bread, to guard ourselves against plague and poison.

units.la: De cepis porro notandum, quod coctæ salubriores sint crudis, tum quia magis nutriunt, tum quia coctione acre illum afperumq; sapore deponunt. Russæ & rubicundæ albis acriores sunt & calidiores, Carnib.aût. piscibus,ouifq; condiendisaccommodatiffi- mæ sunt. Feruenti cinere coctæ atq; ex oleo, saccharo,acetiq; momento comestæ ad diffi- ciles tusses præltant:aluum quoq; emolliunt, vrinamq; pellunt continuo efficatæ. Vnicum hic omnib. præceptum esto omni auro præ- ftantius, videl. quod vnumquemq; fuiipfius medicū esse deceat,obseruareq; [?], iuuerturne an offendatur ceparum vsu, actum demum ab iis,vel abstinere,auteas vsurpare. Idem de allio,& id genus aliis intelligas.
units.tr: Concerning onions, it should further be noted that cooked they are healthier than raw, both because they nourish more and because cooking removes their harsh and biting taste. Red and reddish onions are sharper and hotter than white ones, and are most suitable for seasoning meat, fish and eggs. Baked in hot ash and eaten with oil, sugar and vinegar, they are excellent for stubborn coughs; they also soften the bowels and, taken continually, drive out urine. This one rule applies to everyone and is worth more than all gold: each person ought to be his own doctor, observing whether the use of onions harms him or not, and then either abstaining from them or using them accordingly. The same is to be understood of garlic and that kind of thing.

units.la: Atridæ deniq; & coctæ virentibus & cru- dis vtiliores sunt , namin his sapor ille mor- dax & acris, odorq;lacrymosus (qui tamen tempore elanguescit) oculorum caliginem, capitisq; dolores gignit. Idem & nonnun- quam salutaris est , oculorumq; caliginem pellit,id quod expertus sum in me ipso,capi- tis grauedinem ex natium obstructione sen- tieus[?].Cepam autem vel mando cum pane,vel per medium scindo, odoremq; exhalantem ad oculos penetrare sino, verum caute obser- uandum est,tabidis naturā aridisq; , flaccidis & languidis,ac biliosis,hunc vtendi modum noxium esse, humiditas enim radicalis & nu- trimentalis eo absumitur , contrario autem modo se habētibus vsi est. Leguminibus, vt fabis,pisis,lentibus,salutariter cepas adiectas expertus sum , ad flatus discutiendum,diffi- pandumque crassum , qui ab his gignitur, succum. Somnum quoque conciliare viui-dumque colorem creduntur. Hæc de ce-pis.
units.tr: Finally, leeks too are more useful cooked than raw or green. In them that biting, sharp taste and tear-provoking smell (which however fades with time) produce dimness of the eyes and headaches. Sometimes they are also wholesome and drive away dimness of the eyes, as I have experienced in myself, when I felt heaviness of the head from an obstruction of the nose. I chew a leek with bread, or cut it in half and let its exhaling odour reach my eyes. But it must be carefully observed that this manner of use is harmful to those of wasting nature, dry, flaccid and languid, and to the bilious, for radical and nourishing moisture is consumed by it; it suits those disposed in the opposite way. I have found that leeks added to pulses, such as beans, peas and lentils, are wholesome for dispersing wind and dissipating the thick juice generated by them. They are also believed to bring on sleep and a lively colour. These are my remarks on onions.

units.la: De allio.
units.tr: On Garlic.

units.la: NOn minor verò allio autoritas est apud gentes quasdam. In algidicribus quibusdam regionibus ab ipsius esu non possunt arceri incolæ. Rusticorum quoque theriaca est. Qui natura sunt calidiori ac biliofiori pernitio-so errore eo utuntur, insigniter enim calefacit, quare oleum addunt igni. Vini auiditatem quaerunt nonnulli vno a q, altero nucleo commanducato. Galenus, Aegineta, Aetius q, minime esse siticulosum constanter affirmant. Dioscorides vero & Plinius sitim gignere prodiderunt, quod experimento constat. Siticulosi enim allii esu reddunt & somniculosi, caput enim tentatur, oculorumq; hebetudo infertur, quod tamen de crudo potius quàm elixo intelligas velim, coctum enim crudo, elixumq; tosto, Plinio teste, vtilius. Elixatur vt acrimoniam amittat, succoq; sit melioris. Nihil enim tam est medicamentosum, quod coctione & elixatione aliqua ex parte non sit alimentosum. Contra aquarum autem & quorumlibet locorum mutationes insignem praestat vtilitatem, quod nautis optime esse notum scio, qui nauigantes in lintea id coniiciunt. Qui carnes & cumprimis verueecinam torrentes verubus, verbus, alio eam implent ac infigunt, non faciunt infalubriter. Hoc miror principes quosdam foeminas alio plurimum gaudere. Quin & magnates quidam (cum primis in Gallia) ineunte vere cum butyro recenti eo viuntur, valetudinis per totum annum custodiendae gratia. Colico dolori nobile & praesens medicamentum esse Galenus promisit, inueteratae quoq; tussi, & urinae cienda, mensibus & fecundinae extrahendae. Vnū detestandum in alio est, foetidus videl. ac ingratus ille edor cerebro officiens, ob quem Horatium puto, illud tantopere execratum esse, cum scribit lib. epodon ode 3.
units.tr: Garlic has no less authority among certain peoples. In some cold regions the inhabitants cannot be kept from eating it. It is also a theriac of the country folk. Those of hotter and more bilious nature use it with a harmful error, for it heats markedly, which is why they add oil to the fire. Some seek a desire for wine by chewing one clove or one kernel. Galen, Aegineta and Aetius firmly affirm that it is by no means thirst-producing. But Dioscorides and Pliny have reported that it produces thirst, which experience confirms: those who eat garlic become thirsty and sleepy, the head is troubled, and dullness of the eyes follows. I would, however, have this understood of raw rather than cooked garlic, for cooked is more useful than raw, and roasted more useful than boiled, according to Pliny. It is boiled so that it loses its sharpness and becomes better in juice, for nothing is so medicinal that it is not in some part nourishing after cooking and boiling. On the other hand, changes of water and of place bring remarkable benefit, which I know is very well known to sailors, who put garlic into their linen when they sail. Those who roast meats, especially a pork belly, on spits do not do so unhealthily when they stuff and pierce it with garlic. I wonder that certain princes and women greatly enjoy garlic. Indeed some great men (especially in France) take it with fresh butter in early spring, to keep their health through the whole year. Galen promised that it is a noble and ready remedy for colic, also for long-standing cough, for provoking urine, and for drawing out the menses and afterbirth. One thing is to be detested in garlic: its foul and unpleasant smell, which harms the brain, and on account of which I think Horace execrated it so much when he writes in Epode 3:

units.la: Parentis olim si quis impia manu Senile guttur fregerit, Edat cicutis allium nocentius O dura messorum ilia.
units.tr: "If anyone has ever with an impious hand broken the aged throat of his parent, let him eat garlic more harmful than hemlock, O hard bellies of the reapers."

units.la: Est in exemplis multos odore alii non secus atq; pestilentis rei olfactu affici. Didymus asse-rit, allium, si luna infra terram existente, sera-tur, idemq;, luna sub terra latente, vellatur, o-doris foeditatem amittere & dulcescere. Alii apii liberaliori esu, halitum eius restingui prodiderunt.
units.tr: There are examples of many people being affected by the smell of garlic no less than by the smell of some pestilential thing. Didymus asserts that garlic, if sown while the moon is below the earth and pulled up while the moon lies hidden under the earth, loses the foulness of its smell and becomes sweet. Others have reported that its breath is quenched by a fairly generous eating of celery.

units.la: Didymus crudae fabae manducationem probat: alii betae radicem in prunis tostam: alii rutae folia: ego laudo panem tostum aceto vel vino intinctum. Antipathiam magnetis & alii hic silentio praeterire nefas est, ille enim hoc affri-catus catus ferum non trahit. Sed de hoc mysterio di- cetur alibi.
units.tr: Didymus approves of eating raw beans; others of beet root roasted on coals; others of rue leaves; I praise bread toasted and dipped in vinegar or wine. It would be wrong to pass over in silence here the antipathy of the magnet and garlic: for when rubbed with garlic it does not draw iron. But more will be said of this mystery elsewhere.

units.la: De porro.
units.tr: On the Leek.

units.la: Eiusdem cum cæpis & allio est naturæ, quare nõ incõuenienter de eo hic verba fiunt. Culinæ carnes eo decoquũt, vt gallinas, capones, veruecinamq;, quibus adiiciunt crocum, suaui & grato sapore: Itaque certum est in cibis admodum esse vtile, licet in huius viribus & natura autores varient. Thadeus Florentinus experimento compertum habebat, porrum crudum ex sale primo cibo esitatu ventriculu à crassis lentisq; humoribus, crudisq; succis liberare. Biliosas veró ac calidiores naturas, eosq; qui infirmiori sunt capite, grauiter ab illius esu affici certu est. Alii venerem irritare, ebrietatemque discutere prædicant. Quædam rura edunt ex sale, panemque eo æque atque allio fricant, ad condiendum panis atri ingratitudinem. Alsatiæ agricolæ & vinitores allium, cæpam & porrum inter prima & vltima habent fercula. Præstat autem allium, antequam caules faciat, si intorqueatur ac humi prosternatur, quod Iulio faciendum est, hoc enim pacto cautur, ne in frondem luxuriet, vnde grandiora fiunt capita. In Germania nostra foliis porri, sicut & absynthii, melissæ,
units.tr: It is of the same nature as the onion and garlic, so it is not out of place to discuss it here. Cooks boil meats with it, such as hens, capons and mutton, adding saffron, for a pleasant and agreeable flavour. It is therefore certain that it is very useful in foods, although authors differ about its powers and nature. Thaddeus of Florence had found by experience that raw leek eaten with salt as the first food cleanses the stomach of thick and viscous humours and of crude juices. It is certain, however, that bilious and hotter natures, and those who have weaker heads, are seriously harmed by eating it. Others claim that it stirs up desire and dispels drunkenness. Some country folk eat it with salt, and rub bread with it just as they do with garlic, to season the unpleasant taste of black bread. Farmers and vintners in Alsace count leeks, onions and leeks among their first and last dishes. It is better, however, to twist the leek before it makes stalks, and lay it flat on the ground, which should be done in July; for in this way it is prevented from running to leaf, whence the heads become larger. In our Germany the leaves of the leek are used, as are those of wormwood, balm,

units.la: menthæ Sarracenicæ, rosmarini, amenthæ vulgaris, matricariæ, & similibus. ad placen-tas quas taganitas vocant (Pfanfuchen) ó-diendas vsus frequentissimus est, præsertim verno tempore, estq; harum vsus & esus isto tempore noninfalutaris, ventriculo enim & medicamento & alimento sunt. Hactenus de alimentis quæ veniunt ex radicibus, quibus, quia ciborum potius cõdimenta sunt, quàm cibi, qui proprie alimentum præstare ex-sti- mantur, annumerari possunt, femina, quæ in præcipuis ac laudatissimis saluberrimisq; ho- die condimentis escarum variarum habetur, vt sunt, anisi, feniculi, cari, apii, anethi, sina- pi, quod præcipuam nobilitatem in condi- mentis carnium, vt bubulæ præsertim insu-matæ, item piscium obtinuit: matres familiâs obsonatricis artis non imperitæ per vinde-mias multo id diluunt temperantq; ad acri-moniam eius retundendam, vnde adhuc mu-stardæ nomè à multo & ardore retinuisse vi-detur. Insigniter autem prodest, quibus pala-tum torpescit, quosq; cibi fastidium mole-stat, cerebrum quoq; purgat, sed inualidio- ribus aridisq; oculis infigniter noxium: ari-dos oculos voco tabidos, saccidos, debiles, roridæ sc. humiditatis ratione, ea enim deficiente oculos aridos existere debilesq; necesse est.
units.tr: Saracen mint, rosemary, common mint, feverfew and the like, most frequently for seasoning the flat cakes which they call taganitae (Pfanfuchen); and their use and eating at that season is not unwholesome, for they serve the stomach as both medicine and food. So far concerning foods which come from roots. Since these are rather seasonings of food than food, which are thought properly to provide nourishment, they may be counted among them: seed, which today is held among the chief and most praised and most wholesome seasonings of various dishes, such as anise, fennel, caraway, celery, dill and mustard. Mustard has gained especial distinction in seasoning meats, particularly unsalted beef, and likewise fish. Housewives skilled in the art of cooking, not unpractised, dilute it with much must during the vintage and temper it to blunt its sharpness; whence the name "mustard" seems still to retain the notion of much must and heat. It is especially beneficial to those whose palate is dulled and whom a loss of appetite troubles; it also purges the brain, but it is notably harmful to weaker and dry eyes. I call dry eyes those that are wasted, dim, weak, lacking, as regards the moisture of dew; for when this is lacking, the eyes must become dry and weak.

units.la: CAP. X. De alimentis, quæ suΜuntur ex plantarum foliis.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. Of foods taken from the leaves of plants.

units.la: HÆc plerag{que} sunt hortensia, ut brassica, caulis capitatus, lactuca, endivia, seu cichorium hortense, atriplex, beta, spinachium. Hæc cæteris oleribus, agrestibus & domesticis magis salutaria utiliorꝙ iudicantur, tum quia natura illorum longo experimento vitæ hominum est probata, tum quia rem alimentariam eximiæ augent.
units.tr: These are mostly garden plants: cabbage, head cabbage, lettuce, endive or garden chicory, orache, beet, and spinach. They are judged more wholesome and more useful than other vegetables, both wild and cultivated, partly because their nature has been proven by the long experience of human life, and partly because they greatly enrich the diet.

units.la: De Brassica.
units.tr: On Cabbage.

units.la: IN Græcia Crambe vocitabatur, quasi Coramble, quod oculis inimica existimabatur, pupillam enim oculorum, quæ κόρη gr. dicitur, hebetare dicitur. Galenus excitandi vim insignem obtinere, ideoque vi-sum hebetare, nisi quis oculos habeat hu-mentiores, scriptum reliquit. Alii solam interolera atram bilem procreare, eamqꝛ iniqui & graueolentis succi esse prodiderunt.
units.tr: In Greece it was called crambe, as if coramble, because it was thought hostile to the eyes, for it is said to dull the pupil of the eye, which the Greeks call kore. Galen left it written that it has a remarkable power of stimulating, and therefore dulls the sight unless a person has moister eyes. Others have declared that it alone among vegetables produces black bile, and that its juice is harmful and foul-smelling.

units.la: Sunt qui plurimis mirisque laudibus eam celebrent cum primis vero sativam crispam, hanc enim probe paratam stomacho imbecillo conuenire, concoctionem adiuvare, bilem & phlegma sensim educere asseuerant. rant, ad quod pofterius adhuc magis com- mendantur cymata feu cauliculi braffice te- neriores & delicatiores. Sexcentis annis po- pulum Romanum braffica vfum effe, nul- lumque extitiffe morbum, quem non hoc o- lere curarent graues autores teftantur. Se- ptentrionis gentes, ficut & Weftphali, apud quos magna in copia optima prouenit, braf- ficam in gloria palati habent, coquunt eam cum perdicibus, columbis, carnib° pinguio- ribus, & anferibus infumatis, quidam adiici- ciunt piper falutari inuento, fic eniminfalu- brior & afperior fuccus falubrior euadit & mitior. Hibernis frigoribus & gelicidiis me- dullam caulium quidam in delitiis habent, paratur q; eodé modo quo paftinaca:lautior quoq; & fuauior ipfa braffica redditur in fri- goribus & rigoribus hiemis, tefte experien- tia. Qui humaniorem ac nitidiorem lequun- tur vitam, caules leuiter coquunt, coctos paropfidibus imponunt, faleque ac oleo co- diunt, quoapparatu guftatu gratiffimi eua- dunt. Ebrietatem arcere, crapulamque dif- cutere bina aut terna braffica folia cruda cū fale & aceto, ante & poft cibum comefta, ex- perimento haud fallaci conftat, ob antipa- thian quæ eft braffica cum vitibus, quæ iuxta confitæ non coalefcunt. Podagri- cos, neruosque paralyticos & tremu- los braffica efu plurimum iuuari Erafiftra[?] fcholatestatur, annotante Plinio, vt ita non necesse sit exotica, peregrina & pretiosa expetere, cum vulgaribus sæpe ac notissimis remediis auxilium sentiamus.
units.tr: Some praise it with very many and remarkable commendations, especially the curled garden cabbage, for they assert that, when properly prepared, it suits a weak stomach, aids digestion, and gradually draws off bile and phlegm. For this reason the cymata, or tender and delicate little shoots of cabbage, are commended even more. Serious authors bear witness that for six hundred years the Roman people ate cabbage, and that there was no disease which they did not treat with it. The peoples of the North, and the Westphalians too, among whom it grows in great abundance and excellent quality, hold cabbage in high regard for the palate: they cook it with partridges, pigeons, fattier meats and smoked geese. Some add pepper, a wholesome discovery, for in this way the harsh and sharp juice becomes more healthful and milder. In the frosts and icy cold of winter some take delight in the marrow of the cabbage stalks, and it is prepared in the same way as parsnip. Cabbage itself also becomes more refined and sweeter in the frosts and rigours of winter, as experience attests. Those who follow a more civilized and elegant way of life lightly boil the stalks, set them on platters, and season them with salt and oil; by this preparation they become most pleasing to the taste. That cabbage keeps off drunkenness and dispels the after-effects of excess is established by no deceptive experience: two or three raw cabbage leaves eaten with salt and vinegar before and after a meal. This is due to the antipathy that cabbage has toward vines, which, as is said, do not thrive when planted near it. Erasistratus testifies, and Pliny notes, that cabbage greatly helps those with gout, paralysed nerves and trembling limbs, so that there is no need to seek exotic, foreign and costly things, since we often find help in common and very well-known remedies.

units.la: De caule capitato.
units.tr: On Head Cabbage.

units.la: HVius oleris vsus in Germania nostra ita innaluit, vt vino potius aliúq; necessa-riis ad vitam rebus quam eo carere ma-lit. Bene enim præparatum, conditum & co-ctum longè gratius, salubriusq; est peregrinis illis, sumtuosis, eq; longinquo accitus non nisi ad ina-nem prodigi luxus ostentationem, condimentis, vt olivis, capparibus, & similibus. Multis autem modis præparantur atque condiuntur caules capitati, quibus hodie culina principatum attribuunt: ad cocturam præcipue medullas ex bouum ossibus quærunt aut carnes pinguiores. Germania nostra caules capitatos sale condire didicit, qui postea accescunt, diuq; ita referuan-tur incorrupti, ne putrescant: constat enim decoctorum aquam humi effusam fœtere, quin etiam ipsos (quod de Brassica quoque intelligen-dum) in hortis putrefactos intolerabilem odo-rem exhalare: qua ratione non immeritò à prudentioribus quibusdam in cibis damnantur. Probe itaq; conditi stomacho effuanti‐ latranti, sicut es fastidienti prodesse experimen‐to quotidiano constat. Hoc velim prudenti patresfamilias meminerint, conditura adiicien‐da esse femina anisi, foeniculi, cyminii, anethi, apii, baccas iuniperinas, es similia crasso modo contusa, hac enim saporem conciliant es odo em cerebro gratum es ventriculo salutarem, flatum discutiunt, inflationes impediunt, urinam promovent. Secus praeparatos, cottos es conditos ventriculo, quae illis non affuerunt, infiguiter nocent cuiusque compertum est. Quamobrem hoc olim non protinus planeque contemnendum est, es inscienter, meo iudicio, errant, qui indifferenter coeco es vago iudicio, omnibus hoc cibo interdi‐cunt.
units.tr: The use of this vegetable has so taken hold in our Germany that people would sooner go without wine and other necessities of life than without it. For when well prepared, seasoned and cooked, it is far more pleasing and wholesome than those costly foreign vegetables brought from far away, which serve only to display empty and wasteful luxury, with condiments such as olives, capers and the like. Head cabbages are prepared and seasoned in many ways, and today kitchens give them the first place: for cooking they especially seek the marrow of ox bones or fattier meats. Our Germany has learned to salt head cabbage, which then keeps and remains sound for a long time, so that it does not rot. For it is well known that the water of cooked cabbage, poured out on the ground, stinks, and indeed the cabbages themselves, rotting in the gardens (which is to be understood of cabbage too), give off an intolerable odour; for this reason some of the wiser sort rightly condemn them as food. Properly seasoned, however, it is established by daily experience that it benefits a stomach that is windy and rumbling, and one that is squeamish. Let prudent heads of families remember this: seasoning should be added, namely seeds of anise, fennel, cumin, dill and celery, juniper berries, and similar things, coarsely crushed. For these give flavour, a smell pleasing to the brain and a taste wholesome to the stomach; they disperse wind, prevent bloating, and promote the flow of urine. Cabbage prepared otherwise, cooked and seasoned without these additions, is known to harm the stomach considerably. Therefore it should not be wholly and hastily despised; and those err unwisely, in my judgment, who with blind and vague judgment forbid this food to everyone without distinction.

units.la: Acetaria, quae ex caule capitato crudo, tempore, ut plurimum autumnali concinnari confuerunt, ex oleo es aceto, (quorum usus efficiens ita apud nos frequens est, ut prima mensa, tum magnatum, tum pauperum, is exornari multipliciter gestiant.) lupini, rustici ac stupidi palati esse exstimo. Videant igitur studiosi literarum, ne inter coenam eiusmodi acetario‐rum plenos bolos devorantes ex affumta quadam es permitiosa consuetudine crudiatum copiam inglutiant.
units.tr: Salads made from raw head cabbage, usually put together in autumn with oil and vinegar (whose use is so common among us that every table, of the great and of the poor alike, eagerly seeks to be adorned with them in many ways), I consider the food of boors and of rustic and dull palates. Let students of letters therefore take care, lest, by a certain assumed and harmful custom, they swallow down a quantity of raw indigestion, devouring full mouthfuls of such salads at supper.

units.la: NB. Admonitio.
units.tr: NB. Admonition.

units.la: De Lactuca.
units.tr: On Lettuce.

units.la: DE Lactuca diversæ sunt autorum sententiæ. Quidam præ cæteris oleribus bene eam nutrire, purumq; generare sanguinem, scriptum reliquerunt. Alii aliter sentiunt, non admodum eam expetentes. Serapio utilem sibi fuisse lactucam testatur, æstuantem enim choleram eâ expurgavit. Plinius quoque doctissimum medicum musam, Augusto lactucâ vim morbi repressisse tradit. Et Galenus ipse summis eam laudibus prosequitur. Et certum est, quibus assiduo os ventriculi superius bile efferuescit atque ebullit, lactucæ usum prodesse, sitim extinguere, eximieq; conciliare somnum, quam ob causam æstate feruente, morbo quoque vel ætate calidiori frequentissime in cibo ubique gentium adhibetur.
units.tr: Authors disagree about lettuce. Some have written that, above all other vegetables, it nourishes well and produces pure blood. Others think differently and do not much favour it. Serapion testifies that lettuce was useful to him, since it purged his burning choler. Pliny also reports that the very learned physician Musa, by means of lettuce, checked the force of a disease in Augustus. Galen himself praises it with the highest commendations. And it is certain that lettuce is of benefit to those whose upper stomach constantly boils and froths with bile, that it quenches thirst and brings on sleep remarkably well. For this reason it is eaten everywhere in the world in the heat of summer, and also in fevers or in hotter periods of life, very frequently.

units.la: Magnam in acetariis obtinuit auctoritatem, sicut & præcipuam fere inter olera ei tribuunt graves scriptores. Plinius æstate gratam, stomachoque fastidium auferre, cibique appetentiam inducere memoriæ prodidit.
units.tr: It has held great authority among salads, and serious writers have assigned it almost the chief place among vegetables. Pliny recorded that in summer it is pleasant, removes loathing from the stomach, and induces an appetite for food.

units.la: Ob refrigeratricem, qua prædita est, naturam intemperatas libidines præsertim eas, quæ per somnos contingunt, coercere ducum excaule fcere cœpit cibis, non amplius est idonea, quare culinis abdicatur. Cocta lactuca in pulticulam corpori deficienti bonum præbet nutrimentum, aluumq; emollit, quare edentulis inque senium vergenti-bus salutaris est. Galenus tamen neque multum generare sanguinem, nec tamen improbi succi esse asserit, quin medium temperamentum inter ea, quæ boni sunt succi sunt, & inter ea, quæ mali.
units.tr: Because of its cooling nature, it was thought to restrain intemperate lusts, especially those that arise during sleep. But when cooks began to warm it with other foods, it was no longer suitable for this, and so it is excluded from the kitchen. Cooked lettuce, made into a poultice, gives good nourishment to a weakened body and softens the bowels, so it is wholesome for the toothless and for those growing old. Galen, however, asserts that it does not produce much blood, yet is not of bad juice either, but holds a middle position between those things that are of good juice and those that are of bad.

units.la: Qui ficcioris sunt cerebri, vsum ejus non respuent, similiter, qui concumbendi desiderio nimis vrunt & prıriunt.
units.tr: Those with a rather dry brain will not reject its use, and likewise those who burn and itch too much with desire for intercourse.

units.la: Ad extremum mirari subit, tot laudi- bus celebratum olus oculorum claritati ossi- cere, spiritus visorios incrassando, humo- remque crystallinum efficiendo turbidum, ab aliquibus grauibus autoribus proditum esse, cum neque Galenus, neque cæteri græ- ci medici, (quod quidem ego inuenerim) id annotarint.
units.tr: Lastly, it is surprising that a vegetable so highly praised should be reported by some serious authors to harm the clearness of the eyes, by thickening the visual spirits and by making the crystalline humour cloudy. Yet neither Galen nor the other Greek physicians (so far as I have found) have noted this.

units.la: Immodico ejus vsui id fine dubio af- scribendum est, non secus ac femen genitale immoderato ejus vsu plus fatis dilutum, ineffıcax minufq; idoneum ad pro- creandos liberos effici- tur.
units.tr: Without doubt this must be ascribed to immoderate use of it, just as genital seed, when diluted beyond what is proper by immoderate use of it, becomes ineffective and less fit for producing children.

units.la: De.
units.tr: On.

units.la: De Endiuia, cichorio, atriplice, beta, portulaca, spinachio, &c.
units.tr: On endive, chicory, orach, beet, purslane, spinach, etc.

units.la: Esculenta hæc olera sunt ac culinis grata, interque hortensia folertissima cura excoluntur. Itaq; minime cibis abdicanda, quod experimento longo horum salutarem usum vita probarit.
units.tr: These edible herbs are pleasing to the kitchen and are cultivated with the greatest care among garden plants. Therefore they must by no means be removed from food, since long experience has proved their wholesome use in life.

units.la: Endiuia seu Scariola hibernas hodie menses subit, & hibernis inseruit acetariis: tantus nunc honor per frigora ei debetur & attri-butus est. Folia enim vbi adoleuerint exili fi-lo, quasi in fasciculum solent colligari, & in fictilibus cooperta seruari, sic enim fit, ut & eximiæ candorem, suavemq; teneritudinem adipiscan-tur, vix enim sentitur amaritudo in candidioribus, quam diligenti olitorum cura & cultura deponunt atq; amittunt.
units.tr: Endive, or succory, nowadays comes into season in winter and is included among the winter salads. Such honour and esteem is now paid to it through the cold months. For when the leaves have grown to a slender thread, they are usually gathered into a little bundle and kept covered in earthen vessels. In this way they acquire both an excellent whiteness and a sweet tenderness, for bitterness is scarcely felt in the whiter leaves, which gardeners remove and lose by careful tending and cultivation.

units.la: Quidam, si foliis stramentis adoperiantur putant candorem illum, gratiamq; in cibis posse conciliari. Quâ de causa octobri mense vel etiam septembri seri oportet ad hiberna aceta-ria. Qui Endiuiam hiemis impatientiorem esse feruntur, ut Plinius iis experientiam oppono, quæ in summa etiam rigoris iniuria in terris fri-gidioribus seruari eam testatur.
units.tr: Some think that by covering the leaves with straw that whiteness and pleasantness can be secured in the food. For this reason it is best to sow for winter salads in October, or even in September. As for those said to be less able to endure winter, I set against them the experience which Pliny cites, which attests that endive is kept even in the harsh injury of cold in colder lands.

units.la: Cichorium satiuum seu hortense inte-nera adhuc ætate cibis utiliter adhiberi cœpit concoctionem enim adiuvat, epatisq; ac lienis obstructiones insigniter tollit. In vsu est herba & radix. Sed Erraticum Cichorium seu Sylvestre radicem habet præclaros ad vsus in medicina, ex aceto commanducata, veletiam condita. Quidam singulariter salubrem calidiori temperaturæ præditis promittunt. Abstrusas in hoc olere vires esse, flores indicant, qui Sole oriente se pandunt, quotidie cum eo nubilo etiam cœlo circumaguntur, eodem vero occidente se recludunt, unde & Solsequium vocitatur.
units.tr: Cultivated chicory, or garden chicory, while still young and tender, began to be usefully eaten as food, for it aids digestion and notably removes obstructions of the liver and spleen. The herb and the root are both in use. But wild chicory, or sylvestre, has a root which has excellent uses in medicine, eaten raw with vinegar or even preserved. Some promise it a singular wholesomeness for those of warmer temperament. That hidden powers are in this herb the flowers indicate, which open when the sun rises, turn daily with the sky as it moves, and close again when it sets; whence it is also called sunflower.

units.la: Certissimum & indubitatum superiorum cum inferioribus sympathia documentum. Sed in hoc mysterio nosse oportet cichorium cœli.
units.tr: A most certain and undoubted proof of the sympathy of higher things with lower. But in this mystery one must know the chicory of heaven.

units.la: Atriplex, Beta & Spinachium olus fe-dulo quoq; bodie feruntur atq; excoluntur, in-sculis & cibis, qui alui elicienda atque laxanda gratiâ, parantur, utilia, inter quatamen Beta alutum magis ad excretionem stimulare depre-senda est: inter catera vero olera leniùs alunt, sanguinem q; gignunt pauciorem, eumque mali succi, si non recte probeq; coquantur. Cocta enim tantum edi inueniuntur.
units.tr: Orach, beet and spinach, a vegetable also commonly grown and cultivated today, are useful for soups and dishes prepared to loosen and relax the bowels; among them, however, beet is found to stimulate the bowels more towards evacuation. Among the other vegetables they nourish more gently and produce less blood, and that of bad juice, unless they are cooked properly and thoroughly; for they are found to be eaten only when cooked.

units.la: Hoc nota, minus ventriculo nocere, si cum sinapi aut saltem cum aceto edantur. Candida Beta magis commendatur, rubra medicamentosa est. Tenella quoque præfertur adultæ,
units.tr: Note this: they harm the stomach less if they are eaten with mustard or at least with vinegar. White beet is more commended, red beet is medicinal. Tender beet is also preferred to the mature.

units.la: Spinachium olim in recibaria nullum habuit vsum, nunc vero maximam autoritatem assecutum folertiffime excolitur. Coqui-tur autem aquâ leuiter cultello prius minutim conscissum [?], prius tamen manibus, aut asserculis aquâ, aut vligine. Quæ inest plurima expressa. Varios autem atq; diuersos apparandi modos re-linquemus cocis.
units.tr: Spinach once had no use in the kitchen, but now that it has gained the greatest authority it is cultivated most diligently. It is cooked in water, after being lightly chopped finely with a knife, yet first washed by hand, or pressed with boards in water or moisture, which contains a great deal of liquid. The various and different ways of preparing it we shall leave to the cooks.

units.la: Vulgo in sartagine ex oleo aut butyro fri-gitur, gratiaq; conciliandae gratiâ, piperis, zin-giberis, & cinnamomi pulline [?] aspergitur. Alij in olla ex largiori butyro lento igne coquunt, identidem versant, deinde saporis gratiâ, con-siliandi gratiâ aceti momentum [?], & melligi-nem inducunt, saleq; condiunt.
units.tr: Commonly it is fried in a pan in oil or butter, and sprinkled with pepper, ginger and powdered cinnamon for the sake of pleasantness. Others cook it in a pot in a generous amount of butter over a slow fire, stirring it often; then, for the sake of flavour and to give it a pleasing taste, they add a spoonful of vinegar and honey, and season it with salt.

units.la: Certum est innocentiorem succum salua briorem [?], in corpus diffundere spinachium quam atriplex aut blitum. Acetariis non miscetur nisi tenellum, & parcius quidem, quia immodice sumptum prorsus nauseam.
units.tr: It is certain that spinach diffuses a more innocent juice into the body than orach or blite. It is mixed into salads only when tender, and even then sparingly, since taken to excess it causes nausea.

units.la: Portulacâ astiuis feruoribus eximiam obtinere gratiam, nemo est qui id non norit, manditur in acetariis, nostroq; euo studiosissime in hortis magnatum feritur, quorum etiam cu-lina cum gallinaceis pullis, aliisque lautioribus carnibus eam astate incoquunt.
units.tr: That purslane obtains an extraordinary favour in the summer heats, no one is unaware; it is eaten in salads, and in our age is most eagerly sown in the gardens of the great, whose kitchens also cook it in summer with young chickens and other more refined meats.

units.la: Quibus ventriculi os atq; iecur bile astuans, quæ efferuescunt, utilissimus sit erit cibus frigidæ fumentisq; est natura, quam ob causam adjungunt cepas, ut harum acrimoniâ gulam, irritet.
units.tr: For those whose stomach mouth and liver seethe with boiling bile, it will be a most useful food, since its nature is cold and moist; for this reason they add onions, so that its sharpness may stimulate the palate.

units.la: Cauliculi sale & aceto condiuntur, inque cibos[?] hiemales astiuosq; reseruantur, aquâ deinde calidâ abluuntur aut vino, ut salsugo & acrimonia contracta ex conditura hebetetur, abluti oleo superimfuso apponuntur.
units.tr: Cabbage stalks are seasoned with salt and vinegar and kept for winter and summer foods; then they are washed in warm water or wine, so that the saltiness and sharpness acquired from the seasoning are blunted, and, rinsed, they are served with oil poured over them.

units.la: In horum olerum censu sunt mercuria-lis, asparagus, malua, rumex, buglossa, quae in-re cibaria non postremam dignitatem atque autoritatem reportauit; propterea quod in vi-hum[?] conjecta[?] potantibus[?] animi hilaritatem cre-at melancoliam, pellit.
units.tr: Among the number of these vegetables are mercury, asparagus, mallow, sorrel, and bugloss, which have gained no small dignity and authority as food; for when mixed into wine it creates cheerfulness in those who drink and drives away melancholy.

units.la: Verum in hac & similibus peculiariter ac privatim naturam, ac vim singulorum considerari oportet, quatenus videl. vel sedulâ curâ excoluntur, vel certis ac receptis experimen-tis salutaria & utilia hominum vitae observata sunt.
units.tr: But in this and similar cases one ought to consider the nature and power of each particular plant, namely whether they are cultivated with diligent care, or have been observed by certain and accepted experience to be wholesome and useful for human life.

units.la: Herbarum enim in cibis alia placent, saepe[?] alia folio, alia radice, nonnulla flore, quadam cymis, hoc est, tenerioribus caulicu-lis; aliqua capite & summitati-bus, &c.
units.tr: For among herbs for food some please, often for the leaf, others for the root, some for the flower, some for the tender shoots, that is, the young stalks; some for the head and tops, and so on.

units.la: CAP. XI. De alimentis quæ sumuntur ex fructibus.
units.tr: CAP. XI. Of foods that are taken from fruits.

units.la: Arias, multiplices ac infinitas esse fructuum species atque differentias in natura rerum, ei etiam fatendum est, qui à patrio solo non longe receßitquin annus variorum fructuum feracißimus abunde id testatur.
units.tr: That the kinds and differences of fruit in the nature of things are many and countless must be admitted even by one who has not travelled far from his native soil; a year of exceptional abundance of various fruits amply bears witness to this.

units.la: Verum quoniam non omnes in cibo admittuntur, nimisque operosum foret ac prolixum de omnibus fructib. feorsim pertractare (tum quod in horum multis magnæ vitæ insidiæ subsint, tum etiam, quod major fere eorum pars voluptatis gratia magis, quàm vtilitatis ac salubritatis causa vsurpatur) eos hic annotabimus solum, qui salubritatem magis, quam voluptatem respiciunt. Gorgias Siculus Rhetor, Empedoclis discipulus, natus annos 109. interrogatus, quanam vitæ ratione tam optime vixisset, respondit, nihil voluptatis gratia faciendo. Hodie voluptatis gratia nihil intentatum relinquit gula in arborum fructibus, qui palatum sæpe torpidū, ventremq; cibis aliis refertissimum, alliciût atq; inuitant magno sæpe valetudinis incommodo. Utinam ventri gulæque imperare quan-
units.tr: But since not all fruits are admitted to the table, and it would be too laborious and lengthy to treat each of them separately (partly because many of them carry great dangers to life, and partly because most of them are eaten more for pleasure than for usefulness or health), I shall note here only those that have regard to health rather than pleasure. Gorgias of Sicily, a rhetorician and pupil of Empedocles, who lived to 109, was asked by what manner of life he had lived so well; he replied, by doing nothing for the sake of pleasure. Today the gullet, for the sake of pleasure, leaves nothing untried among the fruits of trees, which often entice and invite a palate grown sluggish and a belly already crammed with other foods, frequently to the great detriment of health. Would that we could sometimes command our belly and gullet,

units.la: quandoque possemus, ne praeter modum & intempestiue nociturus vesceremur.
units.tr: so that we would not eat things that harm us beyond measure and at the wrong time.

units.la: Sed quia difficile est in tanta fructuum varietate jucundo horum aspectu blandis- fimisque saporibus sibi temperare, dandum est aliquid nonnunquam irritanti gulæ, po- monæque inuitanti, obseruato tamen vt di- xi, modo. Plærique enim arborum fructus omnes, ( vno atque altero excepto ) tenue dant exiguumque nutrimentum, crudosque succos aggenerant. Itaq; nimius eorum vsus cauendus.
units.tr: But because it is difficult, amid such a variety of fruit, to restrain oneself from their pleasing appearance and most alluring flavours, we must sometimes give something to the irritated appetite and the tempting fruit, provided the measure I mentioned is observed. Most tree fruits, all but one or two, give thin and scanty nourishment and breed crude juices. Their excessive use must therefore be avoided.

units.la: Prius vero quam fructuum naturas explicare aggrediar, meminisse oportebit, quosnam ex fructibus primâ mensa, & quof- nam secundâ apponi conueniat? Nullo enim discrimine hic fero plane modo peccatur, etiam à magnatibus, qui plus aliis valetudi- nem tueri studebunt. Prima mensâ abdican- da sunt, necessingenda, quæ astringendi vi pollent, neque ita promte corrumpuntur, hæc enim cum bellariis secundas mensas salubri- ter subeunt, cuiusmodi sunt cotonea, malo- rum fere omne genus, pyra, sorba, mespili, nuces amygdalæ, pistacia, castanea : Primâ mensa primoq; cibo apponentur, quæ facile vitiantur ac corrumpuntur, quæq; humen- tiora sunt, talia enim aluo molliendæ & la- xandæ sunt idonea, si videl. prima sumantur, ab aliis antea sese aluum constipant, & co, s 3 &tio-
units.tr: Before I begin to explain the natures of fruits, it will be fitting to recall which fruits belong at the first course and which at the second. Here people go wrong in the same way without any distinction, even great men, who are most eager to preserve their health. Fruits that are astringent and not quickly corrupted should be banished from the first course; they go wholesomely with the sweetmeats at the second course. Such are quinces, nearly every kind of apple, pears, sorbs, medlars, nuts, almonds, pistachios and chestnuts. Fruits that spoil and corrupt easily, and are moister, belong at the first course and before other food, since they are suited to soften and loosen the bowel when taken first. If taken after other foods, they constipate the bowel and disturb digestion.

units.la: & 3 ctionem interturbant : sicut astringendi vi prædita, vt cotonea, secunda mensa sumta, subducendæ aluo conueniunt, comprimen-do enim ac astringendo os ventriculi robo-rant, quo fit vt citius aluus deiiciat. Primam igitur mensam subibunt, cerasa, pruna, perfi-ca, mora, & id genus alia fugacia & præcocia, quorum videl. gratia statim ttansuolat, mu-stea[?] item & mellita plæraq;. Videant igitur, qui secundas mensas cerasis, prunis ac perfi-cis exornant, qui tamen mos adeo in lautioribus mensis inualuit, principumque aulis, vt gulæ ac palato detractum putent, si non apposita fuerint. Eadem ratione valetudinem non parum infirmant, qui primis mensis vescuntur solidis cibis & duris, vt sunt carnes infumatæ indurataque, & quæ vel de prandio vel cœna sublatæ reseruataque sequenti die iterum apponuntur. Sanitatis enim tuendæ præceptum non postremum est, calida, quatenus calida, frigidis, mollia duris, humida siccis sunt præmittenda. Sic poma ante cotonea, hæc vero ante castaneas esitasse conuenit. Et hæc ἐν πρώτῳ[?] & proemii loco præmonuisse placuit.
units.tr: Astringent fruits such as quinces, taken at the second course, are best eaten after the meal, since by compressing and binding they strengthen the mouth of the stomach, with the result that the bowel is emptied more quickly. Cherries, plums, peaches, mulberries, and the other fleeting early fruits of that kind, which are eaten for their own sake and pass quickly, therefore belong to the first course, as do must and most honeyed things. Let those who grace second courses with cherries, plums and peaches consider this. Yet the custom has so prevailed in more luxurious tables and in princely courts that people think their palate is cheated if these are not served. By the same reasoning, those who eat solid and hard foods at the first course seriously weaken their health: smoked and hardened meats, and meats taken away from dinner or supper, kept, and set out again the next day. For a not unimportant rule of preserving health is that warm things, so far as they are warm, go before cold; soft before hard; moist before dry. Thus it is fitting to eat apples before quinces, and quinces before chestnuts. I have thought it right to set out these points first, by way of preface [ἐν πρώτῳ].

units.la: Fructus igitur salubriores adq; rem ci-bariam pertinentes sunt poma, pyra, cerasa, mora, fraga, pruna, persica, melones, pepones, cucumeres, cotonea, mespila, sorba, ca-staneæ, nux juglans, auellana, amygdalæ, piftacia, nux pinea, malum citrium, oliuæ, ficus, uuæ, capparis. Horum tamen quædam diuersam naturam participant, ut dicetur suo loco.
units.tr: The fruits more wholesome and pertaining to the food supply are these: apples, pears, cherries, mulberries, strawberries, plums, peaches, melons, pumpkins, cucumbers, quinces, medlars, sorbs, chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds, pistachios, pine nuts, citrons, olives, figs, grapes and capers. Some of these, however, share a different nature, as will be explained in its place.

units.la: De Malis.
units.tr: On Apples.

units.la: MAlia dicuntur, quæ vulgo appellantur poma. Saporum in his multiplex differentia pro foli, cœlique natura & conditione, quæ magnas efficiunt mutationes. Pomorum in mensis fecundis quoniam magna est autoritas, palmamq; sibi ante alia vendicant, ab iis quoq; exordiri nō inconueniens duxi. Verum nominatissima persequi operosum est & parum vtile, nam pro nationum & populorum libidine nomi-naplerumq; variant. Ordinem præcipue modumq; edendi obseruandum est, & arctissime hic tenendum est. Galen. esum pomorum abdicandum censet iis, qui valetudine tueri student. Is enim quoties pomis cæterisq; frugib. immodice vescerentur, morbo tentabatur, vnde patris sui consilio (qui naturæ erat peritissimus) cautior factus, à pomis abstinuit, firmamq; sanitatem est adeptus. Sunt autem quædam prædulcia, quædam acida, aufteraq; alia & acerba. Cruda nondum matura ante cuncta fugienda sunt, gelidioris enim naturæ sunt, crudiq; plane succu accumulant, vnde non mirum, si grauib. variisq; morbis conflictetur pueri.
units.tr: Apples are what are commonly called pomes. Among them there is a manifold difference of flavour, according to the nature and condition of soil and climate, which make great changes. Since apples carry great weight among the fruits of the second course and claim the palm before others, I did not think it inappropriate to begin with them. To pursue all the most famous varieties, however, would be laborious and of little use, for names often vary according to the fancy of nations and peoples. The order and measure of eating must be observed, and here they must be kept most strictly. Galen judges that those who strive to preserve their health should renounce eating apples. Whenever he ate apples and other fruits immoderately, he fell ill; so, made more cautious by the advice of his father, who was most skilled in nature, he abstained from apples and attained firm health. Some apples are very sweet, some sour, and others astringent and bitter. Unripe raw ones must be avoided above all, for they are of colder nature and pile up crude juices. It is no wonder, then, that boys are afflicted with grave and various diseases.

units.la: NB.
units.tr: NB.

units.la: pueri & fœminæ, ventriculum potius vix dū incoatæ maturitatis explentes.
units.tr: Boys and women, who fill a stomach scarcely yet of full maturity.

units.la: Qui humanioribus dant operam lite- ris à fructuum crudorum esu plane abstinebunt, sensus enim heberant, mentis arcem caligine replent, capita infirmiora admodum conflictant, cutimq; {scabie vlceribusq;} commaculant.
units.tr: Those who devote themselves to the humane letters will abstain entirely from eating raw fruit. For it dulls the senses, fills the citadel of the mind with darkness, greatly afflicts the weaker heads, and stains the skin with scabies and ulcers.

units.la: Belle matura, quæ in hiemem & æstate tem seruari poslunt, commendantur, salutares enim vitæ hominum præstant vsus. Coctæ præterea, vel tosta ex butyro cum saccharo salubriora sunt, inque cibis magis grata. Generosa tamen quæ sunt, raro ignem exuunt periuntur, cruda enim à magnatibus edunt tur, ignobiliora, vt acerba & austera focum defiderant, coctione enim astrictionem auferitatemque amittunt.
units.tr: Well-ripened apples, which can be kept through winter and summer, are commended, for they offer wholesome use to human life. Moreover, apples cooked or roasted in butter with sugar are more wholesome and more agreeable to eat. Choice kinds, however, rarely lose their quality by cooking, and great men eat them raw. The baser kinds, such as the sour and austere, need the fire, for cooking takes away their astringency and harshness.

units.la: Quapropter pernitiofum non est, vt quidam volunt, adaluum emolliendam potius ma coćta primo cibo & mensaassumere, præsertim vero dulcia, quæ medium tempe- ramentum obtinent, adque calorem nonni- hil vergunt: cætera gelidioris sunt naturæ, inprimis vero fera & syl uestria, quibus ferox quoque & sapor, & succus est. Acida, au- fteraque stomacho robur afferunt, astrin- gendoque aluum fluentem sistunt, stoma- chique vomitiones compescunt præsertim acerba, coćta ac parata.
units.tr: Therefore it is not harmful, as some wish, to take cooked apples at the first course and before the meal in order to soften the bowel, especially the sweet ones, which hold a middle temperament and incline somewhat to warmth. The others are of colder nature, especially the wild and woodland apples, which also have a fierce flavour and juice. Sour and astringent apples give strength to the stomach; by binding the loose bowel they check it, and they restrain vomiting of the stomach, especially the bitter ones, cooked and prepared.

units.la: Insipida & aquosa cibis plane abdicada sunt, stomacho enim aduersant fenfibiliter. Dulcia quaedam & vinosa olfactu mire, cor familiaritate quadam singulari recreant, unde in pharmacopoliis sirupus de pomis celebratur. Vino hausto sapore & odore ingratissimae euadunt. Quae prima aestate fere quibusdam in locis maturescunt Paradysea à quibusdam, aestiua & poma S. Ioh appellantur, parua quidem, sed odore suaui & praedulci, odoreq; iucundo. Haec prima mensa & alios cibos efficanda sunt, vitiantur enim in ventriculo, si sequantur alios cibos. Hodie in magnatum aulis fecundae mensae frequenter imponuntur, adeo praepostere & confuse omnia administrantur. Melimela enim omnia, multea, & mellea fecundis mensis abdicanda esse, inter primas vero mensae volu-ptates salubriter vsurpari ratione & experientia constat. Cortex pomorum odorato-rum carbonibus iniectus, suauem suffitum reddit, pestilentiaeque resistere inuentus est. Caeterum in quibusdam Germaniae locis pomafolent (praesertim cum vberior hornm est prouentus, aut cum vermibus teredinibus quoq; corroduntur, quod plurimum fieri solet, si ante perfectam maturitatem decerpuntur) in minutas easque oblongas partes dissecari, adq; fornacem filo appensa, vel etiam in fur-no, vt pyra quaedam, exiccari, quae ad rei esca-
units.tr: Insipid and watery apples must be entirely banished from food, for they plainly oppose the stomach. Some sweet and winy apples refresh the heart wonderfully by a singular affinity, which is why syrup of apples is celebrated in the apothecaries' shops. Once wine has been drunk, they become most unpleasant in taste and smell. Those that ripen in early summer in some parts of Germany, called Paradise apples by some and summer or St John's apples by others, are small but have a sweet and very pleasant smell. These are to be set at the first course and before other food, for they spoil in the stomach if they follow other food. Today at the tables of the great, second courses are frequently set out, so topsy-turvy and confused is everything managed. For it is established by reason and experience that all honey-apples, mellow and honeyed ones, must be banished from the second course, but may be taken wholesomely among the first pleasures of the table. The peel of fragrant apples thrown on charcoal makes a sweet fumigation, and has been found to resist pestilence. Moreover, in some parts of Germany apples are dried (especially when the crop is abundant, or when they are eaten by worms and woodborers, which very often happens if they are picked before full ripeness). They are cut into small, oblong pieces, hung on a thread over a furnace or even in an oven, like certain pears, and dried; they are then kept for a long time for use as food, uncorrupted.

units.la: S 5 ria riz vsús longo tempore feruantur incorru- pta. Verú coctainter alios cibos primò sunt attingenda,vt ocyus deiiciantur,poftalios e- nim cibos sumta in ventriculo vitiantur,atq; corrumpuntur. Salubritati igitur minime student,qui primo sumtis carnibus,tum aífis tum elixis, piscibusque poma cocta supere- derint, Qui mos hodié pertinaciter durat ob coquorum errorem & inscitiam. Quae- ftio deniq; hic prātermittenda non est,quae fēpe in hilarioribus ac Platonicis conuiuiis controuersiam excitare solet, an vinum ab esu pomorum crudorum fit protinus super- bibendum?&an meracum,an vero dilutum? Qui vinum fuperbibi non debere conten- dunt,hac fe muniunt ratione, quod videlicet vinum meracius, in venas cibos incoctos de- ducat,crudumque sanguinem efficiat , vnde omnis generis morbos existere necesse est; cruditates enim illæ cum sanguinea massa permixtæ malignamque qualitatem adeptæ, sanguinem ita inficiunt, vt morbi principa- lis causa existat. Qui in contraria sunt o- pinione aiunt, vinum fuperbibitum obtun- dere pernitiosos atque gelidos succos, eosq; concoquere. Experientia notum est,& re- centiorum quorundam scriptis euulgatum, quosdam vini haustu ab esu pomorum & pyrorum intolerabiles cruciatus & dolo- res perculisse, ( abefu pyrorum quendam plane planè cereuisiæ potu periisse, ipse testis esse possum ) alios quoque à ficuum esu, vini potu interisse, testis est Italia, quamuis Itali, qui hac in parte cautiores videntur, vinum meracum optimum à pomis & pepo-nibus superbibunt. Hìc vt certi aliquid statuatur, sequens prius quæstio, oportu-nè mihi hic occurrens, discutienda est, an poma cæterìque fructus cum pane sint e-dendi?
units.tr: Cooked apples, however, must be eaten first among other foods, so that they pass through more quickly, for eaten after other foods they spoil and rot in the stomach. Those, therefore, who eat cooked apples after meats first taken, whether roasted or boiled, and after fish, pay little heed to their health. This custom persists stubbornly today through the error and ignorance of cooks. Finally, a question must not be passed over here, one that often stirs up controversy at merry and Platonic banquets: must wine be drunk straight after eating raw fruit, and should it be undiluted or watered? Those who contend that wine ought not to be drunk on top of fruit defend themselves by this reasoning: undiluted wine draws the undigested food into the veins and makes crude blood, from which diseases of every kind must arise. For those crudities, mixed with the blood and acquiring a malignant quality, so infect the blood that it becomes the principal cause of disease. Those of the contrary opinion say that wine drunk on top blunts the harmful, cold juices and concocts them. It is known from experience, and has been published in the writings of some more recent authors, that some people, after drinking wine on top of eating apples and pears, suffered intolerable torments and pains. (I myself can testify that one man, after eating pears, died from drinking beer alone.) Others too died from wine after eating figs; Italy is witness. Yet the Italians, who seem more cautious in this matter, drink strong wine on top of apples and melons. So that something certain may be settled here, the following question, which occurs to me opportunely at this point, must first be discussed: are apples and other fruits to be eaten with bread?

units.la: Distinctione hìc opus esse video, inter fructus videlicet præcoces, qui citò maturescunt, & citò corrumpuntur, vt sunt cerasa, dulcia, fraga, pruna, persica, mora, & inter eos, qui per integrum feruantur annum, vt poma quædam, castaneæ, auellanæ, iuglandes. Quidam mediam naturam participant, vt ficus[?], vuæ, pyra & pomorum genera quædam, hæc enim nō ita facilè putrescunt, nec tam longo tempore perdurant, vt castaneæ, &c. Quidam non infimæ eruditionis atque grauitatis autores, primi ordinis fructus in vniuersum absque pane comedi debere existimant, quoniam sunt substantiæ tenuioris aqueæque, facilimeque putrescunt.
units.tr: Here I see a distinction is needed: between early fruits, which ripen quickly and spoil quickly, such as cherries, sweet cherries, strawberries, plums, peaches and mulberries, and those which keep for a whole year, such as certain apples, chestnuts, hazelnuts and walnuts. Some share a middle nature, such as figs[?], grapes, pears and certain kinds of apples, for these do not rot so easily, nor last so long, as chestnuts and the like. Some authors of no little learning and weight hold that the first class of fruits should on the whole be eaten without bread, since they are of a thinner, watery substance and very easily rot.

units.la: His verò ego regero, eò magis cum pane vitandos[?] esse, quia panis firmissimū esculentorūq; potulentorumq; vinculum, facilem eorum putredinem & corruptionem retardat
units.tr: To this I reply that they are all the more to be avoided with bread, because bread is the firmest bond of foods and drinks and slows their easy putrefaction and corruption

units.la: & impedit, tenuioremque ipsorum fubftan- tiam crassiorem reddit, quò minus in ventri- culo fluctuent. Verissimum est, quicquid etiam hic statuatur, cerasa, pruna, persica, fi fecunda mensa apponuntur fine pane efficate insalubre prorfuseffe, praesertim fi multum fuperbibatur, id quod omnibus sanitatis có- feruande studiosis diligenter obseruandum relinquo: cum pane enim ita commixti non adeo facile corrumpuntur, nam panis veluti refrenat Itorum malitiam. De fecundi ordi- nis fructibus sciendum, illos à cibo edendos esse, & quidem aliàs cum pane, aliàs fine eo. Cum pane, fi superbiendum est, vt in lautio- ribus conuiuiis: fine pane at cum sale, fi exic- care, nec multum fuperbibere animuseft, substantia enim eorum magis est terrea, hu- moribusque non redundat, tum etiam, nefi primò sumerétur, quia grauia sunt, cibi par- ticulam crudam ac incoctam per venas fecū rapiant, vnde putredines h imorumque cor- ruptiones (praesertim fi in venis permanse- rint) generari necesse est.
units.tr: and hinders it, and makes their thinner substance thicker, so that they do not churn so much in the stomach. It is most true, whatever is held here, that cherries, plums and peaches, if set out at the second course without bread, are commonly harmful, especially if much wine is drunk on top of them, a point I leave to be carefully observed by all who are keen to preserve their health. For when mixed with bread in this way they do not corrupt so easily, since bread, as it were, restrains their malice. As for fruits of the second order, it should be known that they are to be eaten as food, sometimes with bread, sometimes without it. With bread, if they are to be drunk over, as at more lavish banquets; without bread but with salt, if one wishes to dry them out and does not intend to drink much over them, for their substance is more earthy and does not overflow with moisture. Then also, unless they are taken first, because they are heavy, they drag along with them through the veins raw and undigested particles of food, whence putrefactions of the humours and corruptions (especially if they have remained in the veins) must inevitably arise.

units.la: Ex medii ordinis fructibus ficus, cumpri- mis recentes vuaeque ante alios cibos, & qui- dem cum pane edantur, pyra veró pomaque fugacia & praecocia, quae videlicet citò ma- turefcunt, fecunda etiam mensa concedi pof- sunt fine pane, fi nihil fuperbibatur, est enim id valdè noxium, cum multo ... (et)
units.tr: Of the fruits of the middle order, figs, especially fresh ones, and grapes are to be eaten before other foods, and indeed with bread; pears and apples that are fleeting and early, that is, which ripen quickly, may be allowed at the second course without bread, provided nothing is drunk over them, for that is very harmful, since with much ... (and)

units.la: humore & corruptioni facilè ebnoxia. In dysenteria omnes fructus, prasertim astrin- gentes, vt pyra,mora,sorba,cotonea,cum pa- ne edi debere recte voluit Alexander Tralli- anus. Horum enim succus cum panis sub- stantia mixtus,perque intima corporis pene- trans,aluum sistit. Sine verò pane comesta ventrem repente & facilè penetrant,parum- que aut nihil de facultate sua in intestinis re- linquunt. Experimento didici, pyrorum, cerasorum prasertim acidorum, mororum, prunorum,&c. succum post cibum degluti- tum minus noxæ inferre, quam si cum tota substantia deuorentur, succus enim ille vino exhilaratis fumos reprimit,absolutoq; pran- dio efficit, vt quis minus ebrietati succum- bat,mensque minus ex vapore vini debilite- tur. In hoc casu quoque praestant poma suc- culenta,citria,arantia,&c. Quidam distin- ctione vtuntur in determinanda hac quaesti- one. Fructus enim nunc medicamenti,nunc cibi rationem subeunt.Si sumuntur vt medi- camentum, absque pane estari debent,alui sc. emolliendi corporisque alterandi gratiā, vt refrigerandi,astringendi,humectandi,&c. Si enim cum cibis sumerentur,vis & facultas spissorum obtunderetur, fungiqúe officio suo minimè possent. Si vt cibi sumuntur,cum pa- ne,efficacissime expedit, ne velociter aluum subeant, sed inventriculo paulisper remaneant. Præceptū Vnum deniq; probè animaduertendum hīc notatu dignum est, si minus malum esse, si fructibus vescentes sint, quod tot diuersarum qualitatum ac virium cibos non admiscuerint, manifestum enim est, si naturæ cibis appetitum excitari quidem, sed multò plus ingerere quam conueniat, vnde cruditates multas humos-rumque putredines existere necesse est, tandemque morbos. Vno igitur victus gene-re simus contenti.
units.tr: moisture and easily liable to corruption. In dysentery all fruits, especially astringent ones, such as pears, mulberries, service-berries and quinces, should rightly be eaten with bread, as Alexander of Tralles held. For their juice, mixed with the substance of the bread and penetrating the inner parts of the body, checks the bowel. But eaten without bread they penetrate the belly suddenly and easily, and leave little or nothing of their virtue in the intestines. I have learned by experience that the juice of pears, especially sour cherries, mulberries, plums and so on, when swallowed after a meal, does less harm than when they are gulped down whole, for that juice checks the vapours of those who are cheered with wine, and, when the meal is over, makes it so that a person succumbs less to drunkenness and the mind is less weakened by the fumes of wine. In this case also juicy apples, citrons, oranges and so on are useful. Some use a distinction in settling this question. For fruits sometimes take the place of medicine, sometimes of food. If they are taken as medicine, they ought to be taken without bread, namely for the sake of softening the bowels and altering the body, as for cooling, astringing, moistening and so on. For if they were taken with foods, the power and virtue of their astringent qualities would be blunted and they could not perform their office. If they are taken as food, it is most expedient to take them with bread, so that they do not pass quickly through the bowel but remain a little while in the stomach. Finally, one thing should be carefully noted here as worth remembering: it is less harmful, if one is eating fruits, that one does not mix in many foods of different qualities and powers. For it is clear that the appetite is indeed aroused by such foods, but one takes in far more than is fitting, whence many crudities and putrefactions of the humours must arise, and at last diseases. Let us therefore be content with one kind of diet.

units.la: Prætereà in fluxu alui & dysenteria nonnopus semper est astringentia ante omnes ali-os cibos exhibere ; sed quandoque etiam post exhibita & medicamenta, & alimenta pro uentriculi scilicet corroboratione, vt ita ventriculi os corroboratū phibere possit, nè humores amplius in intestina confluant. Vere rū iudicio hic opus est, quàdo videl. & quo-modo astringentes fructus in statu etiam sa-nitatis sint exhibendi. Ex hactenus igitur dictis, facilè iudicare est de proposita supra quaestione, an vinum post crudorum pomo-rum essum statim sit superbibendum? Cesso igitur ne minima prolixitate lectorem fatigare videar. De potu ex pomis multis gentibus vsitato, vide cap. de potulentis.
