units.tr: Moreover, in a flux of the bowels and in dysentery it is not always necessary to give astringents before all other foods; sometimes, however, they are also given after medicines and foods, namely to strengthen the stomach, so that the strengthened mouth of the stomach may prevent the humours from flowing any further into the intestines. But here there is need of true judgment: namely when, and in what manner, astringent fruits are to be given even in a state of health. From what has been said so far, it is easy to judge the question raised above: whether wine should be drunk immediately after eating raw apples? I will therefore cease, lest I seem to weary the reader with any excessive length. Concerning the drink made from apples, which many peoples use, see the chapter on drinks.

units.la: De pyris.
units.tr: On pears.

units.la: GEnera pyrorum enumerare nemo poterit, & quae de pomis sunt dicta, pariter de pyris fere intelligi possunt. Quaedam ad maturitatem properant, suntque prima quae decerpuntur, ac saporis gratissimi deprehenduntur. Sunt & alia quae tardius ad maturitatem perveniunt, ut amümno[?], quae etiam reservata durant in hiemem, crudaque, & coctissimè manduntur, sunt autem quae mirum in modum grandescunt, ac viridiora cernuntur, à nostris hominibus vocantur Winterbieren / quod in menses durent hibernos. Inter muscatellina, omniaque alia quae palato grata sunt, trimas tenent, quae vulgo appellantur Alandsbie-ren / saporis suavissimi ac jucundissimi, unde prae caeteris omnibus nutrire bonumque corpori succum praebere creduntur: perfecte autem matura tales praestant usus, & alteram partem rubescunt, eáq; una flauescunt. Verum hic tenendum, pyrorum sicut & pomorum musteorum nimio e-su homines quandoque strangulari seu suffocari, saporis enim tanta est gratia, ut nec appetendi nec edendi finis sit. Itaq; servandus modus. Quidam ex pyris concinnant potum, qui tamen tanta gratia utilitatisque non est, quam potus ex pomis, qui saepe subiicitur pro vino inter epulas, quique sunt crassiori palato, vix fraudem[?] deprehendunt.
units.tr: No one could list all the kinds of pears, and what has been said of apples can be applied almost equally to pears. Some ripen early, and these are the first to be picked; they are found to have a most pleasant flavour. Others ripen later, such as the amümno[?], which also keep when stored and last into winter; these are eaten raw or thoroughly cooked. Some grow to an astonishing size and look rather green; our people call these Winterbieren, because they last through the winter months. Among the muscatels and all other pears that are pleasing to the palate, the best are the trimas, commonly called Alandsbieren. Their flavour is most sweet and agreeable, and they are believed to nourish more than all the others and to give the body good juice. When fully ripe, they show their best qualities; they redden on one side and turn yellow on the other. But here we must keep in mind that people are sometimes choked or suffocated by eating too many pears, just as with must-apples, since their flavour is so charming that there is no end to desiring or eating them. So moderation must be observed. Some make a drink from pears, which however does not have the same charm or usefulness as the drink from apples, which is often served instead of wine at feasts; people with coarser palates hardly notice the difference.

units.la: Occurrit mihi hic admodum lepida & facete tofa historia, de perfido quodam Iudeo à pagano quodam huius loci, anno 1604. emturo vinum, Is vinariam cellam pagani ingressus, vina eius vendibilia, quae peculiaribus in dolis feorfim re- ponsa continuebantur, degustans inter pituitandi elegit dolium cotinens potus ex fele&u pomum ob- mas 4. Piganus, vix fore exi&imans, ut Iudeus hunc, cuius perfidia & impostura toti vicinia erat nota & permissa, dolo circumveniret, confirmando, de pretio consensus, Iudeus vinum ex pomis, quod principii vel potius stupido sup- pius palato magis placuerat, letus ad suos defer- ri cura, gloriam non defiles, miserere fraudis illum paganum a fe deceptum effecit, emptus fe pro tolerabili pretio vinum, quo vix praestan- tius aliud. Verum praestanti illo vino acorem acquirens & mucorem (quod facile ex dolio vel non usqueque, pleno, veletiam non probe occlu- fo contingere potuit, vel etiam, si doli ano exque- sire plena, alio quam ipsa continent liquore, ope- rantur) cum fe deceptum intelligeret, paganis perfidia & malitia incusat. Venum est ad ina- dicem, actum est, pronunciatum, Iudeus damnatum vinum retinere, quod ipse sibi ex multis aliis elegerat, iura coegerunt. Hactenus de Iudeo, nunc adrem.
units.tr: Here there comes to my mind a very witty and amusing story about a treacherous Jew and a certain pagan of this place, in the year 1604. The Jew, about to buy wine, entered the pagan's wine cellar, tasted his saleable wines, which were kept stored separately in their own casks, and chose from among them a cask containing a drink made from apples. The pagan, scarcely thinking that the Jew, whose treachery and trickery were well known and tolerated by the whole neighbourhood, could be taken in by a trick, agreed on the price. The Jew, pleased that the apple wine had appealed to his palate more than the others, had it carried home happily, and, not sparing his boasting, made the pagan he had cheated pay a tolerable price for the wine, which was hardly any better than the others. But when the wine, which had been excellent, began to turn sour and mouldy (which could easily happen if the cask was not completely full, or was not properly sealed, or if the bunghole was left open and the air worked on the liquid it contained), the Jew, realising he had been deceived, accused the pagan of treachery and malice. The matter was taken to court, the case was argued and judgment was given: the law compelled the Jew to keep the spoiled wine, which he had himself chosen from many others. So much for the Jew; now back to the subject.

units.la: Pyrorum bodie quadam torrentur furno, a- liacinere feruente, quadam ex butyro coquun- tur cum saccharo culina, cum vino, cinnamomo & & saccharo: pistores dulciarii cinnamomo confi-guntur, & incrustata coquunt, idq; pro variis gulae irritamentis. Solent etiam concidi pyra, sicut & poma ac cotonea, siccataq;, reseruari advsum ci-barium durant enim in annum & ultra. Quidam non leues autores omnia pyra astringere exiccareq;, aperte scripserunt, quod falsum esse (pace eorum) experientia testatur, quædam enim adeo succosa sunt mitia & suauia, vt astri-[?]lam aluum molliant, lubricamq; reddant.
units.tr: Today some pears are roasted in an oven, others are cooked in an ashen fire, some are cooked in a pan with butter, wine, cinnamon and sugar; confectioners prepare them with cinnamon and sugar and bake them in crusts, and all this for various stimulants of the appetite. Pears, like apples and quinces, are also commonly cut up and dried and kept for food; they last for a year or more. Some not unimportant authors have openly written that all pears are astringent and drying; this is false, as experience shows (with due respect to them), for some are so juicy, mild and sweet that they soften the bowels and make them loose.

units.la: Decerafis.
units.tr: On cherries.

units.la: Ominantur hæc à Ponti oppido Ce-rafunte, vnde Mithridate & Tigrane deuictis à Lucullo in Italiam sunt de-uecta, anno vrbis DCLXXX. teste Plinio & Atheneo, quamuis longè ante Luculli vi-ctoriā cerasa cognita fuisse Diphilus Siphni* ipso Lucullo multis annorum curriculis vetu-stior, testatur, qui de iis scripsit. Distinguuntur colore & sapore, quædam enim rubent, quæ-dam nigrescunt, alia albescunt simul & rube-scunt: quædam item dulcia sunt, quædam a-mariuscula, alia acida quæ principatum obti-nuerunt, quædam subacida, gratiqué saporis sunt. Varias autem sortiuntur appellationes, quædam enim vocantur Macedonica, alia aproniana, nonnulla actiana, luliana & Du-racina. Sed de nominib° nolumus esse super-stitiosi ftitiofi & solliciti , viribus explorandis in- cumbamus. Quæ tardius maturitatem adi- pifcuntur vtacida, principatum obtinent,ci- bi enim appetentiam excitant, pituitamqué incidunt,aftringendiqe sua vi ventriculum roborant, inest enim illis succus vinosus & miré gratus. Prædulcia & matura aluum e- molliunt,ocyusq; deiiciuntur,adeò quidem,
units.tr: These take their name from the Pontic town of Cerasus, from which they were carried to Italy by Lucullus after he had defeated Mithridates and Tigranes, in the year 680 from the founding of the city, according to Pliny and Athenaeus; although Diphilus of Siphnos, who wrote about them and was much older than Lucullus by many years, attests that cherries were known long before Lucullus' victory. They are distinguished by colour and flavour: some are red, some blacken, others are both white and red; some are sweet, some slightly bitter, and others sour, which have gained the first place; some are somewhat sour and have a pleasant flavour. They receive various names: some are called Macedonian, others Apronian, some Actian, Julian and Duracine. But we do not wish to be superstitious or anxious about names; let us devote ourselves to examining their powers. Those that ripen late and are sour take first place, for they stimulate the appetite, cut phlegm, and strengthen the stomach by their astringent power, since they contain a wine-like juice that is wonderfully pleasant. The very sweet and ripe ones soften the bowels and are quickly voided, so much so

units.la: vt fi quis manè roscida ea deuoret,in tantum leuetur aluus,vt pedes podagrici morbo li- berentur. Omnia cerasa inprimis veró acida & rubentiora bonum generare succum te- nuitrque[?] alere,cum peruetufto scriptore & medico Diphilo constanter affirmo. Acida quoq; insolantur, saccharoque condiuntur, quæ sitientibus ægris linguaq; ariditati ma- gnum afferunt auxilium.Siccantur etiam fo- le vel furno dulcia,sicut & acida,vbi id mira- ri subit , quod illa acescant,hæc verò dulce- fcant. Non probantur quæ arte fiunt præco- cia,calce fc.viua aut aqua calida arborum ra- dicibus affusa,
units.tr: that if someone eats them fresh in the morning, the bowels are so relieved that gouty feet are freed from the disease. I affirm, together with the very ancient writer and physician Diphilus, that all cherries, and especially the sour and redder ones, produce good juice and nourish thinly. Sour cherries are also dried in the sun and preserved with sugar, and they bring great relief to sick people who are thirsty and to tongues parched with dryness. Sweet cherries are also dried in the sun or in an oven, like sour ones, and it is remarkable that the sour ones become sweet in this way, while the sweet ones... [become sour]. Those that are forced early by art, by applying quicklime or warm water to the roots of the trees, are not approved of.

units.la: Ex acidis deniq; vel solis vel etiam dulci- bus permistis, diligentes matresfamilias no- runt concinnare edulium electuarii instar, quod magni est vsus in re cibaria & familia- ri. In amplo vase æneo coquuntur luculen- to igne: semicocta cribrātur nucleis abiectis, quod per cribrum traiectum est, coquitur denuò perpetuò agitando,donec iustam ele- ctuarii [?]uarii consistentiam adipiscatur, lautiores condiunt id zinzibere, cinnamomo, pipere, garyophyllis &c.
units.tr: Finally, diligent housewives know how to make from sour cherries, or from sour and sweet mixed together, a sweetmeat in the manner of an electuary, which is of great use in food and in the household. It is cooked in a large bronze vessel over a clear fire; when half cooked it is passed through a sieve after the stones have been removed, and what has passed through the sieve is cooked again, stirring constantly, until it reaches the proper consistency of an electuary. The more refined cooks season it with ginger, cinnamon, pepper, cloves, and so on.

units.la: Dixi superstitiosum esse denominibus al-tercari, sed potius in rebus ipsis versari atque perfiltere, distinguenda enim cetafa, sicut & cæteri fructus sunt non ex nominum appel-latione, in qua autores maxime dissentiunt, facilifq; lapsus est, sed ex adiunctis ipsis qua-litatibus, vt sapore, odore & colore, natura ac vites omnium fructuum inuestigantur.
units.tr: I said it is superstitious to dispute over names, but it is better to dwell on the things themselves and examine them closely; for cherries, like other fruits, are to be distinguished not by the use of names, on which authors disagree most and where mistakes are easily made, but by their own qualities, such as taste, smell and colour, and their nature and powers are to be investigated.

units.la: Quis enim Cerasorum omnium sicut & py-torum genera, species & figuras enumerare quèat, taceo appellationes & nomina, quæ cuique fere terræ & genti sunt peculiaria.
units.tr: For who could list all the kinds, species and forms of cherries, just as with pears? I say nothing of the names and appellations that are almost peculiar to each land and people.

units.la: Itaq; curiosius ea diftinguete fupertacuum puto, cum nemini non sint notissima. Dura-cina saltè ea appellari ab autoribus animad-uerti, quæ duriori sunt callo & nucleo.
units.tr: So I think it is superfluous to distinguish them more carefully, since they are all very well known to everyone. I have noticed that the authors call by the name Duracine at least those which have a harder skin and stone.

units.la: De moris.[?]
units.tr: On mulberries.

units.la: Nouissimis florent, & inter prima matu-refcunt. Arbor exatlo frigore quia germinat, prudentissima dicitur. Algida loca reformi-dat, propterea, non vbiq; prosenit. Ex moris co-fectlæ eclegma adoris & colli vlcera interna vti-liter adhibetur cum melle rofarū. Memorabile, quod Pythagoras apud Atheneum memoriæ pro-didit, l.2.c.20, moros in sua patria per 20. annos fructū[?] nulla[?] protulisse, atq; tanta podagra omnes [illegible, ~3 letters] fuisse, vt homines nō solum pueri, item puellæ; Eunuchi & mulieres, eo morbo tentarentur, sed etiam caprarum ouium, q; gregem ita infe-stârit, ut vix tertia earum pars extaret libera.
units.tr: They flower last, and among the first they ripen. Because the tree sprouts only after the hard frost, it is called the wisest. It shuns cold places and therefore does not grow everywhere. An electuary made from mulberries, with rose honey, is usefully applied to internal ulcers of the mouth and throat. Pythagoras, as Athenaeus records (book 2, chapter 20), reported something memorable: in his homeland the mulberry bore no fruit for twenty years, and there was such gout that not only boys, girls, eunuchs and women were attacked by the disease, but also the goats and sheep, which so infested the flock that scarcely a third of them remained free.

units.la: An vero hoc ita euenerit, quia more podagram arcent, in controuersiam venire potest. Testatur Galenus atq; Hippocr. mora qua fatis maturue-runt, ventrem subducere, stomachumq; squalli-dum astuantem, consolari, preferim frigida si-sint, & paulo ante alios cibos sumantur, moxq; fiat deambulatio, unde Horatius non immerite dixerit, cecinit, Ille salubres, Æstates peraget, qui nigris prandia mo-ris. Finiet, ante grauem quæ legerit arbore solem.
units.tr: Whether this happened because mulberries ward off gout can be disputed. Galen and Hippocrates testify that ripe mulberries loosen the bowels and soothe a foul, heated stomach, especially when they are cold and are eaten shortly before other foods, and when a walk follows. Hence Horace not unreasonably said: "He will spend healthy summers who takes his breakfast of black mulberries, gathered from the tree before the heavy sun."

units.la: Peculiari verò facultate podagricis auxilia-ri, quæ minus illi infestentur, ànemine adhuc vi-di obseruatum. Experimenti via facilis est. Ve-risimile tamen est, ac fieri potuisse credibile mo-ra frequenter Pytharini etate ab omnib. essitat stomachis recreatis aliud, liquatis & emollitę eorum humorum lapsum & prouentum, qui si articulos decumbentes podagram gignere con-sueuerunt, intercipere. Id quod & Galenus con-firmat, dicens, aliquos habentes affectus podagriæ esse obnoxios. Verum de capris & oribus, quæ mororum fructus non attingunt, & tamen ab eâ luce immunes nō extiterunt, quid sentiam, nō oc-currit, nisi quod ex aere inclementia quadammoris inimica, in pedum morbos inciderint. Morus enim, teste Theophrasto quia nouissime omnium germinat, si quando pruina ledatur, vel frigoribus, quemadmodum ledi productum est, Pfal. 77. ex apud Plinium lib. 16. cap. 26. intemperiem coeli insignem esse conflat, quâ etiam ad pedes deducit ac delabi defluxiones non est à ratione alienum. Trinus inest moris color, primo candidus, mox rubens, maturus niger: rubea acerbiora sunt, matura vinosa. Certum est abstrusum quid & magneticum hanc arborem, certis indicare indiciis, isq; externis, de qua tamen re firmiore experientia auctus, dicam aliquid amplius alibi.
units.tr: I have not yet seen anyone observe that mulberries help gouty people in any special way, so that they are less troubled by it. The test is easy to make. It is nevertheless likely, and credible that it could have happened, that in Pythagoras' time mulberries, eaten frequently by everyone, refreshed the stomachs, and by softening and loosening the humours, prevented the downward flow and outpouring of those humours which usually settle in the joints and cause gout. Galen too confirms this, saying that some people with a tendency to gout are liable to it. As for goats and sheep, which do not touch mulberry fruit and yet were not spared that plague, I do not see what to think, except that from the unseasonable air, some quality hostile to mulberries, they fell into diseases of the feet. For mulberry, as Theophrastus testifies, since it sprouts last of all trees, if it is harmed by frost or cold, as was reported in Pliny (book 16, chapter 26), clearly signals an extraordinary intemperance of the sky, which also drives downward to the feet, and it is not unreasonable that such fluxes fall there. The mulberry has three colours: first white, then red, and when ripe black. The red ones are more sour, the ripe ones wine-like. It is certain that this tree indicates some hidden and magnetic thing by certain external signs; I will say something more on this elsewhere, when the matter is supported by firmer experience.

units.la: De moris albis cur ânullofere antiquorum men-tio factâ fit (excepto Ouidio, qui in fabula Py-rami & Tisbes, vbi eorum sanguine mora alba rubrum contrax: ffe colorem canens videtur po-tius vlla candida inueniri negaffe) facile est illis intelligere, qui norunt, id arboris genus ex insitio-ne super populum albam facta emanasse, que cum in Europa ac sub Romani imperii ditione fere apparuerit, sicut complures alia insitiones, mirum non est, si pauca de ipsis ab autoribus tra-dita legantur. Quam etiam causam esse puto, quod sericum ad Galeni vfq; tempora rarum fuerit, qui in 13. lib. method. scribit, id in vrbibus Romanorum magnis tantum opulentisque mulieribus familiare fuisse. Ea enim animalcula, que sericam nobis diuina quadam arte labam fundunt, quia potissimum folijs mori nutri-
units.tr: Why the ancients mention white mulberries so rarely (apart from Ovid, who in the story of Pyramus and Thisbe, where the white mulberry turned red with their blood, seems to have denied that any white ones are found at all) is easy to understand for those who know that this kind of tree arose from grafting onto the white poplar. Since it appeared mainly in Europe and under Roman rule, as were many other grafts, it is no wonder that few accounts of it are handed down by writers. I think this is also the reason why silk was rare until the time of Galen, who writes in the thirteenth book of his Method that its use was confined to the great cities of the Romans and to very wealthy women. For those little creatures which, by a certain divine art, spin silk for us feed mainly on mulberry leaves, and grow more fruitful and fatter on them,

units.la: T 3 uniuer, untur, iisq, pinguefatla fœcundiora euadunt, sicut varioratuncfuerunt, & pauciora, itaet- iam moyorum tenuis erat & rarus prouentus, Tejlatur enim in vita luftriani Zonaras, Im- peraoris illius tempore sericam telam à Roma- nis texi ceptam, quæ prius à Perficis mercatori- bus adzech-batur, quomodo, ex vermium iflo- rum tela filiq, fieret, ignorabatur. Duos enim monachos ex India Byzantium profectos origi- nem illius declaraffe, vtq, ex perexigua ouis per fotum vermes isti educerentur, eaubi mori foliis alerentur, postmodum ipsis natura magistrà fi- lum reddentibus sericum texeretur, nó fine mul- tis muneribus edocuisse idem auctor est. De eo- gypria moro nobis ignota, qui aliquid [cire deli- derat,videat Theophr. l.4.c.2.
units.tr: and as these were few and scarce, so the yield of mulberries was also thin and rare. For Zonaras records in the life of the emperor Justinian that under that emperor the Romans began to weave silk cloth, which had previously been bought from Persian merchants, and that how silk was made from the threads of these worms was unknown. The same author says that two monks who had travelled from India to Byzantium explained its origin, and taught that these worms are hatched from a very small egg, are fed on mulberry leaves, and that afterwards, with nature as their teacher, they yield thread from which silk is woven; and they taught this not without many gifts. As for the Egyptian mulberry, which is unknown to us, whoever wishes to learn anything about it should see Theophrastus, book 4, chapter 2.

units.la: De fragis.
units.tr: On strawberries.

units.la: Ehis parum à veteribus medicis pro- ditum reperitur. Quidam fructum terræ nominant, & fraga terrestria, ad differentiam mororum Celsi, de quibus in præcedente cap. & mororum rubi, quæ vulgus Himbeeren und Brombeeren appellat. Fructus sunt pulcrè rubentes,fuauisq; odoris. Reperiuntur & fraga à maturitate candida, sed rariora sunt. Feminarum nobi- le genus fraga in maximis habet delitiis, e- dunt enim ea ex lactis cremore saccharo insperfo:aliæ vino irrigant,facchariq; pollinem adiiciunt, quædam statim lectaac decerpta vorantur.Pulticulæ quoq; ex fragis concinnantur pro delicatioribus aduersus iecoris, stomachi,renumq; æstum[?] utiles. Cui etiam rei miré conducit aqua destillata, calentem enim nimis sanguinem refrigerat & recreat, faciẽq; plurimum rubentibus auxilio est.Hic verò errorem coarguere oportet, quod ple- riq; omnes potissimum feré Magnates secú- das suas mensas iis exornant, cum ut cerasa[?], mora,cæteraq; fugacia primo cibo fumi de- beant,aluum enim molliunt, refrigerant & humectant,sitimque leniunt, peracto enim ptandio[?],aut cœna in corpus admissa putref- cunt, morbisq; ex putredine excitatis seminaria ministrant. Adnotasse[?] præterea hoc in loco oportebit, fraga, ut quæ parum à terra distent,facilè à serpentibus,bufonibus, & id genus venenatis animalibus calcari, arrodique,nec tamen virus accipere, autalienum saporem affumere, quod argumento est nullamiis cum venenis esse cognationem: neq; enim scriptum aut auditum vsquam est, quenquam e[?]u horum veneno infectum fuisse. Nihilominus tamen decerpta, antequam deuorentur, frigidâ purâ abluantur.
units.tr: The ancient physicians have left little about this. Some call it the earth's fruit and "terrestrial strawberries", to distinguish it from the mulberries of Celsus, discussed in the previous chapter, and from the bramble berries, which the common people call Himbeeren and Brombeeren. The fruits are beautifully red and sweet-smelling. White strawberries are also found when ripe, but they are rarer. Women of noble birth hold strawberries in the highest delight: some eat them with cream of milk sprinkled with sugar, others steep them in wine and add sugar dust, and some are eaten straight away as soon as they are picked. Poultices are also made of strawberries, counted among the more delicate remedies, useful against heat of the liver, stomach and kidneys. Distilled water is also wonderfully suited to this purpose, for it cools and refreshes blood that is too hot, and it is a great help to those who blush easily. Here, however, one must correct an error: most people, especially the great men, adorn their second courses with them, whereas, like cherries, mulberries and other perishable fruits, they ought to be taken with the first course. For they soften the bowels, cool and moisten, and calm thirst; but when eaten after breakfast or supper they rot in the body and provide a seedbed for diseases arising from putrefaction. It will also be worth noting here that strawberries, since they lie close to the ground, are easily trodden on and gnawed by snakes, toads and that kind of venomous animal, yet they do not take on poison or acquire a foreign taste. This is evidence that there is no kinship between them and poisons; for it has never been written or heard anywhere that anyone was infected with poison from them. Nevertheless, before they are eaten, those that have been picked should be rinsed in cold pure water.

units.la: Quibus deniq; eparest frigidum[?], ventri-culusq; eadem intemperie laborat, vel à ni-mio fragorum vsu abstinebunt, vel come-dent ea ex vino cum saccharo & cinnamo-mo.
units.tr: Finally, those whose stomach is cold, and who suffer from the same intemperance, should either abstain from eating strawberries too much, or eat them with wine, sugar and cinnamon.

units.la: De prunis.
units.tr: On plums.

units.la: Pruna feré omnia post Catonem cœpisse certum est. Plura sunt eorum genera, sa-pore, colore, figura & magnitudine distin-cta[?]. Principatum obtinent Damascena, quorum quedam nigra sunt, quedam rubent, quedam violacea cernuntur. Sic appellata à celeberrima urbe Damasco, alii vocant Syriaca: deportantur sicca in omnem feré terram, inq; coquinis magnatum non postremum tenent locum. Consici-tur ex his confectio, quæ diaprunum appellatur, ad febres siccas commodissimum, ob humectan-di & refrigerandi vim. Recentia omnia aluum laxant, emolliunt, insigniter enim humectant probè matura, immatura enim acerbiora sunt, unde ob acriorem quendam qui illis inest, succum, crudum, intestina vellicant, fluxum, dy-sentericum excitant.
units.tr: It is fairly certain that nearly all plums began to be known after Cato's time. There are many kinds, distinguished by taste, colour, shape and size. The Damascene plums hold first place: some are black, some red, and some appear violet. They are so called from the famous city of Damascus, though others call them Syrian. They are exported dried to almost every land and hold no small place in the kitchens of the great. From them is made a confection called diaprunum, most suitable for dry fevers because of its power to moisten and cool. All fresh plums loosen the bowels and soften them, for well-ripened ones moisten markedly. Unripe plums are more sour, and because of a sharper juice in them they irritate the intestines when raw and bring on flux and dysentery.

units.la: Eligenda autem quæ amplitudine, suavitate, saporisq; gratiā commendantur, ea enim ceteris plus alunt, vino aut mulso incocta. Verum memineris, ante alios cibos horas aliquot commanducanda esse, nec cum aliis cibis miscenda. Recentium gratia quia non diu durat, siccari solent feruariq[?], viq; ad alia nascen-tia, ad varios in re cibaria usu. Succus quicq[?] prunorum a matribus quibusdam familiis decoquitur, ad sitim febricitantium levandam, linguae, ariditatem humectandam. Diosco-ridem mirantur multi, quod scripserit, siccata Damascena alvum nequaquam devicere, cum in confessio fit ea id praestare, brodio enim seu jus culo eorum nihil fere in alio leniter laxanda frequentius.
units.tr: One should choose those commended for size, sweetness and flavour, for these nourish more than the others when stewed in wine or mulled wine. But remember that they should be eaten some hours before other foods and not mixed with them. Since fresh plums do not keep long, they are commonly dried, or preserved, and used in many ways in cookery. Some housewives boil down the juice of plums to relieve the thirst of the feverish and to moisten a dry tongue. Many marvel at Dioscorides, who wrote that dried Damascene plums by no means loosen the bowels, since in the confection they do exactly that. For in broth or soup, scarcely anything is more often used for gentle laxative effect.

units.la: De Perficis.
units.tr: On peaches.

units.la: Persica mali succi esse, ut quo deterius in cibis esse nihil possit, doctissimi quique statuunt. Plinius l. 15. c. 12. pomum Persicum innocuum esse, experique undique ab aegris aperte scripsit, Et l. 23 c. 7. Persica utiliora esse stomacho quam pruna prodidit.
units.tr: The most learned all hold that the peach is of bad juice, so that nothing in food can be worse. Pliny, book 15, chapter 12, wrote that the peach is harmless, and from everywhere it is clearly reported that the sick use it. In book 23, chapter 7, he stated that peaches are more useful to the stomach than plums.

units.la: Sed a veritate eum aberrare, refellendumque propterea esse quidam contra scripserunt. Verum, quod pace illorum dixerim, innoxium esse malum Persicum aegris recte scripsisse Plinium sentio, in ardentibus enim febribus ob qualitatem frigidam
units.tr: But some have written against him, saying that he strays from the truth and must therefore be refuted. Yet, with their leave, I think Pliny rightly wrote that the peach is harmless to the sick, for in burning fevers, because of its cold

units.la: humidam persica mala prodesse nemo est qui inficias iturus est.
units.tr: and moist quality, peaches do good; no one would deny it.

units.la: Stomacho enim, cumprimis zftu tur-gidonon incommodant, modo ante alios ci-bos fumantur, quemadmodum 2. dealim.bene monet Galenus. Et quod hic de perfi-cis dicitur, debere ea alias escas precedere,id deomnibus temperariis & fugacibus fe-melfit dictum. Immodico liquore perficaluxuriare constat, vnde promtissime celeri-terque putrescere solent, qua de causa con-tinuus multiplexque eorum vsus improba-tur; præsertim ventriculo existente humi-do & flatulento. Paulus Æginetha coacesce-re statim in ventriculo docuit, & admodum esse improbi succi. Delicatiores ea decorti-cata vino madefaciunt, sic enim tolli nozam existimant. Verum videant, nein venas fuc-cusille crudus celerius deducatur, Maurita-ni remedium præclarum esse aiunt contra a-nimæ grauitatem, quæ à vitio ventriculi ex-halat.
units.tr: For they do not harm the stomach, especially if they are swollen with wind, provided they are eaten before other foods, as Galen rightly advises in book 2 on the alimentary faculties. What is said here of peaches, that they should precede other foods, was said of all watery and quickly passing foods. It is well known that peaches abound in excessive liquid, so that they very readily and quickly go bad. For this reason their continual and manifold use is disapproved, especially when the stomach is moist and windy. Paul of Aegina taught that they curdle at once in the stomach and that their juice is very bad. The more dainty soak them peeled in wine, thinking this removes the harm. But let them see that the raw juice is not drawn more quickly into the veins. The Moors say that a famous remedy against the foul breath which rises from a disorder of the stomach is...

units.la: Armeniaca & præcocia, quæ circa fe-stum D. Joh. apparent, caeteris omnibus præ-stant, quia intus magis sicca spectantur, ea intra 30. annos reperta fuisse, dum historiam suam conderet, Plinius testatur, & primo singula denariis venundata, hoc est, sestertiis quaternis, postea, augescente gratia, gulaque titillante pretium ad tricenos nummos eua-sse. fisse. Unde mirum non est singulas arbores bina millia nummûm annuo reditu meruisse, cum septem & sexaginta malaillam summam conficere potuerint, tricenis nummis singula venundata. De nucleis persicorum non pretereundum est ex oleo rosaceo, & aceto temperatos capitis dolores sedare, efitatos[?] autem tormina ventris. Flores saccharo conditi stomacho utiles sunt. Eligenda quae minus succulenta sunt persica, quorumq; fissa caro ligno minime adhæret. Succosa enim nimis damnantur.
units.tr: Apricots and early apples, which appear about the feast of St John, surpass all others, because they look drier inside. Pliny attests that these were discovered within thirty years of his writing his history, and that at first each was sold for four sesterces, but afterwards, as their favour grew and gluttony was tickled, the price rose to thirty coins. Hence it is no wonder that single trees earned two thousand coins a year, since sixty-seven fruits, sold at thirty coins each, could make up that sum. It should not be passed over that kernels of peaches, mixed with rose oil and vinegar, soothe headaches, and when crushed, the pains of colic. Flowers preserved with sugar are useful for the stomach. Choose peaches that are less juicy and whose flesh does not cling to the stone, for very juicy ones are condemned.

units.la: De cucumere, cucurbita, melone, pepone.
units.tr: On cucumber, gourd, melon and pepo.

units.la: Melonum, peponum, cucumerum, cucurbitarumq; varia genera nouit Italia & Gallia, quorum plerasq; in Germaniam nunc quoq; nostram commigrarunt. Non enim indiligenter in hortis excoluntur, expetuntur enim tum à magnatibus, tum à pauperibus, non sine valetudinis sæpe incommodo. Calidioris enim temperaturæ hominibus, & ab ineunte ætate iis assuetis magis conueniunt, frigido humidoq; ventriculo incommodant. Semina vero omnium in renum vesicaq; affectib. ut stranguria, calculo &c. valde commendantur.
units.tr: Italy and France know many kinds of melons, pepons, cucumbers and gourds, and many of them have now also migrated into our Germany. They are cultivated with care in gardens, and are sought after both by the great and by the poor, not without frequent harm to health. For they suit people of a warmer constitution, and those accustomed to them from early life; but they harm those with a cold and moist stomach. The seeds of all of them are highly commended for disorders of the kidneys and bladder, such as strangury, stone, and so on.

units.la: (Cucurbita in cibos decoquuntur, cruda enim non estur, fatua siquidem & insipida sunt.
units.tr: (Gourds are cooked for food; they are not eaten raw, for they are insipid and tasteless.

units.la: Itali ma- ximae- state (e suamque[?] familiä oleribus atq; pe- ponibus iuften- tant.
units.tr: Italians, in the greatest heat of summer, feed their families with vegetables and pepons.

units.la: Apparandi modus variat, Quidam cum Sinapi efitant, alii cum Salsis coquunt, nonnulli cum malo cydonio bodie addunt crocum & piper, sic enim humor eius immoderatus coercetur: vescentes autem cito satiat, ob redundantem humorem alimentum, prabet humidum. Efflate vero potissimum elixae cum juculis edi debent, autumno in oleo aut butyro frixae vel asse farina prius circumlita, acerba, vnae succo asperso.
units.tr: The method of preparing them varies. Some stew them with mustard, others cook them with salted meats, and some now add quince, saffron and pepper, for thus their excessive moisture is restrained. Eaten, they quickly satisfy, since their redundant moisture provides only watery nourishment. They should be eaten chiefly boiled with broth; in autumn they may be fried in oil or butter, or roasted after being dusted with flour, and eaten sour, with juice sprinkled over them.

units.la: Cucumeres, melones, pepones, crudi frequenter in cibos veniunt. Itali, Galli, & Hispani liberaliffime iis vescuntur & frequentissime.
units.tr: Cucumbers, melons and pepons often come to table raw. Italians, French and Spaniards eat them most freely and most often.

units.la: Vidi in Italia multos tanta cum auiditate pepones vorasse, ut satis putarint ad justum prandium aut liberalem coenam, peponibus Saturari. Edunt autem cum pane, pipere & Saccharo, vinum, superbibunt. Sed certum est & indubitatum, licet nonnulli reclè eos coquant in ventriculo, eoq; fifi affatim ius & frequenter sese replent, temporis tractu & protegelidos vitiosq, succos in venis coacernari, quicum in bonum sanguinem convertit, non possint, clam fenimq, lenissima putredinis occasione arrepta, contumaces fauaq, febres excitare confuenerunt. Id quod praeter experientiam praedictae gentes fateri coguntur, fauioribus frequentioribus morbi, quam alia obmoxia.
units.tr: I have seen many in Italy devour pepons with such eagerness that they thought melons were enough for a full lunch or a generous dinner. They eat them with bread, pepper and sugar, and drink wine over them. But it is certain and undoubted that although some digest them well in the stomach, and fill themselves with them freely and often, over time cold and vicious juices gather in the veins, which the body cannot turn into good blood. Seizing the occasion of a slight putrefaction, these juices secretly excite stubborn and foul fevers. The said peoples are forced to admit this from experience, since diseases are more frequent among them than among other peoples.

units.la: In promtu causa est, quia vinum mera-cum superbibunt, quod tanquam vehiculum eruditates ingestorum sursum secum in ve-nas deducit atq; rapit, unde obstructiones pu-tredinesq; existere tandem verisimile est.
units.tr: The cause is ready to hand: they drink wine neat over them, and this, like a vehicle, carries the crudities of what has been swallowed up into the veins and draws them along, whence it is at last likely that obstructions and putrefactions arise.

units.la: Italorum tamen & Hispanorum maxima pars innoxie iis vescitur, ex consuetudine, ut ipsi putant, tum etiam, quia vinum meracum malitiam eorum obtundere vomitumq; coercere expertisunt, &c. Verum consuetudinem istam illis relinquamus, valeantq; qui istorum fructuum esu impensius gaudent. In exemplis est Paulum secundum Pontificem esu pepo-nis interiisse, quin & Clementem septimum avi-diffimum eorum fuisse inde constat, quod in morbo, quo etiam extinctus est, avi de eos vora-vit.
units.tr: Yet the greater part of Italians and Spaniards eat them without harm, from custom, as they themselves think; and also because they have found that neat wine blunts their harmfulness and restrains vomiting, and so on. But let us leave that custom to them, and let those who take great delight in eating these fruits enjoy them. Among the examples: it is said that Paul the Second, the Pontiff, died from eating pepons, and that Clement the Seventh was most greedy for them, which is clear from the fact that during the illness of which he also died, he devoured them greedily.

units.la: Quare perpetuo illud cogitandum, ne ad satietatem quis eos ingerat. Diphilus apud Athenaeum non vult cucumeres assumi primo cibo, propterea quod sursum ferantur, raphani infur[?], ultimo innocentiores concoctuq; faciliores arbitratur, quod tamen quidam non probant.Verissimum & indubitatum est, Cucumeres peponesq; copiosius sumtos nisi probe coquantur, atq; ventriculo conficiantur, vel etiam boni suc-ci cibis non una assumantur, in ventriculo corrumpi atq; vitiari, succumq; parere lethalibus venenis non absimilem. Vide de hac re Galen. librum de cibis boni & mali succi. Item lib.
units.tr: Therefore one must always bear in mind not to eat them to satiety. Diphilus, in Athenaeus, does not want cucumbers taken as the first course, because they rise upward, and thinks that radishes, taken last, are more harmless and easier to digest; some, however, do not approve this. It is most true and undoubted that cucumbers and pepons, eaten in quantity, unless well cooked and digested in the stomach, or even if eaten together with other foods of good juice, corrupt and spoil in the stomach and produce a juice not unlike deadly poisons. See on this matter Galen's book on foods of good and bad juice, and likewise book 2 on the properties of foods.

units.la: lib. 2. de alimentorum facult. Paulum Ægi- netam lib. 1. c. 8o. Plin. l. 19. cap. 5. ubi cucumeres efficatos in stomacho vivere scribit in posterum diem, nec perficipoffe. Videant igitur aulicarum voluptatum sectatores, qui eos in taleolos dissectos ex aceto & sale piperea, vel muria mandunt, sic enim in alienos mensas condiuntur & asseruantur, bocq; modo asseruati pestilenti- fimi [untin commessationibus nocturnis, sicut & in mensis secundis. Chrysippus eos in cibis damnauit. Taurus Philosophus apud Aulum Gellium canam obsonio infruebat ex lente confecto & cucurbita, cuius etiam caulem incibo primum efficie Plinius autores: verum quo longior & tenerior, eo gratior, salubrior, quae pendendo crevit. Secantur autem cucurbita de- raso cortice in tenuia filamenta, qua siccata fervantur.
units.tr: Paul of Aegina, book 1, chapter 80; Pliny, book 19, chapter 5, where he writes that cucumbers preserved in vinegar stay alive in the stomach until the next day and cannot be digested. Let the pursuers of courtly pleasures take note, those who eat them cut into small pieces, seasoned with vinegar, salt and pepper, or brine. For thus they are prepared and preserved for other tables, and so preserved they are most pestilential in nocturnal revels, as also at dessert. Chrysippus condemned them among foods. Taurus the philosopher, in Aulus Gellius, flavoured his dish of soup made from lentils and gourd. Pliny also records that the stalk of the gourd is eaten first as food; but the longer and more tender it is, the more pleasant and healthful, and it grows while hanging. Gourds are cut, with the rind scraped off, into thin strips, which are dried and kept.

units.la: Cucumeres, si quando iis vescitur, vel necessaria tatis, vel voluptatis gratia contingat, sint infantes tenerioris parum, adhuc ventriculo. Suaviores quoq; ac dulciores reddunt, femine eorum lacte vel mulsa temperato ante sationem. Impudicis texticibus venerisq; appetentioribus cucumerem edendum Græcorum est prouerbium, cucumerem enim Veneris cupiditatibus refragari Diphilus autor est.
units.tr: Cucumbers, if one eats them at any time, whether from necessity or for pleasure, should be young and tender, and only a little for the stomach. Seeds steeped in woman's milk or in mulsum (honeyed wine) before sowing make them sweeter and more pleasant. The Greeks have a proverb that cucumber should be eaten by shameless talkers and those more eager for Venus, but Diphilus is the authority that cucumber checks the desires of Venus.

units.la: De Cotoneis.
units.tr: On Quinces.

units.la: Non[?] sunt priuanda, gloriâ sua mala cotonea, ex infulaCreta hujusq; op-pido cydone primum aduecta, unde cydonia mala appellantur. Præclarum quid ante cætera mala præstare Galenus aliique graues autores, tum quotidiana quoque ex-perimenta testantur. Ventriculum enim de-bilem magis aliis malis corroborant astrin-gendi vi, qua etiam aluus firmatur. Flauam etiam bilem coercent, atque cor spiritusque exhilarant. Cruda in cibos non veniunt, de-coctavero hieme summam fecundis in mé-sis autoritatem obtinuerunt. Coctura ha-benda est ratio: Prout enim magis vel minus ventrem firmare astringereque scopus est, pro eo magis vel minus lente diiue coquen-da sunt, certum enim est longa coctura vim constringendi amitti. Delicatior gula ea co-cta saccharo aspergit, cinnamomoq; & ga-ryophillis configit. Succus cotoneorū cum melle coctus ad præftátes vsus seruabilis est. Quin & medicamétū cotoneatū vocát, vul-gatissimi est apud magnates in nocturnis cō-meslationib· vsus, eo náq; moreshuj? seculi venere, ut multa à medicinę leg. ad gulę ven-trisq; delitias trasierint. Vestib. interposita o-doré his conciliär, suspéfa in cubiculis paulo ante maturitaté odore suaui coloreq; aureo, parumq; virescente spiritus recreare insen-subtiliter[?] deprehenduntur. Effi-
units.tr: Quinces must not be denied their own glory. They were first brought from the island of Crete, from its town Cydon, whence they are called cydonian apples. Galen and other weighty authors state that quinces excel all other fruits, and daily experience confirms it. For by their astringent power they strengthen a weak stomach more than other apples, and this power also firms the bowels. They also check yellow bile and cheer the heart and spirits. They are not eaten raw, but when cooked they have won the highest esteem at the second courses, especially in winter. Care must be taken in the cooking: since the aim is to firm and astringe the stomach more or less, they must be cooked more or less long, for it is certain that long cooking loses the astringent power. The more delicate palate sprinkles the cooked quinces with sugar and seasons them with cinnamon and cloves. Juice of quinces boiled with honey can be kept for useful purposes. They even call it quince preserve (cotoneatum), and it is most commonly used among the great at night-time drinking parties. For this age has developed such a taste that many things have passed from the medical art to the delights of the palate and belly. Placed among clothes they lend their scent; hung in bedrooms shortly before ripening, with their sweet smell, golden colour and slight greenness, they are found to refresh the spirits without our noticing.

units.la: Efficaciffimum antidotum, medica- mentumque contra venena & toxica effe malum cotoneum praeter experientiam gra- uiffimi autores prodiderunt. Qui de Par- thorum Scytarumque toxico liteis prodi- derunt, ( vt Plin. l. 11. c. 53. Quid. 1. de Ponto. Lucan. l. 3. Diofc. l. 6. c. 20. Arift. de mirabilib. aufcult.) teftantur humano fanguine viperi- naq; fanie conftare, quo tela fagittafq; fuas inficiebant inungebantque, vt leui etiam ta- ctu mortem accelerarent. Qui hoc pota- runt, his labia intumefcebant, rabiofique lu- porum inftar vociferabantur, quos cotonea mala concifa ac cum pulegio comefta juvifle compertum fuit. Aduerfus Ægyptiorum Pharicum, quod potum refolutionem, con- uulfionemque cum delirio afferebat, effica- ciffimum antidotum effe malum cotoneum velinde praecipue patet, quod folus hujus odor vires Pharici virulentas obtundit atq; eneruat, ita vt fi vna in rifco includantur, hujus virtus illius odore debilitetur. Vnde Philarchus fexto hiftoriarum libro ait, Co- tonea mala fuo odore omnium deleterio- rum vim obtundere. Vide Athen. lib. 3. ex Philarcho, Saepe contingit, vt, qui hefterna in cae- nalargius meraciufque poculis indulferunt, tantam poftero die fentiant capitis grauedi- nem, vt in id cyclopas migraffe jurent, qui alteralternatis illud feriant ictibus. His coro-neum tostum ante somnum vel etiam mane sumtum vapores è ventriculo in cerebrum exhalantes reprimitac coercet, efficitque vt vina minus noceant. Quare cotonea in hunc usum diligenter asseruanda sunt, iis, quos postera die Cepfalalgia ex crapula solet conflictare.
units.tr: Grave authors have written, beyond experience, that the quince is a most effective antidote and remedy against poisons and venoms. Those who have written in books about the poison of the Parthians and Scythians (as Pliny, book 11, ch. 53; Ovid, Ex Ponto, book 1; Lucan, book 3; Dioscorides, book 6, ch. 20; Aristotle, On Marvellous Things Heard) attest that it is made of human blood and viper's venom, with which they smeared and anointed their weapons and arrows, so that even a light touch would hasten death. Those who drank it had their lips swollen, and they howled like mad wolves; it was found that quinces cut up and eaten with pennyroyal helped them. That the quince is a most effective antidote against the Egyptian Pharic drink, which brought on loosening, convulsions and delirium, is especially clear from this: its smell alone blunts and weakens the virulent power of the Pharic, so that if the two are shut in one box, the power of the poison is weakened by the smell of the quince. Hence Philarchus, in the sixth book of his Histories, says that quinces by their smell blunt the force of all poisonous things. See Athenaeus, book 3, quoting Philarchus. It often happens that those who indulged last night too freely in dinner wine and strong drink feel such a heaviness of the head the next day that they swear they have been transported to the Cyclopes' forge, where they strike the head with alternating blows. For them, roasted quince taken before sleep, or even in the morning, checks and restrains the vapours rising from the stomach into the brain, and so makes wine do less harm. Therefore quinces should be carefully kept for this use, for those whom headache from excess usually troubles the next day.

units.la: De Sorbis & Mespilis.
units.tr: On Service-berries and Medlars.

units.la: Sorba & mespila pro medicamine potius, quam pro esca edenda Galenus praecipit, stomachum enim roborant, aluumq; fi-stunt, qua de causa fecundis mensis assumenda sunt.
units.tr: Galen advises that service-berries and medlars be taken as a medicine rather than eaten as food, for they strengthen the stomach and stop the bowels; for this reason they should be taken at the second courses.

units.la: Mespila melle condita referuntur. Inuento nouo in magnatum mensis madent intinctu quoddam qui vino cinnamomite conficitur. Rustici popelluq; cruda, sed mollia (in his enim gratia saporis est) edunt, cocta autem salubriora. De Sorbis torminalibus hoc adnotandum certissimum esse, quod Martialis scripsit, Sorba fumus molles nimium durantia ventres.
units.tr: Medlars are served preserved in honey. A recent invention, a certain dip made with cinnamon wine, is soaked into them at the tables of the great. Country people and the common folk eat them raw but soft (for in these the pleasure lies in the taste), though cooked ones are more wholesome. Concerning service-berries that cause gripes, it must be noted as most certain what Martial wrote: service-berries harden bowels that are too soft.

units.la: Noui quosdam dysenteria gravissime tentatos deploratos, si exitio opem ac medicinam superante, nullo medicamento morbum leniente, consilio fatidica cuiusdam anus sorbis cru-dis largiter voratis postridie vim prope tormi-nalem nalem omnem depuliffe indeq, firmata aluo prs-ftine valetudini fe reftituiffe. Veriffimum igi- tur eft Celfi dictum, temeritatem plerunq; effi-cere in morbis, quod prudentia nequiuerit.
units.tr: I have known some who were gravely attacked by dysentery and given up for lost, when the disease overcame all help and no medicine eased the illness. On the advice of some prophetic old woman, they ate plenty of raw service-berries, and the next day these drove off almost all the griping pain; their bowels being firmed, they recovered their former health. Therefore the saying of Celsus is most true: rashness often accomplishes in diseases what prudence could not.

units.la: De caftaneis, nucibus iuglandibus & auellana.
units.tr: On Chestnuts, Walnuts and Hazelnuts.

units.la: Aftanea igne toftæ, juglandes item & auellanæ fecundis menfis gratiffi-me apponuntur, cumprimis vero ca-ftaneæ, quæ præcipuam obtinuerunt digni-tatem & gratiam. Quin & plebeculæ multis in locis funt folatio, quando fedanda fames animalis eft. In Italiæ quibufdam locis, præ-fertim vero Romæ paffim torrentur in ci-bis, venundanturque voce præconis. Diffi-cilis autem coctionis effe, craffofque humo-res generare, obftructionefque, ii experiun-tur, qui liberalius iis & frequentius vefcun-tur. Quapropter citra fatietatem edendæ funt præfertim calculo colicoque dolorio-b-noxiis: toftæ vel affæ porcellis anferculifq; infarctæ gratiores funt & falubriores. Gale-nus arbores omnes fructus improbi fucci effe, præter caftaneas aftruere non dubitauit. Artius quoq; medicus clariffimus inter cun-ctos agreftes fructus fardinias glandes, fic enim appellat caftaneas, alimentum præfta-re veifcentibus infigne aflerit, verum tentare caput. Peculiare autem genus effe, quod id effiefficiat, dubium non est, Galli enim genero- fiffimas, amplitudine saporisque suauitate commendatissimas prædicant, quas Marro- nes vocant, magnatibus valde expetitas.
units.tr: Roasted chestnuts, and likewise walnuts and hazelnuts, are served most pleasantly at the second courses, especially chestnuts, which have gained the chief dignity and favour. Indeed, in many places they are a comfort to the common people when hunger must be stilled. In some parts of Italy, and especially at Rome, they are roasted everywhere and eaten with meals, and are sold with the crier's call. But that they are hard to digest and generate thick humours and blockages, those find out who eat them more freely and often. Therefore they should be eaten in moderation, especially by those liable to stone and colic pains. Roasted or baked, or stuffed with suckling pigs or young geese, they are more pleasant and wholesome. Galen did not hesitate to assert that all trees' fruits, except the chestnut, are of poor juice. The most famous physician Artius likewise declared that among all wild fruits the Sardinian acorn (for so he calls the chestnut) offers a remarkable food to those who eat it, but it troubles the head. That it is a special kind which produces this effect is beyond doubt, for the French praise their very noble chestnuts, most commended for size and sweetness of taste, which they call marrons, and which are much sought after by the great.

units.la: De nostris adeo magna polliceri non ausim, nisi ex liquore rosaceo saccharato decorti- cata, veletiam porcellis anseribusque infar- cta assaque manducentur. Molitura earum quibusdam gentibus pulmentariorum ac panis vicem præbet, quod tamen panificii genus rusticis magis conueniens est.
units.tr: I would not dare promise such great things for our own chestnuts, unless they are peeled and eaten after being cooked in sugared rose-water, or are stuffed with suckling pigs or geese and roasted. Ground up, they serve some peoples in place of side dishes and bread, though this kind of bread-making suits country folk better.

units.la: De Nucibus.
units.tr: On Nuts.

units.la: E Nucibus strictim & absq; verborum ambage. Nuces vocabulum omnibus commune est, quæ duro sunt operimen- to, vt castanea, avellanæ, nuces juglandes, quæ quia ex Perside primum allatæ perhibentur, per- sicæ, & Euboicæ appellantur. Nucem vero a no- cendo juglandem vero, quod fatis noceat, dictam volut. Nuces juglandes à capitis grauedine græ- cis κάρυα appellantur, foliorum enim vires in cerebrum penetrant, ipsaq; præsertim sicca vbe- rius comeste capitis dolorem inferunt, stomachum grauant, difficulter coquuntur, tussimque excitant certissima experientia. Itaq; quo vetu- stiores eo plus oleo se, cibis itaq; abdicanda. Recē- tes commendabiles sunt saporis, stomachoq; cum sale innocentiores.
units.tr: Of nuts, briefly and without long-winded words. "Nuts" is a word common to all those fruits that have a hard shell, such as chestnuts, hazelnuts and walnuts. Walnuts are said to have been first brought from Persia, and so are called Persian nuts or Euboean nuts. Some derive the name "nut" from "to harm" [nocere], and the walnut in particular [juglans] from "it harms enough" [satis noceat]. The Greeks call the walnut karya from heaviness of the head, since the strength of its leaves penetrates to the brain. Above all, dry walnuts, when eaten in quantity, certainly cause headache, weigh down the stomach, are hard to digest and provoke coughing, as very certain experience shows. Therefore the older they are, the more harmful they are, since they contain more oil; they should be avoided as food. Fresh nuts are pleasant to taste, and with salt they are gentler on the stomach.

units.la: Ve · Vz Venenis eas repugnare certum est in ci-bus praesumtas, qua de re etiam Plinius l.23. c.8. Antido- scribit in hunc modum.. In sanctuariis mitri-datis maximi Regis Ponti devicti Cn. Pompeium inuenit in peculiari commentario ipsius manu scriptam compositionem antidoti, duabus nuci-bus ficus, ficus totidem ʒ[?] ruthae[?] foliis 20. simul tritis, addito salis uno atq; altero grano, quod qui ieiun? sumat, nullum venenum nociturum illo die. Hac Pln.[?] Porro pugnante quadam v: ʒ[?] antipathia piscium malignitati, aquosiq, ipsorum ac pituitosis humoribus adversari nu-meris, ces juglandes compe[?]itum est, quare a efius[?] utendum.
units.tr: It is certain that walnuts oppose poisons when taken as food. On this point Pliny also writes, Book 23, chapter 8, in this way: "In the storehouses of Mithridates, the greatest king of Pontus, whom Gnaeus Pompey conquered, he found in the king's own hand, in a private notebook, the recipe of an antidote: two walnuts, two figs and twenty leaves of rue, all ground together, with one or two grains of salt added. Whoever takes this fasting will on that day be harmed by no poison." Thus Pliny. Furthermore, it has been argued that walnuts, by a certain antipathy, counter the malignity of fish, and the watery and phlegmatic humours, and therefore they should be used accordingly.

units.la: Virentes adhuc ligneo sc. putamine non-dum duritiem adepto, garyophyllus ac cinnamo-mo confixe saccharo condiuntur, servantur in multos annos ad varios usus, ventriculo enim refrigerato ʒ[?] imbecillo utiles sunt, senti-bus item ʒ[?] pituitosis, maritisq, in venerem pi-gris.
units.tr: Green nuts, whose wooden shell has not yet hardened, are preserved whole in sugar with cloves and cinnamon, and they keep for many years for various uses. For a cooled and weak stomach they are useful; likewise for those who are phlegmatic, and for husbands who are sluggish in sexual intercourse.

units.la: Avellanae nuces plus quam notae sunt. Patrio nomine appellantur Abellina ab Abelli-no Campania oppido, Graecis [illegible, ~8 letters] quasi nuces exigue : alii Ponticas vocant, quo-niam e Ponto in Graciam primo venientur. Praenestine etiam quod Praenestini abun-dent. Largius efitata aquae ac juglandes ca-pit noxia sunt. In cibo gratissime sunt rubentem tuis-eam nactâ, exactam tamen omnino maturita-tem non adepta, alexdi[?] enim praestantiâ praepol-lent ob substantiam illarum solidam minusque pingue[?]centem, qua de causa juglandibus in ci-bus postponi oportere medicina prudentes asseue-rant.
units.tr: Hazelnuts are better known than most. In their native name they are called "Abellinae," from Abellinum, a town in Campania; the Greeks call them by a name meaning "small nuts"; others call them "Pontic nuts," because they were first brought from Pontus into Greece; also "Praenestine," because the Praenestines grow them in abundance. Taken in too large amounts, they are harmful, like walnuts. As food they are most pleasant when they have a reddish skin but have not yet reached full ripeness, for they excel in quality because their substance is solid and less oily; for this reason, physicians assure us, they should be placed ahead of walnuts in diet.

units.la: Quaestionem hic video obrepere, quae mi-nime praetermittenda est. Cum vulgo dicitur: Unica nux prodest, nocet altera, tertia mors est, Quaeritur, quia triplicis hic nucis fit mentio, quaenam fit innocens, quae nocens, & quae plane mortifera. Resp. per primam intelligunt quidam nucem moschatam, per secundam nucem juglandem, per tertiam nucem metel-lam seu vomicam, quae duarum drachmarum quantitate sumta mortem accelerat. Alii de solis juglandibus intelligendum id esse, sic expo-nunt, unica prodest, mane, id est pauca, (synec-dochicos) scilicet & jejuno stomacho adue[?]: sus venenâ sumta, veletiam ventris laxandi gratiâ: altera nocet sc. immodico esu: tertia mors est, continuatus enim & praeter modum immodicus earum usus dysenteriam parit, sæpeque mortem.
units.tr: Here I see a question creep in, which must not be passed over. The common saying is: "One nut helps, a second harms, a third is death." It is asked, since three kinds of nut are mentioned, which is harmless, which harmful, and which plainly deadly. Some understand by the first the nutmeg, by the second the walnut, and by the third the metella or vomit-nut, which, taken in a quantity of two drachms, hastens death. Others say that this must be understood of walnuts alone, and explain it thus: "one helps," that is, taken in the morning, a few (by synecdoche), and on an empty stomach, as a remedy against poison, or also for loosening the bowels; "a second harms," namely by eating too many; "a third is death," for continual and immoderate use of them produces dysentery and often death.

units.la: De amygdalis & nucibus pineis.
units.tr: On almonds and pine nuts.

units.la: IN cibis ex amygdalis valent dulces, ama-rae enim cibis abdicantur. Naxiae & Cy-
units.tr: Among foods, sweet almonds are valued; bitter ones are excluded from food. Those of Naxos and Cyprus

units.la: priæ magis laudantur. In delitiis habentur dulces saccharo conditæ vel obductæ. Culi-nas amygdalas ad varios escarum vîusadhi-bere, nemiui non constat.
units.tr: are most praised. Sweet almonds preserved or coated in sugar are regarded as delicacies. That cooks use almonds for various dishes is known to everyone.

units.la: Varia deniq; ex amygdalis concinnan-tur, quæ amygdalata nuncupantur, ficutex pineis pignolata, & hodie vix fine amygda-lis Ptisana paratur, quæ fine iis colore & fa-pore ingratior est, de viribus autem Ptisanæ vide supra cap. de tritico & hordeo. Lac amygdalinum in febribus quid præstet, pul-mentum quoque ex iis & nucibus pineis, quam gratum fit vtileq; pthificis, experien-tia testatur. Mensas fecundas abunde implét atq; exornant variis modis.
units.tr: Finally, many things are prepared from almonds, which are called "almond confections"; likewise pignolata is made from pine nuts. And today barley-water is hardly made without almonds, and without them it is less pleasing in colour and taste. On the powers of barley-water, see above, the chapter on wheat and barley. What almond milk does in fevers, and how pleasant and useful a broth made of almonds and pine nuts is for consumptives, experience testifies. They abundantly fill and adorn the second courses of the table in various ways.

units.la: Nolo hic omittere, vt crapulæ quoq; nonnihil consuleretur, potores quinis vel pluribus præfumtis ebrietatem non sentire. Plutarchus memoriæ prodidit, fuisse apud Drufum Tiberii Cæsaris filium medicum quendam, facile omnes potando fuperan-tem: is autem paulo ante potum quinq; vel sex amygdalas amaras præsumere solitus est, ne crapulæ cogenti deesset: existimauit enim nucum amaritudine siccari abforberiq; hu-morem immodicum. Verum quæritur, cur amaritudo in amygdalis ebrietatem arceat, & non etiam in absinthio, centaurio, aloë? an quia occultum dissidium est & antipathia
units.tr: I do not wish to omit here that, for the relief of hangover too, something may be done: drinkers who have taken five or more, it is said, do not feel drunkenness. Plutarch records that a certain physician at the court of Drusus, son of the emperor Tiberius, who could easily outdrink everyone, used to eat five or six bitter almonds shortly before drinking, so that he would not lack protection against the compulsion of a hangover; for he thought that the bitterness of the nuts dried up and absorbed the excessive moisture. But it is asked why bitterness in almonds should ward off drunkenness, and not also in wormwood, centaury or aloes. Is it because there is a hidden discord and antipathy

units.la: inter amygdalas amaras & liquorem vini ? perfúafum habe : non enim amaritudo id prꝫftat quatenus amaritudo eft , fed quates nus in amygdalis amaris eft.
units.tr: between bitter almonds and the liquid of wine? Be persuaded of this: it is not bitterness as such that accomplishes this, but bitterness as it is found in bitter almonds.

units.la: De piftaceis & nucibus pineis non dif- ficile eft recte judicare, fi,quæ deamygdalis dicta funt,accurate quis obferuauerit,græcis ftrobila dictæ. Grandiffimæ autem funt nu- cespinee , nucleofque exiles inclufos in fe continent,qui probiac craffi fucci funt, va- lenterque alere exiftimantur. Aquá au- tem fimplici vel rofacea macerandæ funt, ad refinofam illam acremque vim deponen- dam, hocq; modo faucibus exafperatis,ex- ulceratifque præclare medentur. Pliniusac Diofcorides fitim fedare, virilium infirmi- tatem roborare,renibufque vtiles effe fpon- dent. Diocles thoracem purgare proditob vim refinofam. Menefitheus corpus imple- reait,vnde ptificis & tabidis vtiles. Saccharo incruftatæ bellariorum vicem fupplent.
units.tr: It is not difficult to judge correctly about pistachios and pine nuts, if one carefully observes what has been said about almonds; the Greeks call them strobila. Pine nuts are the largest, and they contain slender kernels enclosed within themselves, which are thought to be of a good and thick juice and to nourish strongly. They should be soaked in plain or rose water, to remove that resinous and sharp strength, and in this way they are excellent remedies for throats that are rough and ulcerated. Pliny and Dioscorides promise that they quench thirst, strengthen male weakness, and are useful for the kidneys. Diocles records that they purge the chest because of their resinous power. Menesitheus says they fill the body, and therefore are useful for consumptives and the wasting. Coated with sugar, they take the place of sweetmeats.

units.la: De piftaciis,quæ é genere quoque nu- cum funt,autores variant. Ea in Italiam ex Syria Vitellium primum intulifle, & in Hi- fpaniam Flaccum Pompeium equitem Ro- manum qui cum eo militabat , Plinius dili- gentiffimus naturæ fcrutator , autor eft lib. 15.cap.22.Eofdem autem vfus & effectus ha- bere cum pineis idé Plinius reftaturl.23. fuæ V historiae cap. 8. ad quem lectorem remitto, pluribus enim ibi de amygdalis, pineis, juglandibus, castaneis disserit. Gilenus non esse sibi compertum tradit, an sint stomacho amica, quod tamen Diofcorides aperte tradit.
units.tr: Authors differ about pistachios, which are also among the nut family. Pliny, the most diligent investigator of nature, writes in Book 15, chapter 22, that Vitellius first brought them into Italy from Syria, and that Flaccus Pompeius, a Roman knight who served with him, brought them into Spain. In Book 23 of his Natural History, chapter 8, the same Pliny maintains that they have the same uses and effects as pine nuts; I refer the reader to that passage, for there he discusses at greater length almonds, pine nuts, walnuts and chestnuts. Galen says he has not learned whether they are friendly to the stomach, although Dioscorides plainly states so.

units.la: Quin etiam an aluo subducendæ, an cohibenda vtilia sint, se exploratum non ha-bereait. Mira hominis integritas in re me-dica posteris tradenda, quia ne posteritati im-poneret, nihil inexpertum scriptotradere voluit, sed potius in cognita sibi, assidua ex-perientiâ magna cum fide exploraui. Et certe magis ingenuum est, de ignorantia confiteri, quam turpes & ridiculas causas atque rationes promere. Saccharo à se-plastariis incrustantur, gratia tamen eorum vetustate perit, rancida enim vt caeteræ nu-ces, seuadunt.
units.tr: Indeed, he also says he has not ascertained whether they are useful for loosening the bowels or for constipating them. The remarkable integrity of this man in medical matters is to be handed down to posterity: he did not wish to impose on posterity by handing down anything untested, but preferred to set forth with great trustworthiness only what he knew from his own constant experience. And certainly it is more honourable to confess ignorance than to put forward shameful and ridiculous causes and reasons. Pistachios are coated with sugar by confectioners, but their charm fades with age, for, like other nuts, they become rancid.

units.la: De Capparibus & oliuis.
units.tr: On Capers and Olives.

units.la: MEnsas magnatum opulentant ad avi-ditatem excitandam, sed gulosorum inventum est. In iis regionibus, ubi vberrimum oliuarum est proventus, vt in Gallia, Narbonensi, singulis prandiis caenisve ab inco-lis apponuntur. Seruantur autem sale, aceto, oleo. Apud veteres condiebantur, muria, ipsisque faeniculum admiscebatur. Ex defruto quoque & palso condiri solitas Celsus autor est, lib.2.cap.19. e Æginetæ oximelite conditas lau-dat. e Attius ace o 6 oleo conditas ad excitan-dum appetitum coctionem q, iuuandam nobilif-simas (esse ait, minorig[?], negotio à ventriculo perfi-ci,quæ iucundiores sunt.
units.tr: Magnates enrich their tables to stimulate appetite, but this is the invention of gluttons. In those regions where olives yield most abundantly, as in Narbonese Gaul, the inhabitants serve them at every lunch and supper. They are preserved with salt, vinegar and oil. Among the ancients they were seasoned with brine, and fennel was mixed in with them. Celsus records that they were customarily seasoned also with defrutum and pickle, book 2, chapter 19. He praises those seasoned with the oxymel of Aegina. Attius says that those seasoned with vinegar and oil are the most excellent for arousing appetite and aiding digestion, and that they are processed by the stomach with less effort, and so they are more pleasant.

units.la: Acerbæ enim & virides omnes crudæ, nam certissimum[?] est omnem acerbitatem difficillimè domari ac vinci, ē Albas oliuas (quæ scilicet mediæ sunt inter virides & maturas, quarum illæ acerbæ sunt haueo[?], quæ & nigræ sunt, stomachum suâ pinguedine relaxant) sto-macho utiles esse prodiderunt Plin.lib.23.cap.3. Cels.lib.4.cap.20. Galen.s.de compos.me-dic. secundum loc. necnon Oribasius libr.7. Omnes enim bis in stomacho astringendo utun-tur.
units.tr: For all sour and green olives, being raw, are hard to tame and subdue, since all sourness is most certainly very difficult to master. White olives, which are of course midway between green and ripe (the green being sour, the black being ripe and relaxing the stomach with their richness), have been reported useful for the stomach by Pliny, book 23, chapter 3; Celsus, book 4, chapter 20; Galen, in On the Composition of Medicines according to Places; and also Oribasius, book 7. For all of these are used to astringe the stomach.

units.la: Villis enim stomachi relaxatis appetitus per-ditur, & ventriculus sit debilis, corroboratur iidem astrictis. Quæ igitur magis astringunt, se-cundis mensis adhibendæ sunt, vt roborato ore ventriculi deorsum pellantur catera cibaria. Sed hodie eruditi pariter atque inerudiri, pri-mo,medio & postremo cibo,vt carnibus, piscibusq, eas sine vllo discrimine intermiscunt, (Capparis fructus crudi stomacho nocent,quare cuctos prius,deinde ex oleo & aceto mandere seos conuenit, sic enim appetitum excitant pituitam, in ventriculo incidunt, arq, educunt. Continuus Capparum vsus difficulter vrinam, neruæ sa-red dentibus podagricis,plenetico, magno ad-cra fit.
units.tr: When the villi of the stomach are relaxed, the appetite is lost and the stomach becomes weak; the same things that astringe strengthen it. Therefore those foods which astringe more are to be eaten with the second courses, so that, with the mouth of the stomach strengthened, the other foods may be pushed downward. But today learned and unlearned alike mix them without any distinction with the first, middle and last courses, together with meats and fish. (Raw caper fruits harm the stomach, so it is fitting to eat them first, and then with oil and vinegar; for thus they excite appetite, cut phlegm in the stomach and expel it.) Continual use of capers makes urination difficult, and they are harmful to the nerves, to those with toothache, to the gouty, and to those with phrenitis.

units.la: Olei ex oliuis fa-culrates omnes explicare nemo po-teft,adeo frequens multi-plexq; e-ius vius est. Ipsa autem o-lea apud veteres Romãos tante fuit autorita-tis, vt lex lata fuerit,quà cautum erat, ne quis oleã stringeret, pro-pterea q illa Mi-netuæ sacra fit.
units.tr: No one can explain all the uses of olive oil, so frequent and manifold is its employment. Among the ancient Romans oil itself had such authority that a law was passed forbidding anyone to press olive oil, and for that reason it was sacred to Minerva.

units.la: remento est. Radicis vsus maioris momenti est experimenti est. Germani nostri fampridem its affuerunt in cibis liberalius vti, ficus et oliuæ nor fine valetudinis incommodo, licet magnum sibi inde commodum promittant, vel potius ima- ginentur. Gallis, Hispanis et Italis, quorum ventriculi acquisita per consuetudinem proprie- tate in corpora ad alimoniam eius modi fructus dicentur, frequentiorem ac liberaliorem vsum re- linquamus.
units.tr: …remains. The use of the root is of greater moment, as experience shows. Our Germans have long been accustomed to use figs and olives more freely in their food, not without some harm to their health, although they promise themselves, or rather imagine, great advantage from them. Let us leave the more frequent and free use of such fruits to the French, Spanish and Italians, whose stomachs, by acquired habit, are adapted to this kind of food.

units.la: De ficubus.
units.tr: On Figs.

units.la: Icuum naturam breuiter & vt rei veri- tas postulat, perstringemus. In magna autem auctoritate atq; admiratione fuit. Ie ficum indicio est, quod multi ex Græcis multa de ea memoria prodiderunt, eamque omnibus arboribus fructus bonitate præ- tulerunt. Galenus ficus in fenestrate inter omnia poma minus sibi nocuisse testatus est, ab omni enim fugaci pomo abstinuit, exce- ptis maturis vuis & ficub*. Plato Διάσκος, id est, ficuum amator cognominatus est. Re- centes plenamque maturitatem adeptæ in- nocentius eduntur, aluum enim laxant, cele- riterq; per eam deiiciuntur, quin & insigni- ter abstergunt, in cibis namque sumtæ est cal- culofis renibus arenularum vim magnam detrarbant, valentissimum quoque corpori alimen- tum præstant, licet id non sit vfq; adeò soldum, sed sublaxum & tenue. Immodicè esitatæ, frequenterque devoratæ improbum sanguinem pariunt, ventremque inflationibus implent, quæ tamen citò evanescunt, modo non aliorum ciborum copia impediat. Itaq; non ignorandum est, in his quoq; non exiguas vitæ subesse insidias. Est in exemplis, quosdam blandidissimis ficuum saporibus prolectatos, usq; adeò ab earum esu sibi temperare non potuisse, ut supra modum tumidum, turgidum, distentumque in amplitudinem ventrem adepti, prope perierint, nisi matura remedium iis fuisset adhibitum. Scio in Italia id contigisse quibusdam Germanis, nā hi avidius plerunqç cibos eiusmodi exoticos & inconsuetos expetere consueverunt. Ita-que, quibus Italiam, vel Galliam perlustrare ac persuadere animus est, me consultore fru-ctibus vescendis paulatim assuescant.
units.tr: We shall briefly touch on the nature of figs, as the truth of the matter demands. They were held in great authority and admiration. Evidence of this is that many Greeks handed down much about them and preferred them to all trees for the goodness of their fruit. Galen testified that among all fruits figs harmed him least in the stomach; for he abstained from every fleeting fruit except ripe grapes and figs. Plato was surnamed Diaskos, that is, lover of figs. Fresh figs that have reached full ripeness are eaten more harmlessly: they loosen the bowels, are quickly voided, and cleanse remarkably. Taken with food, they greatly expel grit for those with stones in the kidneys, and they provide a very strong nourishment for the body, though not so solid, rather loose and thin. Eaten immoderately and devoured often, they produce bad blood and fill the belly with wind, which however soon passes, unless an abundance of other foods hinders it. Therefore it must not be overlooked that in these too lie no small dangers to life. There are examples of some who, enticed by the most delightful flavours of figs, could not restrain themselves from eating them so that, having the belly swollen beyond measure, tumid and distended, they almost perished unless a timely remedy had been applied. I know this happened in Italy to some Germans, for they are wont to desire such exotic and unaccustomed foods more eagerly. Therefore let those who intend to travel through Italy or France, with me as their adviser, accustom themselves gradually to eating these fruits.

units.la: De uvis.
units.tr: On Grapes.

units.la: Innumeras uvarum esse differentias, ostendunt, color, figura, sapor, amplitudo, duritiesque, mollitiesque. Quin & acini, qui in quibusdam exiles & parui, in aliis grandiores, rotundi vel prælongi sunt differentias constituunt, quas omnes ac singulas persequi operosum esset & difficile. Legatur Plin. l. 14. c. 2 & Dioscor. l. 5. c. 5[?], qui diligentissimè vitiū & vini etiam genera descripserunt. Quædam tamen,ne nihil seciffe videar,adnotabo,cum-primis de uvarum in annuos usus conditura. In uvis autem non pictura , sed natura confi-deranda venit. Nō enim omnia dici possunt, sed maxime utilia & necessaria. Notandum itaque dulces uvas probeque maturas corpus mediocriter alere,calidiorisque esse tempe-raturæ,ob idque sitim afferre pariterque al-uum emollire,idque præstant eò magis quò sunt humidiores. Maximum enim benefi-cium commodumque in iis est,quæ celeriter aluum mouent,velociterque subsident , & quæ ventrem non inflant,quod sit,si postali-os cibos sumantur,quod in primis hic obser-uandum est contra prosperæ valetudinis mi-nus studiosos,nec non contra receptam usu-que pene sed male confirmatam in Germa-nia consuetudinem, quà, quæ tenuiori in-ucluuntur cortice,ut sunt uvæ,cerasa, pru-na,persica,secundis semper mensis imponi-tur,more rationi probatissimorumq; medi-corum placitis,quin & experientiæ ipsi ad-uerso. Sed de hoc errore,quo in omnib.fere Magnatū aulis nihil frequentius est,alibi sa-cta est mentio.Porro q austera sunt acidæq; gelidioris sunt naturæ,quapropter choleram ardoremque restinguunt, mitescunt autem acidulæ diutius pendentes, austera in perse-cta etiam maturitate suspensæ mitiores non reddunredduntur: vtraque vero alimento parum a- pta deprehenditur. Galenus commendat eas uvas, quæ duriori sunt callo & acino(vn- de duracinæ appellantur) solidioris quæ substantiæ, minusque liquoris habeant, has e- nim valentius nutrire affirmat.
units.tr: The differences among grapes are innumerable, shown by colour, shape, flavour, size, and hardness or softness. Moreover, the berries themselves, which in some are slender and small, in others larger, round or very long, make further distinctions, all of which to pursue one by one would be laborious and difficult. Let Pliny, book 14, chapter 2, and Dioscorides, book 5, chapter 5, be read, who described most diligently the kinds of vine and wine. Still, I will note a few things, lest I seem to have done nothing, especially concerning the preserving of grapes for the year's use. In grapes, one must consider their nature, not their appearance. For not everything can be said, but chiefly what is useful and necessary. It must be noted, then, that sweet grapes, properly ripe, nourish the body moderately, are of a warmer temperament, and for that reason cause thirst and also soften the bowels; and they do so the more, the juicier they are. The greatest benefit and advantage lies in those that move the bowels quickly and pass through swiftly, and do not puff up the belly; this happens if they are eaten after other foods. This must be especially observed against those less attentive to good health, and against the custom, received and almost universal in Germany yet badly grounded, by which grapes, cherries, plums and peaches, which have thin skins, are always put on at the second course. This is against reason, the approved opinions of the most reputable physicians, and even experience itself. But this error, than which nothing is more common in almost all magnates' courts, has been discussed elsewhere. Moreover, the austere and sour grapes are of a colder nature, and therefore they quench bile and heat. Sourish grapes become milder if left hanging longer; austere ones do not become milder even when hung in full maturity. Both are found poorly suited to nourishment.
