Galen commends those grapes which have a harder skin and berry (whence they are called duracinae), and which have a more solid substance and less liquid, for he says these nourish more vigorously.

units.la: Verum de conditura vuarum operæ pre- tium est aliquid meminisse, multiplici enim modo in annuos reseruantur vsus. Principio adnotaffe hic lectorem oportet, vuam fine noxaferuari, fi luna decrescente serenoque cælo colligatur, id quod & de feminibus & fructibus intelligendum. Rationem in promtu esse animaduertes, fi consideraueris, vim alimentorum insuauem crudumq; fuc- cum, qui sæpe in feminibus fructibus usque de- litefcit, solis virtute castigari corrigique, hu- iusque actione inutilem humiditatem exugi, sopitumque ac deperditum saporem restitui atque reuocari. Cæterum Columella re- fert inter multos feruandarum vuarum mo- dos huncextitiffe fere precipuum, quando in labello fictili nouo, paleis quam ficciffimis cribatis, vt fine puluere effent, impleto, vuæ condebantur, deinde labellum luto paleato circumlinitum in tabulato ficciffimo paleis ficciffimis obruebatur, talesq; vuas paleales vocarunt, quæ humore superuacaneo spolia- tæ ægris impune concedebantur. Quæ autem in officinis fabrorum ferrariorum suspende-
units.tr: But it is worth recalling something about the preserving of grapes, for they are kept for the year's use in many ways. First, the reader must be told that grapes can be kept without harm if they are gathered when the moon is waning and the sky is clear; and this is to be understood of seeds and fruits too. The reason is easy to see if you consider that the unpleasant, raw juice of nourishment, which often lurks in seeds and fruits, is corrected by the power of the sun, that by its action the useless moisture is drawn out, and the dulled and lost flavour is restored and recalled. Columella, moreover, reports that among the many methods of keeping grapes, this was almost the chief: when they were stored in a new earthen jar filled with sifted chaff, as dry as possible and free of dust, the jar was smeared with chaff-mixed clay and buried in very dry chaff on a very dry shelf. Such grapes were called chaff-grapes, and, stripped of their superfluous moisture, they were given to the sick with impunity. Those hung in the workshops of iron-smiths, to be dried by fire and smoke so that they could be kept uncorrupted for longer, were called smithy-grapes. Pliny teaches that they are kept in earthen pots, and in casks enclosed and packed around with sweating grape-skins.

units.la: bantur,vt igne atque fumo exiccatæ diutius possint incorruptæ seruari ,fabriles appella-tæ sunt. Plinius doceteas seruari in ollis ficti-libus,atq; in doliis inclusas, vinaceis stipatas circumsudantibus. Quæ in ollis fictilibus asseruantur, obturato atq; etiam picato ore earum ventriculum infirmum corroborant & firmant, appetentiam torpescentem exci-tant,sed liberalius voratæ caput tentant,idq; ob nullam aliam causam quàm vinaceorum halitum. Aliæ musto condiuntur,quæ ftoma-choinimicæ censentur. Alii in granariis eas suspendunt, putantes sic pensilibus pulue-rem optimo operimento esse. Matresfa-milias in quibusdam locis in alta eas crucé seruabiles faciunt, durantq; per hiemem,ac etiam inæftatem. Duracinæ fine vllis vasis sunt in vite seruabiles. Quidam solem prius passas in aqua cœleftirecondunt, quas Pli-nius saluberrimas dicit, sicut sapà conditas improbat,nec non quæ in multo fuerunt. A-theneus invino reponi scripsit.Alii denique vuas per vindemiam legunt,quas foliis vitiis implicitas atque inuolutas furno siccant, fo-lent etiam per fe in furno exiccari, ægrisque reponi.
units.tr: Those kept in earthen pots, with the mouth stopped and even pitched, strengthen and firm up a weak stomach and excite a sluggish appetite; but if eaten too freely they trouble the head, and that for no other reason than the vapour of the grape-skins. Others are preserved in must, which are considered harmful to the stomach. Some hang them in granaries, thinking that dust makes the best covering for hanging grapes. In some places housewives keep them in high racks, making them last through winter and even through the summer. Duracinae can be kept on the vine without any vessels. Some first dry them in the sun and then store them in sweet water; Pliny calls these most wholesome, while he disapproves of those preserved in sapa, and of those kept in must. Athenaeus wrote that they are kept in wine. Finally, some gather grapes at the vintage, wrap them up tied in vine leaves, and dry them in an oven; others commonly dry them alone in an oven, and store them for the sick.

units.la: De vuis passis.
units.tr: On Raisins.

units.la: Vanta vero in ciborum gloria bodie sint [?] vua passe,nemini non constat. Bonum enim prebent nutrimentum, stomacho, optimè conueniunt, ac in cibo ficubus suauiores sunt & utiliores. Laudatissime sunt pingui teneroq; callo predite: dulciores quoq; palato & stomacho magis arridentes. Austere ventrem firmant, alvumq; cohibent, ad vinosum enim accedunt saporem. Dulcium autem ingens est turba, adq; nos in magna copia uncęs fiscellis inclusę deportantur plurimum ex Hispania, quæ grandes mittit & suavitate praestantissimas. Minimas, quæ videl[?] acinus carent, Galen. 2. de aliment. facult. scri- bit, in Cilicia provenire: alias non satis constat, ubi & ut gignantur, nisi quod calida eas opus habere terra, facile potest contingi.
units.tr: How great a place dried grapes hold in the esteem of foods today is known to everyone. They provide good nourishment, agree very well with the stomach, and are both pleasanter and more useful as food than figs. The most praised are those with a thick, tender skin: they are also sweeter to the palate and more agreeable to the stomach. Being astringent, they firm the belly and check the bowels, since they have a wine-like flavour. There is a great variety of sweet fruits, and large quantities are brought to us packed in baskets, most of them from Spain, which sends large grapes of outstanding sweetness. Galen, in De alimentorum facultatibus book 2, writes that the smallest, which lack stones, grow in Cilicia. Otherwise it is not well established where or how they are grown, except that they can easily be guessed to need a warm soil.

units.la: De malis citreis & arantiis.
units.tr: On Citron and Orange Apples.

units.la: Hæc poma colore, odore & succo infi- gnia sunt, myropoliis magis quàm culinis nota. Distinguuntur autem amplitudine colore, figura, odore, sapore. In nostra Germania citrea malus non perinde frequens reperitur, atque in Italia & Gallia, propterea quod rigida illi apud nos obstet hiems, siquidem frigoris impatientissima est. Porro q aureo colore refulgent, odoratissimi; sunt halitus arantia dicuntur vulgo & chrysomela: ovata specie turbinata luteoq; colore nitétia[?] citrangula & citrea vocat: her- baceo verò colore virentia limones dicuntur, quæ si prægrandia sunt melonumque modo orbiculata facie turgent ponceria vocantur, sed vernacula hæc specierum nomina sunt, quæ sicut & alia sollicitè disquirere superstitiosum est. Ad facultates igitur quibus pol-lent, veniamus.
units.tr: These fruits are remarkable for their colour, scent and juice, and are better known to perfumers than to cooks. They are distinguished by size, colour, shape, smell and taste. In our Germany the citron tree is not nearly as common as in Italy and France, because a harsh winter stands in its way here, since it is most intolerant of cold. Those that shine with a golden colour and have the strongest scent are commonly called oranges and golden apples. Those of an egg-shaped, tapering form with a bright yellow colour are called citrangulae and citrea. Those of a greenish colour are called lemons, and if they are very large and swell into a round shape like melons, they are called ponderosa. But these are local names of kinds, and it is superstitious to inquire into them carefully, as into other such names. Let us therefore come to the properties in which they excel.

units.la: Præsentissimum exhibet remedium con-tra deleterium pharmacum potum, si quis femina cum pomorum succo contusa cum vino biberit, per ventrem enim pharmacum extrurbat. Tempore Theophrasti & Plinii pomum non edebant, sed veluti thesaurum, teste Athenæo lib.3. in scriniis cum vestimentis reponebant, iis enim interiectum tineas necat, vestesque ab illarum rosione inoffen-sas conservat. Unde Homerus & Nevius Poeta vestes citrosas nominant. Quam verò sit contra omne virus remedium efficax, ex Athenei de duobus latronibus historia consi-lii potest, quos ad virulentas bestias condemnatos in Ægypto refert: verum cum ad supplicii theatrum, bestiis virulenta atrocitate efferatis plenum deducerentur, mulier caupo-naria illis obvia [?] horum quæ miserta, citrium quod manu tenebat illis edendum præbuit, quo comesto, cum illæsi & citra noxam, cum Draconibus colluctarentur, accersito a præ-fide carceris præfecto, ecquid Alexipharmaci præbibissent vel edissent, percontatus, nihil præter citrium respondit. Præses igitur de viribus citrii mali certius periculum factu- rus,alteri tantum de eo praebuit,cui item be- stiarum virus nihil nocuit,alter vero ab aspi- de morsus quamprimum in theatro conci- dit & expirauit. Anhelitus praeterea gra- ueolentiam arcet, si decocto pomorum os colluitur. Praegnantium quoque malaciae prosunt mala citria. Sed Plinius femen tan- tum laudat.
units.tr: The citron offers an immediate remedy against a poisonous drink: if someone pounds its seeds with the juice of the fruit, mixes them with wine and drinks it, the poison is expelled through the bowels. In the time of Theophrastus and Pliny people did not eat the fruit but kept it, as a treasure, in chests together with clothes, since placed among them it kills moths and keeps the garments unharmed from their gnawing. For this reason Homer and the poet Naevius call garments citrine. How effective it is as a remedy against every poison can be seen from Athenaeus's story of two robbers, whom, he reports, were condemned in Egypt to be thrown to venomous beasts. But when they were led into the theatre of punishment, which was full of beasts driven to a venomous fury, a female innkeeper who met them, moved with pity for them, gave them a citron she was holding in her hand to eat. After they had eaten it, they wrestled with the dragons unharmed and without injury. The governor of the prison was summoned and asked whether they had taken or eaten any antidote, and he answered that they had taken nothing but the citron. The governor, wishing to test more certainly the power of the citron, therefore gave some of it to another man, on whom the venom of the beasts likewise did no harm; but the other was bitten by an asp and immediately fell and expired in the theatre. Moreover, if the mouth is rinsed with a decoction of the fruit, it drives away bad breath. Citrons also help pregnant women who suffer from nausea. But Pliny praises only the seed.

units.la: Inter arantia quae acida sunt praeclaros in- tinctus cibariis praestant,durantque in maxi- mam aestatis partem, calorem enim tem- perant, fastidium abigunt, auiditatem- que excitant. Dulcia tufficulofis, thora- ci,pulmonibus exasperatisque faucibus sunt amica. Ex acidis liquor magis expetitur. Sed dissecta vinoque iniecta non paruam ei gra- tiam conciliant. Cortices Citriorum & a- rantiarum saccharo varie praeparantur,nunc incrustando,nunc integendo,nunc condien- do ad varios vsus & delitias gulae. Vnum no- ndum carnem horum pomorum crassi iucci esse ac pituitosi: succum acidum refri- gerare & siccare: cortices vero odoratos qui- dem esse conftatacres & efficaces,praesertim contra venena & ventris tormina,sed in ven- tre difficulter conficiuntur,quia praeduti ru- gofi & callosi sunt,quare conditi, vel deco- cti vel etiam macerati vino,ventriculum ma- gis firmabunt. Nuclei eandem pene cum cortice obtinent vim calefaciendi scilicet discutiendi & exiccandi. Ad extremum de liquore acido sciendum, cum saccharo coqui, seruariq; ad aestatis aestuantis febres, pestilentiæq; contagia certo experimento. Ipsa vero poma in Magnatum aulisin taleo-las conciduntur, sacchariq; polline aspersa manducantur prima mensa, acetariorum vi-cem supplentia; sed ita comesa difficulter in ventriculo confici extra dubium est, prædu-ra enim caro est, pituitosa ac gelida, unde colicos excitari dolores necesse est, si immodi-cè & frequentius efitetur[?].
units.tr: Among the oranges, those that are sour provide excellent flavourings for food, and they keep for most of the summer, for they temper heat, drive away loathing and stir up appetite. The sweet ones are friendly to those with a cough, to the chest, to the lungs and to a rough throat. Of the sour kinds, the juice is more sought after; but when the fruit is cut up and added to wine, it gives no small pleasure. The peels of citrons and oranges are prepared in various ways with sugar, now by candying, now by covering, now by preserving, for various uses and the delights of the palate. One should note that the flesh of these fruits is of a thick, phlegmatic juice: the sour juice cools and dries, while the scented peels are, as is established, sharp and effective, especially against poisons and gripes of the bowels; but they are digested with difficulty in the stomach, because when they are raw they are wrinkled and tough, so that if they are preserved, boiled, or even steeped in wine, they will strengthen the stomach more. The kernels have almost the same power as the peel, namely to warm, to dispel and to dry. Finally, it should be known from sure experience that the sour juice, when boiled with sugar and kept, is useful for the fevers of the summer heat and for the contagions of plague. The fruits themselves are cut into slices in the courts of the great and eaten, sprinkled with sugar dust, first at table, taking the place of salads; but it is beyond doubt that when eaten in this way they are digested with difficulty in the stomach, for the flesh is hard, phlegmatic and cold, so that colic pains are bound to be stirred up if they are eaten to excess and too often.

units.la: Submonitio ad locum de citriis, &c.
units.tr: Note on the passage about citrons, etc.

units.la: Graeci & Arabes in qualitatibus citrii mali recensendis nequaquam conueniunt. Auicenna corticem citri calidum esse ait, in primo, & siccum in gradu secundo. Galenus siccum absolute in secundo, nec calidum contra asseruit[?]. Idem Auicenna carnem dicit calidam, Galenus & Æginetæ frigidam. Semen decoctum suauem ori conciliare odorem, corpusq; reddere pingue scribit, quorum postremum a nullo Græcorum traditum est, omnemq; excedit rationem. Acidam ciusparem[?] bonum esse nutrimentum gutturi[?] & pulmoni contendit, quoniam utrumq; rationi, alierum[?] Serapioni etiam contrarium est, nocere pulmoni affirmanti. Verum Avicennæ sententiam confirmat experientiâ ipsa, cui refragari ineptum est. De cortice aurantiarum certum est, calidioris eius naturæ vires nō perco-quam citriorum, frigidos enim stomachi humores [?] discutit atque educit. Poma ipsa adhuc viridia, corticem habent maturitatem adhuc viridia corticem habent quamvis s[?]uiuentem, qui recens compressus acre reddit oleum, attrahendi exiccandique vim in signe.
units.tr: The Greeks and Arabs by no means agree in listing the qualities of the citron. Avicenna says that the peel of the citron is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Galen asserted that it is dry absolutely in the second degree, and not hot, against him. The same Avicenna says that the flesh is hot, while Galen and Aegineta say it is cold. He writes that a decoction of the seed makes the breath pleasantly scented and renders the body fat, and the last of these has not been handed down by any Greek and goes beyond all reason. He maintains that its acid part is a good nourishment for the throat and lungs, since both of these are... (the text is corrupt here), and Serapion, too, is opposed to this, affirming that it harms the lungs. But experience itself confirms Avicenna's opinion, and it is foolish to contradict it. It is certain that the peel of oranges has a hotter nature than that of citrons, since it dispels and expels cold humours of the stomach. The fruits themselves, while still green, have a rind which, when freshly pressed, yields a sharp oil with a power of drawing and drying.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAP. XII.

units.la: De alimentis quæ veniunt ex floribus, vbi commodè deacetariis ritè præparandis.
units.tr: On foods that come from herbs, and how salads are properly prepared.

units.la: ACetariis nullum ab antiquis scriptoribus, Græcis præsertim, peculiare nomen impositum reperitur, qui-bus tamen maxima in assignandis & imponendis rebus vocabulis erat licentia.
units.tr: No special name for salads is found in the ancient writers, especially the Greeks, though they had the greatest freedom in assigning and applying names to things.

units.la: Sunt autem acetaria non tantum, vt vulgò putatur, herbæ virentes, quæ ex aceto, sale, oleoque guttatim infuso concinnantur, ad languentem scilicet appetitum excitandum, ventriculum-que corroborandum, nec non humores in ore ventriculi residentes appetitum extin-guentes, extergendos, verum etiam cappa-res, bulbi, oliuæ,oua indurata,carnes minu-tim concisæ & ex aceto sumtæ, suilla salita, citria saccharo conspersa, & id genus alia.
units.tr: Salads, however, are not only, as is commonly thought, green herbs dressed with vinegar, salt, and oil poured in drop by drop, to rouse a flagging appetite, strengthen the stomach, and wipe away the humours that settle at the mouth of the stomach and dull the appetite. They also include capers, bulbs, olives, hard-boiled eggs, meats cut small and taken with vinegar, salted pork, citrons sprinkled with sugar, and other things of that kind.

units.la: Vnde videre est, acetaria non recte ab aceto nominari,cum ab accipiendo potius nomen flectatur,quoniam horti igne nonindigeant, ac ligno parcant, sin'que res expedita & pa-rata semper,testante Plinio l.19.c.4. Antiqui enim hortos suos acetaria quasi acceptaria appellabant. Acetaria autem nobis voca-ta veteribus mensæ frigidæ fuerunt appella-ta,inque vltimo mensæ apponebantur, quæ tamen tempore Plutarchi primo in mensas loco ferri ceperunt,cui Martialis, qui iisdem temporibus quibus Plutarchus vixit, adfti-pulatur,qui lactucam vltimo prius loco pofi-tam, sua verò ætate ante alias dapes efitatam testatur hoc disticho,
units.tr: From this it is evident that salads are not rightly named from vinegar (acetum), since the name is derived rather from receiving (accipere), because they need no heat from the fire and spare the wood, and the thing is always ready and prepared, as Pliny attests, book 19, chapter 4. For the ancients called their gardens acetaria, as if acceptaria. What we call salads were called by the ancients cold tables (mensae frigidae), and they were served at the very end of the meal. Yet in Plutarch's time they first began to be brought in at the start of the table. Martial, who lived in the same period as Plutarch, agrees with this. In the following couplet he testifies that lettuce, which had once been placed last, in his own day was served before the other dishes:

units.la: Claudere quæ cœnas lactuca solebat anno-rum, Dic mihi cur nostras incipit illa dapes?
units.tr: Lettuce, which used to close the dinners of our elders, tell me, why does it now begin our courses?

units.la: Causam autem cur veteres cœnam lactucis finire sint soliti, vide loco de lactuca.
units.tr: For the reason why the ancients were accustomed to end dinner with lettuce, see the place on lettuce.

units.la: Cæterum,quia acetaria (hoc enim vocabulum neotericum ab omnibus receptum esse video) diuersi sunt temperamenti pro variatum rerum, ex quibus conflantur natura & proprietate, cum etiam, quod liberaliorem eorum & frequentiorem vsum mi nus salubrem esse pro comperto habetur, modum in iistenendum esse ante omnia me- minifle oportebit. Non enim palati tan- tum gratia ea inuenta sunt,sed & valetudinis causa, iisquenon vtepulis semper & cibariis, sed & vt medicamentis vti oportet. Con- stat herbis crudis crebriusimmoderatiufque vsos grauibus aegritudinibus tentari, quoni- am ex his succus, qui in corpus diffunditur, maxima ex parte crudus ac vitiosus est. Vi- rens certe ille succus, quem bilem porrace- am appellant, & plerique euomere solent, (german. <bl>die grüne Gallen</bl>) non panis aut carnis,aut alterius escae culpa gignirur,sed al- terius cuiuidam feruidioris acriorisque fuc-ci noxa,qualis est ceparum,allii,porri,rapha-ni:& licet plurima huiusmodi modice sumta salutaria deprehenduntur, immoderata ta-men & frequentiora graues adferunt mor-bos: Quod obiter hic noto propter gentium quarundam morem,quae talia in quotidiano habent victu.
units.tr: Moreover, since salads (for I see this modern word is accepted by everyone) differ in temperament according to the variety of the things from which they are made, in nature and property, and since it is held as established that a generous and frequent use of them is less wholesome, we must above all remember to keep to moderation. They were devised not only for the sake of pleasure but also for health, and they should be used not always as food and ordinary fare but also as medicines. It is established that those who eat raw herbs often and immoderately are troubled by serious illnesses, since the juice that is diffused through the body from these is for the most part raw and faulty. That green juice, which they call porraceous bile and which most people are accustomed to vomit (German, <bl>die grüne Gallen</bl>), is not produced by the fault of bread, meat, or any other food, but by the harm of some other juice that is hotter and sharper, such as that of onions, garlic, leeks, and radishes. And although many such things taken in moderation are found to be wholesome, taken immoderately and frequently they bring grave diseases. I note this in passing because of the custom of certain peoples who have such things in their daily diet.

units.la: Quibusdam etiam acetaria adeo sunt vsi-tata, vt in cibis aestate praesertim, vix habeant aliquid frequentius, stupido enim & bruto plane palato ea deuorant & inglutiunt nulla habita distinctione & discrimine ipsarum, quae in ea ingrediuntur, rerum. Exemplo est Antuerpienfium conuiuarum interitus, qui in acetariis radice luparie seu aconiti vefcen-tes diem suum obierunt. Ventriculo natu-rá frigido & imbecillo, cerebroque nimis humido acetaria frigida, vt quæ ex la&uca,a-cetof ,portulaca,endiuia,& similibus paran-tur,nocent,quare ventriculus ita affectus in vniuersum ab eiusmodi crudis abstinebit, nisi eiusmodi frigida calidis contempe-rentur, vterucá, fœniculo, aniso, cori-andro,mentha,hissopo,thymo,satureia, tra-gopogo,& similibus,quæ commodè frigidis possunt commisceri,hæc enim frigus lactuce calore immisto temperant. Commodissimè quoq; acetariis immiscentur flores buglof-sæ,borraginis,cichorii,rosarum,saluiæ,his-sopi,flores persicæ arboris,saporem enim iis conciliant gratum & salutarem. Quibus verò ventriculus immodica bile efferuescit, acebullit,iis acetaria frigida conceduntur: bilis enim feruorem sitimque extinguunt. Conficiuntur quoque acetaria palato deli-catiori noningrata,ex asparago lupuloque, sed recentibus adhuc,cum scilicet in caulem nondum prorupuerunt,quod fit ineunte vere. Nafturtium quoque aqua-ticum in acetariis celebratur hieme,state verò hortense ad fastidium difcutien-dum,lienisque obstructiones aperien-das.
units.tr: Some people use salads so commonly that, especially in summer, they hardly eat anything more often. With a plainly dull and brutish palate they devour and swallow them, making no distinction or discrimination among the things that go into them. An example is the death of the diners at Antwerp, who died of their salads made with wolfsbane, or aconite. Cold salads, such as those made of lettuce, sorrel, purslane, endive and similar herbs, harm a stomach that is by nature cold and weak and a brain that is too moist. So a stomach so disposed will in general abstain from such raw foods, unless these cold things are tempered with warm ones, such as fennel, anise, coriander, mint, hyssop, thyme, savory, goat's beard, and similar herbs, which can conveniently be mixed with cold ones; for a warm admixture tempers the coldness of lettuce. Flowers of bugloss, borage, chicory, roses, sage, hyssop, and the flowers of the peach tree are also very suitably mixed into salads, for they give a pleasant and wholesome flavour. For those whose stomach boils over with excessive bile, and who are hot, cold salads are allowed, since they quench the heat and thirst of the bile. Salads are also made, not unwelcome to a more delicate palate, from asparagus and hops, but while they are still fresh, that is, before they have shot up into a stalk, which happens at the beginning of spring. Watercress is also used in salads, in winter, and in summer garden cress, to dispel weariness and open up obstructions of the spleen.

units.la: Notandum tamen, olei non multum acetariis immitti debere, ventriculi enim tra[?] com-osrelaxat, appetentiamque restinguit magis munem[?] quàm excitat. In ventriculo enim robo-prepara- rando incidentia & astringentia adhibenda di modi[?] sunt non relaxantia, vt sunt oleosa & vn- guinofa. Quare improbantur eiusmodi acetaria, quæ in quibusdam locis paran- tur ex immodico butyro feruefacto, olei vicem supplente ob causam iam comme-moratam. In vniuersum quoque damnan- tur acetaria, quæ multis in locis præfer-ti[?]ima a- tim circa autumnum fiunt ex caule capita-cetaria to minutum dissecto acetoque perfuso: quæ fiunt (vulgus nominat weissen Salat) cuius ex caule tanta est cupido, vt in lautioribus etiam capitato & fplendidioribus conuiuiis inter primas crudo am- mensarum delitias habeatur, primumque fumnali mereatur locum: eo enim venere mores vtpluri- luxuriaque, vt gulæ potius quam vitæ mum te- habeatur ratio. Abdicanda denique ace-pore. Gu- taria sunt, quæ calidis herbis vel aromati-lidosenim bus,vt pipere, saleque non sunt contempe-humores rata, quod hodie ab omnibus feré negligi crudosq, animaduerto, etiam nitidiorem & delica-accumu- tiorem vitam sequentibus, qui non raro pe-lant. cudum instar ea turgidis buccis ingluti- unt,quod sæpe ad stuporem vsque miratus tra ace- sum. tarioph- X 4 Stultè gos.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that not much oil should be put into salads, for it relaxes the stomach and dampens appetite rather than arousing it. In strengthening the stomach, one should use things that are incisive and astringent, not relaxing ones such as oily and greasy foods. For this reason salads of that kind are disapproved, which in some places are made with excessive butter melted down, standing in for oil for the reason already mentioned. Generally, too, salads are condemned which in many places are made, especially around autumn, from a head of cabbage finely chopped and drenched in vinegar (the common people call it white salad, weissen Salat). Such is the desire for it that even at more elegant and splendid banquets it is counted among the first delicacies of the table and deserves the first place. Customs and luxury have reached such a point that people think of the palate rather than of life. Finally, those salads must be rejected which are not tempered with warm herbs or spices, such as pepper and salt. I notice that today nearly everyone neglects this, even those who follow a more refined and delicate life, who not rarely gulp them down with swollen cheeks, a thing I have often marvelled at to the point of astonishment. Foolishly they persuade themselves and imagine that their stomach is hot, and that because of this they must avoid hot things, being of a warmer temperament.

units.la: Stultè enim sibi persuadent & imaginan-tur, ventriculum se habere calidum, eoque calidioris essè temperaturæ, propterea à ca-lidis abstinendum.
units.tr: Foolishly they persuade themselves and imagine that their stomach is hot, and that because of this they must avoid hot things, being of a warmer temperament.

units.la: Sed sciant isti facilius esse & tutius mem-brum nimio calore efferuescens refrigerare quam nimio algore emortuum excalfacere. Similia enim similibus sunt conferuanda & roboranda, nam destructio fit per contraria. Modus tamen seruandus præcipitur. De ace-to[?] illud non omittendum, quantò fuerit acri-us, tantò minus id frigidæ naturæ esse: hu-iusque acorem saccharo aut vuis passis in eo decoctis mitigari: acetum igitur quò acrius, eò ad acetariorum vsum accommodatius est.
units.tr: But let them know that it is easier and safer to cool a part that boils over with excess heat than to warm one that has died from excess cold. Like must be preserved and strengthened by like, for destruction comes about through contraries. Yet a measure must be kept, as is prescribed. Regarding vinegar, it should not be omitted that the sharper it is, the less cold its nature; and its sharpness is softened by sugar or raisins boiled in it. Therefore the sharper the vinegar, the better suited it is for use in salads.

units.la: Hactenus de alimentis quæ veniunt ex vegetabilibus, quib. nó inepté subiici possunt tu-bera & fungi quos terra vegetabilium mater sponte protrudit.
units.tr: So far concerning foods that come from plants, to which tubers and mushrooms, which the earth, the mother of plants, puts forth of her own accord, may not inappropriately be added.

units.la: De fungis.
units.tr: On mushrooms.

units.la: Emirandum, eo vsque nostri seculi fa-riosam & insanam deuentisse gulam, vt in cibos adhibere velit ea quæ vitæ sunt pestis. Quid enim quæso nobis esse potest commu-ne cum piscibus illa arborum (sic enim recte nominant Plinius l.22.c.13.) & terræ vitiis, inter quæ pestilens fungorum succus? [illegible, ~12 letters] eorum [illegible, ~10 letters] interemisse cos [illegible, ~8 letters] cum [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: It is astonishing that our age has grown so mad and insatiable a gluttony that it wishes to put into food things that are a plague to life. For what, I ask, can we have in common with those tree growths (for so Pliny rightly calls them, book 22, chapter 13), which are the defects of earth, and among which is the poisonous juice of fungi? [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible].

units.la: Serenus[?]
units.tr: Serenus[?]

units.la: Serenum præfectum Neronis vigilum, & tribu- nos, & centuriones, idem Plinius est teste. Ni- bilenim[?] aliud esse fungos quam terræ, arbo- rum, lignorum, aliarumq; putrilaginum super- fluas humiditates, inde colligi potest, quod omnes fere è tonitribus & pluuioso cœli statu frequen- tius soleant enasci absq; radice floribus & femi- ne. Vnde veteres, cum animaduerterent fun- gos absq; femine procreari, crediderunt cogna- tionem illis aliquam cum cœlo esse. Repente vero è medio iterum tolluntur, nam ortus occasuq; eorum qui humi prouenient, septem plerunq; in- cluduntur diebus, cuius ortus interitus q; causa est abundans, qua[?] catent, humiditas. Merito igitur à fungorum esu se deterreri[?] sisent[?] fanitā- ti consulentes, primo quod à clarissimis scripto- ribus inter venena collocantur, & à funere a- gendo disiles quidam existimant, tum etiam, Fungi ci- quod pituito[?]um, gelidum, crassum, lentum, bis abdi- iniquiq; [?]ncci alimentum præstant, magna enim candi, ex parte vix conficiuntur, sed cum alii excre- mentis [?]ape reiiciuntur integri & non confecti. Caneant igitur sibi, qui funginis istis delitiis gaudent. Sed bodie fine modo vorantur etiam a magnatibus, qui singulari studio ad dubias eos cœnas exquirunt. Noui, quibus pituita illa fungosa cibo- rum excrementis nihil delicatius est, d: cunt, enim non omnes fungos venenatos esse & perni- ciales, ut sunt qui communiter tuberā dicuntur,
units.tr: Pliny is witness that Serenus was prefect of Nero's watchmen, and of the tribunes and centurions. From this it can be gathered that fungi are nothing other than the superfluous moistures of earth, trees, wood and other rotting matter. For nearly all of them spring up more often after thunder and in rainy weather, without root, flower or seed. Hence the ancients, noticing that fungi are produced without seed, believed they had some kinship with the sky. Yet they are suddenly taken away again, for the rise and fall of those that grow on the ground are usually confined to seven days, and the cause of both their birth and their death is the abundant moisture which [illegible]. Rightly, therefore, some have judged that people who care for their health should be deterred from eating fungi: first, because the most distinguished writers count them among poisons, and some think they are a cause of death; then also because they provide a food that is phlegmatic, cold, thick and viscous, and, for the most part, is barely digested, but is often cast out again with the excrement whole and undigested. Let those who take delight in these fungous dainties beware. But today they are devoured without limit, even by great men, who seek them out with special eagerness for these doubtful dinners. I know some people for whom that fungous phlegm is nothing more delicate than the excrement of food; they say that not all fungi are poisonous and deadly, as are those commonly called truffles,

units.la: germ. Morchel(n/vernoq, potissimum tempo- reab Aprili ad Majum usq, cernuntur : hos aqua feruente bulliere sinunt, postmodum aro- matibus & bu y o conditos mensis imponunt : Item amanita & boleti german. Helderling/ in campis & jumentorum pascuis proventen- tes Iunio primum mense, durante, usq, in Au- gustum : Hos, membranula tamen linida prius detrafta, similiter butyro aromatibus condiunt : alij super ignitos carbones eos af- fant, faleq, asperso mandunt, sed quo fructu, ipsi experiantur.
units.tr: which the Germans call Morchel, appear mainly from April to May; these they allow to boil in boiling water, and afterwards set them on the table seasoned with spices and butter. Likewise the amanita and the boletus, which the Germans call Helderling, growing in fields and cattle pastures, from June at first and lasting into August. These, after the thin skin lining them has first been stripped off, they season similarly with butter and spices. Others roast them over glowing coals and eat them sprinkled with salt, but what benefit they get from this, let them find out for themselves.

units.la: Sic inter esui aptos fungos annumerant.
units.tr: In this way they count among the fungi fit for eating:

units.la: Orbiculatos, german. Pfifferling / ab acri & piperis gustu, fracti enim lacteum fundunt fuc- cum feruentiffimi saporis, ac proveniunt in al- tiffimis & tenebrosis montibus colore prorsus candidi, disco interdum lat ores. Hos, qui fyl- lam Odentwalde cognominatam incoluntos carbonibus ignitis affare solent, faleq, aspersos mandere.
units.tr: The round ones, which the Germans call Pfifferling, from their sharp and peppery taste; for when broken they pour out a milky juice of the hottest flavour. They grow in the highest and shadiest mountains, quite white in colour, sometimes with a broad disc. Those who live in the region called the Odenwald are accustomed to roast these over glowing coals and eat them sprinkled with salt.

units.la: Ad horum catalogum quoque referunt, quos Brottling appellant in altissimis montibus nascentes puniceo colore, bi a quibusdam crudi devorantur, sed qua utilitate nescio.
units.tr: To this list they also refer those which they call Brottling, growing on the highest mountains, of a purple colour. Some eat them raw, but to what advantage I do not know.

units.la: Illi fiunt pracipui, qui hodie in delitiis habentur, inque usum ciborum trahuntur. Preeipuam tamen gratiam & praflantiam obtinuerunt. parte membranulis liquidis obducti, quae, ante- quam in cibos veniant, sunt detrahenda.
units.tr: Those are the chief ones that today are held in delight and drawn into use as food, and they have won a special favour and prominence; they are covered with a liquid membrane, which must be removed before they go to the table.

units.la: runt tubera, & boleti, qui inter fungos ab anti- quis semper sunt habiti optimi. Sed quis hoc sfondebit in venalibus ? Certum est omnes venenis esse accommodatissimos, improbiqué sucçi, quibus nominibus omnino vitari debent.
units.tr: truffles, and boletes, which among fungi have always been held by the ancients to be the best. But who will vouch for this in the market? It is certain that all of them are most liable to be poisonous and of wicked juice, and on these grounds they must altogether be avoided.

units.la: Fungorum enim temerario esu magnas vitæ fruti insidias exemplo est Claudius Tiberius princeps, cui boletorum avidissimo vene-num datum conflat ab Agrippina conjuge, quo facto illa terris venenum alterum sibi ante omnes Neronem dedit. Verisimilius tamen videtur Claudium non vitio boleti, sed vi me-dicamenti quo imbutum fuit boletus exinde fuisse.
units.tr: For a clear example of the snares that rash eating of fungi lays for life, there is the emperor Claudius Tiberius, who is generally said to have been given poison by his wife Agrippina, he being very fond of boletes; and by this deed she then gave poison to herself, before all others, to Nero. Yet it seems more probable that Claudius died not from a defect in the bolete, but from the power of a drug with which the bolete was soaked.

units.la: Submonitio de fungis.
units.tr: A warning about mushrooms.

units.la: NE fungorum me autoritatem prorsus abrogare velle quis existimet, voluptuariofque ac hydnophagos plane mihi inuisos reddam, tum etiam vt ventriac gulæ nonnihil consulatur, sciendum est, vt sum quidem me minime damnare, (per me enim licebit cuique ad satietatem etiam iis vesci,) sed modum feruandum præcipere nec ita liberaliter iis vescendum esse.
units.tr: Lest anyone think I wish to abolish the authority of fungi altogether, and make myself wholly hateful to lovers of pleasure and to mushroom-eaters, and also so that the belly and the palate may be somewhat consulted, it must be known that I, indeed, condemn them not at all (for each may eat of them to satiety, as far as I am concerned), but I advise that moderation be kept and that they should not be eaten so freely.

units.la: Gratum etiam hydnophagis me factarum spero, fi non omnes fungos ab antiquis damnatos esse, planum fecerim. Galenus ex fungis boletos orbiculatos tantum attin- gendos censuit. Celsus item alios fungos vtiles, alios inutiles esse dixit, & hos coctura genere fieri vtiles. Quod fi verum est, vt c[?] te est, etiam muscarii fungi, qui partim rubri, partim albi cernuntur, coquendi modo in-noxii reddi possunt, præsertim diligenter elixentur, mox ex oleo aut butyro[?] additis cæpis & pipere frigantur. Quidam addunt acetum, quod eos eximie debellat.
units.tr: I also hope I shall have made it plain, to the gratification of mushroom-eaters, that not all fungi were condemned by the ancients. Galen judged that only the round boletes should be touched. Celsus likewise said that some fungi are useful and others useless, and that by a particular method of cooking the useless ones become useful. If this is true, as it is, then even the fly agaric, which is seen partly red and partly white, can be made harmless by the manner of cooking, especially if it is carefully boiled and afterwards fried in oil or butter with onions and pepper added. Some add vinegar, which utterly defeats them.

units.la: Alii vino coquunt fungos adjecto origano vel hissopo. Qui vero eduntur expolire piperis, vel ex jure pingui cocti, omnino veneris irritamenta sunt. Diofcorides crudos edi docuit, sed qui crudis vesceretur, nemo adhuc visus est, nisi id fiat à pauperibus, & in summa rerum penuria. Aduersus pernitiales radiculam antefumtam cum sale & aceto prodesse Scribonius Largus testis est. Quercum & Castaneam boletos ferre probatiffimos omniumq; maximos, vt vnus pluribus sufficiat conuiuis, quidam afferunt.
units.tr: Others cook fungi in wine with marjoram or hyssop added. But those that are eaten dressed with pepper, or cooked in rich broth, are altogether incitements to lust. Dioscorides taught that they may be eaten raw, but no one has yet been seen to eat them raw, except poor people, and that in extreme scarcity of food. Scribonius Largus is witness that a little root taken beforehand with salt and vinegar is helpful against deadly ones. Some assert that boletes which grow on the oak and the chestnut are the most approved and the largest of all, so that one is enough for several guests.

units.la: Tutissimos existimant qui coquendo mollescant, qui enim duriores fiunt, noxii deprehenduntur. Venenis etiam accommodatissimi sunt in quibus dilutus rubor est, ranci-dus aspectus, color intus liuidus, pallidum per ambitum labrum, rimosæ striæ. Multi etiam venenosi fiunt, si serpentis cauerna iuxta fuerit, si chalybis rubigo, aut panni marcor: quae sane nec immerito ab esu & v- su fungorum aliquem deterrebunt. Egocer- te caute eos attingendos existimo. Clemens VII. Pontifex tam auide expetebat fungos, qui e spinetis vere nascuntur rotunditate clusili, vocantque Spinulos Cardeolofque, vt solus iis coenaret nullo non die. Edixerat iis in locis quae ditioni suae parebant, ne cui alteri demeterentur. Immatura autem morsindicio fuit, quantum intemperata vi- uendi ratio, noxiorumque esculentorum af- fiduus vsus hominibus ad vitam breuian- dam valeat. Nam & Peponibus immodera- tius vescebatur. Martialis quoque feruorem gulae Ceciliani detreftatus est carminib. suis, qui vocatus ad coenam ab amicis solus ipse boletos vorabat, carmina haec sunt, Dic mihi quis furor est? turba pectante vocata
units.tr: They judge those to be safest which become soft when cooked; for those that become harder are found to be harmful. Those most liable to be poisonous are those in which there is a washed-out redness, a rancid appearance, a livid colour within, a pale border around the edge, and cracked streaks. Many also become poisonous if a serpent's den is near, or the rust of steel, or the mustiness of cloth. These things will certainly deter some from eating and using fungi, and not without reason. I, for my part, think they should be touched with great caution. Pope Clement VII so eagerly sought the fungi that grow in spring among the thorn bushes, round and compact, which they call spinuli and cardeoli, that he dined on them alone almost every day. In the places that obeyed his rule he had issued an edict that they were not to be given to anyone else. His early death was a sign of how much an intemperate way of life, and the constant use of harmful foods, can shorten a man's life. For he also ate pumpkins immoderately. Martial, too, condemned in his verses the ardour of Cecilianus' gluttony, who, invited to dinner by his friends, devoured the boletes alone. The verses are these:

units.la: Solus boletos Ceciliane vorās.
units.tr: Tell me, what madness is this? A crowd invited, expecting dinner,

units.la: Quid dignum tanto ventri gulae, precabor?
units.tr: What worthy of so great a belly and gullet shall I pray for?

units.la: Boletum qualem (laudius edit, edat.)
units.tr: Such a mushroom as Claudius ate, let him eat.

units.la: Pestiferos denique esse fungos breuis illa vita fatis indicat, terrā enim eruti ocyffi- me putrescunt atque contabescunt, & in ipsa hærentes terra vix diem vnum atqueal- terum vigere animaduertuntur. Proinde, nisi probe coquantur, aromatibusque con- diandiantur, suffocationis periculum inferre, præter experientiam graues autores tradunt. Hæc vis strangulandi illis vt adimatur, para-ri eos oportere ex aceto aut oxymelite, aut etiam ipso melle & sale, Diphilus docuit.
units.tr: Finally, that short life of theirs shows by its very fate that mushrooms are deadly. Once dug up from the earth, they rot and decay more quickly, and while they still cling to the ground they are seen to stay alive scarcely a day or two. Therefore, unless they are thoroughly cooked and seasoned with spices, serious authors report, apart from experience, that they carry a danger of suffocation. Diphilus taught that to take away this power of strangling, they should be prepared with vinegar or oxymel, or even with honey and salt.

units.la: Qui vero ex intempestiuo auidoque illo-rum esu strangulatus similitudinem persen-tifcunt, vt sæpe magnatum aulis, apud quos maxima fungorum est autoritas, iis vo-mitu ex oleo, aut potu lixiuii è sarmentis, aut pyrastri furculis succurrendum: quin & ipsa pyra mansa præclare auxiliantur, funtq; hæc remedia parabilia, ac cuique in promtu, hucque obiter apposita, quoniam ancipitis hujus escæ maxima vbiuis fere locorum per-cipitur fœcunditas ac abundantia.
units.tr: But those who feel something like strangling from the untimely and greedy eating of them, as often happens in the courts of great men, among whom the authority of fungi is greatest, must be helped by vomiting with oil, or a drink of lye from vine-twigs, or the twigs of the wild pear; indeed, the pears themselves, chewed, give excellent help. These remedies are easy to obtain and at hand for everyone; I add them here in passing, since the greatest abundance and plenty of this dangerous food is found almost everywhere.

units.la: Hactenus de fungis eorumq; natura.
units.tr: So much for fungi and their nature.

units.la: CAP. XIII. De alimentis quæ veniunt ab animalibus.
units.tr: CAP. XIII. On foods that come from animals.

units.la: Commodum[?] nunc est differere de ciba-riis, quæ ab animantibus veniunt, ordi-nem vitæ sequendo.
units.tr: It is now fitting to discuss the meats that come from living creatures, following the order of life.

units.la: Nam prima illa ætas carnis desideria in-primis damnauit, pecora agricultura tantum-nasci existimans, ideoq; tam capitale erat bovem[?] occidisse, quam civem, primumq; pecudes interimendi morem ac modum a victimis deorum & placationibus alimenti hominum gratiâ emanasse nonnulli diligenter observarunt: unde postea non pauci natura rerum viri calentissimi in lucem emiserunt commentarios, quibus explicarunt, mitiores longe salubriores q; escas, praebere mortalibus animantia, quam olera, aut arborum poma, glandesq;.
units.tr: For that earliest age especially condemned the desire for flesh, thinking that cattle were born only for farming, and so killing an ox was as serious a crime as killing a citizen. Some have carefully observed that the custom and manner of slaughtering animals first arose from the sacrifices to the gods and their propitiation, and only then for the sake of human food. Hence later not a few men, very warm in their enthusiasm for the nature of things, published commentaries explaining that animals provide mortals with food that is far milder and far more wholesome than vegetables, or the fruit of trees and acorns.

units.la: Sed id non factum est ab omnibus pari industria & scientia. Numerosa enim animalium, quæ in cibos hominum admittuntur genera, haud dubie omnibus non percognita, earum varietas copiaq;, coquendi parandiq; diuersitas, ipsorumq; animalium partes diffidentes causam, præbuerunt perplexitati. Nos, quantum nobis licet in hoc præclaro naturæ munere commemorando per exiles ingenii vires assequi, cibaria, quæ ab animantibus sumuntur studiosius & methodice persequemur.
units.tr: But this was not done with equal diligence and knowledge by everyone. For the many kinds of animals admitted into human food, which were doubtless not all known to everyone, their variety and abundance, the differences in cooking and preparation, and the parts of the animals themselves, have caused perplexity by their diversity. We, as far as our slender abilities allow us to follow this excellent gift of nature in describing it, will pursue with care and method the foods taken from animals.

units.la: Alimenta autem ab animalibus petita vel sunt animalium sanguineorum vel exanguium.
units.tr: Foods taken from animals are either from animals with blood or from bloodless ones.

units.la: Sanguinea vel simplicis vitæ sunt, vel amphibia.
units.tr: Those with blood are either of simple life, or amphibious.

units.la: Simplicis vitæ vel solum in aere viuunt, vel in aqua tantum.
units.tr: Those of simple life either live only in air, or only in water.

units.la: Ex aereis alia volucria sunt, alia gradientia. Volucria, quod in aere volent, dicta sunt aues.
units.tr: Of the airborne, some are winged, others walk. Winged creatures are called birds, because they fly in the air.

units.la: Humi gradientia vel ambulant, vt homo & quadrupedes, vel reptant vt reptilia.
units.tr: Those that walk on the ground either go on foot, like man and the quadrupeds, or creep, like reptiles.

units.la: Amphibia animalia dicuntur, quae an-cipitis sunt natura, inter aerea & aquea, hoc est, partim in aere, partim in aqua viuunt, vt rana, crocodilus, lutra, laxus, fiber, natrix, mer-gus, anas.
units.tr: Animals are called amphibious which are of a doubtful nature, between air and water, that is, which live partly in air and partly in water, such as the frog, crocodile, otter, laxus, beaver, water snake, merganser and duck.

units.la: Huiusmodi sunt sanguinea, succedunt ex-sanguia, sanguinis scilicet expertia, vt sunt polypus, sepia, lolligo, crustacea item, vt cancer, locu-sta, squilla, & testacea, vt limaces terrestres, cochlea marina, ostrea, pectines, concha.
units.tr: Of this kind are the blooded animals; the bloodless ones follow, namely those without blood, such as the polyp, cuttlefish, squid, and likewise the crustaceans, such as the crab, lobster, and prawn, and the shelled ones, such as land snails, sea snails, oysters, scallops and mussels.

units.la: Hec est compendiosa animalium familia. Nunc opera pretium erit recensere quibus animantibus, horumq; partibus, tam externis, quam internis hominis potissimum alantur, ex-ordium sumendo ab auibus.
units.tr: This is the brief catalogue of animals. Now it will be worth listing which animals, and which of their parts, both external and internal, feed humans most, beginning with birds.

units.la: De auibus in genere, earumque differentiis in re cibaria.
units.tr: On birds in general, and their differences as regards food.

units.la: NE nihil, quod vitae interest, omittatur, vtque lectorem pleniori atque vlteriore obsequio demereat, adnotare hic oportebit, complures in auium genere reperiri differentias, tum à tempore, ætate, victu, tum loco, cœloq;, quæ auium ipsarum carcarnes salubriores aut infalubriores reddunt, cibisque; magis aut minus idoneas. Quo enim tempore libidine prüriunt coeuntque mactrescunt præsertim syluestres : quin etiam quando incubant pullosque excludunt, tunc enim minus comedunt, vnde extenuantur.
units.tr: LEST anything that concerns life be omitted, and in order to oblige the reader with fuller and further service, it will be necessary to note here that many differences are found in the class of birds, arising from time, age, diet, place and climate, which make the flesh of the birds themselves more or less wholesome and more or less suitable as food. For at the time when they are inflamed with lust and couple, they grow thin, especially the wild ones; indeed, also when they sit on their eggs and hatch their young, for then they eat less, and so grow lean.

units.la: Ex domesticis & villaticis, vt sunt gallinæ, columbæ, anseres, anates, pauones &c. nemo facile edit incubantes. Porro aliæ omnino vere, aliæ magis placent æstate quæ scilicet frugibus vescuntur, aliæ autumno, quæ vuis, ficubus & cæterarum arborum pomis baccisque. Quibusdam hiemis frigora gratiam conciliant, vt turdis, merulis, anseribus feris, gruibus, aquaticisque; fere omnibus. Complures quoq; hieme latent, nec omnes ad loca tepidiora abeunt, vt merula, turdus, alauda. Turtur latere incipit præpinguis, nec vspiam per hiemem videtur, & licet pennas dimittat in latibulo, pinguedinem tamen seruat. Palumborum aliqui latent, aliqui non. Sturnus latet qui per vindemias obesatur eximie. Certum est ad algores æstusque, mutationes temporum aues sentire, natura quippe iis indidit sensum, à quo mutationes frigore vel calore factas cognoscant, ideoq; loca, quæ possunt, permutant, nonnullæque subsidium in locis istis sibi consuetis comperiunt : aliæ peregre proficiscuntur, ut grues ex Scythicis campis ad paludes Ægypto superiores veniunt. A[?] victu quoque differentiæ non paucæ sunt.
units.tr: Among the domestic and farmyard birds, such as hens, pigeons, geese, ducks, peacocks, etc., no one readily eats those that are sitting. Further, some are pleasing chiefly in spring, others more in summer, when they feed on grain, others in autumn, when they feed on grapes, figs and the fruit and berries of other trees. Some are made agreeable by the cold of winter, such as thrushes, blackbirds, wild geese, cranes, and almost all water birds. Many also hide in winter, and not all go off to warmer places, such as the blackbird, thrush and lark. The turtle dove begins to hide when very fat, and is seen nowhere during winter; and although it sheds its feathers in its hiding place, it keeps its fat. Some kinds of woodpigeon hide, others do not. The starling hides, having grown exceptionally fat at the vintage. It is certain that birds feel the chill and heat, and the changes of the seasons; for nature has given them a sense by which they know the changes made by cold or heat, and so they change their places where they can, and some find refuge for themselves in those customary places; others set out abroad, as cranes come from the Scythian plains to the marshes above Egypt. There are also not a few differences in diet.

units.la: Quibus adunci vngues sunt omnes carniuoræ, ut aquilæ, milui, accipitres, vultures, buteo, nocturnæque aues, bubo, noctua, vlula: quædam frugiuoræ sunt & omniuoræ, ut cornices, & ut summatim dicam, omnium fere auium, aliæ victum à terra petunt, aliæ à fluuio, aliæ à lacu, aliæ à mari.
units.tr: All the birds with hooked talons are carnivorous, such as eagles, kites, hawks, vultures, buzzards, and the night birds, the owl, the screech owl and the eagle owl. Some are grain-eaters and omnivores, such as crows; and, to sum up, almost all birds: some seek their food from the land, others from rivers, others from lakes, others from the sea.

units.la: Ubi notandum, auium carnes, ipsarum quo vtuntur, alimenti semper fere refertæ[?] sa-porem: quæ enim formicis vescuntur, for-micarum, quæ culicibus culicum, quæ ver-miculis vermiculorum saporem repræsen-tant. Sic sylvestrium carnes prope refe-runt saporem pabuli. Quæ aluntur pisci-bus, pisces olent, & quæ circa aquas viuunt, lutum cœnumque, quæ circa mare, virus il-lud marinum redolent, proindeque cibis ab-dicandæ.
units.tr: Here it should be noted that the flesh of birds almost always carries the flavour of what they feed on. Those that eat ants taste of ants, those that eat gnats of gnats, those that eat worms of worms. Thus the flesh of wood-dwelling birds nearly reproduces the taste of their pasture. Those fed on fish smell of fish, and those living by waters of mud and sludge, and those around the sea smell of that marine stench; therefore they must be rejected as food.

units.la: Ætatem quod attinet, aliæ placent in infantia, aliæ cum adoleuerint: Senecta semper improbatur. Pulli columbacei generis, pulli perdicum, pulli coturnicum, pulli gal-linarum, ut pullastri & pullastræ parentibus semper præstant, gallinæ iuvencæ quoque anniculæ veteribus anteponuntur. Sicut & capi iuuenes suauitate præstant. Quid? quod & castratione gallinaceum genus suasuauius efficitur & vtilius, quin & fœminas nunc castrare gula luxusque didicit. Ad extremum non prætereundum caueis conclusas, altilesque redditas, inque vrbium domibus vagantes & saginatas gulosis ganeonibus, suauius quidem sapere, sed vitæ minus esse salutares, propterea quod vberiori excremento scateant, probumq; succum non gignant, nam quæ in agris versantur præstantiores exiltunt, vnde caponesfaluberrimi existimantur, qui circa tritici metas pinguescunt, necfine exercitio, difcurruntenim vltro citroq;. Idem judicium fit de omni genere animantium, tum ferorum, tum cicurum, quæ mortalibus cibaria præbent, in quib. faginailla atq; adipofa obelitas carcere otioq; conciliata vitæ insidiosa deprehenditur & pestifera. Sic columbæ quæ turres incolunt salubriores sunt domesticis, & quæ in locis humilib. educantur, volatus enim salubritati gratiam adiicit. Aues item montanæ campestribus, &quein locis paluftrib. degunt, sicut & apri montani campestribus præferuntur. Atq; hæc de auium differentia in genere, sequitur nunc de singulis feorfim. Immensam autem ac Numerosam volucrum multitudinem esse, testatur cœna illa Vitellio à fratre data, in qua septem avium millia ap-posita traduntur, tantus fuit istius seculi luxus tantaque vorago. Y
units.tr: As for age, some are pleasing when young, others when grown; old age is always disapproved. Chicks of the pigeon kind, partridge chicks, quail chicks, and the chicks of hens, such as cockerels and pullets, are always better than their parents, and young hens and year-old ones are preferred to old ones. Just so young capons are superior in tenderness. What of this, that by castration the cock kind is made both more pleasing to the palate and more useful? Indeed, gluttony and luxury have now learned to castrate hens too. Finally, one must not pass over birds shut up in coops, fattened for the table, and wandering in city houses and crammed by greedy gluttons: these indeed taste sweeter, but are less healthy for life, because they abound in more copious waste and do not produce good juice. For those that live in the fields turn out more excellent, which is why capons are thought most wholesome when they grow fat around the wheat stacks, and not without exercise, for they run here and there of their own accord. The same judgment holds for every kind of animal, both wild and tame, that provides food for mortals: in those in which fattening, obesity and fat are produced by confinement and idleness, the life is found to be treacherous and harmful. Thus pigeons that dwell in towers are healthier than domestic ones, and those reared in low places; for flight adds grace to health. Likewise mountain birds are preferred to those of the plains, and those that live in marshy places, just as mountain boars are preferred to those of the plains. So much for the differences among birds in general; now follows an account of each one separately. That the multitude of birds is immense and numerous is shown by that feast given to Vitellius by his brother, at which seven thousand birds are said to have been served up, so great was the luxury and so vast the gullet of that age.

units.la: Aquatilium volucrum genera 177. esse, quæ nominatim percognita sint, Plinius autor est, sed in terrestribus id fieri nequit, tantum enim abest, vt in consideratio-nem omnes venire possint, vt etiam omnes Indiæ, Æthiopiæ, Scythiæ, aut aliarum Septentrionalium occiduarumq; terrarum de-fertorumq; aves non sint notæ: Omitto Ta-probanæ[?], infularumq; nuper patefactarum immensam multitudinem, aliasq; fabulosæ magis quam vere narratas. Quare notas magis, nobiscumque degentes perseque-mur.
units.tr: Pliny is the authority that 177 kinds of water birds are known by name, but this cannot be done for land birds; for not only can they not all come under consideration, but even the birds of all India, Ethiopia, Scythia, or of the other northern, western and desert lands are unknown. I say nothing of the immense multitude of Taprobane and of the islands recently opened up, and of others reported more as fable than as truth. Therefore I shall pursue the better known birds, those who live among us.

units.la: Ex avibus autem escas hominum prae-cipue adjuvant, gallinacei, vrogalli, gallinæ, pulli gallinacei, columbæ, palumbi, anseres, anates, perdices, attagines, rusticulæ, roftrulæ, turdi, merulæ, sturni, coturnices, cornices, pi-cæ, pici, monedulæ, phasiani, alaudæ, fringil-læ, passeres, galguli, aliæq; complures, quæ in minuto avium genere sunt, quas singulas persequi immensi esset laboris & difficulta-tis, præsertim cum multæ inter eas sint vitæ & colore ignobiles.
units.tr: Among birds, those that chiefly serve human food are: the cock, capon, hen, chicks, pigeons, wood pigeons, geese, ducks, partridges, woodcocks, snipe, thrushes, blackbirds, starlings, quails, crows, magpies, woodpeckers, jackdaws, pheasants, larks, finches, sparrows, nightjars, and many others of the small kinds of birds. To pursue each of these would be a task of immense labour and difficulty, especially since many of them are obscure in both life and colour.

units.la: Ex grandioribus vero non prætermit-tendi sunt struthiocameli, grues, ciconiæ, cygni, gallopavi, pavones, ardeæ, & id genus alia.
units.tr: Among the larger ones, which must not be passed over, are ostriches, cranes, storks, swans, turkeys, peacocks, herons, and other such kinds.

units.la: Nec omiserim carnivorum genus, ut aquiaquilas, coruos, miluios, accipitres ambos, fringillarium & palumbarium, hirundines &c, aues item nocturnas, & falcones.
units.tr: Nor would I omit the carnivorous kind: eagles, ravens, kites, both goshawks and sparrowhawks, the falcons used for finches and for pigeons, swallows, etc., and likewise the night birds and falcons.

units.la: Atque hic est præcipuarum magisque confeflarum ac nostris terris familiarium avium catalogus, externas, peregrinas, & nouas persequi parum ad institutum norum attinet. Nunc in vsu mensarum quæ præcipuæ sint, dispiciendum.
units.tr: This is the catalogue of the chief and most familiar birds, and of those that are familiar in our lands. To pursue foreign, exotic and new birds has little to do with our purpose. Now it must be considered which of them are the chief ones in the use of the table.

units.la: De gallis gallinaceis.
units.tr: On Capons.

units.la: Gallinaceos ex Perfide primum in alias terras tranfiffe prodiderunt graeci. Ex his fiunt capi, lautiorum hodie mensas plurimum opulentantes. Castrantur autem galli tum vt facilius pinguescant, tum vt suaui-ores reddantur ac delicatiores. Castrantur nouissima parte sua alui eximendo testiculum, vtrumq;. Quod fi enim alter relinquatur, cu-rietur ac canet, coitumq; repetet. Elegantiores quoq; & maiores euadunt, fi castrentur dum crescunt.
units.tr: The Greeks reported that domestic fowls first crossed from Persia into other lands. From these come capons, which now greatly enrich the tables of the wealthy. Cocks are castrated partly so that they fatten more easily and partly so that they become sweeter and more delicate. They are castrated by cutting out the testicles through an incision in the lower belly, both of them. If one is left, the bird remains restless, crows, and seeks to mate again. Cocks also grow more elegant and larger if they are castrated while still young.

units.la: Vetulorum gallorum carnes ingrata sunt & insuaues, sed jus in quo decoquuntur in aluo soluenda celebratur, juniorum vero gallorum & gallinarum carnes & jus eximie nutriunt.
units.tr: The flesh of old cocks is unpleasant and tasteless, but the broth in which they are boiled is prized for loosening the belly. The flesh and broth of young cocks and of hens are exceptionally nourishing.

units.la: Cerebrum gallorum gallinarumq., exignum quidem est, sed tanto quadrupedum ce-rebro prastantius, quanto durius. Hodie primo elixum, deinde prunis tostum manduntur à delicatioribus. Vitellius Phasianorum & Pavonum cerebella in delitiis gulæ habuit, ea enim apposuit in patina sua, quam Minerua clypeum appellabat.
units.tr: The brains of cocks and hens are indeed tiny, but they are far more excellent than the brains of quadrupeds, in proportion as they are firmer. Today they are eaten by the more refined, first boiled and then toasted over coals. Vitellius kept the little brains of pheasants and peacocks among the delights of his gluttony; he served them on his dish, which Minerva called her shield.

units.la: Gallorum testes miris laudibus extulit Galenus præsertim eorum, qui cibariis lactè ma-ceratis saginantur, veleducantur, succum-enim laudabilem præbent, facile concoquuntur, valenterq; nutriunt acVenerem stimulant cer-to experimento.
units.tr: Galen praised the testicles of cocks with great commendation, especially those of birds fattened or fed on food soaked in milk. They yield a laudable juice, are easily digested, nourish vigorously, and, by certain experience, stimulate Venus.

units.la: Incidit mihi hic historia admodum face-tofa cujus meminit Amatus Lufitanus cen-tur. 2. curationum medicinalium, de nobili quadam fœmina, quæ marito suo gallorum quos castrauerat testes melle-pipere, aliisq; aro-matibus laute præparatos in cœna comedendos obtulit. His cum alacriter avideque palatum explevißet, subsequente nocte tantus concu-bandi appetitus, tantaq; ei tentigo excitata fuit, vt vxor ex nimia continuatione coeundi plu-satis delassata & fatigata, vt tandem evaserit, ino, aliud cubiculum se abdiderit. Ipse vero eam insecutus pruriente adhuc materiâ, in an-cillarum dormitorium irrupit, easq; similiter ad sugam usq; subegit.
units.tr: A very amusing story comes to mind here, which Amatus Lusitanus mentions in the second century of his Medicinal Cures, about a certain noblewoman. She served her husband, to be eaten at supper, the testicles of castrated cocks, elegantly prepared with honey, pepper and other spices. When he had gladly and eagerly satisfied his palate with them, that night such a desire to lie with her came over him, and such an erection was roused in him, that his wife, exhausted and worn out by the excessive continuation of intercourse, at last escaped and withdrew to another bedroom. He, however, still burning, followed her, and burst into the maids' dormitory, and likewise subdued them to the point of exhaustion.

units.la: Ex quibus patet, testes gallinaceorum inter ea, quae venerem excitant, feminisque ac spi-rituum generationi sunt accommoda, non po-stremum obtinuisse locum.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the testicles of cocks have held no minor place among the things that arouse lust and are suited to the generation of seed and of vital spirits.

units.la: Verum tenendum, veterum gallorum testes virosos esse & effœtos, quare juniorum ad hanc rem assumendi sunt.
units.tr: It must be held, however, that the testicles of old cocks are rank and barren, so young ones should be chosen for this purpose.

units.la: Delicatiores quoque fœmina in deliciis gula habent oropygia gallinaceorum & gallinarum, praesertim altilium & praepinguium, ac certum est ea boni succi esse, licet veterani milites oropygiorum voratores a quibusdam appellentur.
units.tr: Delicate women too, in their gluttonous delights, prize the rumps of cocks and hens, especially of those that are fattened and very fat. It is certain that they are of good juice, although some call the rumps the gluttony of veteran soldiers.

units.la: De Gallinis.
units.tr: On Hens.

units.la: Gallinaceae carnes, ut graves testantur autores, ipsaque experientia, praestantissimae sunt, facile enim concipiuntur, omnibusque naturis & temperamentis peridoneae sunt, ideoque alimenti precipui. Quapropter in villatica pastione cum suis pullis merito obtinent primas, ex iis enim numerosissima epularum genera fiunt, infinitosque mortalibus in re cibaria usus subministrant, nec alius cibus est, qui innocentius, tum aegris, tum sanis possit exhiberi. Nullo quoque magis cibo juvamur in repentino amicorum hospitumque aduentu quam gallinaceo:qua de causa multa tradita reperiuntur quomodo tenerefcant,sic enim repente jugulatæ plerumque duræ admodum sunt.
units.tr: Hen's flesh, as grave authors attest and experience itself shows, is most excellent. It is easily digested, suits every constitution and temperament, and is therefore a chief food. Hence in farmyard rearing, along with its chicks, it rightly holds first place, for from it come very many kinds of dishes, and it supplies mortals with countless uses in food. Nor is there any food that can be given more harmlessly, both to the sick and to the healthy. Nothing helps us more than a hen when friends or guests arrive unexpectedly. For this reason many methods are recorded for making it tender, since birds killed on the spur of the moment are generally very tough.

units.la: Horatius eleganter, quomodo id fiat docuit his carminibus,
units.tr: Horace taught elegantly how this is done, in these verses:

units.la: Si vespertinus subito te oppresserit hospes, Nec gallina malum responset durapa- lato, Doctus eris vivam misto mersare fa- lerno, Hoc teneram faciet.
units.tr: If an evening guest suddenly drops in on you, and the hen does not answer the hard palate badly, you will be wise to dip the living bird in mixed Falernian wine. This will make her tender.

units.la: Atque hunc morem à multis obseruari constat. Cæterum in prandia elixas,in cœ-nas vero inaffatas gallinas fumere ganeæ proceres jubent, inuento non insalubri, sed in paucis hodie id obseruari video mensis. Non prætereundum miraculum naturæ, fi auro liquescenti gallinarum membra misce-antur, consumi hoc in fe, ita hoc venenum auri est. Saginare gallinas primum coepe-re Deliaci, unde pestis exorta opimas aues & suopte corpore inunctas deuorandi.
units.tr: And it is established that many follow this custom. Otherwise, the leaders of gluttony order hens to be eaten boiled at lunch and roasted in sauce at supper. This is not unwholesome, but I see it observed today in few kitchens. A wonder of nature must not be passed over: if the limbs of hens are mixed with molten gold, the gold is consumed within them, so great is the poison of gold. The people of Delos first began to fatten hens, whence a plague arose of devouring rich birds anointed with their own fat.

units.la: De gallinaceis non omittendum, quod circulo è sarmentis ipsorum addito collo non canunt.
units.tr: Concerning cocks it should not be omitted that when a circle of their own twigs is placed around their necks, they do not crow.

units.la: De pullis gallinaceis.
units.tr: On Chicks.

units.la: Bimestres & trimestres magis laudantur, nec non qui ante solstitium nascuntur, mense scilicet Martio, Aprili, Maio, qui enim post solstitium nascuntur iustam magnitudinem non implere creduntur, idq; tanto minus quanto serius proveniunt. Inventum est ut omni hiberno etiam tempore contingant & haberi possint. Qua calido in loco, posita paleis igne modico fouentur, verfanturq; pariter die & nocte, statutoq; tandem die illinc erumpit fœtus: quem morem & hodiè durare audio Hierosolymis, & in Syria, Rhodo, & Ægypto: quinetiam apud nos huius rei extiterunt ingeniosi artifices praesertim in Magnatum aulis. Aristoteles praeter id asserit ova in vasis quibusdam tepidis sponte pullos prompsisse. Fabulosum quibusdam videtur, (quanquam a gravibus autoribus proditum reperiatur) quod de quodam vini potore Syracusano reperitur, quem tamdiu potare soli-tu[?] tradunt, donec ab eo cooperta in terra fœtu e-derent ova, quo etiam nomine inter bibaciissimos sui temporis habitus est.
units.tr: Chicks two or three months old are more praised, as are those hatched before the solstice, that is, in March, April and May, for those hatched after the solstice are believed not to reach full size, and the later they come, the less so. It has been devised that they may be obtained and kept even in the winter season. They are placed in straw in a warm place, kept warm by a moderate fire, and turned equally day and night; then on the appointed day the chick breaks out. I hear this practice still continues today at Jerusalem, in Syria, Rhodes and Egypt, and indeed among us there have been ingenious craftsmen in this art, especially in the courts of magnates. Aristotle further asserts that eggs placed in certain warm vessels spontaneously released chicks. It seems fabulous to some, though it is reported by serious authors, what is recorded of a certain Syracusan wine-drinker: they say he drank so long that eggs laid by him on the ground hatched chicks. For this reason he was counted among the most bibulous men of his time.

units.la: De usu gallinaceorum & gallinarum, in medicina.
units.tr: On the use of cocks and hens in medicine.

units.la: NOn tantum in re cibaria infinitos u-sus administrant, numerosissimaq;[?]
units.tr: They provide not only endless uses in food, and very many kinds of dishes,

units.la: Note: the drop-cap and the word "epula-" are printed as read; see notes.
units.tr: [Transcriber's note: the drop-cap and the word "epula-" are printed as read; see notes.]

units.la: epularum genera suppeditant, verum etiam in re medica infigne præstant sæpe auxilium & quidem facile, idáque feré quotidianum.
units.tr: but also in medicine they often give outstanding help, and that easily, almost every day.

units.la: Gallinaceorum cerebro vino epoto, (sicut & carnibus illorum tepentibus) serpentum venenum domari tradit Plinius lib. 29. cap. 4. nec non morsum canis rabidi. Parthi gallinæ cerebrum malunt, quod peculiariter etiam debili memoriæ prodesse traditur.
units.tr: Pliny (Book 29, chapter 4) reports that the poison of serpents is tamed by the brain of a cockerel drunk in wine, as well as by its warm flesh, and also the bite of a mad dog. The Parthians prefer the brain of a hen, which is also said to be especially good for a weak memory.

units.la: Carnes gallinarum viperis, saginatarum elixarumque, elephantiafis labe infectis proff uiffe certò obseruatum est. In aeris vero peste maximè inter cibos commendantur.
units.tr: It has been reliably observed that the flesh of hens, fattened and boiled, cures those infected with elephantiasis. In a plague of the air especially, they are recommended among foods.

units.la: Ius gallinaceorum & gallinarum potum præclarè medetur venenis, præsertim fi allium fueritincoctum. Pantherae, Leonesque non attinguntur eo perunctos: aluum præterea mollitac soluit, sed validius è veteri gallinaceo: prodest & contra longinquas febres tor-pentibus tremulisque membris, articulari morbo, renibus, epati, vesicæ, & demum contra suspiria & cruditates. Veneficiis exmuncta stela fylueftri factis contrarium est ius gallinacei veteris largè haustum, sed peculiari ter contra aconitum, adiecto tamen falis mo-dico.
units.tr: Broth of cockerels and hens, drunk, cures poisons admirably, especially if garlic has been boiled in it. Panthers and lions are not touched by those anointed with it. It also gently loosens the bowels, though more strongly when made from an old cock. It helps against long fevers, numb and trembling limbs, joint disease, kidney, liver and bladder complaints, and finally against hiccups and indigestion. Against poisons made from wild stela, a generous draught of broth from an old cock is the remedy, but especially against aconite, with a little salt added.

units.la: Fel gallinacei dilutum aquâ, vlcerationes & oculorum albugines, suffusiones item & calicalgationes fanat,& maximè candidi. Laudatur & gallinæ fel,præcipueque adeps con-tra pustulas in papillis,adiuuatq; mirifice ruptas oculorum tunicas admixto lapide hæmatite.
units.tr: The gall of a cock, diluted in water, heals ulcers and white films of the eyes, as well as suffusions and dimness of sight, especially that of a white cock. The gall of a hen is also praised, and especially its fat, against pustules on the nipples; and it wonderfully helps torn coats of the eyes when mixed with the stone haematite.

units.la: Fimum gallinaceorum,sed rubrum, luscis-esis[?] illinendum suadent, morsisque à rabido canè exaceto : fimum quoque gallinarum candidum in veteri oleo corneisque pyxidibus asseruare solent ad oculorum albugines, miscetur autem cum rosacea, fœniculacea, vel oui albumine. Earundem fimum candi-dam hissopo aut mulso decoctum, venena fungorum[?] astringit, inflationes itè & strangulationes,quod mirari subit, si enim id fimū gustauerit aliud animal, torminibus afficitur & inflationibus. Verrucas quoq; pellit cum oleo & nitro fimum gallinaceorum.
units.tr: They advise smearing the dung of cocks, though red, on those who are blind in one eye, and on the bites of a mad dog after it has been sharpened. They also commonly keep the white dung of hens in old oil and in horn boxes, for white films of the eyes; it is mixed with rose, fennel, or egg white. The same white dung, boiled with hyssop or mead, checks the effects of poisonous fungi, and also swellings and strangulations, which is surprising: if another animal tastes this dung, it is afflicted with gripes and swellings. Cock dung with oil and nitre also drives away warts.

units.la: Non omittam hîc mysterium naturæ. Nam cor è viuente gallina exectum dextreq; coxæ palpitans adhuc alligatum partum dif-ficilem accelerat.
units.tr: I shall not omit here a mystery of nature. For the heart cut from a living hen, still beating and tied to the right thigh, hastens a difficult birth.

units.la: Ventriculi gallinaceorū membrana, quæ in coctionibus abiici solet, vino trita auib[?] purulentis calida infunditur, sic & gallinarū adeps: eadem siccata & potioni inspersa stomachicis, pectoris destillationibus, humidæque medetur tussi. Gallinaceorum iecuras-sum cum prædicta ventriculi membrana admisto papaueris succo dysentericis ꝑdestvé-trisq; malis.
units.tr: The membrane of a cock's gizzard, which is usually thrown away in cooking, is rubbed up with wine, warmed, and poured into purulent ears. So too is the fat of hens. The same membrane, dried and sprinkled into a drink, cures stomach complaints, rheums of the chest, and damp cough. The liver of cocks, mixed with the said gizzard membrane and poppy juice, cures dysentery and bowel disorders.
See Pliny, Book 29, chapters 5 and 6, and Book 30, chapter 7.

units.la: De columbis.
units.tr: On Doves.

units.la: AGallinaceo genere proximum est columbaceum ninoris in re cibaria vsus quàm gallinaceum. Varro columbas diuitias putat, quod in summis columninibus villa nidificent.
units.tr: Next after the hen in the kind of food it supplies is the dove, which is more nourishing than the hen. Varro thinks doves are a source of wealth, because they nest in the upper dovecotes of the farmhouse.

units.la: Xenophon libro expeditionis Cyri primo tradidit Syros columbas habere sacrosanctas, nefas putare eas violare. Ante bellum ciuile Pompeianum in magno fuerunt pretio. Nam L. Axius eques Rom. denarius quadringentis singula pariauerat. Nam magnis in rebus fuerunt interpreti, epistolas annexas earum pedibus obsidione Mutinensi in castra consulum Decimo Bruto mittente.
units.tr: Xenophon, in the first book of the Expedition of Cyrus, reports that the Syrians hold doves sacred and think it wicked to harm them. Before the Pompeian civil war they were held in great esteem. For Lucius Axius, a Roman knight, had a dove that laid four hundred eggs one after another. They were also very useful in serious affairs, since letters were tied to their feet; Decimus Brutus sent them into the consuls' camp during the siege of Mutina.

units.la: Multa sunt illarum genera, quæ omnia percensere superuacaneum est. Aristoteles prolem vernam præstantiorem affirit quàm autumnalem, deterrimamq; estiuam. Galli aliqua vernam fœturam damnant improbantq;, quoniam pulli non perueniant ad volatum tempestiuum, cum sæpe propter imbres veris largiores in nidis intereant, vel etiam ouâ vitiantur. Præstantissimam ad volatum & cibos prolem existimat Iulio vel Augusto mense natam; messis enim tempore pulli maximè pingues inueniuntur propter pabuli copiam. Calor enim columbis, vt & cæteris animantibus generibus, vtilissimus, imbres vero inimicissimi. Delectantur mi-rum in modum sale, ideoq; cibaria illa salsa crescunt.
