units.tr: There are many kinds of doves, and it would be superfluous to list them all. Aristotle asserts that the spring brood is better than the autumn brood, and the summer brood is the worst. Some poultry-keepers condemn and disapprove of the spring hatching, because the chicks do not reach flight at the right time, since often in the heavier spring rains they die in the nests, or the eggs are spoiled. They judge the offspring best for flying and for food to be the one hatched in the month of July or August; for at harvest time the young are found to be very fat, because of the abundance of fodder. For warmth is most useful to doves, as to other living creatures, while rains are most harmful. They take an extraordinary delight in salt, and so those salted foods fatten them.

units.la: Verna columbarum fœtura cur damnentur? briu obiiciuntur. Qui domicilia sua habent in turribus carcere contabescunt, volatu enim exercitioq; exhilarantur atque pinguescunt. Domestica vero, quae intra limina solent educari prapingues fiunt. Mauritiani columbos cibis damnarunt: at Galenus eos qui in turribus degunt, commendat.
units.tr: Why are spring hatchings of doves condemned? Objections are raised against them. Those who keep their dwellings in towers waste away in confinement; for they are cheered and grow fat through flying and exercise. Those kept at home, which are usually reared within doors, become exceedingly fat. The Mauritanians condemned doves as food; but Galen recommends those that live in towers.

units.la: Nec dubitandum pullos columbarum sanis atq; aegriseffe maxime salutares. Damnatur autem gula quae etiam infantissimos, hoc est, plurima nondum tectos mandere inuenit, nec enim novelli nimium nec adulti nimium probantur, acceptissimi sunt medii. Idemq; de gallinaceis, quos similiter quidam in prima infantia edunt, intelligendum. Turturam caro sapientia fe num cibus dicitur, sensus enim omnes corroborat, cogitationem acuit, memoriamq; corroborat.
units.tr: There is no doubt that the young of doves are most wholesome both for the healthy and for the sick. But gluttony is condemned, which seeks out even the very tender, that is, those not yet fully feathered; for neither the very young nor the fully grown are much approved, the middle-aged are most acceptable. The same must be understood of poultry, which some likewise eat in their earliest infancy. The flesh of turtle-doves is said to be a food that promotes wisdom, for it strengthens all the senses, sharpens thought, and strengthens the memory.

units.la: De palumbis.
units.tr: On Wood-Pigeons.

units.la: IN colübaceo genere maximi sunt palumbi, quorum captura in quibusdam locis, ut Aquitania apud Vafates, vberrima est, gloriaq; inter epulas non postrema; conscientia difficiles iudicantur, succiqueque non adeo boni. Torquatum vnum genus dicitur à torque, quo collum insignitur, germ Ring-geltauben/quorum caro ob glandium esum traditur, hebetare venerem, quod non ignorauit Martialis, (scribens,
units.tr: Among the pigeon family the wood-pigeons are the largest. In some places, such as Aquitaine near the Vafates, they are caught in great numbers, and they are no small glory at feasts. They are judged hard to digest, and their juice is not especially good. The ring-dove is one kind, named from the torque (ring) that marks its neck, [German: Ring-geltauben]. Its flesh is said to dull sexual desire, because it feeds on acorns. Martial did not overlook this when he wrote:

units.la: Inguina torquati tardant, hebetantque pedes lumbi.
units.tr: The loins of the ring-dove slow the groin and dull the feet.

units.la: Non edat hanc volucrem, qui cupit esse salax.
units.tr: Let no man who wants to be lustful eat this bird.

units.la: Porro palumborum vitam vel ad 40. annos durare, quibusdam ad 25. & ad 30. protrahi annum, Aristoteles testis est lib. 6. de hist. c. 4. & lib. 9. cap. 1. cui astipulatur Plinius lib. 10. cap. 35. Lauri se foliis purgare palumbos quotannis, idem Plinius testis est lib. 8. cap. 27. Sicut columbæ, turtures & gallinacei herba helxine, anates, anseresque fiderite[?], grues iunco palustri. Venerem denique trime-stres palumbi nosse incipiunt, & fœtificare, quod vberrima eorum copia ostendit. Nam in agrum Volaterranum, ut & alios tractus palumborum vis ingens quotannis aduolat è mari. Pariunt vere, nec plus quàm bis. Hi-bernis mensibus inter elegantiores epulas collocari palumbos, notum est iis, apud quos eorum magna copia est, eosque quidam cum brassica elixant, parum tamen ante inafla-tos.
units.tr: Further, Aristotle is the witness that wood-pigeons live as long as forty years, and some reach twenty-five or thirty, in Book 6, chapter 4, and Book 9, chapter 1, of his History of Animals. Pliny agrees with him in Book 10, chapter 35. Pliny also witnesses, in Book 8, chapter 27, that wood-pigeons purge themselves every year with bay leaves. Like doves, turtle-doves and chickens use the herb helxine; ducks and geese [use] fiderite[?]; cranes use marsh rush. Finally, wood-pigeons begin to know love and to breed at three months old, as their very large numbers show. For a huge flock of wood-pigeons flies in each year from the sea to the territory of Volaterrae and to other regions. They breed in spring, and no more than twice. Everyone who has many of them knows that in winter wood-pigeons are served among the more refined dishes. Some people boil them with cabbage, though only after they have been somewhat fattened.

units.la: Vsus columbarum & palumbium in medicina.
units.tr: The use of doves and wood-pigeons in medicine.

units.la: Columbarum caro recens contra serpentes auxiliatur: integra verò pectus longitudinem viua dissecta phrenetici que[?]. ticique verrici applicata q. miraculo profui-fe sæpe animaduersum est.
units.tr: Fresh dove flesh is a remedy against snakebites. Whole doves, cut open alive and applied to the chest of the frenetic and to the head of the lunatic, have often been observed to help, as if by a miracle.

units.la: Fimum columbarum ex aceto laudatur ad ægilopas, id est, tubercula circa magnum oculi angulum: [?]uatim vero contra viui ar-genti potum, præcipuè fylueftrium. Pulli co-lumbarum paraliticis & senibus conueniunt frequentius efitati cū maiorana & rorifma-rino: iidem elixi febrientibus vtiliter dari possunt, succo limonum vel citronum asper-so, vel corticibus cum iis incocti. Panos de-nique, tumoresque sub faucibus, auribus & inguinibus fimum columbinum cum farina hordeacea discutit, clauos vero pedum ex aceto.
units.tr: Dove dung in vinegar is recommended for the aegilops, that is, the small swellings near the greater corner of the eye. Taken in drink, it is good against swallowed quicksilver, especially that of the wild kind. Young doves, often boiled with marjoram and rosemary, suit paralytics and the old. The same, boiled, can usefully be given to feverish patients, sprinkled with lemon or citron juice, or boiled with their peel. Finally, dove dung mixed with barley meal disperses pustules and swellings under the throat, ears and groin, and vinegar with it clears warts on the feet.

units.la: De ansere.
units.tr: On the goose.

units.la: ANseres Romanis sacrosanctos fuisse fatis constat inter graues auctores, quin & ob iecur solum ab iis saginatos, Athenæus l. 9. diphnof. testis est, scribit enim tanto eos in-pretio fuisse, vt effent apud eos, qui anseres ita a-lerent, vt eorum iecur mirificè augeretur. Idem-que tradit Plinius lib. 10. cap. 22. iecur, inquit, [?]artilibus in magnam amplitudinem crescit, exemplo [?]ꝗ, latè mulso augetur. Id quod Marialis significat, dicens,
units.tr: It is well established by serious authors that geese were held sacred by the Romans. Indeed, they were fattened for their liver alone. Athenaeus, Book 9, in the Deipnosophists, is the witness: he writes that geese were so highly prized that there were people who reared them in such a way that their liver grew remarkably large. Pliny says the same in Book 10, chapter 22: the liver, he says, grows to a great size in the cold months, and it is greatly enlarged when fattened with honeyed wine. Martial refers to this when he says:

units.la: Aspice ꝗ tumeat magno iecur ansere maius Miratus dices, hoc rogo creuit vbi? Inuentum autem hoc alii Scipioni & Metel-lo, alii Marcello viro confuları, nonnulli Marco Sessio eadem atate equiti Romano asseribunt. Hucitem alludit Horatius Sermonum l.2. Sa-tyra 8.
units.tr: Look how the liver swells, larger than a great goose's! You would say, amazed: where did it grow so big? This was discovered, some assert, by Scipio and Metellus, others by Marcellus the consul, and some claim that Marcus Sessius, a Roman knight of the same age, found it. Horace also alludes to this in Satire 8 of Book 2 of the Satires.

units.la: Non fine farre,Pinguibus & ficis pastum iecur anseris albi,
units.tr: Not without spelt: the liver of a white goose fed on rich figs.

units.la: id est, iecur saginatum & auctum pinguibus fi-cis. Candidorum autem in pluma vestigal maximum, unde bis vel etiam ter vellentur quibus-dam in locis anno. Porro iecur anserinum valen-ter nutrire probrig succi esse ab omnibus ferè re-ceptum est. Alas quoq; Galenus commendabiles facit. Sed carnem ipsorum excrementis saʃtere, adg; concoctionem esse peruicaciorem quàm dam existimant. Certissimum est ex omnibus alitibus, solis anseribus, censores magistratum ineuntes, gratiam retulisse, nihil enim agebant, quàm ut eorum alimenta locarent, sacrosanctos enim eos fuisse, Capitolio seruato, vel indecostat quod violare illos sas non erat. Immensos praeter-ea usus in re cibaria & culinis prastant. Britan-nos quoq; anserem in honore habuisse, Casarin-suis commentariis testis est, eum enim gustare sas non putabant: alebant tamen animi volup-tatis causā. Parentes rarius epulas opiparas subeunt, sed pulli & semestres frequentius. In-fantissimi à Magnatibus quibusdam anise ex-petuntur, sed adultiores vt trimestres, magis comcommendantur, illi enim excrementis abundant. Opimantur loco tenebroso, & tepido caueis conclusi. Largioribus autem cibariis opus est & largiori potu, voracitas enim in iis eximia est & bibendi desiderium ingens: atque sic bene curati, duobus ad summum mensibus alii prepinguescunt, euadunt Castaneis, pyrijs, malis, & id genus alijs ad farcturam idoneis solent farciri vetuli & adultiores, sic enim lautiores euadunt, pulli vero oleribus herbisq; ac lardo minutim concijo.
units.tr: That is, a liver fattened and enlarged with rich figs. The greatest tax falls on the feathers of the white geese, which in some places are plucked two or even three times a year. Moreover, it is almost universally accepted that goose liver is a powerful nourishment and of good juice. Galen also makes the wings commendable. But some think that the flesh of geese is more stubborn to digest, and to concoct, because of its excrement. It is quite certain that of all birds, only geese earned gratitude from the censors when they took office, since their only duty was to provide for their upkeep: geese were sacred, and when the Capitol was saved it was held a crime to harm them. Furthermore, they serve many uses for food and the kitchen. That the Britons too held the goose in honour, Caesar is the witness in his commentaries; they thought it unlawful to eat it, yet they kept it for the pleasure of its company. Parents seldom go to lavish feasts, but young geese and half-year-old ones more often. The very young are sought after by certain nobles, but older ones, at three months, are more highly recommended, for they abound in excrement. They are fattened in a dark, warm place, shut in coops. They need richer food and richer drink, for their greed is remarkable and their desire to drink enormous. Thus well tended, they grow fat within two months at most. Old and mature geese are usually stuffed with chestnuts, pears, apples and other things suitable for stuffing, for in this way they become more delicate. Young ones, however, are cut up small with herbs, greens and lard.

units.la: Ceruix, ala, pedes cum palmis, pipere & vino solent elixari, idq; edulii genus prima mensa solet apponi palato gratissimum & saluberrimum, ius enim contra toxica & aconita efficax esse admodum, compertum habetur.
units.tr: The neck, wing and feet with the palms are usually boiled with pepper and wine. This dish is commonly served at the first course, being most pleasant to the palate and very wholesome; for its broth is known to be strongly effective against poisons and aconite.

units.la: Ad extremum adipem anserum fartiliumJ celeberrimos vsus nobis præstare frigoribus hibernis in condienda brassica aliisque oleribus, sicut & aliis obsoniis parandis, omnibus culinis plusquam notum est, omitto nunc, quantum in re medica valeat, de quo hic meminisse nihil attinet.
units.tr: Finally, I pass over the very well-known uses that goose fat gives us in winter cold, in preserving cabbage and other vegetables, as in preparing other delicacies, which is more than known to all cooks. How much it avails in medicine, and about which it is pointless to say anything here, I leave aside for now.

units.la: De Feris anseribus.
units.tr: On wild geese.

units.la: Feros & fyluestres quoq; esse anseres nō ignotum est: quos sedem mutare, perinde vt grues dubium non est, nam & eo ipso tempore solent ad nos redire quo grues. Hieme autem inter magnificas e-pulas reponuntur, inaffantur enim garyo-phyllis confixi, feruanturq; aliquot dies. Nec autem succi boni esse, nec facile confici norunt ii, qui crebrius iis vti licet aliis in ci-bis non sordeant, propter longinquiorem enim volatum aiunt, minus eos esse excre-mentis refertos, quod verisimile videtur.
units.tr: That geese too can be wild and live in the woods is not unknown. That they change their dwelling, just as cranes do, is beyond doubt, for they usually return to us at the same time as the cranes. In winter they are served among the splendid dishes: they are stuffed with cloves and kept for some days. Those who may eat them more often, and do not dislike them as food, say that they are neither of good juice nor easily digested. Because of their longer flight, they are less full of excrement, which seems likely.

units.la: De anate.
units.tr: On the duck.

units.la: Nter amphibia reponuntur anates, petunt enim tum à terra, tum ab aqua alimentum. Quae in urbibus versantur, liberoq, cœlo, ac aquis fluentibus non fruuntur, in cibis sunt inu-tiliores in[?]salubriores q;[?] viuunt enim cibariis ab-iedliffimis & fœtidissimis, vt iis, quae à culinis eiiciuntur in vicos. Conuenit item mire ducrant, sicut & ranas, bufones & serpentes. Et si asse-uelelixa diutius tempore affiso asseruentur, serpentes vermium q, colluuiem iis innasci animad-uersum est. Vnde facile colligere est, carnem ea-rum mali esse succi excrementorum, ac perti-nacius[?] confici in ventriculo. Quare qui eru-[illegible, ~7 letters]
units.tr: Among the amphibious birds are ranked ducks, for they seek their food both from the land and from the water. Those that live in towns, and do not enjoy the open sky and running waters, are less useful as food and less wholesome, since they feed on very foul and stinking scraps, such as the cooks throw out into the lanes. Likewise they strangely resemble frogs, toads and serpents. And if roast or boiled meat is kept for a long time, it has been observed that worms and serpents breed in it. Hence it is easy to gather that their flesh is of bad juice, full of excrement, and is digested with more difficulty in the stomach. Therefore those who have a more refined palate [illegible]

units.la: ditioris sunt palati, facile poterunt discernere inter eas quæ in urbium lacunis ac paludibus degunt, & quæ in riuulis aquiq; fluentibus, hæ e-nim longè maiorem saporis habent iucunditatem. Pulli autem earum in maiori sunt gloria. Pectus verò & ceruicem delicatius sapere Martialis ganea[?] peritus docuit hoc carmine,
units.tr: can easily tell apart those that live in the pools and marshes of cities from those that live in streams and running waters, for the latter have a far greater pleasantness of flavour. Their young, moreover, are held in higher esteem. The breast and neck, however, taste more delicate, as Martial, an expert in gluttony, taught in this couplet,

units.la: Tota tibi ponatur anas, sed pectore tantumEt ceruice sapit, cætera redde coquo.
units.tr: Let the whole duck be served to you, but only the breast and neck have flavour; give the rest to the cook.

units.la: Anserum & anatum in medicina vsus varius.
units.tr: The varied use of geese and ducks in medicine.

units.la: Adeps anserinus celebratissimi vsus est : cum melle morsui canis rabidi occurrit : medeturque vulneribus cum foliis cucurbitæ syluestris tritis. Sonitum auriumque grauitatem emendat cum succo cepatum. Cum pipere albo & similibus vtiliter illinitur ad perfrictiones, conuulsiones, cæcos ac subitos dolores, omniaque quæ acopis curantur. In leniendis verò & sedandis doloribus, ob partium scilicet & substantiæ tenuitatem magis penetrabilis adeps anserinus cætecaeterarum volucrum adipibus longè præ-fertur, vt pluribus in locis patet ex Galeno, præsertim 2. ad glauc. vbi de fcirrhis. At veró sanguinem profluentem à cerebro, fra-&to scilicet capite, idem vel etiam anatum cum rosaceo co&tus sistit, vel etiam vtriusque infusus sanguis. Sed peculiariter sanguis anatum contusis medetur oculis cum melle.
units.tr: Goose fat is most celebrated in use. With honey it meets the bite of a mad dog, and it heals wounds with crushed leaves of wild gourd. With onion juice it corrects noises and heaviness of the ears. With white pepper and similar things it is usefully smeared on chills, convulsions, blindness and sudden pains, and all that is treated by soothing remedies. In easing and calming pains, however, goose fat, because of the thinness of its parts and substance and its greater power to penetrate, is much preferred to the fats of all other birds, as is shown in many places by Galen, especially in the second book to Glaucon, where he discusses scirrhi. But the blood of ducks, or of either bird, boiled with rose oil, stops blood flowing from the brain when the skull is broken, or the blood of either, infused, does the same. Duck's blood in particular heals bruised eyes when mixed with honey.

units.la: Sanguinem anatum Ponticarum à Mi-thridate Rege nobilitatum inuenimus, spis-fatum enim miscuit antidotis felici fuccellu, quoniam veneno viuerent, de nostris pol-liceri id non ausim, nisi experimento facto.
units.tr: We find that the blood of Pontic ducks was made famous by King Mithridates, for he mixed it, thickened, into antidotes with happy success, since they lived on poison. I would not dare to promise the same for our own ducks unless it were tested by experiment.

units.la: Contra lepores quoque marinos sanguis valet anserinus cum olei æqua portione: contra mala item medicamenta omnia fer-uatur cum Lemniaterra & spinæ albæ succo in pastillos redactus.
units.tr: Goose blood with an equal portion of oil is also good against sea hares. Likewise it is kept against all bad drugs, reduced into lozenges with Lemnian earth and the juice of white thorn.

units.la: Anserum trium linguas inassatas, inque cibo sumtas hydrocelicis, id est, herniæ a-quosa afflictis prodesse, Anaxilaus autor est.
units.tr: Anaxilaus is the authority that the tongues of three geese, roasted and taken as food, benefit those afflicted with hydrocele, that is, watery hernia.

units.la: Porro in peste aeris carnes anserinæ, in peste verò aquæ anatinæ magis celebrantur: quæ verò pestis aeriæ aquæ que sint signa, vide cap. de aere.
units.tr: Moreover, in a plague of the air, goose flesh is more celebrated, and in a plague of water, duck flesh. What the signs of an airborne or waterborne plague are, see the chapter on air.

units.la: De perdicibus.
units.tr: On partridges.

units.la: Perdicum carnem à coturnicum carne non longum differre constat ex Aristotele, qui de perdicibus & coturnicibus eodem capite tradidit, vt natura inter se non multum differentibus.
units.tr: It is agreed, on Aristotle's authority, that the flesh of partridges does not differ much from the flesh of quails. In the same chapter he records that the two birds are of nature not very different from one another.

units.la: Præstantiorem tamen & succi bonitate & concoctionis facilitate esse carnem perdicum norunt proceres & magnates. Infantes enim pulli regum sunt epulæ, adultiores factí, & qui peruolare possunt, non in minori sunt pretio & gloria.
units.tr: Yet the nobles and magnates know that partridge flesh is the more excellent, both for the goodness of its juice and the ease of its digestion. For young partridge chicks are the food of kings; once they have grown and can fly well, they are no less prized and esteemed.

units.la: Annicula perdices in cibos quoque admittuntur, vltra vero displicent. Vetulæ & adulte non nisi per frigora mensas subeunt, tunc enim parum inassatæ lardoq; transfixæ incoquuntur eum brassica, vel solum inassantur.
units.tr: Partridges of one year old are also admitted to the table, but older ones displease. Old and full-grown birds appear at the table only in cold weather; then they are cooked, barely roasted and pierced with bacon, together with cabbage, or else simply roasted.

units.la: Libidinosissimas autem esse perdices, sicut & coturnices, inde palam euadit, quod crebrius eas efitantes, aduenerem prorituent potenter, cumprimis externis saporibus magis inunctæ vi- noq; delibutæ. Gula eas hodie cicurari & mire opinari docuit.
units.tr: That partridges, like quails, are very lustful is plain from this: when they are frequently excited they stir up desire strongly, especially when they are anointed with exotic spices and moistened with wine. Gluttony has taught people nowadays to tame them and to marvel at them.

units.la: Non omnibus præterea terris eas esse datas planum est, in Attica enim non transuolant Beotiæ fines, necin Anaphi insula fuerunt, priusquam eo delatæ. Superiorum seculorum memoria notum est legatos Regis Anglorum cameis conclusas perdices in Britanniam deportaS[?]quoniam illic nulla effent, non tamen potuisse vere. Gr[?]mania nostra, vt est omnium barum rerum ita & perdicum fertilissima quae inter primarias etiam escas reponit: quae rostro pedibusque sunt rubentibus, palmam in cibis obtinuerunt apud gentes quasdam: griseã, quibus neque pedes neque rostrum rubent, pretio- sissimi sunt saporis: rubra quibusdam in locis, præsertim Francia, fordescunt: candidae, quae in Alpibus Allobrogicis nascuntur, fatuo sunt gustu, vt & nigra, has enim innuunt literis pro- ditum est.
units.tr: Moreover, it is clear that they are not given to every land. In Attica they do not fly across the borders of Boeotia, nor were they on the island of Anaphe before they were carried there. It is recorded in the memory of earlier ages that envoys of the King of the English carried partridges shut up in cages to Britain, since there were none there; yet they could not survive there. Our Germany, which is as fertile in all such things as in partridges, counts them among its chief foods. The red-beaked, red-footed kind won the highest place in the diet of certain peoples; the grey kind, whose feet and beaks are not red, has a most exquisite flavour. The red kind become rank in some places, especially in France; the white kind, which is born in the Allobrogian Alps, has an insipid taste, as does the black; for literature has handed down these things.

units.la: In Paphlagonia bina perdicibus corda se, prodidit Plinius lib. 11. cap. 37. Porro annu- um fastidium lauri folio eas purgare, idem testis est. Fel earum cum mellis aquo pondere mixtis Visus per tum oculis claritatem conciliat. Qua vero ill- dicum in larum cum melle cosla oculorum ulceribus me- medici- dentur. Sanguis vero perdicum, vt & colum- na. barum, turturum, palumbium, oculis eruore Fel.Oua. suffusis eximie prodest, teste Plin.lib. 29 cap. 6. Sanguis. Iusillarum vel ventriculus contritus ex vino nī- lus. Ven- gro dysenterias ventrisq; mala sanat. Quorum triculus. putamen cerae mixtum stantes mammas serua- Caro. re,& à partu custodire, qua vero sorpta foecun- ditatem facere laetisq; copiam, testatur idem lib.30.cap.14. Carnes in peste aeris commen- dantur, quae vero pestis aeris siuna sint, & quomodo discernatur à peste terra, aquae, ignisque, vide principio huius tractatus de aere.
units.tr: Pliny, in book 11, chapter 37, reports that in Paphlagonia partridges have two hearts. The same witness says that they purge themselves of the annual nausea by means of laurel leaves. Their gall mixed with honey in equal weight brings clarity to the eyes when applied. Indeed, the physicians think that the cooked flesh of these birds, with honey, is good for ulcers of the eyes. The blood of partridges, as also of pigeons, turtledoves and doves, is excellent when it is spread on the eyes, as Pliny testifies in book 29, chapter 6. The crushed gizzard of the smaller birds, drunk in wine, heals dysentery and disorders of the stomach and bowels. Their eggshell mixed with wax, placed on the breasts, keeps them firm and guards against them after childbirth; and when taken internally it makes women fertile and increases the flow of milk, as the same author says in book 30, chapter 14. Their flesh is recommended in the pestilence of the air; what the signs of a pestilence of air, water and fire are, and how it is distinguished from a pestilence of earth, see the beginning of this treatise on air.

units.la: De attagena, turdo, merula, sturno, rusticula, roftrula.
units.tr: On the attagen, thrush, blackbird, starling, rusticula, and roftrula.

units.la: Antiquis attagena, vulgo gallina cô-rylorum, maximè celebrata fuit, præ-fertim Ionica, ob succum quem parit bonum, tum etiam quod facilè in ventre eam perfici optimeq; nutrire, nullum est dubium, ob quam causam Martialis carmine suo laudes eius non omisit, lib. 13. Epigr. 60.
units.tr: Among the ancients the attagen, commonly called the hen of the cory, was most highly celebrated, especially the Ionian kind, on account of the good juice it yields; and there is no doubt that it is easily digested in the stomach and nourishes very well. For this reason Martial did not omit to praise it in his poem, book 13, epigram 60.

units.la: Inter sapores fertur alitum primus Ionicarum gustus attagenarum.[?]
units.tr: Among the flavours of birds, the taste of the Ionian attagens is said to be first.

units.la: Cæterum nō abs re addo, tum etiam, quia fires quædam est boni succi, non statim fe-quitur, quod sic bonus cibus, qui multa de- fiderat: Bonus enim cibus est, qui facilè à na-turæ robore edomatur, in calorem ventricu-li non reagit, tempestiuè in eo perficitur, in corporis cedit nutrimentum, putredinisque labem non subit. Eiusmodi verò cibum le-uem oportere atque friabilem, succoque laudabili præstantem, extra controuersiam est: nā cibi crassi & duri crassum concoctuq; difficilé succum generant, vt ex leguminibus sunt faba, lentes, lupini &c. & fructus quidā arborei, pifcesitem saliti, carnesq; nimium infumatæ & durae, crassum enim hæc succum generant, & in calorem nativum reagentem:
units.tr: Moreover, I add this not without reason: that a food is good for its juice, though this does not at once follow, since a food that is truly good requires many things. For a good food is one that is easily overcome by the strength of nature, does not resist the heat of the stomach, is perfected in it in due time, passes into the nourishment of the body, and does not undergo the taint of putrefaction. That such a food should be light and crumbly and excellent in praiseworthy juice is beyond dispute. For thick and hard foods produce a thick juice that is hard to digest, as do beans, lentils, lupins and the like, certain tree fruits, salted fish, and meats that are too dried out and tough; for these produce a thick juice that resists the native heat.

units.la: & licet quaedam ex his succum habeant gra-tum & bonum, non tamen protinus bo-nus cibus sunt, cum possint & obstructione, & qualitate, & coctionis etiam duritie, aliaue ratione multifariam obesse. Ex quibus in-telligitur, multa licet existant inter alimenta boni quidem succi, exinde tamen non sequi, bonum etiam esse cibum, qui, vt dictum, multa requirit, quorum vnum fi defit, bonus esse nequit. Et fi succus alicuius rei nulla alia ratione peccat vel obest, certa sola quali-tate noxius deprehenditur, corpusque hu-manum alterat immutatque, vel exiccando, id est, humores valide absumendo, vt acetum forte, muria, lixiuium, alumen, calx, petrole-um, fucciquerum valide purgantium, nec non nimius calidorum ac resoluentium v-sus, vt balnei, vini, veneris, vel incrassando, hocest, humores fluxiles reddendo confi-ftentiores, vt sunt omnium crassarum, terre-narumque, ac citra actiimoniam amarorem-que frigidarum rerum succi liquoresque, vt hypociftidis, acaciae, sorborum, gailarum, cupressi, mororum immaturorum, balau-ftiorum, malicorii, mespilorum, corti-cis & foliorum quercus, myrthi, coto-neorum, &c. vel acrimonia nimia, qua in-situs calor vel extinguitur absumitur; vel etiam mutatur in igneu, hocest, intenditur ad maiomajórem gradum, secundum hujus enim intentionem & augmentum generátur morbi calidi: hujus generis sunt piper, zinziber, & similia linguam acriter vellicantia.
units.tr: And although some of these have a pleasant and good juice, they are not for that reason at once good food, since they can do harm in many ways, by obstruction, by quality, by the hardness of their digestion, or by some other cause. From these things it is understood that, although among foods there are many that have a good juice, it does not follow that the food is also good; for, as has been said, it requires many things, and if one of them is lacking it cannot be good. And if the juice of some thing is not faulty or harmful in any other respect, but is found noxious by a certain quality alone, and alters and changes the human body, either by drying, that is, by vigorously consuming the humours, as perhaps vinegar, brine, lye, alum, lime, petroleum, and the juices of powerfully purging resins, and likewise the excessive use of hot and dissolving things, such as baths, wine and sexual intercourse; or by thickening, that is, by making flowing humours more viscous, as are the juices and liquors of all thick, earthy and cold things that are without sharpness but bitter, such as hypocist, acacia, sorbs, galls, cypress, unripe mulberries, balaustines, pomegranate rind, medlars, the bark and leaves of oak, myrtle, quinces, and the like; or by excessive sharpness, by which the innate heat is either extinguished or consumed, or is changed into fire, that is, is intensified to a greater degree (for by its intensification and increase hot diseases are generated). Of this kind are pepper, ginger, and similar things that sharply pluck at the tongue.

units.la: Vel humectando & emolliendo, ut Spinachium, Beta, Malua, Mercurialis, cau-lis capitatus & id genus alia culinis nota.
units.tr: Or by moistening and softening, as spinach, beet, mallow, mercury, the headed cabbage and other kinds of this sort well known in the kitchen.

units.la: Veldetergendo, viscosofque humores visceribus adhærentes eluendo, ut succus ab-sinthii[?], aristolochiæ, centaurii minoris, sabinæ, gentianæ, agrimoniæ, dracunculi, hellebori, ari, falisq; liquor.
units.tr: Or by cleansing, washing away the viscous humours that cling to the bowels: as the juice of wormwood, birthwort, lesser centaury, savin, gentian, agrimony, dragonwort, hellebore, arum, and the liquor of salt.

units.la: Velaftringendo, hoc est, meatus, venarumq; ac arteriarum ora coarctando, ut succus tormentillæ, cotoneorum, prunorum fyluestrium, pyrorum fyluestrium, malorum granatorum, citriorum, arantiorum acidorum, aliaque plura, quorum facta est mentio interincrallantia[?]: & certum est magnas hic strui vitæ insidias: difficile enim est à blandissimis suauissimisque malorum quorundam nostratium & exoticorum, ut citriorum & arantiorum, succis sibi temperare, quibus multi porcorum more saginam explent, unde postea insignem corporis alterationem sustinere & perpeti coguntur: alii enim succi sunt prædulces, alii acidi, alii austeri, acerbi alii, quidam vero ex horum multis vel duobus temperati sentiuntur. Hic vero meminisse oportebit, rectam cuiuis hominiæ[?] natu-
units.tr: Or by astringing, that is, by constricting the passages and the mouths of veins and arteries: as the juice of tormentil, quince, wild plums, wild pears, pomegranates, citrons, sour oranges, and many others, of which mention has been made among the astringents. And it is certain that great snares of life are laid here; for it is hard to restrain oneself from the most delicious and sweetest juices of certain apples, both native and foreign, such as citrons and oranges, with which many fill themselves with fat like pigs, and afterwards are forced to suffer and endure a remarkable alteration of the body. For some juices are very sweet, others sour, others austere, others bitter; and some are perceived as mixed from two or many of these. Here it will be well to remember that reason has been given to every human being's proper nature, so that it may avoid what is harmful and embrace what is beneficial,

units.la: naturam tributam esse rationem, vt nocitura declinet, profutura vero ampleſtatur, vtque triqueac gulae constanter imperet, ne prae-ter modum & intempestiue iis vescatur, in quibus plus voluptatis, quam vtilitatis in-esse deprehenditur. Vitam enim salubriter prorogare cupienti, duo inprimis confide-randa sunt; primum: praeferuare corpus à praepostera siccitate, deinde vitare nimium ac immodicum, intempeftiuumq; rarefacti-entium, hoc est, solidam compactamq; ma-teriam disiungentium ac relaxantium vsum; hac enim quia plurimum calida sunt tenuif-que substantiae, alte penetrant, humoresque per resolutionem & euaporationem tenui-ores partium à crassioribus & terrestribus abfu-muntur, vnde tandem corpus exiccari ac con-tabescere necessario contingit.
units.tr: and that it may constantly govern the belly and the throat, so that it does not eat of them beyond measure and out of season, in which more pleasure than usefulness is found. For whoever wishes to prolong life healthily must first consider two things: first, to preserve the body from unnatural dryness; second, to avoid the excessive and immoderate use of things that rarefy, that is, that loosen and relax the solid and compact matter. For these, because they are very hot and of thin substance, penetrate deeply, and by dissolution and evaporation the humours are consumed, thinner parts being drawn away from the thicker and earthy ones; whence it necessarily follows that the body at last becomes dried out and wastes away.

units.la: Pessime igitur sanitati consulunt, qui ventriculo relaxato, debili & imbecillo ad-hibent relaxantia, vt maluaticum, piper, fi-napi, theriacam, mitridaticum, & similia, iisque quae vires prostratas vel languidas recuperare re student & corroborare, cum potius aftrin-gentia & austera, quae fc.corrugando vnien-do; ventriculi villos, calorem congregent, ejaculando dissolutionem impediant, appetitu-que excitent, sint vsurpanda. Atq; haec monuif-hic & meminifle, quoniam inter meditandum ita occurrebant, studiose volui, vt lector &c. delectatus recedat, & fideliter monitus ad reliqua quoq; perlegenda reuertatur.
units.tr: Those therefore do the worst for health who, when the stomach is relaxed, weak and feeble, apply relaxing things, such as mallow, pepper, mustard, theriac, mithridate and similar things, and those things which strive to recover or strengthen powers that are prostrate or languid; whereas astringent and austere things, which by contracting and uniting the villi of the stomach gather its heat, and by checking the flow prevent dissolution, and stimulate the appetite, ought to be used. I have wished to note these things here, and to call them to mind, because they occurred to me thus while I was meditating; so that the reader, delighted, may depart, and having been faithfully warned, may return to read through the rest as well.

units.la: De turdis inter autores non conuenit.
units.tr: Authors do not agree about thrushes.

units.la: Multi mirantur, quod Horatius scripserit,
units.tr: Many people wonder that Horace wrote:

units.la: Nil melius turdo, vulua nil dulcius ampla,
units.tr: Nothing is better than a thrush, nothing sweeter than a plump sow's belly,

units.la: Et Martialis,
units.tr: and Martial:

units.la: Inter aues turdus si quis me iudice certet,
units.tr: If among birds a thrush contests with me, in my judgement,

units.la: Inter quadrupedes gloria prima lepus:
units.tr: among four-footed creatures the hare has the first glory:

units.la: inque eam venerunt sententiam, vt veteres tanquā rei alimentariæ indoctos damnârint.
units.tr: and they came to the opinion that the ancients, as ignorant of food, condemned them.

units.la: Sed & illud non parua admiratione di-gnum est, quod Gal.3. de alim. facult. scripsit, turdos & passerculos, perdicibus, attagenis, columbis, gallis, phasianis & gallinis concoctu esse duriores, & posset hunc locum men-do scatere[?] quis suspicari, nisi eadem verba Oribasii & Aëtii notata haberétur.
units.tr: But it is also no small cause for wonder that Galen, in book 3 of De alimentorum facultatibus, wrote that thrushes and little sparrows, partridges, attagens, pigeons, cocks, pheasants and hens are harder to digest. One might suspect the text is full of error, were it not that the same words are also noted in Oribasius and Aëtius.

units.la: Cur autem in admirationem hoc veniat, po- tissimum in causa est, quod idem 7. methodi & alibi scriptum reliquit, quæcunque magis nutriunt, difficilius à calore naturali confici. Vnde si turdis & passerib. perdices, gallinæ, & calore ve- phasiani magis nutriunt, funtq;, vt loquitur triculi cō Celsus, firmioris materiæ, par quoq; est diffi- cili? concoq. At ver o phasianos, quo, quātu sunt. ad coctionis nutriendiq; vim attinet, gallinis pares, edendi vero suauitate superiores facit solis va-porib. à culinarum effectis magi- ... trifq; maiore ob gulæ iucunditate coq cosue-
units.tr: The reason this causes wonder is mainly that the same author wrote in book 7 of his Method, and elsewhere, that whatever nourishes more is digested with more difficulty by natural heat. Hence, if thrushes, sparrows, partridges, hens and pheasants nourish more, and are, as Celsus says, of firmer substance, then they too must be hard to digest. But pheasants, as far as digestive power and nourishment go, are equal to hens, though superior in the pleasantness of eating; the vapours of kitchen preparations, which are usually given for the greater delight of the palate, ...

units.la: {*} D. Hier. testis est, in epist. n. ad Ocean. §3. Sacerdotis munera typice enarrans sic eum depingit, debere esse domum suam bene regentem, non ut opes augeat, non ut regias paret epulas, non ut caelatas struat patinas, non ut phasidas aues lentis vaporibus coquat, qui ad ossa perueniant, superficiemque carnis non disloluant artificii temperamen-to: atque hoc pacto quoque fructus coqui solitum pro valetudinariis meminit Galenus 2. de compos.medicament. & Alexan-der Trallianus l.12.cap.de tertiana. Verum enimuero exactius re considerata apparebit veteres non male judicasse: quantam enim nutriendis faginandisq; turdis majores im-penderint operam M. Varro 3.de re rust.li.& Columell, testatum fecerunt. Agrippina Claudii Caesaris conjunx turdum habuit imitantem sermones hominum, quod nunquam ante visum, teste Plin.l.10.c.42. Certum est tanta fuisse Romæ turdorum auiaria, tamque breui in tantam multitudinem excreuisse, ut ex eorum fimo agri stercoraren-tur, teste Varrone qui principatum turdorum fimo ex auiariis tribuit; quamobrem non immerito exclamauit Plinius apud Varronem id legens, Bene ait sperandum est de moribus nostris, si tanta fuerunt apud majores auiaria, ut ex iis stercorarentur agri. In tanta tamen copia stupendum, tam memorabilia fuisse turdorum pretia, singulos enim Ro-
units.tr: {*} St Jerome is a witness, in his letter to Oceanus, §3. Describing the duties of a priest typologically, he portrays him thus: his own house ought to be well governed, not to increase wealth, not to prepare royal feasts, not to furnish embossed dishes, not to cook Phasian birds in thin broths, which penetrate to the bones and do not loosen the surface of the flesh by the skilled blending of their seasoning. In this way also Galen, in book 2 of *De compositione medicamentorum*, mentions the fruit of the cook prepared for the sick, and Alexander of Tralles, book 12, chapter on tertian fever. Yet, if the matter is considered more exactly, it will appear that the ancients did not judge badly. For Marcus Varro (*De re rustica*, book 3) and Columella have testified how great an effort the men of old spent on fattening and nourishing thrushes. Agrippina, wife of the emperor Claudius, had a thrush that imitated human speech, something never seen before, as Pliny attests in book 10, chapter 42. It is certain that there were such great thrush-aviaries at Rome, and they grew so quickly into so vast a multitude, that fields were manured with their dung. Varro testifies to this, and he gives the first place among manures to the dung of thrushes from the aviaries. Hence Pliny exclaimed, not undeservedly, when he read this in Varro: "We may well hope for our morals, if there were once such great aviaries among our ancestors that fields were manured from them." Yet amid such abundance it is astonishing that thrushes fetched such remarkable prices.

units.la: Romæ denariis ternis, hoc est, duodecim nummis venditatos constat, vt ita turdorum quinque millia tali pretio diuendita sexaginta nummorum millia faciant, hoc est, æstimatione nostra coronatos 1500. Vnde constat mira & immensa auium fuisse pretia apud Romanos, vrbemque Romam quasi arcem quandam expilatorum totius orbis fuisse. Hodie turdorum saginandorum nulla geritur cura, sed quales capiuntur, mittuntur in culinas, vnde manducandi in illis tanta suauitas non percipitur, enutriti enim & saginati jucundissimi euadunt, cum macri ignobiliores ciboque minus commendabiles sint. De his enim verum est, quod Galenus scripsit, perdicibus, gallinis & phasianis eos esse duriores in cibatu, propterea q; dif-ficilius concoqui ac perfici. Non enim abso-lute accipiendum est, quod scribit, quæcunque magis nutrire debent, difficilius ea à ca-lore naturali perfici oportere, verum id est, datis cæteris paribus. Vox difficilius limi-tanda est & secundum quid aliud intelligenda, vt sensus sit, quæcunque magis debent nutrire, necesse est, vt diutius in ventriculo & intestinis (nam & hæc habere vim chylum conficiendi, qui scil. in ventriculo πλέωσιν acquirere non potuit, ostendunt heluones, quibus ob ventriculum nimis dilentum alimentum in intestina prolabitur) com-
units.tr: It is well established that at Rome they were sold individually for three denarii, that is twelve coins. Thus five thousand thrushes sold at that price would make sixty thousand coins, which by our reckoning is 1500 crowns. From this it is clear that the prices of birds among the Romans were wonderful and immense, and that the city of Rome was, as it were, a citadel of plunderers of the whole world. Today no care is taken in fattening thrushes. Those that are caught are sent straight to the kitchens, and so their eating is not found to have such sweetness; for the fattened and well-nourished ones turn out most delightful, while the lean are baser and less commendable as food. It is of these lean ones that Galen's words are true, that they are harder to eat than partridges, hens and pheasants, and therefore harder to digest and bring to perfection. For his statement, that whatever ought to nourish more must be perfected with more difficulty by natural heat, is not to be taken absolutely, but holds only when other things are equal. The word "more difficult" must be limited and understood in another respect, so that the sense is: whatever ought to nourish more must of necessity remain longer in the stomach and intestines (for that these have the power of perfecting chyle, which the stomach could not bring to completion, is shown by gluttons, in whom the stomach is so overstretched that food slips down into the intestines), so that

units.la: commorentur, vt alimentum penitus confi- ciatur : venis enim mefaraicis necessarius succus interciperetur, fi chylus cito & cum impetu, debitam moram non prastans, dila- beretur.
units.tr: it remains, so that the food is wholly perfected. For if the chyle were carried off quickly and with force, not allowed its due delay, the mesaraic veins would fail to intercept the necessary juice.

units.la: Cæterum turdorum carnes probitate succi insignes sunt, cumprimis qui apud nos capiuntur per hiemem, quo tempore maxi- me cernuntur, illaqueanturque in dumetis juniperinis, baccis enim juniperi vi&itant, qua de causa in peste aeris insignes sunt, by- dropicis quoque, calculosis & colica confli- &atis frequens esus prodest : cum myrthi vero baccis & cydoniis turdus inaslatus, dy- sentericis.
units.tr: Moreover, the flesh of thrushes is distinguished by the excellence of its juice, especially that of those caught here in winter, when they are most abundant and are snared in juniper thickets, since they feed on juniper berries. For this reason they are beneficial in a pestilential air. Frequent eating of them also helps dropsical people, those troubled by stones, and those afflicted with colic; but a thrush roasted with myrtle berries and quinces helps the dysenteric.

units.la: Merularum & turdorum amicitia est. Dicta merula quod sola volet, & solitaria pascatur, quasi mera volans. Merularum ge- nus alterum vndiquaque nigrum est, rostro etiam nigro, alterum rostro croceo, quod canorum magis est. Cantu enim maxime vocales hujus generis in auiariis passim ho- die cernuntur, nam docentur secreto, & vbi nulla alia vox miscetur auditurque, assiden- te qui crebro præcinat, cibisque abblan- diat. Tertium genus candidum est, idque nusquam reperiri, quam circa Cyllenen Ar- cadiæ montem vult Plinius. Sed & in Norvegia aliisque locis septentrionem ver- sus albicant, necnon in Heluetia albas mé-
units.tr: Blackbirds and thrushes are friends. The blackbird (merula) is so called because it flies alone and feeds in solitude, as if it were a mere flier. One kind of blackbird is black all over, with a black beak; another has a saffron beak and is more tuneful. For this kind is the most vocal and is everywhere seen today in aviaries, since they are taught in seclusion, where no other voice is mixed in and heard, with one who sings often beside them and coaxes them with food. A third kind is white, and this, Pliny says, is found nowhere except near Cyllene, the mountain of Arcadia. But in Norway and other northern places they are also whitish, and Gesner testifies that white blackbirds with yellowish beaks have been caught in Switzerland.

units.la: rulas captas esse, rostro tamen flauente, Gefnerus testatur, Carnes merularum bonitate succi quidam turdis pares esse vo- lunt, sed quo inuento, vel fundamento, nondum mihi adhuc constat. Alii succum melancolicum & paucum generare asse-runt paridubio. Inconfeffo est, succi praeftan- tia merularum carnes turdis non posse esse pares,ob victus, quem partim in sepibus & vepribus, partim circa loca palustria quae- runt, dissimilitudinem & improbitatem. Sunt enim quaedam, quae vermiculos quae- runt in fimo equino, quaedam vescuntur vermiculis aquaticis, vnde & riuales & a- quaticae nuncupantur.
units.tr: Some hold that the flesh of blackbirds is equal to thrushes in the goodness of its juice, but on what discovery or foundation this rests is not yet clear to me. Others assert that they produce a melancholic and scanty juice, a doubtful claim. It is beyond dispute that the flesh of blackbirds cannot be equal to thrushes in excellence of juice, on account of the difference and inferiority of their food. They seek it partly in hedges and brambles, partly near marshy places. For some look for little worms in horse dung, and some feed on aquatic worms, whence they are also called rivals and water-birds.

units.la: Optimae tamen esse creduntur tor- Merulae quatae, sic dicta ab alba linea totum earum torquatae collum ambiente, vulgo merulae fyluaticae, & montanae, quod in fyluis & circa montes degant : nec non fuscae saxa circa & fruti- ceta degentes, magnitudine paulo mino- res. Ubi magna harum frequentia est, ca- piuntur noctu ad ignis splendorem retibus Capturae extensis: alibi vero visco, quibusdam & plu- ribus in locis laqueis aut tendiculis, vt turdi, & sturni, estque haec captura, infimae etiam hodie plebi ruricolis, equisonibus, & agaso- nibus notissima, qui captosin vrbes, ma- gnatumque ac delicatorum culinas ven- dant.
units.tr: Yet the best are believed to be the ring ouzels, so called from the white line that encircles the whole neck of these birds. They are commonly known as wood and mountain blackbirds, because they live in woods and around mountains. Also the dusky ones, which live among rocks and thickets, are somewhat smaller. Where these are plentiful they are caught at night by nets spread out towards the glow of a fire. Elsewhere they are taken with birdlime, and in some places in great numbers with snares or nooses, as thrushes and starlings are. This method of capture is well known even today to the lowest common people, country folk, horsemen and carters, who sell the birds they catch in the towns, to the kitchens of great men and of the refined.

units.la: Galenus l.6. de fanitruend. esum ftutno-rum concedit iis, qui gracili, attenuato, sic-catoque sunt habitu . carnes enim eorum ab attagenarum carnibus proximas collocat. Alii illaudabilis eos nutrimenti esse conten-dunt decepti errore Arabum, qui fturnosa-conito velci tradiderunt, cum non aconito, sed cicuta sturnos nutriri apud certos auto-res & præsertim apud Galenum notatum re-periatur. Verum an propterea mensis cibif-que sint abdicandi, non inconuenienter hic quæritur. Hujus quæstionis explicationem inueniet æquus lector titulo de coturnici-bus, ibi enim fufius eam tractandi occasio erit. Unum hic adiicere libuit vuas matu-rescentes eos mirifice appetere, quo etiam tempore pinguiores capiuntur, & meliores seipsis jucundioresque, vuarum enim preti-osus ille succus carnis ipsorum improbum succum aboletac emendat. Apud Romanos fuisse sturnos (item luscinias) latino sermo-ne græcoque dociles, prætereaque medita-tos in diem affiduoq; noua locutos esse lon-giori etiam contextu memoriæ proditum est. Quod minus mirabile est, cum vbique fere in Galliarum amplis vrbibus gallicum sermonem longiori etiam contextu expla-nent atque exprimant: fœminas autem ad idineptas existimant.
units.tr: Galen, in book 6 of De sanitate tuenda, allows the eating of starlings to those of a slender, attenuated and dry habit; for he places their flesh nearest to that of attagens. Others contend that they are a poor food, deceived by the error of the Arabs, who handed down that starlings are fed on aconite. Yet it is recorded in certain authors, and especially in Galen, that starlings are fed not on aconite but on hemlock. Whether for this reason they are to be excluded from tables and from food is not an unfitting question to raise here. The fair-minded reader will find an explanation of this question under the title on quails, for there the matter will be treated more fully. Here I wished to add one thing: starlings eagerly seek grapes as they ripen, and at that time too they are caught fatter, better and more pleasant, for the precious juice of the grapes corrects and removes the bad juice of their flesh. It is recorded that starlings (and likewise nightingales) at Rome were apt at speaking Latin and Greek, and moreover, having practised daily, spoke new things in a longer connected speech. This is less surprising, since almost everywhere in the large cities of France people explain and express French in a longer connected speech as well; they consider women unfit for this.

units.la: Ad gallinarum sylvestriũ, quarum permulta sunt genera, figurâ magnitudine, locisque in quibus degunt, diffidentia, clas-sem, qui volet, rusticulas, gallinagines & ro-strulas seu rostratulas referre poterit.
units.tr: Of the wild hens (gallinae sylvestres), of which there are very many kinds differing in shape, size, the places they live, and their wariness, anyone who wishes can list the woodcocks (rusticulas), the snipes (gallinagines) and the rostrulae.

units.la: Est autem rusticula perdix rustica est <bl>Schnepffhun</bl>[?]/ adque differentiam minoris dicitur rusticula major.
units.tr: The woodcock (rusticula) is a rustic partridge, called in German Schnepffhun[?]. To distinguish it from the smaller kind, it is called the greater woodcock.

units.la: Rostrulæ vero à rostro cognominatæ sunt, quod in quibusdam porrectius ac lon-gius, in quibusdam breuius est. Natura o-mnium circa cibos exploranda est à locis, ut plurimum in quibus degunt, & tempore, quo visuntur. Quædam enim sylvaticæ sunt gallinam fere æquantes: quædam turmatim iuxta sepes decurrunt celeriter, humiq; nidulantur: quædam locis humidis gaudent & palustribus: quædam circa æquinoctium vernum aduenient, à lacuum & stagnorum marginibus quoquam vix discedentes: aliæ vere & æstate non visuntur, sed sub autumni fere finem totaq; hieme spectantur, degunt-que in dumetis & genistis, vbi laqueis capi constant: has vermibus viuere, terræ intestinis excrementisque, aliisque bestiolis pla-num est, quædam inter gramina latent: aliæ in agris novalibus & quiescentibus. In de-litiis autem mensarum & gulæ celebrantur omnes. Quæ tamen amplitudine sunt perdicis, ejusdemque prope coloris, rostriq; parui, vel eâdem cum rusticula majori, for- marostri ; capitis, corporisque, (nisi quod longé minores sint) aulicarum delitiarum Proceres quidam perdicibus non dubitant anteponere. Sed certum est, sæpe subesse fraudem. Itaque notandum, quàrum car- nes sunt candidiores, teneriores, suauio- rifque saporis, eas probum quoque genera- re succum & facilius concoqui, quàrum ve- ro carnes nigrę sunt & dure, gustatuq; refe- runt aliquid auium palustrium, difficilius quoq; consici.
units.tr: The rostrulae are named from their bills (rostrum), since in some the bill is longer and more projecting, and in others shorter. The nature of each kind as food must be judged chiefly from the places where they live and the season when they are seen. Some are woodland birds, nearly the size of a hen. Some run quickly in flocks along hedges and nest on the ground. Some like damp and marshy places. Some arrive around the spring equinox and scarcely leave the edges of lakes and ponds. Others are not seen in spring or summer but appear towards the end of autumn and through the whole winter; they live in thickets and broom, where they are known to be caught in snares. It is clear that these live on worms, the entrails of the earth, excrement and other small creatures. Some hide among the grasses; others in fallow and resting fields. All of them are celebrated as delicacies of the table and the appetite. Those which are of the size of a partridge, nearly the same colour, with a small bill, or the greater woodcock with the same bill, and which in head and body (except that they are much smaller) resemble the partridge, some leaders in courtly delicacies do not hesitate to prefer to partridges. But it is certain that deception often lies behind this. Therefore it should be noted that those whose flesh is whiter, more tender and of more pleasant flavour, these produce good juice and are more easily digested; but those whose flesh is black and tough, and which taste somewhat of marsh birds, are also harder to digest.

units.la: Quæ tota spectantur hieme, inter hiemales cibos non postremum obtinent locum: Sed bruti ac rustici plane palati sunt, qui eas inassaras, interaneis non re-purgatis, hoc est, vna cum fimo suauissime deuorant, vt in Suecia & Norvegia, vbi ma-gna illarum copia est.
units.tr: All of these are seen in winter, and they hold no small place among winter foods. But coarse and rustic men, who have no refinement at all, eat them most gladly roasted without drawing them, that is, with their dung, as in Sweden and Norway, where there is a great abundance of them. ## Noteworthy things about quails.

units.la: De Coturnicibus scitu digna.
units.tr: De Coturnicibus scitu digna.

units.la: DE Coturnice veteres & recentiores dis-sentire reperiuntur. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 23. antiquorum Romanorum cibis damnatas scribit, quod veratro vescerentur, eoque pinguescerent, simulque ob comitialem morbum, quem sola animalium sentiant, prater hominem. Hæc Plinius. Galenus lib. sext. epidem. comm. 5. ait, in Doriæ, Beotia & Thessa[?]
units.tr: Ancient and more recent writers are found to disagree about the quail. Pliny (Book 10, chapter 23) writes that the quail was condemned by the ancient Romans as food, because it fed on hellebore and so grew fat, and at the same time because it alone of animals, apart from man, suffers the comitial disease (epilepsy). Thus Pliny. Galen, in the sixth book of his Epidemics, commentary 5, says that in Doris, Boeotia and Thessaly

units.la: Hæc Plinius. Galenus lib. sext. epidem. comm. 5. ait, in Doriæ, Beotia
units.tr: Thus Pliny. Galen, in the sixth book of his Epidemics, commentary 5, says that in Doris, Boeotia

units.la: Thessalia, plurimos ex esu coturnicum muscu-lorum distentionibus correptos, quoniam scilicet vescantur veratro; atque idem quibusdam Athenis[?] accidisse, qui coturnicibus largiùs sese impleuerant. Plinii sententiam, quod attinet dubitandi illa occasionem prabet, solas videl. coturnices inter animalia, praeter hominem morbum pati comitialem, cum & alia sint animalia, quae hoc malo conflictantur, ut cati, capi, alaudae, equi, sciuri, quod vidi ipse, picè & sues: nisi quis dubitationem hanc tolli posse pro Plinio dicat, coturnices animalium solas praeter hominem, talem potissimum sentire morbum, quemadmodum etiam de canibus scripsit Aristoteles[?], nam & mulos, aliaq; animantia rabie corripi videmus.
units.tr: and Thessaly, many people were seized with cramps of the muscles after eating quails, since of course they feed on hellebore; and that the same thing happened to some Athenians who had gorged themselves on quails. As for Pliny's opinion, it gives occasion for doubt, since he says that the quail alone among animals, apart from man, suffers this comitial disease, whereas there are other animals afflicted by this illness, such as cats, goats, larks, horses, squirrels (which I myself have seen), magpies and pigs. Unless someone says, in defence of Pliny, that this doubt can be removed by taking his words to mean that the quail alone among animals, apart from man, suffers this particular kind of disease, just as Aristotle wrote about dogs; for we see that mules and other animals also fall into madness.

units.la: Verum his missis, inquirendum, cujus succi & nutrimenti sit coturnix, seu qualea, sic enim a voce quidam nominant? Quidam in-cibo eas reformidant, ob causas antea a Galeno commemoratas, alii mensis minime abdicandas censent, ob bonum quem prabent succum quin-carnes earum turturum carnibus aequiparant, quasapientum senum[?] cibus habentur, sensus enim roborare, cogitationem acuere, & memo-riam confortare creduntur. Aristoteles de perdicibus & coturnicibus tradit in eodem capite, quasi natura non multum inter se differant, sed eiusdem sint generis. Unde non ita, ut vulgus putat, prauisucci coturnices esse credendum est, sed potius tenendum, conueniens ac inculpatum prabere eas nutrimentum. Nec pro-pterea etiam ab illarum esu abstinendum omnino, quod morbo comitiali corripiantur, venenoq; pascantur, cum nonnulla sint animalia, quae licet venenis quandoque nutriantur, quemadmodum de sturnis dicitur, qui exci-tatae pastu pinguescunt, inter boni tamen succi cibos connumerantur, quo Galenus etiam stur-nos 6. de tuenda sanitat. lib. refert. Sic cotur-nici veratrum est alimentum, hominis medica-mentum, liquidem coturnicis natura est in substantiam suam veratrum conuertere. Sic anati bufo alimentum est, ciconiæ serpens, bo-mini vero venenum. Sic veratrum purgat hominem, non etiam coturnicem. Cicuta refrigerat hominem, non etiam turdum, vel sturnum. Licet igitur veneno vescantur coturnices, nec ipsis tamen, nec aliis animalibus aut hominibus, qui horum esui asseruerunt, sunt venenum.
units.tr: But, setting these aside, we must inquire what juice and nourishment the quail (or qualea, as some call it from its voice) provides. Some shun it as food for the reasons Galen mentioned earlier; others think it should by no means be excluded from the table, because of the good juice it supplies. Indeed, its flesh is compared with that of turtle doves, and it is regarded as food for wise old men, for it is believed to strengthen the senses, sharpen thought and fortify the memory. Aristotle, in the same chapter, teaches that partridges and quails do not differ much in nature but are of the same kind. Hence we should not believe, as the common people think, that quails yield bad juice; rather we should hold that they provide wholesome and blameless nourishment. Nor on that account should their eating be avoided altogether, because they are seized with the comitial disease and feed on poison. For there are some animals which, although sometimes nourished on poisons, as is said of starlings, which grow fat when fed on hellebore, are nonetheless counted among foods of good juice; Galen too reports this of starlings in the sixth book of his On the Preservation of Health. Thus hellebore is food for the quail and a medicine for man; for it is the nature of the quail to convert hellebore into its own substance. So too the toad is food for the duck, and the serpent for the stork, yet poison for man. So hellebore purges man but not the quail. Hemlock cools man but not the thrush or the starling. Therefore, although quails feed on poison, it is not poison to them, nor to other animals or to men who have accustomed themselves to eat them.

units.la: Nam teste Theophrasto, omnium Pharmacorum vires debiliores deprehenduntur in ​assuetis in nonnullis etiam plane inertes.
units.tr: For, as Theophrastus testifies, the powers of all drugs are found weaker in those who are accustomed to them, and in some they are wholly inert.

units.la: Quicquid enim a natura acceptatur, de-vincitur, conficitur, caloreq;, aut congenita, vel ex consuetudine acquisita, corporis proprietate alte-ratum in corporis alimentam digeritur, id aliud venenum esse non potest. Hoc modo puella illa Indica, & annus illa attica, a momento cicuta quod
units.tr: Whatever nature receives, overcomes, digests, and, altered by the heat of the body or by a property acquired from habit, turns into the body's nourishment, that cannot be poison. In this way that Indian girl and that old woman of Attica, from the moment they took hemlock, were unharmed, and they could devour whole handfuls without injury.

units.la: Quara-tione ve-nena alàr & non obsint? quod natura evincere ac concoquere posset, integros affuere manipulos devorare innoxie. Sic venena quotidie, præsumtis tamen remediis, hausit Mithridates, & à tali consuetudine ei fuerunt innoxia, adeo, ut captus à Pompeio magno, in carceribus veneno interimere sese non potuerit. Succum vero cicutæ non affuetis, & pulverem quoq; esse lethale & soporiferum venenum, Athenien-sium supplicia indicant, qui morte condemnatos sorbitione cicutæ interemerunt, quam & Socrates impietatis condemnatus in carcere hausisse fertur, ut ita plurimum hic valere consuetudinem naturæ, acquisititias fatendum sit.
units.tr: Why, then, do poisons feed and not harm? Because nature could overcome and digest them. Thus Mithridates drank poisons every day, though with preventive remedies, and by such habit they were harmless to him; so much so that, when captured by Pompey the Great, he could not kill himself with poison in prison. But that the juice of hemlock, and even its powder, is a deadly and narcotic poison to those not accustomed to it, the executions of the Athenians show, who killed condemned men by making them drink hemlock; and Socrates, condemned for impiety, is said to have drunk it in prison. Thus it must be admitted that habit has so great power over nature, though acquired.

units.la: Porro & illud meminisse hic lectorem oportebit, quod alibi etiam monuimus, veneni fœminaria calore concitata in vivorum corporibus energia longe esse vegetiora & efficaciora, in defunctorum corporibus, calore extincto fere consopita. Unde in veneris cum muliere, Spiritus morbo gallico infecta, conflictu, quo corpus & veneni spiritus, veneni vehicula, incalescunt, contagii vehicula fœminaria fiunt nocentiora, qua in feris ac volucribus toxico interemtis, præcipue si in veru torreantur, vel in lebete elixentur, igni ferventissimū re dissipata diffiantur ac evanescunt. Fera veneno igitur volucresve veneno pasta, vel capta optimis carbonibus tosta, vel etiam elixata menses correcto minime sunt abdicanda. Et ut ad coturnices rium. redeamus,
units.tr: Moreover, the reader should remember here what we have also noted elsewhere: the venomous energy, stirred up by the heat in living bodies, is far more lively and effective than in the bodies of the dead, where it is nearly lulled to sleep once the heat is extinguished. Hence, in intercourse with a woman infected with the French pox, the spirits of the body and of the poison, the vehicles of the poison, grow hot, and the vehicles of contagion become more harmful. But in wild animals and birds killed by poison, especially if they are roasted on the spit or boiled in a pot, the poison is dissipated and vanishes when dispersed by the most fierce fire. Therefore game or birds fed on poison, or caught and then roasted over the best charcoal or even boiled, are by no means to be rejected from the table. And to return to quails,

units.la: Et certum est pullos messium tempore suavissimos esse, inque lautiorum ciborum habere censu. Pinguescunt autem ocyssime, opimanturque maxime frugibus, semine canabis & milio. Iusto diutius in aviariis reservate adipofam illam, propter molem emori exploratum habetur, nec tamen ob id in cibo reformidantur. Ex quibus manifestum evadit, helleboro illis magis, quam coturnicibus opus esse, qui coturnices in cibi damnant, ob nullam aliam causam, quam quod vescantur elleboro, quasi helleborus nascatur omnibus locis, ubi sunt coturnices, tum etiam, quod veteres eas improbârint, tanquam ventriculo ob nimiam pinguedinem infestas, nauseamque parientes & fastidium. Galenum de simplicit. medicam. ubi docet discernere, facileque cognoscere alimenta bona & mala, si quis diligentius inspexerit, intelliget coturnicem praesertim assam boni gratique odoris esse & saporis, ac boni etiam nutrimenti. Illud quoque non omiserim, DEVM Israelis populum, quem ardentissime diligebat, dum per deserta illa transfiret loca, ad satietatem usque coturnicibus pasturum non fuisse, nisi probati illa fuissent alimenti & salutaris.
units.tr: It is certain that young quails in the harvest season are most delicious and count among the costlier delicacies. They fatten very quickly and are most richly fattened on grains, hemp seed and millet. If they are kept too long in aviaries, they are known to die from their own fat's bulk, yet they are not on that account rejected as food. From these things it is plain that those who condemn quails as food have more need of hellebore than the quails do, and do so for no other reason than that quails feed on hellebore, as if hellebore grew in every place where quails are; and also because the ancients rejected them as troublesome to the stomach on account of their excessive fatness, causing nausea and loathing. If anyone examines Galen's On Simple Medicines, where he teaches how to distinguish and easily recognise good and bad foods, he will understand that the quail, especially when roasted, has a good and pleasant smell and taste, and also good nourishment. I should not omit this too: God, who loved the people of Israel most ardently, when they passed through those deserts, would not have fed them with quails to the point of satiety, unless those birds had proved to be wholesome and healthful food.

units.la: Quid multa ? Coturnices bene in ven-triculo confici, inque corporis alimoniam verti probæ temperaturæ & substantiæ indicium est. Nam in omnibus cibis ad boni succi generationem tantum requiritur, ut probe in ventriculo concoquantur, quicquid enim venter concoxerit, ad jecur transit, ab hoc vero ad nutriendum partes transmittitur.
units.tr: What more is there to say? That quail are digested well in the stomach and turned into bodily nourishment is a sign of good temperament and substance. For in all foods, to generate good juice, it is required only that they be properly digested in the stomach, since whatever the stomach has digested passes to the liver, and from there is sent on to nourish the parts.

units.la: Ubi interim hoc adnotandum a pravi succi eduliis, licet a nonnullis interdum probe conficiantur, abstinendum esse, clam enim sensim longa dierum serie pravum in venis succum, humoresque ex iis coacervari, qui vel leuissima putredinis arrepta occasione febres contumaces accendant, quotidiana docet experi-entia.
units.tr: Meanwhile it must be noted here that foods of bad juice are to be avoided, even though some people sometimes digest them well. For daily experience teaches that bad juice and humours gather in the veins from such foods gradually, over a long series of days, and that these, seizing upon the slightest occasion of putrefaction, kindle stubborn fevers.

units.la: Verum, quia delectissimorum ciborum copia non semper, & ad voluntatem nobis suppe-tit, unice studendum, ut, quicunque etiam & qualescunq; fuerint, proba eorum fiat concoctio. tum etiam , quia nullum magis aptius admi- niculum , ad sanitatem tuendam succorum bonitate inveniri potest , ut , quoad fieri potest , bona sint temperatura & substantia. Nam pravi succi cibi , licet concoquantur, si tamen vel minimam putredinis occasionem fuerint adepti, morbos excitant , quamvis Galenus 2. aphor. 28. cibum cum voluptate sumtum , licet deterior paulo sit , aut non modo, non manere deteriorem , sed quandoque reddi meliorem. Idem confirmat 2. de alimento facult. & in consilio pueri epileptici.
units.tr: But since a supply of the most delightful foods is not always available to us at will, the one thing to aim at is that, whatever and of whatever kind they are, they be properly digested. Also, because no more suitable aid for preserving health can be found than the goodness of the juices, the temperament and substance of our food should be as good as possible. For foods of bad juice, even when they are digested, if they have obtained even the smallest occasion of putrefaction, stir up diseases; although Galen, in the second book of the Aphorisms, aphorism 28, states that food taken with pleasure, even if it is somewhat inferior, does not remain worse, but sometimes is made better. He confirms the same in the second book On the Faculties of Food and in the consilium on the epileptic boy.

units.la: Hoc coronidis loco addo , modice coturnicibus vesci [?] posse, qui convulsionibus obnoxios se sentiunt ; plane vero ab illarum esu abstinere, vanum est & insanum.
units.tr: As a coronis to this, I add that people who feel themselves prone to convulsions may eat quail in moderation [?]; but to abstain from eating them altogether is vain and foolish.

units.la: Non me latet Pfellum inter illa, quae boni succi non sunt , coturnicem etiam connumerasse, sed quoniam nullis id rationibus probat , non multum in praesens, testimonium ipsius magnificandum existimo, ut qui turturem etiam damnârit, quae tamen à Galeno et aliis plurimum laudatur.
units.tr: I am not unaware that Psellus, among those things which are not of good juice, also counted the quail, but since he proves this by no reasons, I think his testimony is not to be greatly magnified for the present, just as he also condemned the turtle-dove, which nevertheless is greatly praised by Galen and others.

units.la: Isti namque autores graeci , qui longe post Galeni seculum sunt secuti, quique Arabum doctrinam degustârunt, in plerisque à praecepto- re Galeno declinârunt , ut exempli gratiâ, in sectione venae , extrema manus venam magis eligentes , quam curuatura brachii, & in nonnullis aliis nunc non recen- sendis: sendu:quia tamen pauca admodum isti memoriae mandarunt, quae Galenus ipse non scripserit aut animaduerterit, magis etiam ipsorum monumenta imitanda sunt & amplexanda, ut quae Galeni Hippocratisq; doctrinam magis redoleant, quam barbarorum istorum. Galenus quidem 2. ad glaucon. lib. sectionis vena in manu facit mentionem, vbi passione existente in dextra locorum parte, a dextra manu aut crure eodem sanguinem mitti praecepit.[?]
units.tr: For those Greek authors who followed long after Galen's age, and who tasted the doctrine of the Arabs, departed in many matters from their teacher Galen: for example, in venesection, choosing the vein at the extremity of the hand rather than the bend of the arm, and in some other matters which I will not list now. Since, however, these men committed very few things to memory that Galen himself had not written or observed, their monuments are all the more to be imitated and embraced, as those which smack more of the doctrine of Galen and Hippocrates than of those barbarians. Galen, indeed, in the second book To Glaucon, on venesection, mentions the vein in the hand, where, when the affliction is in the right part of the body, he orders blood to be drawn from the right hand or leg.

units.la: Verum sciendum Galenum ibi manus vocabulo synecdochicos pro brachio Graecorum morem usum fuisse, ut saepius consueuit alibi, & ipse etiam explicauit in libello de motu musculorum, manum in tres partes dividens: brachium, vlnā, & summam extremamq; manum.
units.tr: But it must be understood that Galen there used the word "hand" synecdochically for the arm, according to the custom of the Greeks, as he often does elsewhere; and he himself explained this in his little book On the Motion of the Muscles, dividing the hand into three parts: the upper arm, the forearm, and the extreme hand.

units.la: Rationes igitur, cur coturnix non fit laudabilis succi nutrimentiq;[?] quia a Psello afferuntur nulla, aut certe exigua, coturnicem inter boni probiq; succi ac nutrimenti aues retinebimus tantisper, donec contrarium quis probauerit.
units.tr: Therefore, since the reasons why the quail is not to be praised as food of good juice and nourishment, which are brought forward by Psellus, are none or certainly slight, we shall keep the quail among the birds of good and sound juice and nourishment, for as long as someone proves the contrary.

units.la: De aue alauda, cæterisque minutis.
units.tr: On the lark and other small birds.

units.la: Vulgatissimus alaudarum cibus est apud gentes quasdam, vbi etiam captura earum largissima praesertim hibernis mensibus, quo tempore obesae admodum spectantur.
units.tr: The lark is the most commonly eaten food among certain peoples, where also they are caught in very great numbers, especially in the winter months, when they are seen to be quite fat.

units.la: Quibusdam in regionibus senas aut duodenas ligneo transfixas bacillo, cum saluia lardoque inaffant. Elixantur etiam, piperéque, garyophyllis, & id genus aliis condiuntur. Quin & piftorio opere includuntur madentes cinnamomi condimento. Verum locupletum & ditiorum ventriqué ac gulae obedientium is cibus est. Cristatæ, quas corydalos & galeritas à crista appellant, licet rarius in cibis expetantur, experimento tamen certo inter graues autores conuenit, elixas, assasque in cibo sumtas assiduè, colicos debellare dolores. Alii cineres galeritae adustae commendant ad eosdem vsus. Est in exemplis, quosdam corde huius in armilla aurea inclusò gestatoque à colicis doloribus ex antipathia quadam liberatos fuisse: quod ideo hic meminisse volui, quia morbo isto nunc nihil fere frequentius, tum quod Democritus de vna hac aue priuatim commemorârit.
units.tr: In some regions they skewer six or twelve on a wooden spit and baste them with sage and lard. They are also boiled, and seasoned with pepper, cloves, and that sort of thing. Indeed they are also enclosed in a pastry, soaked in a seasoning of cinnamon. But this food is for the wealthy and richer, and for those who obey their belly and gullet. The crested larks, which they call corydalos and galeritae from the crest, though less often sought as food, nevertheless by certain experience agreed upon among grave authors, when eaten constantly boiled or roasted, overcome colic pains. Others recommend the ashes of the burnt galerita for the same uses. There is an example of some people who, wearing a heart of this bird enclosed in a golden bracelet, were freed from colic pains by a certain antipathy; I wished to mention this here because nothing is now almost more frequent than this disease, and because Democritus alone recorded this bird in particular.

units.la: Et Plinius lib. 30. cap. 7. de hac aue sic scribit, Coli vitium efficacissimè sanatur aue galerita assa & in cibo sumta: quidam in vase nouo cum plumis iubent exuri, conteriq; in cinerem, bibiqué ex aqua cochlearibus ternis per quatriduum: quidam cor eius adalligare femori, alii recens tepensq; deuorari. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: Pliny also, in book 30, chapter 7, writes thus about this bird: "Colic is most effectively cured by the galerita roasted and eaten as food. Some order it to be burnt in a new vessel with its feathers, and reduced to ash, and drunk in water, three spoonfuls for four days; some order its heart to be tied to the thigh; others order it to be swallowed fresh and warm." Thus Pliny.

units.la: Galeno quoque experimento comper-tam esse auis huius aduersus colicos dolores vim literis traditur, bonum praeterea largiri succum, colique doloribus subuenire praeter communeratos[?] autores, etiam Dioscorides testatur, sed cuique experimenti via facilis est, praesertim qui isto morbo frequentius & acerbius conflictantur.
units.tr: It is also recorded in writings that Galen found by experiment the power of this bird against colic pains, and that it bestows good juice besides, and helps against the pains of colic beyond the commonly cited authors; Dioscorides also bears witness to this. But the way of testing it is easy for anyone, especially for those who are more often and more severely afflicted with this disease.

units.la: De Luscinia.
units.tr: On the Nightingale.

units.la: Vfciniam, fringillam, passerem, & in summa, minuta auitia persequi im-mensi & laboris effet & difficultatis, praesertim cum maior pars cantus magis, voluptatisque quam mensarum causa alatur, complures namque earum Latino, Graeco, Germanico, Italico, Gallicoque sermone dociles spectantur. Memorabilia pretia harum fuisse olim Romae, testatur impendiosa ista coena Aesopi, qui multas luscinias in patina sua appositi. Non sumuntur in cibo ab elegantioribus, ut & caeteras pleraque huius generis, quae caveis inclusae, cantu tantum oblectant.
units.tr: To pursue the nightingale, the finch, the sparrow, and in short all small birds would be an immense labour and difficulty, especially since most of them are kept more for song and pleasure than for the table. Many of them, indeed, are seen to be taught to speak in Latin, Greek, German, Italian and French. That these birds were once highly prized at Rome is attested by that extravagant dinner of Aesop, who served many nightingales on his platter.
