They are not eaten as food by the more refined, nor are most other birds of this kind, which, kept in cages, delight only by their song.

units.la: Dignissima autem Luscinia miratu anis, inquit Plinius, lib. 10. cap.28.[?] cuius in tam paruo corpusculo tanta vox, tamque pertinax, tam paruulis in faucibus spiritus, ut in vna perfecta Musicae scientia modulatus edatur sonus, qui nunc continua
units.tr: Indeed, says Pliny (book 10, chapter 28), the nightingale is the most admirable of birds: in so tiny a body there is so great and so persistent a voice, and in such small throat a breath, that in it alone the perfect science of music is produced in a sound that now

units.la: continuo spiritu trahitur in longum, nunc variatur inflexo, nunc diftingnitur conciso, copulatur intorto, promittitur reuocato, infcatur exinopinato : interdum & secum ipse murmurat, plenus, grauis, acutus, creber, extentus, vbi visum est, vibrans, fummus, medius, imus: breuiterque omnia in paruulis tam faucibus, quae tot exquisitis tibiarum tormentis ars hominum excogitauit, vt non fit dubium hanc suauitatem praemonftratam efficaci auspicio cum in ore Stefichori ceci- nit infantis.
units.tr: is drawn out at length with unbroken breath, now varied with a bent note, now broken into distinct parts, now joined with a twisted one, now sustained with a recalled note, now roused by an unexpected one. Sometimes it even murmurs to itself, full, deep, sharp, frequent, extended, trembling where it seems fitting, high, middle, low. In short, everything that human art has devised with so many exquisite pipes is found in those tiny throats, so that there is no doubt this sweetness was foreshadowed by a favourable omen, when the infant sang in the mouth of blind Stesichorus.

units.la: Ac ne quis dubitet artis esse, plures fingu- lis sunt cantus, neciidem omnibus, sed fui cuique. Certant inter fe, palamque animo- fa contentio est. Victa, morte fz,e vitam fi- nit, spiritu prius deficiente quam cantu. Me- ditantur aliae iuniores, versusque quos imi- tentur, accipiunt. Audit discipula intensione magna, & reddit vicibus cantum. In- telligitur emendatae correctio, & in docente quaedam reprehensio. Ergo feruorum illis pretia sunt, & quidem ampliora, quam qui- busarmigeri olim parabantur. Scio candidam sestertiis sex (hoc est, 1ṡo.coronatis) alii- oquin, quod est propeinufitatum, veniisse, quae Agrippinae Claudii Caesaris coniugido- no daretur &c. Hactenus Plinius. Idem cap. 42. Caesares iuuenes habuisse luscinias, ftur- nosque graeco & latino femone dociles, prae-
units.tr: Lest anyone doubt that this is art, each nightingale has its own songs, and not the same as all the others. They compete with one another, and there is open rivalry in spirit. The defeated one ends its life in death, its breath failing before its song. Others, younger, practise and receive the verses they are to imitate. The pupil listens with great attention and gives back the song in turns. The correction of the one who has improved is understood, and in the teacher some reproach. Therefore these singers fetch prices, and indeed higher ones than those which armed men once fetched. I know that a white one was sold for six sestertii (that is, 1½ gold crowns), which is quite unusual, and was given to Agrippina, wife of Claudius Caesar, and so on. So far Pliny. The same author, chapter 42: young Caesars had nightingales and starlings taught to speak in Greek and Latin, and

units.la: tereaq; meditantes in diem, & assiduè noua loquentes longiori etiam contextu. Docentur autem secreto, & vbi nulla alia vox misceatur, assidente qui crebrò dicat ea quæ cōdita velit, ac cibis blandiente. Memorabile est & admirabile, de lusciniis duabus hominum sermones imitatis Ratisbonæ in Comitiis, an. 1546. de quibus Gesnerus ipse sic scribit : Ego profecto nunquam Plinio nostro credidissem, multa adeo miranda de auicula hac scribenti, nisi ipse has bestiolas talia promentes & oculis vidissem, & auribus hisce audiuissem. Hæc Gesnerus. Placuit hoc reponere in gratiam Lectoris Carmen T. Vespasiani Strozæ in philomelam, lib. 6. Erotien:
units.tr: moreover practising daily and constantly speaking new things in even longer sequences. They are taught in secret, and where no other voice is mixed in, someone sitting beside them repeatedly says the words they wish to be learned, and coaxes them with food. It is a memorable and wonderful thing that at Regensburg, at the Diet in 1546, two nightingales imitated the speech of men. Gesner himself writes of them thus: "I should certainly never have believed our Pliny, writing so many marvellous things about this little bird, unless I had seen with my own eyes and heard with my own ears these little creatures uttering such things." So Gesner. I thought fit to set this down for the reader's pleasure: the poem of T. Vespasian Strozza on the nightingale, book 6, Erotica:

units.la: Æmula diuini suauissima carminis ales Quæ virides umbras & loca sacra tenes. Mollibus & variis quæ tot discrimina vocum, Flexibus humana dulcius arte refers. Munere protali tibi quid philomela rependam? Premia quæ tanto digna labore putem? Dum vagus huc illuc hortis genialibus erro, Miror & artifici culta vireta manu, Hospitio officio tu protinus, usa benigni, Fingis in aduentu carmina mille meo, Nec procul hinc densis canis abdita frodib°, alta Ilicis in ramo, populeisque comis, Verùs hic Iuniperi infidis mihi proxima trunco, Non imitabilibus me venerata modis.
units.tr: Rival of the divine, most sweet of songs, bird, you who haunt the green shadows and sacred places, you render, in soft and varied changes of notes, more sweetly than human art can do. What reward shall I give you, nightingale, for such a gift? What prizes do I think worthy of such labour? While I wander here and there through the pleasant gardens, marvelling also at the greenery tended by a skilful hand, you, using kindly hospitality, straightway at my coming fashion a thousand songs. Not far from here, hidden among the dense leaves, high on an oak branch and in the poplar's foliage, ... here, next to me by the juniper's faithless trunk, you, who are honoured by me, sing in inimitable measures.

units.la: Et licet hac praestem tibi tam vicinus in umbra,
units.tr: And though you stand so near me in this shade,

units.la: Dic, tua suaui garrulitate loquar.
units.tr: tell me, and I will speak with your sweet chatter.

units.la: Nil tamen ipsa times, nec guttur is ista canori,Sedulitas ideo dulce remittit opus.
units.tr: Yet you fear nothing, nor does that melodious throat of yours tire; your diligence, therefore, lets the sweet work pause.

units.la: Grata sed in longum luco resonante querelaDucitur argutis continuata modis.
units.tr: Yet a pleasing lament, continued at length, is led through the resounding grove in clear-toned modes.

units.la: Nos vero tali quoniam dignaris honoreDicimus in laudes hac tibi pauca tuas.
units.tr: But since you deign to honour us with such an honour, we say a few words in praise of you:

units.la: Humanas auium quæ mulcent cantibus aures,Cedere carminibus carmina cuncta tuis.
units.tr: You who soothe human ears with the songs of birds, all songs yield to your songs.

units.la: Viue dum similisq; tui generata propago,Finiat extremum non nisi fera diem.
units.tr: Live long, and may your like-born offspring end its last day only in death.

units.la: De luscinia quoque autor Philomela sic canit:
units.tr: About the nightingale, too, the author Philomela sings thus:

units.la: Scribere me voces auium Philomela coegit,Quæ cantu cunctas exuperat volucres.
units.tr: Philomela compelled me to write of the voices of birds, she who surpasses all birds in song.

units.la: Dulcis amica veni nobis[?] solatia præstans;Inter aues etenim nulla tibi similis.
units.tr: Sweet friend, come, bringing comfort to us; for among birds none is like you.

units.la: Tu Philomela potes uocum discrimina mille,Mille potes varios ipsa referre modos.
units.tr: You, Philomela, can produce a thousand differences of voice; you yourself can render a thousand varied modes.

units.la: Nã quamuis aliæ volucres modulamine tentent,Nulla potest modulis æquiualere tuis.
units.tr: For though other birds try with their measures, none can equal your measures.

units.la: Insuper est auium spatiis garrire diurnis[?];Tu cantare simul nocte dieq; potes.
units.tr: Moreover, you can chatter through the long spans of the day among birds; you can sing together by night and day.

units.la: Extat & Philippi cuiusdam carmen inter Epigrammata græca de luscinia, quæ boream fugiēs cum per mare volaret, delphini dorso suscepta fit vectaque, illumque natantem carminibus suis delectarit, vt ita hoc Arionis historiæ fidem faciat, qui cum Tarentho Corinthum peteret,ac videret sibi à nautis insi-dias strui, petiit ab iisdem, vt cythara paulu-lum canere liceret, ad cuius sonum cum del-phini conuenissent, excussit se supra vnum, atq; ita imminens periculum effugit. Seruius in Vergilii Eclog.8.
units.tr: There is also a poem by a certain Philip, among the Greek Epigrams, about the nightingale, which, fleeing the north wind as it flew over the sea, was taken up and carried on a dolphin's back, and delighted the swimming creature with its songs. Thus it lends credence to the story of Arion, who, when he was sailing from Tarentum to Corinth and saw that the sailors were plotting against him, asked them to allow him to play his lyre a little; at its sound the dolphins gathered, and he threw himself upon one and so escaped the imminent danger. Servius on Virgil's Eclogue 8.

units.la: De passeribus.
units.tr: On Sparrows.

units.la: Passeris nomen licet ad omnes fere aues minutas extendatur, priuatim tamen certam significat speciem, vt Graecis [?]στρουθός[?], quod sc. cum furore quodam ad libidinem feratur, unde hominem salacem, & supra modum libidinosum [?]στρουθὸν[?] dicimus, & quae stridunt potius quam canunt, [?]στρουθίζειν[?] graece dicuntur, ex passerum voce. Memorandae autem salacitatis & libidinis sunt passeres, & propterea vitae breuissimae: ob quam etiam causam Mauritanorum medicina cibis in totum abdicandos eos censuit: Venerem in cibatu sumti excitant, unde mariti in venerem pigri solent id genus auium crebro & large mandere.
units.tr: The name "sparrow" is extended to almost all small birds, but it properly denotes one definite species. The Greeks call it στρουθός [strouthos], because it is carried along with a kind of frenzy towards lust. Hence we call a lecherous man, one excessively given to lust, a strouthos [στρουθὸν], and those that chirp rather than sing are said in Greek to strouthizein [στρουθίζειν], from the voice of sparrows. Sparrows are notable for their salaciousness and lust, and for that reason their life is very short. For this reason too the medicine of the Mauritanians judged that they should be wholly excluded from food: when eaten they stir up desire for sex, which is why husbands sluggish in love are accustomed to eat this kind of bird often and in quantity.

units.la: Galenus naturae peritissimus Pyrgitas, id est, eos qui in turribus habitant, parvos item merularum carnibus habere carnes proximas, praecipueq; autumno esse commendabilissimas asserit, quoniam per messes & vindemias mire pinguescunt, succiq; acquirunt probitatem.
units.tr: Galen, most skilled in nature, asserts that the Pyrgitae, that is, those who live in towers, and likewise the smaller birds whose flesh is close to that of blackbirds, are most commendable especially in autumn, since during the harvests and vintages they grow wonderfully fat and acquire good juice.

units.la: Quibus propterea in cibis iis abstinent, quod temperaturae sint vulgi iudicio, caliditoris & siccitatis, & nimis super stituose vitae prorogandae cupidi sunt atque solliciti, vulgi se opinionibus magis quam rationi subiicientes. Passerculi minimi troglodytae dicti, sepes iuxta ac muros vitulu quae-ritantes, miram, & Aetio teste, contra calculos renum & vesicae vim habere dicuntur a natura. Sale conditi fenantur. Porro cinerem passerum iuniorum sarmentis crematorum ex aceto infri-gatum auri um dolores minuere Plinius testis est, cap.3.lib.30. ubi quoq; adidem laudatur paf-ferum fimus cum oleo calfactio infusis, &c. Qui renum vel vesicae calculo confl[ictantur], passer & motacillas in cibos affumere frequentius de-bent, modo assas, modo elixas cum infculo, adiecto anisi & foeniculi feminibus, vel etiam petroselino.
units.tr: For these reasons people abstain from them as food, because by popular judgment they are of hot and dry temperament. Those who are excessively superstitious, eager and anxious to prolong life subject themselves more to popular opinions than to reason. The very small sparrows called troglodytes, which seek hedges as well as walls and vines, are said by nature to have a remarkable power against stones of the kidneys and bladder, as Aëtius testifies. They are eaten preserved in salt. Moreover, Pliny (book 30, chapter 3) attests that the ash of young sparrows burned in vine-twigs and rubbed in with vinegar eases pains of the ears; in the same place the dung of sparrows, warmed and infused with oil, is also praised, and so on. Those suffering from a stone of the kidneys or bladder ought more often to take sparrows and wagtails as food, now roasted, now boiled in broth, with added seeds of anise and fennel, or even parsley.

units.la: De phafianis.
units.tr: On Pheasants.

units.la: Phafi amne, (ad cuius ostia phafiano-rum multitudinem cibi gratia conue-nire tradiderunt graeci) qui Colchorum arua facit ditissima, primum in Graeciam ab argonautis inuectas esse, testatur Martialis, Argiua primum fuerit alportata carina, Ante mihi notum nil nisi Phasis erat.
units.tr: The river Phasis, at whose mouths the Greeks report a great multitude of pheasants gathered for food, and which makes the fields of the Colchians most rich, was first brought into Greece by the Argonauts, as Martial bears witness: "Though first an Argive ship brought it here, before this I knew nothing but the Phasis."

units.la: Auis nobilissima, nunc Germanis quoq; nota, Regum tantum & Magnatum mensas exorexornans atque opulentans. Galenus quantum ad coctionis nutriendiq; vim spectat gallinis Phasianos pares, edendi vero suauitate facit superiores. Carnis enim succiq; bonitatem, concoctionisq; facilitatem praedicant omnes. Solonem ad Croesum Regem in regali folio, diademate & purpura auroq; superbum, interrogantemq; nunquid speciosius quicquam spectasset, dixisse fuerunt phasianos & pauones, venustiores sibi videri, quoniam ornamento naturali decoratæ, non ascititio fuco spectabiles essent. Plutarch.
units.tr: A most noble bird, now known also to the Germans, which adorns and enriches the tables of kings and magnates alone. Galen, as far as the power of digestion and nourishment is concerned, judges pheasants equal to hens, but superior in the pleasantness of eating. All praise the goodness of their flesh and juice and the ease of their digestion. Plutarch reports that Solon, when King Croesus, proud on his royal throne with diadem, purple and gold, asked whether he had seen anything more splendid, replied that pheasants and peacocks seemed to him more beautiful, since they were adorned with natural ornament and were conspicuous not by borrowed dye.

units.la: De cornice, pica, monedula, psittaco, coruo, caeterisq; carniuoris & aduncis.
units.tr: On the crow, magpie, jackdaw, parrot, raven, and other carnivorous and hook-clawed birds.

units.la: Obstupescere fere solet nostra ætas, siquem miluum, aut picam, aut cornicem, aut ancipitrem edisse conspexerit, cum antiquis ciconiæ & Struthiocameli auium grandissimæ, peneq; bestiarum ferin[?]q; genetis in deliciis fuerint. Eduntur psittaci ab incolis nouæ Indiæ, nam apud eos volant gregatim. Et certum est, monstrifica animalia quædam, hominis gulam euadere non posse. Nam quis non admiretur admira-bilem aquatilium, vt balenarum, delphino-rum rum,vitulorum marinorum, canum, &c. in re cibaria usum?
units.tr: Our age is usually astonished if it sees anyone eat a kite, a magpie, a crow or a hawk, whereas among the ancients storks and ostriches, the largest of birds and nearly of beasts and wild animals, were delicacies. Parrots are eaten by the inhabitants of the New Indies, for among them they fly in flocks. And it is certain that some monstrous animals cannot escape the human gullet. For who would not marvel at the admirable use in food of aquatic creatures, such as whales, dolphins, sea-calves, dogs and so on?

units.la: Cornices coloris ex cinereo albicantis à non paucis septentrionis gentibus mandun-tur, frigoribus enim pinguescunt, & gratissi-mi in cibo sunt, nutrimentum namq; firmum præbent, & non facilè fluens. Quidam tostas parum cu ı brassica coquunt eodem modo quo palun bes. Sunt omniuorae, vescuntur enim carnæ, nucibus, pomis, quin & in litto-ribus animalia ab unda eiecta, petunt. Carnes earum in morbis diuturnis esse utilissimas, clari quidam auctores tradiderunt, Plin. lib. 30. cap. 11. Quidam, ut inauspicatæ sunt garrulitatis, ita & inauspicati alimenti esse volunt, sed nulla probabili ratione. Porro prodigiosam huic avi vitacitatem tribuunt. Hesiodus, qui primus de spatiis vitæ longissi-mis quædam prodidit, multaque de hominum ævo retulit, cornici novem nostras attribuit ætates, quadruplum eius cervis, id triplicatum corvis, sed fabulosè magis quàm verè, ut novem videatur accipiendum pro multis per synecdoch. quasi sit πολύγηρως[?], ut interpretatur Theon. Centum autem vivit iuxta Ægyptiorum morem computatis annis, annus Ægyptiacus verò constat quatuor usitatis & communibus. Verum de vera & certa ætate adhuc inter autores non convenit. Hoc adnotasse non inconveniens hic est, cornicicornices temperamenti esse firmioris & sic-cioris,obque id longæuas,gaudereque plurimum frigidis atq; humectantib9. Tempesti-tes præsentiunt, vt & corui,quod Virgilius expressit carmine suo,
units.tr: Crows of an ash-whitish colour are eaten by not a few northern peoples, for they grow fat in the cold and are most pleasant as food; they provide firm nourishment that does not easily flow away. Some roast them lightly and cook them with cabbage, in the same way as coots. They are omnivorous, for they feed on flesh, nuts and fruits, and even seek out animals cast up by the waves on the shores. Certain famous authors have taught that their flesh is most useful in long-lasting diseases (Pliny, book 30, chapter 11). Some, as the crow is of inauspicious chatter, so also want it to be of inauspicious food, but on no probable ground. Moreover, they attribute a prodigious longevity to this bird. Hesiod, who first set down certain very long spans of life and related much about the age of man, assigned nine of our ages to the crow, four times that to the stag, and three times that again to the raven; but this is more fabulous than true, and "nine" should be taken for "many" by synecdoche, as if it were polygēros [πολύγηρως], as Theon interprets. The crow lives a hundred years, reckoning years in the Egyptian manner; an Egyptian year, however, consists of four of the usual and common ones. But among authors there is still no agreement about the true and certain age. It is not out of place to note here that crows are of firmer and drier temperament, and so long-lived, and delight greatly in cold and moist things. They foresee storms, as do ravens, which Virgil expressed in his verse:

units.la: Tum cornix plena pluviam vocat improba voce, Et sola in sicca secum spatiatur arena,
units.tr: Then the crow, full of rain, shamelessly calls for rain with its voice, and alone wanders about by itself on the dry sand.

units.la: Et Horatius 3. carm.
units.tr: And Horace, Odes book 3:

units.la: Antequam stantes repetat paludes, Imbrium diuina (præscia) aus[?] (cornix) immi-nentum.
units.tr: Before the divine bird, the crow that foresees the coming showers, returns to the standing marshes.

units.la: Nec non Lucretius,
units.tr: And Lucretius likewise:

units.la: Mutant cum tempestatibus vnà, Raucisonos cantus cornicum secla verusta Coruorumq; greges, ubi aquà dicuntur & imbres Poscere, & interdum ventos aurasq; vocare.
units.tr: They change along with the storms, the ancient generations of crows and the flocks of ravens with their hoarse-sounding songs, where they are said to demand water and rain, and sometimes to call the winds and breezes.

units.la: Nec prætereundum,in pluviarum denun-ciatione cornicem contra naturam suam cro-citare voce crassa & rauca,coruos vero non in pluviis rauca voce, sed purissima contra naturam denunci-suam[?],non solitarios,sed plures, pluviæ dare signum.
units.tr: Nor should it be passed over that in announcing rain the crow, contrary to its nature, caws with a thick and hoarse voice, while the raven does not use a hoarse voice when rain is coming but the purest voice, contrary to its own nature; and not singly but in numbers they give the sign of rain.

units.la: Ad extremum carnes earum aeriæ pestis tempore conferre plurimum creditur. quia Carnes venenis putredinique obsistunt, qualitate cum manifesta, tum etiam antipathetica Manifesta est in sicco,& ad frigiditatem ver-gente temperamento, tale enim putredinem prohibet. Galenus & Philosophi ac Medici omnes.
units.tr: Finally, their flesh is believed to contribute greatly in the time of a pestilence carried by the air, because meat resists poisons and putrefaction, both by its manifest quality and by its antipathetic property. The manifest quality lies in dryness, and in a temperament inclining to cold, for such a temperament prevents putrefaction. Galen, and all philosophers and physicians.

units.la: Experientiæ quoque testimonium hic il-lustre est in vento Borea naturâ frigido & sicco,quo omniaquàm diutissimè imputria durant. Siccarnes & alia, quæcunque al- seruari ab hominibus assolent, sale, muria, a-ceto, vel alio quopiam ex iis, quæ siccandi naturam habent, commodè præparantur. Galenus 1. de temper. & passim alibi. Calida autem & humida facilimè putrescere, nisi re-frigerari ac exiccari contigerit, idé 2. de febr. differentiis fafius explicat. Qua de causa etiam Hippocrates siccitates imbribus falu-briores multo existere non fine ratione scri-psit 3.lib.aphor.15. In siccitatibus enim super-fluxus humiditates dissoluuntur & absorben-tur, perimbres autem in corpore collecta putrefiunt,nisi quis singulis diebus collectas exercitiis expurget,vel purgantib° pharma-cis exturbet, veletiam per balnea euacuet, vbi tamen diæte & consuetudinis ratio, commoda ac incommoda exactè cogno-scenda sunt.
units.tr: The testimony of experience is also clear here, in the north wind Boreas, which is cold and dry by nature, and in which all things last longest without rotting. Dried meats and other things which men are accustomed to keep are conveniently prepared with salt, brine, vinegar, or some other of those things which have a drying nature (Galen, On the Temperaments, book 1, and passim elsewhere). Hot and moist things, however, putrefy very easily unless they happen to be cooled and dried; Galen explains this more fully in On the Differences of Fevers, book 2. For this reason Hippocrates also wrote, not without reason, that droughts are far more beneficial than rains (Aphorisms, book 3, aphorism 15). For in droughts the superfluous humours are dissolved and absorbed, but rains, collected in the body, putrefy, unless one purges them daily by exercise, or expels them with purgative drugs, or even evacuates them by baths; yet here the reasons of diet and habit, with their advantages and disadvantages, must be exactly known.

units.la: Corui cibis omninò abdicantur ob pabu-lum, quod magna ex parte ex hominum,alio-rumque animantium cadaueribus affumunt: si quis tamen horum esui sensim assueuerit, comperiet,solidi eos esse & firmi nutrimen-ti, licet non ita suauis sint succi. Sed quid tum? quasi omne, quod gustui ac palato sua-ue estac gratum, protinus etiam nutriendi, vim habeat? Non certè,si quippiam est boni succi, sequitur, quod idem fit bonus cibus, qui plura defiderat, vt supra demonstratum est: In coruo quaedam sunt partes,quae sumtae bonum alimentum praebent,iis praesertim partibus,quae substantiae quadam familiarita-te cum illis concordant, licet eae non sint adeo probi succi, quod forsan aliquibus videbitur paradoxon. Nec abs re: quia inquiunt,fi res quaedam fit boni succi,sequitur, quod fit etiam bonus cibus: falsum autem id esse,inque nutritionis opereac mysterio rem aliter longè fe habere ex hactenus dictis facile quis intellexerit.
units.tr: Crows are altogether excluded from food on account of their pasture, since they take in for the most part the corpses of humans and other animals. If anyone, however, gradually accustoms himself to eating them, he will find them to be of solid and firm nourishment, although their juice is not so pleasant. But what then? As if whatever is pleasing and agreeable to taste and palate immediately also has the power of nourishing! Certainly not. If something has good juice, it does not follow that it is good food, since good food requires more, as has been shown above. In the crow there are certain parts which, when taken, provide good nourishment, especially those parts which agree with our substance through some familiarity of material, although they are not of so good juice; this will perhaps seem a paradox to some. Nor is this beside the point: for they say that if a thing has good juice, it follows that it is also good food; but that this is false, and that in the work and mystery of nutrition the matter stands quite otherwise, one may easily understand from what has been said so far.

units.la: Cibi boni virtus est esse bene alterabilem, facile transmutabilem ad coctionem,ab instrumentis,quib. coctionis munus est à natura demandatum : facilè coctibilem, totà substantia nobis amicum & familiarem , facile denique assimilari,cumq; corpore quod nutritur , naturae beneficio coalescere seu coadunari aptum.
units.tr: The virtue of good food is to be easily alterable, readily transmutable towards digestion by the instruments to which nature has assigned the function of digestion; easily digestible, wholly friendly and familiar to our substance; and finally, easily assimilated, and apt to coalesce or unite, by the benefit of nature, with the body that is nourished.

units.la: In coruis,& id genus aliis quibusdam car-niuoris aduncisq; auibus quasdam esse partes, quae substantiae occulta quadam familiaritate cum corporis nostri certis partibus co-spirent,inque cibis sumtae eas nutriant, vfq; assimilentur,fi quis negauerit, is in toto anti-pathias & sympathias mysterio plane caecu-tit, alimentorumque ac ciborum naturam viresque parum habet cognitas. Non e- nim intelligunt, coctionem fieriab ea fub- fit a folis ftantia,cum quaineft fimilitudo, nonà folis elementio- elementorum qualitatibus. Simile enim nu- rum qua- trit fimile,eodemque nutritur, cot corde, e- luatibus. parepate,pulmo pulmone,&c. Quapropter non fimpliciter verum eft, quod Plutarchus aliorum Philofophorum opinioni reclamat, prodens,animalia ftomacho & calore valen- tia ferpentes & fcorpiones digerere poffe. Nam ftruthiocamelus non digerit ferrum folius caloris ventriculi ratione, fed quia in- ter hunc & illud ineft, vel potius intercedit fubstantia quaedam latens & abdita fimilitu- Quod fi folo calore concoctio abfol- ueretur,leo,ftruthione longè calidior,aurú, ferrum, & zs quoque digereret,quae quam- uis ignis calore fint inexpugnabilia,ftruthio- nes tamen ex hisconflata numifmata deglu- tire & concoquere tam experientia clarum eft,vt in horto ducis Ferrariae id fe vidiffe Lá- gius in Epiftolis aperte ceftetur. Quin & mu- res, quia metallorum fcobem adeò appe- tunt,metalla concoquere, iifque nutriri ve- rifimile eft : Et Theophraftus in Syaro In- fula, expulsis incolis, ferrum arrofiffe eos tradit, quos etiam arrofis Lauinii argenteis clypeis Marcii portendiffe bellū, magnāq; ad chalybas, in ferrariis officinis fecifie ia- duram cturam,constat ex Plinio libr.8 cap.17. Sed quis hæc solo calore, quæ vix igne domari possunt, in corporibus animalium confici posse putabit? Vix id, opinor, quispiam credet, nisi congenitæ torius membrorum sub-stantiæ coquendi istam virtutem ac proprietatem attribuerit.
units.tr: Among crows and other such carnivorous, hook-beaked birds, there are certain parts which, by a hidden affinity of substance, agree with certain parts of our own body, so that when eaten they nourish it and are assimilated. Whoever denies this is wholly blind to the mystery of antipathies and sympathies, and knows little of the nature and powers of foods and aliments. For they do not understand that digestion is effected not by the qualities of the elements alone, but also by a certain similarity of substance. Like seeks like, and is nourished by like: heart by heart, liver by liver, lung by lung, and so on. Therefore it is not simply true, as Plutarch maintains against the opinion of other philosophers, that animals with a strong stomach and heat can digest serpents and scorpions. For the ostrich and the camel do not digest iron by the heat of the stomach alone, but because some hidden and concealed substance of likeness lies between the one and the other. If digestion were completed by heat alone, the lion, far hotter than the ostrich, would digest gold, iron and stones too. Yet ostriches swallow and digest coins made of these metals, which are proof against fire's heat, and this is so clearly established by experience that Lagus, in his Letters, openly testifies that he saw it in the garden of the Duke of Ferrara. Moreover, mice, because they so eagerly seek the scrapings of metals, probably digest metals and are nourished by them. Theophrastus relates that on the island of Syros, after the inhabitants were expelled, mice gnawed through iron; and that they gnawed the silver shields of Lavinius, portending the war of Marcius, and made great ravages among the chalybes in the iron workshops, is established by Pliny, book 8, chapter 17. But who would think that things which can scarcely be subdued by fire can be accomplished in the bodies of animals by heat alone? Hardly anyone, I think, would believe it, unless he attributed this power and property of digesting to the innate substance of all the members.

units.la: Verum, vt ad coruos nostros reuertamur, sciendum, carnes eorum mirè conducere iis, qui natura temperamentum compaginemque corporis habent laxiorem, hoc est, minus solidam firmamque ac compactam, hu-midumque radicale nimis fluxile: ob-sucum inquam incrassantem ac consolidantem, qui coruorum carnibus inest, prodest coruis vesci, iis, qui se natura sentiunt minus vegetos, viriumque dissolutarum. Vnde evi-dentissimè vitæ longioris breuiorisque causam in-notescere diligens lector facilè per-spexerit.
units.tr: But, to return to our crows: it must be understood that their flesh is remarkably suitable for those whose natural constitution and bodily make-up is rather lax, that is, less solid, firm and compact, and whose radical moisture is too fluid. I mean that the thickening and consolidating moisture which is in crows' flesh benefits those who feel by nature less vigorous and with dissolved strength. From this a diligent reader will easily see clearly what causes a longer or shorter life.

units.la: Assi autem in cibis præstant elixis, & hieme quoque quam æstate salubriores sunt, per æstatem enim in autumnum morbo cor-uos conflictari Plinius autor est, libr. 29. cap.3.
units.tr: Roasted, crows are better as food than boiled, and in winter they are healthier than in summer; for Pliny is the authority that crows are afflicted by disease in summer until autumn, book 29, chapter 3.

units.la: Cæterum inauspicatissimos eos esse omnium consensu traditur, sed tum maximè cum vocem glutiunt, velut strangulati, tunc enim pessima eorum significatio est.
units.tr: Moreover, by universal agreement they are held to be most ill-omened, and especially when they gulp down their voice as if strangled, for then their omen is at its worst.

units.la: De coruorum intelligentia mira refert.
units.tr: He reports remarkable things about the intelligence of crows.

units.la: Plinius lib.10. cap.43. Soli enim in auspiciis videntur habere intellectum significationi suarum, nam cum Medic hospites occisi sunt, omnes, è Peleponnefo & Attica regio-ne volauerunt. Ab ortu accinentes clara voce præfentem felicitatem, ab occasu veró vel læua clamantes, exitium denunciasse ob-seruatum est. Hominum voces fermonemq; imitantur. Augusto ex Actiaca victoria re-uertenti occurrit inter gratulantes quidam tenens coruum, quem instituerat proferre hæc verba, aue Cæsar Victor Imperator. Mi-ratus Cæsar tam officiosam auem viginti millibus eam emit, hoc est, quingentis aureis solatis, multasque præterea similes compa-rauit. Quo exemplo commotus pauper su-tor, instituere ipse quoque aggressus est cor-uum ad parem salutationem, sed impendio exhaustus ad auem non respondentem dice-re folebat opera & impensa periit. Cepit tamen aliquando coruus optatam salutatio-nem exprimere, ac forte audita, dum transi-ret Cæsar, respondisset, satis aliquid salutato-ri habeo domi, superfuit coruo memoria, ut & illa, quibus Dominû querente folebat audire, verba subiungeret, opera & impensa periit: ad quod subridens Cæsar emi a-uem iussit, quanti nullam aliam emerat.
units.tr: Pliny, book 10, chapter 43: Crows alone seem to have an understanding of the meaning of their omens. For when the guests from Media were slain, they were observed to fly out of the Peloponnese and the region of Attica. Singing out clearly from the east, they announced present happiness; but calling from the west, or on the left, they announced ruin. They imitate human voices and speech. When Augustus was returning from the victory at Actium, among the well-wishers there met him a certain man holding a crow, which he had trained to say these words: "Hail, Caesar, victorious Imperator." Caesar, amazed at so obliging a bird, bought it for twenty thousand sesterces, that is, five hundred gold solidi, and besides this he acquired many similar birds. Moved by this example, a poor cobbler also set about training a crow to give the same greeting, but, exhausted by the expense, he used to say that his work and outlay were lost because the bird did not answer. Yet the crow did at last manage to produce the desired greeting, and, as chance would have it, when Caesar was passing by, it replied: "I have enough of something to give the greeter at home." The crow retained the memory to add the words it had often heard its master complain with: "my work and outlay are lost." At this Caesar smiled and ordered that the bird be bought, at whatever price he had paid for none other.

units.la: Perottus. Vide Macrob. lib.2. Saturn. cap.4.
units.tr: Perottus. See Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 2, chapter 4.

units.la: Plinius loco citato refert, sutorem quendam coruum pullum religione sibi ab officinæ Domino commendatum educasse, matureque sermoni assuefactum, omnibus matutinis euolasse in foftra, in forum versus Tiberium principem, dein Germanicum & Drufum Cæsares, nominatimque eos falutasse, mox transfiise populum Romanum, postea ad tabernam remeasse plurimorum anno-rum, assiduo officio mirum. Hunc fiue æmulatione incitatus manceps sutrinæ proximæ, five iracundia subita, vt videri voluit, ab excrementis eius aspersa calceis maculâ, examinauit, tanta plebei consternatione, vt primo pulsus ex ea regione, mox & interim-tus fit, funusque innumeris aliti celebratum exequiis, constratus lectus fuit super æthio-pum duorum humeros, præcedente tibici-ne, & coronis omnium generum, ad rogum vsque, constructum dextrâ via Appia ad fe-cundum lapidem in campo Rediculi appel-lato. Tanta fuit coruis gratia apud Pop. Ro-manum indignatione testata & conscientia.
units.tr: Pliny, in the place cited, relates that a certain cobbler had reared a young crow which the owner of his workshop had entrusted to him as a religious charge; once it was early accustomed to speech, every morning it flew out to the Rostra, toward the Forum, to the emperor Tiberius, then to the Caesars Germanicus and Drusus, and greeted them each by name; then it passed on to the Roman people, and afterwards returned to the shop, a wonder of constant duty for many years. Then the master of the neighbouring cobbler's shop, either driven by rivalry or by sudden anger, as he wished it to appear, struck it dead, having its droppings splashed on his shoes as a stain. Such was the consternation of the common people that he was first driven out of that district and soon afterwards killed. The bird's funeral was celebrated by countless birds with funeral rites. A couch was laid on the shoulders of two Ethiopians, a flute-player going before, and garlands of every kind were carried, all the way to the pyre, which was built beside the Appian Way at the second milestone, in the field called Rediculus. So great was the favour in which crows were held by the Roman people, as shown by their indignation and their conscience.

units.la: Non prætereundum denique, quod Plinius l. 10, cap. 12. prodidit, grauidas, fi ede-rint corvinum ovum per os partum reddere, atque in totum difficulter parere, & lib. 8. c. 49. corvum, occiso chameleonte, qui etiam victori nocet, lauro infestum virus extin-guere. Hactenus de corvis.
units.tr: It must not be passed over either what Pliny reports in book 10, chapter 12: that if pregnant women eat a crow's egg, they bring forth the child through the mouth, and altogether give birth with difficulty. And in book 8, chapter 49, that a crow, having killed a chameleon (which is also harmful to its killer), extinguishes the poison, which is hostile to laurel. So far concerning crows.

units.la: Bb
units.tr: Bb

units.la: Coruini generis sunt graculi seu mo-nedulæ,sic dicti quod gregatim volent,vel à sono oris, quasi garruli, sunt enim clamoli: vel ut alii putant à gerendo,quod jacta femi-na segetum legant, monedulæ vero à mone-ta, quasi monetulæ, solis enim his miram auri, argentique furacitatem inesse tradit Plinius lib.10. cap.29. Vnde Cicer. in orat. pro Flacc. non plus aurum tibi, quam mo-nedulæ committebatur. Insitionis tene-raque inferendi emplaftrationis causam & inuentionem monedulis tribui, condenti-bus femina in cauernarum thesauros, idem lib.17.capit.13.testis est. Qu busdam in locis habentur in cibatu, & tonstrinæ ibidem eas educant in caveis, docentque humanas exprimere voces. Mira autem his in vino lasciuia, à cuius potu evadunt loquaciores. Quidam existimant mone-dulas, ut & picas comitiali morbo tentari, quoniam plerunque velut extinctæ ex arbo-rum tectorumq; culminibus decidere inter-ram conspiciuntur, ob eamq; causam à vul-go mensis etiam abdicantur.
units.tr: Of the crow kind are the jackdaws, or daws (graculi or monedulae). They are so called because they fly in flocks, or from the sound of their voice, as if garrulous, for they are chatterers; or, as others think, from gathering (gerendo), because they collect the grain thrown by sowers. Monedulae, however, are named from moneta, as if they were little money-birds, since Pliny, book 10, chapter 29, says that this bird alone has a remarkable thievish appetite for gold and silver. Hence Cicero in his speech for Flaccus: no more gold was entrusted to you than to the jackdaws. Pliny, book 17, chapter 13, also attests that the invention of grafting and of plastering wounds is credited to jackdaws, since they store seeds in the treasure-caves. In some places they are kept in the kitchen, and barbers there rear them in cages and teach them to imitate human voices. Their fondness for wine is remarkable, and after drinking it they become more talkative. Some think that jackdaws, like magpies, are afflicted by epilepsy, since they are often seen falling from the tops of trees and roofs to the ground as if dead; for this reason they are even banished from the table by the common people.

units.la: Linguam reliquis animantibus habet latiorem, unde loquacissima & humanæ vocis magis æmula est. Expressior lo-quacitas certo generi picarum est, ait Plinius lib.10. cap.42. adamant verba quæ lo-quantur, nec discunt tantum, sed diligunt, meditantesque intra semet, cura atque cogi-tatione intentionem non occultant.
units.tr: They have a broader tongue than other animals, whence they are the most talkative and the most like human voices. A more distinct talkativeness belongs to a certain kind of magpie, says Pliny, book 10, chapter 42. They love the words they speak, not only learning them, but meditating on them inwardly, and they do not conceal their attention, which they give with care and thought.

units.la: Constat emori victas difficultate ver-bi, ac nisi subinde eadem audiant, memoria falli, quaerentes mirum in modum hilarari, si interim audierint id verbum: nec vulgaris iis forma, quamuis non spectanda: sat illis decoris in specie sermonis humani est. Ve-rum addiscere alias posse negant, quam, quae ex genere earum sunt, quae glandibus ve-scuntur, et inter eas facilius, quibus quini-sunt digiti in pedibus, ac ne eas quidem ipsas, nisi primis duobus vitae annis. Haec Plinius. Astus quoque earum insignis in eo cernitur, quod, cum diligentius, visum ab homine nidum sensere, ova alio transferant. Pulli mire in cibis a quibusdam expetuntur, magnaque cum voluptate manducantur, licet a nitidiorem splendidiorem-que vitam sectantibus damnati, quos cibis minime abdicarent, si carnem eorum visui acuendo conducere, facilisque coctionis esse animaduertissent.
units.tr: It is agreed that they die when overcome by the difficulty of a word, and that unless they hear the same words repeatedly they forget them; and they rejoice wonderfully if they hear that word in the meantime. Nor is their appearance vulgar, though not to be admired; they have enough beauty in the form of human speech. But they cannot, it is said, learn any others than those of the kind that feed on acorns, and among these more easily those which have five toes on their feet; nor can even these learn, except in the first two years of life. Thus Pliny. Their cunning is also notable in this, that when they perceive that a man has more closely observed their nest, they transfer their eggs elsewhere. Chicks are eagerly sought after as food by some, and eaten with great pleasure, although they are condemned by those who pursue a more refined and splendid way of life, who would by no means abstain from them as food if they had noticed that their flesh sharpens the sight and is easy to digest.

units.la: Aduncas aves & carnivoras fere omnes, urbaniores atq; liberaliores homines in ci-bos non admittunt, ut sunt aquilae, vultures, milui, accipitres ambo, fringillarius & pa-lumbarii, multo inter se magnitudine differentes, & buteo, magnitudine miluum aequans, quem graeci aefalona vocant, solus enim eiim[?] omni tempore apparet , caeteri hieme as[?] eunt : triorchis etiam à testium numero dicitur, principatumque ei in auguriis Phœ-moinoe dedit : buteonem appellarunt Ro-mani, familiaque ex eo cognominata, cum pro spero auspicio in ducis naui sedisset. In me[?]nfarum autem honore hic fuisse inueni-tur, sicut & accipitrum pullos suaues admo-duineffe[?], pinguesque reddi Aristoteles te-stir[?], est l.9. histor. animal. Palumbarios quoq; ac cipitres cibis omnino abdicare inhumani &c insipidi palati est, quod tamen lautiorum vnenfarum venià dictum volo. Plura au-tem eorum genera , quæ ex auiditate distin-gui possunt. Alii enim nonnisi ex terra a-vem rapiunt, alii non nisi circa arbores voli-tantem, alii sedentem in sublimi, alii volan-tem in aperto : vnde columbæ nouére ex iis periculum , visoque eo confidunt , vel subvolant,contra naturam ejus sibi auxilian-tes. Caeterum non prætereundum, accipi-tres scalpendo lactucam, quæ hieracium di-citur,succoque oculos tingendo obscurita-tem, cum sensere, discutere. Et certissimi experimenti est, oculorum vitiis, hunc suc-cum apprime mederi.
units.tr: Hooked and flesh-eating birds, nearly all of them, are not admitted to the food of more refined and well-bred people. These include eagles, vultures, kites, both kinds of hawk, the sparrowhawk and the falcon, which differ greatly from one another in size; and the buzzard, equal in size to the kite, which the Greeks call aefalon, since it alone is seen at all times of year, while the others leave in winter. The triorchis is so named from its number of testicles, and Phoenix gave it the first place among birds of augury. The Romans called the buzzard buteo, and a family took its surname from it, because one of that name sat on a general's ship as a favourable omen. I find that this bird was held in honour at tables, just as young hawks are said to be pleasant to eat and to grow fat, as Aristotle testifies in book 9 of the History of Animals. To exclude pigeon hawks from food altogether is, however, the mark of an inhuman and insipid palate, though I wish this said with the pardon of the more discerning gourmets. There are several kinds of these birds, which can be distinguished by their rapacity. Some seize a bird only from the ground, others only while it is flying around trees, others while it sits on a height, others while it flies in the open. For this reason doves recognise the danger from them, and when they see one they either trust to it or fly beneath it, using its own nature against it. Nor should it be passed over that hawks, when they feel their eyes dimmed, scratch at lettuce, which is called hieracium, and by dipping their eyes in its juice they clear the darkness away. It is a most certain experiment that this juice is especially good for diseases of the eyes.

units.la: De Vulturis, inexplebilis scilicet eda-citatis alitis pelle seu plumoso tegmine Le-mnius l.4. de occ. naturæ miraculi scribit, fo-ris admotum robur ventriculo debili afferre, coctionique adminiculari, cibique avidita-tem efficacius excitare, quam zinziber con-ditum. Est autem cæterarum pellium modo arte pellicea subigenda ac concussione có-planan-da. Cum enim omnia hæc avis, & quidem avide appetat, inoffenseque consu-mat, tegmini ejus ea est visinsusa[?], ut ventri-culum humanum roboret, naufeantiq; sto-macho vires appetendi concoquendi cibi conferat: qua de causa etiam carnes ejus ci-bo[?] sumtas ventriculo debili, appetentiaeque dejectæ ac postratæ prodesse, extra omnem dubitationem affirmo ex sympathetico in-fluxu & operatione. Plinius l.29.c.4. scri-bit, cor hujus alitis habentes, tutos non so- luum[?] à serpentum impetu esse, sed etiam se-rarum, latronumque insidiis & Regum ira.
units.tr: Concerning the vulture, the skin or feathered covering of that greedy and insatiable bird, Lemnius in book 4 of On the Hidden Wonders of Nature writes that when applied externally it brings strength to a weak stomach, aids digestion, and stirs the appetite more effectively than preserved ginger. It is prepared, like other skins, by the art of tanning and softened by beating. For since this bird devours all such things eagerly and digests them without harm, its covering has this virtue, that it strengthens the human stomach and restores the strength to appetite and digestion in a queasy stomach. For this reason I affirm beyond all doubt that its flesh, eaten as food, benefits a weak stomach and those whose appetite is lost and cast down, by a sympathetic influence and operation. Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, writes that those who have the heart of this bird are safe not only from the attack of serpents but also from the snares of thieves and robbers and from the anger of kings.

units.la: Sed hæc Magiæ Studiosis ulterius per-scrutanda relinquimus, parum enim ad no-strum institutum.
units.tr: But these matters we leave for students of magic to examine further, since they have little bearing on our purpose.

units.la: Ex nocturnis avibus unum asionum[?] genus affert Aristoteles corpulentia pingui, autumno quandoque apparens, ac uno tan-tum atque alrero[?] die immorans, esui est val-deque probatur, perennes vero omnibusque anni temporibus apparentes esui non esse affeueratob carnis vitium, malum succum, coctionisque contumaciam. Pullinihilo-minus nocturnatum avium, aquibusdam non insalubriter appetuntur. Carnes no-ctua. ctuarum[?] membris paralyticis auxiliari com- pertum habetur, cerebrumque vino co- ctum capitis doloribus. Porro bubones funebres & maxime abominatos publicis praecipue aufpiciis, defertaincolere, nec tantum defolata, fed dira etiam & inaccefla, no- ctis monftrum, nec cantu aliquo vocales ef- fe, fed gemitu potius, nemo fere eft, quinon norit. De babonis augurio hiftoria memo- tatu dignifima eft apud Nicolaum Cle- mangium Bajocenfis Ecclefiæ in Gallia olim Archidiaconum, qui Pifani concilii impro- bitate offenfus, in quandam de conciliis di- fputationem incidit. Agens autem de conci- lio Romano, quod Johannes XXI V.Ponti- fex, in Efquilino monte &de D. Martini ce- lebrauit, fequens natrat prodigium. Con- vocauerat, inquit, ante 4. annos Romę Con- cilium, maxima quorundam impulfus con- tentione, Balthafar Cofla perfidiffimus, nu- per è Petri fede, quam turpiffime fœdabat, ejectus in quo pauciffimis præfentibus, ex aliquibus, qui aderant, Italis & aulicis fuis, feffiones aliquot tenuit de rebus fuperuaca- neis, nihilq; ad ecclefiæ utilitatem pertinen- tibus. Cum autem ante primam concilii có- greffionem pro inuocatione Spiritus S. facra de more fuiflent facta, Patres afflederunt, & Balthafar fublimi in loco præfedit, ecce di- rus ac feralis bubo, funeris aut alterius calamitatis fere semper nuncius, è latebris prorumpens, voce sua illa horrifica, continuo aduolat, superque trabem templi mediam, oculis in Balthasarem intentis, astitit. Uniuersis mirantibus, quod nocturna auis & lucifuga, in turbam diurna luce aduolasset, malumq; ex prodigio ominantibus, Balthasar, in quem fixa acie oculos intendebat, angi, sudare, atque intra semetipsum cœpit æstuare, & dimissis patribus, solutoque conuentu discessit. Aliqui prodigium verterunt in risum, dicentes, specie bubonis in congregationem improborum aduenisse Spiritum S. Secuta altera deinceps sessio, in quam eodem modo rursus bubo aduenit, uerso semper in Balthasarem contuitu, qui maiore pudore, quam prius perturbatus, auem ominosam clamoribus abigi & manuum supplosione terreri præcepit, sed illa non prius amota fuit, quam fustium ictibus pulsata in conspectu omnium examinis decideret. Hic autem bubonis aduentus augurio suo non caruit: nam & concilium cum dedecore Pontificis dissolutum, & Balthasar paulo post Constantiæ exauctoratus est, Monheimiique in oppido Principis Palatini in vinculis fuit detentus. Refert Haithonus in libro de tattaris[?], Changium Can Imperatorem tartarorum victum ab hostibus inter arbusta latitasse, inter quæ, cum forte buboinsideret, victores dum perquirunt. victos passim occultatos neminem latere putárunt, quasi aveillic minime mansura, fi hominum quisquam adesset. Itaque factum est, vt silentio noctis secutæ Imperator ad suos euaserit, & salutis suæ caulam expo-suerit.
units.tr: Among nocturnal birds, Aristotle mentions one kind of owl, thick with fat, which sometimes appears in autumn and stays for only a day or two; it is good to eat and is well approved. The perennial owls, however, which appear at all seasons of the year, are not used for food, since their flesh is noted for a bad quality, a bad juice and a stubborn resistance to digestion. Nevertheless the young of nocturnal birds are eaten by some without harm. It is known that the flesh of owls helps paralysed limbs, and that the brain cooked in wine cures headaches. Moreover, that the funereal owl is carried about, and is especially hated as a bad omen in public affairs, and that it dwells not only in deserted and dreadful and inaccessible places, a monster of the night, and is vocal not with any song but rather with a groan, nearly everyone knows. There is a most memorable story about the owl as an omen, told by Nicolaus Clemangius, once archdeacon of the church of Bayeux in France. Offended by the wickedness of the Council of Pisa, he fell into a discussion about councils, and in speaking of the Roman council which Pope John XXIII held on the Esquiline Hill, at the church of St Martin, he relates the following prodigy. He says that four years earlier, at Rome, a council had been summoned, pushed on by the great contentiousness of certain men, by Balthasar Cossa, the most treacherous man, recently ejected from the Chair of Peter, which he had most shamefully defiled. In that council, with very few present, out of those who were there, Italians and his own courtiers, he held several sessions on trivial matters that had nothing to do with the good of the Church. Now before the first meeting of the council, a sacred service had been held as usual to invoke the Holy Spirit; the Fathers took their seats, and Balthasar presided from a high place. Behold, a dreadful and deadly owl, almost always a messenger of death or some other calamity, burst out of its hiding place with its horrible cry, flew straight up, and stood above the middle beam of the church, its eyes fixed on Balthasar. While all marvelled that a nocturnal and light-shunning bird had flown into a crowd in daylight, and foretold evil from the portent, Balthasar, on whom it kept its gaze fixed, began to be troubled, to sweat, and to seethe inwardly; dismissing the Fathers, he broke up the assembly and left. Some turned the portent into a joke, saying that the Holy Spirit had come to the gathering of wicked men in the form of an owl. Then followed another session, into which the owl again came in the same way, always turning its gaze upon Balthasar. He, more disturbed than before and with greater shame, ordered the ominous bird to be driven away with shouts and frightened off by clapping of hands. But it was not moved until, struck by blows of clubs, it fell down in the sight of all. The coming of the owl did not lack its omen: for the council was dissolved with dishonour to the Pope, and Balthasar was soon after deposed at Constance and was held in chains at Monheim, in a town of the Prince Palatine. Hayton, in his book on the Tartars, relates that Changium Can, emperor of the Tartars, after being defeated by his enemies, hid among the bushes, and that, while an owl happened to sit there, the victors, searching, thought that no one could be hiding there, as the bird would certainly not have remained had any man been present. So it came about that in the silence of the following night the emperor escaped to his own people and secured the means of his safety.

units.la: A quo tempore Tartari bubonem seu auem felicem, auspicatam & sacram reue-rentur, plumasque ejus ceu amuletum & prosperitatis causam in capitibus gestant, ac felices se prædicant, quicunque eas habe-re possunt.
units.tr: From that time the Tartars revere the owl as a lucky, auspicious and sacred bird, and they wear its feathers on their heads as a charm and a cause of prosperity, and count themselves fortunate whoever is able to have them.

units.la: De grandioribus alitibus.
units.tr: On the Larger Birds.

units.la: Vium grandissimi & pene bestiarum generis sunt Struthocameli. In Africa & Æthiopia altitudinem equitis infi-dentis equo excedunt, celeritate vincunt, nec tamen volucres, nec a terra tolluntur. Xenophon expeditionis Cyri lib. 1. tradit in Arabia repertos Struthocamelos, quos nemo ex toto exercitu capere potuerit. Athenæus Arabicos Regum Persarum mensis epulis, adhibest foli-tos scripsit. Galenus quoque in ciborum cen-tu eos reposuit, horum alas deteriores caterasque superiores lucrum alius non esse promisit, carnes tamen ex-crementis abunde refertas concoctione, esse pertinaces. Concoquendi fine delectu devorant.
units.tr: The largest of all, and almost a beast rather than a bird, are the ostriches. In Africa and Ethiopia they stand taller than a horseman sitting on his horse, and they outrun it, yet they neither fly nor are lifted from the ground. Xenophon, in the first book of the Expedition of Cyrus, reports that ostriches were found in Arabia, and that no one in the whole army could catch one. Athenaeus writes that they were customarily served at the feasts of the Persian kings. Galen too lists them among foods, and says that their wings are of inferior quality and their other parts of little profit, but that their flesh, abundantly stuffed with excrement, is hard to digest. They swallow whatever they find, indiscriminately, in order to digest it.

units.la: sic mira in iis natura est, nam ipsum ferrum perfi-cere certo dicuntur, quod absurde & inepte quidam ventriculi calori vehementiori crassitudiniq; ejus attribuunt, ut supra quoq; anno-tatum est. Ex ovis ipsorum caput infantis ma-gnitudine referentibus olim vasa fiebant potoria ex transverso secta, teste Plin. l. 10. cap. 1. Mira vero stol[?] ditatis esse idem auctor est in tanta enim corporis altitudine, cum colla frutice occulta-uerint, toto se latere corpore existimant.
units.tr: So marvellous is their nature: for they are said to digest even iron, which some foolishly and absurdly attribute to the greater heat of their stomach, as has been noted above too. Their eggs, which are the size of an infant's head, were once cut crosswise and made into drinking vessels, as Pliny testifies in book 10, chapter 1. The same author says that their stupidity is marvellous indeed; for when they have hidden their necks in the bushes, they think that their whole body is concealed.

units.la: De Gruibus.
units.tr: On Cranes.

units.la: Altitudine carnisque duritie succe-dunt, frugilegæ grues, Augusti Prin-cipatu in cibis gratæ, teste Nepote Cornelio: Plinii vero ætate inter primas expetebantur: hodie hibernos cibos nobi-litant, & præsertim in claris amplisque fa-miliis.
units.tr: Next in size and in the hardness of their flesh come the grain-gleaning cranes, which were pleasing as food in the principate of Augustus, according to Cornelius Nepos. In Pliny's day they were among the most sought-after dishes, and today they grace winter meals, especially in distinguished and wealthy households.

units.la: Inaflantur autem, garyophyllisq; perfodiuntur & pipere, solidæque postea apponuntur. Quibusdam repositæ & infrigidatæ placent magis quam calentes, & sic paratæ durant in multos dies.
units.tr: They are inflated, pierced with cloves and pepper, and then served whole. Some people prefer them cooled after cooking rather than hot, and prepared in this way they keep for many days.

units.la: Cæterum, quia fibrosæ ac præduræ carnes ipsarum sunt, tenerescere eas sinunt pendendo, si scil. graue aliquod pondus pe-dibus alligetur. Inuenitur quoque aues præ-duras teneritudinem adipisci, si e ficu pendeant, tantam enim arbori huic inesse vim dicunt. Minores grues vipiones appella-tæ in maximo quondam mensarum honore fuerunt Balearicis. Extremos fluvii Gan-gis accolas spithamæos, pygmæos, ternos spithamas longitudine, hoc est, ternos do-drantes non excedentes à gruibus infestari Homerus prodidit. Quin & Plinius l.4.c.11[?], ex Gerania, Thraciæ regione, eos ab illis su-gatos, autor est.
units.tr: Moreover, since their flesh is fibrous and very tough, they let it grow tender by hanging, provided some heavy weight is tied to their feet. It is also found that tough birds become tender if they hang from a fig tree, for they say this tree has such a power. The smaller cranes, called vipiones, were once held in the highest honour on the tables of the Balearic islanders. Homer reported that the pygmies, the dwellers on the farthest banks of the Ganges, who are a span tall and three spans long, that is, not exceeding three dodrantes, are harassed by cranes. Pliny, in book 4, chapter 11, also states that they were put to flight by them, from Gerania, a region of Thrace.

units.la: Cæterum de volatu & migratione gruum mira sunt, quæ apud Aristor, Ælianum, Plinium, Plutarchum, Isidorum, & Gillium scripta reperiuntur. Thraciam in quana-[?]scuntur, ut patriam amore prosequuntur, in eaque æstiuo tempore patriæ sedis amore & studio captæ, ætatem ducunt, medio autu-mno, salutis ergo frigoris vim non sustinen-tes[?] tanquam cœli mutationem temporum-que varietatem scientia & cognitione, com-prehenderint, frequentes in Ægyptum, Li-byam ac Æthiopiam proficiscuntur. Septembri autem discedere incipiunt, ac more Regis Persarum æstiua & hiberna confici-unt. Inducias autem habet Pygmæorum gens abscessu gruum cum iis dimicantium. Cum verò jam proximum est, ut auolent hiberni, circa Nilum victus desiderio incen-si, grus quæ inter alias extremo ætatis tempore affecta fuerit, ter circa universum gregem volans, supremum vitæ diem conficit. Hanc primo sepultura reliquæ afficiunt, reétaque deinde in Ægyptum iter faciunt, neq; imensa pelagi spatia alarum robore transmittentes usquam interquiescunt. Volant autem alte, ut procul possint prospicere, & si nubes tempestatemq; viderint, confugunt se in terram humiq; quiescunt. Volantes trianguli figurâ formant, ut facilius hac forma aerem adversum secent, & ex triquetra figura quandoq; edunt sexangulum. Prouectiores ætate in primum ordinem volando collocant, ne se fatigent nimium sequendo, si juniores præcederent; Clamorem etiam edunt, ne seperentur nimium aliæ ab aliis. Siq; quam sensere defessam, aliæ duæ utrinq; eam alis subleuant, aut etiam super dorsis aut pedibus ferunt, retrorsum enim sereno cœlo pedes solent extendere, secundos ventos & retro flantes obseruare norunt. Ducem habet etiā, & eos qui clament dispositos in extremo agmine, ut vox percipi possit. Cū consistūt, cæterae dormiunt, capite subter alā condito, alternis pedib. insistentes. Dux nudo capite spicit, & q; senserit, voce significat. Cū inter-rā descederint cibi gratiâ, dux earū caput in altum erigit in custodiam omnium, cæteris secure pascentib. In tergo præuolantiū colla & capita reponūr, quod quia duxipse facere nō potest, nō habes quo nitas, revolat, utipse quiescat quoq; in ejus vero locū succedit alia
units.tr: Furthermore, the marvels concerning the flight and migration of cranes are recorded in Aristotle, Aelian, Pliny, Plutarch, Isidore and Gellius. They are said to pass into Thrace, where they love their homeland and spend the summer there, held by affection and longing for their native seat. In mid-autumn, unable to endure the force of the cold for their own safety, and as if they had grasped by knowledge and understanding the change of the sky and the variety of the seasons, they set out in large numbers for Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia. They begin to depart in September, and, like the king of the Persians, they arrange their summer and winter quarters. The race of pygmies has a truce while the cranes are away, since they have been fighting with them. When the time draws near for the winter birds to fly off, and they are inflamed with desire for the food around the Nile, a crane that has grown old among the others flies three times around the whole flock and completes its last day of life. The rest first give it burial, and then, having set out again, they make their journey to Egypt; they do not cross the vast spaces of the sea on the strength of their wings and rest nowhere along the way. They fly high so that they can see far, and if they see clouds and a storm, they take refuge and lie low on the ground. In flight they form a triangle, because this shape cuts the opposing air more easily, and sometimes out of the triangle they make a hexagon. The older birds they place in the front rank, so that they do not tire themselves too much by following, as they would if the younger ones led. They also make a clamour, so that the birds are not separated too far from one another. If they sense that any one is tired, two others on either side lift her with their wings, or even carry her on their backs or feet; for in clear skies they are accustomed to stretch their feet backwards, and they know how to watch for favourable winds and to notice backwinds. They also have a leader, and those who cry out are stationed at the rear of the column, so that their voice can be heard. When they stop, the others sleep with their heads tucked under their wings, standing on alternate feet. The leader keeps watch with bare head, and whatever she senses she signals with her voice. When they have come down to the ground to feed, their leader raises her head high as a guard over them all, while the others feed in safety. The necks and heads of the birds are laid on the backs of those flying in front; and since the leader cannot do this, having no support to lean on, she flies back, so that she too may rest. Another from those following takes her place, and this alternation is observed by them throughout the whole journey.

units.la: ex sequentibus , eaque vicissitudo in omni cursu ab iis obseruatur. Custodes semper ac duces circumeunt, & fiue homo,fiue feraac- cedat, exclamant , altaq; voceinfidiasindi- cant, vt de fuga reliquz in tempore fibicon- fulant. Vigiles etiam constituunt, & decima quzq; excubias custodit. Quz noctu excu- bant in terra crurum alterutri corpore inni- tuntut , alteroq; adducto prehensum tenent lapillum. Quz in retinendo jugitas obrepe- re diutius somnum non finit , sed statim vt remisére,decidens calculus excitat, arguitq; negligentem. Igitur non est, curiftud Her- culis quisquam admiretur,quod ale subdens arcum hzrentem brachio, & dextra clauam regens manu quiesceret. Certum deniq; est pontum transuolaturas , primum omnium angustias petere inter duo promontoria Criumetopum & Carambin , mox saburra stabiliri,cum medium transierint, abiici la- pillos e pedibus , cum attigerint continen- tem & e gutture arenam. Lapidibus vero non omnes inter volandum, sed quzdam fe onerant , quzaliis leuiores sunt & velocio- res , ne reliquas celeritate volandi praueni- ant, & defesse posteriores aciem deferant. Lapides abeis proiici a nautis obseruatum est,in quorum aliquando naues inciderunt, quos ideo etiam ferunt , vt ex eorum casu percipiant supra mare ne an terram volent, fi enim ad mare lapides deferantur, iter su-fceptum facere pergunt, sin ad terram decidant, à volando requiescunt. Fessis aliquibus ad terram omnes descendunt, ut se invicem expectent.
units.tr: The sentinels and leaders always go about, and whether a man or a beast approaches, they cry out and announce the ambush with a loud voice, so that the rest may take counsel in time about flight. They also post watchmen, and every tenth bird keeps guard. Those that keep watch at night stand on the ground, resting the weight of the body on one leg, and they hold a pebble grasped in the other, drawn up. Since the pebble, while they hold it, does not let sleep creep over them for long, as soon as they relax, the falling pebble wakes them and convicts the negligent one. Therefore no one should be surprised that Hercules is said to have rested with his bow hanging on his arm and his club held in his right hand. Finally, it is certain that when they are about to fly over the sea, they first seek the narrow passage between the two headlands, Criumetopon and Carambis. Then they steady themselves with ballast: when they have passed the middle, they cast stones from their feet, and when they reach the mainland, sand from their throat. Not all of them take up stones during the flight, but some load themselves with them, since these are lighter and swifter, so that they do not outrun the rest in speed and so that the exhausted hindmost do not fall behind. Sailors have observed the stones being dropped by them, and sometimes ships have struck these stones; the birds carry them so that from the fall they may perceive whether they are flying over sea or land. For if the stones fall into the sea, they continue the journey they have undertaken, but if they fall on land, they rest from flying. When some are tired, all of them descend to the earth, so that they may wait for one another.

units.la: Hæc de volatu gruum, quæ licet ad pro-positum nostrum nihil faciant, utilem tamen commonefactionem ob oculos ponunt de societate & amicitia fideliter colenda, nec temere dirimenda. Rara avis in terris, mihi crede, est fidus amicus.
units.tr: These things about the flight of cranes, although they contribute nothing to our purpose, nevertheless set before our eyes a useful reminder that friendship must be faithfully cultivated and not rashly broken off. A faithful friend is a rare bird on earth, believe me.

units.la: De Cygnis.
units.tr: On Swans.

units.la: Inter epulas lautiorum quoq; spectantur oleres[?], & præcipue pulli, qui laudabilis succi sunt. Inassantur[?] autem et solidi apponuntur. Elixi insuaues[?] sunt. Temperamenti, quidam ajunt, eos esse cholerici, quibus non assentior, contrarium probante experientia. Corporis quippe amplitudo victusq; ratio naturam ipsorum satis indicant non absimilem ceteris palustribus alitibus. Degunt in aquis, Proceresq; ac Magnates eos alunt in aquis perennib. & riu-lis, qui domos arcesq; alluunt. Aquilam si pugnam coeperit, vincunt, nunquam enim nisi lacessiti dimicant. Socrates apud Platonem Apollini cygnos consecratos asserit, ob divinationem quandam, quâ providentes, quid in morte beni sit, cum cantu moriuntur. Cantant autem, ait Plato, non ex tristitia, sed potius laetitia, propterquante fato, quod immortales fe sentiant, & ad Apollinem, suum remigraturos. Itaq; allegorice cygnus anima boni viri comparari potest, qui latus mortem obit. Cælus tamen cygnum canentem, ait, paucissimos audiuisse, etiamsi vulgatior fama tenet, ingruente fatali momento. Et Ælianus l.1 biftor. varia, inquit, nunquam fe audiuisse cygnum canere, & fortasse neq; alium. Alexander Mindius apud Atheneum complures fe cygnos morientes secum affert, nec unquam eorum cantum audiuisse. Mea sententia est tunc canturos cygnos, cum graculi tacuerint.
units.tr: Among the feasts of the wealthier, even vegetables are served, and especially young chicks, which have a praiseworthy juice. They are also roasted whole and served. Boiled, they are unpleasant. Some say they are of a choleric temperament, but I do not agree, since experience proves the contrary. Indeed, the size of their bodies and their diet show that their nature is not unlike that of other marsh birds. They live in the water, and great men keep them in ever-flowing waters and streams that wash their houses and fortresses. If an eagle begins a fight, they overcome it, for they never fight unless provoked. Socrates in Plato asserts that swans are consecrated to Apollo, because of a certain prophetic power by which, foreseeing what is good in death, they die singing. They sing, says Plato, not from sadness but rather from joy, because they feel they are immortal and are about to return to Apollo, their god. So allegorically the swan can be compared to the soul of a good man, who dies cheerfully. Caelius, however, says that very few have heard a swan singing, although the more common report holds that it sings when its fatal hour is approaching. And Aelian, in the first book of his Varia Historia, says that he never heard a swan sing, and perhaps no one else did either. Alexander Myndius, in Athenaeus, says that many dying swans were brought to him, and that he never heard their song. My opinion is that the swans will sing when the jackdaws have fallen silent.

units.la: De Ciconia.
units.tr: On the Stork.

units.la: Augusti principatu gruibus in cibis ci-conias prælatas Cornelius Nepos auctor est, postea vero nemo attigisse voluit: unde inventorum auctoritatem pre-tiofiores res facere dubium non est, ideoque Si quis nunc mergos fuanes edixerit aßos, Parebit pravi docilis Romana juventus.
units.tr: In the reign of Augustus, Cornelius Nepos reports, storks were served at the tables of the great, but afterwards no one wished to touch them. There is no doubt that the authority of the inventors made the dishes more prized, and so the verse: If anyone should now decree that the storks be eaten, the docile Roman youth would obey the depraved order.

units.la: Hodie magnatum mensæ nullum iis honorem tribuunt, cum tamen carnes ipsarum oculis lippientibus venenifq; aduersari inex-perimentis fit, tum etiam comitiales adjuua-re. Verum de ciconiarum esu pluribus à me supra est annotatum, vt & in tractatu meo de peste. Cæterum admiranda naturæ do-tes, vt ingenium, prudentia, justitia, & gratitudo in hoc alite historiarum monumentis celebrantur. Magna cura exacta ætate pa-rentes alunt, etsi humanis hoc facere legi-bus nullis iubeantur, sed sola naturæ boni-tate ad id impelluntur. Quantum enim curę in sobolis curam & educationem conferunt, tantum senio cofectis rependitur, quod vere ἀντιπελαργὴν [?] est, hoc est, mutuum benefi-cium & gratitudinem iis, àquibus vel enu-tritus, vel institutus fueris, exhibere. Vnde ab Aristophane νόμῳ πελαργικὸς dicitur, quā liberi parentes alere iubentur. Æliani historiam de ciconiarum gratitudine, & Oppiani in Ixeuticis Paraphraftes sic expressit. Mirabilis omnino & folertis ingenii ciconiæ sunt, sive iniuria causa, sive gratitudinis aliquod edendum signum fuerit. Nam & hoc accidisse fertur. Cum quidam ciconiæ crus lapide confregisset, eaque, in nidum, vt poterat, se reciperet, à mulierib. quæ claudicantem videbant, restituta est, & cum ceteris aduolauit. Sequenti deinde anni vere cum ad eundem locum rediisset (agnoscebatur autè ex claudicationis signo) & mulieres conspectu fui, ceu quæ libenter apud ipsas diuerteret, exhilarasset, mox è rostro oblongo egregiam & pretiosam gemmam ad pedes mulierum evomuit, quod quidem illæ gratitudinis ergo fieri intellexerunt.
units.tr: Today the tables of the great pay no such honour to storks. Yet their flesh is said to be harmful to inflamed eyes and poisonous, though it is said by experience to help epileptics. I have already noted more about eating storks above, and also in my treatise on the plague. Meanwhile, the admirable gifts of nature are celebrated in the records of history in this bird: its intelligence, prudence, justice and gratitude. Storks feed their parents with great care when they grow old. Although they are not commanded by any human laws to do this, they are driven to it by the goodness of nature alone. For as much care and upbringing as they give to their offspring, so much is repaid to them in old age. This is truly antiperargē [ἀντιπελαργὴν], that is, a mutual kindness and gratitude, to be shown to those by whom you were either nourished or instructed. Hence Aristophanes calls the law by which children are ordered to feed their parents nomos pelargikos [νόμῳ πελαργικὸς]. Aelian and the paraphrast of Oppian's Halieutica set out the story of the storks' gratitude in these words: "Storks are truly wonderful, of a clever nature, whether they act from a cause of injury or whether they show some sign of gratitude. For this too is said to have happened. When a certain stork had broken its leg with a stone, it withdrew to its nest as best it could. Women who saw it limping restored it, and it flew away with the others. Then in the spring of the following year it returned to the same place (it was recognised by the sign of its limp), and it gladdened the women at whose sight it came, as one that gladly lodged with them. Soon it dropped from its long beak a splendid and precious gem at the feet of the women, which they understood to be done out of gratitude."

units.la: Huic plane similis historia est, quam Juftinus Goblerus J. C. abavis & majoribus suis sæpe commemoratam scripsit fe audi-uifle, contigisse videl. non procul ab ipsius patria (Sanctogoarinum appellant) in civi-tate quondam imperii libera Wefalia fupe-riore, vt civiconia nidum in cujufdam ciuis tecto haberet, in quo per multos annos ova ex more excluderet, & pullos nutricaret. Tanto autem tempore eadem avis benigni hospitis clementiam experta, vt, quæ à ne-mine domesticorum, (pio patrefamiliâs ita cavente) infestaretur, quotannis suo tempo-reauolare & redire, eundemq; nidum repe-tere folebat. Habuit autem in more præter cæteras fui generis aues hæc bestia, hospitis frugi modestia & humanitate ducta, fiue có-moditate loci ædiumq;, fiue, quod verifimi-lius est, naturâ ad hoc ipsum irritante, vt bis, nimirum sub veris & autumni tempus pri-die feré antequam auolaret, &postridie cum rediret, circum limen ac porticum dom° ho-fpitis fui volitaret, & ftriderti rostro fe præ-fenté velut indicaret, femp lætabundo acceu-applaudente gestu voceq; à patrefamilias ac-ceptaac rursus dimissa. Hæc cŭ jâ multis an-nis inter auè & hospité consuetudo fuisset, tâ-dé aliquando ex more sub autumnû auolatu-ra ante ad porticum dom° obstrepo imperu fert, ac crepitanti rostro, ceu hospiti valedi-&ura insolentius aliquâto gestire vila est, cui benè precatus herus amico ore avem quasi alloquens, iubet ut salua & incolumis redeat. Sub verigitur postmodum reuersa ex more hospitem in foribus ædium rostri crepitu sa-lutat, ac mox ante pedes viri, radicem magnâ recentis zinziberis è gutture exerens tanquâ gratulabunda collocat, rostro ut plurimum obstrepero, in symbolum hospitalitatis. Ad-miratus hospes, peregrinum & informe quodammodo munus accipit, vicinisque vi-dendum præbet, certo cognoscentibus gu-stando veram ac viridem zinziberis esse radi-cem. Et quandoquidem hactenus apud multos fuit dubium, & quodammodo in-compertum, (inter quos etiam Plinius est) quoniam è loco veniant, aut quo se referant ciconiæ, vel ex hoc facto constabit, calidas eas terras & ultramarinas, vbi zinziber ho-die nasci dicitur, cum à nobis auolant, pete-re. Verum & hoc exemplo qualicunque, si non aliud, certè admoneri nos arbitrarer, inter homines cum pietatem, tum hospitali-tatem plurimi fieri oportere. Extat & aliud luculentum super ciconiarum mirifica grati-tudine exemplum in Ixeuticis oppiani. In Italia, inquit, vt fertur, cum serpens quidam ad nidum prorepens ciconiarum pullos de-uorasset, & alteram deinde sequentis anni fe-tuam similiter perdidisset, ciconiae tertio de-mum anno reuersæ, nouam quandam auem
units.tr: A story quite similar to this is one that Justinus Goblerus, a doctor of law, wrote that he had often heard recounted by his forefathers and elders. It happened not far from his homeland (they call it Sanctogoarinum), in a city once a free imperial city of Upper Westphalia, that a stork had its nest on the roof of a certain citizen's house. For many years it hatched its eggs there, as is customary, and reared its young. The bird, having experienced the kindness of a generous host over so long a time, was not harmed by anyone in the household, for the good householder took care of this. Each year it used to fly away and return at its proper time and seek out the same nest. This bird, moved by the modest thrift and kindness of its host, had a custom beyond the other birds of its kind. Whether because of the convenience of the place and the buildings, or, what is more likely, because nature itself prompted it to this, it would twice a year, namely at the time of spring and autumn, fly about the threshold and portico of its host's house on the day before it departed and again on the day after it returned, clattering its beak in his presence, as if to announce itself. Always it showed joy, with a gesture like applause, and was received by the householder and then let go again. When this custom had gone on between the bird and the host for many years, it happened one autumn, as it was about to fly away as usual, that it made a noise at the portico of the house and seemed to show more than usual excitement, clattering its beak as if bidding farewell to its host. The master, who had blessed it kindly, spoke to the bird as if to a friend and bade it return safe and sound. In the spring it came back, as was its custom, and greeted the host at the door with a clatter of its beak. Soon, as if rejoicing, it set down before the man's feet a large root of fresh ginger, pulled from its throat, clattering its beak for the most part, as a symbol of hospitality.
