The host, amazed, received this foreign and somewhat shapeless gift and showed it to his neighbours, who, by tasting it, knew for certain that it was a true and fresh root of ginger. And since until now it has been doubtful to many, and in some way unknown (among them Pliny), where storks come from or where they go, this deed will confirm that they fly away from us to those hot and overseas lands where ginger is said to grow today. Yet this example, of whatever kind, if nothing else, ought surely to remind us that among men both piety and hospitality should be cultivated greatly. There is also another splendid example of the wonderful gratitude of storks in the Halieutica of Oppian. "In Italy," he says, "as it is reported, when a certain serpent crept up to a stork's nest and devoured the young, and then in the following year likewise destroyed the next brood, the storks, returning in the third year,

units.la: & prius non visam, (quæ breuior quidem ci- coniis erat, sed rostrum magnum & acutum, instar ensisè capite exerebat)secum adduxe- re, indicatá nimirum ei fœtus fui calamitate, vt opem ferret inuitatam, fiue pollicitationi- bus vllis fiue verbis. Nam vtrum aues & animantesalię, suum inter se colloquium nobis ignotum misceant, in dubium vocari potest. Auis hæc nondum absoluto cico- niarum fœtu, coniunćta eis non erat, pullis verò iam exclusis, cum parentes ad compa- randum pullis auiq; custodi victum longius auolarent, ipsa nidum non deferunt, vt ser- penti obsisteret. Serpens igitur paulò post progressusè latibulo, pullosaggreditur, & licet ab aue custode rostro impeteretur, non tamen statim recessit, sed erectus corpore, caudæque innitens se opposuit, & secundò iam ictus spiris inuoluere custodem frustra molitus est, vtcunq; pluribus se flexibus infi- nuaret, nam facilè euasit auis in sublime se recipiens, sic dum ille perdere, hæc seruare pullos annituntur, pluribus tandem ille vul- neribus consossus iacuit, at non impunè, a- uem enim in conflićtu dentibus venenatis adeò læsit, vt omnes ei pennæ defluerent. Cum verò reuertendi tempus appetisset ac reliquæ ciconiæ iam auolassent, parentes sum pullis feruatis, vt beneficii se memores declararent, tandem sper mansére, donec nouis ei pennis renatis simul auolarent. Hæc Opianus.
units.tr: brought with them a new bird never seen before, somewhat smaller than storks but with a large and sharp beak that stood out from its head like a sword. They had evidently told it of the calamity to their offspring, so that it would bring help, invited by no promises or words. Whether birds and other animals share a conversation among themselves unknown to us can be called in doubt. This bird, while the storks' brood was not yet fully grown, was not joined to them; but once the young had hatched, when the parents flew farther away to find food for the chicks and for the guardian bird, the guardian did not leave the nest, so as to stand against the serpent. Then the serpent, having crept out a little later from its hiding place, attacked the young. Although the guardian bird struck at it with its beak, the serpent did not at once withdraw, but raised its body, leaning on its tail, and resisted. Struck a second time, it tried in vain to coil its rings around the guardian; though it twisted itself in many folds, the bird easily escaped by lifting itself into the air. So while the one tried to destroy and the other tried to save the young, the serpent at last lay down, worn out by many wounds, but not without harm to itself, for in the struggle it wounded the bird with its poisonous teeth, so that all its feathers fell out. When the time for returning had come and the other storks had already flown back, the parents, with their young saved, remained in that place, so as to show themselves mindful of the kindness, until the guardian bird, with its feathers renewed, could fly away together with them." Thus Oppian.

units.la: Riuali quoque inuidia laborare ciconias Ælianus testatur. Nam cum in Cranone Thessaliæ eximia forma mulier, cui nomen Alcinoe, à coniuge peregrè profecto domi relicta stupri consuetudine fecisset, hoc quidem ipsum ciconia intelligens, seruiles iniu-rias in Dominum non sustinuit, quo minus mox facto impetu eum oculorum sensu or-bans, iniuriam in Dominum illatam vlcisce-retur. Sed hæc virtus potius castitatis quam ritualis inuidia in hac aue appellanda. Nam, vt autor libri de natura rerum scribit, non dubium est ciconias castitatis sectatrices esse, fœdusq; coniugii inuice seruare. Fertur enim quod in eminentiori loco domus cuiusdam par ciconiarū habitarit: vnde mare ad pastum recedente, frequenter alius mas adueniens fœminam adulterina coniunctione pollue-bat. At illa statim eminus in fonte se merge-bat, sic scelus adulterii per aquæ lauacru de-lens, marem proprium deludebat. Huiusmodi factum dominus habitationis frequenter aduertit, & quodam post adulterium die eam à fonte, ne lauaretur, prohibuit: nec mora masculus è pastu rediens in fœmina sua sce-lus adulterii deprehendit, & in præsentia dis-simulans abiit. Reuersusque secunda die maximam multitudinem secum adduxit, quæ singulæ adulteram aggressæ miseram crudeli morte dilaniarunt. Auentinus id factum esse scripsit sub duce Bauariæ Hum- berto , in pago quodam Bauarico nomine Thengen/in quo frequentia fuerint adulte- ria : additque hanc ciconiam adulteram coa- &tam fuisse solam educare & pascere pullos exclusos , mare opetam ipsi suam negante, hunc vero sub illud tempus, quo à nobis in alias migrare terras ciconiæ solent , venisse comitatum agmine ciconiarum , à quibus adultera confixa & dicerpta fit.
units.tr: Storks, Aelian tells us, also suffer from the jealousy of a rival. At Cranon in Thessaly there was a woman of outstanding beauty, named Alcinoe, who, when her husband had gone abroad and she was left at home, gave herself to the habit of adultery. A stork noticed this and would not put up with the wrong done to its master by such a servile act. Soon it attacked the adulteress and blinded her, avenging the injury done to its master. This quality, however, should be called chastity rather than rivalrous jealousy in this bird. For, as the author of the book On the Nature of Things writes, there is no doubt that storks pursue chastity and keep the marriage bond in return. It is said that a pair of storks lived on a high place in a certain house. When the male had flown off to feed, another male often came and polluted the female with an adulterous union. She, however, would at once plunge into a spring at a distance and, by washing away the stain of adultery in the water, deceive her own mate. The owner of the house often noticed this happening, and on a certain day after an adultery he forbade her to go to the spring to wash. The male returned from feeding without delay and caught his mate in the crime of adultery; but he dissembled in front of her and went away. On the second day he came back with a great crowd of storks, and they attacked the adulteress one by one and tore the wretched bird apart with a cruel death. Aventinus wrote that this happened under Humbert, duke of Bavaria, in a certain Bavarian district called Thengen, where adulteries were frequent. He adds that this adulterous stork was left alone to hatch and feed its chicks, since the male refused to mate with her; and that at the time when storks usually migrate from us to other lands, this male came back with a troop of storks, by whom the adulteress was pierced and torn to pieces.

units.la: Ad extremum honos ciconiis in Thessa- lia tantus,vt capitale sit occidisse, eademque legibus pœna,quæ in homicidam, teste Plin. lib.10.cap.23. In ea namque regione tan- tàm aiunt serpentum prouenire vim, vt,nisi à ciconiis conficerentur , incolas pellerent.
units.tr: Finally, storks are held in such honour in Thessaly that killing one is a capital offence, and the penalty is the same as for killing a man, as Pliny attests (book 10, chapter 23). For they say that in that region there is such a swarm of serpents that, unless storks destroyed them, they would drive the inhabitants out.

units.la: Præsensionum quoque quandam vim inesse ciconiis testatur Alexander ab Alexandria, Annoenimà Christi natiuitate 454.cum At- tila Aquileiam obsideret, ciconias animad- uertit , quæ in turribus ciuitatis nidificaue- rant,vno impetu ex vrbe migrare,atque suos fœtus exportare, vnde milites hoc auspicio exhortatus tanquam vrbem interitui proxi- mam ciconiæ deferrent, vrbem cepit. Pru- dentia denique ciconiarum ex eo apparet, quod ante abitum vno in loco cögregentur, consilia quasi publica de abitione ineuntes & commurmurâtes, tum verò maximè, quod abiturę aquilonis secundum flatum prudenter expectent, in calidas & meridionales terras se recipientes, ex his enim illas ad nos redire multorum non incerta persuadet opinio. Hæc de ciconiis.
units.tr: Alexander of Alexandria also testifies that storks have some power of foreboding. In the year 454 after the birth of Christ, when Attila was besieging Aquileia, he noticed storks which had nested in the city's towers leave the city all at once and carry off their young. Encouraged by this omen, he urged the soldiers to attack, as if the storks were bringing the news that the city was close to ruin, and so he took the city. Finally, the prudence of storks is shown by the fact that before they depart they gather in one place, holding, as it were, public deliberations about their departure and murmuring together. Above all, they wisely wait for the north wind to blow in their favour before leaving, and then they retreat to warm and southern lands. Many people hold, not without reason, the firm opinion that they return to us from there. So much for storks. ## On the heron.

units.la: De ardea.

Ardeam quasi arduam, quod alte volet, dictam[?] putant. Circa aquas & in aquis vistum quærit. Quæ coloris cinerei est, in maximo apud gentes quasdam nunc honore est, non ob cibos tantum, sed ob voluptatem, quam Magnates hodie in venatu eius per falcones, qui ad eius capturam mansuefiunt &, cicurantur, impetuoso volatu eam prosternentes capiunt, quo quidem in Magnatum aulis nihil admirabilius ferè iucundius, cernitur. Hieme autem potissimum potentiorum subit mensas, vere enim astateq; fœtificat, quo tempore pulli magis expetuntur. Pestore vero tantum placere in cibatu gulæ norunt artifices. Porro splendabilis & plane nobilis est ardearum cum accipitribus dimicatio, quibus podicem chuertentes pennas earum conspurcant, quæ postea compu-trefcunt. Optimum augurium aiunt esse, cum ad austrum volant vel Septentrionem, solui enim periculâ & metus. Plinius l. ii. cap. 37. In mediis arenis tristes futuram tempestatem sentire atque prasagire[?] animadwersum est, quod tamen delencis[?] seu albis intelligendum Plinium vult.
units.tr: They think the heron (ardea) is so called as if it were "arduea," because it flies high. It seeks its food around and in the waters. Its colour is ash-grey. Among certain peoples it is now held in the highest honour, not only for its food but for the pleasure that the magnates today take in hunting it with falcons. These are tamed and trained for its capture, and by swooping in headlong flight they strike it down and seize it. Indeed, nothing is more admirable or pleasing to watch in the courts of the magnates. In winter especially it comes to the tables of the powerful, for it breeds in spring and summer, and at that time the young are more sought after. Cooks know how to please the palate with the breast alone. Moreover, the fight of herons with hawks is a splendid and truly noble spectacle, in which the herons foul their feathers by turning their rear toward the hawks, and these feathers afterwards rot. They say it is the best omen when herons fly toward the south or the north wind, for then dangers and fears are dispelled. Pliny, book 2, chapter 37: it has been observed that herons, sitting sadly in the middle of sandy places, sense and foretell a coming storm; Pliny wants this, however, to be understood of the white ones.

units.la: Submonitio de aquaticis alitibus.
units.tr: Preliminary note on water birds.

units.la: Tractus[?] Oceano vicinos aquaticarum avium omni genere abundare cóstat, quarum captura hibernis praecipue mensibus fit ingens. Veré enim appetente abeunt gregatim, cateruatimq; volant;capi-unturq; in pratibus retibus protentis: earum autem quaedam in cibis ob carnium suauitatem magnam obtinuerunt auctoritatem, quaedam etiam rariores sunt, ideoq; pretio-fiores epulisq; commendabiliores.
units.tr: It is well known that water birds of every kind abound in the regions near the Ocean, and their capture is very great, especially in the winter months. For when spring approaches they depart in flocks and fly in droves, and they are caught in the meadows with nets spread out. Some of them have won great authority as food because of the great sweetness of their flesh, while others are rarer, and therefore more costly and more recommended for banquets.

units.la: Hoc obferuatu hicdignum, omnium a-quaticarum carnes pro corporis magnitudi-ne duras esse, concoctionisq; sua natura diffi-cilis, ac excrementis abundantes: quasdam etiam algae odorem, limiq; ac piscium subo-lere, unde stomacho nausea fastidium profertur, quasdam sapore suaui abblandiri, quarumq; assiduo usu graues sensim accersuntur morbi. Itaq; vt concoctu euadant facilio-res, ventriculoq; minus noxae inferant, tene-ritudiné eas adipisci oportet, postmodum culinis cómendentur & coquis. Videlocum de gruibus, vbi hæc fusius explicantur. Assis deniq;, cuiuscunq; generis etiā sint inter aquaticas, bonitate ac suauitate elixis salubriores esse, longo experimento cóprobatū habet.
units.tr: It is worth noting here that the flesh of all water birds is tough for its bulk, difficult to digest by its very nature, and full of waste matter. Some smell of seaweed, mud and fish, so that they cause nausea and disgust in the stomach; others flatter the palate with a pleasant taste, but frequent eating of them gradually brings on serious illnesses. Therefore, to make them easier to digest and less harmful to the stomach, they should be made tender before being seasoned and cooked by the cooks. See the place about cranes, where these matters are explained at greater length. Finally, it has been established by long experience that, of whatever kind they are among the water birds, roasted birds are healthier than boiled ones in respect of goodness and flavour.

units.la: De cuculo.
units.tr: De cuculo.

units.la: Avium, quae in humanos usus & cibos ad-mittuntur, agmen claudet cuculus, cuius carnes omnium esse suavissimas, gravissimus Philosophus, locupletissima, velut alterum copiae cornu, veterum autorum bibliotheca, Plinius lib.10 cap.9. prodidit. Nec mirum, quod in alienis pariat nidis, maxime palumbium, alauda & curruca atque etiam lute-la[?]; singula quoque ponat ova, bona rarò quod nulla alia avis; pullus item eius subdatur & educetur, avidumque, is ex natura cibos reliquis pullis praripiat, indeque pinguescat, nitidumque nutricem in se convertat ac devoret, ut nullam ita avium suavitate carnes comparari cum cuculi carne posse verisimile sit quidem, dubium tamen, an nutriendi vi succique probitate cum aliis sit aequiparanda. Ego quod hic statuam, non habeo, nec scio, gula proceribus experimentum relinquo. De pullis cuculi, minus certi aliquid licet affirmare, quos Aristoteles ait, neminem vidisse, nam in lib.6.& 9.histor. cuculum non facere nidum constantem asserit. Et hac de cuculo. Hactenus de alimentis quae veniunt à volucribus, seu volatilibus, sequuntur hu-mi gradientia.
units.tr: The cuckoo closes the list of birds that are admitted to human use and food. The most weighty philosopher, Pliny (Book 10, chapter 9), has stated that its flesh is of all the most delicious, and it is, as it were, a second horn of plenty, a most abundant storehouse of the ancient authors. It is no wonder that it lays its eggs in other birds' nests, especially those of the wood pigeon, the lark and the whitethroat, and even of the [?]; it lays a single egg each time, and only rarely a good one, which no other bird does. Likewise its chick is placed under another bird and reared; by its nature it snatches the food from the other chicks, and so grows fat, and draws to itself and devours the foster-mother's attention. It is indeed probable that no flesh can be compared with the flesh of the cuckoo in sweetness of taste, as with that of no other bird, but it is doubtful whether it is to be equated with others in the nourishing power and purity of its juices. What I should decide on this point I do not have, nor do I know; I leave the experiment to the gourmands. Concerning the chicks of the cuckoo one may affirm something less certain, since Aristotle says that no one has seen them, for in Books 6 and 9 of his History of Animals he asserts that the cuckoo makes no constant nest. And so much on the cuckoo. Thus far on the foods which come from birds, or flying creatures; there follow those that walk on the ground.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: De alimentis, quae veniunt ab animalibus humi gradientibus.
units.tr: On foods that come from animals that walk on the ground.

units.la: Vmi gradientia vel ambulant, ut bo- mo, & quadrupes vel reptant, ut re- ptilia.
units.tr: Animals that move on the ground either walk, like man and the quadrupeds, or crawl, like the reptiles.

units.la: De carne humana.
units.tr: On human flesh.

units.la: Cytharum multa genera esse, qui corporibus humanis vescerentur, olim fuisse, & esse nostro seculo in nova India Cannibalos vocatos, historiarum monumentis proditum legimus. Quin & in remediis ac deliciis summis quidam habuerunt, viscera ossaq; humana vorare, in epulis praesertim funebribus & parentalibus.
units.tr: We read in the monuments of history that there were once many races of people who fed on human bodies, and that in our own age in the New World there are people called Cannibals. Indeed, some even counted human entrails and bones among their greatest delicacies and remedies, especially at funeral and memorial feasts.

units.la: Effedones Scythiæ populi parentum[que] & ferina rum funera cantibus laeti prosequi fuerunt parenta- soliti, conuocatisque propinquorum caeti- lia. bus, cadauera ipsa dentibus laniârunt, pecorumque visceribus mixta, conuiuiis inter epulas apposuerunt: cranio autem poculi loco fant vsi, quod & auro circum ornârunt, teste Solino cap. 20.
units.tr: The Essedones, a people of Scythia, used to accompany the funerals of their parents and of wild beasts with joyful songs. When their relatives had been gathered, they tore the corpses apart with their teeth, mixed the flesh with the meat of cattle, and served it at the feast among the courses. They also drank from the skull, which they even decorated with gold, as Solinus reports in chapter 20.

units.la: De Padæis Indica gente, scribit Herodotus, ægrotantes eos interimere, ac epulari, mulieresque mulieribus idem officii praestare,
units.tr: Herodotus writes of the Padaei, an Indian people, that they kill their sick and feast on them, and that the women perform the same service for the women,

units.la: Solino cap. 20. re,etiamsi se negent ægrotare, qua de causa, inquit, pauci apud eos ad senectutem peruenire dicuntur, etsi perueniant, mactati itidē comeduntur. Sic Mallagethæ quoque Scythiæ gens, eos miserrimos ac infelicissimos putabant, qui infirmitate ac morbo decumbentes morerentur, talesque feris bestiisque devorandos proiiciebant. Vnde cum parentes ac propinqui in senium vergerent, iugulabant, eosque in frusta concisos, & ouiū pecudumque carne permixtos in mensa appositos absumebat, sarius rati à se illos, quam à vermibus consumi. Herodot. l. 1.
units.tr: as Solinus reports in chapter 20, even if the sick deny that they are ill. For this reason, he says, few among them are said to reach old age, and even those who do reach it are slaughtered and likewise eaten. Likewise the Massagetae, a Scythian nation, thought those most wretched and unfortunate who died lying sick of infirmity or disease; they threw such people to be devoured by wild beasts. Hence, when parents and relatives grew old, they slaughtered them, cut them into pieces, mixed them with the flesh of sheep and cattle, and served them at table, thinking it better to be consumed by themselves than by worms. Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: Idem Ponticis quoque gentibus ascribit Tertullianus in libris aduersus Marcionem. Parentum, inquit, cadauera cum pecudibus cæsa conuiuio conuorant, qui non ita decesserat, vt escatilis esset, maledicta mors existimabatur.
units.tr: Tertullian in his books against Marcion ascribes the same custom to the peoples of Pontus. He says that they devour at their feasts the corpses of their parents, slaughtered together with cattle; a death that did not come in such a way as to furnish food was thought accursed.

units.la: Indorum, ac eorum inprimis qui Calati nominantur, parentes suos, priusquam annis aut morbo aliquo in maciem Seniumq; abirent, velut Deorum hostias mactare, cæsorumque visceribus epulari mos fuit, idque maxime pium iudicabant. Quare Darius accitos, qui in sua ditione erant, græcos, percontatus est, quanta pecunia vellent defunctis parentibus vesci. Illis negantibus, vlla se pecunia hoc esse facturos, Darius deinde græcis præsentibus, & quæ dicebantur per[?] interpretem discentibus, interrogauit illos Indos, quantum accipere pecuniarum vel-lent, vt patres defunctos comburerent, Indi vehementer reclamantes, meliora illum omi-nari iubebant, vnde Herodotus horum o-mnium testis addit, rectè Pindarum dixisse, morem omnium esse regem.
units.tr: Among the Indians, and especially among those called Calatians, it was the custom to slaughter their parents, as if they were sacrificial victims to the gods, before they wasted away with years or some disease into frailty and old age, and to feast on their flesh. They thought this most pious. So Darius, having summoned the Greeks who were under his rule, asked them how much money they would want to eat their dead parents. When they refused, saying that no sum of money would induce them to do this, Darius then, with the Greeks present and learning through an interpreter what was being said, asked those Indians how much money they would want in order to burn their dead fathers. The Indians strongly protested and bade him speak better omens. Whence Herodotus, a witness to all these things, adds that Pindar had rightly said that custom is king of all.

units.la: Derbices similiter gens Scythica, Hircanis proximi, eos qui sexagesimum annum iam excessissent, iugulabant, & in conuiuis appo-sitos, necessarios & propinquos adepulas conuocabant, abstinebant verò vetularum carnibus, vt virosis, eas enim tantum praefo-catas condebant. Atqui si anteid tempori spatium fato aliquis cessisset, non esse, sed tet-racondere folebant. Atq; hæc de antiquis illis antropophagis, ferissimisq; ac immanissimis eorundem epulis, in quibus potiora fer-cula demortuorum fuerunt carnes.
units.tr: Similarly, the Derbices, a Scythian people near the Hyrcanians, killed those who had already passed their sixtieth year, and they summoned their necessary kin and relatives to the feast, serving the flesh at the table. But they abstained from the flesh of old women, as being unwholesome; these they merely strangled and buried. Yet if anyone had yielded to fate before that time, they were not eaten but buried. These things are said of those ancient man-eaters, and of their savage and most inhumane feasts, in which the choicest dishes were the flesh of the dead.

units.la: His persimiles sunt Americenses, aliique nostri sui anthropophagi, qui hostiū fuorū, quos præsertim in bello ceperunt, per dies aliquot prius bene saginatorum cadauera sa-fata, ceu suavissimas delicias magna cum la-scivia, lasciuia, atque triuudiis deuorare con-sueruntprodente Joh. Leryensi Gallo o-culato teste, in sua illa navigationis historia, gallico sermone in lucem edita. Verum seii-num illum morem anthropophagis istis re-linquamus, ac Christiano homine indignum existimemus hominis viscera persequi, quae aspicere horret animus, quanto magis mandere. In confesso quidem est, etiam à Christianis cadavera hominum in morborum & vulnerū auxilia adhiberi, mumiam appellant: ipsumq; sanguinem humanum destillatum & praeparatum comitiali morbo vexatis propinari, verum ex homine ipso illum adhuc calidum, & quidem vena secta sorbere, vt quidam literis prodiderunt, horror est. Galenus alias carnes humanas gustatu dulces, parumq; à bubula differre, à quibusdam, qui eatum periculum fecerant, se accepisse tradit.
units.tr: Like these are the Americans and other man-eaters of our own time, who, having captured their enemies, especially in war, used to fatten them for some days beforehand and then devour the slaughtered bodies with great lust and triumph, as if they were the sweetest delicacies. Jean de Léry, the one-eyed Frenchman, is the witness who reports this in his history of that voyage, published in French. But let us leave that savage custom to the man-eaters, and let us judge it unworthy of a Christian man to pursue human entrails, which the mind shudders even to look at, much less to chew. It is certainly well known that even Christians use human corpses as remedies for wounds and diseases, which they call mummy; and that human blood, distilled and prepared, is given to those afflicted with epilepsy. But to drink it straight from the man himself, still warm, and indeed by opening a vein, as some have written, is horrifying. Galen reports that he had heard from certain people, who had made trial of it, that human flesh, otherwise, is sweet to the taste and differs little from beef.

units.la: Etapud Graecos fuerunt, qui scrupulosè hominis viscera sunt persecuti, eorumque sapores. Nos anthropophagis valere iussis, ad cibos, qui ex quadrupedibus homini veniunt, progrediemur.
units.tr: Among the Greeks, too, there were those who examined human entrails and their flavours with scrupulous care. Having bidden farewell to the man-eaters, we shall proceed to the foods that come to humans from the quadrupeds.

units.la: De alimentis ex quadrupedibus.
units.tr: On foods from quadrupeds.

units.la: ORdinem vitae materiaq; tractanda sequendo vt nullum praetermittatur naturae & artis munus, commodum nunc est differere de cibariis, quae sumuntur ex quadrupedibus, cumprimis vero pecoribus. Experimento enim compertum est, ac quotidianus vsus id comprobat, mitiores longe salubriores que esca praebere mortalibus animantia, quam olera, arborum poma, aut glandes. Vnde non pauci etiam rerum naturae callentissimi certe commentarii in lucem emissi docuerunt explicarunt, quam multipliciter hominibus pecora praestent alimenta, quamquam eleganter tum lautiorum tum rusticorum mensas instruant, exornent, ac opulentent. Prima quidem illa ac innocens vita et asq; carnis inprimis desidia-ria damnauit, pecora agricultura tantum nasci existimans, idcoq; tam capitale erat bouem occidi, quàm ciuem, primumq; morem alimenti hominum gratia pecudes interimendi à vitiis placationibus Deorum, quae ex iis laudatiffima erant, emanasse quidam statuunt, ficq; ad posteros transfiuffe.
units.tr: Following the order of the life and the matter to be treated, so that no gift of nature or of art is passed over, it is now fitting to discuss the foods that are taken from quadrupeds, especially from cattle. For experience has shown, and daily use confirms, that the animals, being much milder and more wholesome, provide food for mortals better than vegetables, tree fruits, or acorns. Hence not a few writers, very learned in the nature of things, have published works explaining and demonstrating in how many ways cattle furnish nourishment for humans, and how elegantly they furnish, adorn, and enrich the tables of both the wealthy and the rustic. That first and innocent life indeed condemned the eating of flesh, especially as a luxury, since they thought cattle were born only for farming, and therefore killing an ox was as serious a crime as killing a citizen. Some hold that the first custom of killing animals for human food arose from the sacrifices to the gods, which were most praised among them, and so passed down to posterity.

units.la: Caeterum ex quadrupedibus animalibus in ci-bus veniunt, menfiq; adhiberi possunt, leo, elephantus, panthera, vrsus, camelus, equus, asinus, canis, feles, mustela, mus, mele, fcirus, erinaceus, vulpes, cuniculus, lepus, cervus, bircus, capra, pecus, ouilli, bubulus, suillus. Quae vero ex hominis natura et temperatura magis sint familiaria ac amica, vel longius ab ea, vitaq; humaniore discedant, suo dicetur loco, ad quem le-gatorem remitto. Hoc ἐν παραπόδῳ[?] hic, et obiter addo, esse gentem aliquam quae lupinis vescerit[?], adhuc me legisse vel audiisse non memi-nisse.
units.tr: Moreover, the following quadrupeds come to us as foods and can be brought to the table: lion, elephant, panther, bear, camel, horse, donkey, dog, cat, weasel, mouse, badger, hedgehog, squirrel, fox, rabbit, hare, stag, buck, goat, sheep, ram, ox, and pig. Which of these are more familiar and friendly to human nature and temperament, or which depart further from it and from a more humane way of life, will be said in its own place, to which I refer the reader. I add here, by the way [ἐν παραπόδῳ], that there is some people who feed on lupins; I do not remember having read or heard of this before.

units.la: De carne generatim, notatu digna.
units.tr: On meat in general, worthy of note.

units.la: CArnes, inquit Aristoteles, & quicquid iis, simile est, in genere sanguineo sunt, cui astipulatur Galenus 2. de tem-per. per. Carnis abundantiam, dicens, à sanguinis copia nasci, ubi mediocri corporis habitu præditos eusarcos nominat, ut quibus humidum non abundat. Idem in fine lib. 1. carnem dicit multi sanguinis esse & calidum, ut ita caliditatem humiditatemq; quam continet, à sanguine acceperit, aq; boni sanguinis copia corpulentiam augeri in confesso sit. Unde pro confesso etiam & confirmato tenendum, carnem fere talem esse, qualis sanguis, ex quo tota constat, colorem etiam à sanguinis bonitate, cuius index est, dependere. Cæterum, plus alimenti inesse carnibus quam in ullo cibo alio, ob affinitatem scilicet quam habent cum natura nostra, copiosum etiam, quod suppeditant, nutrimentum, & sanguinem, præsertim si sint animantium boni succi, nemo est qui non norit. Verum differentias carnis in re alimentaria corporis salubritatem desideranti ad unguem explo-ratas habere utilissimum erit.
units.tr: "Flesh," says Aristotle, "and whatever resembles it, belongs to the sanguine kind," and Galen agrees in book 2 of De temperamentis. He says that an abundance of flesh arises from an abundance of blood, and he calls those of moderate bodily habit eusarcous, since moisture does not abound in them. At the end of book 1, the same author says that flesh is rich in blood and warm, so that it takes its warmth and moisture from the blood. It is generally agreed that bulk of body increases with a good supply of blood. Hence it must be held as established that flesh is for the most part of the same kind as the blood from which the whole body is made, and that its colour too depends on the goodness of the blood, of which it is the sign. Moreover, everyone knows that flesh contains more nourishment than any other food, because of its affinity with our nature, and that it supplies abundant nutriment and blood, especially when the animals are of good juice. But for anyone who wishes to preserve bodily health, it will be most useful to have examined carefully the differences between flesh and flesh as food.

units.la: Ab animalium enim ætate, à pabulo, à se-xu, à castratione, parandi ratione, & ut uno dicam multa, pro proportione & temperatura eorundem multifaria. In genere quidem primo sciendum omnem carnem naturâ esse calidam & humidam, aliam tamen plus, alia minus, pro ætatis & nutrimenti ratione.
units.tr: For these differences are many, depending on the age of the animals, their fodder, their sex, whether they are castrated, the method of preparing them, and, to say much in a word, their proportion and temperament. In general one must first know that all flesh is by nature warm and moist, though some more and some less, according to age and diet.

units.la: 2. Non omnes quemuis hominem nutrire, sed quasdam quibusdam esse lethales.
units.tr: 2. Not every kind of flesh nourishes every man; some kinds are deadly to some people.

units.la: 3. Sicut extenuatorum nimis & macrorum, ita obesorum & nimis saginatorum carnes improbantur, illic ob nimiam siccitatem[?], probiq; succi[?] carentiam, hic ob contrarium.
units.tr: 3. Just as the flesh of the excessively thin and lean is disapproved, so is that of the very fat and overfed: the former because of excessive dryness and lack of good juice, the latter for the opposite reason.

units.la: 4. Vetulorum quoq; & nuper natorum deteriores sunt, illorum enim aridæ sunt & prædurae, concoctuque contumaces, horum verò immodicè madescunt, excrementisque abundant, præsertim verò quæ humidioris sunt naturæ, vt oues, sues.
units.tr: 4. The flesh of the old and of the newly born is also inferior. That of the old is dry and very hard and resists digestion, while that of the young is immoderately watery and abounds in excrements, especially that of animals of a moister nature, such as sheep and swine.

units.la: 5. Et certè standum hic iudicio, quod longo experimento innititur, standum ab antiquorum obseruatione præsertim rationibus consentientibus, inter quas plurimum valet quæ ab ipsius carnis sumitur substantia: ductities enim in carne facit, vt ferò & paulatim nutriat, teste Gal. in expositione aph. 18. l. 2. Quemadmodū enim, inquit idem, in sin. l. 3. de temper. quod facilè concoquitur & citò nutrit, respectu nostri calidum est, ita è contrario, tarde & paulatim frigidum: facilè n. in substantiam nostram cōuertitur, quod cum ea habet maiorem similitudinem, difficilius id quod magis dissimile. Præterea eadem duricies euidens indicium siccitatis est, teste Gal. l. 2. de temper. Licet enim nō omne durum sit siccum, id tamen durum, sed à vehementi calido induratum est, neq; à frigore vehementi congelatū, siccū procul-dubio censebitur. Tantam auré caliditatē in quibusdam carnibus esse non posse constat, ut ab ea indurentur, nec tantâ etiam frigidi-tate, ut congelet. Quare cum sint nihilomi-nus durae, siccas etiam esse oportebit, ob idq; ænumero bonarum carnium excludendae.
units.tr: 5. Here certainly one must abide by a judgment that rests on long experience, and by the observation of the ancients, especially where reasons agree. Among these, the one taken from the substance of the flesh itself carries the most weight: toughness in flesh makes it nourish slowly and gradually, as Galen testifies in his commentary on Aphorism 18 of book 2. For, as the same author says at the end of book 3 of De temperamentis, what is easily digested and quickly nourishes is warm relative to us, and conversely what is slow and gradual is cold. What is very like our substance is easily converted into it, and what is more unlike is converted with more difficulty. Moreover, the same hardness is clear evidence of dryness, as Galen testifies in book 2 of De temperamentis. For although not everything hard is dry, what is hard because it has been hardened by intense heat, not congealed by intense cold, will undoubtedly be judged dry. It is clear that there cannot be so much heat in certain flesh that it is hardened by it, nor so much cold that it congeals. Therefore, since such flesh is nonetheless hard, it must also be dry, and on that account must be excluded from the number of good meats.

units.la: 6. Animalium quoq; non exercitatorum carnes Galen. damnat, ob nimium illorum humorem excrementitium, contra vero montanorum, sylvestrium & exercitatorum, quaeq; idoneis vescuntur pabulis, liberamq; agunt vitâ, laudat. Certissimum enim est, quod in plenum dixisse sufficiat, pro temporum, pascue-rumq; ac pabuli ratione pecora macrescere, aut obsari, succiq; melioris aut peioris fieri.
units.tr: 6. Galen also condemns the flesh of animals that are not exercised, because of their excessive excrementitious moisture; on the contrary, he praises that of mountain and woodland animals, of those that are exercised, that feed on suitable fodder and lead a free life. For it is most certain, to say enough in brief, that according to the season, the pasture and the fodder, cattle grow lean or fat, and their juice becomes better or worse.

units.la: 7. Quae domi aluntur, ut sues &c. aut frumentorum farina, aut rapis, aut alio huiusmodi, lardi quidem plus obtinebunt, verum non perinde utilis in cibis censetur caro.
units.tr: 7. Animals raised at home, such as pigs, fed on flour of grain, or on turnips, or on other such things, will indeed have more lard, but their flesh is not judged equally useful as food.

units.la: 8. Recenter edita animalia & adhuc la-ctentia plurimum lentoris & viuidi humoris obtinere obscurum non est: ac veterib. maximè in cibis commendata testatur Plin. l. 29. c. 4., tantoque magis sicca efficiuntur, quanto ab-sunt à partu longius, aetateque processerint.
units.tr: 8. It is not obscure that recently born animals, and those still suckling, have much viscosity and lively moisture. Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, testifies that the ancients especially commended them as food, and that they become drier the further they are from birth and the more advanced in age.

units.la: 9. Dulcę ac delicatissimum sanguine habetia, quemadmodum de sanguine leporino scripsit Gal. 3. de alim. fac. bonitatis alimonia pstare creditu difficile non est. Sed de lepore suo loco.
units.tr: 9. Flesh that has sweet and most delicate blood, as Galen wrote of hare's blood in book 3 of De alimentorum facultatibus, is not hard to believe to supply good nourishment. But of hare, in its own place.

units.la: 10. Assas [?] & in sartagine frixas sicciores esse, in aqua v. dulci elixas humidius corpori alimentū ꝑbere, testat Gal. 3. de al. fac. & idipsum
units.tr: 10. Galen, in book 3 of De alimentorum facultatibus, testifies that roasted meats and those fried in a pan are drier, while those boiled in water or sweet water give the body more moisture, and

units.la: comprobat quotidiana experientia. Vnde il- læ naturis humidioribus,hæ verò ficcioribus temperaturis magis conueniunt.
units.tr: everyday experience confirms this. Hence the former suit moister natures, and the latter drier temperaments.

units.la: II. Ad extremum in ouillo pecore mares præstare fœminis, & in bubalo quoq;, quod calidiores sint, minusque excrementis abun- dent: caßrarorum verò etiam quadrupedum carnes plurimum suauitatis ac salubritatis afferre immò plus quam non castratorum præter experientiam multorum cōsensu tra- ditur, rationem hanc quidam assignant, quod ipsa qualitas carnium in non castratis simile quid testium qualitati præ se ferat graue, & virosum adodorem vsq; similitudine porre- ctatum etiam quod castrata nullo à calido & sicco morbo subiecta sint. Hoc inuento ca- strantur gallinæ cæteris gratissimæ. Galenus l. 1. de fœmine, sues fœminas castrari in Asia, & in superioribus nationibus Cappadociam vs- que docet, quæ castratis maribus similes euadunt. Obestantur enim admodum, carnisque suauitate aliis præstant fœminis, quemadmo- dum & castrati mares non castratis. Error de- niq; quorundam detegendus hic est, qui car- nes quomodolibet teneras recentibus fem- per præferunt, haud cogitantes teneritudinè illam velut putredinè quandā, aut saltem ad putredinem, quandam præparationem esse, q cibū dentib? quidé facilioré reddat & gra- tioré, sed q pofteain venis deteriores succos, & & longo tempore prauas affectiones pignat. Recentes enim carnes plus roboris afferre corporibus praeter Hippocr. rationem 2. de diaeta (vbi recentia omnia plus virium aliis praebere dicit, eo quod viuenti sint proximiora, vieta vero & marcida recentibus excernantur magis, quod ad putredinem proximè accedant) bruta omnia carniuora demonstrant, quae carnes recentissimas, immo calentes & quasi viuentes comedentia omnium aliorum sunt robustissima. Verum aliquam hic rationem habendam, tum hominum edentium, tum carnium edendarum etiam, patescet ex speciali singulorum tractatione: in generalibus hisce non sine ratione praemissis, haud pigebit nec poenitebit paululum immorari lectorem.
units.tr: II. Finally, among sheep the males are better than the females, and likewise among oxen, since they are warmer and abound less in excrements. The flesh of castrated quadrupeds also, as is handed down by the consensus of many beyond experience, brings much sweetness and wholesomeness, indeed more than that of uncastrated animals. Some assign this reason: the quality of flesh in uncastrated animals bears a certain resemblance to the quality of the testicles, which is heavy and has a strong odour, extending even to a likeness of smell; also, castrated animals are not subject to any disease of the hot and dry kind. From this discovery capons are castrated, the most pleasing of all fowls to others. Galen teaches, in book 1 of his work on the seed, that sows are castrated in Asia, and in the upper nations as far as Cappadocia, and that they become similar to castrated males; for they fatten greatly, and in sweetness of flesh they surpass other females, just as castrated males surpass uncastrated ones. Finally, the error of certain people must be exposed here, who always prefer meats that are tender, however they are, to fresh ones. They do not consider that such tenderness is a kind of putrefaction, or at least a preparation towards putrefaction, which indeed makes food easier on the teeth and more pleasant, but afterwards engenders worse juices in the veins and long-lasting bad conditions. For fresh meats bring more strength to the body, as all the carnivorous beasts demonstrate, contrary to Hippocrates' reasoning in book 2 of the Regimen, where he says that all fresh things give more strength than others because they are nearer to the living, while stale and withered things are more readily excreted because they approach putrefaction. Those beasts, eating the freshest meats, even warm and almost alive, are the most robust of all. But that some account must be taken here, both of the men who eat and of the meats to be eaten, will become clear from the special treatment of each. In these general matters, premised not without reason, it will be neither tedious nor regrettable for the reader to linger a little.

units.la: De Leonina, Elephantina, Camelina, Pantherina, Vrsina, & Lupina carne.
units.tr: On the flesh of the lion, elephant, camel, panther, bear and wolf.

units.la: Griephagos Æthiopia gentem, Pantherarum carnibus atque Leonum vi&ctitasse, sicut & orientis populos quosdam Africae leonina, vera historia proditum est. Solinus c.33. Plin. l.6. c.30. Elephantos similiter in vi&ctu quorundam Nomadum frequentes fuisse idem testis est.
units.tr: Ethiopia's Griephagi are reported, on true history, to have lived on the flesh of panthers and lions, as did some peoples of Africa's East on lion flesh. Solinus ch. 33; Pliny bk. 6 ch. 30. The same witness says that elephants were similarly a frequent food of certain nomads.

units.la: Verum ab hominis temperatura horum anianimalium carnes alienas esse, praesertim pan-theraram [?] leonum, arbitrandum est, nam Leonis tradunt tantum esse virus, ut halitus sue odorem cibis foedum relinquat, eoq, proscisse [?] interiora ejus gravissime olent: flatus prae-rea emittit acerrimos, urinamque graviter o-lentem, quemadmodum tefantur, quiin Magnorum Principum aulis Leonum domiterunt fuerunt custodes.
units.tr: Yet it must be judged that the flesh of these animals is foreign to human constitution, especially that of lions (and panthers). They report that the lion has such a strong venom that its breath leaves a foul smell on food, and its entrails stink very badly when cut open. Besides, it gives off very sharp breath and urine with a heavy smell. This is why, as they say, lion-tamers were keepers in the courts of great princes.

units.la: Orientis gentes quasdam, ut Battros, Camelorum carnibus vesci certum est. Aristoteles lac as carnes camelorum omnium fauiffimae esse testatus est, qui tamen locus eruditiorbus quibusdam fwpectus est, ut Hieron, Mercuriali variar. Lett.l. 2. putat enim ab aliquo ex marginibus interferta, tum etiam quod Plinius l. 28. solum lac non carnes Camelorum ab hominum lacte facit dulcissimum. Ac de lacte convenit inter omnes. Galenus 3. de aliment. carnes camelinas valde damnat.
units.tr: It is certain that some eastern peoples, such as the Bactrians, eat camel flesh. Aristotle testified that camel milk and flesh are the most wholesome of all, though this passage has been suspected by some learned men. Hieronymus Mercurialis, in his Variae lectiones bk. 2, thinks it was interpolated by someone from the margins. Pliny bk. 28 also says that camel milk alone, not the flesh, makes human milk sweetest. Everyone agrees about the milk. Galen, in book 3 of On Foods, strongly condemns camel flesh.

units.la: Solinus c. 52. scribit lutulentas aquas Camelos captare, refugere puras, nisi cœnosior fuerit liquor, assidua conculcatione limum excitare, ut turbetur, quod vel maxime ab illorum ese aliquem deterrere debeat.
units.tr: Solinus (ch. 52) writes that camels seek out muddy water and shun clear water, and unless the liquid is rather thick, they stir up the silt by constant trampling so that it becomes cloudy. This alone should deter anyone from eating them.

units.la: Antiphanes Comediarum scriptor apud Atheneum tradit, Graecos aliquando solitos Camelum solidum affamz apponere etiam regibus. Quidem orbis posteris monumenta reliquerunt quaequaedam esse Insulas affirmant, quarum incolae camelina vescantur, illicq; esse armenta camelorum ingentia, quin etiam Ægyptii, dum Sultano parebant, Camelos in cibatu habuerunt, ut ita non plane extra humanos mores sit Camelis vesci.
units.tr: Antiphanes, the writer of comedies, reports in Athenaeus that the Greeks once used to serve a whole camel at table, even to kings. Some monuments left by the ancient world affirm that there are certain islands whose inhabitants eat camel flesh, and that huge herds of camels are kept there. Moreover, the Egyptians, while they obeyed the Sultan, kept camels for food, so that eating camels is not entirely outside human custom.

units.la: Sed ursinum plane videbitur ursos in cibos vocare, quorum tamen catulos, seu ursulos conditos tanta esse suavitatis quidam produderunt, ut non minorem saporis gratiam habeant, quam alia ferina. Heluetios quosdam & Allobroges, nec non Septentrionis gentes plurimas ursorum venatu deditas, horumque carnibus vesci, dubium non est. Omnivorum animal est, & carnivorum etiam, non solum enim cervos, sed & feros sues invadit. Cerebro eius inesse veneficium Hispaniae existimasse Plinius testatum reliquit l.8.c.36. ideoque occisorum capita in spectaculis cremasse, exploratum enim, potum in ursinam rabiem egisse.
units.tr: But it will seem quite absurd to invite bears to the table. Yet some have reported that their cubs, preserved, are of such sweetness that they have no less pleasant a flavour than other game. That some Helvetians and Allobroges, and many peoples of the North given over to bear-hunting, feed on their flesh, is not in doubt. It is an omnivorous animal, and carnivorous too, for it attacks not only deer but also wild boars. Pliny has left it on record (book 8, chapter 36) that Spain thought poison lay in the bear's brain, and therefore burned the heads of slain bears at the shows, since it is well known that drinking it drove men into bear-madness.

units.la: Unde illiberalem plane escam, & insalubrem ursinam carnem esse quidam arbitrantur, ut qua iniquum creet succum & atrabilia-rium, stomachoque ut difficilius concoctu adversetur, praesertim vero genitorum catulorum tolerabilior foret. Adipes ursorum multis remediis nobilitantur. Animam ferunt ius adeo virosam esse, ut contactu ea nulla fera attingat, cuius rei causam nullam video aliam produci, quam quod omnivorum animal ursus est, vescitur namq; fructibus arborum, leguminibus, apibus formicis & carnibus praemaceratis ac pene pu-tridis, tum etiam, quod veterno in antris recon-diti pinguescant.
units.tr: Hence some think bear flesh a wholly base and unwholesome food, since it breeds bad juices and black bile and is hard for the stomach to digest, though the flesh of young cubs is more tolerable. Bear fat is valued for many remedies. They report that the broth of the bear is so rank that no wild beast will touch anything it has touched. I see no other cause given for this than that the bear is an omnivorous animal: it feeds on fruits of trees, pulses, bees, ants, and flesh pre-steeped and nearly putrid; and also because, hidden away in caves, it grows fat through lethargy.

units.la: Lupinam vllam gentem in cibatu ba-buisse, nec me legisse, nec audiuisse meminì, cum tamen cetera animantia asperrima & ferocissima cibatum venerint. Quidam non minus maleficii in carne esse credunt, quam in eorum visu.
units.tr: I neither have read nor have I heard it recorded that any people has eaten wolf, although other most savage and fierce animals have been brought to the table. Some believe that wolf flesh carries no less harm than the wolf's gaze does.

units.la: Pastores oves à lupis jugulatas, boves, sues, caeteraque pecudes plurimum in cibis reformidant, credentes aliquod inesse iis venefici-um.
units.tr: Shepherds greatly dread eating sheep, oxen, pigs and other cattle killed by wolves, believing that some poison lies in them.

units.la: Epar eorum, si vescatur, epatici prodesse, eparq; vitiatum reoreare medicorum docent placita, sicut & cor eorundem torre factum asservatum, bonum de se odorem praebere, Comitialibus quoq; tritum in potu auxiliari. Dentem lupi caninum dextrum in magnis habere operibus Plinius autor est l.11.c.37. Tantamq; inesse huic animali vim, ut vestigia eius caleata equis torporem afferant, ac re[?]flat, ob id, villarum portis praefigatur eundem effectum praestare & pellem, è cervice solida idem testis est l.28.
units.tr: Physicians' doctrines teach that the liver of the wolf, if eaten, benefits those with jaundice and restores a diseased liver; likewise its heart, roasted and kept, gives off a good smell, and rubbed into a drink it helps those with epilepsy. Pliny is the authority that the right canine tooth of a wolf is held in great esteem for important works (bk. 11 ch. 37). Such great power is in this animal that its footprints, if touched by horses, cause torpor; for this reason it is fixed to the gates of country houses to produce the same effect. The same witness (bk. 28) says the skin of its solid neck does likewise.

units.la: cap. 10. tuiores & gratiores epulas subministrantes, memoriæ proditum reperitur. Mæcœnasa- pud Romanos epulari eos primus instituit, eoq; tempore magnam autoritatem iis facl- ebant vescentes. Erat autem Mecœnas Au- gusto Imp. mite cætus, suo pene nutu Remp. gubernans, post eum tamen autoritas saporis interiit. Nostro suo Galliarum & Hispania- rum proceres quidam ( inter quos Ant. Pratensis Gall. Cancellarius Javid. [?]issimi Me- cænatis extitere in eo escæ genere imitato- res, sed cum ipsis carnis quoque illius gratia sepulta est.
units.tr: Ch. 10. It is recorded in memory that Maecenas first established among the Romans the practice of holding more refined and pleasing feasts, and at that time those who dined with him gained great authority. Maecenas was a gentle companion of the Emperor Augustus, governing the state almost at his nod; after him, however, the authority of good taste died out. In our own times some nobles of France and Spain (among them Antoine Duprat, chancellor of France, a most distinguished Maecenas) became imitators of him in this kind of eating, but with them the pleasure of that meat too was buried.

units.la: Certum autem est priscis illis tempo- ribus Mecœnatem greges asinarum genero- sissimarum habuisse exagro Rheatino, vbi amplitudinis dignitate præstabant. Popea, Neronis conjunx, asinarum greges secum duxisse fertur, propter lactis gratiam adcane- dorem cutis coriciliandum, quoties enim è balneo exiret, lacte asinino corpus abluisse legimus.
units.tr: It is certain that in those ancient times Maecenas kept herds of very noble she-asses from the Rhaetian territory, where they excelled in distinction. Poppaea, wife of Nero, is said to have led herds of she-asses with her, for the sake of the milk's benefit in softening the skin. For we read that whenever she came out of the bath she washed her body with asses' milk.

units.la: Unde facile conjectare licet, tempori hujus animalis pretium admodum fuisse adauctum. Meminit Plinius asinam Rheatinam suo suo diuenditam quadrin- gentis millibus nummûm, quæ summa intra fidem stabit, si quis æstimationem ejus ad calculum retulerit, lib. 8. c. 43. Porro deasi- narum lacte eiusque viribus dicetur seorsim
units.tr: From this one may easily guess that the price of this animal had risen greatly in those times. Pliny mentions a Rhaetian she-ass sold for four hundred thousand sesterces, a sum which will be credible if anyone reckons its value by calculation (bk. 8 ch. 43). Further, the milk of she-asses and its powers will be discussed separately.

units.la: Cap,de Lacte. In medicinis præcipuè commendantur splen, pulmo, lingua, jecur, ungulæ. Tradit Plin. ex ungulis & ossibus asini confectum annulum, non tamen nigri coloris à comitiali morbo præseruare.
units.tr: Ch. on milk. In medicines the spleen, lung, tongue, liver and hooves are especially recommended. Pliny reports that a ring made from the hooves and bones of an ass preserves from epilepsy, though not if it is of black colour.

units.la: Gulæ insaniam aliquando apud Romanos experti sunt, & canes fidelissimi ante omnia homini: lactentes enim catulos adeo puros exiftimarunt ad cibum, vt placandis etiam numinibus hostiarum vice iis vteren-tur, teste Plin. l.29. c.4. Hippocrates quoque gravissimus autor pluribus in locis non parum eos in variis ægritudinibus commendauit, sicut etiam Oribasius in primo collect. ex sententia Mnesithei Athenien-sis. Galenus catulos præpingues similiter videtur commendare, quos tamen nostér orbis in epulas non admittit. Qui in ædibus educantur ad custodiam, aliisq; animalib. non insidiantur, in cibis non damnari possunt, ob victú non plane ferinum. Africæ gentes quasdã, vt Ptoembaros & Sambris proximos, canè pro rege habere, motuq; ejus imperia augurari Solinus autor est c.33. Genito mane catulo ré apud Prisco s fieri diuinam, Plin. testis est, ca. 4.l.29. & in cœnis Deum etiam num ponicatulinam. Plautinq quoq; fabulę indicio sunt, adiicialib. in epulis cœnisq; catulinam fuisse celebré, Præclarus hujus animalis est in medicinis vsus. Sanguine enim eius contra toxi-ca nihil præstantius putatur.
units.tr: At times the Romans experienced the madness of gluttony, and dogs, the most faithful of all creatures to man, were eaten above all. They considered suckling puppies so pure for food that they even used them as victims in place of sacrificial animals to placate the gods, as Pliny testifies (bk. 29 ch. 4). Hippocrates too, a most serious authority, in many places commends them not a little for various diseases, as does Oribasius in the first book of his Collections, on the view of Mnesitheus of Athens. Galen seems similarly to commend rather fat puppies, which our world nevertheless does not admit to its feasts. Dogs raised in houses for guarding, which do not lie in wait for other animals, cannot be condemned as food, since their diet is not wholly savage. Solinus is the authority that some African peoples, such as the Ptoembari and the neighbours of the Sambri, hold a dog as king and draw omens from its movements. Pliny witnesses (bk. 29 ch. 4) that among the ancients a divine rite was performed on the morning after a puppy was born, and that at feasts a little dog was even served up as a dish. The fables of Plautus also show that puppy meat was a celebrated addition at banquets and suppers. The medical use of this animal is outstanding, for its blood is thought to be most effective against poisons.

units.la: Vomitiones quoque homini canis monstrasse videtur, aliosque ex eo maire[?] lau-datos vsus,hic referre operæ pretium erit, quia hoc animali nullum fere familiarius homini. In canis rabidi morsu tuetur ab hydrophobia seu pauore aquæ,capitis canini cinis illitus vulneri. Oportet autem,inquit Plinius l.29.c.5.omnia comburi in vase fictili nouo argilla circumlito atque in furnum indito. Idem & in potione proficit. Quidam obid edendum dederunt: alii vermem è ca-dauere canino adalligauere, menstruauein panno subdidere calici,aut intus ipsius cau-dæ pilos combustos infuêre[?] vulneri. Cor ca-ninum habentes fugiunt canes. Non latrant vero linguâ canina in calceamento subdita pollici. Iecur caninum vtilissime in rabie morsis datur, si possit fieri,crudum manden-dum, si minus, quoque modo coctum, aut jus coctis carnibus. Saliuntur & carnes eo-rum qui rabidi fuerunt ad eadem remedia in cibo dandæ. Quin & catuli statim necan-tur in aqua, ad sexum ejus qui momorderit, vt iecur crudum ex iis deuoretur. Caninus dens sinister maximus, circumscarificato eo, qui doleat, dolorem tollit. Idem præstat collutio caninis dentibus decoctis in vino ad dimidias,nec non cinis eorum, qui rabie perierunt, capitum crematorum fine carni-bus. Lien caninus viuenti exemtus inque cibo sumtus à lienis vitio liberat. Alii recentem superalligant. Alii duorum dierum catuli lienem ex aceto scillitico dant ignoranti. Lacterum[?] doloribus rabiosi canis caluariæ cinis medetur potioni inspersus. Sedis vitiis canini capitis cinis efficacissimus est, nec non fimi canini candidi cinis cum rosaceo, feruntq; inuentum Æsculapii esse, eodemq; verrucas efficacissime tolli. Ac verrucas quidem omnium generum vrinam canis recentem cum suo luto illitam auerruncare Plin. 30.c.8. & 9.testis est. Nigri canis masculi fel amuletum esse domus totius suffitæ eo puri-ficaræue, contra omnia mala medicamenta Magia naturalis docet. Sanguineitem canis respersis parietibus, genitalique ejus sub limine januæ defosso. Minus autem mirandum hoc, cum fœdissimum animalium ricinum, vermiculum seu pediculum canum, (cui vni, inquit Plinius, nullus est exitus saginæ diutius in fame viuenti) in tantum magnificent: huncenim ex aure sinistra canis, adalligatum omnes dolores sedare ajunt. Eundemque in augurio vitalium habent, nam si æger ei respondeat qui intulerit, à Pe-dibus stanti interrogantiq; de morbo, spem vitæ certam esse, moriturum respondere nihil, voluntque evellendum ex aure læua canis, cui non sit alius, quam niger color. Lac porro canis primi pactus cum ci-nere per se mixtum depilatorium est, evulsis prius pilis quos renasci noiumus.
units.tr: The dog seems also to have shown men the use of vomiting, and other uses from it have been praised. It will be worth the effort to report them here, since almost nothing is more familiar to man than this animal. For the bite of a mad dog, the ash of a dog's head smeared on the wound guards against hydrophobia, or fear of water. "Everything must be burned," says Pliny (bk. 29 ch. 5), "in a new earthen vessel coated with clay and put into the furnace." The same ash also helps when drunk. Some have given it to be eaten for this purpose; others tied on a worm from a dog's carcass, put menstruum in a cloth under the cup, or put singed hairs from the dog's own tail into the wound. Dogs flee from a dog's heart. A dog's tongue placed under the thumb in shoes stops barking. A dog's liver is most usefully given to those bitten in madness, to be eaten raw if possible, otherwise cooked in any way, or as broth of cooked meat. The flesh of those who were mad is also salted and given in food for the same remedies. Indeed the puppies are at once drowned in water, according to the sex of the one who bit, so that the raw liver may be eaten from them. The largest left canine tooth, scarified around the painful part, removes the pain. A rinse of canine teeth boiled in wine to half does the same, as does the ash of those who died of rabies, their heads burned without flesh. A dog's spleen, taken from it while alive and eaten, frees from disorders of the spleen; others apply a fresh one above it. Others give the spleen of two-day-old puppies with squill vinegar to one who does not know. Ash of the skull of a rabid dog, sprinkled into a drink, cures the pains of rabies. Ash of the canine head is most effective for disorders of the seat, and likewise the ash of white dung of a dog with rose oil; they say this was discovered by Aesculapius, and warts are most effectively removed by it. Indeed Pliny (bk. 30 ch. 8 and 9) witnesses that the fresh urine of a dog, smeared with its own mud, drives away warts of every kind. The gall of a black male dog is an amulet for a whole house fumigated or purified with it, against all evil drugs, as natural magic teaches. Its blood sprinkled on the walls, and its genitals buried under the threshold of the door. This is less to be wondered at, since they magnify so much the most foul of animal parasites, the little worm or louse of dogs (for which alone, says Pliny, there is no exit, as fat as it grows while living on hunger). For they say that when hung from the left ear of a dog it calms all pains. They also have it in a kind of augury of life: if the sick man, standing at its feet, asks about his illness and the dog answers the one who brought it, hope of life is certain; if it answers nothing, he is to die. And they want the left ear of a dog plucked out, which has no colour but black. Moreover, the milk of a dog that first bore young, mixed by itself with ash, is a depilatory, provided the hairs are first plucked out, which they say grow again.

units.la: Adextremum, anginæ, dysenteriæ, ul-ceribusque inueteratis, stercus canis, solis ossibus per biduum nutriti, durum, candidum, minimeque fœtens exiccatum, inque pollinem redactum, aliis conuenientibus his affectibus medicinis admixtum, mederi ac opitulari, multis documentis manifestum est. Addysenteriam lacti decocto, aut quod filices candentes extinxerit, iniiciendum. Felle denique canino cum melle suffusiones & albugines oculorum curauit Apol-lonius.
units.tr: Lastly, for quinsy, dysentery and long-standing ulcers, dog dung is shown by many instances to heal and help. It should be dried and reduced to powder, from a dog fed on bones alone for two days, and it should be hard, white and least foul-smelling. It is mixed with other medicines suited to these complaints. For dysentery it is to be given in a decoction of milk, or in the water in which red-hot ferns have been quenched. Finally, Apollonius cured suffusions and films of the eyes with dog's gall and honey.

units.la: De murium acerrimo hoste, fele.
units.tr: On the Cat, the Mouse's Most Bitter Enemy.

units.la: GUlæ insidias & feles effugere nonpotue-runt. Sunt enim qui pro delicatissimis epulis vtantur, tantum potestatis habet venter pro cibo[?] porrigendi quicquid velit. Ho-die in confessa damnatione relinquuntur. Ce-rebrum namq; veneficio infamatur, animam illorum adeo esse ajunt pestiferam hominibus, ut tu-bem[?] afferat, qua de causa etiam minus eos quidam contrectant. Excrementum felis cum digitè bubonis adalligata quartanis febribus adversari tradit Plin. l. 28. c. 15. & ne recidant, non remoueri septena circuitu quidam jubent. [illegible, ~3 letters] hac quaeso inuenire potuit? quaue est ista miftura, & cur digitus potissimum bubonis electus est? antipathias certe mysterium hic admirandum fatendumq; concordiam istam rerum, aut repugnantiam medicinas gignere & genuisse. Alius jecur felis decrescente Luna occisi sale inueteratum, bibendum ex vino ante accessionem quartanarum mandant.
units.tr: Neither have cats been able to escape the snares of gluttony. For some use them at the most delicate feasts, so much power has the belly to demand whatever it wishes as food. Today they are left under an admitted condemnation. The brain, indeed, is defamed by witchcraft; they say the soul of these animals is so pestilent to men that it brings on a swelling, and for this reason some handle them even less. Pliny, book 28, chapter 15, hands down that the dung of a cat, tied on in a finger of an owl, opposes quartan fevers, and some order that it be carried seven times around in a circle, so that they do not return. [illegible] From where, I ask, could this have been discovered? And what is this mixture, and why was the owl's finger chosen above all? Surely here we must confess a mystery of antipathy, and that the concord or repugnance of things produces medicines and has produced them. Another orders the liver of a cat, killed when the moon is waning and kept long in salt, to be drunk in wine before the attack of quartan fever.

units.la: De Muftelina.
units.tr: On the Weasel.

units.la: MAgna autorum asseueratione commendantur multæ mustelæ partes aduersus comitialem morbum, vt cerebrum, jecur, (quod peculiariter etiam jecinoriis vitiis medetur) testes, ventriculus, vulva. Et quidem Comitiales tota in cibo sumta liberare dicitur: quod tamen catulus præstat efficacius. Sylueftrem Plinius totam in cibis prædicat. Vetustate non corrumpi, & à muribus non attingi caseos, affirmant, fi coagulo misceatur mustelæ cerebrum. Cæterum Italos mustelas inter cupedias ponere ac comedere non est ignotum.
units.tr: Many parts of the weasel are commended by writers with great assurance against epilepsy: the brain, the liver (which also cures diseases of the liver in particular), the testicles, the stomach and the womb. Indeed the whole animal, taken in food, is said to free epileptics, though the whelp does this more effectively. Pliny praises the wild weasel, taken whole in food. Cheeses are said not to spoil with age and not to be touched by mice, if the weasel's brain is mixed into the curdling agent. It is no secret that the Italians place weasels among their delicacies and eat them.

units.la: De Muribus.
units.tr: On Mice.

units.la: OVi portenta terrarum verterunt in ga-neam, torpidique palati extiterunt, in-delitiis gula quoque habuerunt mures, & a quos omnes quadrupedes conscia refugiunt, sola fele excepto: ex putredine enim maxim[?]ae ex parte ortium eos habere conflat, ingentemq, eo- rursum usum vim navibus innatasci[?]. Pontici duntaxat albi sunt. In annalibus reperitur veritisse mu- rem ducentis nummis Cafilinum obsidente Han- nibale, eumq; qui vendiderat, fame interisse, extorem vixisse. In Hispania murium copiam pestilentem strabo auctor est.
units.tr: Whatever monsters of the lands have turned to the throat and become sluggish in taste, mice too have been among the pleasures of gluttony, and all quadrupeds, knowingly, shun them, except the cat. For it is established that they arise for the most part from putrefaction, and that they bring great harm to ships by gnawing. Only the Pontic mice are white. In the annals it is recorded that a mouse was sold for two hundred coins when Hannibal was besieging Casilinum; the seller died of hunger, while the buyer lived. Strabo, the author, says that the abundance of mice in Spain was a plague.

units.la: Pulmonum vitiis detracta cute, exenteræ tosq; sale oleoq; decoctos, & in cibo sumtos, me- deri Plinius auctor est. Urinam quoq; non con- tinentes, ut pueri, elixatis epotatisq; praeclare ju- vantur. Dissecti & impositi serpentum fibris efficaciter medentur, verrucasq; exedunt, estq; eorum natura hic non sperneda, praesertim in se- derum assensu, cum Luna lumine fibrarum nu- mero crescente ac decrescente, quod de epate pe- culiariter quidam intelligendum afferunt. Capitum caudarum, murinarum cinerem ex melle inunctum claritatem visus restituere gra- ves autores prodiderunt, Commendantur autem magis sylvestres, aut glandes. Sed in hoc spectatur vel maxime natura potentiæ, si verum est, quod alvum laxare muscerdam potu sumtum, qui- dam se expertos ajunt. Expe-imentum[?] cuiq; relinquitur liberum.
units.tr: Pliny, the author, says that for diseases of the lungs, mice are cured by skinning and gutting them, boiling them in salt and oil, and eating them. Those who cannot hold their urine, like boys, are greatly helped by them boiled and drunk. Mice cut open and applied with the fibres of serpents cure effectively and eat away warts, and their nature is not to be scorned here, especially in the consent of the seasons, with the moon's light, the number of fibres increasing and decreasing; some understand this particularly of the liver. Severe authors have reported that the ashes of the heads and tails of mice, rubbed on with honey, restore clarity of sight. Woodland mice, or those that feed on acorns, are commended more. But in this the power of the nature is especially to be examined, if it is true what some say they have tested: that mouse dung taken in drink loosens the bowels. Each person is left free to make his own trial.

units.la: De Gliribus.
units.tr: On Dormice.

units.la: Tanta fuit vorago, tantusque gurges, tam insanus gulæ ventrisque luxus prisci illius seculi, ut cognata moribus animalia, glires, in epulis lautioribus Romanorum gloriam non obscuram obtinuerint.
units.tr: So great was the abyss, so vast the whirlpool, so mad the luxury of gullet and belly in that older age, that the animals akin to it in habits, dormice, won no small fame at the more lavish banquets of the Romans.

units.la: Nam qui apris vivaria primus instituit Fulvius Hirpinus, gliribus quoque in doliis instituisse fertur. Et glirarium quo pacto construendum sit Varro docuit. Sed in coenis censoriâ tandem lege prohibiti, non alio modo, quam conchilia aut aves peregrinæ quædam. Pinguia glirium soricumque decoctorum paralysin timentibus utilissima esse graues autores tradunt. Quin & de-plorata[?] aurium vitia sanari gliribus, detracta pelle, inestinis exemtis, melle in vase nouo decoctis, vel è nardo, ut malunt alii, vsque ad tertias, atque ita asservatis, cumque opus fit, tepide infusis, Plinius testis est l.29. c.ult. Estq; hoc remedii genus in secretis.
units.tr: For Fulvius Hirpinus, who first set up boar-preserves, is also said to have established dormice in jars. And Varro taught how a dormouse-garden must be built. But at last they were forbidden at dinners by a censors' law, in no other way than shellfish or certain foreign birds. Serious authors hand down that the fat of dormice, and of boiled shrews, is most useful for those who fear paralysis. Indeed Pliny is witness (book 29, last chapter) that even desperate diseases of the ears are cured by dormice: skinned, with the entrails removed, boiled in honey in a new vessel, or in spikenard, as others prefer, up to the third (boiling), and so kept, and poured in lukewarm when need arises. This kind of remedy belongs among the secrets.

units.la: De Melina.
units.tr: On the Badger.

units.la: Mellis hoc animal avidissimum[?], alveariisque infestum semper perhibetur. Carnes ejus ferum[?] gustatu saporem redolere, ac virosum quid exhalare tradunt, potissimumq; cum canibus exagi-tatum.
units.tr: This animal is always said to be most greedy for honey and a constant pest to beehives. Its flesh is said to smell of a wild taste and to give off something foul, especially when it has been hunted down by dogs.

units.la: tatum [?] capitur, ideoque liberaliorem ac humaniorem sectantibus vitam in epulis eo abstinendum. Septentrionis tamen gentibus quibusdam in cibis meles non sordere scio. Adeps huius animalis ad multa millia remediorum utilis est, inprimis vero renum iunctarumque doloribus commodat. Sanguis ejus distillatus in canicularibus ad sii lumtus pestifero veneno adversatur.
units.tr: ...and captured; therefore those who pursue a more refined and humane way of life should abstain from it at feasts. Yet I know that among some northern peoples the badger is not despised as food. Its fat is useful for many thousands of remedies, and above all it helps pains of the kidneys and joints. Its blood, distilled in the dog days and taken in drink, opposes deadly poison.

units.la: De Sciuro.
units.tr: On the Squirrel.

units.la: Vt [?] aridius & atrabiliarium alimentum Sciurus praestare scripserunt, mea quidem judicio, quod tamen pace illorum dixerim, anniversalculi [?] huius naturam plane non habuerunt cognitam. Dulci enim gaudet cibo, quem in recentibus tum fructibus, tum omnis generis succibus studiose exquirit, has etiam in cavernas suas comportat, ad futuram sibi prospiciens hiemem. Quare inter delicatiores suaviusq; succi cibos non immerito quidam Sciuros reponunt: & fuisse olim Martialis testatur. Assos [?] mire gratos ipse suum expertus in Suecia & Dania, ut verisimile sit, qui cibis eos abdicarunt, nunquam degustaffe. Summa in eorum venatu voluptas est, quippe ex arbore in arborem transiliunt, cursu acre-cursu pernici, quo libuerit, exulcant. Porro amnem aliquem transiturus Sciurus lignum leve cui insidet, aqua imponit, canda vela vice, vento flante, utens. Vulgus comitia- li tentari existimat fabulose magis, quam vere.
units.tr: Those who have written that the squirrel provides a drier and melancholy-producing food, I say with respect to them and in my own judgement, have plainly not known the nature of this little animal. It delights in sweet food, which it eagerly seeks out in fresh fruits and juices of every kind, and it stores these in its dens, providing for the winter to come. For this reason some people not unreasonably count the squirrel among the more delicate and pleasant foods, and Martial testifies that it was so in former times. I myself have found roasted squirrel wonderfully pleasant in Sweden and Denmark, so it is likely that those who reject it as food have never tasted it. The hunting of squirrels gives the greatest pleasure, since they leap from tree to tree and, with swift and nimble running, go wherever they like. Moreover, when a squirrel is about to cross a stream, it sits on a light piece of wood, sets it on the water and uses its tail in place of a sail when the wind blows. The common people think this is more a fable than a truth.

units.la: De Erinaceo.
units.tr: On the Hedgehog.

units.la: ET hoc animal ventribus humanis nascı portentosæ culinarum artes ganeæ- queque artifices docuerunt: licet alii vitæ hominum supervacuum esse dicere non dubitârunt.
units.tr: Clever cooks and gluttonous craftsmen have shown that this animal can be fed to human stomachs with extravagant arts, although others have not hesitated to say that it is superfluous for human life.

units.la: Certum est carnes eius ventrem soluendi, ventriculumque corroborandi, nec non vrinas exinaniendi vi pollere, iisqʒ proдesse in cibis, quorum natura ad lepram vergit & malignas pustulas. Tergum viuis detrahitur, postea curatur, interaneis abjestis, & inssatur. Urinam in extrema spe, seu desperatione tergori suo spinisque noxiam & tabificam reddere Plinius testatur, l. 8.c.37. quo maleficio non potest fieri, quin & caro perfundatur, unde plus periculi timendum, quam suauitatis sperandum, quamobrem exinanita prius vrina venari, ars est. Capite autem percusso, si vno ictu perimatur, minus periculi est.
units.tr: It is certain that its flesh has the power to loosen the bowels, strengthen the stomach and also empty the urine, and it is useful as food for those whose nature tends toward leprosy and malignant pustules. The skin is removed from the living animal, afterwards it is treated, the entrails are thrown away, and it is stuffed. Pliny testifies (book 8, chapter 37) that in extreme hope or despair the animal makes its urine harmful and corrupting to its own back and spines; by this trick it cannot be avoided that the flesh too is soaked, so there is more danger to be feared than pleasure to be hoped for, and therefore it is an art to hunt it after its urine has been emptied out. If the head is struck and it is killed with one blow, there is less danger.

units.la: De Vulpina.
units.tr: On the Fox.

units.la: Autumno, quo tempore maxime vulpes pinguescunt, esu fe.vnarum, palatagra-tissimas esse icci[?] coq, Venatores apud Gracos tunc ipsas[?] efitaffe[?] confuentiffe[?], Galenus 4. de vi&t. acut. commen.§ 3. de alim. facult. scri-psit. Seipsis enim circa id tempus meliores eva-dunt. Rursus in multis locis diligenter eas venan-tur, captasq; elixant & inaffant[?], fuavissimeq; mandunt. Nitidior vita eas damnavit. In Magnatum tamen aulis non raro degustantur.
units.tr: In autumn, when foxes grow especially fat, the hunters among the Greeks, as Galen wrote in his commentary on the book On Acute Diseases (book 4, §3) and in On the Properties of Foods, then used to have them as a most delicate dish. For at that time of year they become at their best. Again, in many places they are hunted with care, and once caught they are boiled and roasted and eaten with great relish. A more refined way of life has condemned them, yet they are not rarely served at the tables of the great.

units.la: Sed fraudem detexit virosum quasi quiddam, & in carne agreste. Pulmo vulpis ad pulmonis vitia insignis est, sumitur enim in cibis à lauti-oribus etiam, qui pulmonis tabem reformidant. Adeps ad podagras & convulsiones nobilita-tur. Pellis humidioribus naturis prodest, calida enim est, & confortat humidum, frigidumque ventriculum foris admota.
units.tr: But a certain rankness and something wild in the flesh betrays the fraud. The lung of the fox is notable for curing diseases of the lung, and it is taken in food even by the more refined, who dread wasting of the lungs. The fat is esteemed for gout and convulsions. The skin benefits moist constitutions, for it is warm and strengthens what is moist, and when applied externally it warms a cold stomach.

units.la: De Cuniculis.
units.tr: On Rabbits.

units.la: Fertur in occultis habitare cuniculus antris,Monstrauit tacitas hostibus ille vias.
units.tr: It is said that the rabbit lives in hidden caves; it showed to its enemies secret paths.

units.la: Quo carmine Martialis cuniculorum in bello inuentionem huic animali ascribere visus est. Innumerae autem foecunditatis animal est cuniculus, vrbib.[?] quandoq; oppidisq; fodiendo parans exitiū, vt M. Varro autor est.
units.tr: In this verse Martial seems to ascribe to this animal the invention of tunnelling in war. The rabbit, however, is an animal of unbelievable fertility, and, as M. Varro is the authority, it digs and prepares ruin for cities and towns at times.

units.la: Balearicis insulis famem frugibus populatis attulisse, Balearicosque auxilium militare per legatos ab Augusto petiisse adauerfus eorum prouentum, Strabo, qui sub Augusto vixit, & Plinius certò prodiderunt. Satis autem patet veteres Romanos horum fecisse mentionem. Obtinent vero in opiparis epulis summam gratiam, praesertim vero infantibus pullis habetur honor. Foetus ventre exectos vel uberibus ablatos non repurgatis interaneis, gratissimo in cibatu esse Plinius testatur, lib. 8. cap. 55. Certum est, carnem eorum capacem esse alterius odoris saporisque. Itaque cuniculi, quo in loco alantur, plurimum interesse arbitrantur, pabuli enim, licut & perdices, gratiam referunt, aut vitiu: à leporario genistis confito genistâ referent, si iuniperis iuniperum, si pinastris pinastrû, aut aliud huiusmodi odoratius vibrans, quod in leporibus contingere non deprehenditur. Porro inassantur omnes, & nunquam aut rarissimè elixantur, sunt enim humentioris naturae. Non pinguescere, vt & leporem Plinius lib. 11. cap. 37. affirmat, & senfusid confirmat.
