Venantur multis modis cuniculos, sed maximè viuerris, ad hoc gratia est, quas in fpecus inii-ciunt, in quos subeuntes mirabili pernicitate cuniculos inuadunt, qui perterriti ab iis vel iugulantur, vel foras prorumpunt inque casses praetenfos incidentes capiuntur. E cuniculoEe f niculoniculorum quoq; genere videntur esse, quos porcellos Indicos nominant, passim nunc ali educariq; coepti.
units.tr: Strabo, who lived under Augustus, and Pliny have clearly reported that the Balearic Islands, having been ravaged by rabbits, brought famine on their crops, and that the Balearics sought military help from Augustus through envoys against this plague. It is quite clear that the ancient Romans made mention of them. They enjoy the highest favour at lavish banquets, and especially the young are held in special honour. Pliny testifies (book 8, chapter 55) that the young taken from the womb, or taken from the teats, with their entrails not yet cleansed, are a most pleasant food. It is certain that their flesh takes on a different smell and taste. Therefore people think it matters very much where the rabbits are fed, for they take on the quality of their fodder, as partridges do; if they are fed on broom they taste of broom, if on juniper of juniper, if on pine-cones of pine, or of anything else of that sort that gives off a stronger scent, which is not found to happen with hares. Moreover, all rabbits are roasted, and they are seldom or never boiled, for they are of a moister nature. Pliny (book 11, chapter 37) affirms that they do not grow fat, as also the hare, and experience confirms this. Rabbits are hunted in many ways, but most of all with ferrets, which are used for this purpose: they are put into the burrows, and the rabbits, going in, are attacked by the ferrets with wonderful speed; frightened by them, the rabbits are either killed or rush out and, falling into the nets set in front of them, are caught. Among the kinds of rabbit there seem to be also those which they call Indian pigs, now begun to be bred and raised everywhere.

units.la: De leporina scitu digna, & ad vitam prorogandam necessaria.
units.tr: On the hare, things worth knowing, and necessary for prolonging life.

units.la: VEnatio huius animalis peculiaris est nobilitati & Magnatibus, & nisi natura benignitas tantam lepori fuscun ditatem tribuisset, genus iam dudum defiffet, nam omnium fere praeda nasci videtur, aliarum s.ferarum, volucrum & hominum. Supersunt are lepores, aliud educantes, aliud in utero pilis vestitum, aliud implume, aliud incoato partu gerentes, & v-tramq; vim singulos habere, fineq; mare concipere posse, Herodotus auctor est. Quare definit illi mirari, qui nihil mirabile se videre aiunt, quod quotidianis epulis matres atq; infantes absumantur, & tamen gula populationi tam constanter resistere atq; sufficere.
units.tr: The hunting of this animal is a peculiar pleasure of the nobility and great men, and if the kindness of nature had not given the hare such great fertility, its race would long ago have died out, for it seems to be born as prey for almost all others: beasts, birds and men. Herodotus is the authority that hares still survive, some bringing forth young that are born already, others carrying in the womb young clothed with hair, others unfledged, others in an unfinished birth, and that each has both kinds of power and can conceive without a male. Therefore they cease to wonder, those who say they see nothing marvellous, that mothers and infants are consumed in daily meals, and yet the throat resists the devastation so steadily and is sufficient.

units.la: Caterum de animalis huius natura & temperatura inter ventres non conuenit. Quidam carnem eius faciunt boni succi, facilitate concoctionis, eamq; ab omni melancholica face abesse aiunt, adducti auctoritate Galeni, qui 3. de alim. leporum sanguinem bonitatis & alimonia praestantia, aliis omnibus prefert ob suauitatem & dulcedinem, qua de causa plerisq; consuetudo est, illum cum opase caeterisque leporis visceribus decoquere ac comedere. Indeq; concludunt, leporinam carnem melancholicum non esse, quia sanguis talis non est, tum etiam, quod grauissimi autores, (inter quos est Plinius) qui rerum naturalium historiam conscripserunt, & Poetae tradunt, (inter quos Martialis) ejus leporis venustatis decorem in 7. aut 9. usq; diem prorogari. Alii leporinas, ut & omnium oblongas aures habentium an malum carnes, melancholicum succum parere, proindeq; ex leporum esu puellarum genas rosarum rubore efflorere non posse contra statuunt, pro se adducentes venerandam antiquitatem, & per tot se-cula inculcatam mordicusq; receptam sententiam, quae ab Hippocrate vetustissimo coepit autore. Scribitur enim in lib. 1. de diæt. qui Hippocrati ab omnibus ascribitur, in hunc modum, Leporina caro sicca & astringens, lotium aliquatenus movet. Post hunc Galenus, vel quisquis ille fuerit, l. 2. de escis ait, leporum caro sanguinem gignit crassiorem: & in comment. de attenuante victu, utilem eam esse ait in victu exiccante, non autem attenuante, quia crassum sanguinem gignit. Et lib. 3. de locis aff. magnam eam habere vim dicit in melancholici sanguinis generatione. Psellus & Paulus iisdem fere verbis subscribunt Galeno, & post hos omnes Simeon Sethi lib. de esculentis inter cibaria atrabile gignentia leporinam connumeravit, Carnes inquiens, leporis hu[?] con-ducunt, quibus exiccare corpus animus est, minime vero siccioris temperaturae praeditis, sanguinem enim crassarum partium gignunt & melancholicum. Circa hanc opinionum diuersitatem primo lessorem haud dubito meminisse, quod in verè philosophiâ Scholasticorum receptum est, s.c. variant-ium. Sed sperandum esse non autoritate, sed rationum pondera ac momenta consideranda esse. Quod si nos in præ-senti velitatione conabimur, Sciendum primùm verò, si certi quid concludatur, Medicos, cùm de temperatura aliquid rei loquuntur, nō de eâ loquuntur, quæ, si quælibet rēs per se considerata adepta est, (ad philosophum enim spectat hæc consideratio) ad hominis respectu, ut calidum, humidum, frigidum, siccum dicatur, quod humanum corpus calefacere vel frigefacere potest. Nō igitur cibo ũ natura, ut & leporinæ carnis temperatura exter-nā cum similitudine vel comparatione metienda est, sed relatione ad corpus hominis cibum sit, manuꝰ iudicium formandum, ex eo enim quid hominis cibus sit, an talem habeat cum homine similitudinem, ut conuerti in eius substantiam possit, dignoscitur, atq; hoc est ꝗ non aliud, quod facit aliquam rem, & dici ꝗ esse escam homi-nis. Si quis igitur restè indicare voluerit leporinā carnis temperaturam, ut escæ est, cognoscere ꝗ imprimis oportet, in quibus humores à calore humanô non vertat s, quod certè longam requirit expe-rientiam, teste Hipp. in Epidem. Cibi & potus experientia egent. Hoc s-go indicio standum, huius ꝗ inuendum, quod experientia ac obser-uationes, nec non rationibus consentientibus est. suffultum. Inter has validior aliis omnibus est, quae a carnibus substantia sumitur, quae in lepore satis dura est: quaecunque autem dura carnes constant, ut Galenus in expositione aphorif. 18.lib.2 c.s.de san.tuen. radius[?] nutriunt, idq; non leue frigiditatis & siccitatis argumentum existimant, exanguis enim & veluti vita vaporeq; omni aqueq; humore [illegible, ~10 letters] leporina videtur, quin & friabilis fibrisq; abundans, quae omnia siccam, duram, difficilem concoctu leporinam offendunt. An vero omne durum sit siccum, supra, ubi de carnium differentiis, annotatum reperitur.
units.tr: Yet opinions about the nature and temperament of this animal do not agree among the physicians. Some make its flesh of good juice, easy to digest, and say that it is free from all melancholy, moved by the authority of Galen, who in book 3 of On the Properties of Foods prefers the blood of hares to all others for its goodness and excellence of nourishment, on account of its smoothness and sweetness; for this reason it is customary for many to boil it with the liver and the other entrails of the hare and eat it. From this they conclude that hare flesh is not melancholic, because such blood is not; and also because the most weighty authors, among whom is Pliny, who wrote the history of natural things, and the poets, among whom is Martial, hand down that the beauty and grace of the hare are preserved to the seventh or ninth day. Others maintain that hare flesh, like that of all animals with long ears, produces melancholic juice, and that therefore girls cannot make the roses of their cheeks bloom from eating hare; they bring forward in support the venerable antiquity and the opinion drummed in through so many centuries and clung to stubbornly, which begins from Hippocrates, the most ancient author. For it is written in book 1 of On Diet, which everyone ascribes to Hippocrates, in this way: hare flesh is dry and astringent and moves the urine somewhat. After him Galen, or whoever he was, says in book 2 of On Foods that hare flesh generates thicker blood; and in his commentary on On Attenuating Diet he says it is useful in a drying diet but not in an attenuating one, because it generates thick blood. And in book 3 of On the Places Affected he says it has great power in generating melancholic blood. Psellus and Paulus agree with Galen in almost the same words, and after all of these Simeon Seth, in his book on foods, counted hare among the foods that generate black bile: "The flesh of the hare," he says, "is of such a kind that it draws together, and those who wish to dry out the body should use it, but by no means those of a drier temperament, for it generates thick and melancholic parts." Regarding this diversity of opinions, I do not doubt that the reader first recalls what is accepted in the true philosophy of the Scholastics, namely the distinction of variants. But it should be hoped that the weight and force of reasons, not authority, should be considered. If in the present skirmish we attempt this, it must first be known, if anything certain is to be concluded, that physicians, when they speak of the temperament of something, do not speak of that which belongs to a thing considered in itself (for that consideration belongs to the philosopher), but in relation to man: that something is called hot, moist, cold or dry according as it can warm or cool the human body. Therefore the temperament of hare flesh, as of food, is not to be measured by an external similarity or comparison with its nature, but judgement must be formed in relation to the human body that it feeds; for from this it is known what is human food, and whether it has such a likeness to man that it can be turned into his substance, and this is what makes a thing be called human food and nothing else. If anyone, then, wishes to indicate rightly the temperament of hare flesh as food, he must first know in which humours the human heat does not change them, which certainly requires long experience, as Hippocrates says in the Epidemics: "Food and drink need experience." I say that we must stand by this judgement, and that it must be found, that it is supported by experience and observations, as well as by consenting reasons. Among these the most powerful of all is that taken from the substance of the flesh, which in the hare is quite firm; and whatever flesh is firm, as Galen in his exposition of the eighteenth aphorism of book 2, chapter 5 of On Preserving Health, they think nourishes slowly, and they take this as no slight proof of coldness and dryness. For the hare seems bloodless and, as it were, devoid of life and vapour and every watery humour, and moreover friable and abounding in fibres, all of which show the hare to be dry, hard and difficult to digest. Whether, however, everything hard is dry, has been noted above, where the differences of flesh are discussed.

units.la: De altero, dura, quaeq; tardius & paulatim nutriunt, frigida, ut vulgo[?] Manardus, ea vero quae celeriter concoquuntur & nutriunt, esse calida, qui affirmant, vehementer mihi videntur errare.
units.tr: As for the other claim, that hard foods which nourish slowly and gradually are cold, as Manardus commonly holds, and that foods which are quickly digested and nourishing are hot, those who assert this seem to me to be seriously mistaken.

units.la: Multa enim sunt dura substantia cibaria, quae quidem longo post assumtionem tempore atque paulatim nutriunt ut sunt casei duri, carnes infumatae & salitae, nec non ova ad indurationem elixata: nam & haec inter duras efficas Galenus connumerat loco citato: Quis autem haec frigida dixerit, propterea quod duriora sint substantia, tardiusq; conficiantur, ac tardiorem habeant excretionem? (Nam quae velociter nutriunt, veloces habent deiectiones, inquit Hipp. aph. citato.) Et econtra multa velociter concoquuntur, velocesq; habent deiectiones, quae tamen calida omnia nemo sanus recte dixerit, nisi qui velociter, leniter ac infir-
units.tr: Many foods are hard in substance and nourish only long after they are taken, and only gradually: hard cheeses, smoked and salted meats, and eggs boiled hard. Galen counts these among the hard foods in the passage cited. But who would call them cold merely because they are harder in substance, are digested more slowly, and are evacuated more slowly? (For, as Hippocrates says in the aphorism cited, foods that nourish quickly have quick evacuations.) Conversely, many foods are digested quickly and have quick evacuations, yet no sane person would rightly call all of them hot, unless he wishes to be nourished quickly, gently and feebly.

units.la: mius nutriri cupit. Quin potius contrarium affirmi optimâ ratione posse exiſtimo, quo ſcilicet quicquam ſolidius est ac durius, cò firmius: humiſdum & calidum innatum id afferſunt & contiſnere, & é contra quò quiàtenerius est ac tenuium, eò citius & facilius etiam calidum innatum exſhalare & difflaſe. Firmius igitur nutriunt, esca duriores, licet tardius & concoquantur & deiiciantur. Fundamentum huius aflertionis rationibus; experientia & autoritate nititur. Galenus namq; ipse teſtatur, in fine expoſui citati aphor. 6, quæ cunq; tenuem habent humorem, distribuendum, celeritate quidem distributionis atq; appositionis exuperare, ſtabilem verò natu-ram non habere, ſed facile diffluxque verò crasſiores habent humores & tenaciores, tardius qui-dem distribuuntur, ſed ſtabilitas adherent partibus alendis. Qua de causa verè & recte Ariftote-les assa elixis humidior aſtatur, congenita vidisti humiditatis ratione, quæ in affatione asservatur, elixatione deperditur, nam elixa aduentitio, af-fa proprio humore abundant. Intelligentia verò Ariftidemodice assis est, alias in conso eſt igne affantem, ſ immodicus ſit, exterior & interior plus nimio exiccare, imò non rarius exurere.
units.tr: Rather, I think the opposite can be affirmed with the best reason: the more solid and hard a thing is, the firmer it is. It holds its innate moisture and heat together and contained, whereas the more tender and thin a thing is, the more easily and quickly it lets its innate heat escape and dissipate. Harder foods therefore nourish more firmly, although they are digested and evacuated more slowly. The basis of this assertion rests on reasons, experience and authority. For Galen himself testifies, at the end of his exposition of the sixth aphorism, that foods with a thin humour are distributed quickly and surpass the others in speed of distribution and apposition, but do not have a stable nature and flow away easily, whereas thicker and more tenacious humours are distributed more slowly but adhere stably to the parts to be nourished. For this reason Aristotle rightly says that roast meat is moister than boiled. You see that the innate moisture is kept in roasting and lost in boiling, since boiled meat takes up extraneous moisture while roast meat abounds in its own juice. It must be understood, however, that the meat is roasted in moderation. Otherwise, if the fire is immoderate, roasting dries the outside and the inside too much, and not infrequently burns them.

units.la: Ex his itaſe habetur, ibu(ita autem ſe habere, cer-tis documentis patefactum est, facile est pronuncia-re, duritiem in leporina(vt & in cerumina, de qua in ſequentibus frigiditatis indicium certum non est, nec unquam esse posse, argumento inter alia, quod sanguis eius saporis ac dulcedinis suauitate præstet, nec dilutus tenuisq; nimis nec crassus nimis sit, sed consistentia mediocris: carnem autem sanguinis sequi temperaturam & dispositionē, præter alia color, qui à sanguinis bonitate vel vitio dependet, ostendit. In hyposarca enim, mensium suppressione, febribus & splenetiçis, quibus lien vel epar, alterum vel virumq; procreandi aut depurandi sanguinis organum, induratum vel obstructum, aut quouis modo affectum est, lienore vultus pallescere animadvertimus, qui melancholicis peculiaris color est. At Alexandrum Senerum[?] Imper. quotidiano leporum esu venustatem ruboremq; vultus adeptum esse testatur notum illud, & non illepidum hendecasyllabum,
units.tr: From these things it is held, and it is easy to state, now that this has been shown by certain proofs, that hardness in hare (as also in venison, about which in what follows there is no sure sign of coldness, nor can there ever be) is not a sure indication of coldness. One argument among others is that its blood is outstanding in flavour and sweetness, is neither too diluted and thin nor too thick, but of medium consistency. The flesh, however, follows the temperament and disposition of the blood, as colour shows, among other things, which depends on the goodness or fault of the blood. In dropsy, suppression of the menses, fevers and splenetic disorders, in which the spleen or liver (either or both of which are the organs for producing or purifying the blood) is hardened, obstructed or otherwise affected, we notice that the face turns pale with a livid colour, which is the peculiar colour of melancholics. But the well-known and not unpleasant hendecasyllable tells us that the emperor Alexander Severus obtained beauty and a ruddy face from daily eating hare:

units.la: Pulcrum quod vides esse nostrum regem,
units.tr: The handsome king you see before you,

units.la: Quem Syrum sua detulit propago,
units.tr: Whom the Syrian line has brought forth,

units.la: Venatus facit, & lepus comesus.
units.tr: Makes hunting, and eats hare.

units.la: Ex quo continuum capit leporem.
units.tr: From which he constantly takes the hare.

units.la: Et Plinius l. 18. c. 19. gratiam corpori conci-liare leporem essum in 7. dies, vel etiam 9. venu-statisq; decore[?] prorogare scribit, ac in tanta per-suasione addit causam aliquam subesse debere.
units.tr: Pliny, book 18, chapter 19, also writes that eating hare for seven or even nine days brings grace to the body and prolongs beauty and comeliness; and, given so great a persuasion, he adds that some cause must lie behind it.

units.la: Quapropter leporina, licet melancholicæ sit temperaturæ (tales autem escæ firmiores apponunt nutrimentum, ut alibi demonstratum est) sicca, dura, non tamen ideo frigida, dura, siccaque procreabit sanguinem in corporis officina. Veterū n.omnium li-teris & memoria celebratum & proditum est omne & obid alimentum calidũ tñ frigidũ,cũ in sanguinem abierit, nutrit. abierit, calefacere, nen quidem sanguinis & calidi lidi innati qualitatem caloris, g-adum[?], ut Fer-nelius quod annotaut[?] lib.1. de morb.causis,c.
units.tr: Therefore hare, although of melancholic temperament (such foods, however, supply firmer nourishment, as has been shown elsewhere), is dry and hard, yet it does not for that reason produce cold, hard and dry blood in the workshop of the body. For it has been celebrated and handed down by the writings and memory of all the ancients that every food, however cold, nourishes once it has turned into blood, and warms it, not indeed to the quality of blood and innate heat, but in its own degree, as Fernelius notes in book 1 On the Causes of Diseases, chapter 14.

units.la: 14. Sed horum substantiam: latiuscam[?] enim æque calidum sanguinem, atque vinum, aut piper vel alium gignere qui censuerit, omnium sufficientia causarum vires & naturas succiret. E go etiam leporina sanguinem humoreq[?], sue natura con-sentaneos proferet, hoc est, consistentia crassiores, firmiores & tenaciores, sanguinemq; talem, qui spiritus contentos, calidumq; innatum non facile patitur exhalare ac diffl[?]are, & quoties externa occursu erroreq, dissipari, in quo unu[?] vel maxi-me vitae nostrae prorogandae ars consistit. Ad ex-tremum, quod quidam leporinae carnis frigidita-tem ex animalis timiditate offendere mordicus contendunt, eamq; ex sanguinis crassitie nigro-re[?], veletiam tenuitate & aquositate aiunt. promanere, sciendum, hoc obiectum non magni momenti esse. Quemadmodum enim crassi-ties aterq[?], sanguinis color non semper sunt frigi-ditatis indicium (cauri[?] enim sanguis, Aristotele etiā esse, crassissimus est & nigerrimus, spissiq;, animal calidum valde est) sic etiam ex sanguine ne dilutiori, tenuiori & aquositate quocunq; frigi-ditas, & ex hac timor tanquam illius signum, non semper & protinus est arguenda. In leone quidem siccitati coniuncta calidi[?] as facit audaciam & magnanimitatem, in lepore vero no[?]. Item. Itaq; omnis prorsus ratione caret, & comi-ferandum[?] ferandum potius quam vlterius refutandum est illorum obiectum, quo leporina frigiditatem defendant. Caliditas inquiunt, & siccitas in leone faciunt audaciam, ergo etiam in lepore, si talis esset, eam excitarent.
units.tr: But whoever thinks that the substance of hare makes blood as hot as wine, or pepper, or some other thing, would overturn the powers and natures of all the sufficient causes. Therefore hare too will produce blood and humours agreeing with its nature, that is, thicker, firmer and more tenacious in consistency, and blood of such a kind that does not easily allow the contained spirits and innate heat to exhale and dissipate, and that, whenever it meets external error or harm, is not dispersed; and in this, above all, the art of prolonging our life consists. Finally, as for those who stubbornly insist that the coldness of hare flesh arises from the timidity of the animal, and say that it arises from the blackness, or the thinness and wateriness, of its blood: it should be known that this objection is of no great importance. For just as thickness and dark colour of blood are not always a sign of coldness (for the blood of the ox, as Aristotle says, is very thick, very black and dense, and the animal is very hot), so too from blood that is thinner, more dilute and watery, coldness, and from it fear as its sign, is not always and immediately to be inferred. In the lion, indeed, heat joined with dryness produces boldness and magnanimity; in the hare, not so. Therefore their objection, by which they defend the coldness of hare, lacks all reason and is to be pitied rather than refuted at length. They say that heat and dryness in the lion produce boldness; therefore they would also excite it in the hare, if the hare were such.

units.la: Amygdala amara resistunt ebrietati, ergo omnia amara resistunt ebrietati. Logicus artib. vel leuiter initiati vitium agnoscent. Caliditas enim & siccitas in leone excitant audaciam, non quia tales, sed quatenus in leone excellunt, est enim summe calidus & siccus. Sic amygdalina amaritudo, non etiam alia quæuis, ebrietatem arcet, exindiuiduifica enim & specifica totius substantiæ familiaritate ac proprietate potentiam illam promanare occultior philosophia docet. Hactenus de lepore, cuius in cibatu gratia, succiq; bonitas ac præstantia paulò diutius me degustantem immorata est, foecundi namq; lepo-ris armos sapienti stellandos Horatius docuit, ganea non imperitus. Sunt qui clunes sectentur aridissime. Vetulorum armi totaq; anterior pars a culinis elixatur, ex aqua & vino addito pipere, postrema vel inassantur, vel panificio incrustantur, siccq; durant in multos dies, potissimum hiberno tempore. Pulli & iuuenes inter lautissimas dapes apponuntur, bimestres, & trimestres pretiosiores sunt & suaviores, ostimestres quoque commendantur, nec non semestres. Anniculi iam sordescere incipiunt, ultra in confessa damnatione sunt apud quosdam. Vulgata enim paræmia dicitur, veteres lepores anfereã, malo-rum denionum escam (ff:Certissimum est, tanto deteriores reddit, quàm ò magis as proceffrit. Antiqui loco clauso faciebant pingues è lepo-ris exceptos, (veteres enim Romani lepores non neglexerunt) quod hodie non ob feruatur, passim enim omnifere è tempore capiuntur, nã sic clauf virus quoddam redolere deprehenduntur. Le-porum fœcundiffimam effeinfulam Aftipalcam Hefiz,ander Delphicus scripsit, idq, euenif- ose-ra cuiu'dam Anaphai, qui in infulam istam, perdisibus refer am, duos lepores imuli, indeq, tanta exorta multi udo est. ut quotannis capentur multa millia, ancea vero non fuisse id a-nimal in infula illa, sed perdices. Sale affernati ac comesi insalubres censentur, perinde ac mustela falsa.
units.tr: Bitter almonds resist drunkenness; therefore all bitter things resist drunkenness. A logician, even one slightly initiated in the arts, would recognise the fault. For heat and dryness in the lion excite boldness not because they are such, but insofar as they excel in the lion, which is supremely hot and dry. So it is the bitterness of the almond, and not any other bitterness whatever, that keeps off drunkenness, since a more hidden philosophy teaches that this power flows from the individual and specific familiarity and property of the whole substance. So much for the hare, whose delicious flavour, and the excellence and goodness of its juice, kept me lingering a little long over tasting it. For Horatius, no novice at the gourmet's table, taught that the shoulders of the fruitful hare should be garnished for the wise. Some pursue the haunches, which are very dry. The shoulders and the whole front part of old hares are boiled in water with wine added and pepper; the hind parts are either roasted or crusted with pastry, and they keep dry for many days, especially in winter. Young hares and leverets are served at the most lavish feasts; those two or three months old are more prized and sweeter; eight-month-old ones are also recommended, and six-month-old ones as well. Yearlings already begin to go off, and beyond that some condemn them outright. For there is a common proverb that old hares are food for evil demons. It is quite certain that the older they become, the worse they become. The ancients used to take fat hares in an enclosed place (for the ancient Romans did not neglect hares), a practice not kept today, since now they are caught everywhere in every season, and in this way they are found to smell of some enclosed-place taint. Hesiander of Delphi wrote that the island of Astypalaea is very fruitful in hares, and this came about thus: a certain man of Anaphe put two hares into that island, which was full of partridges, and from these so great a multitude arose that many thousands are caught every year; before that, however, there was no such animal on that island, only partridges. Hares preserved in salt and eaten are considered unwholesome, just like salted weasel.

units.la: De ceruina.
units.tr: On venison.

units.la: Vlæ delitiis & ceruinam seruire in-primis, notum est, Magnatum enim Procerumque mensas opulentant. Est in exemplis fœminas quasdam Principes omnibus diebus matutinis, carnem ceruinam degustare solitas, longoque ævo caruisse febribus, quoniam id animal febrium morbos non sentire, Plinius tradit l.8.c.32. quin potius huic timori mederi. Verum ita demum id ra-tum existimatur, si vulnere vno interierit. Libidinis tempore caro cervorum vitiatur, fœtet enim perinde ac hircorum, quare cibis omninò tunc abdicanda, sicut & æstatis tempore, quo viperis vescuntur & serpentibus, unde siticulosi [?] fiunt, sitim tamen tolerant, eaque incenduntur, ipsi enim nolunt, quod, si aquam ante illorum coctionem hauserint, intereant:per hiemem tutius sumuntur, meliusque concoquuntur. Ex hinnulis verò ge-nerosæ principibus ac potentibus epulæ cō-cinnantur, eorū enim carnes salubres, sapo-req; mirè suaues sentiuntur. Porro vita cer-vis in confesso longa, post 100.annos aliquos captos cum torquibus aureis, quos Alexander Magnus addiderat, adopertis iam cute in magna obesitate, Plin.l.8[?].c.32. testis est. Aristoteles tamen videtur dubitare, cum nec ge-statio nec incrementum hinnuli ita eueniat, quasi vita esset prælonga. Certum est, si ad tantam senectutem pertingerent, carnes eorum omnis succi esse expertes, cibisq; hominum penitus abdicandas. Singulis annis Aprili mense cornua amittere dicuntur, quo tempore etiamnū occultantur interdiu, noctuq; pascuntur, donec cornua recipiant, quę primum quasi cute vestita, & molli lanugine plumata emittuntur, quibus portentosa ex-jam gula non pepercit, elixata enim in frustula postea friguntur, Regumq; is cibus habetur, de cuius natura dici aliud nihil potest, quam sunt. quam quod vires habere fit existimandum, quales ceruorum cornua, quę millibus remediorum nobilitantur, præcipuè verò aduersantur venenis, suffituque eorum abiguntur serpentes. Admultos quoq; vsus celebrantur adeps, medulla & sanguis.
units.tr: It is well known that venison is especially prized as a delicacy, for it enriches the tables of magnates and nobles. Pliny reports (book 8, chapter 32) that certain noblewomen used to eat venison every morning and lived a long time without fevers, since this animal is not thought to suffer from fevers, and the flesh was even believed to cure the fear of them. But this is held to be true only if the deer died from a single wound. At the time of rutting the flesh of deer is spoiled, for it smells just like that of he-goats, so it must then be wholly avoided as food, as also in summer, when they feed on vipers and serpents. From this they become thirsty, yet they endure the thirst and are inflamed by it, for they will not drink, since if they drink water before their food has been digested they die. Venison is safer to eat in winter and digests better. Meat from young stags is served at the tables of princes and the powerful, for their flesh is held to be wholesome and remarkably pleasant in taste. Moreover, the long life of stags is generally admitted: Pliny (book 8, chapter 32) is witness to a stag that was captured after some hundred years, still wearing the golden collar which Alexander the Great had put on it, its skin now worn and its body very fat. Aristotle, however, seems to doubt this, since the growth and carrying of a young stag do not happen in such a way as would suggest a very long life. It is certain that if they reached such great old age, their flesh would be entirely devoid of juice and wholly unfit for human food. Every year, it is said, they shed their antlers in April; during this time they are hidden by day and graze by night until the antlers grow back. These first emerge as if covered with skin and clothed in soft down. Even the monstrous gluttony of men has not spared them: they are boiled, cut into small pieces, and then fried, and this is regarded as food for kings. Nothing else can be said of their nature except that they are thought to have the powers for which the antlers of stags are celebrated in countless remedies, and that they are especially effective against poisons; by burning them, serpents are driven away. Many uses are also commended for the fat, marrow and blood.

units.la: De caprilla, hoedina, hircina.
units.tr: Of goat, kid, and he-goat.

units.la: CApris[?] sacerdotem adeo abstinere voluerunt prisci, ut non modo attingere, sed ne nominare quidem aut appellare liceret, siue quod id animal luxuriosum & olidū abhorrent, siue q; tanquā morbidū timerent. Comitiali enim morbo laborare caprās, nec non febribus graues autores tradūt, ideoq; animam forsan iis quam ouibus ardentiorem, concubitusq; calidiores esse. Flatus ructusq; ciere, choleramq; morbum parere, Hippocr. auctor est, quod tamen de nimis[?] tenellis, nimisq; adultis, & non probè coctis vel præparatis accipiendum esse quaedam existimant. Suauiorem caprinam esse, minusque malam, cum syluæ primum noua frequentiq; fronde germinant, virgultaque turgescunt, experientia docuit. Est in exemplis, athletam quendam Thebanum cunctos alios robore præcelluisse, quod sc.caprilla carne vesceretur, quam valentissimi esse alimēti, ob firmū, lentumque succum, nec facilē dissipabilem apud Arheneum reperitur.
units.tr: The ancients wanted priests to abstain from goats so completely that it was not lawful even to touch them, let alone name or mention them, either because they abhorred the animal as lustful and foul-smelling, or because they feared it as diseased. Serious authors report that goats suffer from the falling sickness and also from fevers, and therefore that their spirit is perhaps fiercer than that of sheep and their couplings hotter. Hippocrates is the authority that goat's flesh causes flatulence and belching and produces cholera, though some think this must be understood of goats that are too young or too old, and not properly cooked or prepared. Experience has shown that goat's flesh is sweeter and less bad when the woods first put forth new and thick foliage and the shoots swell. There is an example of a certain Theban athlete who surpassed all others in strength because he ate goat's flesh, which Athenaeus finds to be a most powerful food, on account of its firm and tenacious juice, not easily dissipated.

units.la: Sed hoedina inter eximias & præcipuè salubres epulas perpetuò adnumerata est, ficciorem enim agnina, esuiquè aptiorem esse communi conlenfu traditur,qnin & cætero-rum quadrupedum carnibus anteponitur: Hefiodus l.2. ωτ' ἐργων [?] &c. hoedorum primogenitorum carnem maximè commendat, vt boni succi,facilisque coctionis. Gedeoné [?] hoedum caprarium coxisse,angeloq;, quem inuitarat,in conuiuio apposuisse, sacra monimenta testantur. Sapiunt autem tunc maximè hoedi cum herbarum sunt expertes,bi-meftres,atque etiam trimestres, si mater la-ctea-bundet,adultiores enim & ab vbere depulsi saporis suauitatsq; gratiam amittunt. Nullam autem aliam magis idoneam à morbo se recolligentibus quidam promittunt, quin etiam otio deditis, & non laborantibus salubriter editur, grauiores verò operas exercentibus insalubriter, facilè enim alimentum eius dissipatur atque euanescit. Galenus l.de fan.tuen. Senibus non incommodam spondet. Manditur elixa pariter atque tolta [?], & quidem recens. Cocta, quæ refrixerit,ca-lente cesetur vtilior Mauritanorum opinione. Galenus frigidam esse edendam voluit in commentario l.4.de rat.vict.in acutis. Quod Plutarchus prodidit de caprina,qui eam gustarint aut attigerint,comitiali morbo affici, auditur verius quam creditur. Caeterum praeclaram in medicinis laudem ad varios vfus obtinuerunt, caprinū lac, fan-guis, fel, adeps, pilus, fimus, vrina, cornu, ie-cur, femina, caput. Delacte eiusq; inprimis fero fuo loco, vbi delactis differentiis. San-guis cum medulla coctus cotra toxica vene-na fumitur, nec non dyfenteriam & hydropi-fin, arefactus vero calculi medicamentis vti-literadhibetur. Iecur caprinum efitatum ve-fpertinam aciem reftituere dicitur his, quos lufciofos & ny&talopas vocant. Fel plurimis modis ad oculorum caligines, cicatrices, al-bugines, pterygia, rupturas tunicularū, cele-bracur cum melle vel mulieris lacte, autalio cōueniente liquore diftemperatū. Adeps in forbitione aliqua fumptus inteftina laxa & corrofa miré fareit, itatamé vt protinus hau-riatur frigida: hoedi vero feminū cineré rupta inteftina efficaciter refarcire à grauib.autori-bus proditū reperio. Cornuū pilorū q; fumo fugari ferpentes prifcæ autoritatis eft. Pilorū verò cinis calculos pellit. Cornu ipfo fuffiri vuluam vtiliffimū puatur. Vrinā apoftemata & fuppurationes lanari, cum melle permixta, quidam certo promittunt. Caprini capitis cū fuis pilis decocti fuccū laudatiffimū aiunt in inteftinis ruptis. Sed caprarū fimus, cuius cre-berrimus vfus eft, Galeno tefte, digerentis & acris facultatis eft, vt induratis fcirrhorum in modū tumoris. congruat. Ad aquā in-tercuté, fplenis affectus, calculos pellendos, duratus, dolodolores podagricos & Ischiadicos mitigandos varius eius usus est, nec non in extergendis psoricis humiditatib°, digerendi disq; paro-tidib°, ac diuturniorib° bubonibus. Hœdorū deniq; sanguinem recentem cum aceto cal-factum vtilissimè dysentericis propinari cer-tis documentis parefactū est. Superest hircina, q omniū animalium ab omnib° fœdissima habita est. Sicut ipsum animal fœdissimū esse in confesso est, ideoq; in cibo damnatū. Caprâ-tos tamen eximiè obesi ari ac pinguescere, gustatuq; non ingratos esse quidā experti sunt. Sanguinē hircorū præsentissimū ac validum lithontribon esse experimenta docuerunt. Iecoris eorū dissectā laniēs efficaciter sanguinē sistere dicitur. Hircinus verò adeps cū ca-præ fimo & croco, sinapiq; podagricis non inutiliter illinitur. Carnes deniq; hircinas epilepticis auxiliari Clem. Alexandrinus tradit, quod equidē mirum, cū de capris contrarium sit proditū, quod tamen de ouib. verisimilibus videri quidā non vulgaris literaturæ exīstimant, nempe, quoniā capite fere semper in terrā inclinato, halitus prauos, humiditatemq; sæpe maligna in caput trahunt, subindeq; obid in sacrū morbū incurrant: caprae verò, q alto capite vtplurimū pascunt, ficcēq; sunt, ac febrire magis dicunt, quomodo ouibus epilepsiæ magis, vt q à larga pituita oriat, subiiciant, nō admodū se intelligere fatētur, nisi ceteris animalib.comitiali morbo magis capras tentari quis dixerit ob meatuü densitatem & angustiam, quam arguit vocis tenuitas. Arift.in probl. quærens, cur homines foli vel maximè interanimalia oculis peruertantur, interalia hanc affert causam, quod fc.foli in animalium genere fiant epileptici, epilepsia auté oculorü peruerfione inducat.
units.tr: But kid's flesh has always been counted among the choice and especially wholesome dishes. It is generally agreed to be drier than lamb and better suited to the stomach, and it is even preferred to the flesh of other quadrupeds. Hesiod, in his Works and Days, especially commends the flesh of firstborn kids as having good juice and being easy to digest. Sacred records testify that Gideon cooked a kid of the goats and set it before the angel whom he had invited to dinner. Kids taste best when they have not yet eaten herbs, at two months and even at three, provided the mother is still giving milk; older kids, weaned from the udder, lose the delicacy of their flavour and sweetness. Some claim that no other meat is more suitable for those recovering from illness, and it is wholesomely eaten by those who are idle and not labouring; but it is unwholesome for those who perform heavier work, since its nourishment is easily dissipated and vanishes. Galen, in his book On the Preservation of Health, promises that it is not unsuitable for the elderly. It is eaten boiled or roasted, and indeed fresh. Meat that has been cooked and then allowed to cool is more useful than when eaten warm, in the opinion of the Mauritanians. Galen wished it to be eaten cold, in his commentary on book 4 of the Regimen in Acute Diseases. What Plutarch reported, that those who taste or touch goat's flesh are afflicted with the falling sickness, is heard more readily than it is believed. Moreover, goats have won high praise in medicine for many uses: goat's milk, blood, gall, fat, hair, dung, urine, horn, liver, testicles, and head. I shall treat of milk and its especially important uses in its proper place, when I discuss the differences of milks. Blood boiled with marrow is taken against poisons, and likewise against dysentery and dropsy; blood dried and powdered is used with success in remedies for stones. The liver of a goat, roasted, is said to restore evening sight to those whom they call purblind and nyctalopes. Gall, mixed with honey or a woman's milk or another suitable liquid, is used in many ways against dimness of the eyes, scars, white films, pterygia, and ruptures of the eyelid membranes. Fat taken in some drink marvellously heals slack and corroded intestines, provided it is swallowed at once and cold; and I find it reported by weighty authors that the ashes of kids' testicles effectively repair ruptured intestines. It is an ancient authority that the smoke of horns and hair drives away serpents, and the ash of hair dissolves stones. Fumigation of the womb with horn is said to be most useful. Some promise with certainty that urine mixed with honey heals abscesses and suppurations. They say the decoction of a goat's head with its hair is most praised for ruptured intestines. But goat dung, whose use is most frequent, is, according to Galen, of a digestive and sharp quality, and so it suits hardened scirrhous swellings. Its use is varied: for dropsy, for diseases of the spleen, for expelling stones, for easing gouty and sciatic pains, and likewise for cleansing the humours of psora, for dispersing parotid swellings, and for longstanding buboes. Finally, it has been shown by certain evidence that fresh blood of kids, warmed with vinegar, is most usefully given to those with dysentery. The flesh of the he-goat remains. Of all animals it has been regarded as the foulest by everyone. Just as it is agreed that the animal itself is most foul, so it has been condemned as food. Yet some who have tried it have found that he-goats grow exceedingly fat and plump, and that their flesh is not unpleasant to taste. Experiments have shown that the blood of he-goats is a very effective and strong stone-breaker. The liver of these, cut up and applied as a dressing, is said to stop bleeding effectively. Fat of the he-goat, mixed with goat's dung, saffron, and mustard, is smeared on gouty joints with some benefit. Finally, Clement of Alexandria teaches that the flesh of he-goats helps epileptics. This is indeed surprising, since the opposite has been reported of goats; yet some learned men think it is likely true of sheep, namely because sheep, with their heads almost always bent to the ground, draw foul vapours and often moisture harmful to the head into it, and so they readily fall into the sacred disease. Goats, on the other hand, which mostly graze with their heads held high, and are dry and more prone to fever, are not, as they confess, easily subjected to epilepsy in the way sheep are, which arises from a large amount of phlegm. They admit they do not understand this at all, unless someone should say that goats are more often attacked by the falling sickness than other animals, on account of the density and narrowness of their passages, which the thinness of their voice proves. Aristotle, in the Problems, asks why men alone, more than any other animals, are perverted in their eyes, and gives this cause among others: that man alone among the animals becomes epileptic, and epilepsy induces perversion of the eyes.

units.la: Quam sententiá falsam omnino esse quidam arbitrantur moti duobus: vnú est, quod ipse Arift.l.de animalib, nonnulla recenset, quæ iisdem morbis, quib.hominestentari scribit, vt ouesalterū, quod in lib.de sacro morbo, qui vt Hipp. à Galeno in progn.text.4.& lib.an sanguis in arteriis contineatur, nec non à Cælio Aureliano l.1.paff.chron.c.4. citatur, scriptum est, oues & maximè capras epileptico morbo nó parū obnoxias esse. Quicertè Hippocratis locus Ariftoteli repugnat, cuius sententiá sic moderandá esse Mercurialis l.4. var. lect. docet, quod homo vel maximè oculis peruertitur, quoniá vel solus vel maximè in infantia epilepticus fit. Vnde in l.de somno & vigil præceptú dedit, vt non solum pueri verum etiá nutrices à vino, præsertim nigro abstinerent, tanquá id magis quam album ad caput euaporet.
units.tr: Some think this opinion is entirely false, moved by two things. The first is that Aristotle himself, in his book On the Parts of Animals, lists some animals which he writes are subject to the same diseases as humans, such as sheep, the other point being that it is written in the book On the Sacred Disease, which is cited by Galen as Hippocrates in his prognostics, text 4, and in the book On Whether Blood Is Contained in the Arteries, and likewise by Caelius Aurelianus in book 1 of the Chronic Diseases, chapter 4, that sheep, and especially goats, are not a little liable to the epileptic disease. Indeed this passage of Hippocrates contradicts Aristotle, whose opinion Mercurialis in book 4 of the Various Readings teaches must be qualified: man is perverted in his eyes most of all because he alone, or most of all, becomes epileptic in infancy. Hence in his book On Sleep and Waking he gave the rule that not only boys but also nurses should abstain from wine, especially black wine, as it rises to the head more than white.

units.la: Pueros autem & infantiam epilepsia maxime tentari experientia notum est, tum quia fuperfluitatibus abundant, tum quia neruosas partes non habét validas, teste Galin expositione aphor.25.l.3.
units.tr: It is well known from experience that epilepsy attacks boys and infants especially, both because they abound in superfluities and because they do not have strong nervous parts, as Galen teaches in his exposition of Aphorism 25, book 3.

units.la: Galin expositione aphor.25.l.3.
units.tr: Galen, in his exposition of Aphorism 25, book 3.

units.la: De caprilla ferina.
units.tr: On the wild goat.

units.la: Numerosissimum ferarum caprarum ef-fegenus[?] constat, inq; plurimas similitudines reperire est transfiguratas. Sunt, caprea, sunt rupicapra, sunt ibices velocitatis admirandae, & dama seu caprea platycornes à cornuum latitudine. Inter agrestia autem animalia posterior & moderna medicina jucunditatis saporis carnes capreas & capreolos obtinere, facile concoqui, probumque praestare alimentum experimento vult, eaque omnia pernicitati, cursi-bus recursibusq; accepta refert. Elixas vero quam assas salubriores quidam putant, sic enim siccitatem ajunt temperari. Hodie magna-tum ac potentiorum mensas exornant, sed inas-sata magis quam elixa. De caprarum porro ferarum jecoris efpectabilior[?] potentia in medicina est, quam villicarum, tostum enim id & commanducatum aciem oculorum recreare, obtusamque clariorem reddere locupletissimis autoribus est proditum. (Caprarum meminit Marti-alis, cum inquit,
units.tr: The very numerous kind of wild goats consists of many species, and one can find many resemblances in them, transformed. There are the chamois, there are the rock-goats, there are the ibex of admirable swiftness, and the fallow deer or the goat with flat horns, so called from the breadth of its horns. Among wild animals, the later and modern medicine holds that the flesh and the kids of wild goats have a pleasant taste, are easily digested, and provide a wholesome food, as experience shows; and it attributes all these qualities to their agility, their running and their returning. Some think that boiled meat is more wholesome than roast, for they say that dryness is thus tempered. Today they grace the tables of great men and the powerful, but roasted rather than boiled. Moreover, the more notable power of the liver of wild goats in medicine is greater than that of domestic goats; for it has been handed down by the most authoritative writers that this liver, roasted and chewed, restores the sharpness of the eyes and makes dull sight clearer. (Martial mentions the goat when he says,

units.la: Pendentem summâ capream de rupe vi-debis, Casuram speres, decipit illa canes, quod tamen de rupicapris, quae cursu atque recur-su pernici per petras & montes, quo libue-rit, exultant, intelligendum est.
units.tr: "You will see a goat hanging from the top of a rock; you may hope it will fall, but it deceives the hounds." This, however, must be understood of the rock-goats, which leap about by their swift running and returning over rocks and mountains wherever they please.)

units.la: De agnina, vervecina, arictina, ovilla.
units.tr: On lamb, mutton, wether and ewe meat.

units.la: Ecus ovillum mille in re alimentaria praestat vsus: quanta enim gloria est in lanificio pro corporis tutela, tanta est carni, lacti, cafeoque ad idem cibandum. Extraordinarily, Ex-ordiri autem prius placuit ab infantibus, quae à parentibus.
units.tr: The use of sheep's meat is superior to a thousand other foods. For as great as the glory of wool is in protecting the body, so great is the value of its flesh, milk and cheese for nourishing it. But I think it best to begin with the young, and then the parents.

units.la: Agninam in antiquorum epulis preti-osam fuisse Graecorum latinorumq; monu-menta testantur. Frequentius hodie mandi-tur hieme assa magis quam elixa, sunt enim agni humidioris & vividioris naturae, qua de causa ficcioris temperaturae naturis, tabidis item & exteriuatis praestant. Summam nobilitatem & gloriam obtinuerunt in elegantioribus mensis, qui à binis ouibus diutius aluntur, nec herbarum nouerunt pabula, tum enim suauiores salubrioresque depre-henduntur, quanto enim junior agnus, tanto pituitofior concoctuque difficilior. Ut autem suaues, salubrioresque evadant agni, requiritur ouium plenus nutricatus, hae-nim fi bene alantur, bonos praestabunt fe-tus, à parentibus enim male enutritis mor-bidiue, fieri qui potest, vt foetus vitiatum temperamentum non contrahat? Apud Homerum in epulis agnina celebrata repe-fitur, quam tamen Samaritanis & Hierosolymi. lymitanis[?] Amos cap.6. exprobrat, vt qui co-mederent agnos de grege, hoc est, egregias, pingues, & ex toto ouium grege lectissi-mas. Tenellas oues, quod omittere hic noluerim, ante maturum tempus venere prurientes futurae pestis indicium esse quidam affirmant, quod quidem ego quotidianę observationi relinquo.
units.tr: Monuments of the Greeks and Latins attest that lamb was prized at the feasts of the ancients. Today it is eaten most often in winter, roasted rather than boiled, for lambs are of a moister and more lively nature. For this reason they suit drier constitutions, and also those who are wasted or emaciated. Lamb has gained the highest reputation and glory at the tables of the more refined, where it is fed on the milk of two ewes for a long time and has not yet known the pasture of herbs. Then it is found to be sweeter and more wholesome, for the younger the lamb, the more phlegmatic and harder to digest it is. But for lambs to turn out sweet and wholesome, a full suckling by the ewes is needed. For if the ewes are well fed, they will produce good offspring; but how can the young avoid acquiring a faulty constitution from parents who are badly or poorly nourished? In Homer, lamb is recorded as a dish at feasts, though Amos in chapter 6 reproaches the Samaritans and Jerusalemites for eating the lambs from the flock, that is, the choicest, fattest and most select of the whole flock of sheep. Some affirm that tender sheep, which I would not want to leave out here, when they come to their ripe age before the proper time, are a sign of coming plague. I leave this to daily observation.

units.la: Ouillam, sicut & arietinam, elegantio-rum quidem in epulis damnari inuenio, propterea, quod illa excrementosior fit fuc-cique pariter iniquioris, hæc vero odorem & saporem virosum referat, succi bonitate careat, vixque conficiatur, & ab hircina de-terrima habeatur. Verum multorum men-tas[?] ovillam opulentare, nec infimam grati-am retinere notum est. Pabula ovium sale respersa efficaciora sentiuntur, magisque eas opimant, carnesq; reddunt salubriores. An-niculæ non improbantur, sed quo plus ultra, eo difficilioris censentur coctionis. Vere porro primo ac medio ovillum pecus præstantius haberi, sicut omnia animantia, quę humili vescuntur herba, Galenus voluit. Juvenibus etiam ovillam non malum ci-bum esse, senibus vero eandem minus commodare, atque hac multo minus agni-nam idem 5.de sanitat. tuenda scriptum reli-quit.
units.tr: I find that ewe meat, like ram meat, is condemned at the tables of the more refined, because it is more full of waste matter and correspondingly poorer in juice, while ram meat has a rank smell and taste, lacks the goodness of juice, is scarcely digested, and is held to be the worst after goat. Yet it is well known that the palates of many make ewe meat rich and keep it in no low esteem. Pastures sprinkled with salt are felt to be more effective, and they fatten the sheep more and make their flesh more wholesome. Lambs are not disapproved of, but the further one goes, the harder they are judged to be to digest. Moreover, Galen held that in spring and midsummer the flock is considered finer, as are all animals that feed on low herbage. He also held that mutton is not a bad food for the young, but less suitable for the old, and he wrote in his fifth book on preserving health that lamb is much less suitable still.

units.la: Mirabilis hujus animalis merito ducitur fœcun-
units.tr: This animal is rightly regarded as remarkably prolific-

units.la: foecunditas, ut quæ quotidianæ populationi gulæ sufficere queat, quippe locupletes, plebs media, pariterq; infima vervecinam vorant: & paucos reperias, qui eam fastidiant. Mauritanam autem Medicinam auſtoritatem illam, quam in cibis tenet, verve- cinæ tribuisse reperitur, antiquior non inue- nitur. Verueces porro appellant arietes ca- stratos, quibus fc. testiculi exemti sunt, habi- tioris acquirendi corporis gratia, qui enim ad prolem generandam tenetur, dicitur a- ries. Anniculos verueces, bimos etiam trimosve, inprimis commendari certum est, quos & altiles facere inuentum est. Constat Ludoicum Borbonium Cardinalem in Belgica Gallia, nec non plures alios, nostris vulgaribus proceriores amplioresque ver- vecesaluisse, quos obefitare insignes aulicis proceribus ostentabat, dabatque epulan- dos. Generofissimos & suauissimos ad cibos educant Germania & Gallia. Italia non vsq; adeo his nobilitatur, Pistorienses tamen in gloria esse compertum est. Castrari denique agnos, nisi quinquemestres, præ- maturum tradunt.
units.tr: ity, since it can supply the daily gluttony of the palate. Rich people, the middling sort and the lowest common people alike devour wether meat, and you will find few who turn up their noses at it. The Moorish physicians are not found to have attributed to wether meat the authority it holds over foods, and earlier writers do not record it. Wethers are castrated rams, from which the testicles have been removed to gain a larger body; for a ram is the one kept for producing offspring. It is certain that wethers of one, two or three years old are especially recommended, and it has been found that they can be fattened. It is established that Cardinal Louis of Bourbon, and several others in Belgic Gaul, preferred wethers taller and larger than our common ones, which he displayed as distinguished to courtly nobles and gave them to eat. Germany and Gaul breed the most noble and sweetest wethers for food. Italy is not so famous for them, though the people of Pistoia are found to be well regarded. Finally, they report that lambs should not be castrated before five months.

units.la: De bubula, bubalina, vaccina, vitulina, taurina, iuvencorum & iuvencarum carnibus.
units.tr: On beef, buffalo, cow, veal, bull, and the flesh of steers and heifers.

units.la: Posteritati minime probro dandum est, quod ad vitæ usu bubulum pecus, in tanta præsertim fœcunditate transtulerit:
units.tr: It must by no means be cast as a reproach upon posterity that it has turned cattle to the use of life, especially given such abundant fecundity.

units.la: Licet enim apud majores olim bubulis visceribus vesci, scelus haberetur, maxima tamen & innumera mortalibus præstare cibaria expertum & compertum habetur.
units.tr: Although among our ancestors it was once considered a crime to eat beef, it has been tested and found that it supplies mortals with very great and countless foods.

units.la: Bubulam summo olim apud Græcos in honore fuisse, satis testatur Heroum usus apud Homerum, conviviorumq; & nuptialium epularum structura: Constat enim non solum bubulam, sed quorumvis animalium carnes, assas semper fere fuisse appositas. Agamemnon Rex convivio excipiens Ajacem aut Nestorem, costas boum assas posuit: Menelaus Telemacho, Ulyssis filio, hospitio comiter accepto, costam bubulam apposuit, ac in summa, bubula esum Homeri temporibus usitatum fuisse Atheneus quoque probat 1.lib.cap.4. Nullo autem non tempore epulas prebet bubula. Verum hieme magis placet & frequentior est: Elixatur pariter atque inassatur, & utraq; cultura gratissima est, præsertim opima & prapinguis [?]. Aulicis culinis ampla & pinguedine refertiora vocantur frusta regia, regia, quae si regiam menſa digna, ſolentſ prima fere menſa apponi elixa, eque ſinapis intinſlu eduntur magna gula aviditate & irritamenſto: varius aſſantur, praeter enim coſlas ex toto bove verubus nihil torreri ſolet, que inter elegantiores eſcas hiemis reponuntur a quibusſ dam, ſalviaque confixa expetuntur: crebrius eduntur ex condimento atro, vini aceto, mo-
units.tr: That beef was held in the highest honour among the Greeks of old is sufficiently shown by the custom of the heroes in Homer and by the arrangement of their feasts and wedding banquets. For it is well established that not only beef but the flesh of every kind of animal was almost always served roasted. King Agamemnon, entertaining Ajax or Nestor at dinner, set out roasted beef ribs. Menelaus, having courteously received Telemachus, son of Ulysses, as a guest, set before him a beef rib. In sum, Athenaeus also shows in Book 1, chapter 4, that beef was eaten in Homer's time. Beef provides a dish at any season. In winter, however, it is more pleasing and more frequent. It is cooked both boiled and roasted, and either way of preparing it is most agreeable, especially the fat and very fatty cuts. The large pieces, fuller of fat, which court kitchens call "royal morsels," since they are worthy of a royal table, are usually served first, boiled, and eaten with mustard dip, with great greed and appetite. They are roasted in various ways. Apart from the ribs, almost nothing is roasted on the spit from a whole ox. Among the more refined dishes of winter some reserve these, and they are sought after when stuck with sage. More often they are eaten with a dark seasoning of wine vinegar and [a sauce], with salt and pepper mixed together. The more luxurious call it a peppered seasoning.

units.la: mento, ſale ac pipere concinnato. Lautiores piperatum condimentum vocant. Caterum laniarum fraus & dolus hic detegenda mor-boſ ſepe bones mactantium, quos tamen ma- clare in ampliori bus urbibus lege cautum eſt. Cognoscuntur autem morboſ, cum fœno aut pabulo objecto abstinent, quo neglecto certum eſt magnas ſepe clades veſcentibus accidiſſe, praeſertim cum deprehenſum ſit, tabe pulmonis, morbisſ, alias pene confectos jugulatos eſſe, ini cibos admissos, carnibus ſilicet ſale alendo fa-multitudo aſſervatis. Qua avaritia quid quaque peſtilentius? vitiatam enim carnem vitio-ſos humores ac ſanguinem generare non veriſ-mile, ſed veriſſimum eſt. Idem qui ſilicet ad cultrum boves emunt, non conſiderant, qua reiruptice & paſtoritie periti examinant, sitem ſilicet calorem & nutricatum, tantumſ ſi pinguet ſint & habitori corpore, pragrandi-bus enim amplius, dignitas, & laus maxima, cumjusmodi nobilissima graminofiſimaq, regiones alunt, perá univerſum fere Germaniae orbem altialtiles pleneque saginatos mittunt. Sed & hodie in plerusque Germania locis saginati amplitudinisq; dignitate spectabiles atque insignes cernuntur. Est vero certa boves saginandi ars, qua ad tantam pinguitudinis molem eos extumescere faciat. Galenus herba adulta & proceriore facta, jamq; ad semen properante boves optimiores, crassiores bonoq; succo pleniores fieri censet.
units.tr: But here the fraud and trickery of butchers must be exposed, who often slaughter diseased cattle, though in the larger cities the law has forbidden this. Diseased animals are recognised when they refuse the hay or fodder put before them. It is certain that great harm has often come to those who eat such meat when this sign is neglected, especially since it has been found that animals nearly worn out by consumption of the lungs or other diseases were slaughtered and admitted into food, and that a great quantity of meat was preserved by salting. What is more pestilent than this greed? For it is not merely likely, but most certain, that tainted flesh generates bad humours and bad blood. Those who buy oxen for the knife do not consider what experts in cattle and herding examine: the age, the warmth and the nourishment of the animal, and whether it is only fat and of a good body. For the larger animals have more dignity and the greatest praise, and the most noble and grassy regions raise them, and from nearly the whole of Germany they send very tall, plump and well-fattened beasts. Even today, in very many places in Germany, fattened and remarkable cattle are seen, conspicuous for their size and dignity. There is indeed a sure art of fattening oxen, by which it makes them swell to such a bulk of fatness. Galen thinks that oxen are made better, fatter and fuller of good juice when they feed on grass that has grown tall and mature and is already hastening to seed.

units.la: ¶Multi herba autumnali & post prata secta proveniente, eleganter saginari boves existimant, quem morem multi germania populi studiose observant, in isto enim pabulo mul-tum emolumenti esse compererunt.
units.tr: Many think that oxen are elegantly fattened on autumn grass that springs up after the meadows have been mown, and many peoples of Germany diligently follow this custom, for they have found that there is much advantage in this fodder.

units.la: Quidam bubula al mentum in sanitate proroganda improbant; atramq; bilem, crassiorem q; gene-rare sanguinem affirmant, propterea q; largius crebrius q; ea vescentes, si obnoxii fuerint, alicui aegritudini splenicae, ut quartanae, scabiei, lepra, cibo esuq; eius oportuniores reddi, facili-usq; tentari. Verum de sale condita & suspen-sa id accipiendum. In amplis enim familiis boves ma es[?] simul ac foemina conduntur ad ci-baria annua famulorum operarumq;, deinde muria exemta pensilis servatur caro, qua adeo induratur, ut longiori etiam coctura postea per-tinacissime dometur, gustatuq; interdum suavi-tatem referat nullam. Potores hac commendata sibi habent tanq; acerrimum situs stimulü, aq; ac pernas sullas[?]. Ego otiosis et sellularis[?], literarumq; studiosis parcius hanc attingendam praemoneo, utpote parum vel nihil alentem, diutiffimeq; in stomacho morantem, concoctuq; difficilimam, & coctam licet vel confectam, peffimum tamen craffumq; succum in corpus distribuentem, dissecta enim rubet & infiguiter dura est. Interim negari non potest, appetentiam quandoq; momento eius affumto excitari atq; vecreari praesertim in vini avidioribus.
units.tr: Some reject beef as food for preserving health. They affirm that it generates black bile and thicker blood, and therefore that those who eat it too freely and often, if they are prone to any splenic ailment, such as quartan fever, scabies or leprosy, are made more liable to it by this food and are more easily afflicted. But this must be understood of beef that has been salted and hung up. For in large households bulls, males as well as females, are salted down for the year's provisions of servants and labourers; then the meat is taken out of the brine and hung up, and it becomes so hardened that it is afterwards subdued only with very long cooking, and on tasting sometimes has no sweetness at all. Drinkers esteem it as a very sharp stimulus for thirst, as well as for their legs. I advise that students and sedentary people, who are idle, and devoted to letters, touch it only sparingly, since it nourishes little or nothing, lingers a very long time in the stomach, is very hard to digest, and, even when cooked or thoroughly done, distributes a very bad and thick juice into the body; for when cut it is red and unpleasantly tough. Meanwhile it cannot be denied that the appetite is sometimes stirred up in an instant by taking some of it, especially in those more eager for wine.

units.la: Adextremum non praetereundum, Galenum 2. de simplic. medicam. referre, coquos, antequam vel pisces, vel carnes assarent, oleo in-ungere solitos, creditq; ideo hoc ab ipsis factitatum tum esse, ne exteriores partes vignis exustæ con-sumerentur, interiorumq; coctionem impedi-rent.
units.tr: Finally, I must not pass over the fact that Galen, in book 2 of On Simple Medicines, reports that cooks used to rub oil on fish or meat before roasting it. He believes this was done so that the outer parts would not be burnt up by the fire and the inner parts would not be hindered from cooking.

units.la: Mercurialis l. 1. variar. lect. id factum etiam potius esse existimat, ne carnium intestinum & proprius humor extra fluerent, sed intus cohibitus bitus coctusq; iucundiorem cibum palato red-deret. Oleum enim occludere eximos corpo-rum meatus, quo minus quicquam effluere que-at, & Galenus fasse est, & Alexander, quia in-probl.ea ratione animalia infectas ab oleo enecaridiputat, prohibita ex olei obftipatione nativa eorum spiratione: & hoc pacto affata intellexit: fe Ariftotelem verisimile est, quando in 4. demixtorum affectibus lib.ea elixatis humidiora facit. Quinquam affata etiam intus humi-diora evadunt, cum multo igne flatim extimiscrusta cem lorica inducitur, qua inducta humorintranem non ita promte valet exorbere atqueforas. foras erumpere, quod in affandum cumprimis observandum. in pluribus enim humor ille nutri-mentalis vi ignis, elicitur atq; consumitur, nihilq; [?]huius humoris retinetur, unde minus etiam nutrimenti vescentium con partibus accedere in confesso est.
units.tr: Mercurialis, in book 1 of Variae lectiones, thinks it was done rather so that the meat's own juice and natural moisture would not run out, but would stay inside and cook, making the food more pleasing to the palate. For oil closes the finest pores of bodies so that nothing can flow out. Galen says this, and so does Alexander, who in his Problems holds that animals killed by oil die because the oil clogs their natural breathing. Aristotle probably understood it in this way too, when in book 4 of On the Affections of Mixed Bodies he makes boiled foods moister. Yet roasted foods also become moister inside, because with a strong fire a crust forms at once like a coat of armour, and once it is formed the moisture cannot easily force its way out. This must be especially observed in roasting, since in most cases that nutritive moisture is drawn out and consumed by the force of the fire, and none of it is kept back. It is therefore agreed that less nourishment reaches the body of those who eat.

units.la: Bo ves fœminas notum est plerunq; vetulas lanio tradi, cum aut senectute sterilescunt, aut alia de causa inutiles evadunt. Sed sic effœ-ta ad elegantiores cibos damnantur, pauperum-que precipue vulgiq; mensas subeunt, magis e-nim insalubris earum caro, quam vetulorum bovum censetur.
units.tr: It is well known that cows are generally handed over to the butcher when they are old, either because they have become barren with age or because they have become useless for some other reason. Such worn-out animals, however, are condemned to cheaper food and mostly end up on the tables of the poor and common people, for their flesh is judged less wholesome than that of old oxen.

units.la: Veteribus bubalum seu bufalum (quo nomine bovem ferum & sylvestrem significari inuenio) non fuisse incognitum (ut quidam putarunt) probari potest ex Flavio Iosepho l. 8. antiquit. vbi quotidianos sumtus mensæ regiæ Salomonis enumerans etiam feros bubalos vna cum cervis refert. Quin & Amos horum mentionem facit, Numquid, inquit, currere queunt in petris equi, aut arari potest in bubalis? vbi Bened. Arias [?] Montanus stupidius, quam bovi bubalo ingenium esse & indocilius. Armenta horum in Italia circa Pisas videntur, & in Romanorum agris, nam Roma carnem eorum non venalem tantum esse, Judais in gratissimo cibatu, verum etiam ex latte eius animalis caseos confici Roma aliusq; in locis in pretio, maximi etiam cibi, sed qui sumti difficilius transeant,
units.tr: That the bubalus or buffalo (a name which I find to denote a wild and untamed ox) was not unknown to the ancients, as some have thought, can be proved from Josephus, Antiquities book 8, where, listing the daily provisions of Solomon's royal table, he also mentions wild buffaloes along with deer. Amos too mentions them: "Can horses run upon the rocks? Or can one plough with buffaloes?" Benedictus Arias Montanus, however, rather foolishly says that the buffalo has a nature more stubborn and less tractable than an ox. Herds of them are seen in Italy around Pisa and in the fields of the Romans. Their meat is not only sold in Rome but is a great favourite with the Jews as food, and cheese is made in Rome and other places from the milk of this animal. It is highly valued and is a very great delicacy, but when eaten it passes through the body with difficulty.

units.la: Columnella scribit. Phil. Camerarius in medit-tion. lib. cent. 2. testatur de caseo hac vera esse, enim cum nanseaid expertum, aitq; bubali-nam carnem infustis dura esse coctionis, dulce-req; suo insipidam. Alii tanto lentore pre-dicam eam afferunt, ut in parietem adastatene-cuissime adhæreat, quæ de causa menstruat-bus abdicandam censent, idq; juratissimis affir-mant verbis. Sed forsan ventriculo silli non ma, adeo fuerunt robusto.
units.tr: Columella writes of this. Philipp Camerarius, in his Meditationes, century 2, testifies that what is said of the cheese is true, for he tried it and felt nausea, and he says buffalo meat is hard to digest and, though sweet in its own way, insipid. Others say it is so sticky that it clings to the wall of the stomach, and for this reason they think it should be avoided by menstruating women, and they affirm this with the most solemn oaths. But perhaps those people's stomachs were not so weak; they were very robust.

units.la: Bovis adulti nondum castrati, quia ad-missura servantur, tauri vocantur. Horum carnem omnium fere sententiis proscriptam re-perio atq; damnatam. Castrati autem ante ma-turam (postea enim non dibent, nam dura sunt, Varrone teste) nondum laboris fracti, mediq; ætatis, utiliores habentur, vehementer enim alit, alimentumq; quod subministrant, non facile dissipatur. Raro tamen macellum intrant, mus srure fracto, aut aliacaufa nutriles ad agricul-turam fuerint. Laudem tauroruṁ siluesse hic naturalium rerum peritiqvitio vertent, qui ob-feruarunt, licet hoc animal in libidinem admo-dum esseratum sit s concitatum, non tamen se-pius quam bovis in direfcendere, a concepta vero spiritus vacca, modestum castum, ultius nihil moliri, unde tanta in hieroglyphicis Egyptiorum temperantia s continentia suit symbolum. Quo libidinosi monentur, ut ab hoc brutæ exemplum sumentes in conjugio alienos amores non sectentur.
units.tr: An adult bovine that has not yet been castrated and is kept for breeding is called a bull. I find that almost everyone condemns and rejects its meat. Oxen castrated before full growth (for afterwards they are not fit, since they are tough, according to Varro) are considered more useful; they are not yet worn out by labour and are of middle age. They nourish strongly, and the food they supply is not easily dissipated. They rarely enter the butcher's, unless they have been broken in strength by an accident or some other cause, or have been kept for farm work. Here those experts in natural things who have observed this say that, although this animal is very inflamed and stirred to lust, it nonetheless does not mount more often than a cow in heat; but once it has conceived, the cow becomes modest and chaste and attempts nothing further. Whence such temperance and continence became a symbol in the hieroglyphics of the Egyptians. By this the lustful are warned: taking example from this brute beast, they should not pursue other men's loves within marriage.

units.la: {a} Tautina.
units.tr: {a} Tautina.

units.la: Vitulinam, suauitatemq; saporis ac odoris in ea fragrantiam celebrat Mauritanorum omnium acerrimi ingenii Auerrhoes, quam etiam gallinaceae anteponit. Quare intrepidè tutoque à se semper ægris datam constanter af-ferit. Secuta medicina ex hujus sententia in præcipuam salubritatis admirationem eam evexit. Verum commendatio illa examina-tione indiget. Certum est recenter editos plu-rimum & lentoris, & vividi humoris obtinere, tantoq; esse ficciores, minus autem humentiores, quanto à partu longius recesserunt. Multi Germania tractus vitulos & vitulas, mensem unum & quandoq; eo minus natos, aut etiam sesquimensem laniis tradunt. Sunt alii tractus, in quibus macellum non subeunt propter majorem utilitatis spem. Sunt qui plane in cibis iis abstinent, oletum citius, quam vitulinam expetentes, ut septentrionales quidam, quibus ferum plane & insipidum palatum est. Romani Italorumq; complures semestri, aut etiam anno toto à lacte eos non depellunt, caventq;, ut herbarum expertes aliorumq; pabulorum, per id tempus degant, sic enim jucundiores, pretiosiores, & salubriores ipsorum fieri carnes experimento didi-cerunt, proindeque Cardinalitias, Pontificias, nec non Regias mensas lautissimas esse persua-sum habent, si vitulina apponatur. Hoc cibo inire delectatus[?] dicitur Franciscus Galliarum Rex huius nominis primus: nec nō hodie in splendidis amplisq, vrbibus vulgatissimi cibi est vitulina, inter grandiorum animalium carnes facile tenens primas, siue elixetur, siue assetur: vnde ru-stici[?] ita rem suam dispensant, vt nullo non tempore supersint, ex quo commodum percipiant lucrum. Caeterum vitulinam jurulentam magis alere quam assam, assamque magis quam frixam, seu butyro lossam, experiuntur, qui crebrius ac largius ea vescuntur. Magnicum etiam artificium hic jure requiritur, vt exquisite sciat vitulina probeq, vel elixetur, vel inassetur, ita quidem, ne humiditas illa nutri-mentalis plane exorbeat, vt supra quasi, annotatum est.
units.tr: Averroes, the sharpest mind of all the Moors, praises the flesh of the calf, its sweet taste and the fragrance of its smell, and he prefers it even to chicken. Therefore he asserts that he always gave it to his sick patients confidently and safely. Medicine, following his opinion, has since raised it to special admiration for its healthfulness. But that praise needs examination. It is certain that recently born calves have a great deal of sticky and lively moisture, and the further they have gone from birth, the drier and less moist they are. Many regions of Germany hand over calves, both bulls and heifers, born a month or sometimes less, or even a month and a half, to the butcher. There are other regions where they do not go to the butcher, because of the greater hope of profit. Some people abstain entirely from these foods, preferring goat to veal, as certain northerners do, whose palate is wholly rough and insipid. The Romans and many Italians do not wean them from milk for half a year or even a whole year, and they take care that during that time the calves live without grass and other fodder. For they have learned by experience that their meat becomes more pleasant, more valuable and more wholesome in this way. Therefore they hold that the tables of cardinals, of the Pope and of kings are most sumptuous if veal is served. Francis I, King of France, is said to have delighted in this food. Even today, in splendid and large cities, veal is the most common food, easily holding first place among the meats of larger animals, whether boiled or roasted. Hence country people manage their stock so that veal is available at all times, and from this they gain a profit. Moreover, those who eat it often and in quantity find that veal broth nourishes more than roast veal, and roast veal more than veal fried or fried in butter. Great skill is also rightly required here, so that one knows exactly whether veal should be boiled or roasted, and in such a way that the nutritive moisture does not wholly escape, as noted above.

units.la: De juvencorum porro, ex juvencarum carnibus, non adeo difficile est aliquid astruere, vel judicare, si modo dicta ad memoriam revo-centur. Etiam eum autem duriuscum ex siccitatem perrerein confesso est. Vitulinis quoq, auctoritate inferiores esse ex precedentibus ex antedistis patere arbitror. Semestres ex annicula, bima, trimestri, in cibis a quibusdam mire expetuntur, vt lenter enim nutrire experimentis multis patefactum est. Invenci tamen rarius a quibusdam mastantur. Invence venerem non expertes labe dabiliores existimantur, ampliusque, ea augentur, quo plus temporis venereorum expertes degunt, recentiores autem, quam annicula vene-rem non patiantur[?].
units.tr: It is not so difficult to make some assertion or judgement about the flesh of yearling and young heifers, if only what has been said is recalled, even though it is admitted that it is somewhat tougher because of its dryness. I think it is clear from what has gone before that they are inferior in quality to veal. Calves of six months, of a year, of two years or of three are eagerly sought by some for food, since many experiments have shown that they nourish gently. Young bullocks, however, are eaten more rarely by some. Young heifers that have not yet experienced mating are judged more delicate, and they grow the better the longer they live without experiencing the sexual act. Younger ones than yearlings do not submit to mating.

units.la: De Suilla memoratu digna.
units.tr: On the pig, worth mentioning.

units.la: EX nullo animali numerosiores ganeæ dapes præparari, suesque[?] nihil habere præter escam, tantumq; donatas à natura ad epulandum, antiquissimi[?] pariter ac prudentissimi Philosophi prodiderunt.
units.tr: The most ancient and most prudent philosophers have recorded that no animal supplies a greater variety of dishes for the gullet than the pig, and that the pig has nothing but its food, and was given by nature for feasting alone.

units.la: Itaq; iis animam pro sale datam, ne caro viuenti putresceret, Chrysippus ait. Nihil enim fere in hac pecude reperias, quod edendo non sit, suamq; propriam suauitatem repræsentet. Hinc abdomina prisci s celebrata, glandia, testiculi, vuluæ, iecinora, verrina, & nostra memoria maxime nobilitantur latera, coxæ tam priores, quam posteriores sale macerate & suffitæ pernæ dictæ & petasones, aures, pedes, costæ, spina, sanguis & intestina ipsa, & operosum esset singula recense-re cibaria, quæ ex illis parantur. Titus Quintius ante tribunatum & prœturam consul designatus, in Chalcide apud hospitem cœnans miratus esse traditur carnium copiam varie-tatemq;, hospite vero affirmasse illas omnes suillas esse, condimentis saltem & præpara-tionib. differentes. Convenit autem inter omnes percelebres medicos, suillam boni fac-ci[?] esse, valentissimumq; omnium escarum nutrire: testantur id fossores, messores, huius-modiq; alii grauiorum operarum, hos enim, si alio cibo pascere velis, imbecilliores reddes. Nam etsi parem alterius obsonii molem pridie assumserint, postridie si æq; laboraverint, infirmiores erunt minusque validi, & ad opera promti. Qui igitur suillam frequenter comedunt, plene se nutriri deprehendent, ce-lerrimeq; excrementorū copia abundabunt, q arctissime meminisse velim literarum stu-diosos, & qui domi sedent otiosi: congesta[?] n. illa excrementa laborib. & vehementiorib, frictionib. dissipanda sunt ac discutieda.
