Ca-terum teterrima antiqui porci caro censetur ut q ægre concoquatur, concoctaq; sanguinē atra bile contaminet: optima vero & ad gulę illecebras & ad corporis alimonią est porco-rum mediæ ætatis caro, non obesa nimis, nec macra nimis, porcorū inq;[?], qui veteris victi-mæ, vel non excesserint, vel nondum annos assecuti sint, hi enim facile concoquuntur, sanguinem; probum generant, & ad bonos gignendos succos carnem habent aptissimā, & probatissimam. recte Gal. l.4. reg. acut. Etin[?] l. 1. ad Glauc. exquisita tertiana affectis, præ-ter testiculos & alas gallorum, vitellaq; ouo-rū sorbilia, porcorum pedes & cerebra, porcel-lorumq; carnes in jure albo liquefactas præ-bet, effœtaq; à morbo convalescentium vires illarum esu reficere præcipit his verbis: Suil-lasait, carnes edere à pedib. in Ptisana elixis incipient, post vero etiam imum crus recte sumét, ab hoc etiam reliquas partes primum quiquidem porcelli juvenis, qui, si hiems sit, et-iam prid e macterur. nam hesternus, quare-cens macatus facilius concoquitur: astatefat fuerit, si mane immolatus porcellus sit, accirca solis occasum comedatur. Gal. 7. meth. Necabs re hoc pcepiffe videtur, omnium n. e fculentorum, q nota sunt, caro porcina valen-tiffime nutrit, si modo concocta fuerit, (nihil enim nutrit, nisi natura viribus concoctur.) adeoq; magna habet cum humana affinita-tem & similitudinem, vt non modo nostro aevo in Gallia, sed & Galeni tempore Romae, scelerati quidam Pandochei & caupones,carnem humanam cum aromatib. in paftilliscoctam pro suilla magni vendiderint, neccomeftores alteram ab altera sapore, odoreaut colore discernere poterant, donec huma-nus digitus per negligentia cum sua vngue coctus & repertus atrox mox coci facinus didit, q& meritas supplicio in furca pepedit poenas. Porro recente suillam, h.e. nuper ma-ctatae fais, faleq; non aspersam, stomacho esse grauem, difficulter concoqui, aliuique quan-doq; fluuium liberali vefcentib. ciere quo-tidiano experimento constat. Mucofa n. & praehumida est, qua de causa pituitosis & fri-gidis naturis crebrior illius vsus noxius est. Porcellos seu lacteos porcos opipara conui-via admittitur, mefaeq; elegatiores, sed magnoerrore prandiis potius, q coenis hodie edunt,
units.tr: Hence Chrysippus says that a soul was given to the pig in place of salt, so that its flesh would not rot while the animal was alive. Indeed, you will hardly find anything in this beast that is not fit to eat and does not show its own particular sweetness. From this, the ancients celebrated and in our own day the following are especially prized: the belly, the glands, the testicles, the womb, the liver, the sow's flesh, and the sides; the hams, both front and back, cured in salt and smoked, which are called pernae and petasones; the ears, feet, ribs, spine, blood, and the intestines themselves. It would be a laborious task to list every dish prepared from them. Titus Quinctius, before he became tribune and praetor, while still consul-designate, is said to have dined at Chalcis with his host and to have marvelled at the abundance and variety of the meats. But his host assured him that they were all pork, differing only in seasoning and preparation. Moreover, all the most renowned physicians agree that pork is of good quality and the most nourishing of all foods. Diggers, reapers, and other men of this kind who do heavy labour bear witness to this: if you wish to feed them on other food, you will make them weaker. For even if they have taken a similar quantity of some other food the day before, if they have worked equally hard the next day they will be weaker, less robust, and less ready for work. Therefore those who eat pork often will find themselves fully nourished, and they will very quickly abound in an abundance of excrement. I would especially wish students of letters, and those who sit idle at home, to remember this, for that excrement, once gathered, must be dispersed and dissolved by labours and more vigorous rubbing. Otherwise, the flesh of an old pig is considered most loathsome, because it is digested with difficulty and, once digested, contaminates the blood with black bile. The best flesh, both for the pleasures of the palate and for nourishing the body, is that of pigs of middle age, neither too fat nor too lean, provided they have not passed the age of the old victim, or have not yet reached their years. For these are easily digested, produce good blood, and have flesh most suitable and most approved for generating good humours. Galen rightly says so in book 4 of the Methodus medendi and in book 1 of the work addressed to Glaucon. For those affected by a tertian fever in its exquisite form, he provides, besides the testicles and wings of cocks, the sorbile yolks of eggs, the feet and brains of pigs, and the flesh of piglets melted in white broth. And for those whose strength has been wasted by disease and who are recovering, he advises restoring their strength by eating these, in these words: "Begin to eat pork flesh from the feet, boiled in ptisana; afterwards, indeed, you may rightly take also the lowest part of the leg, and then the remaining parts from this." Also the young piglet, which, if it is winter, should be salted the day before, since flesh salted the previous day is more easily digested than flesh salted the same morning; in summer, if the piglet has been slaughtered in the morning, it should be eaten about sunset. Galen seems to have understood this from experience as well. For of all the foods that are known, pork flesh nourishes most powerfully, provided it has been well digested (for nothing nourishes unless it is digested by the natural powers). And it has such great affinity and likeness to human flesh that not only in our own age in Gaul, but also in Galen's time at Rome, certain wicked innkeepers and tavern-keepers sold human flesh cooked with spices in pastilles as pork at a high price, and the diners could not tell one from the other by taste, smell, or colour, until a human finger, carelessly cooked with its nail and found, soon revealed the cook's atrocious crime, and he paid the deserved penalty on the gallows. Moreover, that fresh pork, that is, the flesh of pigs recently slaughtered and not sprinkled with salt, is heavy on the stomach, difficult to digest, and sometimes provokes a flux in those who eat it freely, is established by everyday experience. For it is slimy and very moist, and for this reason its frequent use is harmful to phlegmatic and cold constitutions. Suckling pigs, or milk-pigs, are admitted to sumptuous banquets, and people today eat them as the more refined dishes, but with great error they eat them at lunches rather than at dinners,

units.la: in quibus valentiora & vtiliora alimenta plæriq; promittunt. Assi autem frequentisi- me mensas subeunt, elixi raro: calidique e- deadi potius quam frigidi, & absque cute, quamtamen igne retorridam jucundissime quidam vorant. Olim quoq; in pretio eos fuisse testatur. Martialis l.13.
units.tr: in which most people promise more powerful and more useful nourishment. They are served most frequently roasted, and rarely boiled; warm rather than cold, and without the skin, though some eagerly devour them roasted by the fire. The ancients too, Martial testifies, held them in high esteem, in book 13:

units.la: Lacte mero pastum pigra mihi matris alumnæ Ponat, & Æ tolo de sue diuas edat.
units.tr: Let my lazy foster-mother's pampered nursling be served on pure milk, and let the goddesses eat from an Aetolian sow.

units.la: Sed de Suillæ carnis alimonia omnia ha- &tenus dicta, neminini non perspecta esse arbi- tror. Unus Hippocrates l.4. de Pulsana, & 4. regimin. acut. de suillæ carnis differentia multorum ingenia torsit, vbi carnes porci- nas vituperat, suillas vero commendat: Por- cinæ carnes, inquit, siue ambustæ, siue sub- ctudæ, malæ, nam & bilem pariunt, & turba- tionem: Suillis nullæ aliæ meliores sunt, idq; si non admodum pingues, neque etiam per- tenues sunt, ac neque veteris victimæ sta- tem sint assecutæ: at vero rejecta pelle, & subfrigidæ edende sunt. Vbi sciendum, vete- res græcos porcellos lactentes & adhuc sub- rumes χοίρως appellasse, horumq; esum ob viscidos & crudos humores carnis. Hippoc. improbasse, cui subscribit Gal. 3. de alim. & 2. de temper. merito, inquiens porcelli tanto magis excrementitiam prebent nobis alimo- niâ, quanto sunt magnis suib. humidiores, & min° quoq; nutriût. Nap n.editi quoiuis animali terrestri, quo homo vescitur, carnem habent humidiorem, sanguinis à phlegmate viscosi comitem. Differentiam hanc apud Homerum Eumæus Subulcus Vlyssis, quem ex bello Troiano & naufragio sibi tum ignotum, reducem hospitio excepit, obseruat dicens, Ede ô hospes, nam hæc choerea, porcellorum carnes, debentur & supersunt famulis, proci verò Penelopes obesos, & spumantes sues adultos edunt, qui delphaces dicebantur, sicenim nominabant sues corpus robore compactum habentes, & qui adolescant. Ut autem carnes suauitatem adipiscantur & iucunditatem, adq; pinguedinem sues adolescant, glande maximè aluntur, faba, hordeo, cæterisque frumentis, facilè enim ad quoduis pabulum assuescunt. Vrbium pisto-res frugum farina & furfuribus saginant ad tantam sæpe pinguitudinem, ut vix loco se mouere queant, & si alio quis transferre velit, plaustro id faciendum esse. Pinguedo & adeps horum, aptissimum aliarum escarum condimentum est. Carnes pro glandium natura variare certum est: fagineam enim su-em hilarem facere, carnem coctibilem, leue, & stomachoque utilem: ilignam suem nitidam, angustam, ponderosam: quernam diffusam, grauissimam, certi autores tradunt. Montanorum quoque caro domesticarum carni præfertur, grata enim his in lauro voluptatio, locisque obscenis. Quare, qui sues domi alunt, curabunt, vt cubile semper sit mundū, cribroq; ue fuliaverrantur, hæc enim cura ad carnis suauitatem, salubritatemq; pluri-mum facit. Quoad tempora, præstantiores quæ sub hiemis initium nascuntur, determi-næ, quæ æstate, plærunque enim grandini reddūtur obnoxiæ, præsertim autem gran-dinosi fiunt. Aristotele teste, quorum crura, collum & armi carne constant, quibus parti-bus vel plures grandines innatici conspici-untur. Dulcior autem caro est, cum paucio-res sunt grandines. sic multas habet, humida valdè & insipida est. Certum est non parum dotibus, & gloriæ suillæ detrahere grandinè, vt & pretio. Qui grandent probantur ante emtionem, facileque cognoscuntur, parte e-nim linguæ inferiore habentur grandines, & si setam dorso euellas, cruorem in radice pili euulsi videris, cum lactent, grandine carent. Morbosas igitur, visceraque habentes vitia-ta non attingent sanitatis vitæque prorogan-dæ studiosi, sunt etenim, quibus lien in tu-morem attollitur atque induratur, quod non accidit, nisi à corporis temperamento vitia-to.
units.tr: But all that has been said so far about the nourishment from pork I think is known to everyone. Hippocrates alone, in book 4 On the Diet in Acute Diseases and in the Regimen in Acute Diseases, has tormented the minds of many concerning the difference in pork flesh, where he finds fault with the flesh of the wild pig but commends that of the domestic pig: "Wild pig flesh," he says, "whether roasted or boiled, is bad, for it produces bile and disturbance. Of all the swine, none are better than those which are neither too fat nor too thin, and which have not passed the age of the old victim. But they must be eaten with the skin removed and somewhat cold." Here it should be noted that the ancient Greeks called suckling and still tender pigs [χοίρους], and Hippocrates disapproved of eating them because of their viscous and crude humours; Galen agrees with him in book 3 On Foods and book 2 On Temperaments, rightly saying that suckling pigs provide us with more excrementitious nourishment the more moist they are than full-grown swine, and that they also nourish less. For the flesh of young animals of any land kind on which man feeds is moister, and accompanied by phlegm's viscous blood. Homer observes this difference: Eumaeus the swineherd of Ulysses, who received into his hut as a guest the returning Ulysses, then unknown to him, from the Trojan war and shipwreck, says: "Eat, O guest, for these suckling pigs' flesh is owed to and remains for the servants; but the suitors of Penelope eat the fat and frothing mature swine, which were called delphaces, for thus they named swine having a body compact with strength and that are fully grown." Now, in order that the flesh may acquire sweetness and pleasantness, and that the swine may grow fat, they are fed chiefly on acorns, beans, barley, and other grains, for they easily get used to any fodder. The bakers of cities fatten them with flour and bran of grain, often to such great fatness that they can scarcely move from their place, and if someone wishes to move them elsewhere, it must be done by wagon. The fat and lard of these is the most suitable seasoning for other foods. It is certain that the flesh varies according to the nature of the acorns: certain authorities report that beech-mast makes the swine cheerful, its flesh easily cooked, light, and useful for the stomach; holm-oak makes it shining, lean, and heavy; oak-mast makes it loose, very heavy. The flesh of mountain pigs is also preferred to that of domestic pigs, for these take pleasure in laurel and in filthy places. Therefore those who keep pigs at home will take care that their sty is always clean, and that they are cleaned with a sieve or a broom, for this care contributes greatly to the sweetness and wholesomeness of the flesh. As to seasons, those born at the beginning of winter are the best, and those born in summer are inferior, for they are commonly subject to hailstones, and especially become full of hail. According to Aristotle, the pigs whose legs, neck, and forelegs are composed of flesh, and in which several hailstones are seen to be embedded in those parts, are worse. The flesh is sweeter when there are fewer hailstones; if it has many, it is very moist and insipid. It is certain that the hail detracts not a little from the qualities and reputation of the pig, as it does from its price. Pigs with hail are tested before purchase, and are easily recognised: for hail is found on the lower part of the tongue, and if you pluck a bristle from the back, you will see blood at the root of the plucked hair; pigs that are suckling are free of hail. Therefore, those who are eager to preserve their health and prolong their life will not touch diseased pigs, or those having diseased viscera, for there are those whose spleen swells into a tumour and becomes hardened, which does not happen unless the temperament of the body is diseased.

units.la: Ad extremum perfida Iudæorum gens e-fam suillæ temere infamauit. Nam, pro-dente Iustino lib.36. & Cornelio Tacito lib.21. cum hæc gens in Ægypto Diis homini-busque busque inuisa, foeda scabiei porrigine & tabe laboraret, eiusque contagium totam Ægyptum inficeret, Iuppiter Hammonius de remedio per Bochorim Ægypti Regem, consultus, Iudæos Ægypto respondit arcendos, quorum exulum dux designatus Moses, memor quàm foeda scabies & vitiligo ipsorum corpora deturpasset, simulque quod porci grandine & scabie eadem infestarentur, sudæis suillæ carnis esui interdixit, nec verò quod insalubris sit suillæ esus, vetuit, sed, vt hoc Mosis decretum rectius intellexit Eusebius de præpar. Euan. l.8. c.3. cum sus sitamica luto, locisque vliginosis, in quibus se volu-tate, vt ea quæ externè corpus, intus verò animam coinquinarent, sedulò cauerent, & sobriè non vt sues in crapula & sagina viuerēt. Meminit huius quoq; Plutarch in 4. sympos. probl.5. vbi rationem reddit, cur Iudæi carnibus suillis abstineant.
units.tr: Finally, the perfidious nation of the Jews rashly defamed the pig. For, as Justin in book 36 and Cornelius Tacitus in book 21 relate, when this nation, hated by gods and men, suffered from foul scabies and ulceration in Egypt, and its contagion infected all Egypt, Jupiter Hammon, consulted about a remedy through Bochoris, king of Egypt, replied that the Jews should be expelled from Egypt. Moses, leader of the exiles, mindful of how foul scab and vitiligo had disfigured their bodies, and that pigs were likewise afflicted by scab and scurf, forbade the Jews to eat pork. He did not forbid it because pork is unhealthy, but, as Eusebius understood the decree of Moses more correctly in De praeparatione evangelica book 8, chapter 3, since the pig is a filthy animal that delights in mud and marshy places where it wallows, so that people should carefully avoid what defiles the body outwardly and the soul inwardly, and should live soberly, not like pigs in gluttony and fattening. Plutarch also mentions this in Quaestiones convivales book 4, problem 5, where he gives the reason why the Jews abstain from pork.

units.la: De feriis suibus[?].
units.tr: On wild swine.

units.la: A Prugnam[?] Magnates & Potentes studio-fissime[?] hodie venantur, non sine vitae periculo, tantaq; est gulæ insania apud quosdam, vt mori satius existiment, q eo cibo carere. Romani solidos apros epulis apponere soliti sunt, huiusq; luxuriæ auctor fuit P. Seruilius Rullus, primus enim Romanorum primum integrum aprum apposuit, vt testantur annales. In huiusmodi mores clamat Satyricus,
units.tr: Today magnates and powerful men hunt boars most eagerly, not without danger to life, and among some people the madness of gluttony is so great that they think it better to die than to go without this food. The Romans were accustomed to set whole boars on their banquet tables, and the originator of this luxury was P. Servilius Rullus, for he was the first of the Romans to set a whole boar before his guests, as the annals attest. The Satirist cries out against such customs,

units.la: Quanta est gula,quæ sibi totos Ponit apros,animal propter conuiuia natum.
units.tr: How great is gluttony, which sets out whole boars for itself, an animal born for feasts.

units.la: Et sub finem,
units.tr: And near the end,

units.la: Semesum leporem atq; aliquid de cluni-bus apri.
units.tr: A half-eaten hare and something from the haunches of a boar.

units.la: Huius autem lumbus, omnibus aliis partibus praponebatur;quem Plautus & Cato aprugnū[?] vocarunt. Sedidem Martialis uix[?] unquam cœnas aut nobiles escas memorat,quin interipfa[?] apronobiliorem prope locum tradat, quem sicut[?] bodie variis iuribus ac delicatis liquoribus con-diunt, exquisitissimeq[?], apparare confuerunt coqui,ut eius syluestrem[?] adorem occultent, ita quoque maiores nostros fastitasse[?] intelliget, quicunque Apicii illius opsoedeli[?] varias condituras examinauerit, Obseruatum quippe à ganea proceribus est, aprugnam meliorem esse carne suum domesticorum, propterea quod tantas non habeat superfluitates, nec glutinosum adeo tenacem, procreet succum. Caput vero aprinum inter nobiliores cibos bodie predicatur, optimiq, ac grati saporis est, præsertim eorum aprorum qui liberè vagantur, non qui in villa-ruis nati ciuitates, aut feri capti includuntur, hi enim non perinde gratam acitudinem carnes salubrem obtinent. Mortanos enim gula pro-ceres præferunt, ut & medici, minus enim excre-mentis abundant. Hæc enim de suibus.
units.tr: The loin of this animal was preferred to all other parts; Plautus and Cato called it aprugnum. Martial, however, hardly ever mentions a dinner or a noble dish without naming the boar's loin as an especially noble dish, which cooks today prepare with various broths and delicate sauces, most carefully, so as to hide its wild taste. That our ancestors were also fastidious in this way will be clear to anyone who examines the varied seasonings of that gourmet Apicius. It has indeed been observed by the gluttons among the nobles that the loin is better than the flesh of domestic pigs, because it has less superfluous matter and does not produce such a sticky, tenacious juice. Today the boar's head is praised among the more noble foods and is of excellent and pleasing flavour, especially that of boars which roam freely, not those raised in pens or captured wild and shut up in towns; for these do not have such pleasant flesh of healthy quality. Gluttonous nobles prefer mountain boars, as do physicians, since they have less excrement. These are the things to say about pigs.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis, quæ venient ab animalibus humi gradientibus, sequuntur reptilia, ut serpens, vipera, omnisq; generis vermes & insecta, ut formica, scorpius, aranei, cimices, pediculi, pinorum truca[?] : nec non pennata quaedam, ut musca, papiliones, apes, vespae, scarabaei.
units.tr: Further, concerning foods that come from animals that creep along the ground, there follow reptiles, such as the serpent, the viper, and every kind of worm and insect, such as the ant, scorpion, spiders, bedbugs, lice, and pine ... ; nor certain winged creatures, such as the fly, butterflies, bees, wasps, and beetles.

units.la: CAP. XV. De serpentina & viperina.
units.tr: CAP. XV. Of serpents and vipers.

units.la: Est[?] ophiophagos, serpentibus vesci af-suetos, Caudeos vocatos, à grauissimis auctoribus proditum reperitur. Solin. c.36[?]. Plin.l.6.c.29. Et fuisse in Africa Marsos, & Psyllos, nec non Ophiogenes in Cypro, quorum illis exitiale virus serpentibus inge-nitum erat, vt odore solo eas sopirent, his ve-rò[?] serpentum ictus solo cotaculeuare[?], manuque impolita venenum corpori extrahere, huiusque experimenti causa ex Ophiogenarum familia legatus Exagon nomine, à Consulibus Romae in dolium serpentum coniectus circummulcentibus[?] linguis miraculum praebuit : Signumque eius familiae est, si adhuc durat, vernis temporibus odoris virus. Plin.l.28.c.3. Qui Athon montem incolunt viperinis carnibus vescuntur, itaq; nec capiti nec vestibus eorum noxia corpori innasci animalia, certi autores tradunt. Certissimis experimentis patefactum est, viperi-
units.tr: It is reported by very serious authors that there are snake-eaters, accustomed to feed on serpents, called Caudi. Solin. c.36. Plin. l.6 c.29. There were also, they say, the Marsi and the Psylli in Africa, and the Ophiogenes in Cyprus. For the Ophiogenes, the serpents' poison was innate and deadly, so that by smell alone they lulled serpents to sleep, and by touch they soothed the bites of serpents and drew the venom from the body with an unpolished hand. To test this, an envoy of the Ophiogenes family named Exagon was thrown by the consuls at Rome into a tub of serpents, and the serpents licked him all over, which was a marvel. A sign of that family is, if it still survives, that in spring their bodies give off a smell of poison. Plin. l.28 c.3. Certain authors relate that those who live on Mount Athos eat viper flesh, and therefore no harmful creatures breed on their heads or clothes. Most certain experiments have shown that viper flesh

units.la: nam valide ficeare & digerere, proindeque insanabilia eam persanare vlcera, cacochy- miz mederi & elephantiasi, pruritibus cu- tisq; foeditati, nec non pediculos expellere toto corpore,in cibis sumtam;Plinio & Ga- leno testibus,meminitq; Galenus harum be- neficio & vsu, dubs integrae sanitati restitu- tos elephantiasis contagione contaminatos. Cauda autem & ceruice abscissis viperae vi- no pri? suffocandae,vel vt Plinius tradit l.29. c.6.primum occisis sal in eos addunt,donec li- quiscat humor,vtrinque postea praecisas ex- emtisq; interaneis discoquunt cum aqua, vel vino,quod melius est,oleo,sale & anetho, o- mnibusq; aut statim vescuntur,aut pane col- ligunt vt sepius vtantur. Diofcorides viperi- nas catnes claritatem oculis afferre, neruo- rumq; vitiis auxiliari autor est, coctas ac esi- catas. Antonius Musa quoq; insanabilia & maligna vlcera, su vini viperini persanata ef- fe certis experimentis testatus est: eligendas vero esse foetas & iuxta mare degentes praec- piunt. Venenis deniq; vinum viperinum potenter resistere clari autores promittunt. Caetera reptilia & infecta, quibus nihil prae- ter luridum,fuscum,crassumq; lentoré, quia terrae,aerisq; vtplurimum inquinamenta sunt & purgamenta, cibariorum albo excludun- tur. Vnum meminisse tamen non indignum, quod praegrandes arborum vermes, cossi appellati,in delicatiori ciboRomanis olim fue-rint, quos farina [?]aginatos altiles fecerunt, tanta fuit seculi istius prodigiosa & vesana luxuria, vt ventris irritamenta & delicias in foedis etiam infectis quae fuerit saporesq; ex causis & putridis arborum corticibus.
units.tr: strongly dries and digests, and so it cures incurable ulcers, heals cachexia and elephantiasis, and cures itching and foulness of the skin; when taken in food it also expels lice from the whole body. Pliny and Galen bear witness to this, and Galen recalls that by this remedy and its use two men contaminated by the contagion of elephantiasis were restored to full health. Vipers should first be suffocated in wine with their tail and neck cut off, or, as Pliny relates in l.29 c.6, they are first killed, and salt is added to them until the fluid melts. Then, cut at both ends and with the entrails removed, they are boiled with water or wine (better still, oil), salt and dill, and all of it is either eaten at once or kept with bread so that it can be used more often. Dioscorides is the authority that viper flesh, boiled and dried, brings clarity to the eyes and helps with disorders of the nerves. Antonius Musa also attested by sure experiments that incurable and malignant ulcers were cured by viper wine. He instructs that pregnant vipers and those living by the sea should be chosen. Finally, famous authors promise that viper wine strongly resists poisons. Other reptiles and insects, which contain nothing but a livid, dark, thick slime, since they are for the most part pollutions and refuse of earth and air, are excluded from the list of foods. Yet one thing is worth remembering: the very large grubs of trees, called cossi, were once a delicacy for the Romans, who fattened them on meal. So prodigious and mad was the luxury of that age that it sought out stimulants and delights for the belly even in foul infected things, and flavours from putrid tree bark.

units.la: Hactenus de alimentis quae homini in cibos veniunt ex animalibus in aere degentibus, sequuntur, quae in aqua viuunt, vt pisces.
units.tr: So far on foods that come to man as meat from animals living in the air. There follow those that live in water, such as fish.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: TAm apud Graecos antiquos quam Romanos etiam summo semper in mensarum pretio atq; honore fuisse pisces, tot eorundem conscripti de iis libri fatis superq; testantur. Alexander ille Macedo Orientis dominator maximus & potentissimus cupidine animalium naturas noscendi inflammatus Aristotelem praeceptorem inci-tauit, vt studiosissime ac prolixissime animalium, aquatilium vero potissimum naturas & partes fuerit persecutus, proque tam praeclaro & mirabili opere fertur a cep[?]ffe ab Alexandro oc-tingenta talenta quam summam immodicam nemo existimare debet, si huius Regis opulentiam immensam, diuinamque erga omnium bonarum artium Magistros liberalitatem considerauerit.
units.tr: Fish were always held in the highest esteem and honour at table, among the ancient Greeks as well as among the Romans, and the many books written about them bear ample witness to this. That Alexander of Macedon, the greatest and most powerful lord of the East, inflamed with desire to know the natures of animals, urged his tutor Aristotle to investigate the natures and parts of animals most diligently and at great length, especially those of aquatic creatures. For so splendid and marvellous a work, Aristotle is said to have received eight hundred talents from Alexander. No one should think this sum excessive if he considers the king's immense wealth and his almost divine generosity toward masters of all the liberal arts.

units.la: Obtrectatoribus autem non caruit Ari-stoteles maximè verò in iis quæ de piscibus disputauit, in quibus eum plus iusto curiosiorem fuisse & scrupulosiorem prodiderunt, vix enim sciri posse affirmarunt, quæde generatione & coitu aquatilium tradidit.
units.tr: Aristotle, however, did not lack detractors, chiefly for what he argued about fish, in which they reported that he was more inquisitive and scrupulous than was right. They claimed that it could scarcely be known what he taught about the generation and mating of aquatic animals.

units.la: Constanter hoc asserendum, omnia fere, quæ de piscibus cognita sunt, Aristoteli debere accepta referri,& q aliorum libros, quos de piscib. exararunt, (ut sunt Oppian°, Ælianus, Seleucus Tarsensis) evoluerit, comperiet ab Aristotele tanquam limpidissimo & abundantissimo fonte rivulos eorum defluxisse. A-pud Latinos pauci admodum ex antiquis rem piscariam attigerunt. Solus Plinius in hac materia videtur Latinos adiuvisse, in arctum enim fatetur ipse collegisse, quæ Aristoteles de animalibus prodidit, quo nobis labore latine loquitur Aristoteles. Mirari subit à Romanis tam ofcitanter rem piscariam fuisse prætermissam, cum constet statim ab urbe condita piscis marinos in usu fuisse, postea verò orbe deuicto luxuriáque urbem invadente, cœperunt Proceres Romani piscinas instituere, in quibus pretiosissimos piscis alerent educarentque, ex quibus etiam magnos reditus capiebant. Claudebant autem dulcibus aquis piscis marinos, eosque gula maximè probabat, quia in suburbanis litoribus inveniretur, quod ab ipsis Gadibus aut mari alias extremo peteretur. Inprimis vero Luculli Euripus, (quo exciso monte maria admittebat) fuit admirabilis. Reliquorum piscium viuaria inuenit Licinius Murena, quem postea nobilitas secuta est. Philippum & Hortensium Cicero non sine mordaci aceto piscinarios appellasse praedicatur, quod scilicet piscinas, piscibus ad gulae incendia idoneis refertissimas possiderent. Sergius Orata primus omnium ostrearum viuaria in Baiano instituit, non gulae gratia tantum, sed auaritiae etiam, magna enim ex iis vectigalia percipiebat. Constat quoq; nonnullos ex mari externo in freta Italica deuectos, estque in exemplis Optatus Tyberii Cęsaris libertus classisque praefectus, qui Scarum vndis Italicis ignotum nominecq; vacantem latino, inter Ostiam & Campaniae littus in mare sparsum disseminauit, & nouo exemplo nouum Italis dedit incolam. Verum tanta impensa, tantique sumtus & studium ventris gulaeque causa magis fiebant, quam valetudinis prorogandę. Nam quos Magnatum Principumque libido in cibos admittebat, statim alii in pretio atque auctoritate habebant, vt ita indubitatum fit, nullam valetudinis eos rationem habuisse, vt nec rerum naturae cognitionis. Caeterum pisces a maioribus etiam nostris non fuisse neglectos Mosis, libri & sacri vates testatum faciunt. Nam & ipsa aquatilia priprimū à Deo Opt. Max. creata fcribit & crēdit Chrifto quin ipfi pifciū efum fuiffe fami-liariffimum legimus, & poft refurrectionem pifcem affatum deguftaffe, Lucas reftis eft. Merito igitur mirari fubit noftri feculi fa-ctiones quorundam, qui pifcium efum non damnant tantum, fed etiam ex Chriftianorum menfis penitus abdicare anniuntur, cum tres noftros mille quingentis annis in eo vi-&tu perdurasse inuentiantur. Ercerte, (fi hi-storiis fides adhibeatur, aliisque fcriptoribus antiquis) in cibis omnibus fere, nationibus placuiffe reperiuntur. Alexandro potentiffi-mo atque opulentiffimo regi in delitiis fue-runt, ad amicos enim pro summo munere pifciculos mififfe proditum eft. Agrigentini Geloni tyranno gulæ & lu-xui dedito pifcinam extruxerunt magnifice-tiffimam, 7. ftadiatum longitudinis, tum lati-tudinis altitudinis vero continentem cubi-tos viginti. Noftris in terris paffim ad alen-dos pifces, lacuftres vifuntur, omnibus fe-ré in tractatibus pifcinæ, quibus non quidem ad luxum femper omnes, fed ad neceffitatem vtuntur & voluptatem educantur veró tan-tum in iis aut lucii, percæ, anguillæ, cyprini, tincæ & alii quidam, quorum apud antiquos Romanos nullum fuiffe in menfis vsum, sic-ut necaliorum fluuiatilium & lacuftrium, in confeffo eft.
units.tr: This must be firmly asserted: nearly everything known about fish is to be credited to Aristotle. Anyone who reads through the books others wrote on fish, such as Oppian, Aelian and Seleucus of Tarsus, will find that their streams flowed down from Aristotle as from a very clear and abundant spring. Among the Latins, very few of the ancients touched on the subject of fishing. Pliny alone seems to have helped the Latins in this matter, for he himself confesses that he gathered in brief what Aristotle had written about animals, a labour by which Aristotle speaks Latin to us. It is surprising that the Romans so carelessly passed over the subject of fish, since it is established that sea fish were in use from the founding of the city. Later, however, with the world conquered and luxury invading the city, Roman nobles began to set up fish ponds, in which they kept and raised the most prized fish, from which they also drew large revenues. They used to keep sea fish in fresh water, and gluttony especially prized them because they could be found on the shores near the city, whereas otherwise they had to be fetched from Gades or the farther sea. Above all, Lucullus' Euripus, into which he admitted the sea by cutting through a mountain, was admirable. Licinius Murena invented fish preserves for the rest of the fish, and after him nobility followed suit. Cicero is said to have called Philippus and Hortensius fish-pond keepers with biting vinegar, since they possessed fish ponds crammed with fish fit to inflame gluttony. Sergius Orata was the first of all to set up oyster beds at Baiae, not only for the sake of gluttony but also of greed, for he drew large revenues from them. It is also recorded that some fish were carried from the foreign sea into the Italian straits. Optatus, freedman of Tiberius Caesar and prefect of the fleet, is an example: he scattered the scarus, unknown to Italian waters and without a Latin name, into the sea between Ostia and the Campanian shore, and by this novelty gave Italy a new inhabitant. Yet such great expense, such outlay and zeal, were made for the sake of belly and gullet rather than for prolonging health. For whatever the lust of magnates and princes admitted to their food, others at once held in price and esteem. So it is clear beyond doubt that they took no account of health, nor of knowledge of nature. Moreover, that fish were not neglected by our forefathers is shown by the books of Moses and the holy prophets. For they write that the aquatic creatures themselves were first created by God the Best and Greatest, and we read that fish was very familiar food to Christ, and that after the resurrection he ate a fish in the sight of others, as Luke bears witness. It is therefore right to wonder at the factions of our age, of some who not only condemn the eating of fish but strive to banish it altogether from Christian tables, when we find that our forefathers persisted in this diet for fifteen hundred years. Indeed, if credence is given to histories and other ancient writers, fish are found to have pleased nearly all nations as food. They were delights of Alexander, the most powerful and wealthy king, for it is reported that he sent little fish to his friends as a supreme gift. The Agrigentines built for Gelo the tyrant, who was given over to gluttony and luxury, a most magnificent fish pond, seven stades long, and in breadth and depth holding twenty cubits. In our lands, lake fish are kept everywhere: fish ponds for rearing fish are found on almost all estates, used not always for luxury but for necessity and pleasure. In them are reared pike, perch, eels, carp, tench and certain others, of which it is agreed that the ancient Romans had no use at table, nor of other river and lake fish.

units.la: Piscium differentiae variae: quinam & quando in cibis praestantiores [?]
units.tr: Of the varieties of fish: which kinds are the more excellent as food, and when [?]

units.la: Piscium discrimina & species enumerare omnes, immensi foret laboris, & extra institutum. Quis enim marinos seu in mari degentes vastoq; Oceano, totq; fretus ac fluctibus[?] generatos numero explicare queat, cum qui in nostris fluminibus, amnibus, lacubus ac stagnis agentes vix exploratos habeamus & compertos.
units.tr: To list all the kinds and species of fish would be an immense labour and beyond my purpose. For who could explain the number of those that live in the sea, in the vast Ocean, and are born amid so many straits and waves, when we have scarcely examined or identified those that live in our rivers, streams, lakes and pools?

units.la: Differentias tamen piscium praebet generatio & victus eorundem. Sunt enim qui ex coitu proveniant, sunt alii qui in limo vel arena, vel spuma maris, imbribus excitati: alii carne vitiant[?], alii alga & caeno, alii humore dulci & potulento, alii lenitore quodam suo, omnes autem generatione constitutionis suae talem materiam participant, qualem in pastu sibi assumunt, ut ita in coesso[?] sit, innumera piscium genera, variéq; locis varia esse & diuersa, difficile propterea cunctos describere. Sufficiat hic nosse ac de piscibus prodere, quae ad sanorum aegrorumq; commoditatem facere videntur, maximè vero quinam vita sanitatiq; proroganda conducant, nec non boni malique succi existant. Constat inter omnes Medicina scientiâ claros ac peritos, & de piscium alimento & natura sagacissimè ac prudentissimè pariter historiam historiam posteriùs reliquerunt, eorum piscium carnem, quæ in aquis degunt cœnosis, sordidis, sta-gnis tranquillis, & à ventis silentibus, fluctibus minimè commotis, amneque præterea grandes nô admittentibus fontes non habentibus, neque lar-gum effluxum, deterrimam esse maligi, succi.
units.tr: Yet generation and diet make differences among fish. Some come from mating; others arise in mud or sand, or from sea foam, stirred up by the rains; some are fouled by flesh, others by seaweed and mire, others by sweet and drinkable water, others by a certain softness of their own. All of them, however, take on in their generation and makeup the kind of matter they take in as food. So, since fish are of countless kinds and differ from place to place, it is hard to describe them all. It is enough here to know and report about fish those things that seem useful for the health of the well and the sick, and above all which ones help to prolong life and health, and which have good or bad juice. All who are famous and skilled in the science of medicine agree, and they have also left us a very shrewd and prudent account of the food and nature of fish: the flesh of those fish that live in muddy, filthy, still ponds, sheltered from the winds and not stirred by waves, and that have no large streams flowing in, no springs, and no broad outflow, is judged to be of the worst juice.

units.la: Nam stagna, quæ nullas emittunt aquas, sed perpetuo immota tantum permanent, Galen. de alim. facult. testimonio, l. de malis boni, succi cibis, nec noxiis, quæ de alimento facultatibus scripsit volumini-bus suis in confessa damnatione, omninò, carnem im-probissimam obtinent, qui in lacubus ac paludi-bus aquisq; stantibus aluntur. Minus enim natant exercentur, aërea, ventiu & vicin- deteriori, maximè verò si in eorum lacubus aquâ ex magnis custatibus, latrinas, balnea, macellis, ac culinas, fullonum, qui vestes & linteas eluunt, sordes expurgans, effluit, pessima enim in tam fæculenta aqua degentibus caro nascitur, quæ commeste corporis nostri alimoniam facilè con-spurcare apta est. Et è contra, quemadmodum pisces marini saxatiles, in alto aquore degentes sunt salubriores, sic quoq; fluviatiles, qui aduerso torrentium impetu exercentur ac satigantur, atq; occurrentibus abruptis vadorum periculis sì-duntur, hi quo in stagnis limosis, lacubus tran-quille degunt & torpes, castigatiora habere sumi-na, inq; salubri vitæ ratione præferendos esse existimandum est. In aquis rapidis & currenti-bus nati probam carnem habent & succum, sed præst-
units.tr: For still ponds that send out no water but remain perpetually motionless, as Galen testifies in his book on the properties of foods, and as he wrote in his volumes on the powers of foods, the flesh of those fish that are fed in lakes, marshes and standing waters is entirely of the worst quality. They swim and move about less, and they are fed by the air and by the lowest and most stagnant water, especially if into their lakes flows water that washes out filth from great sewers, latrines, baths, butchers' shops, kitchens, and the fullers who wash clothes and linen. For flesh grows very foul in fish living in such muddy water, and it is apt to contaminate easily the nourishment of our body when eaten. Conversely, just as sea fish that live among rocks and in the deep sea are healthier, so too river fish that are exercised and worn out by the opposing rush of torrents, and that are tested by the dangers of rocks and shallows, are thought to have the purest juices, and are to be preferred in a healthy way of living, while those that live sluggish and torpid in muddy pools and quiet lakes have the coarser juices. Fish born in swift and running waters have good flesh and juice, but...

units.la: Marini cur flu-uiatilib' prestent? præferuntur hi[?] marini, quia salsus aquoris liquor & fluxus inter saxa collisio, viscidum illorum li-quorem vel potius mucorem attenuat & digerit.
units.tr: Why do sea fish surpass river fish? These sea fish are preferred because the salt of the sea water and the dashing of the flow among the rocks thin and digest their viscous humour, or rather their slime.

units.la: Unde Cornelius Celsus l.2.c.17. inquit, levior pi-scis est inter saxa editus quam in arena, levior in arena quam in limo, quo fit, ut ex stagno vel lacu eadem piscium genera graviora sint, leviorque qui in alto, quam qui in vado vixit.
units.tr: Hence Cornelius Celsus, book 2, chapter 17, says: a fish caught among rocks is lighter than one from sand, and one from sand is lighter than one from mud; so it follows that the same kinds of fish are heavier from a pond or lake, and lighter when they have lived in the deep than when they have lived in the shallows.

units.la: Saxatiles omnium iudicio celebrantur, quiq; omnibus puris, limpidis, saxeisq; aquis littori-busq; eduntur ac degunt, proinde horum esus fe-bricitantibus nonnunquam conceditur, ut fun-dulorum, auratarum, luciorum, barbatulorum, percarum, quia qualitatem habent febricitanti-bus contrarias, frigiditatem sc. & humiditatem, tum etiam quia excrementis, ut ceteri, non adeo abundant, interq; scopulos & saxa, seu in saxosis locis sese exercent, hæc enim fluxus inter saxa, scopulosq; collisio mucum illorum absorbet atque abstergit. Unde arbitror facile pisces vere saxatiles discerni possunt ab iis qui in levibus, arenosis aut terreis littoribus aquisq; natant, qui improprie & perperam a quibusdam saxatiles nominantur, cum potius ita appellati a græcis auctoribus inveniantur, qui in saxosis locis ac circa promontoria scopulosq; maris delitescunt sefeq; exercent.
units.tr: Rock fish are celebrated by the judgement of all, and those that are bred and live in clear, limpid, rocky waters and along the shores; therefore the eating of these is sometimes allowed to the feverish, such as the fundulus, gilthead, pike, barbel and perch, because they have qualities contrary to fever, namely coldness and moisture, and also because they do not abound in excrement as others do. They exercise themselves among crags and rocks, or in rocky places, for the friction of the flow among rocks and reefs wipes away and cleanses their slime. Hence I think that fish that are truly rock fish can easily be distinguished from those that swim in smooth, sandy or earthy shores and waters, which some wrongly and improperly call rock fish, whereas they are found to be called so by the Greek authors only when they hide and exercise themselves among rocks and around the headlands and reefs of the sea.

units.la: Porro alimentorum, quibus utuntur pisces, habenda ratio est, nam alimenta carnis bonitatem vel malignitatem faciunt, succiq; probitanem velimprobitatem. Certum est, ubi herbarum radicumq; copia nascitur, excellentiores in cibis fieri & salubriores pisces[?]. Qui limosas ber-bas malig[?], succi radices attingunt, improbantur.
units.tr: Moreover, we must consider the food that fish use, for food makes the flesh good or bad, and makes the juice good or bad. It is certain that where there is an abundance of herbs and roots, the fish become more excellent and healthier as food. Those that touch muddy herbs and bad roots are condemned.

units.la: Qui in animibus[?], magnas & populosas urbes praeterfluentibus hominum stercoribus, aliisq; id genus sordidissimis efficis nutrientur, omnino cibi sunt abdicandi, pestilentes. n. succi tales effeinde parent quod paucotempore, si extincti feruentur, putredinem concipiant & foetorem, quod Ausonius de coruo dixit,
units.tr: Those fish that are nourished in the sewers of great and crowded cities, into which flow the dung of men and other most filthy refuse of this kind, must altogether be rejected as pestilential food. For such fish generate a juice that, if kept even a short time after death, quickly takes on putrefaction and stench, as Ausonius said of the crow:

units.la: Nec duraturi post binatrichoria corui.
units.tr: Nor do they last long after the crow's second... [?]

units.la: Quin & lucium à vitu damnare visus est à loco in quo versatur, ait enim,
units.tr: Indeed, he seemed to condemn the pike as food also because of the place where it lives, for he says:

units.la: Lucius obscuras vlua, coenoq; lacunas Obsidet hic nullos mensarum lectus ad vsus Feruet fumosis olido nidore popinis.
units.tr: The pike haunts the dark sedge and muddy pools; no table couch serves its uses; it simmers in smoky cookshops with a foul stench.

units.la: Sic Mosellam idem Poeta à puritate commendat, inquiens,
units.tr: So the same poet praises the Moselle for its purity, saying:

units.la: Tu neq; limigeris ripam praetexteris vluis, Nec piger immundo perfundis littore coeno: (phas. Sicca sed in primas spargis vestigia lymphas:
units.tr: You do not wind along your bank with mud-bearing reeds, nor do you lazily soak the foul shore with filth; but you scatter dry footprints over the first waters.

units.la: Et paulo post:
units.tr: And a little later:

units.la: Spectaris vitreo per lenia terga profundo, Secreti nihil amnis habens, atque almus aperto Panditur intuitu liquidis obtutibus aer: Nec placidi prohibent oculos per inania venti.
units.tr: You are seen through your glassy back over the smooth deep, having no secret of your stream, and the kindly air is opened to the clear gaze in open view, nor do the calm winds hinder the eyes through the empty spaces.

units.la: Sic demersa procul durante per inania visu Cernimus, arcaniq; patet penetrale fluenti.
units.tr: Thus we see things sunk far down through the empty spaces by the flowing gaze, and the inner sanctum of the stream lies open.

units.la: Ex quibus Ausonii verbis piscēs Mosellae mirè salubres esse facile est colligere, vt ita certum sit, & in confesso, vitæ suæ adferre detrimentum nē poenitendum, sanitatiq; parum consulere, qui piscibus vescuntur malo pabulo pastis & enutritis.
units.tr: From these words of Ausonius it is easy to gather that the fish of the Moselle are wonderfully wholesome, so that it is certain, and admitted, that those who eat fish fed on bad pasture and nourished in it do no small harm to their own life, and do little to look after their health, and they have no reason to regret it.

units.la: Sed & locorum, in quibus educantur pisces, de-lectus [?] habendus, à quibus magnæ exurgunt differentia, tum quo ad habitum vegetiorem acquirendum, tum etiam magnitudinem, teste Aristotele, sicut in animantibus cæteris, stirpibusq; ex regionibus plurima spectantur discrimina.
units.tr: But we must also take account of the places in which fish are raised, since great differences arise from them, both as to acquiring a more vigorous condition and as to size, as Aristotle testifies; just as among other animals and plants, very many differences are observed according to regions.

units.la: Sunt enim quædam loca piscibus singulis propria, in quibus rectius valent, commodiora si-quidem sunt ea, qua algarum copia scatent, pinguiores enim iis in locis solent pabulari. Nam quibus alga pabulum est, effatim pascuntur, plu-resq; ibi pisces reperiuntur. Ponunt gregatim petunt cibi gratia, qui uberior & commodior illic est propter dulcium aquarum admixtionem, nam humor dulcior & potulentior ad partum & fœtum educandum commodior. Apud Cretæ insulam gobiones, genusq; omne saxatile satis pinguescit.
units.tr: For there are certain places that are peculiar to particular fish, in which they thrive better; those places are the more suitable which abound in seaweed, for fish are wont to feed more richly in such places. For those fish that feed on seaweed graze freely, and many fish are found there. They gather in flocks, seeking food, which is more plentiful and convenient there because of the mixing of sweet waters; for sweeter and more drinkable water is more suitable for bearing and rearing young. Near the island of Crete, gobies and every kind of rock fish grow fat enough.

units.la: Qui in Eurypo Pyræo sunt, foras omnes per hiemem enatant, excepto uno gobione, sed veris circa principium ad redeunt.
units.tr: Those in the Pyraean Euripus all swim out in winter, except one goby, but they return about the beginning of spring.

units.la: Qui in purissimo mari degunt cæteris perpetuo præstant, maxime ubi littora, quæ aquarum in orbem ambiunt, terra non abundant, nec lenia, sed aut arenosa sunt aut aspera. Quod si præter-ea ad boream vergat, longe erunt excellentiores, puritas enim aquilonis, qui aquæ commiscetur, substantiæ ipsorum probitatem adauget. Aristoteles plurimum interesse volunt aquilonia sint loca an austrina. Lacus aut piscinæ sic posita, ut insequens vel maris unda, vel fluvii aut perennis fontis vel torrentis priorem submoveat, nec intra conseptum veterem sinat remanere, pisces alunt commendabiliores, similes enim sunt pelago eiusmodi lacus, quod ventis confluum[?] assidue renovatur, vel flumini perpetuo decurrenti ac labenti. Ab austro perflante lacus ingratos præbent pisces. Galenus perspicuum esse ait, mare alterum alteri præstare, quod aut maxime purum est, aut fluvios multos & grandes admittit, ut Pontus.
units.tr: Those that live in the purest sea always surpass the others, especially where the shores that surround the waters on every side are not rich in earth, and are neither gentle but either sandy or rough. If moreover the sea lies toward the north, they will be far more excellent, for the purity of the north wind, which mingles with the water, increases the goodness of their substance. Aristotle thought it made a great difference whether places lay to the north or to the south. Lakes or fish-ponds placed so that either the incoming sea wave, or a river, or a perennial spring or torrent drives out the former water and does not let it remain within the old enclosure, rear more commendable fish; for such a lake resembles the open sea, since it is constantly renewed by the winds that blow over it, or by a river that flows and glides on without pause. Fish from lakes exposed to the south wind are unpleasant. Galen says it is plain that one sea is superior to another, namely that which is either very pure or admits many large rivers, such as the Pontus.

units.la: Purissimi maris pisces præferuntur o-mnibus. S.agnales[?] Pontici bonitate quidem vincunt, sed sunt illis inferiores, eodem te-ste[?], propter aquarum dulcium ingentem abundantiam. Itaque multum interest, hoc an illo educentur loco. Nam enim, ut Varro ait, si murena optima sint in Sicilia, & bel-lops[?] Rhodi, continuo bipisces[?] omnes maritales existunt: animum enim & aquarum mira-biles vires, pisces, in iis degentes sentire, nemo dubitauerit: quin & earundem bonitate aut pravitate discrimina memoranda oriri necesse est, tales quippe sunt aquae, qualis terra per quam fluunt, qualesq; herbarum, quas lauant, succi: & iidem amnes reperiuntur parte quadam salubres, alia insalubres. Ctesias tradit in Armenia esse fontem nigris piscibus abundantem, qui in cibis sumti afferant mortem. Theophrastus praeterea in fonte quodam Arcadiae lethales tradidit. Borysthenes amnis suauissimos fert pisces, qui tamen aestate ex rivis influentibus saporemq; eius mutantibus deteriores efficiuntur, influentes enim alias aquas saporem immutare in ponto perspicuum est, in quem multitudo fluminum influit. Tigris a celeritate sic dictus in lacum influit Rhetussam, omnia illa pondera sustinentem, & nitrum nebulis exhalantem, cui unum genus est piscium, quod aquae transcurrentis alveo non miscetur: exsistimantur autem pisces illi e lacu Rhetussa hominibus pestilentes, Tigris vero utiles, nam hi e Tigri in lacum Rhetussam non transnatant, utriusq; autem lacus pisces non nominatos hactenus a quoquam inveni, quod equidem mirum, cum aliA-rum aquarum piscibus suis nominibus, vt plu-rimum appellati reperiantur. Nilum, auctor est Strabo in libris de situ orbis, permultos diversosque educare pisces, propriam quandam & suam habentes formam, omninoq; gratissimi saporis esse praedicantur, pracipue vero qui coracini dicuntur: suntur: latum quoq; piscem pregrandem ad 20 ultra libras in eodem crescentem,omni ap-paratus ratione suauissimum & gratum ali-mentum esse Athenæus testis est. Non tamen de-sunt, qui Niloticos pisces minus salubres existi-mant, forsan quoniam ventus Notus non agite-tur, Gangis anguilla ad tricenos pedes longa sunt memo abiles Borysthenis piscium nomina non inueniuntur, tantum laudantur saporis suauitate, prædicantur, sine ossibus sp. sq. In India amnibus piscium genus est in terram ex-euntium, ac deinde refiluentium. In Eloro amne lupi, anguillaq; magnitudine insignes. Ptolomæus Ægypti Rex apud Athenæum te-statur, circa Berenicen Libyæ fluuium esse lu-porum, murenarum, anguillarum copiâ refer-tissimum. In Aorno vocales reperiri pisces, turdis similes certi autores tradunt, quos varios appellant. In Syria, Xenophonte in expedi-tione Cyri narrante, est Achelois, in quo sunt pisces pregrandes & mansuetissimi, quos violare nefas erat. Salmo fluuiatilis in Aquitania marinis omnibus præfertur. Ticinus in Insu-bria peculiariter alit thynnum piscem odoris suauissimi, teste D. Ambrosio. In Lario Iu-bia lacu perce suaues alluntur & ample, etiam grandissime, quas ad 100, quandoq; libras peruenire testatur Paulus Iouius. Mintium Benacus, quæ est in agro Veronensi, mirabili anguillarum captura mense Octobri mobili-tur. tur. Et quis flumina illa grandia Italia, Gal-liæq; fluviolos item rivos & torrentes piscibus scatentes enumerare queat? non opera pretium duco, cum Paulus Iovius aliiq; Itali, qui de piscium esu monumenta posteris reliquerunt, abunde eorum meminerint. Qui porro pe-regrinationes sponte susceperunt, aut legationi-bus functi terras septentrionales adierunt, te-stantur lacus illic esse ingentes, omniumque ge-nerum piscibus mire abundantes, sponte enim illic nascuntur, & felicissime proveniunt. Moscovia, Suecia, atq; etiam vicini tractus lacubus huiusmodi abundant.
units.tr: Fish from the purest sea are preferred to all others. The Pontic fish, though they surpass others in goodness, are inferior to these, by the same witness, because of the enormous abundance of fresh water there. So it makes a great difference whether they are reared in this place or that. For, as Varro says, if the murenae are best in Sicily and the ... at Rhodes, then all the fish born there are at once marine. Nobody will doubt that the fish living in waters feel the wonderful powers of the water. Indeed, differences in their goodness or badness must necessarily arise, since waters are such as the land through which they flow, and such as the juices of the herbs they wash. And the same rivers are found to be partly wholesome and partly unwholesome in different parts. Ctesias relates that in Armenia there is a spring abounding in black fish, which, when eaten, bring death. Theophrastus has also reported lethal ones in a certain spring in Arcadia. The river Borysthenes bears very sweet fish, which nevertheless in summer become worse when streams flowing into it change their taste; for it is plain that other waters flowing in alter the flavour in the sea into which a multitude of rivers pour. The Tigris, so called from its swiftness, flows into the lake Rhetussa, which bears all those weights, and gives off nitre in vapours. There is one kind of fish there that does not mix with the water of the running stream. Those fish from the lake Rhetussa are thought harmful to men, but those of the Tigris useful, for these do not swim across from the Tigris into the lake Rhetussa. I have found that no one has so far named the fish of either lake, which is remarkable, since the fish of other waters are for the most part found with their own names. Strabo, in his books on the situation of the world, testifies that the Nile rears very many and diverse fish, having a form peculiar and their own, and they are declared to be of the most pleasant flavour in every way, especially those called coracini; and Athenaeus bears witness that a broad fish, very large, growing up to more than twenty pounds in the same river, is in every respect a most delicious and pleasant food. Yet there are not lacking those who consider Nile fish less wholesome, perhaps because the south wind does not stir it. The eels of the Ganges are thirty feet long. Names of the fish of the Borysthenes are not to be found in the memorable authors; they are only praised and proclaimed for the sweetness of their flavour, and are without bones. In India there is a kind of fish in the rivers that goes out onto the land and then flows back again. In the river Eloros there are wolf-fish and eels notable for their size. Ptolemy, king of Egypt, testifies in Athenaeus that near Berenice in Libya there is a river full of wolf-fish, lampreys and eels. Certain authors relate that in Aornos there are singing fish, like thrushes, which they call various. In Syria, as Xenophon relates in the expedition of Cyrus, there is the Achelois, in which are very large and very gentle fish, which it was a sin to harm. The river salmon in Aquitaine is preferred to all marine fish. The Ticinus in Insubria rears in a special way the tunny fish of most sweet smell, as witnessed by St Ambrose. In the lake of Como, Lario, sweet perch are reared and in abundance, even very large ones, which, as Paulus Jovius testifies, sometimes reach a hundred pounds. The Mincio, flowing out of Benacus (Lake Garda), which lies in the Veronese territory, teems with a wonderful catch of eels in the month of October. And who could list those great rivers of Italy, and likewise the small streams and torrents of Gaul teeming with fish? I do not think it worth the effort, since Paulus Jovius and other Italians who have left records for posterity about the eating of fish have amply mentioned them. Moreover, those who of their own accord have undertaken long journeys, or who have travelled as envoys to the northern lands, testify that there are huge lakes there, wonderfully abounding in fish of every kind, for they arise there of their own accord and thrive most abundantly. Muscovy, Sweden and even the neighbouring regions abound in lakes of this sort.

units.la: Caeterum ex aquarum pisculentarum ci-bis in frequentiori apud nos esu sunt, mensarum-que delitiis habentur ut plurimum, delphinus, balena, lucius, cyprinus, seu carpio, accipenser, salmo, trutta, anguilla, prasinus, barbus, perca, mullus, scarus, scombrus, tinca, murena, lampe-tra, salpa, raja, platessa seu pectines, harengi, go-bius, alburnus, aliique complures maritimis populis magis cogniti. Horum autem alii sunt pela-gii, altum tenentes mare, intusque eius penetralibus profundoque degentes, terram littoraque fugientes, cuiusmodi sunt congri, asellii, thynni, raja, &c. alii littorales, qui in vado degunt, ac in littoribus & circa easdem visitantur, ut mulli, gobii, mugiles, cantharii, oculata: alii saxatiles, qui scilicet in mari inter saxa degunt, quos ante cunctos Medicina magnificat. Optime ingt Col.l.9, c.16. saxosum mare mare nominis sui pisces alij, qui quod in petris stabulentur, saxatiles dicti sunt, ut merula, tur-di, melanuri, quos Galenus l.3. de aliment. fa-cult. recenset, & perspicae, scaros, cottyphos, juli-das, phycidas, percas, petraeos nominat pisces, a lo-cis in quibus inueniuntur & diuersantur, non enim in lubricis, arenosis, aut terrestribus æquo-ris littoribus, sed ubi petra & saxosa sunt littera, sese illatebrant & parturiunt. Alimonia ex his non modo concoctu facilis, sed humanis quo-que corporibus saluberrima est, sanguinem enim substantiâ mediocrem generant: unde Ga-lenus in esculento piscium iure albo elixatos, ma-rasmo aut syncope ex spiritus inopia languen-tibus, & lassitudine ulcerosâ defessis salutare eos esse statuit, quibus vires effœtas reficere nouit, nec illorum esum febri aut pleuritide labo-rantibus à morbi statu denegauit.
units.tr: Moreover, among the foods from fish-bearing waters, the following are eaten more commonly among us and are mostly regarded as delicacies of the table: dolphin, whale, pike, carp, sturgeon, salmon, trout, eel, prasinus (a green-backed fish), barbel, perch, mullet, parrotfish, mackerel, tench, moray, lamprey, salpa, ray, plaice or flounder, herring, goby, bleak, and many others better known to maritime peoples. Of these, some are pelagic, keeping to the deep sea and living in its inner recesses and depths, shunning land and shores, such as conger, hake, tunny, ray, etc. Others are littoral, which live in the shallows and are visited on the shores and around them, such as mullet, goby, grey mullet, cantharus, and sea-bream. Others are rock-dwellers, which live in the sea among rocks, and which Medicine above all others extols. Columella rightly says, in book 9, chapter 16: "a rocky sea." Other fish, which are called rock-fish because they dwell among stones, are such as the blackbird, the thrush, and the melanurus, which Galen lists in book 3 of On the Properties of Foods; and he names as rock-fish the perch, the scarus, the cottyphus, the julis, the phycis, the perch, and the petraeus, from the places in which they are found and dwell. For they do not hide and breed on slippery, sandy or earthy shores of the sea, but where the shore is rocky and stony. Food from these is not only easy to digest but also most wholesome for human bodies, for they produce blood of moderate substance. Hence Galen judged that in the edible broth of fish, boiled white, they are beneficial for those languishing from wasting or fainting from lack of breath, and for those worn out by ulcerous weariness, those whose spent strength they know how to restore; nor did he deny their eating to those suffering from fever or pleurisy, once the state of the disease allowed it.

units.la: De Delphino.
units.tr: On the Dolphin.

units.la: [?]Elfus inter eos cibos, qui plurimum præbent alimenti, retulit omnes beluas marinas. Galenus omnes ce-taceos pisces duram prauique succi, excre-mentisque plenam carnem obtinere constanter affirmat; proinde sale eos condiendos esse, quâ conditura alimentum exipsis proveniens, promtius faciliusque in corpus distribuitur faciliusque concoquitur. Delphinum, certum est, in cibos venire, nec fe-rinum ejus gulam fastidire saporem. Ex mari mediterraneo adfertur in Galliam, Italiamque, habeturque in pretio. Maritimis tamen gentibus raro editur, imo nec plebs infima eum attingit. Porro epar commendari video & linguam, ipsam vero carnem, quia praepinguis est, nauseam excitare, ventriculumq; relaxare verisimile est. Adeps eius ad eosdem usus, ad quos græci oleum, in testis repositus inuentus est à Græcis apud Mosynecos, sicut & ex carne ejus salsamenta, teste Xenoph. in expeditionis Cyri L.s[?].
units.tr: Aelian, among those foods which provide the most nourishment, counted all sea beasts. Galen firmly maintains that all cetaceous fish have hard flesh of poor juice and full of excrement; therefore they should be seasoned with salt, since the nourishment arising from them is then distributed into the body more readily and more easily, and is more easily digested. It is certain that the dolphin comes to the table, and that its wild taste does not offend the palate. It is brought from the Mediterranean sea into Gaul and Italy, and is held in high esteem. Yet it is rarely eaten by the maritime peoples; indeed even the lowest common people do not touch it. Moreover, I see that the liver is recommended, and the tongue; but the flesh itself, because it is very fat, is likely to cause nausea and to relax the stomach. Its fat was used for the same purposes as the Greeks used oil; it was found stored in jars by the Greeks among the Mosynoeci, and likewise salted meats were made from its flesh, as Xenophon testifies in the Expedition of Cyrus, book 5.

units.la: De Balena.
units.tr: On the Whale.

units.la: Hujus caro vilissima habetur. Sed lingua in pracipua autoritate est præ-fertim-diebus quadragenarii jejunii apud Pon-tificios. Caro pinguis est & dura, coquitur cum pisis, vicemq; non raro supplet suilla: quidam verubus eam figunt, torrentq;: admodum autem noxia recens deprehensa est, salita innocentior: qui colico dolori sunt obnoxii, abstinere sibi omnino temperent: otiosis quoq; infalubberrima est, graves vero labores subeuntibus aut vehementer exercitatis non adeo inutiles.
units.tr: Its flesh is considered very cheap. But the tongue is in especially high repute, particularly on the days of the forty-day fast among the Papists. The flesh is fat and hard; it is cooked with peas, and often takes the place of pork: some pierce it on spits and roast it; but it is very harmful when freshly caught, less harmful when salted: those who are subject to colic should wholly refrain from it; it is also very unwholesome for the idle, but not so unsuitable for those undertaking heavy labours or who are vigorously exercised.

units.la: De Lucio.
units.tr: On the Pike.

units.la: Lucius NOn leuem inter celebres autores diglatiationem concitauit lucius, fe- re enim omnes lupum appellandum censuerant non luciùm, propterea quod in pisces non secus ac lupus in oues grassetur Verum hic error docte pariter ac diligenter à Paulo Iouio explosus est. Porro Aufonius in Mofella de lucio ita canit: Hic etiam Latio risus praenomine culter Stagnorum, querulis vis infestissima ranis Lucius obscuras vlua cœnoq; lacunas Obsidet, hic nullos mecafarum leclus ad vsu, Fervet fumosis olido nidore popinis,
units.tr: Not a slight controversy has arisen among famous authors over the pike. Almost all of them thought it should be called a wolf (lupus) rather than a pike (lucius), because it preys on fish just as the wolf preys on sheep. But this error was learnedly and carefully refuted by Paulus Jovius. Ausonius, in the Mosella, sings of the pike thus: "Here too is the pike, which the Latins call by the name 'knife of the ponds', most deadly enemy of the complaining frogs. It besieges the dark pools with reeds and mud. Here no table is set for the use of the mena fish, but it boils in smoky taverns with a foul reek."

units.la: Ex quibus intelligere facile est, olim nullo in honore mensarum fuifle.
units.tr: From these lines it is easy to understand that formerly the pike was held in no honour at tables.

units.la: Nunc passim inter lautissimos pisces amnicos annumeratur. Certum autem est quasdam gentes parum luciis delectariorum marinorum præsertim abundantiam. Et Italiparua in gloria eos habent, ob saporem insuauem ac pene fastidiosum. Gulofiffimus enim est & voracissimus, precipueque carniuorus, suique generis piscibus vescitur gratissime, sicut & ranis. Quin tanta est gula hujus piscis, vt anserculosa ana-ticulasque in aquis natantes deglutiat. Qui in fluuiis rapidis ac putis aluntur magis commendantur, limosum virus gustatu re-ferensferentes, cibis ut inutiles, abdicandi. Porro in coquendo elixandoq; artificium adhibetur non paruum, ut durior evadat, dura enim piscium caro gratior est, mollis insalubris.
units.tr: Now it is commonly counted among the most sumptuous river fish. It is certain, however, that some peoples care little for pike, especially where sea fish are plentiful. The Italians also hold them in low esteem, because of their unpleasant and almost loathsome flavour. The pike is very greedy and most voracious, and it is chiefly carnivorous. It feeds most eagerly on fish of its own kind, and on frogs as well. Indeed the gluttony of this fish is so great that it swallows goslings and ducklings swimming on the water. Those raised in swift and deep rivers are more highly commended, since they taste less of the muddy poison; those fed in muddy waters are to be rejected as useless food. Further, a considerable skill is applied in cooking and boiling it, so that it becomes firmer, for the firm flesh of fish is more pleasing, while soft flesh is unwholesome.

units.la: Apparatum hunc culinæ germanorum pri-mum videntur docuisse alios, nam condi-menta, quæ hodie luciis adhibentur, lautio-ra, à populis quibusdam germanica appel-lantur. Fit autem id genus condimenti ex si-napi & butyro prunis liquato. Alii edunt ex aceto piperato: alii & quidem lautiores frigunt, exque liquore mali aurantii affu-munt: alii craticula, præsertim vero lucio-los, torrent, prius tamen utrinque scarifica-tionibus cute aperta, ut butyrum, quo li-quato in craticula humectatur, penitus sub-eat.
units.tr: The Germans seem to have first taught others this method of preparing it, for the sauces now used with pike, which are called more refined, are named German by some peoples. This kind of sauce is made from mustard and butter melted over the coals. Others eat it with peppered vinegar. Others, who are more refined, fry it and pour over it the juice of the bitter orange. Others grill it on a gridiron, especially the small pike, but first they cut the skin on both sides with scorings, so that the melted butter, with which it is moistened on the gridiron, may soak in thoroughly.

units.la: Anglia præcipuæ nobilitatis lucios o-stentat, ventribusque eorum cultro apertis, seuum pingueque, vendentes ementibus o-stendunt, & si non emantur, (mirum dictu) in aquas eos rursum coniiciunt, nec intereunt, sed vulnus celerrime coalescit, quod quidam contactui tincarum ascribunt, rin-ca enim glutinosa admodum est, alii rectius eam vim iis inesse à natura affirmant, inventum enim est interaneis lucii coagulari lac, ac glaciari æque ac coa-gulo.
units.tr: England displays the pike of the highest nobility. Opening their bellies with a knife, the sellers show the fat and suet to the buyers. And if they are not bought, (wonderful to say) they throw them back into the water, and they do not die; the wound heals very quickly. Some ascribe this to contact with the tench, for the tench's slime is very sticky. Others more correctly affirm that this power is inherent in the pike by nature, for it has been found that the milk in the pike's entrails coagulates and freezes just like rennet.

units.la: De Cyprino.
units.tr: On the Carp.

units.la: Cyprinum piscem eruditi existimant esse, qui à nostris Carpio, Carpus & Carpena vocatur, quem Aristoteles inter lacustres & amnicos retulit. Linguam eius seu palatum, lautissimos inter cibos reponunt ganeae periti, de quo Aristoteles 2. de animalium partibus sic prodidit compluribus piscibus carnosum est palatum, & quidem inter fluviatiles ꝯ-prinis admodum carnosum & molle. Est in exemplis Lurco quidam Borbonensis Ferdeletum nomine, qui in vivariis aut piscinis Illustriss. familiae Borbonie ad duo triaue[?] millia Cyprinorum cepit, usq; singulis linguam seu palatum detraxit, ut quid in gloria palati, palatum posset, experiretur, gulamq; suam, quæ postea ob iasaniam tantum a carnifice laqueo elisa est, expleret. Carne autem constant molli & phlegmatica, seu aquea, non glutinosa. Qui educantur stercoribus & sordibus urbium, cibis omnino abdicandos censent eruditiores. Nec enim ullum dubium est, quin pro piscinarum ac vivariorum situ ac natura magnas alimenti sortiantur differentias, cum alibi pinguiores, alibi graciliores, alibi glutinosiores, & lentulentiores, qui omnium pessimi sunt, esse deprehendantur. Itaq;, quo loco piscina instituenda ac ponenda sint, diligenter considerandum. Pabulum namq; gratia & salubritati addit vel detrahit. Porro multifariam coquuntur apud Germanos adq; varios vsus in re cibaria adhibentur. Modos coquendi relinquemus coquis. Ut vero in multos dies coctus duret, sumenda sunt vini & aquae partes aequales, quibus aceti, aut omphacii nonnihil adduitur ad acorem conciliandum, deinde piperis, garyophyllorum, zinziberis & nucis moschatae pollinem liberalius adducere oportet, adq; colorem elegantem inducendum, crocum, quae postea cum cyprino diutius sunt coquenda.
units.tr: The fish called cyprinus is thought by learned men to be what among us is called carp (carpio, carpus or carpena), which Aristotle placed among lake and river fish. Experts in gluttony rank its tongue or palate among the most sumptuous foods. Aristotle wrote of this in the second book On the Parts of Animals thus: in many fishes the palate is fleshy, and among river fish the carp has a very fleshy and soft palate. There is an example of a certain glutton of Bourbon, named Ferdeletus, who in the fishponds or tanks of the most illustrious house of Bourbon caught some two or three thousand carp. From each one he removed the tongue or palate, to test how far the palate could go in its glory and so to satisfy his gullet. Afterwards, for madness alone, he was strangled by the executioner's noose. Carp flesh is soft and phlegmatic, or watery, not glutinous. The more learned judge that those raised on the dung and filth of cities should be rejected entirely as food. Nor is there any doubt that, according to the site and nature of the fishponds and tanks, they acquire great differences of nourishment, for some are found fatter, others leaner, and others more glutinous and slimy, which are the worst of all. Therefore the place where a fishpond is to be set up and placed must be carefully considered, for food adds to or takes away from both pleasantness and wholesomeness. Further, they are cooked in many ways among the Germans and used for various purposes in food. We shall leave the methods of cooking to the cooks. But so that it keeps for many days once cooked, equal parts of wine and water must be taken, to which a little vinegar or verjuice is added to give a sharpness. Then pepper, cloves, ginger and nutmeg powder must be added rather generously, and saffron to give an elegant colour; these are to be boiled with the carp for a long time afterwards.

units.la: (Cum squamis quoque elixare eos expedit, sic enim sapidum illum pinguemq; succum, intus servari, qui desquamatis aliàs deperiret, constat, Aristoteles miram cyprino fertilitatem tribuit, quinquies aut sexies anno parere affirmans. Plinius marinum tantum nominat, eumq; canicula exortu fiderari, tonitruq; sopiri in mari ab aliquibus existimari, prodidit, quod in fluviatilibus nondum accidisse observatum est.
units.tr: (It is also useful to boil them with their scales on, for it is established that this keeps the savoury and fatty juice within, which would otherwise be lost once they are descaled.) Aristotle ascribes a remarkable fertility to the carp, affirming that it spawns five or six times a year. Pliny names only the marine kind, and he reported that it is dulled at the rising of the dog star, and that some think thunder lulls it to sleep in the sea, which has not yet been observed to happen in river fish.

units.la: De Accipenfere.
units.tr: On the Sturgeon.

units.la: PIscium apud antiquos nobilissimum fuisse accipenserem Plin. l. 9. c. 17. autor est, hodieque in summo mensarum honore habetur apud eos, in quorum fluminibus capitur, subit enim è mari flumina. Rhodanum delicatissimos & suavissimos, amplissimosq; praebere constat, ut & Albim, prope Hamburgum inprimis, ubi vasto ore in Oceanum germanicum exoluitur. De nomine inter eruditos non conuenit, alio atq; alio eum appellantes. Paulus Iouius Silurum Aufonii exiftimauit : Hermolaus Hiccam apud Athen. alii Torfionem Plinii efse crediderunt, cuius etiam opinionis fuiffe Chriftoph. Longolium inuenio. Rondeletus his omnibus fcriptor recentior Accipenfe- rem Romanorum literis nobilitatu n Stu- rionem effe putauit, & Dorionis ?, five Galeni galaxian lib. ?aliment. Stacio igitur mire ingenia doctorum torfit, gulam interim fuauiter demulcens, boni enim fuanifque fucci eft, carnifque durae & candidae, adul- tioris vitulae carnibus haud abfimilis: vnde nutriendi vi Scurionem pollere certam eft, modo bene in ventre perficiatur, fecus enim negotium faceffit ventriculo. Coctus in acce- to feruatur ad aliquot dies. Praefertur mas in cibo: Sed foemina ouis grauida autorita- tem quoque retinuit. Quidam foeeum craffum & glutinofum eum obtinere ajunt, quod de crudo, vel etiam non probe coctae ac praeparato conceffero. Potro in magna fuiffe autoritate & honore in menfis Ros manorum accipenferem teftatur Horatius l.2. ferm. fatyra 2. fic fcribens, haud ita pridem. Galloni praeconis erat accipere mensa Infamis.
units.tr: Pliny (bk. 9, ch. 17) is the authority that the sturgeon was the most noble of fishes among the ancients, and even today it holds the highest place of honour at tables among those in whose rivers it is caught, for it swims up from the sea into the rivers. It is agreed that the Rhone supplies the most delicate and sweetest sturgeon, and very large ones, as does the Elbe, especially near Hamburg, where it flows out through a vast mouth into the German Ocean. Scholars do not agree on its name, each calling it something different. Paulus Jovius thought it was the Silurus of Ausonius. Hermolaus called it hicca, according to Athenaeus, and others believed it was Pliny's torfio; I find that Christophorus Longolius also held this opinion. Rondeletius, a more recent writer than all of these, thought that the sturgeon, which is ennobled by the Roman writers, is the sturio, and that it is the [fish] of Dorion, or Galen's galaxias (in the book on foods). So the wits of learned men have been wonderfully tossed about over this, while the sturgeon meanwhile pleases the palate agreeably. It has good and sweet juice, and its flesh is firm and white, not much unlike the flesh of a fully grown calf. Hence it is certain that the sturgeon has great power to nourish, provided it is well digested in the stomach; otherwise it gives the stomach trouble. It is cooked and kept in vinegar for some days. The male is preferred for food, but the female full of roe has also kept its reputation. Some say it has thick and glutinous juice, which must be granted of raw fish, or of fish not properly cooked and prepared. That the sturgeon was of great authority and honour on the tables of the Romans is attested by Horace in Satire 2.2, writing thus, not so long ago: "It was a disgrace for the herald Gallonius to have a sturgeon at his table."

units.la: Et Lucillius apud Cic. l. 2; de finib. O Publi, inquit, o gurges Galloni, es homo miser, coenalti in vita nunquam bene; cum omnia in ista consumis squilla atque accipen-sere cum decumano. Unde apparet hunc Gallonium obsoniorum gurgitem, accipensere, vt carissimo & suauissimo pilce ornasse instruxisseque conuiuium. Archestratus apud Athen. lib. 8. existimat χαλεόν[?] eundem piscem esse, atque eum qui apud Romanos cum tibiis & coronis ad coenas cum pompa quadam circumfertur, corona- tisetiam iis qui eum ferunt, & appellatur accipenser. De eodem quoque Cicerone illa verba ex lib. de fato leguntur apud Macrob. l. 13.
