Nam cum esset apud se ad Lauernium Scipio, vnaque Pontius, allatus est forte Scipioni accipenser, qui admodum raro capitur, sed est piscis, vt ferunt, inprimis nobilis.
units.tr: And Lucilius, in Cicero's De finibus, bk. 2: "O Publius," he says, "O gullet of Gallonius, you are a wretched man, never well in life, when you spend everything on squill and sturgeon with a tithe..." From this it appears that this Gallonius, that glutton of delicacies, adorned and furnished his banquet with the sturgeon as a most costly and sweet fish. Archestratus, in Athenaeus bk. 8, thinks that the chaleon [?] is the same fish which among the Romans is carried round at dinners with pipes and garlands, those who carry it being crowned too, and which is called accipenser. Cicero's words about this same fish are also read in Macrobius, bk. 13, from the book On Fate: "For when Scipio was at his house at Lavernium, and Pontius was with him, a sturgeon was brought to Scipio by chance. It is caught very rarely, but it is a fish, they say, especially noble."

units.la: Cum autem Scipio vnum & alterum ex iis, qui ipsum salutatum venerant, inuitasset, pluresq; etiam inuitatur[?] videretur, in aure Pontius, Scipio, inquit, vide quid agas, accipenser iste paucorum hominum est. Comendatur quoq; à Martiali hoc disticho,
units.tr: When Scipio had invited one or two of those who had come to greet him, and seemed about to invite still more, Pontius said in his ear: "Scipio, see what you are doing. This sturgeon belongs to few people." It is also commended by Martial in this couplet:

units.la: Ad palatinas accipensera mittite mensas
units.tr: "Send the sturgeon to the palatial tables,"

units.la: Ambrosias ornent munera rara dapes.
units.tr: "rare gifts that adorn the ambrosial feasts."

units.la: Ex ouis ejus nigris conditis paratur edulium Venetiis laudatiffimum, quod Caniaco appellatur, inassuetisque mouet nauseam, assuefactis vero gratissimum. Salsamenta quoq; parantur ex eius dorsi spina, reliqua caro sale fumoq; asseruatur.
units.tr: From its black roe is prepared a dish at Venice, most highly praised, called caviar. It causes nausea in those unaccustomed to it, but is most pleasing to those who are used to it. Salted meats are also prepared from the backbone of the fish, and the remaining flesh is preserved with salt and smoke.

units.la: De Salmone.
units.tr: On the Salmon.

units.la: Nec te puniceo rutilantem viscere Salmo / Transierim, late cuius vaga verbera caude, / Gurgite de medio summas referuntur in vndas, / Occultus placido cum prodiit[?] aequore pulsu, / Tu loricato squamosus pectore frontem, / Lubricus, & dubiae fatturus fercula cāme, / Tempora longarum fers incorrupte morarum, / Prafignis maculis capitis,cui prodiga natat / Aluus, opimatoq; fluens abdomine venter.
units.tr: "Nor shall I pass you by, salmon, glowing with purple flesh, whose wide-ranging tail beats the water, and from whose midst in the whirlpool they are carried up on the surface waves, when you come forth hidden on the calm water with a splash. You, scaly, with a breastplate-like chest, slippery, and destined to furnish dishes of doubtful..., you bear the passing of long delays uncorrupted, with spots on your head, and your bountiful belly floats, and the stomach flows with a fattened paunch."

units.la: Ex his Aufonii carminibus facile este-licere Salmonis dotes in re cibaria.
units.tr: From these verses of Ausonius one may easily gather the salmon's qualities as food.

units.la: Intelligit autem Aquitanicum fluuia-tilem, quem Plinius marinis omnibus prae-ferri affirmat, lib.9. cap.18. Maflarius omni-bus,tam marinis, quam fluviatilibus ante-ponere videtur, in quo tamen ab aliis non immerito reprehenditur, cum esu Salmo-nis colica passione plures correptos esse constet, ob crassum & flatuofum succum, quo abundat. Verum probe praeparatus, hoc est, elixatus in vino cum garyophyllis, pipere,cinnamomo, zinzibere, vel etiam craticula tostus in aflulas dissectus, & garyo-phyllis confixus, tum, quod praecipue spe-ctandum, perfecte in ventre coctus confectusq;, alit egregie, extraq; noxam est, quod Rheni, Albis, Rhodaniqueaccolae, Salmo-ne namque clarent isti fluuii, contestantur.
units.tr: He means the river salmon of Aquitaine, which Pliny affirms is preferred to all marine fish (bk. 9, ch. 18). Massarius seems to prefer it to all fish, both marine and river, and on this point he is not undeservedly rebuked by others, since it is agreed that many have been seized by colic from eating salmon, on account of the thick and windy juice with which it abounds. But when it is properly prepared, that is, boiled in wine with cloves, pepper, cinnamon and ginger, or toasted on a gridiron, cut into slices and stuck with cloves, and then, which is the chief point to observe, perfectly digested in the stomach, it nourishes excellently and is free from harm. The inhabitants of the Rhine, the Elbe and the Rhone attest this, for those rivers are famous for their salmon.

units.la: Venter adipofus in praecipua ciborum gloria est: quin caput etiam magnificatur a ganeae peritis. Recens suauissimus est: sale quoque conditus atque, ut ceteri grandio-res pisces, asseruatus, gratus est, nec infalu-bris, mutatoque nomine dicitur esox. E mari flumina subeuntes meliores evadunt, marinum illud virus exuentes, vel ad minimum emendantes.
units.tr: The fatty belly holds the first place of glory among foods; indeed the head too is praised by those skilled in gluttony. Fresh, it is most delicious. Salted too, and preserved like other larger fish, it is pleasant and not unwholesome, and under a changed name it is called esox. Ascending from the sea into the rivers, they become better, shedding the marine taint or at least mending it.

units.la: Constat tamen non semper e mari in flumina ascendisse, sed pluribus in locis natos & educatos. Rhodanicos & Ligerinos praecipue commendatos apud certos autores invenio.
units.tr: It is agreed, however, that they have not always ascended from the sea into the rivers, but are born and raised in many places. I find the salmon of the Rhone and the Loire especially commended by certain authors.

units.la: Mirum vero nullam a graecis Salmonis mentionem factam esse, & a Latinorum, praeter Plinium & Ausonium, nullo: quidam trottam fluuiatilem volunt esse Salmonem, quam opinionem relinquo ego in medio.
units.tr: It is strange that no mention of the salmon is made by the Greeks, and by the Latins none except Pliny and Ausonius. Some want the river trout to be the salmon; this opinion I leave undecided.

units.la: The ornament divider is not printed text and is left out.
Detrutta, aurata & variola.
units.tr: Trout, golden trout and variola.

units.la: NEC tu, trutta, silentio damnanda adeo in mensarum aulicarum gloria prealiis nobilitata, faporeq, suavi celebrata, ut etiam Aufonius in sua Mofella te non conticuerit, sic canens,
units.tr: Nor, trout, are you to be passed over in silence. You were ennobled among other fish by the glory of courtly tables and celebrated for your sweet flavour, so that even Ausonius did not leave you unmentioned in his Mosella, singing thus:

units.la: Teque inter geminas species, neutrumq; & vtrumque, Qui necdum Salamo, nec tam Salarambiguufque Amborum medio sario intercepte sub zuo
units.tr: "And you, between two kinds, neither one nor the other, who are not yet a salmon, nor yet a salar, and are caught midway between the two."

units.la: Ex quibus versibus colligitur, farionem, variolam seu forellam, falarem & falmonem eundem esse piscem, dicit, falarem forellam adhuc teneram, farionem media ætatis, jam vero grandem forellam Salmonem, seu truttam Salmoneam, cujusmodi plurimi Germania amnes, rivi, rivuli, torrentes, fertilissimi [?] sunt. Celebrantur in primis, quae in fluminibus fontium abundantibus capiuntur. Porro elixae assis praeflant, eduntur ex aceto, rarius friguntur, nec alia condimenta patiuntur, suo enim sapore fatis placent.
units.tr: From these verses it is gathered that the fario, the variola or forella, the falar and the falmo are the same fish. He says that the falar is a young forella still tender, the fario is one of middle age, and the forella grown large is the salmon, or salmon trout. Very many such trout are found in the most fertile rivers, streams, brooks and torrents of Germany. Those taken in rivers fed by springs are most highly prized. They are better boiled or roasted, are eaten with vinegar, more rarely fried, and do not admit other seasonings, for they are pleasing enough in their own flavour.

units.la: Sale quoq; condiuntur, laquearibus adium appensa asservantur. Caeterum nobiliores semper habentur & pretiosiores, purpureis aureisq; maculis variegatæ, & quibus caro rubescens, & dura est: candida, & quibus est caro alro albida mollisq; insipida sunt, & minus pretiosa. Illas nobiliores culina commendant precipue ut sapidissimas. Attamen,
units.tr: They are also salted and hung up to be kept from the ceilings of houses. Those with purple and golden spots are always considered more noble and precious, and their flesh is reddish and firm. The white ones, whose flesh is whitish, soft and insipid, are less valued. The cooks commend the former above all as the most savoury. Yet,

units.la: Non omnis laudem pretiumq; aurata meretur, canente Martiali.
units.tr: "Not every golden trout deserves praise or price," as Martial sings.

units.la: De Prasmo, Barbo, Perca.
units.tr: On the prasmus, barbel and perch.

units.la: IN ciborum quoque gloria, palatique delitiis sunt Prasmus seu Erythrophthalmus (sic dictus à rubro oculorum colore) barbus seu barbatus (sic cognominatus à barbula vtrinque in inferiori labro pendente) & Perca. (per antiphrasin sic appellata, quod nemini parcat, iratus namque pisces alios pinnis suis vulnerat.) De hoc pisce Ausonius in Mosella elegant carmine ita cecinit, quem etiam pretiosissimis mullis non veritus est comparare, Nec te delitias mensarum Perca silebo, Amnigeros inter pisces dignande, marinis Solus puniceis facilis contendere mullis, Namq; & gustus iners, solidoq; in corpore partes Segmentis coeunt, sed dissociantur aristis.
units.tr: Among the glories of food and the delights of the palate are the prasmus, or erythrophthalmus (so called from the red colour of its eyes), the barbel, or barbatus (so named from the little beard hanging on each side of its lower lip), and the perch (called by antiphrasis, as it were "sparing," because it spares no one: when angry it wounds other fish with its fins). Ausonius sings of this fish in his Mosella in an elegant poem, which he did not hesitate to compare even with the most precious red mullet: "Nor will I pass over you, perch, worthy to be counted among the delights of tables, you alone among river fish able to vie with the purple mullet of the sea. For your taste is not inferior, and your body is firm, its parts joined in segments yet separated by spines."

units.la: Et hodie certe nobilitatem illam atq; praestantiam pertinacissime retinuit, nec de ejus in cibis salubritate ac suavitate etiam dubitandum est, ob carnem candidam, duram, parumque obtinentem lentoris: amnicatamen & fluviatilis lacustrib. semper prae-fertur, fertur, tum enim bene valentibus, tum etiam aegrotantibus praesertim febricitantibus, in cibatu posterior medicina vtilem eam esse prodidit.
units.tr: And today it certainly keeps that nobility and excellence most stubbornly. Nor is there any doubt about its wholesomeness and pleasantness as food, on account of its white, firm flesh, which holds little sliminess. Yet it is always preferred to the lake fish of rivers. For it is useful both to the healthy and to the sick, especially to those with fever, and later medicine has declared it useful as food.

units.la: De babo praeterea, nullum Latinorum, praeter Aufonium, mentionem fecisse inuenio, cuius elegantissima carmina huc asscribere placuit, graphicè enim barbum ita pingit,
units.tr: Moreover, I find that no Latin writer except Ausonius has mentioned the barbel. I am pleased to add his most elegant verses here, for he paints the barbel vividly:

units.la: Tuq; per obliqui fauces vexate Satani, Qua bis terna fremunt scopulosis ostia pilis, Cum defluxisti fama majore in amnem Liberior, laxos exerces barbe natatus, Tu melior pejore auo, tibi contigit uni Spirantum ex numero non illaudata fenestra.
units.tr: "And you, who are harassed in the jaws of the crooked Satan, where two-and-thirty doors bristle with rocky bristles, when you have slipped down into the river with greater renown, free, you practise your loose swimming, barbel. You are better than your evil grandfather; to you alone of those who breathe has a window not unpraised been granted."

units.la: Haec Aufonius. Adultiores autem & seniores inter lautiores habentur, praesertim &statis temporibus, cibos, tunc enim cum vino & aqua elixantur, aceduntur. Barbu- lones hoc est, minores & juniores in cibos quoq; veniunt, sed non adeo lauti sunt. Porro rostrum barbi, quam sit gulae proceribus gratum, quamq; auide expetatur, neminino est notum. Vnde Germanorum vulgatum jactatur & jocularie prouerbium,
units.tr: So Ausonius. Older and grown fish are counted among the more refined foods, especially at certain seasons, for they are boiled with wine and water, and then dressed with vinegar. Young barbel, that is, the smaller and younger ones, also come to table, but they are not so refined. Moreover, how pleasing the barbel's snout is to the noble gourmets, and how eagerly it is sought, is known to no one. Hence the common German proverb, said in jest:

units.la: <bl>Deß Hechts Zungen / Deß Karpffen Seiten / Deß Barben Mäulchen / brachten mich vmb mein Apffelgrawes Gäulchen.</bl> Ad extremum infamantur barbi ouorum malitia & vitio, esitata enim intolerabiles alui cruciatus concitasse expertum est, tum ipsam etiam aluum immodicè soluisse, quod obiter hic memoriae causâ adiicio.
units.tr: <bl>Pike's tongues, carp's sides, barbel's little mouths: these brought me to lose my dapple-grey little horse.</bl> Finally, barbel are disparaged for the malice and fault of their roe. For it has been found that eating it causes intolerable pains in the bowels, and also brings on excessive diarrhoea. I add this here in passing, to be remembered.

units.la: De anguilla.
units.tr: On the eel.

units.la: AB anguium similitudine videtur nomen sortita, unde Iuuenalis in sua Satyra, Vos anguilla manet, longae cognata colubrae.
units.tr: From its resemblance to snakes, the eel seems to have received its name. Hence Juvenal in his satire: "The eel remains for you, a kinsman of the long snake."

units.la: Sed vulgus falsò coire cum serpentibus credit, hocque modo veneficiis impleri, unde æstiuo tempore mensis plane abdicant. De ortu anguillarum inter autores non conuenit. Aristoteles naturarum callentissimus, sine coitu, sine ouo, anguillas procreari, inq;iis [?] nec masculinum nec fœmininum genus esse constanter affirmat. Priorem rationem videtur afferre hanc, quod scilicet in nonnullis fœculentis stagnis, aqua omnino exhausta, limoque detracto, anguillæ denuo generentur, ubi aqua accesserit pluuia. Plinius atterere se scopulis, eaque frigmenta [?] reuiuiscere, nec esse aliam earum procreationem asserit. Oppianus lib.1. aliter sentit, cuius carmina, Lippio vertente, subnectere, non erit incongruum,
units.tr: But the common people wrongly believe that eels mate with serpents, and that by this means they are filled with poisons; for this reason they abstain completely from eels in summer. Authors do not agree on the origin of eels. Aristotle, most skilled in natural things, affirms firmly that eels are produced without coupling and without eggs, and that they have neither a male nor a female kind. He seems to give this reason: that in some muddy pools, when the water has been entirely drained and the mud removed, eels are generated again once rain water has come in. Pliny says that they are produced when they rub themselves against rocks, and that these fragments come back to life, and that there is no other way in which they are produced. Oppian, in the first book, thinks otherwise. It will not be out of place to add his verses, in Lipsius's translation:

units.la: Anguillæ spiris, multoq; volumine nexæ Concubunt, lentor destillat corpore toto, Qui spumæ similis, bibula cælatur arena,
units.tr: "The eels, knotted in coils and in a great tangle, lie together, and a viscous slime drips from their whole body,"

units.la: Accipit hunc cœnum, quid enim fœcundius illo? Concipit accépto, nascuntur lubrica turba: Sic coeunt congri, sic lubrica membra refol-uunt.
units.tr: "which, like foam, is hidden in the thirsty sand. The mud receives it; for what is more fruitful than that? It conceives when it has received it, and a slippery brood is born. So the conger eels couple, and so they loosen their slippery limbs."

units.la: Sed nobis perinde est, siue ex cœno, siue ex fœno, siue ex limo, siue ex fimo procreentur ur.[?] Quid in glo-ia œsophagi valeant, inquiramus. Certum[?] est anguillarum carnem medicos plerosque, omnes damnasse, tum in sanorum tum in ægrorum cibis, sed nulla probabili ratione, quod tamen pauci illorum dictum volo. Lenta enim illa & glu-tinosa[?] pituita, quam vescentibus pestem, imo largius crebriusq; sumtam, mortem afferre dicunt, elixatione, vel assatione sudando facile extillat, nullo relicto vel alieni saporis, vel lenti illius glu-tini pigmento. Parandi igitur ratio hic, quæ varia est, non ignoranda. In confesso est uberrimi alimenti esse anguillas ob carnem mollem & dulcem, adeoq; suauissimam[?] ad largissima edendum diuturno morbo confectos & extenuatos non al-liciat modo, verum etiam cito reficiat, vi-resq; restauret. Non eo inficias, uberius in cibis, crebriusq; sumtam, pernitiosam esse, vitæq; periculum afferre non assuetis. Itaque gentes in iis locis, ubi anguillarum abundantia est, (sic Homerus Phæacas appellat, ἀλωλιχωτάτας[?] quasi anguillis abundantissimos, & propterea in quotidiano sunt usu, paulatim iis edendis assuefacti, impune postea iis vescentur. Ubi memimeminisse quoq; vitæ prorogandæ studiosum velim, crebro anguillarum cibo calculos gigni in renibus & vesica, glutinoso lento non probè absterso:um quoq; nigra illa venulâ per spinâ medium porrecta, non exemta, antequam coquatur, veneni enim particeps esse creditur. Diphilus apud Athenæum lacustrem anguillam marinæ quidem insuauiorem efferit[?] esse, verum uberioris alimenti.
units.tr: But for us it is all the same whether they are produced from mud, from hay, from slime, or from dung. Let us inquire what they are worth for the glory of the gullet. It is certain that most physicians, indeed all, have condemned the flesh of eels, both in the food of the healthy and of the sick. Yet there is no probable reason for this, and I would like a few of them to say so. For that slimy and gluey phlegm, which they say is a poison to those who eat it, or rather a death if taken in larger and more frequent amounts, is easily dissolved by boiling or roasting, leaving no trace either of foreign flavour or of that gluey slime. So the method of preparation here, which is varied, should not be ignored. It is granted that eels are a very rich food, because their flesh is soft and sweet, and so very pleasing to eat. They not only tempt those worn out and wasted by a long illness to eat them, but also quickly restore them and renew their strength. I do not deny that, eaten in larger amounts and more often, they are harmful and bring danger of life to those not accustomed to them. So the peoples in places where there is an abundance of eels (Homer calls the Phaeacians "[ἀλωλιχωτάτας]," as it were most abundant in eels), and who therefore use them daily, gradually accustomed to eating them, afterwards eat them with impunity. I would also like anyone who is eager to prolong life to remember that frequent eating of eel causes stones to form in the kidneys and bladder, when the gluey slime has not been properly wiped away. Also that dark little vein which runs along the middle of the spine should be removed before cooking, for it is believed to share in the poison. Diphilus, quoted by Athenaeus, says that lake eels are indeed less pleasant than sea eels, but more nourishing.

units.la: Quæ ex fluminibus in mare descendunt, (falsâ enim deleētantur) salubriores effici aquâ maris & nutrimento, omnium consensu traditur, exuere enim illas lentum illud glutinum, periculosamq; illam pinguedinem, hacq; ratione mirè agiles effici, minusq; lubricas, atque esui salubriores, testantur maritimi piscatores, qui circa catarrhactas ( Schlüfen vocā, à claudendo) quæ apertis valvis aquam, quâ hibernis mensibus agri opprimuntur, violento impetu in mare profundunt, inusitatæ magnitudinis anguillas nassis ac sagenis eximunt.
units.tr: It is commonly agreed that those which descend from rivers into the sea (for they are refreshed by the water) become healthier, through the sea water and the nourishment. For they shed that viscous slime and dangerous fatness. In this way they become remarkably agile, less slippery, and more wholesome to eat, as the sea fishermen testify. They catch eels of unusual size with fish traps and seine nets near the sluices (which we call Schlüfen from closing), which, when the valves are opened, discharge in a violent rush into the sea the water by which the fields are flooded in the winter months.

units.la: Porrò coctura rationem quod attinet, elixantur ex aquâ & vino detracto corio, adiectis pipere, cinnamomo, Zinzibere & croco. Alii, & quidem salubriori inuento eas torrent, craticula, & quæ sunt ampliores, verubus. Sale quoq; condiuntur, quibus vulgus suauissimè ve-scitur per illos præsertim dies quibus carnibus abstinet. In vino suffocate[?] abstemios reddere homines, si ex eo bibant, qui plus satis mero indulgent, & hinc offendantur, atq; delinquunt, Mi-zaldus prodidit, cuius quoq; commeminit Plinius l.32.c.10. Ad extremum non prætereundum, singularem anguillis etiam extra aquam vitacitatem esse, aquiloneq; flante plures vivere dies, austro pauciores. Turbidam aquam omnino reformidant, profundam & puram appetentes, non leve salubrioris alimenti indicium. De alimento ipsorum nihil certi proditum invenio, nisi quod quibusdam in locis vescantur limo, atq; aliis eduliis si quis apposuerit. Athenæus se vidisse ait in Arethusa circa Chalcidem anguillas man-suetas, inaureq;[?] aureas & argenteas habentes, & capientes ab offerentibus cibos. Cuius quoq; rei Plinius meminit lib.32.cap.2. Idem in amne Gange ad tricenos pedes longas reperiri lib.6.c.3. autor est. Lacustres carnivoras esse certò constat, piscículos enim ranasq;[?] persequuntur. Vitium indubitatè manifestant odor & gustatus: inculpate nihil virosum sapiunt aut redolent. Examines piscium solas non suitare[?] Aristoteles & Plinius prodiderunt, quod mirum quidem, ratione tamen non plane carens. Capiuntur viplu-[?]rimum rimum circa Virgilias, fluminibus sc. tum prae-cipue urbidis.
units.tr: As for the method of cooking, they are boiled in water and wine, with the skin removed, with pepper, cinnamon, ginger and saffron added. Others, and indeed in a more wholesome way, roast them on a gridiron, or on spits if they are larger. They are also seasoned with salt, and the common people eat them with great pleasure, especially on those days when they abstain from meat. Mizaldus has reported that eels drowned in wine make men abstinent if they drink it, but that those who indulge too much in unmixed wine are offended by it and go astray; Pliny also mentions this in book 32, chapter 10. Finally, it should not be passed over that eels have a remarkable ability to live out of water, and that when the north wind blows they survive for more days, but under the south wind for fewer. They utterly dread muddy water, seeking deep and clear water, which is no slight sign of wholesome food. I find nothing certain reported about their food, except that in some places they eat mud, and other food if someone puts it before them. Athenaeus says that he saw tame eels in the Arethusa near Chalcis, having golden and silver earrings, and taking food from those who offered it. Pliny also mentions this, in book 32, chapter 2. The same author states that in the river Ganges they are found up to thirty feet long, book 6, chapter 3. It is certain that lake eels are carnivorous, for they pursue little fish and frogs. Their defect is clearly shown by smell and taste; when unblemished they have nothing foul in taste or smell. Aristotle and Pliny have reported that only the eels of the sea do not spawn, which is indeed remarkable, yet not wholly without reason. They are caught most often near the Virgilian region, that is, in rivers, especially muddy ones.

units.la: De Mullo, Scaro, Scombro.
units.tr: On the Mullet, the Parrotfish, and the Mackerel.

units.la: Quanta fuerit imperii Romani in alendis piscibus luxuria, quamque infina & portentosa eorundem pretia extiterint, docet vel unus mullus tantopere iactatus ac nominatus à Plinio, Iuuenale, Macrobio. Hunc octo millibus ab Afinio celere viro consulari, Clodio Principe, emtum, Plinius tradidit, id est, aestimatione Budaei, ducentis aureis. Iuuenalis vero quasi dubi-tans ait;
units.tr: How great the luxury of the Roman empire was in keeping fish, and how immense and monstrous their prices became, is shown by the mullet alone, which Pliny, Juvenal and Macrobius all praise and name. Pliny reports that Afinius, a consular man of quick wit, bought one under the emperor Claudius for eight thousand, which by Budé's estimate is two hundred gold pieces. Juvenal, as if doubtful, says:

units.la: Mullum sex millibus emitÆquantem sane paribus sextertia libris.Ut perhibent qui de magnis maiora loquuntur.
units.tr: He bought a mullet for six thousand, one that weighed as many pounds as the sesterces it cost, as those say who speak of great things in grander terms.

units.la: Macrobius septem millibus emtum meminit, ut ita duo millia, teste Budeo, maneant in controuersia. Ex quibus satis superque videre est, in admirabili honore mensarum fuisse mullum, magnopereque gulae placuisse, adeo quidem, ut nec accipenseris apud antiquos pretiosissimi gustus, nec scari, nec lupi celebratissimorum piscium pretium tantopere fit decantatum. Galenus lib. de facult. alimentt. multi in cibis sua aetate auctoritatem non tacuit, ait enim, magnificari ab hominibus, ac si cunctos alios sapiditate praecelleret.
units.tr: Macrobius mentions a price of seven thousand, so that two thousand, on Budé's reckoning, remain in dispute. From these accounts it is plain enough and more than enough that the mullet held a wondrous place of honour at the table and greatly pleased gluttony, so much so that among the ancients neither the sturgeon, the most precious delicacy, nor the parrotfish, nor the pike, the most celebrated fish, had their prices so loudly sung. Galen, in his book On the Properties of Foods, does not pass over the esteem the mullet enjoyed among many in his day; for he says that men extol it as if it surpassed all other fish in flavour.

units.la: Atcaufas cur tantoperè gulæ placeret, capè- re non potuit, quippe nec fapotis gratiam, nec pariter salubritatis ineo fe reperire fate- tur. Refertidem; cumaliquando quendam togaffet, cur ram immani pretio mullos præ- grandes effet mercatus, respondisse, pro oter iecur inprimis, deinde propter caput tantam impendisse pecuniam. Horatius 2. ferm. Satyra 2. epar, caput, & denique ipsas carnes vocat pulmenta. Et épar in delitiis popina- libus fuisse Galenus testis est, qui carné mul- li durissima esse dicit, admodum, friabilem hoc est, lentoris omnis atque pinguedinis expertem, ideoque, fi probé conficiatur, vas- lentius & vberius alere quam czterorum pi- scium. Idem tamen priusquam iis coctis ve- famur, ventres esse referandos præcipit, quod scilicet in ventre crebrò alimenta res- perianrut venenata, quæ abipfisdeuoran- tur, vt nos fzpiffimè in luciis spectamus. Qui enim in cœnosis obfcœnisque littoribus versantur, grauiter olent; gustatuque sunt insuaues, maliqué succi. Sed adhuc peiores, qui lepore marino venenatiffimo vescuntur mullos autem eo vesci clari autores trádunt. Ideoque & mullorum auctoritas in tanto gu- lz desiderio ac pretio, vitæ insidias struit. Sale aßcruati mille remedia præstant, verum cibis minusidonei. Coćti panificioque in- eruftati crustati diutius durant, alias facile compu-trefcunt. Optimos Galenus censer,qui in puro versantur pelago,quiqué bona alimen-ta pascuntur. Oceanus Britannicus fert amplissimos. LXXX. librarum mullam in mari rubro captum Licinius Murianus prodidit,referente Plinio. Bilibres alias, tri-libres,atque etiam quadrilibres vsitati sunt. Certum est, ætatem amplitudinem & pon-dus augere.
units.tr: Yet why it pleased gluttony so much he could not grasp, since he admits that he found in it neither a pleasant taste nor any wholesomeness. He relates that once, when someone in a toga asked a man why he had bought such large mullets at an immense price, the man replied that he had spent so much money chiefly for the liver, then for the head; Horace calls the liver, the head and finally the flesh itself the relishes (Satires 2.2). Galen also bears witness that the liver was among the delicacies of the eating-houses. He says that the flesh of the mullet is very hard, indeed very crumbly, that is, free of all viscosity and fatness, and so, if properly prepared, it nourishes more strongly and abundantly than the flesh of other fish. Yet the same author advises that before we eat them cooked, their bellies should be inspected, because venomous food is often found in the belly, having been devoured by the fish, as we often see in pike. For those who live in muddy and filthy shores smell strongly, taste unpleasant, and have bad juices. Worse still are those who feed on the sea-hare, a most deadly kind of food; and famous authors report that mullets feed on it. Hence the authority of the mullet, which excites such great desire and commands such a price, lays snares for life. Salted and cured, they provide a thousand remedies, but they are less suitable as food. Cooked and encased in pastry they last longer; otherwise they rot easily. Galen judges the best to be those that live in the open sea and feed on good food. The British Ocean produces very large ones. Licinius Murianus, as Pliny reports, recorded a mullet of eighty pounds caught in the Red Sea. Otherwise two-, three- and even four-pound mullets are customary. It is certain that age increases their size and weight.

units.la: Non omittendum hic, Apitium ad omne luxus ingenium mirum, in associorum garo, (quæ quoque res cognomen inuenit) necarieos præcessens putasse, atque è iecore eorum halece excogitare prouocasse. Quod quidem facilius est dixisse,quam quis vicerit, Plinio l.9.c.7.teste. Ex quibus omnibus conspicuum euadit,mullum (sicdictum à mollitie,quod seruitutis sit impatientissimus, & viuariorum claustrorumque indignantissimus) à barbo nostro fluuiatili longe diuisum esse,licet imperitè à quibusdam confundantur, german. nominari potest, ein Meer- barbel/mullus marinus,qui si barbatulus est, inque alto alitur mari,præstantissimus est,& hic in tam mirabili priscis Romanis fuit honore & pretio: barbæ expertes inglorii habentur, german. glatte Meerbarbeln. Solus mullus cer parit,Plin.& Aristotele prodentibus, vnde τρίγλα[?] dicitur græcis.
units.tr: It should not be omitted here that Apicius, remarkably inventive in every kind of luxury, is thought to have had the heads of these fish cut off for his garum of pickled fish (a thing which also gave its name to the sauce), and to have devised a relish from their livers, which is easier to say than to surpass him, as Pliny attests in book 9, chapter 7. From all this it becomes plain that the mullet (so called from mollitia, softness, because it is most impatient of servitude and most indignant at tanks and enclosures) is far removed from our river barbel, although some confuse them unskillfully. It can be called in German ein Meerbarbel, a sea-barbel, mullus marinus, which, if it has a beard and is fed in the deep sea, is most excellent; this is the fish that held such marvellous honour and price among the ancient Romans. Beardless ones are considered without distinction; in German, smooth sea-barbels. The mullet alone, as Pliny and Aristotle relate, bears young, whence the Greeks call it trigla [τρίγλα].

units.la: Scarum quoque in luxus patina principa-tum olim tenuisse non leues autores memo-riæ prodiderunt. Solus piscium ruminare dicitur, (unde à quibusdam ruminalis dici-tur) herbisque vesci, mari Carpathio maxi-mè frequens. Optatus Tiberii Cæsaris clas-sis præfectus scarum piscem nouum incolam mari Italico dedit, aduectumè promontorio Troadis Lecto, quod sponte nunquā transit. Adeò gula ex piscibus sapores sibi admouit. De eius alimento minimè dubitandum, cum omnium eruditorum consensu primatum geratinter saxatiles. Carnem habet, teste Athe-neo, facile coctibilem, & quæ celeriter distribuitur, aluoque molliendæ non inutil-lem: saffari autem solet in craticula aut sarta-gine, quin & elixari. Intestina eius ac iecur inter popinales delitias à ganeæ peritis repo-sita inuenio. Martialis de scaro cecinit,
units.tr: Not slight authors have recorded that the parrotfish too once held the primacy in the luxury of the dish. It alone among fish is said to ruminate (whence some call it ruminalis) and to feed on herbs; it is very common in the Carpathian Sea. Optatus, prefect of the fleet of the emperor Tiberius, introduced the parrotfish as a new inhabitant of the Italian sea, bringing it from Lectum, the promontory of Troas, which it never passes of its own accord. So far did gluttony seek flavours from fish. There is no doubt about its diet, since by the agreement of all learned men it holds the first place among rock fish. Its flesh, as Athenaeus reports, is easily cooked, is quickly digested, and is not useless for softening the bowels. It is usually grilled on a gridiron or fried in a pan, and it is also boiled. I find its guts and liver stored away among the delicacies of the eating-house by men skilled in gluttony. Martial sang of the parrotfish:

units.la: Visceribus bonus est: catera bile sapit.
units.tr: Good in its entrails; the rest tastes of bile.

units.la: Mirum, quod piscium omnibus serrati sunt dentes, vni aquatilium scaro plani. Sed nec conticendus astus scarorum est, nassis enim inclusi non fronte erumpunt, nec infestis viminibus caput inferunt, sed auersum caudi-bus crebris fores laxant, atque ita re-trorsum erumpunt. Quem eorum luctatum, si forsan alius scarus extrinsecus videat, ap-prehensa mordicus cauda adiuuat erumpen-tes nixus. Germ. appellari audio, sin [?] Heuwet/ oder Keutwbraffen/ &c. Usum multi[?], recentisq; eius e capite cineris in medicinis, aduersus omnia venena & venenata animalia insignem esse Plinius graviter prodidit, lib.32. cap.7. Sumitur autem in cibo, vel allinitur.
units.tr: It is remarkable that all fish have serrated teeth, but among the water-creatures only the parrotfish has flat ones. Nor should the cunning of the parrotfish go unmentioned: when shut in traps, they do not burst out through the front, nor push their heads against the hostile wicker, but turning their tails backward they loosen the doors with repeated blows and so force their way out backward. If another parrotfish outside sees such a struggle, it helps the one trying to escape by seizing its tail in its teeth and pulling with all its might. I hear that in German it is called Heuwet or Keutwbraffen. Pliny seriously reports that its head, burnt to ash, is used in medicines, and is a notable remedy, recently discovered, against all poisons and poisonous animals (Natural History 32.7). It is taken in food or smeared on.

units.la: Ex laudatissimorum quoque piscium marinorum & gr[?]alium genere est Scomber, Mafrell/ vel Mafrill/ qui recenter captus melior est, mensisq; lautioribus primis diebus gratior, sed gratia breui perit ob fastidiu, quod ex diuturniori asseruatione parit. Olim ex Scombris, Plinio teste, praestantissimum conficiebatur garum, cuius Atheneus quoq; meminit lib.7. Torrentur autem in craticula, viridi inuoluta foeniculo & butyro: quibusdam in locis irrorantur ex butyro vel oleo, sale etiam condiuntur, & asseruantur. Bene autem alere, boniq; succi esse non est dubium. Scombros in aceto putrefactos vulua strangulatu oppressas excitari Plinius graui-simus scriptor autor est. Sumendus autem est adeps linamentaq; eo sunt accendenda.
units.tr: The mackerel also belongs to the kind of sea and river fish most praised. It is called Scomber, in German Mafrell or Mafrill. When freshly caught it is better, and on the first days of more elegant meals it is more pleasing; but its pleasure soon perishes through the distaste that comes from longer keeping. Formerly, according to Pliny, the most excellent garum was made from mackerels, which Athenaeus also mentions (book 7). They are roasted on a gridiron, wrapped in green fennel and butter; in some places they are basted with butter or oil, and they are also seasoned with salt and preserved. There is no doubt that they nourish well and have good juice. Pliny, a most serious writer, reports that mackerels steeped in vinegar relieve women suffering from strangulation of the womb. The fat should be taken, and linen cloths should be set alight with it.

units.la: De Tinca.
units.tr: On the Tench.

units.la: HOdie in lautioribus mensis exiguam ob-tinet autoritatem tinca sive tencha, per-spicuissimum enim habent, infalubérrimam esse, propterea quod cænosis & limosi loci sponte vel proueniat, vel quod luto & cæno gaudeat & alatur, unde germani Schleyen appellatur, vel à lubricitate, vel muco, quem Germani Schleim nominant. De lacuftribus seu palustribus non item inficias glutinosi eas esse & difficilis succi de aquatilibus non item, bas enim elixas, frixas, vel craticula tostas, oleribus odoratis vel aromatis fartas, commendatas à granibus aut oribus reperto. Popi-nalis lautitiæ & ganeæ studiosissimum quendam, alio laridoq; eas conditas, additis odoratis oleribus multo aromate, ad vaporem tepidiorum furno felicissime percoxisse, Paulus Iouius pro-didit. Discissas per dorsi longitudinem plantiq; pedum appositas, febrium ardentium flammas sedare Medici quidam experti sunt.
units.tr: Today the tench, or tinca, holds little authority at more refined tables, for people are quite sure it is very unwholesome. It either arises spontaneously in muddy and slimy places, or it delights in mud and ooze and is nourished by them. For this reason the Germans call it Schleyen, either from its slipperiness or from the mucus which the Germans call Schleim. I do not deny that fish from lakes or marshes are glutinous and of coarse juice, but the same cannot be said of fish from running water. These, boiled, fried, or grilled on a gridiron, and stuffed with fragrant herbs or spices, are commended by serious men. Paulus Iovius reports that a certain man, devoted to luxury and gluttony, seasoned them with bacon and much spice and fragrant herbs, and then roasted them in an oven to a pleasantly warm steam with great success. Some physicians have tested that tench cut along the length of the back and laid on the soles of the feet calm the flames of burning fevers.

units.la: De Muræna, lampetra, ascellis, raia, pla-teffis, harengis, gobio, al-burno, &c.
units.tr: On the Murena, the lamprey, the asellus, the ray, the plaice, the herring, the gudgeon, the bleak, etc.

units.la: Tanta fuit priscos apud Romanos hu-ius piscis gratia, tantoperequeabiis honoratus, vt etiam nobiles abeo fa-miliæ fuerint denominatæ. Plurimum au-tem inter fe differre murænas Galenus vult, pessimamque earum carnem asserit, qui in ostiis flumi-num degunt lacrinas cloacasque expurgantium, aut culinas aut balnea, aut ve-[?]tium, stium, aut lineolorum sordes, aut si quæ alia sunt in urbibus, per quas medias fluunt, expurganda, potissimum si populosæ fuerint. Itaq; muraenis non semper contingit esse optimas.
units.tr: The murena was held in such high regard among the ancient Romans, and was so honoured, that even noble families were named after it. Galen holds that murenas differ greatly from one another, and he asserts that the worst flesh belongs to those that live at the mouths of rivers, where they feed on the filth of drains and sewers, or of kitchens and baths, or the refuse of tanners and linen-washers, or whatever else in cities must be cleansed where the rivers flow through the middle, especially where the population is dense. Therefore murenas are not always the best.

units.la: Traduntur & alia, quæ muraenas abdicandas cibis suadeant, concipere enim eas ex serpentibus autores non dilutæ fidei affirmarunt. Prodidit id Plinius l.9.c.23. & l.32.c.2, autoritate Licinii Macri, cuius etiam opinionem secutus est Oppianus, muraenam scil. & serpentem mutuo amore ardere, ac serpente veneno mortifero in saxis deposito è littore sibilo muraenam euocare, quem si audiat muraena, ex aquis confestim protuat, expletoq; Veneris desiderio serpentem venenum depositum repetere, quod si non inueniat, dolore emoriatur. Aristoteles tamen videtur negare cum serpentibus eas misceri ac generare, marem enim proprium vocat myrum, qui generat. Porro fuisse in delitiis & hoc mensarum Poetæ multi latini aliique scriptores prodiderunt. D. Ambrosius l.5. sui hexameri ait, Mutæna, quam ferunt aliquid habere noxium, esca pretiosior est. Siculæ pretiosiores erant, testante Iuvenale,
units.tr: There are also other accounts which advise that murenas be excluded from food, for certain authors of no firm credibility have affirmed that they are conceived from serpents. Pliny reports this in book 9, chapter 23, and book 32, chapter 2, on the authority of Licinius Macer, and Oppian followed the same opinion: that the murena and the serpent burn with a mutual love, and that the serpent, having laid down its deadly poison upon the rocks, calls the murena from the shore with a hiss. If the murena hears it, it immediately rises out of the waters, and, when its desire for love is satisfied, the serpent takes up again the poison it laid down. But if it does not find the poison, the murena dies of grief. Aristotle, however, seems to deny that they mate with serpents and produce offspring, for he calls the male, which is the one that generates, the myrus. Moreover, many Latin poets and other writers have recorded that this fish was also among the delicacies of the table. Saint Ambrose, in book 5 of his Hexameron, says: "The murena, which they say has something harmful in it, is a more precious food." The Sicilian ones were more precious, as Juvenal attests:

units.la: Virroni murana datur; quæ maxima ve-nit
units.tr: To Virro a murena is given, the largest that comes

units.la: Gurgite de Siculo. Horatius Sat. vlt. l. 2. Serm. grauidam commendat his versibus,
units.tr: from the Sicilian whirlpool. Horace, in the last satire of book 2, commends a pregnant one in these verses:

units.la: Affertur [?]squillas inter murena natantes, In patina porrecta [?]sub hoc berus, hac granida, in-quit, Capta est, deterior post partum ca-rne[?] futura.
units.tr: A murena is brought in among the swimming squills; placed on a dish under this, a pregnant one, he says, was caught; after giving birth her flesh would be inferior.

units.la: Venenatam viminefle dentibus ipsarum piscatores certò sibi persuasum habent, vi-uam enim manibus non attingunt sed forci-pe. Lactes earum miré commendatur. Refert Ælius Lampridius Heliogabalum aulam omnem & tufticos aliquando iis pauisse. Vi-uarium murænarum primus inflituit & excogitauit C. Hirius ante alios, Plinio l. 9. c. ss[?] teste. Coenis is triumphalibus Coesaris Dictatoris sex millia numero murænarum tuo appendit, nam permutare quidem pro-tio noluitaliaue mercede.
units.tr: Fishermen are firmly convinced that they have venom in their teeth, for they do not touch them alive with their hands but with pincers. Their milt is especially commended. Aelius Lampridius reports that Heliogabalus once fed the whole court, and even the country folk, on them. C. Hirrius was the first, before others, to establish and devise a fishpond for murenas, as Pliny reports in book 9, chapter 55. At the triumphal feasts of Caesar the Dictator, he hung up six thousand murenas in number, for he was unwilling to exchange them for any price or reward.

units.la: Crassus cognomento diues, murænam altilem adeò adamauit, vt fato functam ali-quando luxerit. Cumque à L. Domitio ad-modum obid rideretur, respondit, mirum quidem esse quod extinctum p:fcem lacry-mis prosequeretur, sed multo admirabilius, quod ipse tres à fe elatas vxores non lugeret. Tres enim é medio sustulerat, vt dotibus po-tiretur.
units.tr: Crassus, surnamed the Rich, loved a fattened murena so much that when it died he once mourned it. When Lucius Domitius mocked him harshly for this, he replied that it was indeed strange to follow a dead fish with tears, but much more remarkable that he did not mourn the three wives he had carried out to burial himself. For he had removed three of them from the midst, so that he might come into their dowries.

units.la: Cinerem murænarum cum melle Liche-nas & lepras sanare proditum est.
units.tr: It is reported that the ash of murenas mixed with honey heals lichens and leprosy.

units.la: Non est mirandum, si cibo plures pereant quam gladio, quia nulla extat lex, quæ vesa-nam gulam puniat, solisque culinis homines ta. perimentibus non impunitas solum promit-titur, sed & in summa gloria habetur. Lam-petrociolis enim, hoc est, lampetris exiguis, hœdos configere atq; assare quandoque, gu-læ insanæ inuentum est, quin & capos iis in spiras detortis implicare, verubusque torre-re,quo tamen cibo omnes postridiê cõuiuæ se grauiter narrarunt conflictatos, stomacho enim negotium facesserat. Porro Illustria ingenia torsit lampetra, dum quisque pro e-ruditionis suæ ostentatione nomen eius antiquum docere contendit. Nos de nomine parum contendentes, quæ ad propositum nostrum pertinere videbuntur attingemus. A lambendis autem & fugendis petris lam-petram nominatam reperio, murenæ similem, longam, lubricam, sine pinnis, septem foraminibus læua parte distinctam, quibus muræna caret. Fertur autem primo vere pretiosissimus esse cibus, cum scilicet cartilago illa quæ pro vertebris & spina illiinest, nondum induruit, illa enim indurata infuauio-res esse incipiunt, gratiamque ac pretium amittere. Cæterum apparatus culinarum circa eas varius & operosus magnique impendii est, & verissimum est condimentum multo pretiosius esse & carius quam ipsam lampetram, Vnde facilè quis poteft coniicere, uen[?] admo-dum fuaues falubrefque effe efcas, quæ tot adulteriis & pigmentis placere coguntur: nam lora & coria ipfa eo modo apparata & condita placere poffent veru tofta. Magnates ex liquore arantii fuauiter mandunt: elixan-tur quoque & incruftantur panificio à pifto-ribus dulciariis. Ad extremum lampetram muftelam effe Aufonii Pliniíque inter erudi-tos plerosque conuenit, à maculati huius nominis quadrupedis tegminis fimilitudine, hoc eft, longitudine candoreque ventris, aq; tergoris fuperioris fubluteo colore.
units.tr: It is no wonder that more people die from food than from the sword, since no law exists to punish a raging gullet, and men who kill only with their kitchens are not only not punished but are held in the highest glory. For to skewer and roast little lampreys, that is lampetrae, and sometimes kids, was an invention of a mad gullet. Indeed they also wrapped capons in them, twisted into spirals, and roasted them on spits. Yet from this food all the guests reported the next day that they had been gravely troubled, for it had caused trouble for the stomach. Moreover, the lamprey has tormented illustrious minds, since each man, to show off his learning, strives to teach its ancient name. We, contending little over the name, will touch on what seems relevant to our purpose. I find that the lamprey is named from licking (lambere) and fleeing rocks (fugere petras). It is long, slippery, and without fins, and it is marked on its left side by seven holes, which the murena lacks. It is said to be the most precious food in early spring, when that cartilage which takes the place of vertebrae and spine has not yet hardened, for once hardened it begins to be less pleasant and loses its grace and value. The preparation of kitchen dishes around them is varied, laborious, and very costly, and it is quite true that the seasoning is much more precious and dear than the lamprey itself. From this one can easily conjecture how pleasant and wholesome those foods are that must be made to please by so many adulterations and spices. For the thongs and hides themselves, prepared and seasoned in that way, could please if roasted on a spit. The great men eat them sweetly with a liquor of bitter orange. They are also boiled and encrusted in pastry by bakers and confectioners. Finally, it is agreed among many learned men, such as Ausonius and Pliny, that the lamprey is a kind of weasel (mustela), from the resemblance of the spotted quadruped of this name: that is, in the length and whiteness of its belly, and in the upper part of its back, which is of a yellowish-brown colour.

units.la: Huius generis eft Enneopthalmus[?], lampreta fluuiatilis, ein <bl>Neunauge</bl> / aliàs lum-bricus aquatilis: item lampreta longior, eit <bl>Bricke</bl>. Fluuiatilis quoque muftelæ genus eft pifcis, quivulgò vocatur <bl>Aruppp</bl>[?] pro-pter fimilitudinem quam habet cum anguil-la, cuius pifcis epar cum conueniente fucco oculis obfcuris & caligantibus tenebrico-fisq; miraculo mederi expertum eft.
units.tr: Of this kind is the enneophthalmus, the river lamprey, which in German is called Neunauge, otherwise the water lumbricus (earthworm); also the longer lamprey, which is called Bricke. The river kind of mustela is also a fish commonly called Aruppp, on account of its resemblance to the eel. Experience has shown that its liver, with a suitable juice, cures eyes that are dim and clouded and, to the wonder of all, restores sight to those in darkness.

units.la: Afellorum permultæ funt fpecies, quæ di-ftinguendæ funt. Prima eft marlucius, hoc eft, lucius marinus à fimilitudine lucii fluuia-tilis: huic magnam fuiffe olim auctoritatem Plinius fcribit ex Cornelii Nepotis & Labe-rii Poetæ teftimonio. 2. Merlanus ple-beis in frequentiffimo cibo, quem lautiores etiam quandoque menfæ, tarius tamen, admittunt, voluptatis magis quam utilitatis gratiâ. 3. Tertius asellus capite est magno, oris scissura magna, oculis magnis. 4. Species aselli maris Oceani est, qui ex terræ parte nuper reperta salitus aduehitur. 5. Species est asellus varius, seu molua maior. Est quoque de asellorum genere Anglorum <bl>Golsisch</bl>/ à nigredine forsan sic dictus. Nomen germanicum <bl>Stockfisch</bl>/ (sic appellatus à trunco, cui aridus hic piscis tundendus imponitur) diuersas asellorum species comprehendit. A quo longe alius est piscis, qui salpa dicitur, <bl>ein Goldstriemer</bl>/ à striis seu lineis aureis. Aselli partes circa ventrem & pinnas refectæ & seorsim salitæ, doliisque inclusæ variis nominibus appellantur. Alii qui <bl>Stockfisch</bl> & <bl>Dorsch</bl>/ <bl>Rauchfisch</bl>/ <bl>Flachfisch</bl> vocitant: cuius quoque generis est Capellarius vulgò dictus, <bl>Bolch</bl>/ <bl>Ka-belaw</bl>: quamuis <bl>Kabelaw</bl> vocetur piscis vi-vus aut recens, <bl>Bolch</bl> verò capite iam mutilatus & falsus. Huius quoque census est, quem piscem Rhenanum nuncupant, &cal-larium <bl>Schelfisch</bl>/ à scabra cute ac squamata, unde cum elixandus est, torreri enim recusat, cultro deradendus est ac desquamandus) vel à fluuio <bl>Schelt</bl>/ quod in Oceani ostiis, in quæ flumen hoc se exonerat, vel hamo vel retibus subducatur.
units.tr: There are very many species of asellus, which must be distinguished. The first is the marlucius, that is, the sea pike, named from its likeness to the river pike; Pliny writes that this once had great authority, on the testimony of Cornelius Nepos and the poet Laberius. (2) The merlanus is a food of the common people, very frequent, which more luxurious tables also sometimes admit, though rarely, for the sake of pleasure rather than usefulness. (3) The third asellus has a large head, a wide mouth, and large eyes. (4) There is a species of asellus from the Ocean, which is brought from the part of the land lately discovered, salted. (5) There is a species called the asellus varius, or the greater molva. There is also among the aselli of the English kind the Golsisch, perhaps so named from its blackness. The German name Stockfisch (so called from the block on which this dried fish is beaten) covers various species of asellus. Quite different from these is the fish called salpa, the Goldstriemer, from its golden streaks or lines. The parts of the asellus around the belly and fins, prepared and salted separately and enclosed in casks, are called by various names. Some call them Stockfisch, Dorsch, Rauchfisch, Flachfisch. Of this kind also is the fish commonly called the Capellarius, Bolch, or Kabelaw, although Kabelaw is the name for a fish that is living or fresh, while Bolch is one already beheaded and salted. Included in this class also is the fish they call the Rhenish fish, and the callarium, the Schelfisch, from its rough, scaly skin; when it is to be boiled, since it refuses to be grilled, it must be scraped with a knife and descaled. Or it is named from the river Schelt, which is caught with hooks or nets at the mouths of the Ocean into which this river discharges itself.

units.la: Cæterum Galen. in re cibaria tale profert de asellis iudicium, quod, si incúlpato alan-tur nutrimento, inque puro versentur mari[?], carnis succique probitatem adipiscantur, adque saxatilium carnes proxime acce-dant.
units.tr: Galen, in his remarks on foods, gives this judgment on young asses (a kind of fish): if they are fed on unpolluted nourishment and live in clean sea, they acquire good flesh and juice, and their flesh comes close to that of rock-fish.

units.la: Idem in methodo medendi boni succi & concoctu faciles tradit, minimeque glutino-sos:& alioin[?] loco, molli esse carne, nec minus laudandos quam saxatiles, atque ex iure albo febricitantibus esse adponendos. In libello de boni maliq;[?] succi cibis, molles qui-dem esse carnis asellos asserit, sed non æquè ac saxatilium friabilem. Iecur in popinali-bus delitiis haberi reperio. Eduntur autem aselli, inprimis vero truncus cum suis specie-bus, ex butyro bono & synapi, adiectis pipe-re,cinnamomo vel zinzibere: quin & frixus ex synapi cum pipere: vel ex arantii succo. Sale condiuntur & asseruatur aselli in Anglia, Scotia,Dania, Noruegia, indeque in alias re-giones deportantur. Sic autem sale condi-ti pessimi esse nutrimenti vel inde constat, quod septentrionis & maritimæ gentes fre-quentiori vberiorique asellorum salitorum esu pessimo conducto in corporibus inqui-linoscorbuto, consistentur, huiusque ma-li causam crebriori salitorum esui assignatam reperio.
units.tr: The same author, in his Method of Healing, says they yield good juice and are easy to digest, and are not very glutinous. Elsewhere he says their flesh is soft, no less praiseworthy than that of rock-fish, and that they should be given to feverish patients in white broth. In his book on foods of good and bad juice, he asserts that the flesh of asses is soft, but not as crumbly as that of rock-fish. I find the liver counted among the delicacies of cookshops. Asses are eaten, especially the trunk with its parts, with good butter and mustard, with pepper, cinnamon or ginger added; they are also fried with mustard and pepper, or with orange juice. They are seasoned with salt and preserved in England, Scotland, Denmark and Norway, and from there carried to other regions. That salted ones are of very poor nourishment is clear from this: the peoples of the north and the seacoasts, who eat more often and more abundantly of salted asses, have in their bodies a bad guest, scurvy. I find this evil's cause assigned to the frequent eating of salted fish.

units.la: De harengis sale conditis idem esto iudicii. Messorum,fofloram, bajulorum, & helcia-riorum palato magis sapiunt.
units.tr: The same judgment holds for salted herring. They taste better to the palates of reapers, diggers, porters and rowers.

units.la: Lapillos ex asello pisce plena lunain-uentos in capite linteolo alligatos febrium circuitus tollere Plinius autor est.
units.tr: Pliny is the authority that small stones found in the belly of the asellus fish, tied in a little linen cloth on the head, remove the recurring rounds of fevers.

units.la: Piscis est planus, cartilagineus totus, aculeis præcipue circa caudam asper, fœcun-difsimus, maximeque varius, gustatu jucun-dus teste Atheneo, teneri ris & probi succi, præsertim qui asterias dicitur, ein Steinroch. Lejobatus hoc est, læuis raja, ein glatter Roch/difficulter ventrem subit, virusque redoler. Galenus de nutrimento cartilagineorum differens rajam pastinaca (cui similis est, vnde Pastinacam, rajam quidam appellant) duriorem asseruit, difficulterque in ventriculo perfici. Certum est abundanter alere, quod nautæ, qui eam in deliciis habent, testantur. Subit quoque lautiorum mensas elixata, quandoque frixaque. Jecur gratissimè ediajunt ex aceto pipe-rato. Archestratus apud Atheneum, hiber-num esse cibum voluit. Dorion dixisse fer-tur, rajam perinde bonam esse escam atque pallium elixatum, quod jocose magis, quam verè eum dixisse autumo. Ad Venerem denique incitare rajam largius comesam sæ-pius me audiuisse memini ab iis, qui piscis hujus naturam longo esu probe cognove-rant.
units.tr: The ray is a flat fish, wholly cartilaginous, rough with prickles especially around the tail, very fruitful and most varied. According to Athenaeus it is pleasant to taste, of tender flesh and good juice, especially the kind called asterias, a stone ray. The leiobatus, that is, the smooth ray, a smooth ray, goes down into the stomach with difficulty and smells of poison. Galen, discussing the nourishment of cartilaginous fish, said that the pastinaca ray (to which it is similar, whence some call it the pastinaca ray) is harder and hard to digest in the stomach. It is certain that it nourishes abundantly, as sailors attest, who count it a delicacy. It also appears on the tables of the wealthy, boiled and sometimes fried. People eat the liver most gladly with peppered vinegar. Archestratus, in Athenaeus, wanted it to be a winter food. Dorion is said to have said that the ray is as good a dish as boiled cloak, which I think he said in jest rather than in earnest. Finally, I remember hearing from those who knew this fish's nature well from long eating that eaten freely it often stirs up desire for Venus.

units.la: E planorum piscium genere sunt passe-res, quos Aufonius Plateffas nominat, Lethalisq, Trygon, mollesq, Plateffe.
units.tr: Among the flat fish are the plaice, which Ausonius calls plateffa: the deadly trygon, and the soft plateffa.

units.la: Hodie in iautiorum quidem ciborum albo non habentur, sunt tamen nutrimenti non mali praesertim recentes, & quae in acte-nofis gurgitibus aluntur. Marinos autem fluuiatilibus & ftagnalibus praeferri aequum est. Passeres quoque & planos omnes in limosis locis bene educari Columella testis est. Certum est, aquas quasdam passeres alere saporis miram obtinentes gratiam. Li-gerinas miré audio commendari. Arida, quae ad nos exportantur, quia duriores sunt, diligentem probamq; apparandi coquediq; requiruntrationem. Suauiter eduntur ex ju-repiforum adjecto zinzibere, mace & croci momento, vel etiam ex butyro & lacte, ad-jectis petroselini foliis. Muldandi sunt, qui calce maceratas, vt teneriores fiant & molle-fcant eas vendunt, ac debet magistratus ossi-cii fui memor in has insidias animadverte-re. Injurato mihi aequus lector credat, ma-gna inde incommoda concitari, vt torsio-nes & rofiones in ventriculo, quod expertus ipse sum.
units.tr: Today they are not counted among the foods of the wealthier tables, yet they are not bad nourishment, especially fresh ones and those raised in tidal channels. It is right to prefer sea fish to river and pond fish. Columella witnesses that plaice and all flat fish are well raised in muddy places. It is certain that some waters make plaice of wonderful flavour. I hear that the ligerinae are highly praised. Dried ones, which are exported to us, because they are tougher, require careful and proper preparation and cooking. They are eaten pleasantly cooked with added ginger, mace and a pinch of saffron, or also with butter and milk, with parsley leaves added. Those who soak them in lime to make them tender and soft and sell them should be fined, and the magistrate, mindful of his office, ought to take notice of these frauds. Let the fair reader believe me, who have been injured: great discomforts arise from them, such as twisting and gnawing in the stomach, which I have experienced myself.

units.la: Suauissimi saporis sunt recentes coeli[?]. Sed incautius aclargius efitati facile febres generant, quod mihi contigit Hafniæ. Sa-poris enim suauitas ad vberius vescendum allicit. llicit. Itaque ex jure bene piperato & bu-yro salito edendi sunt. Torrentur etiam in paticula, butyroque irrorantur salubri in-ento. Magnatum quoque mensas sub-unt, exornantque. Saliti & muriati peffi-ni nutrimenti sunt, cibisque omnino abdi-andi. Macerati minus mali, infumati pla-ie difficilis coctionis sunt, nisi aliorum ciba-iorum beneficio vna conficiantur. Quie-uditioris sunt palati, abstineant.
units.tr: The fresh ones have a very sweet flavour. But if they are eaten carelessly or in large quantity, they easily produce fevers, which happened to me at Copenhagen. For the sweetness of their flavour entices one to eat more abundantly. So they should be eaten from well-peppered broth and salted butter. They are also roasted in a pan and sprinkled with a wholesome butter sauce. They also grace and adorn the tables of great men. Salted and pickled ones are of very bad nourishment and must be avoided altogether. Soaked ones are less bad. Smoked ones are hard to digest unless they are eaten together with other foods to help them. Those of more delicate palate should abstain.

units.la: Harengulus, paruus Harengus Sardi-na & Trichis dicitur ob spinarum copiam. Porro sciendum alecem non esse harengum. Significat enim alec pisciculum omnem vi-lem, vel muria conditum, vel etiam liquamq; ex intestinis piscium: unde Horatius,
units.tr: The little herring, the small herring, is called sardine and trichis from its abundance of spines. Moreover, one should know that alec is not herring. For alec signifies any cheap little fish, either preserved in brine, or also the liquor made from the guts of fish. Whence Horace:

units.la: Ego faecem, inquit, primus & alec,
units.tr: I, he says, the first of the dregs and alec,

units.la: Primus & inueni piper album.
units.tr: and the first to discover white pepper.

units.la: Et Hermolaus piscem omnem vilem halecularium dixit. Harengus vero piscis est ex thriffarum genere, qui in Oceano tantum reperitur, minoribus thriffis,& sardinis ma-joribus plane similis. Spinosissimus autem est, adeo vt vescentibus infestissimae [?]finc spi-nae, aeque ac alosarum & thriffarum, deglu-titae enim grauissimam adferunt molestiam & pene strangulant, si gulae haereant in-fixae.
units.tr: Hermolaus also called every cheap fish halecularium. The herring, however, is a fish of the thrissa kind, found only in the Ocean, quite similar to smaller thrissae and larger sardines. It is very spiny, so that for those who eat it the spines are most troublesome, as are those of the shad and the thrissae. When swallowed they cause very grievous discomfort, and if they stick in the throat they nearly strangle.

units.la: Tu quoq; flumineas inter memorande cohortes
units.tr: You too, worthy of mention among the river hosts,

units.la: Gobio, non major geminis fine pollice palmis,
units.tr: the gudgeon, no longer than two palms without the thumb,

units.la: Prapinguis, teres, ovipara congestior alvo, Propexiq; jubas imitatus gobio barbi.
units.tr: very fat, round, more full of eggs than belly, imitating the hanging manes of the barbel gudgeon.

units.la: Hæc Aufonius Mofella. Eundem quoque Martialis laudauit in Xeniis, In venetis sint lauta licet conuiuia terra, Principium cœna gobius esse solet.
units.tr: These are the words of Ausonius in the Mosella. Martial also praised the same fish in his Xenia: Though lavish banquets may be held in the Venetian lands, the gudgeon is wont to be the first course.

units.la: Sunt autem gobii pisces vix excedentes duorum pollicum crassitiem aut palmi longitudinem, lubrici, & tamen squamis tecti: marini sunt & fluuiatiles: fluuiatilis nostris dicitur, Cressio, Kresling / Grun-delen / forsan quod circa fundum leu vadum aquæ degere soleant, limpidis enim aquis gaudent, vnde fundulos alii appellitant. Hujus generis est Cottus, qui inter fundulos capitur, & etiam venditur, aliàs capito Keuling / & papa à capitis mole mitram referente papalem. Marini gobii appellantur Meergoben / Meergroppen: Suntque albi & nigri. Cæterum gobiones in arenosis littoribus, limpidisque aquis degentes optimi sunt, suaues & jucundi, ad coctionem & distributionem faciles, probique nutrimenti & succi: quiin cœnosis aluntur locis, aquisque vrbes expurgantibus à Galeno pro damnatissimis habentur. Candidos ait Diphilus teneros esse, probi succi, concoctuque faciles, deterrimi virides, licet grandes sint.
units.tr: Gudgeons are fish scarcely exceeding two thumbs in thickness or a palm in length, slippery and yet covered with scales. There are sea and river ones. The river kind are called Cressio, Kresling, Grundelen in our language, perhaps because they usually dwell near the bottom or in shallow water, for they delight in clear waters, whence others call them fundulus. Of this kind is the cottus, which is caught among the fundulus and also sold, elsewhere called capito, Keuling; and papa, from the bulk of its head resembling a papal mitre. Sea gudgeons are called Meergoben and Meergroppen; they are white and black. Gudgeons living on sandy shores and in clear waters are the best, sweet and pleasant, easy to cook and to distribute, and of good nourishment and juice. But those that live in muddy places and in waters that drain cities are regarded by Galen as the most condemned. Diphilus says the white ones are tender and of good juice and easy to digest, while the green ones are the worst, even if large.

units.la: Atheneus quoque lib. 7. gobiones plurimi esse nutrimenti scribit, facilesque excretu: differre autem albos ab atris: viridium vero carnem macriorem, aridiorem, tenuiorisq; succi esse, & pinguitudinis expertes. Diocles saxatiles gobios mollioris esse carnis dixit, quod tamen Galenus mullorum respectu vult esse verum, ait enim, gobionum caro saxatilium carne durior est, & mollior, quam mullorum.
units.tr: Athenaeus too, in book 7, writes that gudgeons are of very great nourishment and easily excreted, and that the white differ from the black. The flesh of the green ones is leaner, drier, of thinner juice, and lacking in fat. Diocles said that rock gudgeons have softer flesh, which Galen however holds true only in comparison with mullets; for he says that gudgeon flesh is harder than rock-fish flesh and softer than that of mullets.

units.la: Pisces candidi, Leucisci, Alburni, ger-man. dicuntur <bl>Weißfische</bl> / <bl>Gleißling</bl>/à squamarum splendore, <bl>Zwibelfischlein</bl>/ quod nimirum cum cœpis coquantur, <bl>Roß-äuglein</bl>/ ab oculis rubicundis, & à vilitate <bl>Schneiderfischlein</bl>/ item <bl>Breitling</bl> à corporis latitudine. Meminit horum Aufonius, cum inquit,
units.tr: The white fish, called leuciscus and alburnus, are named in German Weißfische and Gleißling from the shine of their scales; Zwibelfischlein (onion-fish), because they are cooked with onions; Roß-äuglein (horse-eyes), from their reddish eyes; and, from their cheapness, Schneiderfischlein (tailor-fish). Also Breitling (broadling) from the breadth of their bodies. Ausonius mentions these when he says:

units.la: Et alburnos pradam puerilibus hamis.
units.tr: and bleak, prey for boyish hooks.

units.la: Porro carnes eorum molles sunt & pituitosæ. Certum est aquis exemtos diutiusq; seruatos cito corrumpi, vitus[?] enim quoddam redolent, id quod odore facile cognoscitur ventre refecto interaneisque exemtis. Ex jure autem piperato non inutiliter edun-tur.
units.tr: Further, their flesh is soft and phlegmatic. It is certain that when taken from the water and kept longer they quickly spoil, for they give off a certain foul smell, which is easily recognised by the odour when the belly is opened and the innards removed. They are eaten not unprofitably from peppered broth.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis quæ veniunt ab a-nimalibus sanguineis simplicis vitæ, sequuntur amphibia, quæ ancipitis sunt naturæ, vt ranæ, lutra, fiber.
units.tr: Next, concerning foods that come from sanguineous animals of simple life, come the amphibians, which are of doubtful nature, such as frogs, otters and beavers.

units.la: Cap. XVII. De ranis memorabilia & scitu digna.
units.tr: Ch. XVII. Remarkable and noteworthy things about frogs.

units.la: Ranarum in re alimentaria usus non est proscribendus, licet rustici & ineruditi palati homines eas aversentur. D. Am-brosius in suo hexamero omnibus fere alimentis praestare asserit. Et licet Romanorum gentes[?] de iis tacuerit; hac tamen tempestate velut deli-catissima gustantur à multis nationibus, praesertim Italis, quos hoc nomine batrachophagos ap-pellari animadverti.
units.tr: The use of frogs as food should not be condemned, although rustic people and those of uneducated palate shrink from them. Ambrose, in his Hexameron, asserts that they surpass nearly all other foods. And although the Roman peoples have said nothing about them, nowadays they are eaten as a great delicacy by many nations, especially the Italians, whom I have noticed are called batrachophagi (frog-eaters) on this account.

units.la: Certe vivaria Romani instituissent, si ranarum delitias habuissent exploratas, nam-[?] cossos arborumq; vermes in rem cibariam verterunt. Commendantur autem ; edulia sunt, ac valenter alunt, si probe perficiantur, fluviatiles in aqua pura, fluviis, fontibus de-gentes, ac rivulis, palustres & cœnosis in locis na-tae pernitiosæ & venenatae sunt. Refert Alvi-sius Mundella Epist. 8. Seranas sale oleoq; con-ditas, partim ex jure albo coctas, partim frixas in coena sumpsisse, paulo post tribus fere die-bus continuis tanta sensisse symptomata, ut in ve-neni assumti suspicionem venerit, postea uti[?] se comperisse ranas illas stagnantis cujusdam & palustris loci fuisse incolas, longoq; ex itinere al-latas continuo calore & agitatione semicorru-ptas. ptas fuisse. Itaq; recenter capienda sint, & quidem ex aquis puris, diligenterq; denudanda, tum abjecto capite elixanda, inq; sartagine frigenda. aspersa farina, & tandem apio. Gula generosior piperis pollinè salubriores & delicatiores reddit. Cibum non sentientibus, quos graeci ἀτρόφως appellant, nec non tabidis utilissime sumuntur. Antiquitas adversus venena eas magnificavit. Ætius l.2. c.162. & l.13.c.5. Item Æginetá l. 7. prodiderunt, ranarum jus cum sale oleo, haustum mirificè illis prodesse, qui à venenatis reptilibus essent percussi. Plinius his suffragatur l.32.c.5. ubi leguntur sequentia. Fluviatiles rana, si carnes earum edantur, jusq; vel decoctum sorbeatur, prosunt contra leporem marinum & contra serpentes. Item ranarum marinarum ex vino & aceto decoctarum succus contra venena bibitur & contra rubetæ venenum. Est autem rubeta in vepribus tantum vivens rana plena venefitii.
units.tr: Certainly the Romans would have set up frog-ponds if they had known the delights of frogs, for they turned grubs and worms of trees into food. Frogs are recommended and are edible, and they nourish well if properly prepared, provided they are river frogs that live in clean water, in rivers, springs and streams. Marsh frogs, and those born in muddy and filthy places, are harmful and poisonous. Alvisius Mundella, in Epistle 8, reports that he ate frogs preserved in salt and oil, some boiled in white broth and some fried, at dinner. Shortly afterwards, for almost three days in a row, he felt such symptoms that suspicion of poison arose. He later learned that those frogs were inhabitants of a stagnant and marshy place, and had been carried a long way, half-rotted by constant heat and agitation. Therefore they should be taken fresh, from clean waters, and carefully skinned; then, with the head discarded, they should be boiled, and fried in a pan, sprinkled with flour, and finally seasoned with parsley. A nobler palate is made more wholesome and delicate by pepper and powdered spices. They are most useful for those who cannot digest food, whom the Greeks call atrophōs [ἀτρόφως], and also for the wasted and consumptive. Antiquity praised frogs against poisons. Aetius, book 2, chapter 162, and book 13, chapter 5; likewise Aegineta, book 7, have declared that a broth of frogs with salt and oil, drunk, greatly benefits those struck by venomous reptiles. Pliny supports this in book 32, chapter 5, where the following is read. River frogs, if their flesh is eaten, or their broth or decoction is sipped, help against the sea-hare and against snakes. Likewise the juice of sea frogs boiled in wine and vinegar is drunk against poisons and against the poison of the toad. The toad, however, is a frog living only in brambles, full of poison.

units.la: Mira sunt, qua Plinius certatim à scriptoribus tradita de rubeta prodidit. Illatus sc.in populum silentium fieri. Offiento[?] quod sit in dextro latere, in aquam ferventem dejecto, refrigerari vas, nec postea fervere, nisi exemto. Inveniri autem id objecta rana formicis carnibusq; erosis. Et aliud esse in sinistro latere, quo dejecto fervere videatur, apocynum vocari: eo cohiberi canum impetus, amore concitari, et jurgia additó in potionem: venerem adalligatum simulare. Rursus dextro adalligato in pellicula agnina recenti quartanas sanari aliasq; febres : amo- remitem inhibeti eo. Lienem quoq; ex his ra- nis contra ipsarum valere venena, & cor etiam efficacius esse. Hac Plinius de rubeta. Cate- rum rana oculum dextrum dextro, sinistrum laevo suspenso collo natiui coloris panno, lippi- tudines sanare idem c.7 refert: & si per coitum rana eruantur, albuginem quoq; adalligatas si- militer in putamine ovi, reliquas carnes imposi- tas suggillationem [?]vapere. Tussim quoq; sanare ranas expertum est piscium modo è jure deco- ctas, pedibus autem suspensas, destillante in pa- tinam saliuâ earum, exenterandas, abjectiq; in- teraneis condiendas esse idem c. 8. retulit. Ra- nam praeterea esse parvam arbores scandentem, exq; ea vociferantem, in cujus ossi quis expuat, ipsamq; dimittat, tussi liberari narratur, experi- mentum cuiq; liberum.
units.tr: Pliny reported wonderful things, which writers have eagerly handed down, about the toad. He says that when it is thrown in, silence falls upon the people. He says that if it has a bone in its right side, and is thrown into boiling water, the vessel cools and does not boil again unless the bone is taken out. This bone is found when the frog is thrown among ants and gnawed flesh. He says there is another bone in its left side, and when this is thrown in, the water seems to boil; this is called apocynum. By it the attacks of dogs are restrained, love is stirred up, quarrels are caused when it is added to a drink, and it makes a woman seem to be bound to a man by love. Again, when the right bone is tied up in fresh lambskin, it cures quartan fevers and other fevers; and it is said to inhibit the love-potion. The spleen of these frogs is also said to be effective against their own poisons, and the heart even more so. So far Pliny on the toad. Elsewhere, in chapter 7, he reports that a frog's right eye, hung on the neck by a cloth of natural colour and attached on the right side, and its left eye on the left, cure inflammation of the eyes; and if frogs are dug up during mating, the whiteness of the eye is similarly bound in an eggshell, and the other flesh is placed on bruises. In chapter 8 he reported that it has been tested that frogs, boiled in broth like fish, cure coughs, and that when they are hung by the feet, their saliva dripping into a pan, they should be gutted, and the entrails thrown away and the frogs seasoned. He also says there is a small frog that climbs trees and calls out loudly; if one spits into its mouth and then lets it go, one is said to be freed from coughing. Let anyone try this who wishes.

units.la: Ranarum adipe aurium dolores tolli, ar- thritico sq; affectus sedari, tabida membra corro- borari ac refoveri, multis experimentis patefa- ctum est. Nec conticendum, singulas ranas in aceto decoctas, ut dentes collantur, dolorem sedare. Siq; fastidium obstaret, Salustius Dio- nysius suspendebat pluris ranas pedibus posterio- ribus, ut sluerent ex ore virus in acetum feruens, quo maxillares sanari precipue dentes putant, mobiles vero stabiliri. Alii ad idem binarum ranarum corpora precisis pedibus in vino macerant, colluiq, eo labantes dentes jubent: alii totas adalligant maxillis: alii 36. ranarum corda in oleo vetere sub area testa discoxere, vt infunderent per aurem dolentis maxillæ: alii jecur ranæ decoctum & cum melle tritum dentibus imponunt. Ad extremum parvam illam ranam in herbis & arundinetis maxime viventem, mutam & sine voce, viridem, boum ventres distendentem oculis tenebricosis, nebulosisq; mede-ri quidam abstrusorum natura periti in arcanis habent. Præcipue autem id præstare dicitur corporis humor specillis derasus inunctuq;, ipsa vero carnes doloribus oculorum superponuntur.
units.tr: It has been shown by many experiments that the fat of frogs stops earaches, calms arthritic conditions, and strengthens and restores wasted limbs. Nor should it be passed over that single frogs boiled in vinegar, applied to the teeth to chew, relieve pain. And if disgust is an obstacle, Salustius Dionysius used to hang several frogs by their hind feet, so that the poison flowed from their mouths into boiling vinegar, which people think cures especially the molar teeth and makes loose teeth firm. Others macerate the bodies of two frogs, with their feet cut off, in wine for the same purpose, and order those with loose teeth to rinse their mouths with it. Others tie whole frogs to the jaws. Others boiled the hearts of thirty-six frogs in old oil under a potsherd, so that it might be poured into the ear of the one with the aching jaw. Others apply to the teeth the liver of a frog, boiled and ground with honey. Finally, some learned men, skilled in hidden natures, claim to cure dark and clouded eyes with that small frog which lives mostly among herbs and reeds, is mute and voiceless, green, and swells the bellies of oxen. They say the moisture of its body, scraped off with probes and applied as an ointment, cures this, and the flesh itself is placed over painful eyes.

units.la: De Lutra, & Fibro.
units.tr: On the Otter and the Beaver.

units.la: Jusdem fere sunt generis lutra & fiber, nisi quod cauda differant, quam fiber habet piscibus similem, cætera lutræ species. Utrumq; animal horrendi est mortis, & lutra non desistit, nisi fracti offis, vt ajunt, crepitum senserit. Lutram autem in cibos venire notum est, præsertim autem manditur à rusticis circa piscolentos lacus fyluis aut nemorosis locis proximos, habitantibus. Pisces hujus carnem olere certum est, ideoque de natura ejus non difficile est judicare: quidam lenti eam, crassi & pituitosi succi esse affirmant, difficulterque concoqui.
