Infibro, priori parte pro carne, posteriori vero pro pifce vefcuntur nationes quaedam: de viteriori in re alimentaria potentia nihil aut patum conftat. Caeterum Caftorii, h.e. Caftoris feu fibri teftium exectorum, millenii in medicina vfus, Vide Plin. l. 32. c. 3. Diofcor. l. 2. c. 22.
units.tr: The otter and the beaver are almost of the same kind, except that they differ in tail; the beaver's tail is like a fish's, while the rest of its form is that of the otter. Both animals are of deadly harm, and the otter, they say, does not stop until it has heard the crack of a broken bone. It is well known that otters are eaten, and they are especially eaten by country folk who live near fish-smelling lakes or in woodland places. It is certain that their flesh smells of fish, and so it is not hard to judge their nature: some maintain that it is sluggish, thick and phlegmatic, and hard to digest. Some peoples eat the beaver, the front part as meat and the back part as fish; but about its further nutritive power little or nothing is established. Moreover, castoreum, that is, the testicles of the castor or beaver cut out, is in frequent medicinal use. See Pliny, book 32, chapter 3, and Dioscorides, book 2, chapter 22.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis quae veniunt ab nimalibus sanguineis, sequuntur sanguinis expertia.
units.tr: Still concerning foods that come from animals with blood, there follow those that lack blood.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Hic modi sunt sepiae, loligo, polypus item cruftacea, hoc est, cruftis cotecta, graecè μαλακόστρακα, vt cancer, squilla, locusta: Sc. necnon teftacea teftis inclusa, graeci ὀστρακόδερμα, vt limaces terrestres, cochleae, marinae, oftreae, pectines conchae.
units.tr: These are the kinds: cuttlefish, squid, and likewise the octopus; the crustacea, that is, creatures covered with a crust (in Greek malakostraka), such as the crab, squill, and lobster; and also the testacea, enclosed in a shell (in Greek ostrakoderma), such as land snails, sea snails, oysters, scallops, and mussels.

units.la: De Sepia, Loligine, & Polypo.
units.tr: On Cuttlefish, Squid, and Octopus.

units.la: Sepias, Polypos & Loligines germanice vocant <bl>Tintenfisch</bl> / Angli <bl>Cuttel/Kuttelfisch</bl>: catamen recte distinguuntur ftinguuntur longo major fit, <bl>ein grosser langer Blackfisch</bl> differentiam loliginis minoris, lepia generatim <bl>Blackfisch</bl> nominatur: Polypus vero fit <bl>ein Blackfisch mit einem kleinem Leibe und langen Füssen</bl>, <bl>darauff gehen kan</bl>, quib. etiam à pri ribus discernitur, qui pedes habent breuiores, am-pliusq[?]
units.tr: The Germans call cuttlefish, octopus, and squid Tintenfisch, and the English call them Cuttel or Kuttelfisch. Cuttlefish are rightly distinguished from squid: the larger one becomes ein grosser langer Blackfisch (a big long blackfish), which differs from the smaller squid, and the cuttlefish in general is called Blackfisch. The octopus, however, becomes ein Blackfisch mit einem kleinem Leibe und langen Füssen (a blackfish with a small body and long feet), darauff gehen kan (on which it can walk). It is also distinguished from the former by its feet, which are shorter, and by its fuller body.

units.la: pliufq; corpus. Sepia & loligo cruore tantum differunt, qui in sepia ater, in loligine tuber effunditur [?]. Nutrimentum horum piscium quod attinet, graues autores testantur valenter alere polypum, si probè conficiatur, venerenq; ciere vehementer. Unde acetabula & extremitates cirrorum à senibus expetuntur ad parandam sobolem. In aqua & atramento suo si elixetur melior euadit. Venetias adferuntur ex Illyrico & Dalmatia sale inueterati. Loliginem sepiâ concoctu esse facilio-rem, verum insuauiorem graeci auctores quidam tradiderunt. Parua, quam Caf-feronem quidam vocant, interlautas epulas habetur. Diphilus apud Atheneum de sepia ait, tenetam eam esse, ori suauem, concoctu facilem, quin etiam succum ejus sanguinem externare, excretioneq; per haemorrhoidas concitate. Celsus quoq; sepiae atramentum aluum mollire scribit. Recentes fastidium statim pariunt. De atramento sepiae scribit Plinius, tantam ei inesse vim, vt in lucerna addito aethiopas videri ablato priori lumine, Anaxilaus tradat. Porro sepias & loligines binum & quinuum cubitorum captas, polypum vero pendentem pondo 700 inauditae magnitudinis monstrum, subL. Lucullo proconsule Boeticae, Plinius refert, prodente Trebio Nigro Lucullí Comite, cujus etiam polypi reliquae miraculi loco asseruatae. Plin.
units.tr: Cuttlefish and squid differ only in their blood: in the cuttlefish the ink is black, in the squid it is poured out (?). As to the nourishment of these fish, serious authors testify that the octopus nourishes strongly if it is properly prepared, and greatly stirs up desire. Hence old men seek the suckers and the tips of the arms to produce offspring. If it is boiled in its own water and ink, it turns out better. They are brought to Venice from Illyria and Dalmatia, preserved in salt. Some Greek authors have said that squid is easier to digest than cuttlefish, but less pleasant. The small one, which some call caffero, is eaten between the courses. Diphilus, in Athenaeus, says of the cuttlefish that it is pleasant to the mouth and easy to digest, and that its juice even expels blood and promotes excretion through the haemorrhoids. Celsus also writes that the ink of the cuttlefish loosens the bowels. Fresh cuttlefish at once cause loathing. Pliny writes of cuttlefish ink that it has such power that, when it is added to a lamp, the Ethiopians appear once the former light is removed, as Anaxilaus relates. Further, Pliny reports, on the authority of Trebius Niger, companion of Lucullus, that under Lucullus, proconsul of Baetica, cuttlefish and squid of two and five cubits were caught, and an octopus hanging at 700 pounds, a monster of unheard-of size, whose remains were also kept as a marvel. Pliny.

units.la: De Oftracodermis.
units.tr: On the Ostracoderms.

units.la: Omnibus Oftracodermis hoc est, silicea testa intectis commune est, ut falsum in carne succum contineant, qui alvum soluit. Unicuique vero is inest proprium secundum majus & minus, pro quantitatis & qualitatis ratione.
units.tr: All the Ostracodermata, that is, those enclosed in a silicious shell, have in common that they contain in their flesh a watery juice which loosens the bowels. Each has it in greater or lesser measure, according to the quantity and quality.

units.la: Hic falsus succus in ostreis magis abundat, ideoq; ad emolliendum alvum utiles magis, quam cetera dura carnis testacea. Romanos diligentes admodum circa ostreas su[?]se ganeonibusq; earum escam arrisisse in confesso est.
units.tr: This watery juice is more abundant in oysters, and so they are more useful for loosening the bowels than the other hard-fleshed shellfish. It is well known that the Romans were very diligent about oysters and that gluttons admired their food.

units.la: Nam vivaria ostreis instituta inveniuntur, quæ primus invenisse legitur Sergius Orata, primus optimum saporem lucrinis adjudicaunt, hæc enim suaviores & meliores habebantur. Cochlearum vivaria instituisse Hirpinum, eadem altius adeo grandes factas, ut singularum calices so.quadrantes caperent, Plinius autor est. Verum qui absque vitæ suæ infidus [illegible, ~6 letters] noxa testaceis quibuscunque vescitur, unice ventriculi sui constitutionem ac naturam explorare debet.
units.tr: For oyster beds (vivaria) are known to have been established; Sergius Orata is read to have been the first to invent them. They first gave the Lucrine oysters the best flavour, for these were considered sweeter and better. Pliny is the authority that Hirpinus established snail beds, and these grew so large that each shell held roughly a quarter of a pint (quadrantes). But whoever eats any shellfish without danger to his life must carefully examine the constitution and nature of his own stomach.

units.la: Quæ mollissima constant carne, ut ostreæ, humore abundant (quemadmodum in ostrearijs compertum est) humorem suum facilissime effluere [?] exhibenda sunt ventriculo a vitiatis succis vacuo ac expurgato; quæ vero duriores sunt carnis, ut testacea, sunt danda, quibus facile cibi vitiantur in ventriculo ob improbos succos vel ex epate in ipsum confluentes, vel tunicis ipsius infixos atq; contentos. Sicut igitur ostrea magis alvum emolliunt, alunt vero levius, ita carnem haben-tes duriorem difficilius quidem conficiuntur, at valentius nutriunt. Ut autem ostrea dissici-lius corrumpantur, alvum reprimant, nutri-antq; valentius, succum illum salsum, quo abundare ostreas dictum est, eas deponere necesse est.
units.tr: Those with very soft flesh, such as oysters, abound in moisture (as has been found in oyster beds), and this moisture flows out very easily. They should be given to a stomach that is empty and cleansed of corrupt juices. Those with firmer flesh, such as shellfish, are to be given to those in whom food is easily spoiled in the stomach by bad juices, either flowing into it from the liver or fixed in and contained in its coats. Therefore, just as oysters loosen the bowels more but nourish more lightly, so those with firmer flesh are digested with more difficulty but nourish more strongly. But so that oysters may be less easily corrupted, may check the bowels, and may nourish more strongly, it is necessary to remove that salty juice with which oysters were said to abound.

units.la: Mirandum, (deplorandum volebam dicere,) eo gula insaniam rediisse, ut salutaribus escis neglectis, venefica in cibos vertat. Ostracoderma enim omnia & inprimis ostreas humidam nimis mucosamq; obtinere carnem, in confesso est, testante id Galen. quoq; 2. de temper. & per consequens malum genera e alimentum cruda illa pituita in ventriculo non probe confecta[?].
units.tr: It is astonishing (I was going to say deplorable) that gluttony has come to such madness that, neglecting wholesome foods, it turns poison into food. For it is agreed that all shellfish, and especially oysters, have flesh that is too moist and mucous, as Galen also testifies in book 2 of De temperamentis; and consequently they produce bad, crude phlegm in the stomach, not properly digested.

units.la: Gulosissimi igitur phagones sunt, qui ostreas crudas devorant, & quidem cum pituita sua integras. Sunt, qui quinquagenas, sunt, qui centenas devorant prima mensa. Persuasum habent quidem gula illi ganeaq; ostentatores, humiditatem illam pituitamq; crudam, a vino forti largius superbibito confici atq; edomari, ut ita haud facile ventriculo officere e possit. Non attendunt vero, quam promte & incaute vinum cruditatem illam mucumque ostrearum secum rapiens in corpus omne distribuat, venas repleat, corpusq; reddat cacochymum. Qui nitidioris sunt palati, vitaq; salubrioris curiosi, nec non ventriculi imbecil-lioris, ostreas in ollis elixant, adiiciuntq; piper, cinnamomum & garyophyllos: alii reclusas falis momento addito, prunis imponunt, parum concalefactas vorant. Galenus in sartagine coquia quibusdam docet. Alibi sale condita aut garo friguntur, quo cibo gentes quædam utuntur frequenter. Ganeones ad Venerem stimulandam experimento iis vescuntur. Plinius lib. 32. cap. 6. stomachum vnice reficere, indistinctè aserit, fastidisq; mederi, alvum quoque leniter mollire, aitq; omnia testacea modice in cibis oportere collum, quia saporis gratia perit.
units.tr: The most gluttonous, then, are those who devour raw oysters, and indeed whole, with their phlegm. Some devour fifty, some a hundred, at the first course. Those gluttons and show-offs of the throat are convinced that this moisture and raw phlegm is overcome and tamed by strong wine drunk in large quantities, so that it cannot easily harm the stomach. They do not consider how quickly and carelessly the wine, carrying off that crudity and the mucus of the oysters, distributes it through the whole body, fills the veins, and makes the body cacochymic. Those of more refined palate, more careful of a healthy life and of weaker stomach, boil oysters in pots and add pepper, cinnamon, and cloves. Others, opening them and adding salt in a moment, lay them on embers and gulp them barely warmed. Galen teaches how some are cooked in a pan. Elsewhere they are fried seasoned with salt or garum, a food that some peoples eat frequently. Gluttons eat them as a trial to stir up Venus. Pliny, book 32, chapter 6, asserts without distinction that they alone restore the stomach, cure loathing, and also gently soften the bowels; and he says that all shellfish should be eaten in moderation with food, because their flavour is lost.

units.la: Celsus Cornelius lib. 2. eo capite, quo stomacho idoneas explicat, pisces ex mediamarè teriaponit ostrea, pectines, cochleas. Idem tenerorum pisces & ostrea in his cibis numerat, quæ facile corrumpuntur, muricesq; & purpuras inter ea, quæ minus vitiantur.
units.tr: Cornelius Celsus, book 2, in the chapter where he sets out foods suitable for the stomach, places fish from the open sea, oysters, scallops, and snails. The same author counts tender fish and oysters among those foods which are easily spoiled, and murex and purple shells among those that spoil less.

units.la: Præterea alium moventibus contribuit ostrea, omnesq; reconchulas maximeq; jus earum. Veteres in principio cœnæ ostreas præbere consueuisse Plutarchus innuit. 8. (Sympos. 9.) bodie nostros invalui apud quosdam exitiales, ostreas post alios cibos inglutire, cum primis si præcesserint cibi dulciores & astringentes, quiq; difficulter corrumpuntur: cottionem enim sic devorata impedimento, caloremque nativum ventriculi, cottionem. jam aggressurum interturbant. Non parum enim interest, quo ordine fercula aut cibi ingerantur. Galenus lib.3. de fymt. cauf. cap.1. inquit, Cibus parum conveniente ordine aut in-tempestive sumptus concoctionem vitiat. Et cod. in libr.cap.eod. Ciborum inconveniens ordo est, cum fructus primo, deinde alia emolli-entia, ut oleum ex garo sumuntur. Idem lib.2. de aliment.facultat. de sycaminis. Ex cibis qui subducuntur, posteriores quidem sumendi, qui tarde permeant, omnium autem primi, qui celeriter pervadunt, ut sunt ostrea. Celsus lib.1. cap.2. inquit, Cibus a salsamentis, oleribus simi-libusq; rebus melius incipit, tum caro assumen-da, quae as[?]a optima aut elixa est. Secunda mensa stomacho nihil nocet, in imbecillo coacescit, Si quis itaq; hoc parum valet, palmulas pomaq; & similia melius primo assumit cibo. Valeria-lib.[?]1.loc.comm. cap. 6. hunc esse debere ordinem ait, ut quae levia sunt, alvumq; subducentia prius, posterius vero, quae plenius alunt, ingerantur, nec dura mollibus, nec astringentia subducentibus, nec crassiora tenuibus, nec concoctu gravia facilibus præmittantur. Eo igitur ordine alimenta ingerenda esse omnes præcipere videntur, ut aquo tempore omnia coquantur, ne sc.[?] crudum misceatur cocto, vel coctum crudo: quod fit, si ea, quae liquida sunt, lubrica, vitiosiq; succi pro aliis obsonijs comedantur, ita enim & ipsa facile egestantur, & caeteris iter parant. Ex quibus perspicuum evadit, & ostrea fecundo cibo affumta concoctionem vitiare, tum quia a natura superata coctaq; descendere non possunt ob cibos praemissos nondum coctos, in ima ventriculi parte adhuc existentes, & hic retenta, quae jam concocta sunt, corrumpuntur: tum quod hoc modo coctum crudo miscebitur. Expedit igitur praecedere ea, quae facilius coquuntur, ut cocta citius statim descendant, neque ab aliis impediantur, aut eisdem misceantur & confundantur. Quidam pro evidenti veritate affectione & clarioris doctrinae gratia utuntur hac distinctione. Alimentorum quaedam habent liquidam, quaedam solidam substantiam. Ex solidis quaedam citius, quaedam tardius superantur a ventriculo. Ventriculus an-tens[?] non habet in partibus suprema & infima parem calorem, siquidem infima crassior est, carnosior, jecoris propior. Ubi alimenta eam habent differentiam, ut quaedam sint liquida, tenuisq; substantiae, quaedam solida, nihil omnino refert, fi in simul, five praecedant liquida, five sequantur. Exemplo est jus carnis & caroipsa. Si quis enim haec duo eadem mensa assumere debeat, nihil refert jus antecedere, vel subsequi: Si enim antecedat, adveniente carne, facile invicem miscentur, inq; unam deducuntur substantiam mafticata ac comminuta prius carne. Si vero caro praecedat jusq; sequatur, totam carnis substantiam jus pervadet, cui exacte commiscemiscebitur. Et haec ratio est, ob quam sine manifesta noxa quidam ante, quidam post ius ingerunt, porrumq; cum & post cibos assumimus. Quod si vero solida fuerint alimenta, sed naturae disparis, aut liquida, sed crassae substantiae, fercula, quae sunt faciliora concoctu praeire debent, subsequi vero reliqua, docente Gal. 2. de alimēt.fac.[?] c. de piscib. ubi inquit, omnia cibaria pranum[?] cum humiditate succum habentia, ex facili descendere, eaq; prima mensa esse assumenda. Et l. 3. de rat. vict. in acut. comm. 22. inquit, Nam perpetuo prius ingerenda sunt, quae & facilius concoquuntur, & quae subducuntur magis. Quin & valida ratione comprobatur haec sententia. Cum enim alimentum, quod facile coquitur, praeassumitur, prius coquitur, ac descendit, deinde aliud sequitur, quod eo diutius immoratur, quo longiori tempore eget ad coctionem. Non enim coctum alimentum in ventre momento temporis descendit, sed quod in superiori parte continetur, tardius: decet igitur id tardius coqui, uti tardius descendit, ut diu retentum perficiatur, & tam id quod facile quam id quod difficile coquitur, parum a completa coctione descendat. Ubi vero unum alimentum tantum assumatur, quemadmodum pars superior tardius coquetur, ita magis immorabitur, donec perficiatur.
units.tr: Besides, oysters and all shellfish, and especially their broth, contribute to stirring up a second appetite. Plutarch hints that the ancients were accustomed to serve oysters at the start of dinner (Symposiaca, book 8, question 9). Today a pernicious custom has taken hold among some of our people, to swallow oysters after other foods, especially if sweeter and astringent foods have gone before, which are hard to spoil. For in this way the oysters, once swallowed, hinder the digestion and disturb the native heat of the stomach, which is already about to begin its work. For it matters a great deal in what order courses or foods are taken. Galen, book 3 De symptomatum causis, chapter 1, says: food taken in an unsuitable order or at an unseasonable time spoils digestion. And in the same book and chapter: the order of foods is improper when fruits are taken first, and then other softening things, such as oil with garum. The same author, book 2 De alimentorum facultatibus, on sycamine figs: of the foods that are taken away, the later ones should be eaten, which pass slowly; but the first of all should be those which pass quickly, such as oysters. Celsus, book 1, chapter 2, says: the meal should begin better with salted foods, vegetables, and similar things; then meat should be taken, which is best roasted or boiled. The second course does no harm to a strong stomach, but it curdles in a weak one. If anyone is therefore weak in this respect, he takes dates, apples, and the like better first, before the meal. Valerius, in book 1 of the Loci communes, chapter 6, says that this should be the order: light foods, and those which loosen the bowels, should be given first, and afterwards those which nourish more fully; neither hard foods before soft, nor astringent before laxative, nor thicker before thinner, nor foods hard to digest before easy ones. All seem to prescribe that foods should be taken in this order, so that everything is cooked at the same time, lest raw be mixed with cooked, or cooked with raw. This happens if things that are liquid, slippery, and of bad juice are eaten before other dishes; for in this way they themselves are easily passed on and prepare the way for the rest. From these things it becomes clear that oysters taken with the second course also spoil digestion: first, because, overcome by nature and already cooked, they cannot descend on account of earlier foods not yet cooked, still lying in the lowest part of the stomach, and what is already cooked is retained there and spoiled; and second, because in this way the cooked will be mixed with the raw. It is therefore expedient to eat first those foods that are more easily cooked, so that what is cooked may descend at once, and not be hindered by others or mixed and confused with them. Some, for the sake of evident truth and clearer teaching, use this distinction: of foods, some have a liquid, others a solid substance; of the solid, some are overcome by the stomach more quickly, some more slowly. The stomach does not have the same heat in its upper and lower parts, since the lower part is thicker, fleshier, and nearer the liver. Where foods differ in that some are liquid and of thin substance, and some solid, it makes no difference at all whether they are taken together, or whether the liquids come before or after. The example is broth and meat. If someone is to take these two at the same table, it makes no difference whether the broth comes first or second: if it comes first, when the meat arrives they easily mix together and are led into one substance, the meat having been first chewed and broken up. But if the meat comes first and the broth follows, the broth will penetrate the whole substance of the meat, with which it is thoroughly mixed. And this is the reason why some people take broth before and some after, without any manifest harm; and we also take leek with and after food. But if the foods are solid yet of unlike nature, or liquid yet of thick substance, the dishes that are easier to digest should come first and the rest follow, as Galen teaches in book 2 De alimentorum facultatibus, in the chapter on fish, where he says: all foods that have juice with moisture descend easily, and these should be taken at the first course. And in book 3 De ratione victus in acutis, comment 22, he says: for those which are both more easily digested and those which loosen more should always be given first. Indeed this opinion is also confirmed by strong reasoning. For when a food that is easily cooked is taken first, it is cooked first and descends; then another follows, which remains the longer in the stomach the more time it needs for cooking. For cooked food does not descend in the belly in an instant, but what is contained in the upper part stays longer. It is fitting, therefore, that this be cooked more slowly, as it descends more slowly, so that what is retained a long time is completed, and both what cooks easily and what cooks with difficulty descend little before complete cooking. But where only one food is taken, just as the upper part is cooked more slowly, so it remains longer until it is complete.

units.la: Excluditur igitur hic illorum placitum, qui dixerunt, alimenta tardioris difficiliorisq; coctionis antecedere debere ea quae facile coquantur, quoniam, inquiunt, venter magis calidus est in fundo ea scilicet parte, qua carnosior est, & iecori propior: ideoque talí ordine alimenta esse ingerenda, ut æquo tempore coquantur omnia, nec crudum costo misceatur, quod tum fieri aiunt, vbi, quod difficilius coquitur, antece-dat, imamq; ventris partem, quæ calidior est, præoccupet, quod verò facilius coquitur, superiorem & minus calidam. Exploditur quoque illorum opinio, qui statuunt, quod si pari inter-mallo distent ciborum natura cum calore partium ventris, eam antecedere debere, qui coctioni magis reluctatur, ut uno tempore omnino coquantur: inde enim fieret, ut totum alimentum in brevissimo tempore descenderet, aut superior pars corrumperetur. Primum autem non fit, quoniam quivis facile intelliget, plus quam duarum horarum tempore ventrem onus in intestina deponere, quo tempore leuior sensim redditur venter. Secundum igitur, id est, alimentum in ventre corrumpi, accidet, si duarum horarum spatio coctum retineatur in ventre. Vide infra Præceptum 3, capite 3. Ad extremum, ut ad ostreas revertamur, non ignorandum, mensarū palmas tribus Oceanicis, damnari verò fluviatiles, quæ sputrefcente limo, aut facie sumosa circa navigia diutius stante, desixosq; palos adnascuntur. Sic autem generari ostreas Aristoteles & Plinius prodiderunt. Et verissimum id esse nostro seculo approbavit Franciscus Gall. Rex, qui, cum adfossam Mariana Carolum V. Imper. excepturus, nauigasset, sermoq; de ostreis inci-disset, ac ciues illius loci nautaq; constanter affir-marent, mare illud ostreas non alere, statim ins-sit, vt nauigiorum carinas & inferior a foris scru-tarentur diligenter, ipsoq; præsente ostrea inuen-ta sunt tenuem saporem, pelagiis & Oceanicis longè ignobiliorem referentes. Nec prætereun-dum hic, ostrearum, concharumq; corpora, quin & Cancrarium genus vniuersum, lunari pote-state grandescere, augeri, minuiq;, præsertim vtrò plenilunijs restitui, pleniorq; fieri, magisq; in cibis placere, Aristoteles & Plinius grauès au-tores testantur. Id autem non euenit ab vberiore pabulo, vt alii existimăt, sed ob tepidiores noctes, quia plenior lux est, calorem enim desiderant, frigori patentes. Præcipuè vero ait Plinius l.32.c. §[?].circa æstatis initia multo latè pregnantes spe-stantur, atq; vbi sol penetret in vada. Hæc q; vi-detur causa, cur minora aliis in locis reperian-tur: Opacitas enim incrementum prohibet & amplitudinem, adeò rebus omnibus vitali suo lumine sol prodest, etiam in profundo mersis ma-ri. Venenis ostreas aduersari, virusq; pestilentes bubones loco transferre, virusq; omne ad se tra-here non leues autores tradunt, sunt autem bra-chio agglutinande, ea parte qua axillaris de-currit, si bubo in alis est, si verò in-guen obsederit, femo-ribus.
units.tr: This, then, refutes the view of those who said that foods which are harder and slower to digest should come before those which are easily digested, because, they say, the stomach is hotter at the bottom, in the part that is fleshier and nearer the liver. Therefore, they hold, foods should be taken in such an order that everything is digested in the same time, and raw matter is not mixed with the cooked. They say this mixing happens when the harder-to-digest food goes first and occupies the lower, hotter part of the stomach, while the easier-to-digest food occupies the upper, cooler part. The opinion of those who maintain that, if the natures of foods and the heat of the parts of the stomach are equally distant, the food that resists digestion more should go first, so that all are digested at one time, is also exploded. For then the whole food would descend in a very short time, or the upper part would be corrupted. The first does not happen, since anyone can readily see that the stomach takes more than two hours to discharge its load into the intestines, and in that time the stomach is gradually made lighter. The second, that food would be corrupted in the stomach, would happen if it were kept in the stomach after it had been cooked for two hours. See below, Precept 3, chapter 3. Finally, to return to oysters, it should not be ignored that the flat oysters of the sea are esteemed, but river ones are condemned, which grow on rotting mud or on the scum that stands long about ships and on the stakes driven in. Aristotle and Pliny have reported that oysters are generated in this way. And Francis, King of France, proved this to be most true in our century. When he had sailed to Mariana to receive Charles V, the emperor, and the talk had turned to oysters, the citizens of that place and the sailors firmly maintained that the sea there did not nourish oysters. He at once ordered the keels of the ships and their lower outer parts to be searched carefully, and in his presence oysters were found, with a thin flavour, far less noble than those of the open and Oceanic seas. Nor should it be passed over here that the bodies of oysters and shellfish, and indeed the whole crab kind, grow, increase and diminish under the power of the moon, and especially are restored and grow fuller at full moon and please more as food. Aristotle and Pliny, weighty authors, bear witness to this. This does not come from richer pasture, as others think, but from warmer nights, since the light is fuller; for they need warmth, being exposed to cold. Pliny especially says that around the beginning of summer they are seen to be very widely pregnant, and where the sun penetrates into the shallows. This seems to be the reason why smaller ones are found in other places: shade prevents growth and size, so much does the sun benefit all things with its vital light, even those submerged in the deep sea. Not slight authors hand down that oysters counteract poisons, transfer plague buboes to another place, and draw all poison to themselves. They are to be bound to the arm, on the part where the vein of the armpit runs, if the bubo is in the armpit, but if it has settled in the groin, to the thighs.

units.la: Submonitio de oftracodermis.
units.tr: Preliminary remarks on the ostracoderms.

units.la: NE in cæteris oftracodermis & reliquis ceis describendis, enumerandisque diutius immorer, ostrearum naturā & conditionem aliquantò prolixius persecutus sum, aliis, quibus plenior est de his cognitio, quiq; diu multumq; in locis illis maritimis versati sunt, pleniorem scribendi occasionem relinquens. Quæ igitur de ostreis hucusque inserta, de cæteris testaceis quoque intelligantur: In specie vero cochleas, conchasque fluuiatiles virosas esse, vepribus verò adhærentes ventrem turbare, vomitumque ciere. Testudines autem, quas Græcorum patriter atque latinorum auctoritas in vsu cibario reposuit, carnes habere à vitulina non multum discrepantes, tum odoris suauitate, tum odoris gratiâ, graues autores affirmant. Sanguinem earum contra venena præclarè auxiliari vno ore prædicant omnes. Terrestres, quæ formosiores sunt, insque nemoribus & syluis degentes gracilibus & tabidis ab orco reuocandis mirè commendat posterior medicina, càlidicati enim habituali in membris resistunt. Marinæ circa omoplatas posterioraque crura suaues ac delicatæ prædicantur. Certissimum aiunt, probè in ventre confectas valenter alere: elixantur prius exquisitè, deinde in frusta dissectæ friguntur. guntur. Mare Indicum tantæ amplitudinis testudines mittere, Plinius lib. 9.cap 10. autor est, vt singularum superficies habitabiles casas integant, atque inter insulas rubri maris præcipuè his nauigent, velut cymbis. Qui de nouæ Indiæ rebus monimenta tradiderūt, testudines illic reperiri aiunt ex quarum tegumento magni fiant clypei. Vnde à scuti seu peltæ figura Schildkroten appellantur à Germanis. Hactenus de Ostracodermis.
units.tr: So that I do not dwell too long on describing and listing the other ostracoderms and the remaining shelled creatures, I have pursued the nature and condition of oysters somewhat more fully, leaving a fuller occasion for writing to others who have a richer knowledge of these things and who have long and often lived in those maritime places. What has so far been inserted about oysters should therefore be understood of the other shellfish as well. In particular, snails and river shells are noxious, and when they cling to brambles they disturb the stomach and provoke vomiting. Tortoises, which the usage of Greeks and Latins has admitted into the diet, have flesh not much different from veal, in both the pleasantness of its taste and its smell; serious authors affirm this. All authorities declare with one voice that their blood is a remarkable help against poisons. Land tortoises, which are the more handsome and live in groves and woods, are highly commended by later medicine for calling back the thin and wasted from the grave, for they resist the hot habit in the limbs. Sea tortoises are said to be soft and delicate around the shoulder blades and the back legs. They say it is most certain that those well digested in the stomach nourish vigorously. They are first boiled very carefully and then cut into pieces and fried. Pliny, book 9, chapter 10, is the authority that the Indian Sea sends forth tortoises of such size that the surfaces of single ones cover habitable huts, and that people sail among the islands of the Red Sea especially in them, as in boats. Those who have handed down records of the affairs of the New Indies say that tortoises are found there from whose shell large shields are made. Hence the Germans call them Schildkroten from the shape of the shield or buckler. So far on the Ostracoderms.

units.la: De Malacostracis, hoc est, crustis intectis, seu crustaceis.
units.tr: On the Malacostraca, that is, the crustaceans with soft bodies under a shell, or crustaceans.

units.la: CRustatorum nomina tam apud Latinos quam Græcos confundi certum est. Aristoteles quatuor eorum fecit genera, locustas, astacos, squillas, cancros, 4. de animal. lib. Et cancros appellasse visus est, quibus corpus est rotundum, & cauda deest. Capite enim secundo ait, Cancris ex crustaceis solis cauda deest, & corpus rotundum est, cùm locustis squillisque longum sit. Plinius summus alioquin Aristotelis imitator, omnes qui crusta teguntur, tam caudatos, quam non caudatos sub cancri appellatione complectitur. Porro cancrorum genus multiplex esse Aristoteles scribit, nec facilè enumerandum, ob nominum multitu-dinem. Generatim, quæ de his constant, leguntur què, depromant. Dutitate[?] autem ostracodermis similia esse, sed minus quam illa salsi liquoris continere, Galenus lib. de alimentis[?]. Confirmat hoc Simeon Serhi de vsu cancrorum prodens, Cancri, in-quit, salsum quendam succum habent, mi-nus tamen quam testacea: ventrem nihilo-minus sistunt, nec leuiter alunt, in aqua po-tulenta prius elixati, qua ratione salsum suc-cum amittunt. Cæterum nomina malaco-stracorum sic distinguenda sunt, vt cancer sit ein Krabbe/cancer marin*, ein Meerkrabbe/ altacus vero, ein Krebs/ altacus mari-nus, gammarus. ein Meerkrebs/ altacus sluuiatilis, ein süsser Wasserkrebs/ cancer locu-strarius, ein langer Krebs. Cancri maiores, omnium cancrorum maximi, grosse Meer-spinnen / squillæ, kleine Meerkrebs oder kleine Krabben / locustis similes sunt, nisi quod forcipe carent. Utautem nominibus malacostraca distinguuntur, ita etiam viribꝰ & facultatibus, pro sc.aquæ, loci, aeris ac pa-buli natura ac conditione diuersa.
units.tr: It is certain that the names of crustaceans are confused among the Latins as well as the Greeks. Aristotle made four kinds of them: lobsters, crayfish, squills and crabs (4 *de animal.*). He seems to have called cancers those that have a round body and no tail. For in the second chapter he says: "Among the crustaceans, only crabs lack a tail, and their body is round, whereas lobsters and squills are long." Pliny, otherwise a great imitator of Aristotle, embraces under the name of cancer all crustaceans, both tailed and tailless. Aristotle writes that the genus of crabs is manifold and not easy to enumerate, because of the multitude of names. What is generally agreed about them is read and may be drawn from the sources. Galen (*lib. de alimentis*) says that crustaceans are similar to the testaceans, but contain less salty liquid than they do. Simeon Seth confirms this in his work on the use of crabs: "Crabs," he says, "have a certain salty juice, though less than the testaceans. Nevertheless they fill the belly and do not nourish lightly, unless they are first boiled in a potable water, by which method they lose their salty juice." The names of the malacostraca should be distinguished thus: *cancer* is a crab (German *Krabbe*, *Meerkrabbe*); *astacus* is a lobster (*Krebs*, *Meerkrebs*); *gammarus* is a sea-lobster (*Meerkrebs*); *astacus fluviatilis* is a river crayfish (*süsser Wasserkrebs*); *cancer locustarius* is a spiny lobster (*langer Krebs*). The largest of all crabs, the *cancri maiores*, are the big sea-spiders (*grosse Meerspinnen*) or squills; the small crabs (*kleine Meerkrebs* or *kleine Krabben*) are like lobsters, except that they lack claws. Just as the malacostraca are distinguished by their names, so also they differ in powers and qualities, according to the nature and condition of the water, place, air and food.

units.la: Omnia crustacea esse tabidis, extenuatis ac macilentis salubria, feruidos adustosque humores refrigerare ac diluere omnium pe-ne consensu traditur: verum fluuiatilia mari-nis efficacia existere, quoniam his salsugi-
units.tr: It is handed down by almost universal agreement that all crustaceans are wholesome for those who are wasted, emaciated and thin, and that they cool and dilute fiery and scorched humours. But river crustaceans are more effective than sea ones, since a certain saltiness is mixed into the sea ones.

units.la: {y} [?]is aliquid admixtum reperitur, qua quidem appetentiam excitant, ac palato gratificantur, sed magis exiccant, quocirca sanis marini-mi cancri aptiores sunt, nec non iis qui insa-lubri corporis sunt habitu, vitiosisq; humo-ribus scatent, humorum enim putredini ob-sistunt, superuacuaque excrementa exiccant atque absumunt: fluuiatiles vetò humectant ac nutriunt magis, natiuumque [?]homorem, quo corpus subsistit ac nutritur, adaugent, adhibito vino dulci & calorifico, cuius adiumento concoctio perficitur. Efficacius omnia praestant in aqua hordei loti, inque carnium vel capi iure cocti. Salis quoque & aromatum vsum non incosulto hic adhibent, qui ad aquilonios tractus vergunt, hac enim ratione minus pituitosi efficiuntur, minusq; computrescunt, liquescit enim saliis adeps, vt videre est in limacibus, quae asperso sale, minus sunt opimae ac [?]mostrosè obesæ. Squillæ praeterea astacos & locustas in eo quod hecticis aeque morbo extenuatis eximiè prosint, vincere reperio, carnisq; dulcedine superare, easdemq; non in vilibus apud Romanos fuisse cibis, Satyrographorum carmina satis testantur, de qua re Iuuenalis,
units.tr: ...is found mixed in, which indeed stimulate the appetite and please the palate, but dry more. For this reason sea crabs are more suitable for the healthy, and also for those whose body is of an unwholesome habit and full of morbid humours, for they resist the putrefaction of humours and dry up and consume superfluous excrements. River crabs, on the other hand, moisten and nourish more, and increase the natural moisture by which the body subsists and is nourished, when sweet and warming wine is added, with whose help digestion is completed. All these work more effectively in washed barley water and in the broth of boiled meat or chicken. People here also use salt and spices, not without reason, those who live toward the northern regions. For by this method they become less phlegmatic and rot less, since the fat of the salt is liquefied, as may be seen in snails, which, when sprinkled with salt, are less plump and monstrously obese. I find that squills, moreover, are excellent for those wasted by hectic fever, and surpass lobsters and crayfish in this respect, and also in the sweetness of their flesh. That they were not among the cheap foods of the Romans is sufficiently attested by the verses of the satirists, concerning which Juvenal says:

units.la: Aspice quam in magno distinet pectore lancem,
units.tr: Behold how proudly he carries the dish on his great chest,

units.la: Quæ fertur Domino Squilla.
units.tr: Which is said to be a squill for the master.

units.la: Et Horatius,
units.tr: And Horace:

units.la: Adsertur Squillas inter murenas natantes
units.tr: A squill is served among the swimming lampreys

units.la: In patina porrecta.
units.tr: On an outstretched platter.

units.la: Non conticendum hîc remedium cansi crorum fluuiatilium caudâ carentium, in patella crematorum ac deustorum, quorum puluis cinisque singulari pollet virtute, in expugnando exitiali canis rabidi veneno. Ex hibetur cum gentianæ radice thurisque mento cochleari mensura, frequentius ite rando, quo rabies aquæque pauor propulse tur.
units.tr: Nor should I pass over here the remedy of river crabs, which lack a tail, burned and scorched in a little dish. Their powder and ash have singular power in overcoming the deadly poison of a mad dog. It is given with root of gentian and a spoonful measure of frankincense, repeated frequently, by which rabies and the fear of water are driven away.

units.la: Stillatitium quoq; cancrorum liquorem, plenilunii tempore in balneo Mariæ elicitū, sicut & ius eorundem accuratè prius abluto rum, aftmaticis & tabescentibus, nec non apopleċticis bis in die potam, prodesse com pertum est.
units.tr: It has also been found that the liquor distilled from crabs, drawn off in the time of the full moon in a bain-marie, and likewise the broth of the same crabs after they have been carefully washed beforehand, benefits asthmatics and the wasting, as well as apoplectics, when drunk twice a day.

units.la: Oleo coctos aurium dolores calidos fanare, si instilletur id, si verò hauriatur, venena tam potionem aut venenatum morsum dif ficultur ferentibus succurrere, apud doctissi mos autores reperio.
units.tr: I find in the most learned authors that oil in which they have been boiled cures warm pains of the ears if it is dripped in, and that if it is drunk it helps those who with difficulty bear poisons in a potion or a venomous bite.

units.la: De oculis cancrorum sciptum inuenio, collo adalligatos lippitudini mederi: tusos que eosdem aduersus laterum punctuaras bi bi & calculum, necnon venena, & febres.
units.tr: I find written about the eyes of crabs that, hung around the neck, they cure inflammation of the eyes; that crushed, they are good against stitches in the side and kidney stones, and also against poisons and fevers.

units.la: Non omiserim, quod Plinius de fluuiatī libus cancris scribit, eos tritos in oleo & aqua ante accessiones inunctis febricitantibus prodesse: alii decoctos ad quartas in vino è balneis egressis bibere suadent in quartanis: alii sinistrum oculum deuorari iubent: alii oculos eorum ante solis ortum ægro adalligari mandant, ita vt[?] æcæ dimittantur in aquas, sicque tertianas abigi promittunt. Mirabile, & in naturæ maiestate plane recon-ditum atque abstrusum, febricitanti, si vngues in pedibus & manibus resecentur, viuque cancri dorso adalligentur, cancerque in aquam fluentem viuus coniiciatur, febrim remissuram, cuius experimenti, possem, si opus effet, producere testes, qui id non semel documento comprobarunt. Et tantum etiam de animalibus exanguibus, eorumque in re cibaria vsu dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: I should not omit what Pliny writes about river crabs: that rubbed in oil and water before the attacks, they help the feverish when smeared on. Others advise drinking them boiled down to a quarter in wine by those coming out of the baths, for quartan fevers. Others order that the left eye be eaten. Others instruct that their eyes be hung on the sick before sunrise, and then released into the water, and thus promise that tertian fevers will be driven off. Marvellous, and plainly hidden and concealed in the majesty of nature: for the feverish, if the nails of the feet and hands are pared, and a live crab is tied to the back, and the crab is thrown alive into running water, the fever will be dispelled. I could, if it were needed, produce witnesses to this experiment, who have more than once confirmed it by proof. And let it suffice to have said this much about bloodless animals and their use as food.

units.la: Hactenus de esculentis vitæ prorogandæ conducentibus ex animalibus sanguineis & exanguibus : Sequuntur nunc ordine partes animalium quorundam, quæ sunt e-dendo.
units.tr: Thus far on the edible animals, both blooded and bloodless, that conduce to prolonging life. Now follow in order the parts of certain animals that are eaten.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: IN animalibus partes reperiuntur tum carnosa, & sanguinea, tum carnes, sanguinisq; expertes, adipofa item ac pingues, suaq; natura humida ac fluida.
units.tr: In animals there are parts that are fleshy and bloody, and others that are free of flesh and blood, and likewise fatty and rich, and by their nature moist and fluid.

units.la: Primi generis sunt lingua, glandia, testes, vulua, renes, iecur, lien, pulmo, cor, ventres.
units.tr: Of the first kind are the tongue, the sweetbreads, the testicles, the womb, the kidneys, the liver, the spleen, the lungs, the heart, and the stomachs.

units.la: Secundi, pedes, aures, rostra.
units.tr: Of the second kind, the feet, the ears, and the snouts.

units.la: Tertii, ossium[?] medulla, cerebrum, sanguis[?], adeps.
units.tr: Of the third kind, the marrow of the bones[?], the brain, the blood[?], and the fat.

units.la: De Lingua.
units.tr: On the Tongue.

units.la: Sfe animalia, & homines lingua caren- tes. Plinius l.8 & 6. testatur: ell quoque miram linguarum diuersitatem idem eleganter ostendit libro naturalis sua historia 11. Itaque quæ in cibis magis placeant, inqui- rendum. Inuenio autem suillam & bubulam āculinis magis commendari, vtramque qui- dem quandoque elixam, sepius tamen assam, gariophyllisque consixam. In multis Ger- maniæ locis bubulæ sale condiuntur, pensi- lesque asseruantur in annuos vsus. Hac zy- thi meriq; seu vini potores ad excitandam si- tim nihil præclarius habent, vinum siquidē iucundioris gustus fieri huius est assirmant. Verùecinæ elixæ ex aceto febricitantibus, & à valetudine sese colligentibus exhibentur. Cæterum, probum pariunt succum, carnium succo similem, si commodē præparentur, & in ventre conficiantur. Cinnamomo, garyo- phyllis, piperéque ganeæ artifices eas ptæ- parare inuenerunt: ex auibus nullam lin- guam in mensarum olim honore fuisse re- perio, præterquam phœnicopteri, & anserum, quam libidinem monere quidam tra- derunt.
units.tr: There are animals and men that have no tongue. Pliny, in books 8 and 6, bears witness to this, and in book 11 of his Natural History he elegantly shows the wonderful diversity of tongues. Therefore we must inquire which tongues please most at table. I find that pork and beef tongues are most recommended by cooks, both boiled at times, but more often roasted and stuck with cloves. In many places in Germany beef tongues are seasoned with salt and hung up to be kept for the whole year's use. Drinkers of beer or of wine, to whet their thirst, have nothing more excellent than these, for they affirm that wine becomes more pleasant to the taste with them. Boiled tongues are given with vinegar to the feverish and to those recovering their health. Moreover, they yield a good juice, similar to the juice of meats, if they are properly prepared and digested in the stomach. Cooks of gluttony have found that they can prepare them with cinnamon, cloves and pepper. Among birds, I find that no tongue was once in honour at the table, except those of the flamingo and the goose, which certain writers report as provoking lust.

units.la: De glandiis,& glandulis.
units.tr: On the Glands and Sweetbreads.

units.la: GLandia ipsas esse cervices quidam volunt, quod in his glandulæ sint: Plinio pars illa apri, in qua sunt glandulæ, qui-busdam sunt vbera. Censorius olim legibus cœnis interdictas fuisse Plinius narrat. Caterum glandulas inter salubres animalium partes, quæ in cibos veniunt, repositas reperio, alimentum q;, si probè conficiantur, præbere vescentibus carnis naturæ proximum. Si exactè non concoquantur, duriores quæ sunt, crudum, humidior & pituitosum aggenerant succum. Præcipua autem inter hodiernæ gulæ ganeaq; cibaria mammillares glandulas lacte refertas, præcipuam auctoritatem obtinuisse, & etiamnum obtinere video suillas & bubulas, vbera gulæ proceres inprimis magnificant. Assa autem elixis præstant.
units.tr: Some hold that the sweetbreads are the necks themselves, because glands are in them. Pliny says that for some people that part of the boar in which the glands are is their udder. Long ago, Censorius, Pliny relates, forbade these at dinners by law. Moreover, I find that the glands are placed among the wholesome parts of animals that come to food, and if they are properly digested they supply nourishment nearest to the nature of flesh for those who eat them. If they are not thoroughly digested, the harder ones generate a crude and moister, phlegmatic juice. Yet I see that the mammary glands, full of milk, have obtained and still obtain the chief authority among the foods of the modern throat and gullet, and the nobles of the palate especially praise the udders of pigs and cows. Roasted, however, they excel boiled.

units.la: De testibus.
units.tr: On the Testicles.

units.la: TEstes nitidiores in cibos raro admit-tunt, feminis enim virosum odorem redolent. Insalubres autem plane esse taurorum, arietum & hircorum inde constat, quod nemo elegantioris vitæ eos vnquam attigerit. De testiculis vulpis,& gallinaceis, experimento quidam compererunt, venerem lan-guinam & desidiosam eos mire excitare, in cibis adhibitos, Quin gallinaceos probi-tate alimenti praestare graues autores tradunt. Suum testiculos censoriis legibus interdictos cœnis Plin. l. 8. c. 51. autor est.
units.tr: Testicles, being rather delicate, are rarely admitted to food, for they smell of the male's strong odour. That they are plainly unwholesome in bulls, rams and he-goats is clear from this, that no one of more refined life has ever touched them. Some have discovered by experiment that the testicles of foxes and of fowls, when taken as food, wonderfully arouse sluggish and languid desire. Indeed, serious authors report that the testicles of cocks surpass in the goodness of their nourishment. Pliny, book 8, chapter 51, is the authority that the testicles of swine were forbidden at dinners by the censorial laws.

units.la: De vulua.
units.tr: On the Womb.

units.la: Vluam in animalibus interiorem fœtus conceptaculi cauitatem appellant erudi-tiores, quæ in homine uterus dicitur, matrix. Porro ex omnibus, suillam Romani gulæ proceribus in cibo placuisse, agrauibus autoribus reperitur proditum, ferculum enim ex ea conficiebant ab Apitio & Horatio celebrati, Cum fit obeso. Nil melius turdo, vuluá nil dulcius ampla.
units.tr: The more learned call the womb in animals the inner cavity that receives the foetus; in man it is called the uterus or matrix. Further, of all the parts, it is found recorded by weighty authors that the sow's womb pleased the Romans, the nobles of the palate, as food, for they made a dish of it celebrated by Apicius and by Horace, when he says: "Nothing is better than a thrush, nothing sweeter than a full womb."

units.la: Tres autem erant eius differentiæ, cuius deleclum Plinius indicat lib. 11. c. 36. his verbis, Vulua fuit ... eiectio partu melior, quam edito, eiectitia vocatur.
units.tr: There were, moreover, three kinds of it, the choice of which Pliny indicates in book 11, chapter 36, in these words: the womb was... the one discharged after birth is better than the one brought forth; it is called the ejected one.

units.la: Quæ vulua [?] primipara suis optima, convainci-tra effœtus. A partu, præterquam eodem die bis opti-suis occisa, liuidaq; macra. Nec novellarum præterquam primiparum laudatur, potiusq; veterum, dum ne effœtarum, nec bidua ante partum, aut post partum, aut quo eiecerint die. Proxima eiectitia est occiso uno die post partum, huius & sumen optimum, fi modo fœtus [illegible, ~4 letters] hamhauserit, eiectitiæ[?] deterrimum. Vulua verò de virgine, porca sterilis dicta, lasere Cyrenaico pipere, menthæ sicce foliis, addito liquamine, mel-le & aceti modico, condita, in muria tamè prius cocta, cæteris præferebatur, de qua Martialis,
units.tr: The womb of a first-bearing sow is the best, but the barren are inferior. Apart from a birth, unless on the same day, the best is that of a sow killed twice, and a livid, lean one. Nor is that of young sows praised, except of first-bearers, but rather of older ones, provided it is neither of barren ones, nor of one two days before or after birth, or on the day they cast it. Next to the ejected is the one of a sow killed one day after birth; the milk of this one is also best, if only the foetus [illegible, about four letters] has swallowed it; the ejected is the worst. But the womb of a virgin, called a barren sow, was preferred to the others when seasoned with Cyrenaic laser, dried mint leaves, with brine added, honey and a little vinegar, but first boiled in brine. Of this Martial says:

units.la: Te fortasse magis capiet de virgine porca, Me materna graui de sue vulua capit.
units.tr: Perhaps the virgin sow will please you more; but the maternal womb of a heavy sow pleases me.

units.la: Languidum autem ventriculum sterilem vul-uam [?]Apiii conditurâ præparatam reficere proditum est. Celsus Cornelius lib.2.cap.24. de sue scribit, stomacho prosunt vngulæ, rostra, aures, vulvaeque, sterilis. Vulvas quoque proin-cundissimo edulio olim habitas Plutarchus 8. Symp.problem.9.testatur. Qui nostro sacculo in mensas eas recipiant, nulli sunt aut pauci, nisi libidinis proritandæ, vel etiam conceptionis in-vandæ spe, &c.
units.tr: It is recorded that the sterile womb of a sow, prepared with the seasoning of Apicius, restores a languid stomach. Celsus Cornelius, book 2, chapter 24, writes of the sow: the hooves, snouts, ears and the sterile womb benefit the stomach. Plutarch, in Symposiacs, problem 9, bears witness that wombs were once held to be a most pleasant dish. Those who in our age admit them to their tables are none or few, except in hope of arousing lust or even of procuring conception, etc.

units.la: De renibus.
units.tr: On the Kidneys.

units.la: IN Brileto & Tharne Asiæ regionibus cer-vis quaternos renes esse Plinius commemorat lib.ii.cap. 27. Vitulini aliorumque quadrupedum iuniorum, quibusdam in cibis arrident: alias difficulter in ventriculo confici verisimile est, iniquosque & impro-bos succos generare, quia vrinæ naturam quandam iu[?] se receperunt, id quod fœdus etiam odor manifestat, quem renes omnium aliorum alioaliorum viscerum maximè reddunt, corporis enim humores per eos colantur. Quare rusticis relinquantur & messoribus.
units.tr: Pliny mentions that in the regions of Brileta and Tharne in Asia, stags have four kidneys, book 11, chapter 27. Veal and the flesh of other young quadrupeds delight some at table; otherwise it is likely that they are hardly digested in the stomach, and generate unfair and bad juices, because they have taken on a certain nature of urine, which the foul odour also shows, which the kidneys of all other organs give off most of all, for the humours of the body are strained through them. Therefore let them be left to peasants and reapers.

units.la: De iecore & liene.
units.tr: On the Liver and Spleen.

units.la: IEcur[?] cibis lautioribus non est abdicandum, habito tamen respectu animalium, quorum est proprium, natura, status, pabuli. Multum enim refert horum notitia. Est autem epatis caro sanguini proxima, quae optimum epar est, quod puro & sanguineo colore rubet. Porrò multorum animalium iecinora medicinae potius quàm culinae praestant, opem adpraeclara enim remedia magnificantur: epar caprarum, aprinum, hircinum, item pisces, qui dicitur Ἀλλρυππε[?], huius enim epar oculis obscuris, & ex imminuta v sione imbecillis miraculo mederi expertum est, ut & epar caprarum aciem oculorum restituere dicitur vespertinam his, quos νυκτάλωπας vocant.
units.tr: The liver should not be excluded from the finer foods, provided regard is had to the nature, condition and feed of the animal to which it belongs, for knowledge of these matters makes a great difference. The flesh of the liver is closest to blood, and the best liver is the one that is red with a pure, bloody colour. Moreover, the livers of many animals are better suited to medicine than to the kitchen, since they are celebrated as excellent remedies: the liver of goats, of wild boar, and of he-goats; likewise that of the fish called [Ἀλλρυππε], for its liver has been found by experience to cure people with dim eyes and weak sight, just as goat's liver is said to restore the evening vision of those whom they call [νυκτάλωπας].

units.la: In cibis verò sapore salubritateque commendari reperio apud autores non proletarios epar gallinarum & gallinaceorum, anserum, anatum, suum, vitulorum, ratarum, piscium, qui dicitur Ἀλλρυππε. Suillum tum Graecis, tum Romanis in lautioribus ciborum fuit. Inuentum Apitii[?] esse Plinius voluit cari à saginare sues fœminas, easque à satietate necare repente potu mulsi dato. Galenus hac sagina censuit, mulso iucundius iecur esse, aliisque dotibus ac virtutibus cæteris præferri debere. In anserum iecoribus quantam curam veteres Romani adhibuerint, infra, vbi de anseribus dictum est, annotauimus.
units.tr: In foods, however, I find that among non-plebeian authors the liver of hens and cocks, geese, ducks, pigs, calves, rays and the fish called [Ἀλλρυππε] is recommended for flavour and wholesomeness. Pig's liver was a delicacy for both Greeks and Romans. Pliny claims that Apicius invented the practice of fattening sows and then killing them quickly by giving them mulsum to drink until they were full. Galen held that the liver from such fattening is more pleasant than the rest and should be preferred for its other qualities and virtues. How much care the ancient Romans gave to goose livers I have noted below, where I discuss geese.

units.la: Fartilibus enim in magnam crescere amplitudinem, exemptaq; lacte augeri & mulso, Scipio, Metellus vir consularis, & Sestius eques Romanus inuenisse dicuntur. Non obscuram enim esse operarium huius ganea inuentionem[?], Vitulinum in cibis, multis gratissimum est, garyophyllis id confixum assant, eduntq; ex intinctu quodam nigro & pradulci, quod vino, aceto, pipere, saccharoq;, vel in defectu huius, melle, temperatur.
units.tr: For it is said that Scipio, Metellus, a man of consular rank, and Sestius, a Roman knight, discovered how the liver could be made to grow to a great size, by feeding the birds on figs and then, once removed, enlarging the liver with milk and mulsum. The inventor of this delicacy is not obscure. Veal is very pleasing to many as food. They roast it stuck with cloves and eat it with a dark, sweetish sauce, seasoned with wine, vinegar, pepper and sugar, or with honey when sugar is lacking.

units.la: Eodemq; modo & pulmones, lienesq; praeparari possunt, eparitem vermiculum, bubalum & ouillum, quae tamen vulgo peculiariter eduntur in sartagine frixa, vel etiam elixa frustulatim, concisa, cum pipere & butyro, estq; hoc edulium non insuave, nec insalubre.
units.tr: Lungs and spleens can be prepared in the same way, as can the liver of the ... , the buffalo and the sheep, which are commonly eaten in a particular fashion: fried in a pan, or boiled, cut into small pieces, with pepper and butter. This dish is neither unpleasant nor unwholesome.

units.la: Raiae epar ganeae artifices in summo honore habent, elixum id ex aceto piperato editur plerunque, communiter frigitur in sartagine. Aliorum animalium iecinora crassi esse succi concoctuque pertinacia, ac difficulter persuapermeare ventrem, dubium nullum est. Qui indistinctè hæc de omnibus pronunciant, errant, naturæ rerum causarumq; imperiti. Nobile apud quosdam proverbium est, iecinora efitaia[?] vescentium iecinora exhilarare, similia enim si-milibus delectari, conseruariq;. Tabe namq; pulmonis laborantes pulmo humanus, tabe re-num, renes humani ob substantiæ similitudinem, restituunt. Atrophia igitur perire male, velpla-nè contabescere, quam appropriatum remedii adhibere, est vitam sibi ipsi abbreuiare. Multis paradoxon videbitur, hominis pulmones tabidis auxiliari, caliditatemq; habitualem & hecti-cam prepedire. Sed expedimentum cuiq; liberum est.
units.tr: Cooks hold ray liver in the highest esteem; it is usually eaten boiled in peppered vinegar, and commonly fried in a pan. That the livers of other animals are thick in juice, and, because of their stubbornness in digestion, pass through the stomach with difficulty, is beyond doubt. Those who pronounce this indiscriminately of all livers are mistaken, being ignorant of the nature of things and their causes. There is a well-known proverb among some people that eating livers gladdens the liver, for like is delighted and preserved by like. Thus those suffering from consumption of the lungs are restored by the human lung, and those with wasting of the kidneys by human kidneys, because of the likeness of substance. Therefore to waste away, or to perish in a slow decline, is worse than to apply a suitable remedy; it is to shorten one's own life. To many it will seem a paradox that human lungs help the consumptive and check the habitual heat and hectic fever. But each man is free to make his own trial.

units.la: Experiantur tabidi, senes, & marasmo seu marcore aridi, comperient natiuam sibi hu-miditatem iis reparari ac restitui, quod annotasse hic opere pretium duxi.
units.tr: Let the consumptive, the old, and those dried up by marasmus or decay make the trial; they will find that their natural moisture is restored and renewed for them. This I thought worth noting here.

units.la: Lienis carnes rariores, suauiores, leuio-resq; esse quam epatis constat, sanguis tamen minus rubicundus, melancholico enim succo nutritur, unde ad carnis huius speciem ad por-tionem alentis se habebit succi.
units.tr: It is agreed that spleen flesh is rarer, sweeter and lighter than liver flesh, yet its blood is less red, for it is nourished by melancholy juice. Hence the juice that nourishes it will bear a corresponding relation to the kind of flesh it produces.

units.la: Itaque quo is improbior est, fœculentior & crassior, tanto carnem ipsam deteriorem esse veri-simile est. Porro lienē vituli, sicut & bubalum recenrecentem assum velelixum[?] in cibo ad splenis dolores præsentaneum esse remedium quondam tradiderunt. Vrsorum, Luporum, Leonum, Pantherarum, & similium lienes esculentos non esse inde constat, quod, qui horum animalium carnibus vescuntur homines, iis abstineant.
units.tr: Therefore the more corrupt, thick and gross the spleen is, the more likely it is that its flesh is worse. Moreover, it was once taught that the spleen of a calf, like that of a buffalo, eaten roasted or boiled while fresh, is an immediate remedy for pains of the spleen. That the spleens of bears, wolves, lions, panthers and similar animals are not edible is clear from the fact that men who eat the flesh of these animals refrain from their spleens.

units.la: De Pulmone.
units.tr: On the Lung.

units.la: DIfferentiæ Pulmonum variæ sunt, pro sanguinis, quo pulmo alitur, diuersa constitutione; Carnem habet laxissimam & levissimam, quasi ex spuma quadam coagulatam, alitur enim sanguine ad unguem elaborato, flavo, tenui, puro, spi-ritali, ad alentis igitur succi naturam se accommodat. In cibis certum est, tanto facilius jecore & splene perfici, quanto utroque est rarior, tantoque magis vires reficere & spiritus reparare, quanto puriore & tenuiore alitur sanguine. Suilli autem pulmones magis commendantur, habenturque in deliciis: bubali & vervecini inter populares cibos referuntur. Assi quoque & à jejunis præsumti, eo die ebrietatem arcere dicun-tur. Sed hoc miratu & cognitu dignum, quod à Plutarcho de ficubus scribitur, qui in causis naturalibus tradit Mnesitheum medicum à Galeno in Proœmio libri ad glauc.commendatum narraffe , eos qui in principio pulmonariae morbi cepas appetuntferuari, qui vero ficus, interire, ideo, quia appetitus temperaturas, temperaturae aurem morbos consequuntur. Galenus 3.de alim. facult. ait , pulmone jecorem conco-ctu esse faciliorem, minus nutrire, pituito-sumque magis succum facere. At 6.de vita[?] partium cap.10,tradit,pulmonem tenui,levi & vaporofo nutriri sanguine , jecur vero li-mofo & crasso.
units.tr: The lungs differ in various ways, according to the varying constitution of the blood by which the lung is nourished. It has very loose and light flesh, as if coagulated from a kind of foam, for it is nourished by blood worked to perfection, yellow, thin, pure and spirit-like, and so it adapts itself to the nature of the juice that feeds it. As food, it is certain that the lung is digested more easily than the liver and spleen, and the more rarefied it is, the more it restores strength and renews the spirits, the purer and thinner the blood by which it is fed. Pig's lungs are more highly commended and are counted among delicacies; buffalo and sheep lungs are reckoned among common foods. Lungs roasted and eaten by those who have fasted are said to ward off drunkenness on that day. But one thing is worthy of wonder and of study, which Plutarch writes about figs in his Natural Questions, reporting that the physician Mnesitheus, whom Galen commends in the preface to his book addressed to Glaucon, related that those who crave onions at the beginning of a lung disease recover, but those who crave figs perish, because appetites follow temperaments and temperaments bring on diseases. Galen (De alimentorum facultatibus, bk 3) says that the lung is easier to digest than the liver, nourishes less, and makes more phlegmatic juice. But in De usu partium, bk 6, ch. 10, he says the lung is nourished by thin, light and vaporous blood, and the liver by slimy and thick blood.

units.la: Unde fi tale est nutrimentum , qualis est substantia nutrientis , videtur substantia pulmonis, vt est jecore tenuior, sic succum tenuiorem parere non pituitofiorem. Ærius 2.c.127.[?] hanc dubitationem tollit , dicens pulmonis nutrimentum esse magis pituito-sum ob cartilagineum, (e.asperæ arteriæ pulmoni inexiftenti corpus perpetuo madore scatens.
units.tr: Hence, if the nourishment is of the same kind as the substance that is nourished, the substance of the lung, being thinner than that of the liver, seems likely to produce a thinner juice, not a more phlegmatic one. Aëtius (2, c. 127) removes this doubt, saying that the nourishment of the lung is more phlegmatic because of its cartilaginous part, the windpipe, which lies within the lung and is always dripping with moisture.

units.la: Ad extremum monitum vitæ prorogandæ studiosum hic velim, epata, lienes & pulmones in pecudibus mactatis non raro vitiata & infecta videri, quæ postea manda-cata non leue vitæ periculum attulisse experientia fatis comprobauit, & etiam nunc cō-probat. Itaque vitæ ejusmodi insidiæ cauté euitentur.
units.tr: Finally, I wish here to advise those who are studious of prolonging life that livers, spleens and lungs of slaughtered animals are often seen to be spoiled and tainted, and experience has amply shown, and still shows, that eating them has brought no slight danger to life. Such snares to life should therefore be carefully avoided.

units.la: De Corde.
units.tr: On the Heart.

units.la: Symbolo Pythagorico iubebatur, cor non esse edendum. Et elegantioris vitae homines raro in cibos corda admittunt, quia ex fibris multiplicibus contexta sunt, carnemque habent duram, spissam, aegreque alterabilem. Exacte tamen elaborata alimentum validum praestare, minimeque iniqui succi nullum est dubium. Caterum ventriculum frigidum & flaccidum, cibosque retinere non valentem, animalium quorundam corda, ut vituli, leporis, cervi, suumque, ex avibus vero, cornicis gallinarum, phasianorum, turdorum, & similium, leviter ex butyro modicoque aceti affusa garyophyllisque confixa, corroborare ac fovere novis experimentis patefactum est quod reticere hic nolui. Nec enim decet posterorum commodis consulturum, vel praetermittere necessaria scitu & utilia, vel ad caligine involutam doctrinam, inextricabilesque perplexitate lectorem invitare.
units.tr: The Pythagorean precept ordered that the heart not be eaten. People of more refined living rarely admit hearts into their food, because they are woven from many fibres and have a hard, dense flesh that is slow to be changed. Yet, when carefully prepared, they provide a strong nourishment, and there is no doubt that they yield very little unsound juice. However, the hearts of certain animals, such as calves, hares, deer and pigs, and among birds those of crows, hens, pheasants, thrushes and similar birds, have been shown by new experiments, which I did not wish to pass over here, to strengthen and warm a cold and flaccid stomach that cannot hold its food. They are lightly dressed with butter, a little vinegar poured over them, and studded with cloves. For it is not fitting to serve the convenience of posterity by omitting things that are necessary and useful to know, nor to invite the reader into a doctrine wrapped in darkness and inextricable confusion.

units.la: De Ventribus,
units.tr: On Stomachs,

units.la: Ventres animalium, qui in cibos hominum veniunt, nec magnitudine nec specie inter se similes sunt & quibusdam sunt multiplices, ut cornigeris, quibusdam, ut in avium genere gallinae sunt, l.12.2.28 [?]
units.tr: The stomachs of animals that come to human food are not alike in size or kind, and in some they are multiple, as in horned animals, and in others, as among birds, in hens and geese, etc. l.12.2.28 [?]

units.la: sunt, anseres &c. validum, prædurum & car- nofum quid vice illius partis, quæ cibum re- cipit, obtinuerunt, quin & ingluuiem quan- dam habent, in quam cibum recentem & in- confectum recondunt, sed in cibos non ve- nit. Porro fi exacte ventres perficiuntur, quod longiori fit tempore, succum pariunt, nec sanguineum, necinculpatum, gelidum tamen & pituitosum. Qui validos habent ventriculos, laboresque validos aggressuri sunt, minus noxie iis vescuntur. De inte- ftinis idem fit judicium, hoc tamen interest, quod citius conficiantur, & cum pinguedi- ne sua plus nutriant, fine tamen pane, faleq; sufficiente deglutita infigniter noxia depre- henduntur, cogitur enim & concrescit pin- guedo in ventriculo, tunicisque ejus adhæ- refcit.
units.tr: They have taken the place of that part which receives food, being something hard, very tough and fleshy; indeed they also have a kind of crop, in which they store fresh and undigested food, but this does not come into food. Further, if stomachs are thoroughly prepared, which takes a longer time, they yield a juice that is neither bloody nor blameless, but cold and phlegmy. Those who have strong stomachs and are about to undertake strenuous labour eat them with less harm. The same judgment applies to the intestines, with this difference: they are digested more quickly and provide more nourishment along with their fat. But if they are swallowed without bread and sufficient salt, they are found to be remarkably harmful, for the fat gathers and congeals in the stomach and clings to its coats.

units.la: De pedibus, auribus, rostro.
units.tr: On feet, ears, and snout.

units.la: Ubalos, vitulinos, vervecinos, hædinos, ô- villos, pedes & suillos, in cibu frequentius usurpari video, multiplicia, ratione & cu- nis prepa'ari, sed interdum non fine noxa. In pedibus ovillis anterioribus & posterioribus, parte quaterna calcant vermiculos inhærere sub rotunda forma, languinofa intus & crinita con- gerie implicitos, experientia & obseruatio testis est, qui, fi ex incuria aut hujus rei ignorantia, cum cū concretione illa, exemti non fuerint, edenti ovillos illes pedes confestim nauseam stomachiq; cruciatum excitabunt cum ructu & vomitione. Verisimile enim est venenosum quiddam subesse capillata huic congeriei, quod coctioni obsit. Vide Lemn. l. 3. cap. 5.[?] Caeterum aures suilla, rostrum, & pedes in summo honore mensarum sunt, hi tamen illo praestant, hoc vero cruribus. Vervecinos quidam aqua incoctos ex aceto mandunt, apio virente asperso. quandoq; frigunt, prunisq; torrent: bubalos elixos exacte quida frigunt: sed male, quia humiditatem nutrimentalem plane eliciunt.
units.tr: I see that the feet of buffaloes, calves, sheep, kids and lambs, and of pigs, are more commonly used as food, prepared in many ways and by various methods, but sometimes not without harm. In the front and hind feet of sheep, a certain quarter-part, experience and observation bear witness, there cling small worms in a round form, entangled in a bloody and hairy mass within. If these are not removed, through carelessness or ignorance of the matter, along with that clotted matter, those who eat these sheep's feet will at once provoke nausea and stomach cramps, with belching and vomiting. For it is likely that something poisonous lies hidden in this hairy mass, which hinders digestion. See Lemn. l. 3. cap. 5.[?] Moreover, pig's ears, snout and feet are held in high honour at table; yet the first excel the others, and the last excel the legs. Some boil sheep in water and eat them with vinegar sprinkled with green celery; sometimes they fry them or roast them on hot coals. Some carefully fry boiled buffalo, but badly, because they draw out all the nourishing moisture.

units.la: Commendant etiam vitulinos elixos piperū & croci condimento addito: suilli craticula assantur, & ex cœpis concisis aceto q; aspersis sumuntur.
units.tr: They also commend boiled veal with pepper and saffron added as seasoning. Pork is roasted on a gridiron, and taken with chopped onions and sprinkled with vinegar.

units.la: Aures suillas ex garo, veteres aceto q; & sinapi edendas voluerunt, vel ex garo oleoq; affuso vino. Hodie culina ganeaq; artifices pro varia praeparationis principatu certant.
units.tr: The ancients wished Ears of pigs to be eaten with brine, vinegar and mustard, or with brine and oil poured over with wine. Today cooks and gourmands contend for the first place in the various ways of preparing them.

units.la: Anserini pedes, omniumq; fere Planipedum, quod omittere nefas fere duxerim, succi suavitate, elixi praestant multis aliis, cumprimis vero in palati delitiis est membrana illa, quâ interveniente, vngues conjun-guntur.
units.tr: Goose feet, and nearly all of the web-footed kinds, which I would almost count it wrong to omit, are excellent when boiled for the sweetness of their juice, above many others; but especially a delicacy for the palate is that membrane intervening, by which the toes are joined.

units.la: De cerebro, adipe, ossium medul-la, sanguine;
units.tr: On the brain, fat, marrow of bones, and blood;

units.la: EX medullarum genere existere cete-brum Galenus 2: de temperamentis, & 2. de vsu part. scripsit; Gujus quoque sententiæ videtur fuisse Plato in Timæo, ubi medullæ morbum omnium periculosissi-mum esse scriptum reliquit, sub medullæ nomine cerebrum intelligens; non spina-lem medullam, ut aliqui putant, vel alias me-dullas, quod verba Platonis ostendunt. Vide Mercurial. variar. lect.[?] lib. 1. c. 9. Caeterum ce-rebra animalium, tempore Plutarchi man-ducati cæpisse; quæ tamen antiquitas abo-minata projecerit, idem affirmat 8. symp. probl. 9. Hodie inter præcipuas epulas quædam re-poni video, præcipuè verò vitulorum, hœ-dorum, leporum, suum; quin & atiùm mul-tarum atq; piscium. Inter damnatos autem cibos à grauibus autoribus cerebra colloca-ri reperio, ob naturam pituitosiorem, diffi-cilemque concoctionem, tum etiam, quod stomacho adversentur, fastidiumq; afferant. Unde Galenus postremo cibo cerebrum pinguiter conditum vomitu indigentibus exhibendum suadet, sic enim faciliorem fo-re vomitionem. Coquuntur multis modis, elixantur interdum, quandoq; friguntur, vel carbonibus assatur[?]. Suillum marasmo ta-bescenbefcentibus utile est: Galenus affirmat, sed vel diligenter assum, vel in albo jure legitime elixum, porro & anetho injectis. Crudum devoratum laedit summopere, ut & omnium aliorum animantium. Leporis ad tremores membrorum magnificari video, sicut cuniculorum in confessa damnatione reperio, quoniam memoriae, officere creditur: Cerebrum cerebro, eparepate recreari Averrhoistarum proculdubio placitum fuit.
units.tr: Galen wrote in his On the Temperaments and On the Use of the Parts, book 2, that the brain belongs to the kind of marrows. Plato in the Timaeus seems also to have held this opinion, where he left it written that disease of the marrow is the most dangerous of all, understanding the brain under the name of marrow, not the spinal marrow, as some think, or other marrows, as Plato's words show. See Mercurial, Variae lectiones, book 1, ch. 9. Moreover, Plutarch says that the brains of animals began to be eaten in his time; yet antiquity, which abhorred them, rejected them; he affirms the same in the 8th book of the Symposiacs, problem 9. Today I see certain brains put among the chief delicacies, especially those of calves, kids, hares and pigs, and indeed of many other animals, and of fish. But I find that brains are placed among the foods condemned by serious authors, on account of their more phlegmy nature and difficult digestion, and also because they are hostile to the stomach and cause loathing. Hence Galen advises that brain richly seasoned be given at the end of a meal to those who need to vomit, for in this way vomiting is easier. They are cooked in many ways: sometimes boiled, sometimes fried, or roasted on coals. Pig's brain is useful for those wasting away with marasmus, Galen affirms, but only if carefully roasted or properly boiled in white broth, with dill added. Eaten raw, it greatly harms, as does that of all other animals. I see the brain of hares praised for tremors of the limbs, as I find that of rabbits is in a notorious condemnation, since it is believed to hinder the memory. That brain is restored by brain, eparepate, was without doubt the opinion of the Averroists.

units.la: Avium cerebrum tanto quadrupedum praestantius est, quanto durius. Vitellius cerebella phasianorum & pavonum apposuit, in passim illa sua ab autoribus celebrata patina.
units.tr: The brain of birds is so much more excellent than that of four-footed animals as it is harder. Vitellius served the little brains of pheasants and peacocks on the dish celebrated by writers in all places.

units.la: Concretis quosdam ossibus, ac sine medullis viuere Plinius autor est, signumque eorum esse, nec sitim sentire, nec sodorem emittere. Caeterum, quoniam medulla ali-menti est sanguinei in ossa spinamque dorsi distributi, dulcis, pinguis, mollis, & humida, extra dubium est, eam probe ac valenter alere, quin & tabidis membris foris & intus auxiliari, quod multis documentis patefactum est: In exemplis nostris est paupercula, quaedam mulier, si recte memini, Lipsica, cui integrum & ultra annum bacillo innixae & ex cruribus tabescentibus claudicanti, Medici illius loci, publicam tunc anatomen exer-
units.tr: Pliny is the authority that some animals have bones that are solid and without marrow, and that the sign of these is that they feel neither thirst nor give off a smell. Moreover, since marrow is the nourishment of the blood distributed into the bones and the spine of the back, it is sweet, fat, soft and moist; there is no doubt that it nourishes well and strongly, and indeed helps wasted limbs outwardly and inwardly, as has been shown by many proofs. Among our examples is a poor woman, if I remember rightly, from Leipzig, who for more than a year had walked lame with wasting legs, leaning on a stick. The physicians of that place, who were then performing a public anatomy,

units.la: exercentes, porrexerunt tibiam, ut hujus medulla ad ignem crura tabida inungeret: Illa protinus, certâ fiducia ducta, accenso igne, medullam liquefactam & extillantem vasculo excipiens, partim cruribus perunxit, partim, quod tamen Medici non præcepe-rant, in ventrem absumpsit: vnde postridie ejus diei, recuperato & integrato gradu, Medicis gratias actura, quaerentibus, quanam ratione tibiae medullam adhibuisset, omnia exposuit, sicque quasi miraculo fuit resti-tuta.
units.tr: offered her a shin-bone, so that she might anoint her wasted legs with its marrow by the fire. She at once, led by firm confidence, lit the fire, caught the melted marrow dripping from it in a little vessel, and partly rubbed it on her legs, and partly, which the physicians had not prescribed, swallowed it.
