Hence on the following day, having recovered and regained her step, she came to thank the physicians, and when they asked by what method she had used the marrow of the shin-bone, she explained everything, and so she was restored as if by a miracle.

units.la: Caterum bubalorum medullam sua-uiffimum condimentum esse ad olera pin-guefacienda, quin & tosti panis frustis eam cum [?]faleillinere, procerum & delicatorum gula experta est. Laudatiffima tamen me-dullarum Plinio teste, est cervina, mox vitu-lina, hircina & caprina. emolliunt omnes ac excalfaciunt, explentq;.
units.tr: Moreover, the marrow of buffaloes is the most pleasant seasoning for fattening vegetables, and the palate of the great and the delicate has tried spreading it on pieces of toasted bread with salt. Yet the most praised marrows, according to Pliny's testimony, are those of the deer, next those of calves, goats and he-goats. All of them soften and warm, and fill.

units.la: Adeps, & pinguedo licet inter fe diffe-rant, confundi tamen vtramque quandoq;, alterumque pro altero poni testatur Galen, 11. de simplicibus medicamen. Idem tamen ibi-dem distinguit, quod pinguedo humidiori-bus animantibus, vt suibus, proveniat, cele-riterque ad ignem colliquescat, nec semel li-quata, rursus facile concrescat: Adeps vero crassior fit, non facilè fundatur & liquescat, liquatus celerrime congeletur. A renibus autem detractus adeps omnis laudatissimus est, antiqui enim medici eum maxime probarunt, Plinio teste l.20.cap.9. Caeterum ex Aristotelis sententia dicentis, adipem & pinguedinem esse sanguinem concoctum, item ex sanguinis percoctione adipem gigni, facile exploditur illorum placitum, qui volunt, omnem pinguedinem absolute esse malam, pisciũ vero pessimam, pinguedinemque ex alimentorum censu proscribunt. Alimenti enim, & condimenti simul, vt & medicamenti vicem praestant pinguedo, & adeps. Pinguedo quo oleosior & humidior, eo salubrior, quo crassior & siccior, eo insalubrior praesertim largius si fumatur: Illa enim igneam, aeriamque naturam participat, intraque corpus sumta, corpus ab occursu malorum vaporum venenatorumque praeservat immune, permeare enim illos non finit in intimos corporis meatus, praesertim vero hoc praestat jus capi pingue, huic enim pinguedo supernatans inducit pelliculam, quae noxiis halitibus, vna cum cibo vel potu in ventrem exceptis, fortiter resistit, quod crassior & siccior praestare nequit. Unum hic occurrit, quod memoria dignissimum est, videl. pinguia, vini vel zythi liberalius haustì vapores reprimere, eorumque evapo-rationem in cerebrum prohibere, quod iis, qui facile ex vini potu inebriantur, capiteq; postea
units.tr: Lard and fat, although they differ from one another, are nevertheless sometimes confused, and Galen, in book 11 of On Simple Medicines, testifies that one is put for the other. The same author there distinguishes that fat is found in moister animals, such as pigs, and quickly melts in the fire, and once melted, quickly congeals again; but lard becomes thicker, is not easily poured out and liquefied, and once liquefied congeals most quickly. Moreover, all fat drawn from the kidneys is most highly praised, for the ancient physicians especially approved it, as Pliny testifies book 20, chapter 9. Moreover, from the opinion of Aristotle, who says that lard and fat are blood concocted, and that lard is produced by the boiling down of blood, the view of those is easily refuted who wish all fat to be absolutely bad, and fish fat worst, and who reject fat from the list of foods. For fat and lard serve at once as food, seasoning and also as medicine. The more oily and moister the fat, the more wholesome; the thicker and drier, the less wholesome, especially if eaten in large amounts. For it shares in a fiery and airy nature, and once taken into the body it guards the body, unharmed, from the attack of noxious vapours and poisons; for it does not allow them to pass into the inner passages of the body. This is especially achieved by broth made with fat, for the fat floating on top forms a thin film, which strongly resists the harmful exhalations taken into the stomach together with food or drink, something the thicker and drier fat cannot do. One thing here deserves to be remembered above all: that fatty foods restrain the vapours of wine or mead drunk too freely, and prevent their evaporation into the brain, which those who are easily made drunk by drinking wine and afterwards suffer in the head must observe. That this is so is clear also from this, that oil poured into wine or scented waters

units.la: Notes in the right margin, transcribed in place above; the marginal notes are only partly legible at the edge of the scan. postea vexantur, obseruandum præcipitur: & hocita se habere vel inde patet, quod oleum vino aut aquis odoratis affusum exhalare eorum odores non finit, humori enim subiecto pelliculam inducit, per quam sub-ditus humor evaporare non potest: Sic raphanus cum oleo commestus, eructatio-nes ventriculi, quas aliàs solet, ciere non potest. Probè igitur faciunt Westphalie populi, dum cerevisiam tepidè cum butyro, vel oleo affuso jejuno stomacho bibunt, sic enim eo die à veneno se reddunt saluos.
units.tr: Pour the oil over wine or scented waters, and it will not let their odours escape, because the oil spreads a film over the liquid beneath and the liquid cannot evaporate through it. In the same way, radish eaten with oil cannot provoke the belching of the stomach that it usually does. So the peoples of Westphalia act wisely when they drink beer lukewarm with butter or oil poured in on an empty stomach; by this means they are kept safe from poison that day.

units.la: Esse hæmapotas, qui sanguinem & quidem humanum exipso homine calidum adhuc sorbeant cap.14. ostensum est Anigi-[?]tur & qualis in cibum sit assumendus, nunc inquirendum. Sanguinem (de humano lo-quar) omnibus humoribus natura esse tem-peratiorem, humanæque temperaturæ fami-liariorem, nutrimenti totius corporis auto-rem, humorem benignum, dilectum filium naturæ, succum naturæ familiarissimum, vt quem natura semper in superpurgationibus ad extremum tanquam pretiosissimum the-saurum conseruet atque custodiat, omnes, quotquot aut sunt aut exiterunt Philoso-phi & Medici, vno ore professi sunt. Proin-de recte Marsilius Ficinus Z. 7. c.2. è Medico-rum tradidit placiti, talem pene esse con-templationem, qualis est sensus, calif; sen-sus sus,qualis sanguis: quę sententia hanc habet rationem, quia ex cibo fit sanguis, talis igitur fuerit sanguis, qualis cibus fuit, necesse est, & quia sanguis inseruit spiritui, spiritus sen-sibus, sensus rationi & intellectui, sequitur sanguine existente impuro, spiritum turbari, sensus obtundi, rationemque stupescere. Ratio evidentiæ. Sanguinis enim tenuissima pars in cordis fluit fontem, vbi facultas viget vitalis, indeque generati spiritus in cerebri arcem ascendunt, in qui-bus sentiendi mouendique virtus dominatur. Nam vigente spiritu viget motus & sensus. Cacochyma igitur, difficilisque co-ctionis alimenta in sublimium rerum con-templatione versaturo sunt vitanda; crassum enim & prauum sanguinem, unde spiritus turbidi & tenebricosi generant. Qui laboriosum & negotiosum vitæ genus suscepe-runt, peregrinationesque subire coguntur, duri-oribus cibis uti interdum non inconsultum est. Sed ad rem.
units.tr: That there are blood-drinkers, who swallow blood, and indeed human blood, still warm from the man himself, has been shown in chapter 14. Now we must inquire what kind of blood should be taken as food. I shall speak of human blood. All the philosophers and physicians, past and present, have agreed with one voice that blood is, of all the humours, the most temperate and the most familiar to human temperament; that it is the author of all nourishment for the body, a kindly humour, the beloved son of nature, the juice most closely akin to nature. Nature always keeps it, as her most precious treasure, to the very end, even in her greatest purgations. Therefore Marsilio Ficino rightly states, in book 7, chapter 2, of the opinion of physicians, that the state of the blood is almost the same as that of the senses: as the blood is, so are the senses. The reasoning of this view is as follows. Blood is made from food, so the blood must necessarily be of the same quality as the food. Blood serves the spirit, the spirit serves the senses, and the senses serve reason and the intellect. It follows that when the blood is impure, the spirit is disturbed, the senses are dulled, and reason is stupefied. The reason is evident. The finest part of the blood flows to the fountain of the heart, where the vital faculty flourishes, and from there the spirits that are generated rise to the citadel of the brain, where the power of sensing and moving holds sway. For when the spirit is vigorous, motion and sensation are vigorous too. Therefore foods that are corrupt and hard to digest must be avoided by those who devote themselves to the contemplation of lofty things, since they generate thick and bad blood, and from this come turbid and gloomy spirits. Those who have taken up a laborious and busy way of life, and who are compelled to undertake journeys, do well, now and then, to use harder foods. But to return to the matter.

units.la: Cæterum in cibos lautiorum sanguinem præcipuè leporinum, qui Galeni iudicio 3. de aliment. facultatibus, suauissimus est, suillum, qui ad farcimina expetitur, hoedorum, item vervecū & agnorum admitti, notū est: cæterorum animalium raro aut nunquam elegantioris vitæ homines attingūt, nisi sanguinem hirci, caprarū, vel cerui in sartagine tostum aduersus calculum, dysenteriam & toxica, Taurorum & aprorum fibris refertior est, & quia taurorum sanguis celerrime coit, & durefcit, inter potus pestifera recens, praesertim habitus est potus. Hircorū tanta vis praedicatur, vt ferramentorum subtilitas non aliter acrius induretur, scabritia collatur vehementius, quam lima. Quin & inquicta illa vis adamantis, rerum violentiffimarum ferri & ignis contemtrix, hircino sanguine rumpitur, calido ac recenti. Unde remediis aduersus calculum recte admiscent medici.
units.tr: Moreover, it is well known that among the more refined foods the blood most commonly taken is that of the hare, which, in Galen's judgment (book 3, On the Properties of Foods), is the most pleasant; also that of the pig, which is sought for sausages; and that of kids, and likewise of sheep and lambs. Of other animals, people of more elegant life rarely or never touch the blood, except that of the goat, the she-goat or the stag, roasted in a pan, which is used against the stone, dysentery and poisons. The blood of bulls and boars is richer in fibre, and because bulls' blood clots very quickly and hardens, fresh bull's blood has been regarded as a deadly drink, especially as a drink. Such great power is ascribed to goat's blood that the sharpest steel is hardened in it, and the blade is tempered more fiercely than by a file. Indeed, that unconquered force of the diamond, which scorns the most violent things, iron and fire, is broken by goat's blood, if it is warm and fresh. For this reason physicians rightly mix it into remedies against the stone.

units.la: Caprinum celebrauit Homerus: gallinarum quoque & columbarum, & potissimum saginatarum à quibusdam edi compe- rio, qui tum suauitate, tum coctionis facilitate eum commendant : Leporinus cum iecore caeterisque visceribus elixatur. Quocumque autem modo praeparaueris sanguinem, inuenies eum vtplurimum concoctioni contumacem esse & excrementofum. Turrum sanguinis tribus gutturis puero exhibitis, epileptico auxiliari, experimentis indubitatis patefactum est: Vulnerandus autem tem leuiter alter pes est, sanguisque excipiendus. Non conticendum, Hippocratem negare sanguinem esse calidum contra opinionem, rationem affert hanc, quod in animali mortuo calorem non retineat, neat,calidum vero euadere, quod calorem à corde tanquam fonte & foco caloris mutue-tur, spiritūmque beneficio, qui calorem communione quadam sanguini impertit. Grauissimi autoris grauis sententia,& vera, qua quidem omnis sanguis cibo abdican-dus venit, praecipue vero, ex quo farcimina concinnantur, probatur. Conflat san-guinem extra sua vasa effusum atque emis-sum coagulari & putrescere, quod indubita-tum est: Si igitur aliena tantum & non propria etiam caliditate calet, ut Hippocrates vult, extra vero vasa emissus statim putre-scit, quid quaeso[?] aliud est, ex quo hodie far-cimina conflantur, quam quoddam cadauer, sanguisque putridus spiritu & calore destitutus: is vero in alimoniam corporis nostri magna cum auiditate expetitur, animalis, magis famis sedandae, quam naturalis gratiâ, qua quodlibet membrum sibi amicum ac familiare ad se trahit alimentum, inimicum vero auersatur, verum, qua salubritate, iis iudicandum relinquo, qui sanguineis istis farciminibus solis, ventrem probe expleverunt. Quid alimoniae sit in his, nitidiores ventres nondum experiri potuerunt. Sed plura de hoc paradoxo alio loco.
units.tr: Homer praised goat's blood. Blood of hens and pigeons is also eaten by some, especially that of fattened birds, which people commend both for their sweetness and for their ease of digestion. Hare's blood is boiled together with its liver and other entrails. However you prepare blood, you will find that for the most part it resists digestion and is full of excrement. That the blood of a turtle, given to a boy by mouth in three doses, helps the epileptic has been shown by undoubted experiment. One of the boy's feet must be lightly wounded, and the blood collected. We must not pass over the fact that Hippocrates, contrary to common opinion, denies that blood is warm. His reason is that in a dead animal it does not retain heat, and that it becomes warm only because it receives its heat from the heart, as from a fountain and hearth of heat, and through the spirit, which imparts heat to the blood by a kind of communion. The weighty judgment of so weighty an author is true, and it shows that all blood ought to be kept away from food, especially that from which sausages are made. It is established that blood poured and released outside its vessels clots and putrefies, which is beyond doubt. If, then, as Hippocrates maintains, blood is warm only with borrowed and not its own heat, and once it is let out of the vessels it quickly rots, what, I ask, is it that sausages are made from today, other than a kind of corpse, putrid blood deprived of spirit and heat? Yet this is sought with great eagerness as nourishment for our bodies, more for the sake of satisfying appetite than of natural good, by which every member draws to itself the food that is friendly and familiar to it and shuns what is hostile. As to whether it is wholesome, I leave the judgment to those who have filled their bellies well on these blood sausages alone. What nourishment is in them, lean bellies have not yet been able to find out. But more on this paradox in another place.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis, quae veniunt in cibos humanos ex partibus animalium quodam-modo: sequuntur ordine alimenta earum rerum, quæ ab animalibus proveniunt, vt sunt, lac, ova, mel.
units.tr: So far I have dealt with foods which in a certain way come to human tables from parts of animals. In order, the foods that come from animals follow: such as milk, eggs and honey.

units.la: CAP. XX. De Lacte memorabilia.
units.tr: CAP. XX. On the memorable properties of milk.

units.la: Lacte plerasq; vixisse gentes, & hodie quoq; viuere, in confesso est. Gethas, Scy-thas, Nomadas, omnesq; eius tractus, galactophagos, hoc est, lac edentes, alios galacto-potas, hoc est, lactis potores, vocatos, Homerus retulit. Nomadas cynocephalorum lacte viuere Plinius l.6.cap.30. prodidit. Nostrâ memoria satis constat, Belgas, & non paucas septentrionis gentes lacticinijs nihil fere habere in cibis frequentius, ac multa praclara opera lactaria conficere. Et certè mitis, humanaque vita, absq; operis lactarii vsu, nulla dicenda est. Quis ignorat, lac, caseum, & butyrum non rara solum satiare[?], sed etiam vrbium, & nobilitatis elegantiores mensas jucundis & numerosis dapibus exornare. Quare bruti prorsus, stupidi fo-didiq;, palati sunt, qui lactis vsum interdicunt. Verum, quoniam variæ sunt pro diuersorum animantium temperaturâ & natura, tum etiam pabuli alimentiq; varietate, lactis differentia, diligenter inquirendum, quodnam lac optimum, maximeq; nutriat, tum quibus prosit vel obsit, & quo tempore magis conueniat.
units.tr: It is agreed that many peoples have lived on milk, and that many still do today. Homer reported that the Getae, the Scythians, the Nomads and all that region were called galactophagi, that is, milk-eaters, and others galactopotae, that is, milk-drinkers. Pliny (book 6, chapter 30) reported that the Nomads live on the milk of dog-headed men. In our own time it is well established that the Belgians and not a few northern peoples have almost nothing more common in their diet than dairy products, and that they make many excellent dishes from milk. Indeed, a gentle and humane way of life cannot be called such without the use of milk. Who does not know that milk, cheese and butter not only satisfy the poor but also adorn the more refined tables of cities and of the nobility with pleasant and plentiful dishes? So those who forbid the use of milk are utterly brutish, stupid and foul in their palate. However, since milk varies with the temperament and nature of different animals, and also with the variety of their pasture and fodder, one must carefully inquire which milk is best and most nourishing, to whom it is beneficial or harmful, and at what time it is more suitable.

units.la: Sciendum itaq;, præstantissimum omnium, quæ eduntur, succum esse lac, Galeno & Ætio testibus, modo secundum naturam se habeat, minusq; morbidum fit, vitiosum vel virosum, tunc enim sauiora, quam sanguis, symptomata inducit. Constat namq; lac ex sanguine exactissimè coctò in colorem album beneficio glandularum generari, imò cur sanguinem exactiore elaboratione, quam sanguinem, cum coqui, omnem quoq; mutationem in contrariam malo pe-jus abire, omnesq; eius optimas qualitates mutari, & quæ naturaliter optima sunt, contraria ratione præternaturaliter lapsa pejora fieri. Ergo & habiliorem ad corruptionem & putredinem substantiam ipso sanguine ac-quisivit lac, ob exactiorem scilicet & exquisi-tiorem elaborationem & concoctionem, quia fit bonæ vel ex sanguine in venis prius elaborato. Lactis malæ co-autem naturalis ter se habentis & optimi signa & coctio-nota sunt color candidus, vel secundum Aristot.[?] nis signa. ad livorem vergens, odor suauis, sapor dulcis, non salsus, acidus vel amarus, est enim dulcedo lactis peculiaris, substantiâ mediocri & omni ex parte æquali, in ungue hærens & non defluens, non fœtidum quid aut putrilaginem redolente, tum cum probè in ventriculo concoquitur, cuius indicium est, si neq; rursus acidos aut fumidos concitat, præcordiaque & ventriculum non gravat, hæc enim signa, si adfuerint, lactis in ventriculo non probè concoqui arguunt.
units.tr: Know, then, that milk is the most excellent of all the juices that are eaten, according to the witness of Galen and Aëtius, provided it is in its natural state and not diseased, vitiated or poisonous; for then it produces more dangerous symptoms than blood does. For milk is generated from blood that has been most thoroughly cooked into a white colour by the work of the glands. Indeed, since it is cooked with more exact working than blood itself, any change of it turns to something worse, and all its best qualities are altered; and what is naturally best, once it has slipped out of its natural state, becomes worse by the same reasoning. Milk, therefore, has acquired a substance more liable to corruption and putrefaction than blood itself, because of its more exact and refined working and concoction, since it is made from blood that was first well worked in the veins. The signs of good and natural milk, well prepared, are these: a white colour, or one inclining to bluish; a pleasant smell; a sweet taste, not salty, sour or bitter, for milk has a peculiar sweetness of its own; a medium substance, equal in every part, clinging to the fingernail and not running off; no foul smell or smell of putrid matter. And it is properly digested in the stomach when it does not provoke sour belching or fumes, nor weigh down the chest and stomach; for if these signs appear, they show that the milk is not being properly digested in the stomach.

units.la: Nº 4 Huic sententiæ patrocinatur Galenus lib. 1. de sanit.tuen. ubi de lacte nutricis ait, debere id esse bene temperatum, quale certe erit, si sanguis eius, quam optimus sit. Isautem talis est, qui nec flava, nec atra bile, nec serosa aut aquosa abundat substantia. Et paulo post ibidem: Optimum lac est, quod gustanti olfacienti, plane suave aspicienti seu intuenti candidum, et æquale, liquidiq, & crassi medium apparebit, quod vitiosum est, aut crassum, aut caseosum, aut liquidum, aut serosum ac lividum, tum consistentia colore, ipso inæquale videbitur, gu-stantibusq, amarorem, aut salsedinem, aut qua-litatem saltem exhibebit extraneam. Idem l. 7. de morb. curandis bonum lac appellat, quod nullam externam qualitatem odore, vel gustu præ se fert, sed quam dulcissimum est, si-bique ipsi continuum, et prout lacti convenit, splendens, & super omnia, similes habet partes. Hæc Galenus. Caeterum cum probatissimum lac insigni vi nutriendi polleat, perbelleq; alat, usu tamen eius non omnibus æque sit salubris, videndum ulterius, quibus sumpsisse ex usu sit, quibus non. Certum est, si bene concoquatur, nutrire, probosq; humores generare, & dum concoquitur illa attollit & inflat, petitq; caput etiam in sanis, teste Gal. in expositione apho-rism. 64. l. 5. Hipp. Unde, si hoc sanis accidit, quanto magis capite dolen-tibus, vel illa haben-tibus suspensa. In quibusdam etiam acescit, inaliùs euaporat: in ventriculo frigidiore accessit, praecordiaq; flatibus distenditur: in calidiori corpo-ris temperamento aduritur, inq; nidorosos halitus effumat, capitiq; affert grauedinem. Ergo, cum eius natura sit lac, vt calore densescat ac spisse-tur, frigore vero liquescat, fit vt in estuanti sto-macho promtius coaguletur, coagulatum & in grumos conuersum periculosa sepe accidentia excitet, praesertim in faeminis, coagulatio illa nulla re efficacius inhiberi potest, quàm melle vel tum pef-[?]saccharo salisq; momento: Confirmat id Galenus lib. 5. de morbis curandis, his verbis, porro hoc & quid tibi de lactis vsu pro maximo praecepto sit, vt ii quibus eo opus est, omnino id astante animali statim multum bibant etiam melle iniecto, si cui in ventriculo solet, & si ipsum descendere ad alvum citius cupis, etiam sale.
units.tr: No. 4 Galen supports this opinion in book 1 of On Preserving Health, where, speaking of a nurse's milk, he says it ought to be well tempered, as it certainly will be if her blood is as good as possible. Such blood is one that abounds in neither yellow nor black bile, nor in a watery or serous substance. And a little later in the same place: "The best milk is that which, to the taste and smell, is plainly sweet, and which to the eye appears white, even, and of a middle consistency between thin and thick. Milk that is faulty is either thick, or cheesy, or thin, or serous and livid; its consistency and colour will look uneven, and to those who taste it will show a bitterness, or saltiness, or at least some foreign quality." The same Galen, in book 7 of On Curing Diseases, calls good milk that which shows no external quality in smell or taste, but is as sweet as possible, holds together with itself, is shining as milk should be, and above all has parts that are all alike. So far Galen. Yet although the most approved milk has a remarkable power to nourish and feeds very well, its use is not equally wholesome for everyone, and we must consider further for whom it is useful to take it and for whom not. It is certain that, if well digested, it nourishes and generates good humours; and while it is being digested it swells and inflates, and even in healthy people it sends fumes to the head, as Galen testifies in his commentary on Hippocrates' aphorism 64 of book 5. Hence, if this happens to healthy people, how much more so to those who suffer from headaches or who have such complaints. In some people it turns sour, in others it evaporates; in a colder stomach it is curdled and the praecordia are distended with wind; in a warmer bodily temperament it is burnt and gives off fumes of a smoky smell, bringing heaviness to the head. Therefore, since it is the nature of milk to thicken and curdle with heat and to become liquid with cold, it happens that in a hot stomach it coagulates more readily, and once coagulated and turned into clots it often brings on dangerous symptoms, especially in women. This coagulation can be checked by nothing more effectively than by honey or sugar, with a little salt. Galen confirms this in book 5 of On Curing Diseases, in these words: "Moreover, this is the chief precept about the use of milk: those who need it should, while the animal is standing, drink a great deal of it at once, even with honey added, if it usually lies heavy in the stomach; and if you wish it to pass quickly down to the bowels, add a little salt too."

units.la: Quapropter detestandus nobilium quarundam faeminarum adolescentularumq; mos est, quae inter coenae & prandii tempus, vel etiam statim a prandio colostris ac lactis cremore, aliisq; lactariis se infarciunt, vinoq; postea affatim ea perfundere non verentur maximo valetudinis detrimento. Notum est, plurimos ex lacte sic coagulato, eoq; in grumos cocreto strangulari, spirandiq; difficultate, oborto vomitu, opprimi. Vinum enim coagulare facit lac, atque in cafei consistentiam conglobari, quo cum offendatur stomachus, ac inter se repugnantia elaborare nequeat, omnia ad putredinem vergere necesse est, grauiumq; mor-
units.tr: Therefore detestable is the custom of certain noblewomen and young girls, who between dinner and lunch, or even straight after lunch, stuff themselves with colostrum and cream of milk and other dairy foods, and afterwards do not hesitate to drench them freely with wine, to their very great harm to health. It is well known that very many people are strangled by milk coagulated in this way and curdled into clots, and are overwhelmed by difficulty of breathing and by a sudden vomiting. For wine makes milk coagulate and gather into the consistency of cheese; and when the stomach is thus assailed and cannot digest these conflicting things, everything must tend to putrefaction, and the seeds of grave diseases gather together.

units.la: Note: the printed margin notes "coalesce-re." appear beside the last full lines and are part of the same right-margin column. borum seminaria coacervari. Sic pisces & lac, omniaq; acida lactis admixta, vinoq; pfufa fca-biem generant & lepram. Sic enim impro-mifcue ingesta computrescunt, ac corruptioni ef-ficiuntur obnoxia.
units.tr: (marginal note: to coalesce) ...the seeds of these things are heaped together. So fish and milk, and all sour things mixed with milk and drunk with wine, generate scabies and leprosy. For when they are swallowed indiscriminately, they rot and become liable to corruption.

units.la: Colostra fœtantes enixaq; bone quidam gu-la ganeaq; procerus, in delitiis habent, sed nacen-tissimè, adeo ut infantibus etiam triduo à partu lac degustasse maternum perniciosum sit, cùm enim & crassescit in ventre, venaq; ac sanguinis rivos obstruit, ut minus commodè alimenta pof-sint permeare ac distribui. Quæ verò lac coagu-latum dissoluant, multa sunt, præcipua tamen cyminum, angelica, oximel, & acetum scyllitica.
units.tr: Some gluttonous and greedy men of high rank delight in colostrum, the foaming and newly delivered milk, but it is most harmful to them; so much so that it is harmful even for infants to taste their mother's milk within three days of birth. For when it thickens in the belly, it obstructs the veins and the streams of blood, so that the nourishment cannot pass through and be distributed as it should. Many things dissolve milk once it has curdled, but the chief are cumin, angelica, oxymel, and vinegar of squill.

units.la: Lactis porrò differentias ab animalibus sumtas vel ortas opera pretium est hic considera-re. Plinius quodcunque humanum maximè & valentissimè alere prodidit. Verba eius lib. 28. c. 9. placuit subnectere. Maximè autem, inquit, quodcunque humanum alit, mox caprinum, vi-de fortassis fabulæ locum ita nutritum dixere: dulcissimum ab humano Camelinum, efficacissi-mum ex asinis. Magnorum animalium & corporum facilius reddetur. Stomacho accommodatissimum caprinum, quoniam fronde magis quam herba vescuntur.
units.tr: It is worth considering here the differences of milk, according to the animals from which it is taken or in which it arises. Pliny reported which milk nourishes humans most and most powerfully. It pleases me to add his words, from book 28, chapter 9: "Most of all, he says, the milk of whatever animal nourishes humans; next goblin's milk; some have said that from being so fed it has a place in fable; the most pleasant is that of the camel, and the most effective is that of asses. It makes those of large animals and bodies easier to produce. Goat's milk is best suited to the stomach, since goats feed more on leaves than on grass."

units.la: Bubulum medicativum, omnium dulcium & magis alit, stomacho minus utile, quoniam pinguis: omne autem vernum aquatilium esse, & de nomi[illegible, ~3 letters]ellis: Probatissimum vero quod in ungue haeret, nec defluit: Innocentius decoctum praecipuè calculis marinis: alvus maximè solvitur bubulo: minus inflat quodcunque decoctum. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: Cow's milk is medicinal, the sweetest of all and more nourishing, but less useful for the stomach because it is fat. All spring milk, however, is watery, and of the name ... The best is that which clings to the fingernail and does not run off. Innocentius says that decoction is especially useful with sea-stones; the bowels are most loosened by cow's milk; any boiled milk causes less wind. So says Pliny.

units.la: Alii bubulam lac crassissimum & pinguissimum esse volunt, quapropter etiam ocyus in lamacho concrescere ac glaciari, minusque alvo solvendo utile, valentius tamen nutrire: ovillum caprillo crassius habetur, caprillum vero medio habet loco, teste Galeno lib. de bono & malo succo, utrumque tamen pinguitudinis obtinet exiguum, unde & paucum exiis colligitur butyrum.
units.tr: Others wish cow's milk to be the thickest and fattest, for which reason it also curdles and freezes more quickly in the stomach, and is less useful for loosening the bowels, yet it nourishes more strongly. Sheep's milk is considered thicker than goat's, but goat's milk holds a middle place, according to Galen in his book on good and bad juice; both nevertheless have a small amount of fat, and so little butter is gathered from them.

units.la: Alii aliter sentiunt, non certè experti vires & naturam veri & boni lactis. Lubet huc subiicere versus Baptistæ Fierae de lacte, qui sunt eiusmodi, Dulce sapit, subito cur lac putrescit? aquosum est. (uis, Quod praestat? caprae, post? ovis. inde boCui nocuum? capiti, putridis & febribus, ora Inficit & neruos, sed bene pectus alit, Quando bibam? primum cum sugis ab vbere. Somnus Huic (moneo) & motus, mixtaq; mensa nocent. Tot petis? vnum oro, cur in contraria fertur, Et modo lac referat, & modo fluxa tenet. Haec ille,
units.tr: Others think otherwise, though they have certainly not tested the powers and nature of true and good milk. I wish to add here the verses of Baptista Fiera on milk, which run as follows: "It tastes sweet: why does milk turn sour so quickly? Because it is watery. What is its strength, what does it offer? Goat's milk is better than sheep's, after that, cow's. What harms? It harms the head, and those with putrid fevers; it infects the mouth and nerves, but nourishes the chest well. When should I drink it? First, when you suck from the udder. Sleep and movement, and mixing it with food, do it harm (I warn you). You ask so much? I ask one thing: why does it turn in opposite directions, now restoring, now binding the bowels loose?" So he writes.

units.la: Certum est & inconcussum, optimum, lac illud esse, quod in florenti ætate ab animali sano emulgetur, suauibus odoratisq; pascuis enutrito, cum scilicet succis turgent herbæ, ut in vere, medicanturq;, ubera pascuis, ut loquitur Plinius l.2s.c.8. [?] Cum autem omnium horæ sere in herbis sint boues, frondeq; & herba vescantur, sequitur bubulum lac tempore verno præcipuè tamen Maio, in terris verò septentrionem versus sitis, Iunio optimum esse. Cuius sententiæ veritatem ratio ipsa & experientia comprobat, ut nemo opinor, erit, nisi plane ἀλόγος & ratione carens, qui contradicturus sit. Caprarum lac aliàs salubrius. Asininum phthisicis commendant, sed protinus bibendum est nullà interpositâ mora: unde Galenus lib.10.de morb.curand. inducit in ipsum cubiculum asinum subet. Et lib.7. vbi de siccitatum differentiis agit in corpore humano, celeriter, exiccatum & tabidum sanari scribit, si ipse asinam sugeret, id si granaretur, expedire vt quam minimo tempore in aere lac moretur, propterea quod celerrimè mutari sit aptum. Et paulò post ibidem. Acsanè utilissimum lac est, cum ex ipsis mammillis quæ haueserit, veluti Eurypon, Herodotus & Prodicus censent, qui tantum in eò ad corpora reficienda fiduciam habuerunt, ut etiam qui ptisoe tabescerent, ex ipsa mulieris pas-tilla lac sugere iubiret: quod cum pleriq; displi-cat, ceat, asininum ipsis dari conveniet. Hac Galen.
units.tr: It is certain and beyond dispute that the best milk is that which is drawn in the flower of its age from a healthy animal fed on sweet-smelling, fragrant pastures, when the herbs are swollen with juice, as in spring, and the udders are medicated by the pastures, as Pliny says (book 28, chapter 8?). Since cattle spend almost all their hours among herbs and feed on leaves and grass, it follows that cow's milk is best in spring, especially in May, but in lands lying toward the north, in June. Reason itself and experience confirm the truth of this opinion, so that I think no one will contradict it unless he is wholly irrational [ἀλόγος], lacking reason. Goat's milk is otherwise more wholesome. Asses' milk they commend for the consumptive, but it must be drunk at once, with no delay. Hence Galen (On the Treatment of Diseases, book 10) brings the ass into the very bedchamber. And in book 7, where he treats of the varieties of dryness in the human body, he writes that one who is dried up and wasting is quickly cured if he sucks the ass itself; and if the milk is carried, it is expedient that it stay in the air for as short a time as possible, because it is very quick to change. And a little later in the same place: "Indeed milk is most useful when drunk from the very teats themselves, as Eurypon, Herodotus and Prodicus think, who had such confidence in it for restoring bodies that they ordered even those wasting away with phthisis to suck milk from a woman's breast itself. Since this displeases most people, it will be fitting to give them asses' milk instead. Thus Galen." [sic]

units.la: Conferre quoque aliquid & candori mulierum cuti existimantur. Poppæa Domitii Neronis coniux quingentas secum per omnia trahens asinas fœtas asininum nobilitauit, balneorum etiam solio totum corpus illo lacte maceranit, sic candi-dieri cutē extendiq; existimans. Sed longe asinino in pithisi, humanum præstantius est, nam pecu-liariter extenuatis plurimum & frugi alimen-tum confert, corporisq; robur restituit. In expe-rimentis sunt, qui iam tabe & atrophia cofumti solo lacte ex vegeta & florentis mulieris uberibus susto sunt resti uti. Sic Dauid septuagenarius cū senili torpore frigeret, nec pellib. cooperiens inca-lesceret, in speciati decoris puella amplexib° caste condormiuit, vt eius calore robur stomachi soue retur. Equino septentrionis gentes quaedam in cibis & potu viuntur, quod hic meminisse lestore volo, sicut & illud, quod in Ponto fluviu Asiaces ri-gat campos, in quibus pastanigro lacte equa gen-tem alant. Lactaria pulticula, (quæ fiunt ex lacte similagini misto, inq; sartagine decosto, fre-quentissq; cum spatula versato in lenta pruna, s ne sartigini adhærescat, vsq; ad modicam crassi-tudinem, & donec crusta tenui obducatur, ) apud nostratus quasdam fœminas Principes in summis delitiis habentur, sunt enim suauissimi saporis, & odoris, si addatur crocus, optimiq; ac firmi nutrimenti. Sofistratum nullo cibo & potu alio quam lacte toto vita sue curriculo vsum su-isse isse [?] Plutarehus lib.4.Symposiacorum scriptum reliquit.
units.tr: It is also thought to contribute something to the complexion of women's skin. Poppaea, wife of Domitius Nero, brought along five hundred she-asses in foal, made asses' milk famous, and even bathed her whole body in that milk in her bath, thinking this would whiten and smooth the skin. But in phthisis human milk is far superior to asses' milk, for it brings a particularly rich and wholesome nourishment to those who are much emaciated and restores the strength of the body. There are cases of people already consumed by wasting and atrophy who were restored by milk alone, sucked from the breasts of a vigorous and blooming woman. So David, an old man of seventy, when he was chilled by senile torpor and could not warm up even though covered with blankets, slept chastely in the embrace of a girl of remarkable beauty, so that her warmth might foster the strength of his stomach. Certain northern peoples live on horse's milk in food and drink, which I want to mention here, as well as the fact that in Pontus the river Asiaces waters fields where they feed their horse-herds on black milk. Milk porridge (which is made by mixing milk with fine flour, simmering it in a frying pan, and stirring it often with a spatula over a slow fire until it is moderately thick and a thin crust forms) is held in the highest delight by certain noble women among us; for it has a most pleasant taste and smell if saffron is added, and it is of the best and firmest nourishment. Plutarch, in book 4 of the Symposiaca, has left it written that Sostratus lived his whole life on no food or drink other than milk.

units.la: De tribus diuersis lactis partibus, ferosa, caseosa, & butyrosa.
units.tr: On the Three Different Parts of Milk: the Serous, the Caseous, and the Buttery

units.la: TRes in lacte substantias contineri, & praeter has nullam esse quartam, quae lactis nomine designetur, sed totum, quod ex iis tribus legitime temperatis constit, lactis nomen sibi assumere, in confesso est.
units.tr: It is agreed that three substances are contained in milk, and that besides these there is no fourth which is called by the name of milk; rather, the whole that is properly compounded from these three, duly blended, takes the name of milk for itself.

units.la: Serum vnumquodq; lactis genus continet, estq; aquosior & tenuior lactis substantia, à qua caseus, hoc est, crassior & densior pars est separata: graecis ὀρὸς dicitur, quasi separatum à ὁρίζω, id est, findo, sepáro, germ. Molcken. Porro antiquitati celebratissimum semper fuit, obq; vim abstergendi, attenuandi, aluumq; abluendæ ac soluendæ nobilitatum, hodie caprinum in laude magis habet. Estq; serum ipsum tanto melius ac praestantius, quanto lac ipsum melius fuerit. Porro de temperatura seri autores, & inter se & à Galeno dissentire videntur: alii enim calidum, alii frigidum esse contendunt. Galenus lib.4.simpl.medicam. frigidum, libro vero 10. sicut & libro 3.alimentor. calidum id esse asse-rit. Qui serum simpliciter & absolutè idio-tarum tarum more, frigidum pronunciant, crassè hallucinantur. Exploranda enim lactis hic Lac & natura est, quæ in variis eius generibus &dif- ferentiis non est vniufmodi, alterum enim altero frigidius est vel calidius pro temporis sc. pabuli ac foli diuersa cöftitutione. Si itaq; lac & ferum eius dicuntur frigida, non ita ac- cipiendum est, ac fi caliditatis omninò sint expertia, sed quod frigiditas calori præualeat, vel quod eum præ frigiditate habeat imbe-cilliorem. Ioan. Manardus Epist. f. l. 16. lac fe- rumq; eius absolutè frigidum statuit, & tamè idem ibidem fero acrimoniam tribuit, atte- nuandiq; ac detergendi facultatem: quas vi- res inquit, quia lactis tota substantia à ferofis potissimum partibus nanciscitur, minimè mirandum est, fi illis deperditis, simul & vires illæ a lacte in totum fubmoeantur. Quare, pergit, cui ferum ademtum est, ventrem po-tius abstinet quam subducit, & in quantum-uis calido ventriculo ad nidorem non am-plius conuertitur, resolutis fc. non solum fe- rosis partibus, in quibus calor aliquis supra temperamétum inueniebatur, sed & pingui-bus, quæ temperatam habent caliditatem, non autem tantam vt butyrum reddant abso-lutè calidum: Hæc Manardus: ex quibus eui-denter perspicitur, in fero lactis frigiditatem non præpollere, sed calorem potius cum fri-giditate temperatum. Hæc de fero. Cafeum omnem ægrè confici, succosque improbos subministrare, ventriculum flatibus replere, multorum erronea opinio est. Recentes enim laxiores & molliores, ex dul-ci, bono, laudabilíque lacte, butyro non fe-parato, confectos, ac puriores, aliis videlicet succis aut rebus non commixtis, induratis ac veteribus in cibis præferri debere omnia pene consensu traditur. Immodico quoque sale imbuti cafei improbantur, & qui nullo pariter noxii sunt: humore destituti vetusta-teque corrupti, putres quoque vermibusq; scatentes pernitiofiffimi sunt: acriores & ca-lidiores certum est difficulter concoqui. Ve-teres, fi in frequentiorem cibatum admissi fuerint, animæ grauitatem afferre, complu-ribus experimentis percognitum est. Verum facilè ex iis,quæ de lacte fuerunt prodita,iu-dicare est,quinam præstantiores,& qui igno-biliores sint. Operofiffimum enim effero-mnium regionum & tractuum dotes perse-qui. Nominatiffimi sunt hodie,quos mittit Hollandia, Helvetica, Mediolanum, quos placentinos appellant,nec non Weftphalia. Suecia & suos miris effert laudibus, & certe est Parmenfibus parum cedere. In septem-trionis quibusdam tractibus certum est ca-feos in tantam ab incolis molem cogi atque densari,vt vni ferendo vix quatuor robuf-timi bajuli sufficiant. Soli autem ratio pluri-mum mum hic confert.Solum enim graminofissi-mum & restibule, pascuaque generosissi-macaseorum copiam bonitatemq; præbent. Galenus scribit caseum dignosci substantia & gustu,nempe molli vel dura, densa vel la-xa, lenta vel friabili:unde mollem duro, ra-rum & laxum denso præstare ait: gustus quoque certissimus testis est,qui suauitatem nullamq; vehementem & peregrinam qua-litatem in caseo solet deprehendere. Casei quoq; dotes sequenti vetustas comprehen-dit disticho,
units.tr: Whey contains every kind of milk. It is the thinner and more watery substance of milk, from which the cheese, that is the thicker and denser part, is separated. In Greek it is called ὀρός [oros], as if separated from ὁρίζω [horizo], that is, I split or separate; in German it is called Molcken. Moreover, it has always been most celebrated in antiquity, and renowned for its power to cleanse, thin, and loosen and purge the bowels; today goat's whey is more highly praised. Whey is always as much better and more excellent as the milk itself is better. Authors seem to disagree both among themselves and with Galen about the temperature of whey: some contend that it is hot, others that it is cold. Galen, in book 4 of On Simple Medicines, calls it cold, but in book 10, as also in book 3 of On Foods, he says it is hot. Those who simply and absolutely pronounce whey cold, in the manner of laymen, greatly err. For the nature of milk must be examined here, and in its various kinds and differences it is not of one sort; one kind is colder or hotter than another according to the differing constitution of season, pasture and soil. So if milk and its whey are called cold, this is not to be taken as if they were wholly free of heat, but as meaning that their coldness prevails over their heat, or that they have less heat than coldness. Giovanni Manardo, in Epistles, book 16, holds that milk and its whey are absolutely cold, and yet in the same place he ascribes to whey sharpness and the power of thinning and cleansing. He says: "Because the whole substance of milk gets its powers chiefly from its serous parts, it is hardly surprising that if these are lost, those powers are also entirely removed from the milk. Therefore," he goes on, "whoever has had the whey taken away from him rather stops the bowels than loosens them, and in a warm stomach it is no longer turned into a fume, since not only the serous parts, in which some heat was found beyond the balanced mean, are dissolved, but also the fatty parts, which have a tempered warmth, but not so much that they make butter absolutely hot." Thus Manardo. From these words it is plainly seen that the coldness of milk does not predominate in whey, but rather that its heat is tempered with coldness. So much for whey. That all cheese is hard to digest, and supplies bad juices, and fills the stomach with wind, is the erroneous opinion of many. For fresh cheeses, which are softer and looser, made from sweet, good and commendable milk, with the butter not separated out, and purer, that is, not mixed with other juices or substances, are almost universally agreed to be preferable in food to hardened and old ones. Cheeses steeped in excessive salt are disapproved of, and likewise those that are not harmful in any way: destitute of moisture and corrupted by age, they are most pernicious when rotten and teeming with worms; sharper and hotter cheeses are certainly hard to digest. Old cheeses, if admitted into frequent use as food, bring heaviness to the spirit, as has been established by many experiences. Yet it is easy to judge from what has been reported about milk which cheeses are more excellent and which more ignoble. For it would be a laborious task to pursue the virtues of every region and tract. The most renowned today are those sent from Holland, Helvetia, Milan (which they call Placentine), and also Westphalia. Sweden praises its own with wonderful praise, and is certainly not much inferior to Parma. In certain northern tracts it is well known that the inhabitants press their cheeses into such a mass and density that scarcely four very strong porters suffice to carry one. But here the nature of the soil contributes the most. For the most grassy and fertile soil and pastures provide both abundance and goodness of cheese. Galen writes that cheese is judged by its substance and taste, namely whether it is soft or hard, dense or loose, tough or crumbly; hence he says that soft is better than hard, and loose better than dense. Taste too is a most certain witness, which is accustomed to detect in cheese sweetness, and no violent or foreign quality. The old age also sums up the virtues of cheese in the following couplet:

units.la: Non Argus,largus,nó Magdalena,Matuslem[?], Non Abacuc, Lazarus, caseus iste bonus.
units.tr: "Not Argus, not generous, not Magdalene, not Methuselah, not Habakkuk, not Lazarus: this cheese is good."

units.la: hoc est, si non multis oculis lugeat, si non nimium fuerit salsus, si non capillis intrinsecus sordeat, si non nimis vetustus, si non nimis durus,& non fa[?]tens. Ad extre-mum mirum ait esse Plinii lib.ii.c.41. bar-baras gentes, quæ lacte viuant,spreuisse aut ignorasse tot seculis casei dotem. Tradit i-dem Zoroastrem in defertis caseo victitasse annis 20[?]. ita temperato vt vetustatem non sentiret. Sapientes quoque à quibusdam vo-cari repetio,qui à caseo abstinent. Verum extremis epulis parce sumtus parum aut ni-hil negotii faceslit,ventriculum enim sic ro-borat,cibumque vnà digerit.
units.tr: That is, if it does not have too many eyes (holes), if it is not too salty, if its inside is not soiled with hairs, if it is not too old, if it is not too hard, and if it does not stink. Finally, Pliny says in book 2, chapter 41, that it is remarkable that the barbarian peoples who live on milk have for so many centuries disregarded or not known the merit of cheese. The same writer relates that Zoroaster lived for twenty years in the wilderness on cheese, prepared so that it did not taste of age. I also recall that some call wise men those who abstain from cheese. In truth, eaten sparingly at the end of a meal, it causes little trouble, for it strengthens the stomach and helps digest the food along with it.

units.la: Lactis pinguedinem interpretatur buty-tum Rabbi Salomon Prouer.30. Qui exprimitlac , educet butyrum & mel comedet; Deuteron. 32. butyro boum & lacte ouium. Efaiæ 7. butyrum & mel comedet. Hebr. di-citur hæmach à chamam calere, quia semper calet, & nunquam frigescit seu congelatur. Lacti autem demitur pinguedo illa, tundi-turque donec in massam coeat. Plinius la-ctis spumam appellat: quantos in re cibaria & medica præstet vsus, nemini non est no-tum. Est autem butyrum modicè calidum, digerit, nutrit, emollit, laxat & purgat. Edi-tur crudum, adque omnis generis cibos ad-ditur. Belgarum & Septentrionis gentium quarundam laudatissima consuetudo est, mane & ieiuno stomacho butyrum cum pa-ne efficare, omnibusque aliis cibis id præ-mandere. Econtra pernitiose faciunt, qui, postquam impromiscue variis cibis ventré probe infarserunt, tandem butyro quoque eundem aggrauant. Causam huius reiinue-niet æquus lector infra cap. 18. vbi de ordine cibórum ingerendorum prolixius dictum est.
units.tr: Rabbi Solomon, on Proverbs 30, takes the fat of milk to mean butter: "Whoever presses milk will bring forth butter and eat honey" (Prov. 30). Deuteronomy 32: "butter of cows and milk of sheep." Isaiah 7: "he shall eat butter and honey." In Hebrew it is called hæmach [חמאה], from chamam, to be warm, because it is always warm and never grows cold or congeals. That fatness is taken from milk, and it is beaten until it coheres into a mass. Pliny calls it the froth of milk. How greatly it serves as food and medicine is known to everyone. Butter is moderately warm; it digests, nourishes, softens, loosens and purges. It is eaten raw and added to every kind of food. It is a most praiseworthy custom among the Belgians and some northern peoples to eat butter with bread in the morning on an empty stomach, and to eat it before all other foods. On the other hand, those act harmfully who, after they have thoroughly stuffed their bellies with various foods in a mixed way, then weigh them down with butter as well. A fair reader will find the reason for this below, in chapter 18, where the order of foods to be taken is discussed at greater length.

units.la: Hic vnum meminisse lectoré volo, veteres habuisse varia butyri genera, sed pharmaci potius loco quam cibi illis in vsu fuisse, vt non immeritò Plinius butyrum gen-tium barbararum laudatissimum cibum, quique diuites à plebe discerneret, ap-pellarit. pellarit, Et Athenæus, qui in suo conuiuio nullum cibi genus prætériit, butyri nunquam mentionem fecerit. Porro ruffescens & maiale magnificatur, candidum & rancidum virusque redolens damnatur.
units.tr: Here I wish the reader to remember that the ancients had various kinds of butter, but used them as a medicine rather than as a food. So Pliny not unjustly called the butter of the barbarian peoples the most praiseworthy food, one which distinguished the rich from the common people. And Athenaeus, who passed over no kind of food at his banquet, never mentioned butter at all. Furthermore, the reddish and yellowish is praised, while the white and rancid, with its foul smell, is condemned.

units.la: Westphaliæ populi potibus suis butyrum indunt, ac ieiuno bibunt stomacho salubri inuento: alii cum allii capite uno aut altero viridi, vel etiam ruthæ foliis mane aduersus venenorum suspiciones pestilentisque aeris contagia mandunt, nec non ventris animalia. Vires quoque corporis per se cum pane tosto mane comesum conseruat, sed salitum, sic enim in annuos durat usus.
units.tr: The people of Westphalia put butter in their drinks, and drink it on an empty stomach, a wholesome invention. Others chew a head or two of green garlic, or even leaves of rue, in the morning, against suspicions of poisons and the contagions of the pestilential air, and likewise against worms of the belly. Eaten alone in the morning with toasted bread, butter also preserves bodily strength, but it must be salted, for in this way it keeps for a year's use.

units.la: Placentarum quoque innumera genera concinnare norunt pistores dulciarii & matresfamilias, quæ butyro condiuntur uberrime, suntque suauissima & saluberrima gulæ irritamenta probè confecta, alendi enim corporisque vires roborandi vim habent insignem. Liquefactum butyrum atque epotum quidam ad intestinorum ulcerationes commendant, alii in clysteres addunt successu non infelici.
units.tr: Confectioners and housewives also know how to make countless kinds of cakes, which are richly seasoned with butter. They are most pleasant and wholesome stimulants of the appetite when properly made, for they have a remarkable power to nourish and strengthen the body. Some recommend butter melted and drunk for ulcerations of the intestines, and others add it to enemas, not without success.

units.la: Contra sanguisugas potas butyrum teme-dio esse cum aceto ferro calefacto, Plin. au-tor est l.28.c.10. vbi quoq; acetum calefactū per fe venenis aduersari tradit.
units.tr: Pliny says in book 28, chapter 10, that butter drunk is a remedy against leeches when mixed with vinegar heated in an iron vessel. There he also relates that heated vinegar by itself counteracts poisons.

units.la: De butyro Scytharum confecto ex lacte equino digna lectu inueniuntur apud Mer-curialem lib.1. variat. lect. vbi de variis eius generibus apud veteres, vsuque tum in cibo, tum in vngendis corporibus post balneum, olei loco, fit mentio.
units.tr: Remarkable things about butter made from mare's milk among the Scythians are found in Mercurialis, book 1 of his Variae lectiones, where the various kinds of butter among the ancients are discussed, and its use both in food and in anointing the body after bathing, in place of oil.

units.la: Tenuior à butyro separata substantia, dum videlicet lactis pinguedo tufione in massam cogitur, ferum butyri dicitur, germ. Stoßmolcken[?] q. ferum, quod extufione fit, rura vocant Buttermilch[?]/eftiuisq; temporibus haud infalubriter aduersus sitim febriumq; ardores eo vtuntur.
units.tr: The thinner substance separated from the butter, namely when the fat of the milk is pressed into a mass by churning, is called the whey of butter; in German, Stoßmolcken. What is left over from churning, the Germans call Buttermilch, and in summer they use it, not unhelpfully, against thirst and the heat of fevers.

units.la: Sed oxygala,hoc est, lac acidum, plurimi apud veteres aestimatum fuisse reperio. Et Plin.l.11.c.41. scribens, consueuisse barbaras gentes lac in iucundum acorem condensare, & butyrum pingue quod spuma lactis effet, nihil aliud intelligit quam oxygala & aphrogala apud Romanos niue refrigerari foli-tum, testante Galen. 7. meth. Et aphrogala hodie apud multos inter suauissima edulia reputatur. Porro confectionem oxygala do-cet Columella l.12.c.8. cum scribit recipe ol-lam nouam, eamque fundum iuxta terebra-to, deinde surculo cauum obturato, lacteq; ouillo ( ex hoc enim optimum fit) quam recentissimo vas repleto, adiicitoque viridium condimentorum fasciculos, origani, menthę, cepæ, coriandri. Has herbas in lacte demitto, vt ligamenta earum extent. Post diem quintum, quo cauum obturaueras furculum eximito serumq; emittito. Cum deinde lac coeperit manare, eodem surculo cauum obturato, intermissoque triduo, serum iterum emittito, & fasculos condimentorum exemtos adiicito. Deinde exiguum aridi thymi & cunilæ aridæ super lacdistringito concisique sectiui porri quantum satis videbitur adiicito & permisceto : mox intermisso biduo rursus serum emittito, cauumque obtu-rato, ac salis triti quantum satis erit, adiicito & misceto. Operculo deinde imposito & oblito non ante aperueris quam vsus exe-gerit. Plinius l.28.c.9. oxygalæ mentionem faciens, scribit, fieri ex acido lacte in recens quod acescere velit, addito, stomachoque id utilissimum esse: Et cap. eod. quod maxime coactum est, in summo fluitat, id exemtum sale addito appellatur oxygala, reliqua decoquunt in ollis, ibi quod supernatat, butyrum est oleosum naturâ. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: But I find that oxygala, that is, sour milk, was highly esteemed by many among the ancients. Pliny, book 11, chapter 41, writing that barbarian peoples were accustomed to thicken milk into a pleasant sourness, and that the fat butter which was the froth of milk, understands nothing other than oxygala and aphrogala, which among the Romans were customarily cooled in snow, as Galen attests in book 7 of his Method. Today aphrogala is counted among the most delicious foods by many. Moreover, Columella, book 12, chapter 8, teaches how to make oxygala, when he writes: "Take a new pot, bore a hole near the bottom, and plug the hollow with a twig. Fill the vessel with the freshest milk, preferably ewe's milk, since this is the best. Add small bundles of green seasonings: oregano, mint, onion, coriander. I put these herbs into the milk so that their stalks stick out. After the fifth day, when you have plugged the hollow, remove the twig and let the whey run out. Then, when the milk begins to flow, plug the hollow again with the same twig, and after an interval of three days let the whey run out again, and add the bundles of seasonings you took out. Then add a little dried thyme and dried cunila over the milk, and add chopped leek as much as seems enough, and mix it. Soon, after an interval of two days, let the whey run out again, plug the hollow, add and mix as much ground salt as is enough. Then put on a lid, seal it, and do not open it until use requires." Pliny, book 28, chapter 9, mentioning oxygala, writes that it is made by adding to fresh milk that is about to turn sour, and that it is most useful for the stomach. And in the same chapter: what has been most thickened floats on top; this, with salt added, is called oxygala; the rest they boil in pots, and what floats on that is oily butter by nature. So Pliny. Recent medicine has proved by indubitable experiments that oxygala is a great aid in heat, for tempering the inner fevers and the burning of pestilential fevers.

units.la: Magno autem oxygala esse auxilio in ca-loribus ad temperandos internos æstus febriumque ardores pestilentes, indubitatis experimentis recentior medicina compro-bauit. bauit. Aphrogala verò,flos,cremor feuspu-ma lactis,quantam æstate inprimis gratiam Pomeridianis epulis, atque etiam in cœnis fecunda mensa obtinuerit,miscentibus huic nobilibus fœminis humi nascentia fraga facchariq;[?] pollinem (Sic enim innocentio-rem esse vsum eius comperserunt) nemini nonest notum, nisi omnium salubrium re-rum ignaro.
units.tr: Aphrogala, the flower, the cream or froth of milk, which during summer especially holds great favour at afternoon meals and even at banquets on the abundant table, when noble women mix with it wild strawberries growing on the ground and sugar powder (for they have found that this use is more harmless), is known to everyone, except to someone ignorant of all wholesome things.

units.la: De ouis.
units.tr: On eggs.

units.la: NVllum esse alimentum, quod æquè in ægritudine alat,neque oneret, si-militerque vim ac cibi vsum habeat, quam ouum,Plinius lib.29. cap. 3. prodidit. Quemadmodum enim lac quadrupedum sanguis est percoctus, sic ouum est sanguis auium femine[?] conspersus, nutritioni vber-rimè accommodatus. Verum Hippocra-tes lib.de diæta ob nutrimenti dissimilitudi-nem ouum admodum videtur improbare. Naturam enim vitellus & albumen habent contrariam, non colore tantum, sed virtute etiam. Vitellus enim temperatus est, faci-lius concoquitur, magis humet, frigoreque spissatur, album contra frigidius est, & cras-siusac igne spissatur, cum vitellus mollis persistat, magisque in aqua feruente quam ad ignem coquatur atq; induretur. Sed hoc incommodum facile tollitur, si reiiciatur, vel cocturæ, in qua summa differentia est, dili-gens habeatur ratio. Infinitis enim modis culinæ oua parant, sed apparatus non raro euadunt pestilentes ob aliorum societatem & mixturam, vt alibi quoque notatum est.
units.tr: Pliny (Book 29, chapter 3) has declared that there is no food which nourishes the sick equally well without burdening them, if it is similarly strong and taken as food, as the egg. For just as milk is the blood of four-footed animals, cooked down, so the egg is the blood of birds, mixed with the seed of the female, and very well suited to nourishment. Yet Hippocrates, in his book On Diet, seems to disapprove of eggs quite strongly because of the unlikeness of their nourishment. For the yolk and the white have opposite natures, not only in colour but also in their power. The yolk is temperate, is digested more easily, is more moist, and is thickened by cold. The white, on the other hand, is colder and thicker, and is thickened by fire, while the yolk stays soft and is cooked and hardened more in boiling water than over a fire. But this drawback is easily removed if careful attention is paid to rejecting the eggs, or to the cooking, in which the greatest difference lies. For cooks prepare eggs in endless ways, but the dishes often turn out unwholesome because of the mixing and combining of other ingredients, as has been noted elsewhere.

units.la: Modice cocta, seu mediocrem consistentiâ per coctuvam adepta, qualia sunt tremula & mollia, græc. τροφιμα[?], eademque recentia, quemadmodum omnium consensu excel-lentissimè alunt, cæterisq; in virium restau-ratione præstant, ita econtra ἐψηθα[?] dicta, id est, ad indurationem cocta, difficulter pe-fi-ciuntur, crassumq; præbent nutrimentum; q vero in vniuersum cocta sunt, ἀψυχικά[?] græc. cibis abdicata sunt, quamuis sordidi quibusdam palati hominibus ea in astiuis a-cetariis maximè placere sciam non sine valetudinis iactura, & bruto plane appetitu. Sorbilia & ἐυφθαρτα[?] vix parantur calida, vtiliter-que in faucium gutturisque morbis forben-tur, aliquò quoq; probè molliunt, sed propter celerem descensum minus nutriunt: in ventre verò calidiore impuriore q; iusto diutius retenta facilimè alterantur inq; nocentissima vertitur bile, quare in his deglutiendis cau-tio obseruanda est, facilimè enim febrim accendunt, q; ipse voluptatis magis q vtilitatis gratiâ aliquado bina sic absorbes expt sum, idque idq; nullam ob aliam euenire causam verí- simile est, quam ex duabus repugnantibus naturis per coćturam non vnitis & contem- peratis,sed maximam adhuc partem crudis, Vnde celebriores quidam Practici oua fe- bricitantibus,vt omnino pernitiofa interdi- cunt, nouum enim inde febri fomentum suppeditari rectè sibi persuasum habent.
units.tr: Eggs that are lightly cooked, or that have reached a moderate consistency through soft boiling, such as those that are wobbly and soft, in Greek nourishing [τροφιμα], and fresh ones too, are, by general agreement, the most excellent nourishment and are outstanding for restoring strength. On the contrary, eggs called boiled [ἐψηθα], that is, cooked until hard, are difficult to digest and give a thick nourishment. Those that are cooked through and through are rejected as lifeless [ἀψυχικά] by the Greeks, although I know that some men of dull palate are very fond of them in summer salads, not without loss of health and with a plainly brutish appetite. Soups and easily dissolved [ἐυφθαρτα] dishes are hardly prepared hot, and they are usefully swallowed in diseases of the throat and gullet. They also soften somewhat, but because they pass down quickly they nourish less. In a warmer stomach, and one more foul than is right, where they are retained too long, they very easily change and turn into the most harmful bile. So caution must be observed in swallowing them, for they very easily kindle fever. Someone who has sometimes gulped down two eggs of this kind, for the sake of pleasure rather than usefulness, probably did so for no other reason than that two opposing natures had not been united and tempered by cooking, but were still for the most part raw. That is why certain more famous practitioners forbid eggs entirely to those suffering from fever, being firmly persuaded that they supply a new fuel for the fever.

units.la: In cineribus præterea assa,frixa,vel in sartagine coćta & rotundata improbantur.Suf- focata à veteribus celebrata reperio, græc. τυκτά,quæ sc. rupto putamine in patinam, in qua butyrum fit liquatum, coniecta co- quuntur prunis subditis,igne molli & conti- nente,donec vitelli in mediâ coeant, albu- mina autè circûdent, feq; in oras constituãt.
units.tr: Moreover, eggs roasted in ashes, fried, or cooked in a frying pan and turned over are disapproved of. I find that the eggs called smothered [τυκτά] were famous among the ancients. These are cooked by breaking the shell into a dish in which butter has been melted, and placing it over embers, with a gentle and steady fire, until the yolks come together in the middle while the whites surround them and settle at the edges.

units.la: Hæc Græcos Medicos oleo garoq; & vino conspergenda esse,censuisse reperio, fri- xisq; assis ac elixis vtiliora promisisse,sed a- liter tamen præparasse. vbi notandum, per- petuò moderatam in iis coćtionem obser- uandam esse. Vetustate vel incubatu magna ex parte deprauata virosa sunt & pessima, nec fine magna edentis ruina edi possunt.
units.tr: I find that the Greek physicians thought these eggs should be sprinkled with oil, garum and wine, and they promised that fried, roasted and boiled eggs were more useful, but prepared them differently. Here it should be noted that the cooking must always be kept moderate. Eggs that have become old or have been left to incubate are for the most part spoiled, poisonous and very bad, and they cannot be eaten without serious harm to the eater.

units.la: Ad extremum, licet multarum, imò feré omnium auium oua sint esculenta, nulla tamen magis frequentiusq; rem cibariam adiuuant quam gallinarum, hodieq; gallinarum Indicarum oua mirifice commendari coepe- runt,cætera vixà vita lautiori attinguntur, nisi vel voluptatis gratia vel in aliorum penuria, ut anserina, anatumque, quæ, licet minus probè nutriant, quam gallinacea, naturam tamen confortant, Veneremq; prori-tant experimento.
units.tr: Finally, although the eggs of many, indeed nearly all, birds are edible, none helps food more frequently than those of hens. Today the eggs of Indian hens have also begun to be wonderfully recommended. Other eggs are hardly used in a refined diet, except for pleasure or when other food is scarce, such as goose and duck eggs. Though these nourish less well than those of hens, they strengthen the body and, as experience shows, stir up desire.

units.la: De melle apum notatu digna.
units.tr: On the honey of bees, worth noting.

units.la: Non minorem esse mellis in esculentis auctoritatem atque præstantiam quam sacchari, ex multis omniq; ex parte homini utilissimis viribus atque dotibus, quas à natura obtinuit, manifestum est. Quin & veteribus in maximis fuisse deliciis, ut qui innumera escarum genera melle condiebant, multaque ex eo panificia ac potus concinnabant, in confesso est. Id quod hodie quoq; Septentrionis Sarmatiæque populi in Moscouia, Lithuania, terrilque vicinis factitant, uberrimus enim laudatissimi mellis apud eos proventus est, quod apum mellificio ex floribus myricæ, thymi, aliarumque arborum ac herbarum succo in aluearibus elaboratur, nec non in syluis in arborum cauis atque petris etiam copiosissime colligitur, quod mel syluestre propterea vocant. Laudatissimum autem ac optimum præter quod Hymettus Atticæ regionis mons profert, in nominatis Sarmatiæ regionibus provenire testatur nobile illud ac
units.tr: It is clear that honey is no less valuable and excellent among foods than sugar, on account of the many powers and qualities it has received from nature, which are in every way most useful to man. Indeed, it is agreed that honey was a great delight to the ancients as well, since they seasoned countless kinds of food with it and prepared many breads and drinks from it. The peoples of the north and of Sarmatia do the same today in Muscovy, Lithuania and the neighbouring lands, for their yield of very praised honey is abundant. This is made by bees in their hives from the juice of the flowers of the bog myrtle, of thyme and of other trees and herbs, and it is also gathered very plentifully in the woods, in hollows of trees and in rocks; for this reason they call it wild honey. The most praised and best honey, besides that which the mountain Hymettus in the region of Attica produces, is said by that famous and very celebrated mead to be found in the aforementioned regions of Sarmatia. It is sought after so eagerly by everyone that it is exported to other places.

units.la: celebratissimum hydromel, quod tantopere ab omnibus expetitur, indeque in alia loca exportatur. Nam in tanto apud Moscovitas, vicinarumque terrarum Proceres honore est, vt generosis vinis etiam praferrenon vereantur, peregreque aduentantibus missisque legatis etiamnunc felicis ominis aduentúsque ergo plenis id propinent cyathis, & quidem prima statim mensa.
units.tr: For it is held in such honour among the Muscovites and the nobles of the neighbouring lands that they do not hesitate to prefer it even to noble wines. When envoys arrive from abroad, they still drink to them, for good omen and a happy arrival, in full cups, and indeed at the very first course of the meal.

units.la: Porro mel τεοφιμόν esse, corporisque Columell. l. 12. scribit, exanimum corpus hominis per annos plurimos inoxium conseruare. Et Plin. referr, Principatu Claudii se vidisse Hippocentaurum in Thessalia natu, ex Ægypto ad Imperatorem in melle allatu. Ante vero Plin. Xenophon in S. rerum græc. morem quandoque sepeliendi mortuos in melle, ut conseruarentur, extitisse tradidit, quod in 3. Lucret. intellexisse putatur, cum scribit, [?]Aut in melle situm suffocari atq; rigere Frigore, cum in summo gelidi cubat æquore saxi. Insigne quoque exemplum est 1. Sam. 14. quoprobatur mellis utilitas in viribus reficiendis & restaurandis. Cum enim Saul in bello, quod gessit contra Palæstinos graui edicto prohibuisset militibus ante vesperam & partam victoriam cibum ullum capere, Jonathan edicti illius ignarus fame impulsus mel quod in sylua quadam decurrebat, cæteris ab eo abstinentibus, degustauit, cuius esu oculi eius fuerunt illuminati, hoc est totius corporis vires inedia fractæ ac debilitate fuerunt instauratæ. Nam ut inedia oculi exiccantur atque excæcantur & caligant, ita cibo reficiuntur ac q. illuminantur. Est in exemplis Poll' ò Romulus, qui excedes annu centesimu, cu ab Aug. Imp. interrogaret, quana ratione maxime vigore illu animi corporisq; conseruasset, respondit, intus mulso, foris oleo. DeDemocritus quoque Abderides senex,[?] interrogatus, quanam ratione quispiam sane degeret, respondit, si interiora melle, exteriora oleo madefierent, melle enim ipsum plurimum delectatum tradunt, sicut & Pythagoram, qui cum frugalissime viveret, solo sæpe melle fuit contentus.
units.tr: Furthermore, Columella in Book 12 writes that honey is life-preserving [τεοφιμόν] and keeps a lifeless human body harmless for very many years. Pliny reports that in the reign of Claudius he himself saw a Hippocentaur, a dwarf from Thessaly, brought from Egypt to the Emperor in honey. Earlier, Xenophon in his Greek Affairs (Hellenica) recorded that there was once a custom of burying the dead in honey so that they would be preserved. It is thought that Lucretius in Book 3 also had this in mind when he writes: "Or lying in honey they are suffocated and stiffen with cold, when they lie on the surface of a cold rock." There is also a notable example in 1 Samuel 14, which shows the usefulness of honey in restoring and renewing strength. For when Saul in war against the Philistines had strictly forbidden the soldiers to take any food before evening and until victory was won, Jonathan, ignorant of that order, was driven by hunger and tasted some honey that was dripping in a certain wood, while the others abstained from it. By eating it his eyes were enlightened, that is, the strength of his whole body, broken by lack of food, was restored and revived. For just as the eyes dry up, go blind and grow dim through hunger, so they are refreshed and brightened by food. There is also an example in Pollio Romulus, who, having passed a hundred years, was asked by the Emperor Augustus by what method he had preserved the vigour of both his mind and body most of all. He replied: "Mead inside, oil outside." Democritus of Abdera, too, when asked in old age how one might live in good health, replied that if the inside were moistened with honey and the outside with oil. They report that Democritus took great delight in honey itself, as did Pythagoras, who, though he lived most frugally, was often content with honey alone.

units.la: Cyrnios Sardiniam incolentes ideo diutius viuere quidam tradiderunt, quod ipsis mel perpetuum erat escarium. Valleriola in locis suis comm.l.3. melle, ob detergendi calefaciendiq; potestatem insignem, lenibus plurimo utendum consulit, si modo illæsam lenectam in multum æui producere velint, idque probat Antiochi Medici & Telephi Grammatici exemplo, qui senes annosi, attico melle & pane plurimum vtebantur, Gal.f.de sanctuenda teste. Quin & ipse Saluator Christus à mellis usu non abstinuit, testatur enim Lucas spectantibus post resurrectionem discipulis ipsum de mellis suo comedisse, non quidem φυσικῶς, ut inquit Theophylactus, cibo enim non amplius indigebat, sed οἰκονομικῶς, nempe resurrectionis, & veri sui corporis confirmandi gratia. Non omittendum autem in hac de melle historia, Eudoxum Cindium apud Apollonium referre, in Aphrica quandam gentem esse, quæ supra Syrtes & Chartaginem incolat,gyzanteres vocatam, hancque exercere artem, ut flores in istis locis colligat, melque ex iis ea copia & qualitate con-ficiat, ut apum æquet mellificium. Mellis quoque boni vel mali indicia minime prætereunda sunt: judicatur autem optimum, suave, acre, flavum, odoratum, modiceque pingue & tenue, vernum & æstivum. Plinius scriptor inter latinos gravissimus lib. II. ca. 14. sensisse videtur, optimum mel Sirio exoriente produci, & proculdubio ex Aristotelis sententia, nam, ut Mercurialis l. 2. variarum lectionum notavit, in vetustissimo Scipionis Carteromachi codice scriptu reperitur, mel maxime tunc ab aere cadere, cum inter astra Sirius exoritur: eo namque tempore ardere terram, siccitatesque maiores instare, unde roris mellei ubertas generetur, nemo ignorat: ut ita consequens sit mellis proventum maxime præmonstrare summas siccitates, in quibus maior mellis copia super herbas, quas depascuntur apes, abundare deprehenditur. Idem Plin. maxi-me laudabile mel esse scribit quod per se fluit ut oleum. Galenus 7. de morb. curand. optimi mellis indicia esse ait, si colore flavo est, odore suavi, tum purum adeo, ut totum pelluceat, gustantique acutum, jucundissimumque, tamque sibi cohærens, ut si digito attollatur, continuum sibi nec intercisum ad humum defluat. Despumatum quoque minus excrementosum esse, frigido ventriculo optimum nutrimentum, magisque nutrire idem asserit lib. eodem. Crudum enim aluum inflare tuffimq; lacessere deprehensum est. Coquendum est autem supra pru-nas aut arida ligna sine fumo, ac probè despumandum. Unde tutior etiam eius in medicinis est usus, medicique ad occurrendum corruptionibus, putredinemq; compescen-dam in mellis usu sunt audaciores.
units.tr: Some have written that the Corsicans and Sardinians lived longer because they always had honey as their food. Valleriola, in his commentary on the places in his Book 3, advises that those who wish to prolong an unimpaired old age to a great length should use plenty of honey for its special power to cleanse and warm, provided it is mild. He proves this by the example of Antiochus the physician and Telephus the grammarian, aged men who used a great deal of Attic honey and bread. Galen, On Preserving Health, is a witness to this. Indeed, the Saviour Christ himself did not abstain from the use of honey, for Luke testifies that after the resurrection, while the disciples looked on, he ate of a piece of honeycomb. He did this not naturally [φυσικῶς], as Theophylact says, for he no longer needed food, but economically [οἰκονομικῶς], that is, to confirm the reality of his resurrection and of his true body. In this history of honey it should not be left out that Eudoxus of Cnidus, in Apollonius, reports that in Africa there is a certain people living beyond the Syrtes and Carthage, called Gyzanteres. They practise the craft of gathering flowers in those places and make honey from them in such quantity and quality that it rivals the honey-making of bees. The signs of good and bad honey must also not be passed over. Honey is judged best when it is sweet, sharp, yellow, fragrant, moderately thick and thin, and made in spring or summer. Pliny, the most serious of the Latin writers, Book 2, chapter 14, seems to have held that the best honey is produced when Sirius rises. Undoubtedly he follows the opinion of Aristotle, for, as Mercurialis noted in Book 2 of his Various Readings, it is found written in the very ancient codex of Scipio Carteromachus that honey falls from the air most of all when Sirius rises among the stars. For at that time the earth burns and greater droughts threaten, whence the abundance of honey-dew is produced, as nobody is unaware. It follows that the yield of honey especially points to the greatest droughts, in which a greater quantity of honey is found to abound on the herbs that the bees feed upon. Pliny also writes that the most praiseworthy honey is that which flows of its own accord, like oil. Galen, in Book 7 of On the Curing of Diseases, says that the signs of the best honey are these: it is yellow in colour, sweet in smell, so pure that it is clear right through, sharp and most pleasant to taste, and so cohesive that when lifted with a finger it falls to the ground in one continuous thread without breaking. He also says in the same book that skimmed honey is less full of waste matter, and is the best nourishment for a cold stomach, and nourishes more. For raw honey has been found to inflate the belly and to irritate the cough. It should be cooked over hot embers or dry wood without smoke, and carefully skimmed. For this reason its use in medicines is safer, and physicians are bolder in using honey to oppose corruption and to check putrefaction.

units.la: Ad extremum non ignorandum, esse adhuc alia duo mellis genera, unum Saccharum vocatum Indi, quod India fert & Arabia, mel videlicet in arundinib. concretum gummi aut salis modo candidum ac fri-abile, unde Megasthenes graecus Indiam mel, sine apum opificio gignere tradit: alterum ab aeris rore ἀέρομελι [?] id est mel roscidum aut aerium, ab hebr. manna, latin. ros Syriacus dicitur, quoniam interdiu sublato aestiui solis vapore in aera, qui tandem serenae noctis frigore concretus, in Syria & monte Libani, Neapolis, in Oenotria campo, ac Calabria, ante lucano tempore supra saxa, aut laricis arboris, aut thymi, aliarumq; plantarum folia destillat, id collectum inq; mafam globulose effictum ad vsum seponitur. De hoc plura legantur apud Galenum, 3.de alim.& 4. de comp.med. secundum lo-ca:Athen.l 11.
units.tr: Finally, it should not be overlooked that there are two other kinds of honey.
