One is called Indian sugar (saccharum), which India and Arabia produce: honey that hardens in the reeds, white and friable like gum or salt. This is why Megasthenes the Greek writes that India produces honey without the work of bees. The other is aerial honey from the dew of the air, aeromeli [ἀέρομελι], that is, dewy or airy honey, called manna in Hebrew and ros in Syriac. During the day the summer sun's heat draws moisture up into the air, and when this is condensed by the cold of a clear night, it drips before dawn in Syria and on Mount Lebanon, at Naples, in the plain of Oenotria and in Calabria, onto rocks or the leaves of the larch, thyme and other plants. It is gathered, shaped into small round masses, and kept aside for use. More on this may be read in Galen, On Foods, book 3, and On Compound Medicines, book 4, in the passages indicated, and in Athenaeus, book 11.

units.la: Sardiniam, quod praeterire nefas est, ex apum absinthii pabulo mel amarum, Hera-cleam vero ponti ob herbas noxias vi ulen-tum proferre autores non protarii tradunt: mellis autem ita venenati indicia esse, si omnino non densatur, si color magis rutilus est, odoralienus, sternutamenta protinus mouens, quod ponderosius innoxio, & qui ederunt si humi se abiiciunt quaerentes re-frigerationem, Plin.li.21.c.13. scriptum reliquit, vbi quoq; remedium mellis venenati aitcile[?] multum vetus e melle optimo & rutha, salsamenta[?] etiam crebro sumta.
units.tr: Sardinia, which it would be wrong to pass over, produces bitter honey from bees feeding on wormwood. Authors who are not unreliable report that Heraclea on the Pontus produces violently poisonous honey because of its harmful herbs. The signs of such poisoned honey are these: it does not thicken at all, its colour is rather reddish, its smell is strange, and it at once provokes sneezing. Honey that is heavier and harmless does not do this. Those who eat it throw themselves down on the ground, seeking cooling. Pliny wrote of this in book 21, chapter 13, where he also gives a remedy for poisoned honey: a great deal of old honey of the best quality and rue, and salted foods also often eaten. Plin. lib. 21. cap. 13.

units.la: Hactenus de varius cibis & alimentis ad vitam prorogandam conferuandamque ne-ceflariis[?].
units.tr: Thus far on the various foods and nourishments necessary for prolonging and preserving life.

units.la: CAP. XXI. De Condimentis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI. On Condiments.

units.la: Optimum cibi condimentum esse famem, potionis sitim, Cicero l.1.de finibus scribit: Et certe melius habent, qui ita simpliciter cibos suos condiunt, quam qui saccharo, pipere vel garyo-phyllis, sine quibus millia gentium eleganter & feliciter vixerunt ac etiamnunc de-gunt. Sunt enim Condimenta aliud nihil quam gulæ irritamenta, quæ ad condi-enda obsonia fiunt, græcis ὀψύσματα[?] dicta & ἀρτύματα. Varia autem olim fuisse condimentorum genera in confesso est, ut garum, muriam, oxigarum, finapidium, &c. Verum singula ea pertractare immensum foret, præcipua saltem, quæque in vita humana magis necessaria, quorumque vires compertæ habentur, attingam, qualiasunt sal, mel, saccharum, acetum.
units.tr: Cicero, in book 1 of On Ends, writes that the best condiment for food is hunger, and for drink, thirst. Certainly those people fare better who season their food in such a plain way than those who use sugar, pepper or cloves, without which thousands of peoples have lived, and still live, elegantly and happily. Condiments are nothing other than irritants of the palate, made to season dishes, called opsysmata and artymata by the Greeks [ὀψύσματα, ἀρτύματα]. It is agreed that there were formerly many kinds of condiment, such as fish sauce (garum), brine (muria), vinegar-and-fish-sauce (oxygarum), mustard, and so on. To treat each of them individually would be an immense task, so I will touch only on the chief ones, and those which are more necessary in human life and whose powers are known: salt, honey, sugar and vinegar.

units.la: De Sale notatu & lectu dignissima.
units.tr: On Salt, most worthy of notice and reading.

units.la: PRincipem inter condimenta locum merito obtinet Sal, ut, sine quo vita humanior degere non possit, adeoq; ut ait Plin. l.3o.c.7. necessarium elementum sit, ut transierit intellectus ad voluptates nimi quoque: nam ita sales appellantur, omnisque vitæ lepos & summa hilaritas laborumque requies non alio magis vocabulo constat, unde etiam gratiarum nomen salibus à nonnullis impositum videtur, eo quod sales in suavitatem, cibi necessitatem convertant.
units.tr: Salt rightly holds the first place among condiments, since without it human life could not be lived in a civilised way. Pliny (book 31, chapter 7) says it is a necessary element, so much so that the mind passes over even to pleasures; for salts (sales) are so called, and all the charm of life, the highest cheerfulness and rest from labours, are not expressed by any other word. Hence some think the name of the Graces was also given from salts, because salts turn the necessity of food into pleasure.

units.la: Cum igitur Sale & Sole, eodem teste, utilius corporibus nihil sit, adq; excitan-dum sopitum ac deperditum cibariorum saporem, ac putredinem arcendā, ac diuturniorem carnium piscniumque inprimis conservationem Sal praecipue conferat, & in universum memorandos mortalibus praestet usus, merito condimentum iucundissimum, atque adeo obsoniorum & condimentorum obsonium ac condimentum, quibus suavitatem conciliat, censebitur.
units.tr: Since, as the same authority says, nothing is more useful to bodies than salt and the sun, and since salt above all serves to rouse the dulled and lost savour of foods, to ward off putrefaction, and especially to preserve meats and fish for longer, and since it offers many uses to mortals in general, it will rightly be counted the most pleasing condiment, and indeed the seasoning of seasonings and condiments, since it gives them their agreeableness.

units.la: Quare fatui & insulsi plane sunt, qui à sale abstinent, insulsoque pane utuntur & cibo, quod de sacerdotibus Ægyptiis Plutarchus 5. sympos. probl. 10. prodidit, ii enim à salis usu omnino abstinuerunt, forsan ob hanc causam, ut Lemnius quoque l. 2. ca. 36. de nat. miracul. notavit, quod Venerem irritare persuasum haberent: quapropter insipida potius sumenda existimabant, quam condimento omnium vulgatissimo uti & iucundissimo. Sed an satis valetudini consu-luerint, (cum à corporibus hominum pu-trilaginem sal arceat, humores alienos excrementitiosque absorbeat, ac esculenta quaevis sapida reddat gustuique grata) dici non potest, sed potius nimis superstitiosè id eos observasse statuendum est. Adde quod foecunditatem conferat, seu foecunditatis progignendaeque sobolis, atque sterilitatis expugnandae vis sali insit, praeter experientiam eruditiores quosdam literis mandasse, certis enim rationibus persuasum habent, muli-
units.tr: Those people are plainly foolish and insipid who abstain from salt and eat unsalted bread and food. Plutarch (Symposiacs, book 5, question 10) reports this of the Egyptian priests, who abstained entirely from the use of salt. Perhaps this was for the reason that Lemnius also noted (book 2, chapter 36, On the Nature of Miracles): they were persuaded that salt stirs up desire. For this reason they thought it better to take things unseasoned than to use the most common and most agreeable of all condiments. But whether they took sufficient care of their health (since salt keeps putrefaction away from human bodies, soaks up foreign and excrementitious humours, and makes every food savoury and pleasant to taste) cannot be said; it must rather be held that they observed this too superstitiously. Add that salt has a power to promote fertility, or to bring about the increase of offspring and to overcome barrenness. Apart from experience, certain more learned men have committed this to writing, for they are persuaded by definite reasons that

units.la: mulieres obesas, quae magna ex parte sunt steriles & effœtæ moderato falis in cibis vsu fœcundas fieri conceptuiq; idoneas, abstergere enim sic omnem vliginem, matricemque plus iusto vdam madidamque exiccate, efficereque vt genitale semen firmius vtero adhærescat: Viris quoq; tentiginem mouere lumbofq; excitare, testantur populi salitis tum carnibus tum piscibus marinis crebrius vtentes, idq; nullam aliam ob causam eue-nire affirmant quam mordacis caliditatis ratione. Accedit & illud fœcunditatis indu-cendæ argumentum, quod immensa vis mu-rium in marinis nauibus soleat procreari, & quod mulieres salinariæ continenter pruri-ant, multarumq; prolium sint feraces. Hinc quoque in nonnullis regionibus coloniiu-mentorum pabulo nonnihil inspergunt sa-lis, quo sint ad cibum auidiores, gignendũq; magis alacres & erecti: agros deniq; steriles, vbi plus æquo palustres sint & vliginosi fe-races effici illius conspersu experientia compertum habetur. Exiccandi au-tem, abstergendi, corporaque nimia humiditate luxuriantia à putredine con-feruandi, in sale vis vel hoc vno quoq; illu-strior euadit, quod cum Ægyptii plures ha-berent modos, quibus mortuos à putredine conseruarent immunes, primus tamen om-nium atq; etiam frequentius vsurpatus fuit, qui solo constabat sale, unde etiam merito condire corpora dicebatur salire, & condita πεπυχευμένα[?], ut notavit Merc.l.3.variar. lect.c.2.Idem Plutarchi sententiam iuste e- mendat in quest.nat.de carnib.salib.afferen-tis sal & salsa ad pinguefacienda corpora maxime valere, cum sal extenuandi potius quam craffefaciendi facultate praeditum esse experientia comprobet, dulcia vero plus in corporibus craffefaciendis valere, falsorum autem usum esse, sua siccitate aperiendique vi alimentum ad partes nutriendas perferre.
units.tr: women who are fat, and who for the most part are barren and worn out, become fertile and fit for conception through a moderate use of salt in their food. For in this way it wipes away all moisture, and dries the womb which is too wet and damp, and makes the seed of generation cling more firmly to the womb. They also testify that it stirs lust in men and excites the loins, and that peoples who use salted meats and sea fish more often [experience this], and they affirm that this happens for no other reason than the biting heat of salt. There is also this further argument for inducing fertility: that an immense number of mice are usually bred on sea ships, and that salt-workers' women are continually lustful and very fruitful in children. Hence too in some regions they sprinkle a little salt on the fodder of livestock, so that they are keener to eat and more eager and aroused for breeding. Finally, it is established by experience that barren fields, where they are too marshy and wet, become fruitful when salt is scattered on them. But the power of salt to dry, to wipe away and to preserve from putrefaction bodies that are luxuriant with excess moisture becomes clearer even from this one thing: although the Egyptians had several methods by which they kept their dead free from putrefaction, the first and most often used of all was the one which consisted of salt alone. Hence bodies preserved in this way were rightly said to be salted, and the preserved corpses were called pepychemena [πεπυχευμένα], as Mercurialis noted (book 3, Variae Lectiones, chapter 2). The same man rightly corrects the opinion of Plutarch, who in his Questions on Natural Matters, On Meats and Salt, says that salt and salted things are most effective in fattening bodies, whereas experience proves that salt has the power to thin rather than to thicken, while sweet things have more power in thickening bodies, and that the use of salted foods, by their dryness and power of opening, carries nourishment to the parts to be nourished.

units.la: Cæterum non praetereundum, quod Lan-gius epist.17.etiam ex Athen.l.10. annotavit, apud veterum conviuas non illaudatā olim suisse consuetudinem, ut qui gryphum pro-positum dissoluere non posset, is poculum salsuginis humore mixtum uno exhaurire spiritu cogeretur.
units.tr: Moreover, it should not be passed over that Lange (letter 17), also noting from Athenaeus (book 10), records that among the ancient diners there was an custom not to be ignored: whoever could not undo a griffin-shaped cup set before him was compelled to drain in one gulp a cup mixed with the brine of salt water.

units.la: Qui hodie salem poculis inspergunt (utinam vero id fieret crebrius, minus enim tunc noxæ fœculenta vina bibentes contra-herent) ideo id factitare intelligo, ut, si vi-num sit fœculentum, sal id depuret, non modo enim vini fœculentiam ob gravitate suam trahit in fundum, & à corruptione ni-miaq; æstus ebullitione præferuat, sed etiam longe salubrius quàm sulphur efficit. Unde Torcularia marina aqua eluere & irrigare suadent: Græci quoq; & Romani, ut vinum
units.tr: Those who today sprinkle salt into their drinks (I wish they did so more often, since those who drink turbid wines would then incur less harm) I understand to do this so that, if the wine is turbid, the salt may purify it. For salt not only draws the turbidity of the wine down to the bottom by its weight, and preserves it from corruption and excessive boiling-up of heat, but also does this far more healthily than sulphur does. Hence they advise rinsing and wetting the sea wine-presses with seawater. The Greeks and Romans too, in order to make their wine clearer and more delicate, mixed the must, boiled down to a third, with seawater or brine in a fixed measure,

units.la: defœcatius ac delicatius redderent, mustum aquâ maris aut muria ad tertias vsque deco-ƈta certa inensura miscebant, teste Columel.
units.tr: as Columella attests.

units.la: 3. vbi quoque modus decoctionis traditur. Ob eam vero causam sale multum reddide-runt faecatius quidam existimant, quod salis li-quor vini fœculentiam ei implicitam sua terrestri grauitate in fundum cadi velut hy-postafin trahat, quam tamen rationem ab-liis improbari video, obiicientibus salis pinguedinem, ob quam enatare potius de-bebat quam subsidere. Verum plus terræ quam aeris sali inesse paruulus eius grumus in vino vel aqua subsidens claredemonstrat cum vter oleo plenus emergat. Huc com-mode quoque referri potest, quare potato-res sale frequentius vtantur inter bibendum, & an bene hoc ipso sibi profiteantur vbi responderi potestex salis natura, ideo, sal? hocipsos facere, quia comperetunt sal tor-pentem ventriculi excitare appetentiam, stomachique fastidium tollere, testante et-iam Plin.l.31.cap.9. & Plutarch l.de causa-tur.3. tum vt illa salsugo stimulet naturam ad celeriorem excretionem, ne videlicet si-tres nimium distendantur. Ad extremum, quoniam salis natura est, vt exprædictis pa-tet, corporum, quibus inspergitur & admo-uetur superfluos humores extenuare, ac di-rigere, ipsa quoq; corpora in sese cogere, al-ligaligare & condensare, consequens est, ipsâ et- iam experientia suffragante, arida sale aspersa, ut cibis inepta fieri, ut si quis lepores sale asseruare tentet, edentibus admodum noxios reddet: sues contra bene saginatæ obesæq; summam à sale accipiunt commendationem: pilces quoque mollis carnis, excrementisque vacuos ad saliendum ineptos deprehendes, cuiusmodi sunt saxatiles. Grandiores vero humidioresque idonei sunt durantque sale conditi per secula. Quanto enim pituitosiores, humidiores, excrementosioresque carnes extiterint, tanto ad saliendum sunt aptiores, id quod de caeteris omnibus cibariis intellexisse lectorem velim. Quapropter æstate modicum salis usum prodesse experimentis quotidianis compertum est, sicut hieme, terris naturisque frigidioribus & pituitosioribus, obesioribus & crassioribus liberalior usus haud noxius est: atrabiliarios vero, macros, graciles & calidiores praeter modum sumtus laedit, adurit atque reficcat. Unde pessimus in corporibus ipsorum conducitur inquilinus Scorbutus, maritimis accolis, crebriusque ac quotidie fere salsamentis salitisque; tum carnibus tum piscibus vescentibus peculiaris, gingivas primo & pedes inficiens, pluribus latenter lethalis, praecipue vero foeminarum choro. Nouii in Dania Nobiles vere foeminas eo extinctas, quæ sale maceratis piscibus carni-bufq; admodum delectabantur, ac crebrius vescebantur. Certissimum est exta & viscera vitiari ac tabescere, oraq; cum anima grā-ue illius virus exhalare ex fallamentorum omnis generis immodico vsu. Ergo sal, qui defunctorum corpora per secula a putrefa-ctione vindicat, viuentia corrumpit ac ene-cat.
units.tr: 3. where the method of boiling is also described. Some think that for this reason people made their wine clearer by adding a great deal of salt, namely that the liquor of the salt, with its earthly weight, draws down the turbidity of the wine entangled in it to the bottom of the cask like a sediment. Yet I see others reject this reasoning, objecting to the fatness of salt, on account of which it ought rather to float than to sink. But that salt contains more earth than air is clearly shown by a small grain of it settling in wine or water, whereas oil, when poured in, floats on top. To this may also fairly be referred the question why drinkers use salt more often while drinking, and whether they can rightly claim for themselves that they do this, since it can be answered from the nature of salt: they do it because they find that salt stirs the sluggish appetite of the stomach and removes its distaste, as Pliny (book 31, chapter 9) and Plutarch (On Causes of Things, book 3) also testify; and so that this saltiness stimulates nature to a quicker excretion, lest, namely, the bowels be too much distended. Finally, since the nature of salt is, as has been made clear above, to thin and direct the superfluous humours of the bodies it is sprinkled on and applied to, and also to draw the bodies themselves together, to bind and to thicken them, it follows, with experience also lending its support, that dry things sprinkled with salt become unfit for food: if anyone tries to keep hares with salt, he will make them very harmful to those who eat them. Pigs, on the other hand, when well fattened and fat, receive the highest commendation from salt. You will also find that fish with soft flesh, empty of excrement, are unfit for salting, of which kind are the rock fish. The larger and moister ones, however, are suited to salting and last for ages when seasoned with salt. For the more phlegmy, moister and more excrementitious the flesh, the more apt it is for salting; I would have the reader understand this of all other foods as well. Therefore it is established by daily experience that a moderate use of salt is beneficial in summer, while in winter, for cold and phlegmy regions and natures, and for the fatter and grosser, a more generous use is not harmful; but it harms, burns and dries out those who are melancholic, thin, slender and too hot, when taken beyond measure. Hence the worst lodger that settles in their bodies is scurvy, peculiar to those dwelling by the sea and to those who eat salted meats and fish more often and almost daily. It first infects the gums and feet, and for many it is secretly deadly, especially for the company of women. I have known noble women in Denmark who were killed by it, women who took great delight in fish and meat steeped in salt and ate them more often. It is most certain that the entrails and viscera are spoiled and wasted, and that the mouth exhales a heavy poison together with the breath, from the immoderate use of salted foods of every kind. Thus salt, which saves the bodies of the dead from putrefaction for ages, corrupts and kills the living.

units.la: Viri quia in exercitamentis sunt impigri-ores, lentius scorbuto inficiuntur. Qui novi orbis res literis mandarunt, aiunt Nigritas sale valetudinem tueri, & pene cum auro æquare.
units.tr: Men, because they are more vigorous in exercise, are less quickly infected by scurvy. Those who have written up the affairs of the New World say that the Negroes keep their health with salt and almost value it equal to gold.

units.la: Et tantum de sale, quod falso Arist. putant[?] frigore & humore dissolui, calido ac sicco cogi, cū calido & humido quoq; eliquefcat, nā raphano aspersus, aut fi raphani, q natura calidus est & humidus, fruita falis aceruo in-deris, sal totus liquescet. Vide Langium in epist. 28 Plura de falis natura, conficiendi illius ratione singulari, vsu ac differentiis, tum etiam herbis quibusdam maritimis falfugi-nofo fuccoimbutis, & ex quibus sal elicitur, inueniet lector apud Lemnium l.3 de naturæ occult. mirac. c.9. Plin. l.31.c.7. & 9.
units.tr: So much for salt. Aristotle is falsely thought to say that salt is dissolved by cold and moisture and hardened by heat and dryness. It also melts with heat and moisture: if it is sprinkled on radish, or if a heap of salt is laid on a piece of radish, which by nature is hot and moist, the whole of the salt will melt. See Lange, in letter 28. More on the nature of salt, its special method of preparation, its uses and kinds, and certain maritime herbs full of salty juice from which salt is drawn, the reader will find in Lemnius, On the Hidden Miracles of Nature, book 3, ch. 9; Pliny, book 31, chs. 7 and 9.

units.la: Plutarch.7. fympof. probl.10. & 4.
units.tr: Plutarch, Symposiacs, book 7, problem 10, and 4.

units.la: fymp. probl. 4.
units.tr: Symposiacs, problem 4.

units.la: De Melle & Saccharo.
units.tr: On Honey and Sugar.

units.la: De mellis natura & viribus dictum est c. praecedente inter ea quæ ab animalibus proueniunt. Hodie vice eius vsurpari plurimum coepit saccharum, maximaque in tribu medicorum id excitauit lites, quas tandem Lusitanorum ac Hi-spanorum nauigationes ac negotiationes cum Alexandriæ, nouæque Indiæ incolis vi-dentur sedasle[?]. Vix autem explicare est, quantum ad condimenta obsoniaque expetatur, adeo ventri gulæq; exotica magis placent, domestica vero vbiq; sordent, vnde fit, vt mel, quia vbique fere prouenit, & vltro se porrigit, minoris nunc quam olim fit auctoritatis, licet viribus, facultateque tum ci-bariâ tum medica saccharo non cedat. Por-ro de sacchari natura variæ fuerunt eruditorum opiniones, & præsertim Mauritanorum sententiæ mire euariarunt. Constat tamen inter omnes, calidæ, humectantis[?], abstergentisq; naturæ esse, multaque præstare melle inualidius, idemque plurima posse va-lidius. Et vno dicâ verbo, omnium saporum videri potest domitor, acria leniendo, acida retundendo, salsa suauiora reddendo, auste-ra vincendo, acerba mitigando, fatuis & insipidis sensum tribuendo. Æstate & in temperamentis calidioribus verti in bilem, obstructionibusq; nimiū ei[?] vsum implicare viscera proditum reperio, pulmonibus ca-men vesicaeque, gutturi atque tracheae arte-riae vtile ac salutare, sed dentibus inimiciffi-mum, quibus nigredinem, rubiginem indu-cit ac mobilitatem, quare ab eius esu os col-luendum quidam docuerunt. Vires porro pro coctura ratione atque differentia sortiri conflat. Quo enim coctum exactius est, eo calere magis arbitrantur.
units.tr: The nature and powers of honey were discussed in the preceding chapter, among the things that come from animals. Today sugar has largely begun to take honey's place, and this has stirred up great quarrels among the physicians, which the voyages and trade of the Portuguese and Spanish with Alexandria and the inhabitants of the New India seem finally to have settled. Yet it is hard to say how much is sought after for seasonings and delicacies, so much do exotic things please the belly and palate, while domestic things are everywhere despised. Hence it happens that honey, because it grows almost everywhere and offers itself freely, now carries less authority than it once did, although in its powers and qualities, both as food and as medicine, it is not inferior to sugar. Moreover, the opinions of the learned about the nature of sugar have varied, and the views of the Moors in particular have differed wonderfully. Yet all agree that it is of a hot, moistening and cleansing nature, and that it does many things less strongly than honey and many things more strongly. To say it in one word, it can be seen to tame all tastes: softening sharp things, blunting sour ones, making salty things more pleasant, overcoming astringent ones, mitigating bitter ones, and giving sense to the foolish and insipid. I find it reported that in summer and in hotter constitutions its excessive use turns into bile and, through obstructions, clogs the viscera; yet it is useful and wholesome for the lungs and bladder, the throat, windpipe and arteries, but most hostile to the teeth, which it blackens, rusts and loosens; so some have taught that the mouth should be rinsed after eating it. Moreover, it is agreed that its powers depend on the manner and degree of its boiling, for the more thoroughly it is cooked, the more they think it heats.

units.la: Pistores dulciarios in varia panificio-rum genera saccharum digerere, nec non Seplafiarios varias ei figuras effigiesque tri-buere, totque eo incrustari ad delicias femi-na, & vno verbo, nihil hodie pene fine fac-charo condiri, inque eo monstrificum pla-ne esse gulae ingenium plufquam notum est. Panificiis additur, vinis miscetur, aquaeo suauior efficitur salubriorque, carnes eo dem alperguntur & pisces, nec non oua crebrius quam sale. Eruditi palati homines prae ftan-tiffimas eas escas putant, quae suapte natura placent absque eiusmodi exoticis condi-mentis.
units.tr: Confectioners put sugar into all kinds of breads, and sugar-workers give it various shapes and images and encrust things with it to the delight of women. In a word, almost nothing today is seasoned without sugar, and the monstrous nature of the palate's appetite in this respect is more than well known. It is added to breads, mixed into wines, and makes water sweeter and healthier; meats and fish are sprinkled with it, and eggs more often than with salt. Learned men of refined palate think those foods most excellent which please by their own nature without such exotic seasonings.

units.la: De aceto, eiufq; vsu ac viribus in cibo & potu, fitiq; restinguenda.
units.tr: On vinegar, its use and powers in food and drink, and in quenching thirst.

units.la: Irum certe, & vini cereuisiaeque vitium transire in alimentum. Est enim nihil aliud acetum quam vi-num vel cereuisia vetustate corruptum, & in acidi liquoris saporem conuersum: PraePræclarè autem cibos & sapores quosdâ commendabiles reddit atque sapidos, proximumq; à sale in conferuandis eduliis tenet locum, at non tam vi diuturna, nisi enim postaliquot menses priori effuso recens rebus conditiis affundatur, mucore limoque obducuntur. Vires eius in medicorum scho-la excitauerunt controuersias. Omnes ta-men vel maior pars vim ei tribuit refrigerandi, repellendi, exiccandi, penetrandique.
units.tr: Vinegar is, as it were, the fault of wine and beer passing over into food. For vinegar is nothing other than wine or beer spoiled by age and turned into the taste of a sour liquid. It makes foods and certain flavours pleasing and tasty, and it holds the place nearest to salt in preserving foodstuffs, though not with such lasting force: unless fresh vinegar is poured over the pickled things after some months in place of the old, which has been poured off, they are covered with mould and slime. Its powers have stirred up controversies in the schools of the physicians. Yet all, or most, ascribe to it the power of cooling, repelling, drying and penetrating.

units.la: Quitamen absolutè frigidum id cótendunt, hallucinantur. Plinius lib.23.c.1. summam ei vim esse in refrigerando, nec minoré discu-tiendi affirmat, vnde terræ infusum spuma-re, medicosque nesciuisse, quantum aspides contra polleret, ab aspide enim calcata per-cussum vtrem aceti ferentem, quoties depo-suisset, ictum sensisse, illæso aliâs similem.
units.tr: But they are wrong to hold that it is absolutely cold. Pliny, book 23, ch. 1, affirms that its chief power lies in cooling, and no less in dispersing; hence when poured on the ground it foams. Physicians, he says, did not know how strongly it works against asps: a man struck by an asp, when he had set down a skin of vinegar he was carrying, felt the blow whenever he put it down, whereas otherwise he was unharmed by a similar bite.

units.la: Sed mirabile & hoc in eo exemplum, quod idem addit. Nam M. Agrippa suis pre-annis conflictatus graui pedum morbo, cum dolorem illum perpeti nequiret, vnius medicorum portentosa scientiâ, ignorante D. Augusto, tanti putauit vsu pedum sensuque omni carere, dummodo & doloreillo carerer, demersis in acetum calidum cruribus in acerrimo impetu morbi. Galen. lib. 10. de morbis curand. acetum, omnium, quæ nota sunt, potestate refrigerantium tenuissimarum esse partium, admixtam quèaliquam sibi caliditatem habere, propterea corpora, quæ contingit, exiccare, scriptum reliquiæ, vnde in iis affectibus, inquit, qui refrigerationem postulant & humectationem, non solo aceto vtendum, sed aquæ frigidæ tantum admini-scendum, vt bibi possit. Hæc Galen. Qua-propter immodicè aceti vsum cerebro nocet, uisque siccitatem inferre, somnumque excutere, pallorem inducere, exangues[?]q; redderinficiari nemo potest, quia humorem omnem natiuum exiccando absorbet. Modi-cus contra eius vsus ad condimenta & in-ctus stomacho vtilis est, fastidia enim discutit, singultus cohibet, & sternutamentã olfactu, testante Plin. Vnde Seruius, & potu & fotu stomacho conducit acetum. Dioscorides quoque viniaceti dicit esse ἐυσομα-χιὼν li.s.c.11. Hippocrates atram bilem pa-rere inq; massam attollere, biliosis verò sa-lubre asserit lib.3.de rat.victus acut. Etibi-dem tamen Galenus quartanis ad inciden-dum & attenuandum dari meminit. Quod idem 14.de morb.curand.expresse his verbis significauit, siquidem, inquit, aceti vis modò eo quis modicè & debito tempore vtatur, sa-lutaris eiusmodi affectibus est, (loquitur au-tem de scirrhosis) ceu tenaces ac crassos hu-mores dissecans ac resoluens, sin vel immo-deratius vel in tempore non idoneo, te-nuiores[?] [?]uiores partes violenter absumens quod reliquum est finit lapidescere. Sed si quis eo diutius utatur, ipsam neruorum substantiam delibauerit. Obid igitur nec sæpe,ac inter initia, neclongo tempore, medicamentis ex aceto ad ligamenta & tendines utendum: at in liene & carnosis musculi partibus scirrho affectis tutus eius usus est. Hæc Galenus. Alii, quanto fuerit acrius, tanto minus frigidæ naturæ esse contendunt, acoremque illum & mordacitatem saccharo aut uvis passis in eo decoctis corrigunt. Ruellius in Dioscoridem cap.11.lib.5. asserit, acetum crassis partibus, faecibus, seu faeci proportione respondentibus calidum esse, tenuibus vero partibus frigidum, idque magis quam calidum, aut forte frigidum per se, calidum vero per accidens: & quo acrius est, minusq; vini naturam & qualitates repræsentat, tantò tenuium magis esse partium idem affirmar. Vide quoque Galenum lib.1. simplic. lib.de composit.medic. per gen. & lib.1.2.& 6.de comp.med.per part. Experientia quoq; vires aceti manifestat. Nam si ouum in acerrimo aceto triduo maceretur, aut plus paulò, testa in eam teneritatem mollescit, ut veluttenuis membrana per annuli adiga-tur angustiam. Quin & coticula, aut silex aceto septem dierum spatio iniectus digiti attritu in pulnerem redigitur.
units.tr: Yet there is also a remarkable example of this that he adds. Marcus Agrippa, harassed by a severe gout in his feet, could not bear the pain. By the prodigious skill of one of the physicians, without the knowledge of the emperor Augustus, he thought it worth losing the use and all feeling of his feet, provided he was rid of that pain, and so he plunged his legs into hot vinegar at the most violent onset of the disease. Galen, On the Method of Curing Diseases, book 10: vinegar, of all the things known for their cooling power, consists of very fine parts and has some heat mixed into it, and so it dries the bodies it touches. He writes this, and says that in those conditions which call for cooling and moistening one must use not vinegar alone but mix it with cold water, so that it can be drunk. So Galen. Hence excessive use of vinegar harms the brain, brings dryness, drives off sleep, induces pallor and makes the body bloodless, since by drying it absorbs all natural moisture. A moderate use of it, on the other hand, for seasoning and for dressings, is useful to the stomach, for it disperses loathing, checks hiccups, and provokes sneezing by its smell, as Pliny attests. Hence Servius says that vinegar benefits the stomach both as a drink and as a fomentation. Dioscorides also says that wine vinegar is good for the stomach [εὐστόμαχον], book 5, ch. 11. Hippocrates asserts that it produces black bile and raises up the mass, but is wholesome for the bilious, in his Regimen in Acute Diseases, book 3. Yet in the same place Galen mentions that it is given to quartan fever patients for cutting and thinning. Galen expressed this same point in book 14 of On Curing Diseases, in these words: "If one uses the power of vinegar moderately and at the right time, it is salutary for such affections (he is speaking of scirrhous ones), cutting and dissolving tenacious and thick humours; but if used too immoderately, or at an unsuitable time, it violently consumes the thinner parts, and what is left ends by turning to stone. And if anyone uses it for too long, he will damage the very substance of the nerves. Therefore vinegar medicaments should not be used on ligaments and tendons often, nor at the beginning, nor for a long time; but in the spleen and in the fleshy parts of the muscles affected by scirrhus, its use is safe." So Galen. Others maintain that the sharper it is, the less cold its nature, and they correct its sourness and bite by sugar or raisins boiled in it. Ruellius, on Dioscorides, book 5, ch. 11, asserts that vinegar is hot in its thick parts, its lees, or in the parts corresponding to lees, and cold in its thin parts, and that it is cold rather than hot, or perhaps cold in itself and hot only by accident; and the sharper it is, and the less it represents the nature and qualities of wine, the more it consists of thin parts, he affirms. See also Galen, book 1 of the Simple Medicines, On Compound Medicines according to Kinds, and books 1, 2 and 6 of On Compound Medicines according to Places. Experience also shows the powers of vinegar. If an egg is steeped in very sharp vinegar for three days, or a little longer, the shell softens to such tenderness that it can be drawn through the narrow opening of a ring like a thin membrane. Indeed, a pebble or flint placed in vinegar for seven days is reduced to powder by rubbing with a finger.

units.la: Hinc Hannibal Alpes sibi peruias faciens Italiæque inhians feruenti aceto saxa diffol. uere ac dissilire coegit. Vnde sanè penetra- bilis aceti visconspicitur, quâ saxa etiam corrodit & comminuit, & margaritæ refol- uuntur in tabem. Sed & venenis resistit po- tenter, valetque aduersus omnium acula- torum animalium ictus, morsúsque venena- tos, necnon pruritus vlceraque manantia, testante etiam Plinio. Quare non inconsul- tò faciunt, qui, grassante morbo populari & pestilenti modicum aceti vsum sibi reddunt familiarem, dissipat enim ac discutit vitio- sum aerem, & fi quid in corpus est haustum, prohibet humores infici ac putrescere, astu quoq; in corpore vehementiorem insigni- ter arcet. Verum ne cerebro neruorü prin- cipio ipfisq; neruis fit nocumento, pruden- tiores aquam rosaceam admisceri iubent, pauxillum q; vini Rhenani, ac croci momé- tum, ficenim minus capiti incommodaɪe experti sunt. Porró Romanos in expeditioni- bus suis eo vsos plurimum faiffe constat, vt mirum non fit (id quod nonnulli in admira- tionem trahunt) quod Suetonius scribat, A- fiaticum Vitellii Imperatoris libertum, Pu- teolis poscam vendidisse, quon iam is potus non solum medicum in vsum, i ntus & extra adhibetetur, sed etiam, cum mi lites, vilisque plebecula illo in quotidiano vi &tu in magnis prapraesertim caloribus vterentur,infignitere-nim refrigerat & humectar. Fit autem ex a-ceto vel vinoacido & aqua. Secundum ve-teres concinnatur ex aquae partibus ii,& vi-ni acidi part. 3. Ita haec temperanda sunt, vt possint bibi. M. Catonem in militia sem-per aquam b bibere ferunt, nisi quando sitie-bat ardentius, tunc enim acetum potasse le-gimus. Mirum itaque non est, milites Rom. Christo sitienti acetum porrexisse. Et hodie quoque milites acetum semper secum ferre constat.
units.tr: Hence Hannibal, making the Alps passable for himself and longing for Italy, forced rocks to crack and split with hot vinegar. Thus the penetrating force of vinegar is plain, by which it even corrodes and crushes stones, and pearls are dissolved into rottenness. It also resists poisons powerfully and is effective against the bites of all stinging animals and venomous bites, and against itching and running ulcers, as Pliny also testifies. Therefore those do not act unwisely who, when a popular and pestilential disease is raging, make a little vinegar a familiar part of their diet; for it disperses and dispels the foul air, and if anything harmful has been swallowed, it keeps the humours from being infected and putrefying, and also keeps off more strongly the heat within the body. But lest it harm the brain, the origin of the nerves, or the nerves themselves, the more prudent advise mixing in rose-water, a little Rhenish wine and a pinch of saffron, for they have found that this causes less trouble to the head. It is also established that the Romans used it greatly on their campaigns, so it is no wonder (which some regard with amazement) that Suetonius writes that Asiaticus, a freedman of the emperor Vitellius, sold vinegar at Puteoli; for that drink was used not only medicinally, but both internally and externally, and especially when soldiers and common folk used it in their daily life, and in great heats, for it cools and moistens remarkably. Vinegar is made from sour wine and water; according to the ancients it is made of three parts of water to one part of sour wine, and these must be tempered so that they can be drunk. They say that Cato, on campaign, always drank water, except when he was very thirsty; then we read that he drank vinegar. It is therefore no wonder that Roman soldiers offered vinegar to Christ when he thirsted. And it is well known that soldiers today too always carry vinegar with them.

units.la: Sciendum enim & notandum diligen-ter est, nec vinum per se, quia calidum, nec a-cetum, quia siccum, nec aquam, quia tardius permeat & distribuitur, miscentur autem aquâ alterutrum horum certa portione & quantitate sitim probe extinguere. Nam haec vini cali-ditatem acetique siccitatem sua frigiditate& humiditate corrigit atque attemperat. Tam vinum autem quam acetum essentiae suae te-nuitate ipsi aquę celeritatem permeandique promptitudinem impertit. Quare pruden-ter quidam aquam insalubriorem admisto a-ceto corrigunt, praeterquam enim quod, vt celerius hypochondria transfeat, minusq; in-flet, praestat efficitque.
units.tr: It must be noted and carefully observed that neither wine alone, because it is hot, nor vinegar alone, because it is dry, nor water alone, because it passes through and is distributed more slowly, quenches thirst properly. But when either of the first two is mixed with water in a certain proportion and quantity, it does. For this corrects and tempers the heat of wine and the dryness of vinegar by its own coolness and moisture. Both wine and vinegar, by the thinness of their substance, give water speed and readiness to permeate. For this reason some prudently correct less wholesome water by adding vinegar, since it both makes the water pass more quickly into the hypochondria, so that it causes less bloating, and accomplishes other benefits.

units.la: Verum enimuero cum sitis sit humidę substantiae appetentia, (sine qua animalium tota moles, quia in perpetuo fluore est, protinus collaberetur atque concideret, nisi fi-mile quid,quod defluxit, restauraretur)eaq; duplex, vna quæ à feruore calorisq; abunda- tia, altera quæ ab humoris penuria ac in-opia concitatur, discrimen aperiendum est, aqua aceto diluta ac temperata quam sitim restinguat? Certum est & in confesso, vorem & ariditate, si concurrerint, vehemen-tem excitare sitim. Quod si vero humori coniungatur, fiunt quidem homines si-ticulosi, sed moderatè, ideoque facilè illa si-tis sedatur. Unde ex aceti quoque natura consequens est, sitim, quæ à feruore conci-pitur, poscâ salubriter leniri, eam verò, quæ ab humoris oritur penuria, nullum sentire auxilium. Acetum enim infigniter refri-gerare ostensum est, sed levius humectare, ideoque sitiab ariditate humorisque inopia manante, aut caliditate siccitateque coeun-tibus, minimè proderit, si solum poterit, quin potius irritabit acriusque stimulabit. At si humiditas cum caliditate coiuncta est, (quod tamen raro usu venit, nisi in hydro-pisi & ventriculo salsa pituita scatente) gene-rosum levamen est, cuius rei experientia quoque testis est. Non omittam Plinii testimonium lib. 23. cap. 1. afferentis, æstus in ba-lneis calorisque vim acetum arcere ore de-tentum, vel etiam aquâ potum, &c. Quid hic dicitur aliud, quam in vehementibus calocaloribus homines sitientes aquam illam aceto dilutam vtilissimè bibere.
units.tr: But since thirst is a craving for moist substance (without which the whole mass of animals, being in constant flux, would immediately collapse and fall apart, unless something like what has flowed away were restored), and since it is twofold, one kind roused by an excess of heat and warmth, the other by a lack and poverty of moisture, we must explain which kind is quenched by water diluted and tempered with vinegar. It is certain and generally agreed that dryness and heat, when they act together, provoke a violent thirst. But when heat is joined with moisture, people do become thirsty, though only moderately, and so such thirst is easily satisfied. Hence it follows from the nature of vinegar that thirst arising from heat is wholesomely relieved by it, whereas the thirst that arises from a lack of moisture finds no help in it. For vinegar has been shown to cool markedly but to moisten only slightly. Therefore, when thirst comes from dryness and a lack of moisture, or from heat and dryness combined, vinegar will be of little use, if indeed it is of any use at all; rather, it will irritate and sting more sharply. But if moisture is joined with heat (which, however, seldom happens, except in dropsy and in a stomach full of salty phlegm), it is a generous relief, and experience also bears witness to this. I shall not omit the testimony of Pliny, book 23, chapter 1, who says that vinegar held in the mouth, or even drunk with water, keeps off the heat of the baths and the force of warmth, and so on. What else is said here than that people who are thirsty in intense heat drink that water diluted with vinegar most beneficially?

units.la: Cæterum, quoniam plerosque noctu fitis fatigat, nonimmeritò & præter ordinem instituique rationem quæritur, an noctu sitientibus potus fit dandus? Æstate, aliaque temporis conditione feruenti, terrisque æstuosis & calidioribus, quin & victu ciboque tali homines fieri fiticulosiores, ne-mo, nisi omnium rerum iners,ibit inficias. Nihil hic fastidiosi dicetur & fabulosi. Ipsa veritas cum experientia aget. Me quod atti-net, intra limites & metas consistam,nec extra Pomœria euagabor. De fitis nocturnæ origine & causis operæ pretium est aliquid hucapponere.
units.tr: Moreover, since thirst troubles many people at night, it is not without good reason, and beyond the usual order and method, to ask whether drink should be given to those who are thirsty at night. Nobody, unless he is utterly idle, will deny that in summer, or in any hot season, on sultry and warmer lands, and indeed through such a diet and food, people become more thirsty. Nothing fastidious or fabulous will be said here; the truth itself, together with experience, will drive the argument. As far as I am concerned, I shall keep within limits and boundaries and not wander beyond the sacred boundary. It is worth adding something here about the origin and causes of nocturnal thirst.

units.la: Qui ob inexplebilem illam & inex-haustam potandi cupiditatem vitam immaturè relinquunt, studiosèque irritamenta exquirunt, quæ in siticulosam voraginem eos demergant, diligentiori, aiunt, potu potum prouocari, nonaliter ac somno somnum, ideoque nocturnas potationes vespertinasque promtiores & paratiores ad diurnas reddere perfuafiffimum habent. Biben-di enim consuetudo auiditatem auget, monstrificamque sitim comparat, adeò vt lecto fe committentes dormituri cantharos vini plenos aut lagenas condormire & astare velint, dignissimi sanè, qui mediisin vndis æquoris immensi, Tantali instar, perpetua siti excrucientur.
units.tr: Those who, through that insatiable and unending craving for drink, leave life before its time and eagerly seek out incitements that plunge them into a thirsty whirlpool, say that drink is provoked by more drinking, just as sleep is by sleep, and therefore they firmly hold that nightly and evening drinking-bouts make the daytime ones more prompt and ready. For the habit of drinking increases the appetite and produces a monstrous thirst, so that those who give themselves to bed want to sleep and stand beside cups or flagons full of wine. They are certainly deserving of being tormented by perpetual thirst, like Tantalus, in the midst of the waves of an immense sea.

units.la: Sitis verò nocturnæ irritamenta esse præcipua, liberaliorem vini potētis & meraciōris potum, qui fit interdiu, vel etiam à cœna, piperis, zinziberis, & id genus Indica esculenta, adulteria immodicè sumpta, tum acriū quo-que salsorum saporum coacervationem vlumque immoderatum, quibus ventriculus viscerāque intus omnia intolerabili fer-uore incenduntur, abundè testatum faciunt, qui crebrius iis ad vinarias & cereuiliarias cellas exhauriendas, vtuntur. Hinc totam gni sæpe incorpore tumultus immensique æstus non fine maxima valetudinis ruina & noxa, orisq; ac animæ exhalans virus. Constat namque ora vino nimio fœtere, eaque contactis etiam contagionem afferre. Quapropter detestanda illorum sententia est, vel potius nostra memoriā vulgatissimum bibacium prouerbium, nihil æquè sitim sedare, atque afliduos liberalioresque haustus. Indigna certè homine liberali sententia. Iam enim indicatum est intemperantiam illam bibendi auiditate accendi.
units.tr: That the chief incitements of nocturnal thirst are the more generous drinking of strong and undiluted wine, taken during the day or even after supper, pepper, ginger, and that kind of Indian delicacy, and adulterated drinks taken to excess, as well as a heaping up of sharp, salty flavours and immoderate use of salt, by which the stomach and all the inner organs are set on fire with intolerable heat, is abundantly shown by those who often resort to the wine and beer cellars to drain them. Hence a whole fire often rises in the body, a tumult and immense heat, not without the greatest ruin and harm to health, and a poison exhaling from the mouth and breath. For it is well known that mouths stink from too much wine, and that this even passes its contagion to those who come into contact with them. Therefore the opinion of those drinkers is to be detested, or rather the most common proverb of tipplers in our memory, that nothing quenches thirst so well as frequent and more generous gulps. It is certainly an opinion unworthy of a gentleman. For it has already been shown that that intemperance is kindled by the eagerness to drink.

units.la: Quin & errorem illorum detegere hic, vitæ prorogandæ interest, qui volunt vini meraciorem potum magis quam dilutiorem sitim restinguere, cum vinum perpetuo sitim magis fe-calore ac flamma, sitim augeat magis atque prodet[?]? proritet, consequenterque exiccando tabe- faciat, membraq; efficiat tremula, adq; mu- nia obeunda inepta. De aqua grauissimi autores prodiderunt, in hypochondriis diu- tius commorari atque hærere solam, po- tam, nec adeo promptè sitim leuare, pene- trare, adq; partes permeare, nisi modico vi- no mixtam, quo tanquam deductore ac ve- hiculo opus habet, ad quod ipsum etiam a- cetum non parum momenti obtinere statu- endum est.
units.tr: Indeed, it is also important for the prolonging of life to expose here the error of those who think that undiluted wine quenches thirst better than diluted wine, when wine, by its constant heat and flame, rather increases thirst and further provokes it, and consequently, by drying out, wastes the body and makes the limbs trembling and unfit for their duties. The most serious authors have taught about water that alone, when drunk, it lingers for a long time and sticks in the hypochondria, and does not relieve thirst so quickly, nor penetrate and pass into the parts, unless it is mixed with a little wine, which it needs as a guide and vehicle. For this purpose vinegar too must be regarded as having no small importance.

units.la: Nunc ad quæstionem propositam.
units.tr: Now to the question proposed.

units.la: Qui noctu bibere appetunt, inquit do- ctis. Hippoc.aph.27.l.5.iis admodum fitien- tibus, si superdormierint, bonum. Quem a- phorismum explicans Galenus censet omni- no dandum potum iis, qui vehementi siti torrentur, siue à penuria & defectu potus & humidi, siue ex vini meracioris vbetiorisque haustu fuerit prouocata. Nam & defectui, in-quit, succurrere confert, illamque quæ facta est ex vino, caliditate, aquâ restinguere, theo-remasalubre est, & remedium certissimum, est enim aqua frigida maximeq; omniù hu-mida. Quod si verò quis modicè nec adeò vehementer sitiat, iis potum dandū non esse, idem censet, sed confiderandū, nunquid ex defectu humidi tale quid patiatur, an verò ex nimia vini potatione, fatisq; auxilii somnum, præstitutum, qui solet concoquere & propulsare quod sitim induxerit. Si vero aso-mino excitato modica fitis permanserit, vi- gilia porrò medebitur. Verum qui paucum intus calorem habent, ab immodico frigidæ potu abstinebunt. Galenus non proletarius autor affirmat aquæ frigidæ potu Æthiopes extinguí, ob paucum, quem intus obtinent calorem. Unde quæ nitidioris vrbanioris-quæ vitæ sunt omnibus modis aduersus fi-timillam pugnant, sed inprimis aquâ, in qua panem friatum macerant. Alii cautiores adhuc, si vel interdiu vel noctu fitis obstre-pat; solent cibarium panem friatum in calicé cem coniicere, deinde frigidam superadde-re, sæpius tranfuasare, sicque potum efficere, quo liberalissimè salubriterq; vtuntur. Qui carius & pretiosius bibere concupiscunt, aq saccharatam, vel iulepum, & cinnamomiten concinnant, cuius potu mirificè elegantiores atque aulicas fœminas deleCtari norunt, qui extillandis eiusmodi liquoribus aulicam impendunt operam. Præstantissimus ad si-tim quamuis feruoribus inprimis contractam, potus est, qui in quibusdam celebrio-ribus vrbibus conficitur ex radice glycyrrhizæ hordeo, caricis, vuis passis & prunis, ifq; in Seplasiariorum quorundam tabernis pro-stat venalis, aiuntq; eius haustu somnos in-terturbatos mirè reuocari. Quare nocturna inquie-
units.tr: "Those who desire to drink at night," says Hippocrates, aphorism 27, book 5, "if they fall asleep again, it is good for those who are very thirsty." Explaining this aphorism, Galen holds that drink must in every case be given to those who are tormented by a violent thirst, whether it arises from a lack and deficiency of drink and moisture, or has been provoked by a draught of stronger and richer wine. For, he says, it is useful to relieve the deficiency, and to quench with water the heat that came from the wine; it is wholesome above all, and a most certain remedy, for cold water is especially moist of all things. But if someone is only moderately thirsty and not very violently so, Galen thinks drink should not be given to him, but one should consider whether he suffers such a thing from a lack of moisture or rather from excessive drinking of wine, and sleep, which usually digests and drives out whatever has induced the thirst, is enough help, so it is appointed. But if, when sleep has been roused, a slight thirst remains, then waking will further provide the cure. Yet those who have little inner heat will abstain from excessive drinking of cold water. Galen, no mean author, asserts that the Ethiopians quench their thirst by drinking cold water, because of the little heat they have inside. Hence those who live a more refined and urbane life fight against that thirst in every way, but chiefly with water in which they soak crumbled bread. Others, even more cautious, if thirst troubles them either by day or by night, are accustomed to put crumbled bread into a cup, then pour cold water over it, strain it often, and so make a drink, which they use most generously and wholesomely. Those who desire to drink more expensively and luxuriously prepare sugared water, or a julep, and cinnamon-water; the courtly women, who devote their care to distilling such liquors, know how wonderfully they delight in drinking them. A most excellent drink for thirst, especially that caused by burning heats, is made in some well-known cities from licorice root, barley, figs, raisins and plums, and it is sold in the shops of certain druggists; they say that by drinking it, disturbed sleep is wonderfully restored. Therefore a wholesome drink for those troubled by restless

units.la: inquietudine vexatis potus salutaris. Sed de calido frigidoq; potu, pauca, psenti rei conuenientia, attigisse, non displicebit sanitatis & vitæ prorogādæ studiosis. Non solum au- tem hominem, vt Ioh. Bruerinus l.15.de re cibaria vult, sed & alia animantia calidis po- tibus delectari, imò quadrupedum maximā partem iis pinguescere, inq; quibusdam gionibus obessati, mirum videbitur forsan ei, qui à patrio solo nusquam discessit. Maio- rem verò insaniam gulæ in frigidis potioni- bus prodigiosa ingenia commenta esse, di- uerticulaq; omni studio quæsiuisse, quibus ludificetur vita, vel inde patet maximè, quidam potus suos æstate hiemant, niues iis addunt, alii glaciem, seruantq; algoréastib°, vt nix alienis mensibus algeat. Nerosua hic laude non fraudandus est, alioqui tererrim° toto principatu suo generis humani hostis, qui primus aquā decoquere instituit, vitroq; demissam in niues refrigerare, ita enim volu- ptatem sine vitiis niuis contingere. Verum Andromachi medici eius id inuentum fuisse quidam autumant. Galenus qui posteriori seculo vixit & scripsit, aquam calefactam eodem modo refrigerari imperatoribus indicauit. Quin & si nix desit in amnem profluentem, aut puteum demittere vascu- lum præcipit, id quod crebrius à se factitatū restatur, ægrotanti alicui frigidā exhibiturus. Qui in marinauigant, vini lagenas noctu ad malos appendüt, vt à roscido cœlo vina algo-rem affumerent, vbi vero dilucuit, eas multa veste obuelant ; ita enim conceptam illam cœli frigiditatem duraret in conscio habent.
units.tr: restlessness at night. But it will not displease those who study health and the prolonging of life if I have touched briefly on hot and cold drink, matters suited to the present subject. It is not only man, as Johannes Bruerinus holds in book 15 of De re cibaria, who delights in hot drinks; other animals too do, and indeed most four-footed beasts grow fat on them, and in some regions... it may perhaps seem strange to someone who has never left his native soil. That the monstrous minds of greed have devised even greater madness in cold drinks, and have sought out every device by which life is mocked, is clearly shown above all by this: some people make their drinks cold in summer, adding snow to them, and others keep ice, and keep it cold so that snow may freeze in other months. Nero, too, must not be denied his due praise here; otherwise he, the most dreadful enemy of the human race in his whole reign, who first began to boil water and cool it by lowering it into snow in a glass vessel, would be unfairly passed over, since in this way he thought the pleasure of snow could be had without its harms. But some think this invention was made by Andromachus, his physician. Galen, who lived and wrote in a later century, pointed out that warm water is cooled in the same way for emperors. Indeed, if there is no snow, he instructs that a vessel be lowered into a flowing river or a well, a thing he often did himself, he says, when he was going to give cold water to a sick person. Sailors at sea hang flagons of wine at the masts at night, so that they may take on cold from the dewy sky; but when day dawns they wrap them up in thick clothing, for in this way they keep that coldness of the sky which they have taken in.

units.la: Hic vero vinarii negotiatores ementes saepe & facile deludunt, dum etiam infirmissima vina & vappida, quæ generosum pretiosum-que in cellis vinariis algidis rigidisq; acqui-runt saporem, vendunt; obstupescente fcil. hebetatoq; palato algore vini. Quantum autem insidiarum potu eiusmodi frigido vi-tæ obtendatur, ii experiuntur, qui modum nullum adhibent, gulamque in gelidiffimis cellis algidi vini potu emori peneque obftu-pefcere conqueruntur. Certissimum est, ca-ido tepidoq; potu immodico vires ftoma-chi elanguescere, cibi auiditatem minui, fa-ftidia concitari, corporisque totius robur e-molliri atq; effeminari. Frigido contra potu vitiari fauces & pectus, pulmones, stomachi, intestina & ipsa viscera, excitariq; non raro tusses, raucitates, colica tormenta quotidia-na manifestat experientia. Constat epar a-quæ frigidæ potione sæpius adeo corrumpi, vt morbus diuturnus insuperabilis atq; etiā mors sequatur. Felix certe qui alienā sapit insania, Galeno reste, qui frigidiore egere potu arbitratur eos, qui rerumpublicarum magistratus administrant, quiq; assiduis oc-cupancupantur negotiis, qui castra sequuntur & bella, qui peregrinantur ac viatores agunt. Qui liberi sunt & soluti, suiq; iuris ac spon-tis rárò frigida eiusmodi potione indigent.
units.tr: Wine merchants often and easily deceive buyers here, since they sell even very weak and insipid wines, which have acquired a rich and fine flavour in cold, chilly wine cellars, because the palate is numbed and dulled by the cold of the wine. Those who drink in excess of such cold wine know how much danger to life lies hidden in it. They complain that they lose their appetite and nearly lose their senses when they drink cold wine in very icy cellars. It is quite certain that immoderate drinking of warm or hot liquor weakens the strength of the stomach, diminishes the desire for food, provokes loathing, and softens and effeminates the strength of the whole body. On the other hand, cold drink injures the throat, chest, lungs, stomach, intestines and the inner organs themselves, and daily experience shows that coughs, hoarseness and colic pains often result. It is well established that the liver is often so damaged by drinking cold water that a long-lasting and incurable illness, and even death, follows. Happy indeed is the one who is made wise by another's folly, as Galen rightly says, when he holds that those who manage the magistracies of states, who are busy with constant business, who follow camps and wars, who travel abroad and live as wayfarers, need colder drink. Those who are free and unfettered, masters of themselves and their own time, seldom need such cold drink.

units.la: Feruida, inquit, æstate calore presli, exerci-tiisq; non subiecti, bibant fontanâ, niuemq; omninò vitent. Plura de calido frigidoq; po-tu videat lector ap. Athen. l. 3.
units.tr: "In the burning heat of summer," he says, "those who are not subject to exertion should drink spring water and avoid snow altogether." The reader may see more about hot and cold drink in Athenaeus, book 3.

units.la: Porrò non omittenda in hoc discursu est quæstio, quæ inter epulas plerumq; moueri solet, de famis sitisq; tolerantia, famisne sc. an vero sitis facilior tolerantia sit. Tria gra-uissima tormenta esse, quæ hominem suis æ-dibus deturbent, famem, fumum & fœmi-nam, communi apud quosdam iactatur pro-uerbio. Constat autem inter omnes grauis-simos autores animalia propemodum cun-cta diutius perdurare in siti quam fame, ci-tiusq; contabescere ac gracilescere, corrum-pi q; inedia quam potionis penuria. Et lon-gum sane foret referre, qui fame mortem si-bi conscisse antiquorum monumentis re-periuntur. In exemplis est, grauesq; historiæ perhibent, quosdam annos totos sine cibo potuque vixisse, & quod inter ostenta magis & prodigia quam naturæ insignia reponen-dum est, puellam quandam natam plus mi-nus annos 20. sine cibo permansisse salubri-terq; vixisse. Notum est arces oppidaque munitissima validissimaque nec non vrbes inexinexpugnabiles famæ potius quam siti oppugnatoribus sese dedidisse. Sitis enim in-clementia frequentius minuitur atq; sedatur patientia, neq; ei certum attributū mortis diem invenire est, quemadmodum inedia, omnino enim famem inclementiffimū[?] tormentum esse notissimum est. Non continendum hydrope vexatos, cum potus abstinentiā evasissent, postea non ita magnopere bibere appetiuisse, ut ita in totum dixisse liceat, sitim, licet cruciatus sit violentiffimus, nihilominus tamen non æquè vitæ adversari atq; famem, in qua citius contabescere animantia quam in siti dictum est. Unde mirum etiam videri & incredibile non debet, quod quidam fine cibo multos annos vixerint, foloq; potu vitam traduxerint, ob celeriorem enim transitum ac exactiorem distributionē per corporis partes nutriendas celerius quoq; ac facili? nutrire verisimile est.
units.tr: Furthermore, in this discussion we must not omit the question, which is usually raised at banquets, concerning the endurance of hunger and thirst: whether hunger or thirst is easier to endure. It is commonly repeated among some people as a proverb that there are three most grievous torments which drive a man from his house: hunger, smoke and a quarrelsome wife. Yet it is agreed among all the most weighty authors that almost all living creatures endure thirst longer than hunger, and waste away and grow thin more quickly, and are destroyed more by lack of food than by lack of drink. It would be a long task to relate how many people are found in the records of the ancients who killed themselves by hunger. There are examples, and serious histories report, that some people lived whole years without food or drink; and, which is to be reckoned among portents and prodigies rather than natural wonders, a certain girl, born about twenty years earlier, is said to have gone without food and lived in good health. It is well known that strongholds, most fortified towns, and even cities that could not be taken by storm surrendered to their attackers out of hunger rather than thirst. For thirst is more often alleviated and calmed, and the patience to bear it is less easily exhausted; nor can one find a fixed day of death assigned to it, as with starvation, for it is most widely known that hunger is the most merciless torment. Those afflicted with dropsy, who had abstained from drink, afterwards did not desire to drink so much, so that one may say in general that thirst, although it is the most violent torment, nevertheless does not oppose life as hunger does; it has been said that living creatures waste away more quickly from hunger than from thirst. Hence it should not seem strange or incredible that some have lived many years without food, sustaining themselves on drink alone, for because of the quicker passage and more exact distribution of the nourishment through the parts of the body, it is likely that they were also nourished more quickly and easily.

units.la: Hactenus de aceto eiufq; viribus, ubi-biter &hoc meminisse lectorem velim, quoties aceti apud Medicos fit mentio, semper vini acetum intelligi oportere. In quibusdam etiam locis, præsertim Saxonia Braunfuicenfi ex industria acetum sicut cereuisiam coquunt, quod tamé nō fit cereuisia, sed musteum illud decoctum refrigeratum in acetū transit, quo finitime etiam gentes plurimæ in cibis utuntur. Fiunt quoq; aceta faluberrima ex floribus siccatis rorismarini, saluiæ, lavendulæ, lilii convallium, sambuci, hyssopi, rosis siccis, & similibus, quæ vitam sanitatem q; prorogaturo, cumprimis verò politioris literaturæ studiosis, & ut uno dicam verbo, omnibus patribus familiâs tanquam pretiosissimum ad ingenii vires animiq; vigorem custodiendum thesaurum, u-nicè commendo. Præstant autem id fotu[?], olfactu & illitu circa tempora, oculos, os, nares & carpum. Crocata autem omnia præstātiora. Ad extremum, ut tandem lucubrationibus hisce vigiliisq; meis finem imponam, in condimentorum quoq; usum admitti, & aromata, ut gariophyllos, zinziber, piper, cinnamomū, corticé citri, cardamomū, crocū, macin, &c. non ignorandū est quib. suaviter salutariterq; cibi potusq; condiri solent, iisq; innoxiè maximoq; valetudinis commodo uti possum*, si moderatè & mediocriter adhibeantur. Immoderatū verō illorū, usumq; frequentiore, ipsum stomachū visceraq; int* omnia, præcipuè epar, intolerabili feruore incédere manifestū est, id q; sitis bibēdiq; avidi-tas indicat. Ubi pessimè sanitati vitæq; cōsulūt, q, dū ardoré illū vini ingētib haustib*, restinguere student, igněq; igni addētes, oleūq; flamis, ingéres in corpore cruciatus atq; tumult* excitāt, seq; ipsos ad liberali* avidiusq; bibendū, invitāt, proritā, atq; inflammant.
units.tr: So far concerning vinegar and its powers. I would also like the reader to remember that whenever vinegar is mentioned by physicians, it must always be understood as wine vinegar. In some places, especially in the region of Braunfels in Saxony, they deliberately make vinegar from beer, but this is not beer; that boiled and cooled must turns into vinegar, and many neighbouring peoples use it in their food. Very wholesome vinegars are also made from dried flowers of rosemary, sage, lavender, lily of the valley, elder, hyssop, dried roses and similar plants, which prolong life and health. I especially commend them to students of polite literature, and, to say it in one word, to all heads of households, as a most precious treasure for preserving the strength of the mind and the vigour of the spirit. They are of benefit when applied as a lotion, smelled, or rubbed on the temples, eyes, mouth, nostrils and wrist. Those made with saffron are the best of all. Finally, so that I may at last bring these studies and my wakeful labours to an end, one must not forget that spices are also admitted into the use of seasonings: cloves, ginger, pepper, cinnamon, citron peel, cardamom, saffron, mace, etc., with which food and drink are usually pleasantly and healthfully seasoned. They may be used harmlessly and to the great benefit of health, if they are applied moderately and in small amounts. But it is clear that immoderate and frequent use of them sets the stomach and all the inner organs, especially the liver, aflame with intolerable heat, as the thirst and eager desire for drink show. Those who take the worst care of their health and life, while trying to quench that burning with great gulps of wine, add fire to fire and oil to flames, stir up torments and turmoil in the body, and invite, urge and inflame themselves to drink more greedily and freely.

units.la: Quare aromata cautè & modicè cibariis sunt inspergenda, habita ratione ætatis, temporis, temperamenti locique, in terris enim tem-poribusq; frigidioribus, naturis item pituitosioribus, liberalior vsus concedi potest, &, vt, facto fine, quiescam, aduersus stomachi infirmitates, ac cruditates, nec non vilcerum temperaturam frigidam, cunctaq; ante alia ad Venerem concitandam aromata magnificant, ex quibus tamen piper, zinziberque nec suauitate, nec dulcedine, neçacido sapore placere, sed acrimonia tantum stimulante gulam, non immerito quis miretur, saltem quia exotici peregrinió; saporis sunt, & ex India petuntur, illorum auiditas maior inter mortales existit, quibus suarum rerum alioqui satietas ingens est. Tantum de aromatis, quorum vires ac laudes, in potibus, si Deus voluerit, alibi vberius prosequar.
units.tr: Therefore spices are to be sprinkled on food carefully and sparingly, with regard to age, season, temperament and place. In colder lands and seasons, and for those of a phlegmatic nature, a more generous use may be allowed. And, to bring this to an end and rest, they praise spices against weakness and indigestion of the stomach, and against a cold temperature of the inner organs, and above all for arousing desire for Venus. Yet pepper and ginger, which please neither by sweetness, nor by pleasant taste, nor by agreeable flavour, but only by a biting sharpness that stings the palate, are rightly a cause for wonder, at least because they are foreign and of strange flavour, brought from India. Their desire is greater among mortals, even though people are otherwise very sated with their own goods. I shall say more, if God wills, about the powers and praises of spices, in another place, in relation to drinks.

units.la: Ne vero planè atido palato & sine hypno-sit [?] extremam huic libro imposuisse manum, videat, quæstionem Coronidis loco, an cœ-na potu sit finienda, subnectam. Discordes autè quorundam sententias hic esse animad-uerti, præsertim inter cœnandum, quo tem-pore potissimum exagitari videtur, de ea li-gantium. Portentosis commessationibus dediti, si cœnam potu non dauserint, cra-stinam lucem non alpicere nec iecorispulmopulmonisque vitia ac tabitudines effugere posse, persuasum omnino habent. Quin & generosum hodie ducitur & praeclarum strenue & quidem stando, potu coenam fini- re praesertim in Magnatum aulis in quibus, quo quis existit bibacior, eo censetur gene- rosior. Et nemo aestimatur pluris, quam qui egregie censum Domini sui mergit. Imo quod mirari haud immerito quis possit eius modi de grege Epicureo porci, strenuique ca- licum gurgites non infimum obtinere lo-cum cernuntur. Certe eousque creuere im-manes illae propinationes atque monstrifi-cae potationes nocturnae, ut cellae vinariae in-de exhauriantur, corporis animique vires e-neruentur, asotique[?] illi, qui in mensam vo-entes de conuiuiis, ut cum Cicer.de fini- bus loquar, auferuntur, crudique postridie se rursus ingurgitant, funeris ante diem mi- fere pereant. Justæ moderatæque propinati- onis usum legitimum censeri debere carita-tem, amorem, amicitiamq; mutuam, cuius vel ineundæ, vel fouendæ atq; confirmandæ causa olim ab honestis probisque viris eam fuisse adhibitam, passim apud autores videlicet. Immoderatarum vero istarum atq; cyclopicarum propinationum, quibus hodie plerique Christianorum quotidie fere utuntur, finis non est caritas, amor, amicitia, honor, obseruantia, quam tamen helluones isti verbis egregie simulant, sed ebrietas, & quæ illam necessario consequuntur, turpitudo, ignominia, sanitatis viriumque corporis labefactatio, tremor, grauedo, pallor, linguæ titubatio, contentio extremitatum in neruis, torpor, vt plurimum vero resolutio. Et certè constat quotidianâ experientia, plærofque acrium illorum potatorum hoc tantum spectare, vt illos, quos vel amicitiæ, vel honoris specie, atq; simulatione ad immoderatè bibendum inuitant, atq; cogunt, cunctis deridendos propinentatq; comedédos, vt metaphoricós Terentius in Eunuco dixit, vt ita in totum dixisse liceat, nihil esse tam vtile, laudabile atque honestum, quod non deformet abusus hominum; quis enim non videt quotidie, antiquam illam propinandi consuetudinem ac philothefian amoris per se amicitiæque plenam, proindeque honestam, iam à multis seculis in turpissimum flagitiosissimumque abusum degenerasse, & ad Plutonis vsque Cancellos ipsos Christianos hodie sibi inuicem specioso amoris atque amicitiæ obtentu propinare. Atq; hinc promanasse putatur vox crapu-la, quæ pro ebrietate metonymicós vsurpatur, cumtamen proprie sit ebrietatis effectus capitis nimirum lucta, agitatioque, cum sc.ex temulentia caput aggrauatur & tremit. Galenus in aphor. omnem noxam ex vi-no contractam, [illegible, ~9 letters] nominat, [illegible, ~8 letters] id est caput, & [illegible, ~7 letters] hoc est concuti, reuera enim multis ex pri-diana & hesterna temulentia tanta sentitur in capite grauedo, vt cyclopas sibi in cere-brum migrasse iurent, qui alternatis illud fe-riant ictibus, quos dolores Germani non in-cepte <bl>Tröscher oder Schmidtknechte</bl> appellant, q. [illegible, ~10 letters]. Sed ad rem.
units.tr: So that you may not think I have set the final hand to this book with a plainly greedy palate and without thought, I shall append, as a crown, a question: whether a meal should be ended with drink. I observe that the opinions of certain people differ on this, especially during the meal, when the question of this matter seems chiefly to be debated. Those given to monstrous drinking bouts are firmly convinced that, if they do not finish the meal with drink, they cannot see the next day nor escape diseases and wasting of the liver and lungs. Indeed, today it is thought a mark of nobility and distinction to finish the meal with drink, vigorously and even standing up, especially at the courts of great men, where the more heavily a man drinks, the more noble he is considered. And no one is valued more than the one who most splendidly drowns his lord's fortune. Indeed, which one may reasonably wonder at, such Epicurean swine of this sort and strenuous whirlpools of the cup are seen to hold no low place. Certainly those huge toasts and monstrous nightly drinking bouts have grown to such a degree that the wine cellars are emptied because of them, the strength of body and mind is weakened, and those gluttons who are carried from the tables, as I may say with Cicero in De finibus, and the sickly ones who gorge themselves again the next day, perish almost before their time of death. It is commonly found in authors that the lawful and moderate use of toasting ought to be regarded as the bond of charity, love and mutual friendship, which honest and upright men once used either to begin or to foster and confirm these. But of those immoderate and Cyclopean toasts, which nowadays most Christians use almost every day, the end is not charity, love, friendship, honour or respect, which those gluttons nevertheless display splendidly in words, but drunkenness and what necessarily follows it: disgrace, shame, the weakening of health and bodily strength, trembling, heaviness, pallor, stammering of the tongue, cramped and tense sinews, numbness, and, most often, collapse. Indeed daily experience shows that most of these fierce drinkers aim at only this: to invite and force those whom they urge to drink immoderately under the appearance and pretence of friendship or honour, so that they may be mocked by all and drunk up, as Terence says metaphorically in the Eunuch. So that one may say in general that nothing is so useful, praiseworthy and honest that the abuse of men does not disfigure it. For who does not see every day that that ancient custom of toasting, and the fondness of love, full of friendship in itself and therefore honourable, has for many centuries degenerated into a most shameful and disgraceful abuse, and that even in the very prisons of Pluto Christians today drink to one another under the specious pretext of love and friendship? And from this, it is thought, comes the word crapula, which is used metonymically for drunkenness, although properly it is the effect of drunkenness, namely a struggle and agitation of the head, when the head is weighed down and trembles from intoxication. Galen, in the Aphorisms, names every harm contracted from wine [illegible], that is, the head, and [illegible], that is, to be shaken; for in truth, from the previous day's and yesterday's drunkenness so much heaviness is felt in the head by many that they swear the Cyclopes have migrated into their brain, striking it with alternating blows; these pains the Germans call not unskilfully <bl>Tröscher oder Schmidtknechte</bl>, [illegible]. But to the matter.

units.la: An expediat mensas claudere seu terminare potu, supra quasitum fuit. Veterum autem morem poculo quodam certo fiue propinatione cœnam claudere seu termi-nare, idque partim religionis fiue supersti-tionis potius, partim amicitiæ ergo, passim apud autores traditur. Huiusmodi poculum appellârunt poculum [illegible, ~7 letters] forsan boni o-minis ergo, quod illud sibi inuicem bonæ valetudinis ergo propinabant. Profanitate enim & olim propinationes fieri solitas & etiamnum hodie strenue hunc morem continuari maximo sæpe corporis & valetudi-nis dispendio, plus quam notum est. Sunt in exemplis, quos pro [illegible, ~7 letters] poculo for-bendo principatum quærentes & gloriam, truncorum siue stipitum, instar & velut at-tonitos atque resolutos concidisse constat.
units.tr: Whether it is expedient to close the table, or end the drinking, with a drink was discussed above. That the ancients customarily ended a meal with a certain cup, or toast, partly out of religion or superstition, partly for the sake of friendship, is related everywhere in the authors. They called this cup by a name, perhaps for the sake of a good omen, because they drank it to one another for good health. Indeed, it is well known that toasts were commonly made even in profane settings and that, even today, this custom is zealously maintained, often at great cost to the body and health. There are examples of men who, seeking the reputation and glory of outdrinking the rest, are known to have collapsed like tree trunks or stumps, stunned and limp.

units.la: Præterea vltimum illud poculum maxi-mè communi nomine appellatum quoque fuit boni dæmonis siue boni genii, seu for-tunæ; de quo Theophraftus l. de ebriet. scri-bit in hunc modum: Vini meraci, quod in cœna datur, quod quidem boni dæmonis propinationem vocant; parum degustantes, in memoriam rèuocant, quanta fit ipsius Dei vis, quantumque hoc fit illius donum. At postquam impleuerunt, dant quàm mi-nimum haustum, & tertio flexis genibus ad-orantes, ex mensa capiunt, tanquam Deo supplicantes, ne quid designent à decoro-lienum, neue vehementi aliqua illius po-tus cupiditate accendantur, sed hauriant ab illo ea, quæ honesta sunt & vtilia. Philocho-rus similiter apud Athen. lib. 15. de hoc potu sic scribit: more atque consuetudine fuit receptum, vt post cibos vinum meracum omnibus offerretur, illud degustandi gratiâ ceu ad demonstrandam vim boni Dei: reli-quo autem omni conuiuii tempore vinum dilutius bibere consueuerunt, iccircoque ipsas etiam nymphas Bacchi nutrices appel-litarunt. Ex quibus Theophrafti & Phi-lochori verbis colligitur, hunc vini puri ac meraci potum, quem boni dæmonis potum appellarunt, & ab initio cœnæ & in extremo conuiuio, antequam surgerent, mensæ ue a-fportarentur, à conuiuis fuisse vsurpatum.
units.tr: Moreover, that last cup, most commonly called by a general name, was also the cup of the good demon or good genius, or of Fortune. Theophrastus, in his book On Drunkenness, writes about it in this way: "Of the neat wine that is served at dinner, which they call the drink-offering to the good demon, they taste only a little, and so call to mind how great is the power of God himself and how great a gift of his this is. But once they have filled their cups, they give the smallest possible sip, and then, three times, kneeling and praying, they take it from the table as if supplicating God, lest they commit anything unbecoming or be inflamed by some violent craving for that drink, but that they may draw from it what is honourable and useful." Philochorus likewise, in Athenaeus book 15, writes about this drink thus: "By custom and usage it was the practice that after the food, neat wine was offered to everyone, to be tasted as it were for the sake of showing the power of the good God; for the rest of the whole time of the banquet they were accustomed to drink wine more diluted, and therefore they even called the nymphs the nurses of Bacchus."
