From the words of Theophrastus and Philochorus it is gathered that this drink of pure and neat wine, which they called the drink of the good demon, was used by the guests both at the beginning of the dinner and at the end of the banquet, before they rose or the tables were carried away.

units.la: Nec vero in deorum tantum honorem bo-ni ominis auspiciisque causâ victima illa po-tatio fieri consueuit, verum etiam amicitiæ mutuæ testificandæ sanciendæque[?] causâ, unde Philotesia fuit appellata, propinatio fc. quædam post cœnam amicitiæ ergo fieri solita. Dicebatur quoque Tantali poculum, cuius initiatorem & quasi pincernam fecerunt Tantalum, quod is incredibili inter homines benevolentia liberalitateque præcelluisse creditur.
units.tr: Nor was that drink of sacrifice customarily made only in honour of the gods, for the sake of a good omen and auspices, but also for the sake of bearing witness to and confirming mutual friendship; whence it was called the Philotesia, a certain toast customarily made after dinner for the sake of friendship. It was also called the cup of Tantalus, whose initiator and, as it were, cupbearer they made Tantalus, because he is believed to have excelled among men in incredible goodwill and generosity.

units.la: Christophorus à Vega l.1. de arte med. sect. 4. in hanc scribit sententiam de quæst. proposita. An, inquit, expediat mensas claudere potu, an vero cibo, scire oportet eum, cuius os ventris laxum est, aut cuius caput ex vini potu compatitur, egere cibo quopiam astringente postremo loco, quem non sequetur potus. Quorum autem venter siccus est, aut siti molestantur, non longe à cibo bibere debent, sed parum ad finem mensæ. Sic etiam iis, quibus nulla prava adest ventriculi affectio, convenit finito prandio aut coenaparum vini, si ita affuerint, fumere, ut postremus ille cibus è gula descendat, liquetur, commisceaturque aliis cibi partibus; aliis vero æque similis potus convenit: deinde os & dentes vino colluere omnibus ex usu erit, diluatur, si capitis malis tentantur, aliâs non. Celsus lib. 1.[?] vbi expletus est aliquis, inquit, facilius concoquit, si quicquid aliquid sumsit, potione aquæ frigidæ includit, tum paulisper inuigilat, deinde bene dormit.
units.tr: Christophorus a Vega, in book 1 of On the Art of Medicine, section 4, writes this opinion on the question proposed: "Whether it is expedient to close the table with drink or rather with food, one must know that those whose stomach is loose, or whose head suffers from drinking wine, need some astringent food at the last place, which the drink should not follow. But those whose stomach is dry, or who are troubled by thirst, ought not to drink far from food, but a little toward the end of the meal. Likewise, for those who have no bad affection of the stomach, it suits, when the luncheon or dinner is finished, to take a little wine, if they are accustomed to it, so that the last food goes down from the throat, is dissolved, and is mixed with the other parts of the food; but for others a similarly mild drink is suitable. Then rinsing the mouth and teeth with wine will be useful to all; let it be diluted if they are troubled by headaches, otherwise not." Celsus, book 1: "When someone is filled up, he digests more easily if, after taking whatever he has taken, he shuts it in with a drink of cold water, then keeps watch for a little while, and then sleeps well."

units.la: Quam sententiam Celsus videtur deprom-psisse ex Hipp.l.3. de victu acut. sic scribente, vbi timueris, ne vel caput vehementer vino, morboque grauetur, vel mens etiam tentetur, tum vel aquam, vel vinum aquosum & album, & neutiquam odorum exhibere, & deinde paululum aquæ superbibere con-uenit. Sic enim vini potentia non tam fa-cile caput mentemque attingit. Addit Pantimus interpres, perperam etiam non fecerint, qui pro aqua è Cidonii malis conditi portiuncula, aut coriandri ex acce-to[?] præparati cochleari, aut citriorum succo, aut limonum, aut punicorum, aut istorum sirupis, aut denique astringentis alicuius maturique pomi esu ventriculi os occluserint, simul & vini exhalationem ac vim refrænauerint, præsertim, si quis etiam inter quiter ac somnum, & inter aquæ vinique sumtionem paulisper inuigilauerit. Et idem paulo post: Confert quoque neque cœnam, neque prandium potu vnquam finire, quin aliquid ex supe-rioribus, aut quid esce superedatur, unde tritum illud,
units.tr: Celsus seems to have drawn this opinion from Hippocrates, book 3 of On Acute Diseases, who writes thus: "Where you fear that either the head or the mind may be grievously weighed down by wine and disease, it is fitting to give either water, or watered and white wine, and by no means fragrant wine, and then to drink a little more water." For in this way the power of wine does not so easily reach the head and mind. The interpreter Pantimus adds: "Nor do those who have closed the mouth of the stomach, instead of water, with a small portion of quince preserved in honey, or a spoonful of coriander prepared in vinegar, or with juice of citrons, or of lemons, or of pomegranates, or with syrups of these, or finally with the eating of some astringent and ripe fruit, act wrongly, and at the same time restrain the exhalation and force of the wine, especially if someone has also kept watch for a little while between the rest and sleep, and between the taking of water and of wine." And a little later the same writer: "It is also helpful never to finish either dinner or luncheon with drink, without something left over from the earlier courses or some food remaining, whence that well-worn saying:

units.la: Sit tibi postremus semper in ore cibus.
units.tr: Let the last thing in your mouth always be food.

units.la: Innatant siquidem cibi illico post cœ-nam si quis largius biberit, ita ut eos ventri-culi corpus, propter interiectum humorem non contingat. Præterea utendum semper potu est ad desiderio satisfaciendum, & ut cibus nec fit in sicco, nec fluitet, sed modera-to potu madescat.
units.tr: For foods float up immediately after dinner if someone has drunk too freely, so that the body of the stomach does not touch them, because of the moisture that intervenes. Moreover, one must always drink enough to satisfy the desire, and so that the food is neither dry nor floating, but is moistened by moderate drink.

units.la: Confultum quoque putatur intere-dendum non confertim, nec auide, sed sen-sim ac paulatim bibere, quo commodius utraque misceri queant, parique concoctio-ne perfici. Qui vero ea edendi utuntur con-suetudine, ut ad prandii medium potu sibi temperent, affatim illis bibere expediet, ut potus penetret, ac per cibum undique diffundatur. Optimus igitur ac securissimus bibendi modus statuendus est cuique pro sua ætate temporum ratione, inueterata consuetudine, ac pro vini natura ac viribus. Sanis quoque non posse certo aliquid aut determinate circa potum præscribi inde constat quod plæriq; diuersæ potandi consuetudini sint assueti, quam citra valetudinis iacturam mutare nemini fit facile.
units.tr: It is also thought advisable that one should drink between mouthfuls, not in a heap, nor eagerly, but gradually and little by little, so that both can be more conveniently mixed and digested in equal measure. But for those who have the custom of eating in such a way that they moderate their drinking until the middle of the luncheon, it will be useful for them to drink freely, so that the drink penetrates and is diffused everywhere through the food. The best and safest manner of drinking, therefore, is to be fixed for each person according to his age, the seasons, his long-established habit, and the nature and strength of the wine. That nothing certain or definite can be prescribed about drink even for the healthy is plain from this, that most people are accustomed to different habits of drinking, which no one can easily change without loss of health.

units.la: Sic multo potui assueti pleniores possunt tolerari haustus, quam insueti. Cerebrum vero habentes imbecillum, vinum non tolerant. Signum enim fortitudinis cerebri ac bonitatis eius, teste Auicenna est, à vini generosi vaporibus non lædi, vinique popotentiam sustinere. Certissimum est, me-dicaque grauitate ac experientia confirma-tiffimum, à cibo potaffe concoctionem e[?] uertere, flatusque multos ac cruditates gi-gnere[?], ieiuno vero ventre vinum fumptile, neruos ac caput infigniter laedere. Dormi-turis vero & à coena (nisi valida admodum fitis vrgeat) nocentiffimus est omnium me-dicorum consensu potus, obidque recte di-cebat Hipp. §. aphor. Qui noctu bibere ap-petunt, his admodum sitientibus fi super-dormierint, bonum. Somnus enim eam sitim, quæ vtplurimum mendosa est & salsa, sedare soleat atque leuare. Hisita obserua-tis, & caput minus offendetur, omneq; cor-pus somno fruetur iucundius. Non parum quam in-tamen emoluméti aliquem ex eo confecu-turum Auicenna putat, si quis semel inmé-fainebrietur, vt videl, perc brietatem exci-tetur vomitus, quo chronicas diuturnasqué ægritudines ait prohiberi. Verum Rabbi Moses tractat. 4. ad Soltanum Babylonia, hanc illius sententiam cen fallam conuellit omnem ebrietatem & maxime assiduam, nocere affirmans. Pestilentissimam assidue ebrietatem esse dubium non est, quam tamen vt quæ in mense semel contingit, velad summum bis, quibus sdam vt quoties rum ventriculus crudis humoribus est re-sertus, non plane noxiam esse experientia testis est. Qui vero ex vini immodico hau-stu temulenti evaserunt, omnium testimo-nio consilium fuerit ciere vomitum, inedi-am imperare ac somnum, ac succum malo-rum punicorum, vel oxicratum exhibere potandum, aut caulium succum. Sybaritas ferunt olim cramben prius esitasse[?], quo plus deinde bibere possent.
units.tr: Thus those accustomed to much wine can tolerate fuller draughts than those unaccustomed to it. But those who have a weak brain do not tolerate wine. For a sign of the strength of the brain and of its goodness, according to Avicenna, is not to be harmed by the fumes of noble wine and to withstand the power of the drink. It is most certain, and most firmly confirmed by medical weight and experience, that drinking after food can disturb digestion and produce many winds and crudities, whereas wine taken with an empty stomach strikingly harms the sinews and the head. For those who are about to sleep, and who have just come from dinner (unless a very strong thirst presses), the drink is by the consensus of all physicians most harmful of all; and so Hippocrates rightly said in the aphorisms: "For those who want to drink at night, if they are very thirsty and then sleep on, it is good." For sleep is accustomed to quiet and relieve that thirst, which is for the most part faulty and salty. If these things are observed, the head will be less troubled, and the whole body will enjoy sleep more pleasantly. Avicenna thinks that someone who once becomes drunk will gain no small advantage from it, namely that vomiting is provoked by the drunkenness, by which, he says, chronic and long-lasting sicknesses are prevented. But Rabbi Moses, in the fourth treatise to the Sultan of Babylon, overturns this opinion entirely, affirming that all drunkenness, and especially constant drunkenness, is harmful. That constant drunkenness is most pestilential there is no doubt; yet that drunkenness which happens once a month, or at most twice, is, as experience bears witness, not plainly harmful, especially when the stomach is filled with crude humours. Those who have escaped drunkenness from an immoderate swallow of wine, by the testimony of all, should resolve to provoke vomiting, to enjoin fasting and sleep, and to give the juice of pomegranates, or oxycrate, or cabbage juice to drink. The Sybarites, they say, once ate cabbage first, so that they could then drink more.

units.la: Dioscorides quoque ebrietatis & cra-pulæ incommoda tollere prodidit, si cruda edaturante cœnam ex aceto. Inesse autem peculiarem quandam vim vino obsistendi in crambe, inde patet, quod in vineto fata, vinum proveniat dilutius. Proinde apud Ægyptios & Sybaritas solenne erat, ante omnia sumere cramben coctam: quibusdam eius semen ante compotationem capere mos erat, quo citra ebrietatis periculum vi-no possent indulgere. Ebrietatem quoque arcent amata potissimum, omniaq; ea quæ humores aquosos per vrinam expurgant, quibus præsumtis fit ut fumi alio quam ad caput deferantur, vinumque venas subire prohibeatur, exiccante etiam amarore hu-miditatem. Præcipuam vero inter ea ob-tinuerunt laudem amygdalæ amaræ ad fa-stidium usque nobilitatæ, (sed fallaci sæpe experimento) si 6. vel 7. ante compotatio-nem comedantur. Huc pertinent antiquo-tum propomata, siue propinamenta, inter quæ maxime commendantur, quæ exabsin-thio & aromatibus conficiuntur. In frequentissimo hodie usu est propoma absinthites, quod ut Trallianus testatur vim habet stomachum corroborandi, extenuandi, expellendique excrementa in eo contenta.
units.tr: Dioscorides also reported that the ill effects of drunkenness and surfeit are removed if one eats raw cabbage with vinegar before dinner. That cabbage has a special power to resist wine is clear from the fact that wine made from grapes grown among cabbage is thinner. For this reason it was customary among the Egyptians and the Sybarites to eat boiled cabbage before anything else, and some people took its seed before drinking so that they could indulge in wine without danger of drunkenness. Bitter things also prevent drunkenness, as do all those things that expel watery humours through the urine, because when they are taken beforehand the fumes are carried anywhere but to the head, and wine is prevented from entering the veins; bitterness also dries up moisture. The greatest praise among these has been won by bitter almonds, celebrated even to the point of disgust (though often by a deceptive experiment), if six or seven are eaten before drinking. To this belong the propomata of the ancients, or propinamenta, among which those made from wormwood and aromatic substances are especially recommended. Today the most frequently used is the propoma absinthites, which, as Trallianus testifies, strengthens the stomach, thins and expels the excrements contained in it.

units.la: Cinnamomites quoq; propoma vires insignes obtinet in corroborando cerebro & corde. Panis similiter buccella cum melle, cydoniaq; cocta ebrietati resistunt potenter. Plinius adversus ebrietatem & tremulentiam valere pecudum pulmonem allum præsumtum: inprimis vero apri, suis achœdi: hirundinis rostri cinerem cum myrrha tritum, & in vinum bibendum inspersum l. 30.c.15.testatur, huiusq; remedii inventoré [?] esse Horum Assyriorum Regem. Adversus idem & iaspidem pollere affirmant, sed incerto experimento. Ipsam vero ebrietatem discutere ne sentiatur, porrum sectiuum [?], aut crocum prius potum apud claros autores invenio. Sed melilotus multorum etiam antiquissimorum consensu celebratur. Alii radiculam commendant elixam, quod restatur Alexis,
units.tr: The cinnamon propoma also has notable power in strengthening the brain and heart. Likewise a morsel of bread with honey, and quinces cooked, resist drunkenness powerfully. Pliny states that the lung of a beast taken beforehand with garlic is good against drunkenness and tipsiness, especially that of a wild boar or a sow, or of a kid. He also reports (book 30, chapter 15) that the ashes of a swallow's beak, rubbed with myrrh and sprinkled into wine to drink, are effective, and he says the inventor of this remedy was the king of the Assyrians. They also affirm that jasper has power against the same, but with an uncertain experiment. I find in distinguished authors that cut leek (chives), or saffron, drunk beforehand, keeps drunkenness from being felt. But melilot is celebrated by the agreement of many, even the most ancient. Others commend a small root boiled, which Alexis attests:

units.la: Iam vero nonne omnium malorum est ebrietas Maximum hominibus & nocentissimum, Heri subbibisti, ideo nunc crapula vexaris, Obdormito, ac lenaberis, deinde tibi det Radiculam quis elixam.
units.tr: Indeed, is not drunkenness the greatest and most harmful of all evils for men? You drank too much yesterday, so now you are racked by the hangover. Go to sleep and you will be made well; then let someone give you a boiled little root.

units.la: Sed satius effet ita bibere, ut medicamento opus non fit. Studium sobrietatis, ebrietatisq; odium optima temulentiae antipharmaca sunt. Non damnatur crater philotesius, qui amicitiae conciliandae causa alteri praebibi ab antiquis solebat.
units.tr: But it would be better to drink in such a way that no medicine is needed. Zeal for sobriety and hatred of drunkenness are the best antidotes to intoxication. The crater philotesius, which the ancients were accustomed to drink to one another in order to win friendship, is not condemned.

units.la: Pernitiosissimum est sub amicitiae praetextu & specie ad bibendum invitare, imo dirum propinandi hoc seculo certamen apud quosdam Nobiles atque ignobiles. Unum meminisse hic lectorem velim, veteres vinū malum bibisse vomitus ciendi gratia, ut scil. evacuato exinanitoq; per vomitum stomacho tanto maior effet bibendi edendiq; orexis id est appetentia. Vinum pessimum vocant pedibus admotum, siue à pedib. quod ferus apponi fuit solitum, quod [illegible, ~8 letters] id est versionem appellabant, quod stomachum subverteret ac perturbaret. Huc facit illud Martialis, Nec cœnat prius aut recumbit Quam septem vomuit deuncés.
units.tr: It is most pernicious to invite people to drink under the pretext and appearance of friendship, indeed the dreadful drinking contest that in this age is held among some nobles and commoners alike. I would have the reader remember one thing here: the ancients drank wine to provoke vomiting, so that, with the stomach emptied and drained by vomiting, their appetite for drinking and eating would be that much greater. They called the worst wine that which was set before the feet, or from the feet, which was commonly served, [illegible in the scan], that is, they called it a "turning over", because it upset and disturbed the stomach. To this belongs what Martial says: "He neither dines nor reclines before he has vomited up seven deunces."

units.la: Qui sanitati vitaeq; prorogandae daturi sunt operam, ii, praesertim si intemperantius viuere cogantur, ut in aulis Magnatum quorundam vsuenit, singulis mensibus ad summum bis vomitum sibi imperent, multorum namque morborum seminaria una exturbari extra omnem est controuer-fiam. Quod enim ad sanitatem confert prorogandam & conferuandā, prætermittere vel negligere homo mortalis non debet, nisi proprii sui corporis carnifex, tortor ac destructor perhiberi velit, quod ab homine Christiano debet esse quam longe alienum. Et certe nemo existimet, licet temperantissimè etiam circa cibum & potum versetur, non posse in corpore superfluitates inutilesque sensim humores, hoc est, ad nutrien-dum ineptos, coaceruati, qui morborum tandem causam & fomentum sint præbituri: Et tantum de proposita quæst:dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Those who are going to take pains for health and for prolonging life, especially if they are forced to live more intemperately, as happens in the courts of certain great lords, should induce vomiting in themselves at most twice each month. For that many seeds of diseases are driven out by this is beyond all controversy. A mortal man ought not to neglect or overlook what contributes to preserving and prolonging health, unless he wishes to be called the executioner, torturer and destroyer of his own body, which must be far from a Christian man. And surely no one should think that, however temperately he lives in regard to food and drink, superfluities and useless humours, that is, those unfit for nourishment, cannot gradually accumulate in the body, and will in the end provide the cause and fuel of diseases. Let it suffice to have said this much about the question proposed.
